is the third installment of the time management games loosely based on the Greek hero. While this sequel fails to bring anything new to the table, it still provides a nice casual gaming experience.
The
series is a simple time management game, meaning that you direct a cast of workers to gather resources and complete objectives. As levels progress, it tries to spice it up with special abilities, jigsaw puzzles, and additional characters. It has all the elements of a good casual game, and especially so if you like this genre.
I feel a little let down that this game doesn't introduce anything new, and I was a little disappointed to see the removal of clicker minigames. Not that it needs them, but something - anything - to add more variety and punctuate the stages was something I missed. I still feel that the expert difficulty can be very difficult for a newcomer, and some stages almost feel impossible to complete in gold times. Potentially more aggravating are the developer times, which I will be honest, I only did the minimum required for achievements, they're that hard. But some people may love a good challenge, and in this respect, the game definitely delivers.
Achievement hunters: 100% is relatively simple, but once again you may find yourself stuck on "beat 10 developer times." Here's the trick: First, the description is wrong again, only 5 are needed. Second, you can get this easiest in the earliest game stages (since shorter and less complex design), personally I found 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 the simplest. Beyond that, requires some strategy and definitely requires clicking birds that fly by for more points. The forums and guides have some good advice, and with some effort and persistence, it's doable. Don't give up.

Spent about an hour with it here's what I got:
Pros:
1) cars look good (but theres only 6)
2) for the few tracks I tried, they seemed interesting and challenging
3) I did enjoy trying to strategise how I was going to get past cars, and it felt satisfying when you passed someone
4) wait times were around 1:30, 2:00 min max. That might seem high to some, but it's not bad for a new game. The maximum is that you will be pitted against bots; so your not stuck if no one is available.
Cons:
1) Not a fan of the sound track
2) Hoped for more detailed car modding rather than "packages"
3) 2/4 races failed for one reason or another. In one my car got stuck trying to pit and just didn't move. In another the race never started. Had to quit to menu.
4) In another race I did not finish because I ran out of fuel... Now I may be wrong here, but why couldn't I just take a time penalty to get more fuel? Seems silly.
5) Watching the cars felt a bit like watching RC cars race... Steering felt a little rigid.
6) There's a NOS-like feature that fills up after every lap. That's a little 'gamey' if you ask me. (EDIT: I've been corrected that this is a real thing:
7) You collect experience to spend on your team, but I never found a way to do that.
8) You can lobby sponsers for contracts, which is neat, but it feels a bit arbitrary to build a high enough chance to get them to sign. I realize this was a simple way to simulate going out and getting contracts, but it's not terribly immersive and feels more like a mini game that is artificially handicapped by the 'TU' (time units). So its sorta like the TU are quarters and the contract 'game' is a bit of a slot machine you handicap in your favor over time.
9) No camera controls. The follow cam stays on one side of the car, making it difficult to see where the car is going. You could zoom out, but that works dyanmicly so the camera is constantly panning in and out. That's not a huge issue... the main issue, is not knowing when a turn is coming to strategise your abilities (which side to overtake, when you might want to use your boost or overcharge..)
10) I could be wrong, but it felt like you were racing against whomever was available regardless of skill level. That's fine, but it should be spelled out clearly that you might be up against someone with a tricked out car and a number of wins or fresh n00b. It's a little unfair to not know your competition. I expect that will get ironed out in the future, but again, its out of EA so who knows?
I could go on, as I noted far more bugs and oddities than I listed, but I'm trying to be fair. All in all though, this game though I got it on sale wants me to believe its retail price is close to $30CAD. So I will compare it other games I've gotten at that pricepoint - and it really, really is not there. Mainly I was looking for a more serious racing manager... But as one reviewer said, whos warning I really should have heeded more strongly.. This is a game that would work better as an iOS app than a desktop racing manager.
One thing is clear from looking at the game, it's clearly a work in progress. A number of modes for example are "coming soon", and there's also only 6 (albeit highly detailed) cars that are clearly modeled on real life cars. So one expects that in the future one will see more tracks, more cars and probably more features. This makes me think that someone of the game mechanics may simply be placeholders for future, better versions.
In the end though, this isn't EA anymore. What you see, is what you get right now and for a game where the retail price is close to $30. or multiplayer only plus the severe bugs (pathing errors and non-starts are like getting uncooked food at a resturant. Unacceptable in 2016 at this pricepoint). That's too rich for me.
I've requested a refund.
tl;dr;
Not a serious racing manager. Lacks content. Heavy on the bugs. Clearly a work-in-progress still. Priced too high, when it's current version would compete better with App Store games than other titles.

tl;dr:  It's an idling game with a few clever ideas implemented in the worst way
Emporea is an idling game where you can join Alliances(guilds/clans/teams) and build up a city and army to raid monster camps and propsper - or attack players and win.
On the core level, it's actually pretty robust for an idling game - there's a fair number of unit types and progress and the way you can trade between allies is intuitive and useful since the various races require different combinations of resources to be effective.  My Dwarven army was virtually always out of Stone or Iron, but Stone moreso since buildings needed it more.  However, I always had a gross abundance of Wood - and I would trade Wood for Stone with a teammate and this was cool.
It has some Facebook style BS I hate where you have to ask random friends for random items as well as give those random items away (without it reducing your quantity) which is also 90% of the gameplay for WEBKINZ, but because it's only used for Alchemy in this game, which has limited utility, it balances out.
Now, this is where things turn south...  After a few days of upgrades you'll notice that some of the top clans are insurmountably better than everyone else combined.  This is because, ugh, PAY 2 WIN.
Now, ok - Pay2Win is something people just have to accept in this style of game, but it conflicts with another core element...  individual servers reset at the end of every season, which is relatively short (3 months);  Similar to NukeZone.   Both ideas work on their own, but the moment you combine them ANY notion of fair competition flies out the window.  You can have either/or, but not BOTH.
You don't have to Pay2Win, after all - it's not like you NEED to win, it's just a game right?  Well, this brings up the next point - the reseting servers.  The Pay4Play item in this game is called Gems, and like most Freemium games you can find a few of them naturally while playing.  The downside is... GEMS PROGRESS ACROSS SERVERS!!  So now not only can you Pay2Win if you wanted, but you can level up an alt to farm items for your closed realm - completely defeating the purpose of limited servers.
However, ok - maybe you don't care about competition at all... you're just here for the sweet Achievement Score on AStats, well - you're good to go, you can get almost all of them from playing one server of each race concurrently.  If you are very active, the SMALLEST idling period is 5~6 minutes - to raid a portal for a token reward, it's easy to switch realms in this time period and be set for life, maybe even getting GEMs you can use on your other characters.  But you'll NEVER get the victory achievement...  even if you dump tens of THOUSANDS of dollars on the game, you'd have to have an entire alliance doing the same, while also all feeding their own meta progress via alternate servers.  You can't actually win, not ever.
On the other hand, if you simply don't care about winning and just like idling games - there's a lot to do in this game, so it's certainly worth a try, just don't get mad (like me) when you finally cash in 50 quest items only to see the number 1 player cashed in 100'000 of them.

My favorite fighting game of all time. Fast, responsive controls, an eclectic cast of wildly diverse characters for every playstyle, amazing hand-drawn sprites and the most rockin' soundtrack you're likely to ever hear in a video game all come together to create an insane experience that is still second-to-none. The only problem is that the online for this game is dead. Guilty Gear has never been a mainstream series like Street Fighter or Mortal Kombat, so finding people to play online with is hard without arranging something ahead of time. When you do finally find someone to play with, you'll probably get crushed. The Guilty Gear scene has a small, but dedicated niche of players who are really, really good; some of them have been perfecting their skills since 2002, when the original release of XX dropped, and some even earlier than that. Not only that, but the netcode isn't exactly the best. Sometimes, you'll be fighting against the lag more than your actual opponent. There is plenty of content here for solo players to get some enjoyment, and the tried-and-true local multiplayer is still fine, but the online could use some work. Still, GGXX is a game nobody should miss out on, and AC+R is the most complete version of it.

So, obviously with the release of 1.0 I'm going to be re-writing my review along with everyone else. Enjoy! Or don't. You have free will.
With the release of 1.0, as you can read with almost every other review, there's lots of ups and down with the update, and I'm not gonna lie, it's suffered a bit. I still, however, find it an incredibly fun game with less and more than was in the early access game.
Pros
- More, better looking cosmetic items
- No longer needing to follow the main storyline to progress to different planets.
- A coherent storyline as opposed to the various odd jobs you'd do around the outpost
- More blocks that were previously unobtainable/obtainable through destroying them are now craftable
- Crew members
- Steam Worshop
- Achievements! (If you're into that)
- Survival mode (As a roleplayer, I love this!)
- Fleshed out objects, art, items, etc.
- Bugs are fixed pretty fast
- Exploration is still really fun
Cons
- Story is rather cliche, not very imaginative
- Novakids are pretty much just "there". No villages, no missions, no furniture, only some rare colonists if you build your own colony
- Ocean worlds are still a ♥♥♥♥♥ to explore
- Vehicles are pretty much useless, save for the hoverbike when it comes to underwater exploration, though the strobe light it has is annoying
- Progression to the next main storyline mission is incredibly annoying and arduous
- Racial weapons are no longer a thing, for some reason
- Getting furniture is a pain, as most racial furniture can only be found in villages and not bought
- FPS issues
- Shared universes (meaning progress you make on one character is shared with another)
- Bosses are either no challange at all or ridiculously hard (Looking at you, Big Ape)
tl;dr Great game if you're looking for a game to just wander around in, not so much if you're looking for a story heavy game.

In Town of Salem, you are thrown into a town of between 7 and 15 residents made up from other online players. The town is split into three factions; Town, Mafia and Neutrals. Each faction has a selection of roles and you will be randomly assigned a role when you start the game (which also determines your faction).
The catch? Unless you're Mafia, you don't know who your team mates are so you need to use powers of deduction to work out who is with you and who is against you (or use powers of deception to remain hidden if you're Mafia or an evil Neutral role). Think you've found a baddie? The Town can vote on whether to lynch them or not!
With 30 different roles to play, every game of Town of Salem will offer a different experience. Will you be the Town's Jailor, locking up and passing judgement on your fellow players every night? Or will you be the Mafia's Godfather, ordering your team to kill the Town's Doctor whilst you sit safely hidden from view? Or maybe you're the crazed Serial Killer - at odds with everybody else and going on a stabbing spree every night in the hope of becoming the last man (or woman) standing?
This game is available to play for free in a browser if you would like to try it out first but I would highly recommend the Steam version as it removes all the annoying advertisments and pop-ups and is less prone to lag and disconnects. Furthermore, you begin with a stash of Town Coins (in game currency) which you can use to customize your avatar, town house, town map and even your pet and your death animation!
As with any online game, you will encounter offensive and abusive players quite often which is a shame but you do have fillter options for bad language, the ability to ignore other players and there is also an in-game reporting system.
I would also recommend that you read up on the roles available and understand something of how the game plays before you start - and ALWAYS start with Classic Mode (the roles are set and are more limited and this mode is designed to ease in newer players).
Very addictive game and VERY highly recommended.

This is a game that comes close to good but fails to hold together.   There're just a lot of things that aren't explained well, or are poorly designed--for instance, there are crew members you can pick up.  That's cool, but you can only have one at a time initially, upgrading to more is /extremely/ expensive, and a great deal of content is gated behind their abilities.  You can't even store a few different ones to tediously return to the ship for--all crew not currently assigned as direct sidekicks are lost when you change islands.  You find anywhere from 2-4 crew members per island and nearly all of them go to waste.
Crew members can take damage and die, including from your own sword--and the way you move and swing and their idiot AI means you are hitting them /constantly/.  Once, I had a crew member get stuck behind an obstacle and be unable to follow me closely.  No problem, I figured.  Surely the pathfinding algorithm will eventually teleport them back to me.  Nope!  Traveled to the next island, and they were gone permanently--because of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ pathfinding.
There are items available for pickup as well, but you can again only hold one--and the game won't explain to you why you can't pick up or interact with a second item.  Items themselves are much more rare than crew and often require crew gating skills to retrieve, and this can make healing complicated since you don't auto-heal between islands.
The enemies are very repetitive, particularly given that you can't upgrade or change your weaponry.  There appear to be a couple of special attacks buried in the obtuse upgrade menu but they cost a huge amount of XP.  There's a ship upgrade in THAT obtuse menu that reduces XP costs but again it costs a huge number of coins.  Have fun grinding the same five creatures forever!
Lastly, the bosses are gearboxy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  By that I mean they sit on their invincible ledge and you get to dodge around until they show a weak spot for a brief time.  Repeat.  Yawn.
The graphics are nice enough, even if the tile elements repeat a lot, and the music is alright.  There's just a lot of gameplay flaws that make this one fall flat.  I got it on sale for $3 and had an hour or two of amusement with it, and I think that's all it contains for me.

.Story.
You’ve been marooned on an island by a convenient turn of events. You meet a scientist who explains to you that, by finding magical tablets, you can travel from island to island and hopefully escape.
So… You do just that.
.Gameplay.
The game can be played with either keyboard and mouse or gamepad.  I used the latter simply because it was far more comfortable than the keyboard setup.
You begin each playthrough by selecting 1 of 8 characters. These are merely aesthetic and have no bearing on how the game will play.
Then, you hop onto your ship and sail to the first island in the first zone (unless you have warp, but more on that later). Islands have a varying enemy difficulty from easy-hard. On them, you’ll hunt down tablets, which can be found at random, so that you can move from island to island. One tablet means you can move to the next islands in the chain of islands.
You’ll continue doing this until you reach the large island at the end—the one with a huge skull and dark, ominous clouds hanging above it—where you’ll face a boss.
If you die, you’re given a statistical breakdown of what you’ve done in game:
Regions Discovered
XP
Gold
Deaths
Crew Recruited
Enemies Killed
Items Used
Time Played
Then, you choose a character and dive into the game with a fraction of the resources you picked up during your last run and none of the skills you’ve unlocked.
Rinse, wash, and repeat.
Once you clear a zone you unlock the ability to Warp between them freely. There are four in total, not counting the starting area.
The islands also contain collectable treasures and pickups with a variety of effects. These pickups can heal you, add more stats, and the like. Unfortunately, there’s no telling what items do until you use them. Once or twice I’ve tried a mysterious potion that miraculously drained all of my HP or some other awful thing that put me at a horrible disadvantage when fighting the foes on the island.
.Atmosphere.
The islands are rather uniform in appearance, despite their procedural generation. Every area has its own biome, which is visually interesting at the very beginning of the chain of islands, but quickly loses its luster.
The music is nothing special, just a repeating loop that gets lost in the background.
.Longevity.
There are plenty of upgrades to unlock and treasures to discover while you travel the isles. Dying results in you losing all of those upgrades, but the amount of resources retained after you die is pretty generous, so you should have no problem regaining the skills you lost.
There isn’t a story so you could go on playing indefinitely as long as you’re willing.
.Pros and Cons.
.Bottom Line.
Lost Sea is a fun, albeit repetitive experience. Newcomers to the rogue-like genre will find a good starting place here, though veterans will likely get bored with the basic combat and the lacking arsenal of pickups/equipment.
All in all, a title I’d suggest getting at a discount or avoiding entirely.

is a procedurally generated action, adventure, rouge-like game. In Lost sea, the primary objective is to find these secret, hidden items called tablets. Tablets are artifacts scattered across every single island that you must collect and bring back to the ship in order to clear each level. The problem becomes, at the start of the game, you are unable to unlock any ship upgrades that would reveal up to three hidden tablets on your island map, as a result, you have to search through most of the island until a light in the upper left-hand corner of your screen illuminates through your lantern showing you how close the next tablet is. It is not until later on in which you unlock two ship upgrades that you purchase through obtaining gold located in wooden boxes that you destroy through your currently equipped weapon.
These two upgrades are respectfully called crow’s nest and charts. Crow’s nest shows you exactly where a random tablet is hidden on your map which can be brought up through pressing start. The other ship upgrades revealing multiple destinations up to three tablets at a time is charts II. The first upgrade to charts “ensures multiple tablets don’t roll the same sailing distance.”
In the beginning, you play as one of eight different survivors as you uncover your purpose and reason for waking up on an abandoned island. The story uses the classic adventure-based dialogue of early adventure-based games for the PC. The game reminds me of
despite the game having no resemblance or relation to the former. I used to watch my brother play the point-and-click based
series on console long ago by Telltale games. Now, Telltale focuses primarily on story-based movie-driven plots, climax, exposition and character based interactions that give the gamer influence over how the movie-driven story will pan out.
It is rare now to see Telltale re-focus on their beginnings which were some of the earlier point-and-click adventure games that made the genre rise and become so popular among people of all ages. In contrast, in Lost Sea, you wake up as a survivor that has been knocked out, face down in the sand. You awake to experience amnesia for a short while until your memory begins to come back. Once your memory sets in, you find a strange man who is actually a scientist that has lost his assistant. He tells you how you got to the island. There were rough seas in which the ship spun out of control and washed you upshore. Now, after this, you team up with the scientist and help him out as you gather more crew members within your party.
You are limited to only one crew member to follow you and tag along at the beginning until unlocking the leadership tiers found within the ship’s workshop under player upgrades. You use your gold you collect from destroying boxes in order to purchase these, whereas, ship upgrades are bought through a currency you use once defeating enemies, dealing hit points to them.

Lost Sea is an Indie Action , Rogue-like title that features Permadeath Gameplay and Procedular Generation.
Your hero has been stranded onto a tropical island due to a plane crash. With the help of other stranded crew members that you find on your path and upgrades you can purchase at each island's dock , your quest is to navigate through the islands up until you reach the final one which allows you to enter a portal that leads you to an unknown place, presumably somewhere safe.
When you first start your journey or everytime you have to restart due to death , you can select from 8 Equally Powered Characters. There are five male and three female Heroes to choose from.
The tutorial island does a decent job at covering all the basic knowledge you will need throughout your journey. You will meet a Self-proclaimed scientist , that will explain to you your situation and how to deal with it. As soon as you are done with the tutorial island the game sends you straight to the next one.
There are 5 Sections in total. Each section has its own biome theme , monsters and a boss fight on the last island. Beating that boss permanently unlocks you the next section. (Meaning if you die after reaching a new section, you can start at it's beginning as opposed to the very first Tropical Island you start the game at, if you choose to.)
The idea of the game is to search these procedually generated islands for new crew members, items that will aid you, Monsters for their EXP-Currency drops (Which are needed for Player based upgrades), Crates and Barrels for their Coin drops (Which are needed for Ship Related Upgrades) and mainly for Navigation Tablets which are the only way for you to move forward to the next island. Once you require those tablets , you ought to bring them back to the island's dock and then if you decide you are finished with that island you can move to the next ones.
is the Difficulty Curve. While the game has some Pseudo-Difficulty elements which upset me at first , but then I realised there weren't that many (Talking about charging Lizards coming out of nearby harmless-looking coin boxes and Crew Members you're about to rescue suddently turning into monsters that attack you as soon as you get close). It actually came to me by surprise how the game doesn't want to take you by the hand showing you every little way to deal with things easier and that it expects you to learn it by experience by yourself. No Pickup/Item you find in the game ever has description. You have to judge what the Item does based on it's icon and use it atleast once to be sure of what it does. Attack patterns of monsters you've encountered for the first time are not visible from afar. Sometimes you have to get close and personal to learn what they do and although that experience goes away as soon as you learn the pattern , I think its really cool.
The monster design while being basic has a nice variety, making the difficulty curve extremely noticeable for players. Each section you move forward you will find new monsters and revamped versions of old ones with more challenging attack patterns.
While it can be said that the monster design is pleasing, the same thing cannot be said for the Boss Battle(s). Each boss battle features the same boss. An angry pirate captain that each time you meet on a later section has a new trick under his sleeve. Lost Sea is an arcade survival roguelike game, developed and published by Eastasiasoft, releasing on July 5th 2016 on PC, PS4 and Xbox One. Due to a plane crash in the Bermuda Triangle, your character finds themselves stranded on a tropical island so obviously your aim is to find a way off it. In order to do that, you must explore the island in search of food, other stranded people and build yourself a ship capable of getting out of there!
The gameplay in Lost Sea is played from top down view and has very basic hack and slash combat elements. Your character’s main attack is simply a swing of the sword, but you will come across other pieces of equipment too such as a shotgun of sorts. You will be fighting against pretty much what you would expect on a tropical island, wild animals, huge giants, dinosaurs, crazy island dwellers, and more. Due to the game’s very basic combat system, you find yourself having to dodge more and carefully time your attacks on foes as you will soon find out, death in permanent here. If you die, you start right at the beginning again; it oh so annoying but also part and parcel of roguelike games. I think the perma death feature wouldn’t be so bad if they allowed you to keep all of your well earned abilities and skills that you have gathered up to that point but alas we can't have it all.
On the subject of these skills and abilities, any enemies you kill will drop coins and experience points; back at your home base you can trade these in for new skills and abilities which will aid you on your exploration of the island. These can range from straight up health increases, or allowing you to have more people in your party of explorers. I personally really liked the skill and ability system in Lost Sea, but it let me down a tad when I found out they don’t carry over between runs - it almost makes them feel a little pointless at times.
Other part’s of Lost Sea’s gameplay really irk me a tad too; as you progress through the game, you will soon be heavily reliant on the rest of your team mates; these bring along their own unique traits to your party such as being able to dig up hidden treasure, or unlock locked away items in chests - so they become pretty key to your progression. Sadly they have a very poor AI programmed into them. When you get attacked by enemies they will just freeze where they stand and do nothing; common sense would make them run away and hide, but they just knuckle down and do nothing until the danger has passed, this came across as a very poor design to me. Another issue with the AI is that they are so prone to getting stuck behind objects and pieces of the world that you will spend a good portion of time backtracking in order to free them from that hidden wall they are constantly running into.
Lost Sea’s bright and colourful art style gives the game a playful look to it; one that I particularly enjoyed, the character models look well detailed and well animated with the enemies looking impressive too. The game’s environments are definitely well worth exploring if only for the graphical fidelity on them. I would have liked to see some voice acting throughout as the sound effects are a little on the low quality side but nothing overly bad at the end of the day.
This game is difficult, no question about it. It is almost as forgiving as Dark Souls when it comes down to instant deaths, as monsters will literally jump out of trees, charge at you and you’ll die. This happens more times than I can count on one hand and does leave you feeling a little deflated in terms of wanting to pick up the controller again and jumping straight into another run, because quite simply, you are starting the game all over again. Yes you do unlock a portal like system in order to teleport to where you died, but your character is so under leveled and poorly equipped that you would just end up dying even quicker than before.
This game has tons of content, and I found it hard to actually find someone who had managed to complete the game even now 10 days after it’s release. I am not sure it would have much replayability as the actual story and plot does not change from run to run, and to be honest I would be more than happy to get one complete run out of this title, because it is so tough in the first place.
Apart from the issues mentioned with the buggy AI of the other team members, Lost Sea is a pretty technically sound release. The game is definitely going to require you to pick up your controller over keyboard and mouse though.  I feel Lost Sea would have really benefited from a multiplayer mode too; after all everything is better with friends, and this would of been no different. A co-op mode for this game would be absolutely awesome and one that I hope they can add in the future.
Overall Lost Sea is an OK release. There is nothing absolutely mind boggling good coming out of it, but it doesn’t do too much wrong either. The permadeath element definately needs changing to make the gameplay a little more forgiving and to cut down on the amount of rage quits this game induces on its players though. The game’s full price of £10.99 is well marked for a game of this quality and amount of content on offer.

Luckily, for those who can look past the shortcomings, Lost Sea has tight, reactive controls and offers a pretty good challenge, awarding players who take a slow and steady approach to completing each island.
Overall, I enjoyed my time with Lost Sea and if it weren't for the floaty combat, bad AI pathing, and somewhat forgettable skills, I could easily recommend this game to roguelike fans. As it stands right now, I would wait for a sale before you sail.

Lost Sea is an indie action adventure that features some lovely visuals, procedurally generated levels, an absolute ton of loot to collect, and a combat system rather evocative of the old Zelda series, though a whole lot easier and simpler than that. With all of that said, its also worth mentioning that Lost Sea is designed with a more casual audience in mind, so if you're a hardcore fan of roguelikes you will find very little for yourself here. On the other hand, if you're looking for a relaxing game for either yourself or your kid, then you're looking in the right direction.
Since the text area here on Steam is a bit limited, I've broken down this review into various categories to hopefully give you a good idea of what Lost Sea is all about:
For reasons unknown, Lost Sea doesn't feature a way to change the controls from within the in-game menu! You can do so by messing around with a config file buried deep within the Steam folder, but due to the initial controls being awkward on small keyboards I can see this causing a whole ton of frustration, especially for the younger/less experienced players that might not even know about config files. This should be an easy thing to fix, on account of the fix already being "there", so I hope its something the developers correct as soon as possible.
While it might not have the graphical fidelity to match the AAA games of today, Lost Sea features a charming art style that makes exploration a pure joy. All of the islands are filled with vibrant colors, shading is used to great effect in order to create somewhat realistic environments, and the various regions you can visit feel fresh and unique, despite using basically the same "building elements".
To further add on to the atmosphere we have the music, which while not numerous exhibits the same sort of charm as the visuals. To put it simply, all of this combined makes Lost Sea a rather relaxing experience, something I certainly didn't expect to see given the non-optional permadeath.
Lost Sea is a roguelite, and as such it has a need for a massive amount of levels that you can replay over and over again. Thankfully, the procedural generation is done admirably and outside of a few pre-build chunks you won't be able to notice island repeat themselves. The level design is a quite simple, however, so you will start seeing some patterns here and there, but in terms of item placement, enemies and visual elements, the procedural generation does an excellent job.
The main reason you would ever risk your life exploring in a roguelike is the loot, and Lost Sea features an absolute ton of it, most of it in the form of gold. Best of all, the whole process of looting, everything from smacking the barrel to the sound the coins make when you collected them, is an absolute joy to the eyes and ears.
Unfortunately, the majority of the loot is completely pointless as most of the gold-based upgrades are useless, and the entirety of your power comes from combat experience and followers, which also come from combat experience. Its a real shame since the looting does feel just as good as I said, but due to lacking upgrades its almost never worth it to risk even a smidgen of health to acquire entire bundles of treasure.
As I've mentioned in my introduction, the combat in Lost Sea feels like it was taken from an old Zelda game. You only have one attack, your sword swing, and with it you will need to bounce away enemies as they charge at you, stun those that might try and throw coconuts at you, and in general survive through well-timed attacks and positioning. The sword swings themselves feel satisfying, with each one giving off those satisfying swish and thunk noises as you swing your sword around and into enemies, with the end result being a rather enjoyable fighting system.
However, while the act of fighting is enjoyable, its also extremely exploitable and you can downright destroy the difficulty through one simple "trick". Just mash the attack button. Instead of relying on timing and finesse, you can instead create an impenetrable wall of blades infront of you and just mow down enemies by the hundreds, practically impervious to harm from anything but the strongest of foes. If that doesn't make Lost Sea easy enough for you, the follower system further makes it so that any semblance of challenge can swiftly be erradicated.
The followers are by far the most innovative idea Lost Sea puts forward, though sadly they are a bit too underutilized for my liking. Their main purpose is to offer you ways of traversing obstacles or picking up hidden loot, either by building bridges, unlocking chests or digging up buried stashes. Since you start with only one follower slot and need to spend a surprising amount of experience unlocking the other three, one would think that choosing the right follower with the right skills would be a crucial aspect of your survival, but it really isn't.
There are only 3-4 progression-based skills such as Craftsmanship or Lockpicking, with the rest mostly being combat and experience related, and since each follower can have 4 randomized skills its easy to fulfill all of the "requirements" with only one crewmember, and then chose the rest based around their combat benefits. The followers don't fight along with you, they are too cowardly for that, but what they do instead is amplify the amount of damage you do to quite frankly ridiculous levels. Yetis are usually quite tanky enemies and present a significant challenge when you get surrounded by a few of them, but if you have even a couple of followers with the Damage Buff attribute, something that is incredibly easy to achieve, you will be able to one-shot some of the strongest enemies in the game, and thus the challenge gets thrown out of the window.
Lost Sea is a nice and relaxing romp through exotic locations littered with more treasure than a pirate would ever know what to do about. The highlights for me are the exploration of some beautifully rendered and procedurally generated islands, the process of finding and hoarding tons of loot, and the feeling of slowly upgrading your character with newer and better skills. On the other hand, all of the elements that directly relate to combat and the roguelike progression system are just not compelling enough for me to keep playing Lost Sea once I'm done with this review, despite the 4-5 hours I've spent with it being fairly enjoyable.
If you're interested in a hardcore roguelike experience with perfectly balanced combat and items, I'm afraid you won't find any of that in Lost Sea. However, if you're looking for a cheerful and upbeat game to give your kid and guarantee that they will be both entertained and adequately challenged, then Lost Sea might just be the one you're looking for.

Good:

Bad:

TL;DR - Enjoyable as it is, 12 Labours of Hercules III: Girl Power is just like any other game from its series. Now, you have Megara (Hercules' Wife) to play, more interesting levels to play, and a "storyline" to follow. 6.5/10
In this third 12 Labours of Hercules game, the developer tends to focus a bit more heavily on the storyline. Although the storyline still remains insignificant throughout the game, there is a fully-voiced comic-style cutscene once in a while which switches things up a little bit. Pretty interesting if you really want to know mythical lore in a fun comic style.
Apart from that, the game is very similar to its predecessors. In terms of gameplay, Girl Power does not break away from the resource-management game formulaic. At the beginning of each level, a list of tasks will be given to complete by the time that the level finishes. You then need to assign tasks for your workers to do. What we appreciate about Girl Power is the function to assign tasks in advance for workers to follow; this make the game much more fast-paced and less laid-back.
Most of the levels in 12 Labours of Hercules III: Girl Power have the right challenge level. Beginners can learn their way through the game on the Relaxed mode, while more advanced players can enjoy the more intimidating Expert mode. For the usual achievements, Girl Power also featured collectible puzzle pieces; once all of the puzzle pieces are found, a jigsaw mini-game will be unlocked at the end of every 10 levels. Go for it to get that 100%.
Like the first two games, Girl Power has bright and sharp graphics. Still, there is nothing spectacular about the visuals, we still think that the developers need to add some depths into each scene. On the other hand, the soundtracks are pure gold; they are melodic, upbeat and fit the game really well, while not being distracting.

It took me years before I finally played Half-Life, which is considered one of the greatest games of all time. I was skeptical of its quality before I played it. I finally got it during the Steam Summer Sale 2017 in the Valve Classic Collection. I first booted up Half-Life: Source. I got to Blast Pit before switching to GoldSrc Half-Life upon hearing of a glitch involving rockets and Apache Helicopters that was present in HL:S. The opening sequence on the tram was cool, but I'd still want an option to skip it. I appreciate the slower buildup to action thats present, a contrast to other 90's shooters like DOOM and Quake, both games that I love and play frequently. The gunplay was solid and fun. I really liked the amount of diversity in enemy types that kept fights from getting stale. However, the human enemies were not so fun. The soldiers had perfect aim, high HP, and the actual AI was uber annoying. Thankfully the human enemies are only present in about 50-60% of the game. Your weaponry is a nice blend between returning FPS classics like the shotgun, SMG/Assault Rifle, and pistol, and unique weapons, like the Tau Cannon, Gluon Gun, and the Hivehand. Even the .357 Python is a nice little addition. The level design was very high qualiy in parts of the game, but did suffer in other parts. I give Half-Life a pass in some of its confusing level design because it was made in the 90's. As long as I don't have to use a walkthrough online, the level design isn't too obtuse. I never had to use a walkthrough while playing Half-Life.
Despite all this, despite all my praise and two negative comments, I agree that Half-Life is overrated. I HIGHLY recommend playing this game, but do not go in expecting one of the greatest experiences of your entire gaming career. But perhaps that's just me. Keep your mind open if you buy this game. Don't expect disappointment, like I did, but don't expect a Video Game From The Gods. Instead, expect a high quality First Person Shooter with an immersive setting, no cutscenes, good gunplay and occasionally confusing level design. Also, don't expect a great story or great storytelling. The story is OK, but the storytelling is worse. There really are no characters in the game. Half-Life 2 fixes that and adds actual characters, but I'm talking about Half Life 1. I give Half-Life an 8.5/10. I recommend that anyone who likes First Person Shooters buy this game.
EDIT: I can't believe I left this out, but the last four levels, (The Xen levels) are complete garbage. Everything up to this point is great. Thankfully three of the four Xen levels are short.

In this game you become the manager of your own racing team. You won't find here popular car brands like Ferrari or Maserati but just a fictional racing cars.
As a team manager you can sign new sponsor offers and help the driver to drive around the track. By earning money out of every race you can then upgrade the car or buy a new color design. The racing itself is from 3rd person perspective so you see a very small cars. As a team manager you can instruct the driver to: overtake, overload, block or tail the following car. The second set of options is: KERS button, changing the engine's ECU fuel mapping or requesting the driver to make a pitstop. Instructing the driver to overtake the following car can be from the left or right side and it works pretty well but sometimes the AI fails causing strange situations. The rest of the options work pretty well.
Single race or cup mode - new in the game. In the cup mode you also have qualification lap which i felt lacking before. Cup mode provides you also some more fun because of strategy, because there are 3 races that are longer and therefore you can go on one pitstop or two.
The game is all the time on the same level. When you start there are many cars faster than you and some of them are slower. It means that after you do the upgrades to the car your car becomes more competetive and heads to the front of the opponents. After you upgrade your car to the maximum you fight for the first places. It means that after you do it your car is always in the front so if you don't have real players as the opponents, you almost always fight for win. There should be some racing categories or one type of car races to make it more interesting.
It's the first issue - because the game doesn't have singleplayer, the game is always looking for online players. Sadly almost all the time you compete with the bots and maybe 1-2 real players.
Everything looks very nice, has good sounds. The music becomes a little boring after 5 or 10 races but you can turn it off. Some optimalizations must be made to the game because of the high cpu/gpu usage, but so far it works nice.
There are still some bugs like for example disapearing wheels, lapped cars still fight like they were racing while they shouldn't. The game needs some work but the direction is so far very good and i can recommend this game. If you like racing games, you'll definetely like this one!

The learning curve is steep when the "Magic Circle" system is into play. Basically, you can stack your sub-characters together with your main character (the one you physically play with), and the stats get transferred to your Main Character while special tiles like "Growth" will determine your Sub Character's Leveling Parameters.
If this looks like rocket science to you, this may not be the game to pass up and if you want a simpler game, I will forward you to Binding of Isaac or Hack, Slash and Loot. Heck, even Desktop Dungeon (its free, and not on Steam). For a roguelike with a slightly higher learning curve, I recommend Dungeons of Dreadmor.

Until Bastion, I've never played a button-masher/overhead beat-'em-up type game that could actually hold my attention for more than 30 minutes total. I'm no expert on this genre, and I don't intend to inform the reader about anything aside from my own opinion. Awesome. I'm not going to appologize for overhyping every good game because obviously, the games I'm going to be reviewing first are going to be either awesome or terrible, I've seen my share of each.
Bastion conforms to whatever playstyle you choose, as you move through the storyline, more and more weapons types--and by extension, play styles--become available. Now, at first, you're playing and come across a new weapon and think, well why the [heck] do I want a knife when I can have this giant hammer?! My answer to that is upgrades player, upgrades. NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Lost Sea is a classic console-style action adventure game with rogue-like elements.
In Lost Sea, you find yourself on a tropical island in the Bermuda Triangle after your plane has crashed during a storm.
For reasons that I won't go into here, you need to travel to a series of islands of four different types (jungle, desert, swamp, and snow), collecting weird magical tablets on each, in order to open an interdimensional portal and escape the Triangle.
Graphics - Lost Sea uses cel shading to good effect to give its three-dimensional graphics a cartoon feel. Textures are mainly clean, bright colours, continuing the cartoon theme, and models seem to have relatively low poly counts, although are nicely animated.
There's a day-night cycle with nice lighting changes and a rain effect, which is also quite nice, but it seems to me that it never rains during the day part of the cycle and always rains at night, which is a bit disappointing.
The game includes some nice little graphical touches like animated plants blowing in the breeze and a shark swimming around the docks, which serve to give a bit more life to the world. Unfortunately there's no manual camera zoom, though, so if you want to see anything up close you're out of luck.
Sound - Sound effects are suitable. They're not bad, but there's nothing special about them either. There are no voices for the different characters in the game, which leaves it feeling a bit empty. Music is catchy, with a sort of pirate adventure movie feel to it.
Gameplay - Lost Sea plays like a classic console action adventure game. You can play with keyboard (no mouse), but a controller is fully supported and recommended. Controls are simple: left stick for movement, right stick for camera rotation, and buttons for interaction, attack, sprint, dodge, etc.
The game is made up of four zones, each with a different theme. Each zone contains a series of individual islands, culminating in a boss level, although in the case of Lost Sea you don't have to (and can't) visit every island; instead the runes you collect act like dice to determine how many islands you hop over on your next journey. Each island is then made up of a series of hexagonal outdoor areas, each enclosed on all sides except where it connects to an adjoining room. Each island, although outdoors, ends up looking like some sort of modular habitat when viewed on the map, with a few exceptions.
Where Lost Sea differs from classic games in the genre is in its use of rogue-like elements, namely permadeath and procedural generation of islands. Unfortunately, though, neither one really works that well here. The base components for the procedural generation are mostly large, and you'll often see whole hexagonal areas copied from one island to the next, which not only breaks the suspension of disbelief, but also makes for a repetitive game. Permadeath, also, doesn't really work that well in this game, as dying simply causes frustration in making you start again; there's no carry-over benefit outside of normal progression, and the levels are all similar enough that even though you don't end up playing exactly the same islands next time you play, you might as well be doing so for all the variation you'll see.
Lost Sea also includes the concept of crew members: seemingly random people who you find at various points on each island who will join you as your slave without even exchanging a single word with you. Each crew member has up to four skills that he or she can use to boost your abilities in the game, from unlocking chests or repairing wooden bridges, to resurrecting you (once only) if you die. It's a bit silly, but is a good addition to the game. Unfortunately, though, the crew members are also very limited in implementation, with only a handful of skills meaning that you quickly max out your limited quota of crew with the most useful skill combinations, and just ignore anyone else you meet. Poor pathfinding and an inability of the crew to move out of harm's way lead to increased frustration as well.
Finally, making the repetitiveness issue even worse is the amount of backtracking you'll find yourself needing to do on islands to deliver tablets back to the docks, or go back and pick up items or crew that you didn't have space for before. This is especially painful in the early game.
Pros:
+ Rogue-like additions are a great idea, but need more work to fully realise their potential benefits to the genre
+ Crew are a good idea (but, see Cons ...)
+ Good cel-shaded graphics with nice animations
+ Steam Achievements
+ Trading Cards
Cons:
- Lots of backtracking required
- Procedural generation seems to be based on a small number of large sections, making many levels look the same, adding to the repetitiveness
- Limited number of enemy types
- Limited crew skill options make talking to most potential crew members unnecessary after the first couple of islands
- Crew are braindead and easily become stuck on terrain or won't try to avoid even the simplest trap or enemy
- No manual zoom
- No introduction or cut scenes, outside of small in-game scripted events; not everything is explained that well
- Needs a little bit more QA
I've listed a lot more cons than pros in this review, but don't let that give you the wrong impression. I like Lost Sea a fair bit -- enough to have played for over five hours straight in my first sitting, anyway.
It's good, but with a bit more work it could be excellent.

Lost Sea is a cool little exploration, action game featuring rogue-like mechanics such as permadeath and procedural generation.
Journeying from one island to the next you explore through mutliple regions, encounter differnt enemies and collect items, tablets, crew members, gold and experience to help you progress to further reaches of the game.  Rogue-like lovers or players who enjoy exploration and strategy will find a lot to like in this title but it is far from a perfect experience.
Positives ->
+ The music and art are appropriately jaunty and pleasing.
+ Procedrual generation, differing regions and areas within regions, a day/night cycle and dynamic weather keep the game feeling fresh and interesting as you explore.
+ The game adds a layer of strategy and management not often found in rogue-like games.  Crew management, tablet rescuing and rpg style upgrades all give you strategic options for you to mess around with.
+ The game feels fun to explore.  You're rewarded for looking in every nook and cranny of the islands by discovering a myriad of game resources that help you through your journey.
Negatives ->
- The combat can be one-dimensional and begin to become dull.  Player upgrades eventually help to make the combat more dynamic and interesting but don't do enough to completely fix the problem.
- The game suffers from having no minimap.  Having to constantly open the map to check your position relative to where you want to explore merely serves to slow down the gaming experience.
- Boss battles are fairly repetitive.  They are structured, not random and from one battle to the next the mechanics of the fight change only slightly.  It seems like much more interesting and grandiose things could have been done for boss battles.
- The game's AI is unfortunately idiotic.  Getting stuck behind walls is a constant struggle and leaves you needing to run back and collect the crew that got lost behind you.  They can also serve as a massive headache during skirmishes with enemies and it can be difficult to keep them alive in later sections of the game.

Videoreview:
Textreview:
Videogames have 3 very important characteristics, A like atmosphere, B like banging music and C like compelling gameplay! I hope you were able to follow me because while some games are easily implementing A and B, some games just lost sea.
Lost Sea is a fun little game I would let my kids play, if I had any. A light and colorful game, where we’re stranded in the most famous Bermuda Triangle. The goal is to survive against lurking monsters, wildlife and challenges us to get all collectible treasures and tablets to continue our journey forward.
So, how do we play it? Mostly with a gamepad. Keyboard controls are there, but complex and the camera angle to your character doesn’t change, that’s why you need a gamepad. Because it has two sticks…
Basically the controls could be better for mouse and keyboard.
Most annoyingly, and I’m not sure if it’s the fault of my Xbox One Elite controller or not, is that once I plugged my gamepad into the PC, all options and travel screens automatically move to the left. So I can barely even move the cursor to the character that I want to start the game with or properly move the cursor over the next island that I want to visit. Again, not sure if it is the game’s fault or mine. Also it doesn’t really matter which character you pick, because none of them have any percs or advantages other another.
At least we can spam the attack button which is necessary because while some enemies are very easy to take care of, the later zones are giving you enemies which charge you so quickly, you need the reaction time of Flusha or JW or someone in that range. At least the first zone, with all its enemies, it is easy to learn how to approach each enemy type. Another good thing is that enemies are not respawning once you beat all of them.
To progress in the game, we need magic tablets which let us move around in the Bermuda Triangle. The islands have a random generated layout and are set together with hexagons. In those hexagon elements are different spawns for enemies, sometimes an NPC and the tablets that you need to travel the sea between islands.
On your way you can find helpers, NPCs, which have different percs like the ability to revive you, to build bridges to get to new areas and to unlock chests. Other features are the ability to dig, to make your attacks stronger and many more. There is a lot of RNG going on in this game and while it certainly varies the difficulty of this game, it’s mostly just the best way to find the one character with lockpicking, revive and maybe even the builder ability. I ran an entire zone just with one NPC from start to end, thanks to some lucky roll.
But watch out, some NPCs like to bring themself in danger and others can’t keep up with your amazing fast movement and get stuck behind a wall.
But wait, there is more! The RNG is also combined with a deep leveling system. You can extend your own abilities like finding the fastest path back to your ship, running… yeah running is and unlockable, although it has to be said that running only lasts for a few seconds and it takes forever for you to regain stamina to run again… oh and neat stuff like managing more than one crew member at a time. I boggles me, why can’t you just “collect” crew members and switch them out when you need someone with a skill? Ah well, you can switch them out, when you first find them. Just let the current crew member go to your ship and recruit the next one. Back at your ship the previous crew member waits and you can reswitch them again.
What’s also fun to look at is the voice acting for this game. There are basically only two voices ever used in this game as it seems. A male and a female voice. No matter which NPC you find on the islands, they either have the default male or the default female voice. But, that is not even the funny part, the really funny part is when you get to fight the pirate at the end of each zone. At least the first zone features are grumpy redbeard who seemingly has some anger issues and sounds like a twelve year old. Not sure what’s up with that but it does sound somewhat wrong when you see the character.
You know what I wished for? More healing! It’s mostly impossible to get heal items from chests or to find one of those trees that magically give you about half of your lifebar back. There is an ability that you can unlock to get a higher chance of health from beaten enemies, but man I wish it would have been there right from the start, because without it, you quickly die and have to play way more carefully and therefore play the game at a higher difficulty level.
So, while I opened the review with the outlook of giving my possible children this game, I still have to say, that some aspects of the game need some adjustment. The charging enemies should be that powerful, as they were in the desert zone, and I would wish for costumizable controls for the gamepad and the mouse and keyboard combo.
I did not finish this game as of writing this review, because while the game was surely in a proper state without game breaking bugs or other problems, I just could not motivate myself to play more than the about 2.5 hrs that I invested in this game. It’s not my favorite type of game and surely not really aimed at my age group. I hope you can take my review as some buyers guide and I also hope that the developers will continue to improve the game. There is certainly a fun little game to be found here.

Tales of Berseria is a fantastic RPG with the real time action combat that the Tales of series is well known for. Flashy combos of attacks are to be expected, and Berseria offers nearly complete customization of combos, only limited by what you have at the moment. The newest edition to the system offers unique attacks or techniques at the cost of your stamina, which keeps the combat fast and furious.
You play as Velvet Crowe, who wants nothing more than revenge for what happened to her family and is willing to do anything to get it. Right away, veterans of the Tales series will notice that this is different from other Tales games, in that you aren't playing a hero. The game isnt afraid to let Velvet and her party do things that are straight out villainous.
What elevates it over the other games in the series is the absolutely fantastic characters and story that game brings, a near total 180 from the disaster that was Zestiria. I was very engaged with Velvet's story from the beginning, and every main character has an interesting story. Berseria's great characters even extends to the various NPC characters you meet up with Yes, even the mascot character gets development! I won't spoil anything but I will say there were some absolutely shocking moments that I absolutely enjoyed.
It isn't perfect, dungeons and exploration aren't anything special, and can be said to run a bit long. Sometimes the game will expect you to backtrack which can be annoying at times. I played using the english dub, which was mostly good except for one big stinker of a side character. The game does also provide a japanese voice option for those who prefer it. Some of the later skits (little optional party interatction bits) were translated poorly in text, but the english dub was perfectly understandable.
Still, Berseria is an excellent entry in the Tales of series, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who likes JRPG games.

It took me years before I finally played Half-Life, which is considered one of the greatest games of all time. I was skeptical of its quality before I played it. I finally got it during the Steam Summer Sale 2017 in the Valve Classic Collection. I first booted up Half-Life: Source. I got to Blast Pit before switching to GoldSrc Half-Life upon hearing of a glitch involving rockets and Apache Helicopters that was present in HL:S. The opening sequence on the tram was cool, but I'd still want an option to skip it. I appreciate the slower buildup to action thats present, a contrast to other 90's shooters like DOOM and Quake, both games that I love and play frequently. The gunplay was solid and fun. I really liked the amount of diversity in enemy types that kept fights from getting stale. However, the human enemies were not so fun. The soldiers had perfect aim, high HP, and the actual AI was uber annoying. Thankfully the human enemies are only present in about 50-60% of the game. Your weaponry is a nice blend between returning FPS classics like the shotgun, SMG/Assault Rifle, and pistol, and unique weapons, like the Tau Cannon, Gluon Gun, and the Hivehand. Even the .357 Python is a nice little addition. The level design was very high qualiy in parts of the game, but did suffer in other parts. I give Half-Life a pass in some of its confusing level design because it was made in the 90's. As long as I don't have to use a walkthrough online, the level design isn't too obtuse. I never had to use a walkthrough while playing Half-Life.
Despite all this, despite all my praise and two negative comments, I agree that Half-Life is overrated. I HIGHLY recommend playing this game, but do not go in expecting one of the greatest experiences of your entire gaming career. But perhaps that's just me. Keep your mind open if you buy this game. Don't expect disappointment, like I did, but don't expect a Video Game From The Gods. Instead, expect a high quality First Person Shooter with an immersive setting, no cutscenes, good gunplay and occasionally confusing level design. Also, don't expect a great story or great storytelling. The story is OK, but the storytelling is worse. There really are no characters in the game. Half-Life 2 fixes that and adds actual characters, but I'm talking about Half Life 1. I give Half-Life an 8.5/10. I recommend that anyone who likes First Person Shooters buy this game.
EDIT: I can't believe I left this out, but the last four levels, (The Xen levels) are complete garbage. Everything up to this point is great. Thankfully three of the four Xen levels are short.

This game is a gem! Or, at the very least, a diamond in the rough.
After several hours of more fun than I had ever expected (man, those hours flew by fast) I decided it was about time I broke out of my shell and popped the review-cherry on Steam. And I'm not even a petrol head!
The pros:
- The races are fun!
- Car customization is solid, with paint schemes, sponsor placement and may other details to tweak.
- Weather and day/night cycle adds a lot of both tactics and atmosphere.
- Skill system for driver and pit crew is simple and logical.
- Online matchmaking system is good. I was a bit sceptical about this at first, but the solution to add in AI controlled vehicles to fill in the empty seats is very elegant as it completely eliminates queue times.
The cons:
- Would like to see the "management" part get expanded upon, for instance with more detailed control over the driver and pit crew (finding replacement team members, sending them to training camp, etc). This could also add some personal connection to the team, instead of just managing a car.
- Skill system is a bit TOO simple. Some more advanced skill customization options wouldn't hurt. Although I guess that would probably be a result of more advanced management features (if we get individual skills for each team member for instance) so technically not a "con" on it's own, but deserves mention.
- Not enough content. Should have more cars, more tracks, more everything. Leagues, tournaments, random events, counting the days in a season, calendar marking races and event you have signed the team on for, etc, etc.
So, considering most of these Cons may be addressed before launch (this game is still in Early Access after all), I'd say this is looking mighty promising!
All in all: Recommended!
And a tip for those of you just getting started: Go to options and enable tooltips - that will help a LOT. And save you a lot of time trying to figure things out blindly, like I did. *cough*
Seriously though, turn those tooltips on!

Let me preface this review by reinterating this is an Live Launch Review. Having observed the game's development and at times being it's harshest critic. I am finally amending my review to reflect some of the progress and improvement that is TrackDay Manager today. There are still some glaring issues to be worked out, but the game is about 85% there after final release. Which is to say, I'm about 85% towards giving this title the thumbs up. I advise deciding yourself about this title. That said, here are some of the Pros and Cons of TrackDay Manager.
Update Per Live Launch: 5 May 2016
Pros:
1: Overall concept and premise of the game is great.
2: Graphics are solid and suit the concept and focus of the game.
3: Customization of race cars (Not 100% of this content is ingame), both paintschemes and sponsor placement.
4: Online Multiplay, with AI fillers when lacking enough human players.
5: In race chat, allowing folks to chat pre-during-post race.
6: Straight forward Upgrade and Skill system, easy to understand.
7: Tons of Achievements that actually unlock useful and cool ingame content.
8: Highly interactive and communicative development team of 4. So yea it's small but very dedicated team.
Cons:
1: Laggy netcode( Peer to Peer), resulting in lag spikes and sometimes adversely affecting race mechanics. Let me make clear, there are folks from all over the world playing this title and unfortunately the sheer distance between say North American players and European players often results in  laggy races. As of now, you are lucky to see another human player 1 out of maybe 10 races. Sadly MP is pretty much broken.

2: Lack of Career mode, MP Racing Leagues, League Management Tools, etc. There is a Leaderboard, which tracks National, Regional and Global Ranking. The lack of League Management tools really misses the mark in allowing folks to set up (In a convienent fashion) their own racing leagues. There is a "Cup" format newly added, which is a 3 random tracks mini-race series, queued up for just like single quick race. ***Edit*** Custom races have been added, which will allow leagues to form and manage themselves externally. Though there are plans for alternate mode and Reward Cup Series coming to the game in trhe future.
3: Limited amount of vehicles (6) and tracks (6), albeit there is more content incoming, no ETA.
4: Microtransactions where mentioned at point, seems this may be a dead issue and no longer in this game's future. We hope.
5: Rudimentary Matchmaking. New(er) Drivers are not matched with Drivers whom have Max Skills and Maxxed out Cars for 50 races. After that, time to dine the freshbloods.
6: Absence of an Open Game Lobby, where folks can hangout chat, swap strategies, ask advice, arrange races.
7: Inability to preset custom setups for each track, like real race teams would in real life. One setup and random assigned race tracks, so you end up using the same setup for road courses and ovals alike, etc.
8: The New GUI has some work to be done, as it does error and give improper information.
9: This game should have been developed as a iOS/Android Application.
10: Since launch the Developement team has been slow to patch and often breaking more than fixing. Which was a problem during Early Access also. Communication has also all but dried up, the Devs seem to be paying less attention this newly launched title.
11: Arctic Hazard Games did little to promote this title, barely a whisper on any social media and ignored Early Access Player advice to ultilize Twitch and other Social promotion venues.
In the End, avoid this already dead title. Was a great idea, implemented poorly.

Until Bastion, I've never played a button-masher/overhead beat-'em-up type game that could actually hold my attention for more than 30 minutes total. I'm no expert on this genre, and I don't intend to inform the reader about anything aside from my own opinion. Awesome. I'm not going to appologize for overhyping every good game because obviously, the games I'm going to be reviewing first are going to be either awesome or terrible, I've seen my share of each.
Bastion conforms to whatever playstyle you choose, as you move through the storyline, more and more weapons types--and by extension, play styles--become available. Now, at first, you're playing and come across a new weapon and think, well why the [heck] do I want a knife when I can have this giant hammer?! My answer to that is upgrades player, upgrades. There are a ton of alternate paths to take in order to collect more pieces that unlock upgrades, and if you play enough, you can buy the last few pieces in the shop towards the end. The game gets much harder as you continue but at a gradual enough tempo to not overwhelm. Its fun, just don't try to beat it all in oone sitting and you'll get the most enjoyment out of it, replay levels, try to complete the genie lamp bonus levels, try to play with each weapon and by the end of the game you'll wish you could play more...which you can, in game plus, which I haven't given a go yet, but it is no doubt, going to be a fun speed run.
P.S.: The voice-acting! I almost forgot! It's fantastic! A deep voiced cowboy narrates everything you do, sort of like the Big Lebowski. Shoot the shot gun for the 10th time, "Yeeeaaah, the boy took a likin' to that new fangled blunderbuss almost too quick. But it worked for him and it became... his saving grace." Or some cowboy thing like that.
Overall: 9/10 (

Warning: Super vague spoilers.
This game seemed interesting at first, and I especially enjoyed the idea of the narrator looking for his wife, even though what happened to her was completely obvious just from the game's description. However, once opening the game (heeding warnings that you must play the whole thing in one sitting - the esc button simply kicks you out of the game), I quickly got confused. As it turns out, to get through the game, you must click the same objects and spaces around the cabin numerous times until you trigger something other than the idle text (things along the lines of "I'm so confused" and "It's too painful to remember"). There is literally no instruction for gameplay at all, and the only reason I realized I had to trigger events to move on was that the clock made noise, then produced new text when I examined it for the ten millionth time. Furthermore, the climax of the game is so underwhelming that what should have been a gruesome scene was simply a moment of "Oh. Finally." Lastly, the ending of the game was just flat-out confusing and leaves so many loose ends even the newest of writers would cry (and I am no new writer). There is no explanation as to who the figures outside are or what they are even doing - though I did take some context clues and made an assumption. I don't know if the photograph so indicating of the narrator's progress through the game changed to show what he discovered, or whether it becomes clear how he managed to do what he did - all I noticed before the final text and the credit roll was that a place on the floor changed to be more what I expected of what he did. By the end of the game, even the narrator's status as a living human being comes into question - we know by the end what his fate is, but was he even alive in the first place? There are far too many unanswered questions at the end of the game for me to enjoy even a part of the story.

You play a man with partial memory loss, confined to a cabin where he and his wife stayed as you try to figure out where she is and what happened to her. Typical point-and-click deal.

The gameplay is fairly simple (You load a cannon and fire it, you fire swivel guns, you command the ship as a captain, you repair the ship with a hammer or you pump water out from the ship. And die here and there.), but the destruction mechanics are pretty nice and it seems like a pretty fun game.

Still in early access, but worth the purchase. Whatever bad things you've heard about updates, forget that. The developers work hard every day and they release updates every month or so.
There are still quite a few things wrong with this game, but that's expected from an early access. I've had this game for a while now, and it's great.
If you're into exploring around space, awesome music, and lots of variety, then I urge you to buy Starbound.

This game really is  a work of art. It's got truly beautiful graphics, an outstanding soundtrack and a narrator with a voice that would make Morgan Freeman jealous.
You play a character known only as The Kid who wakes up one day to find his homeland has been destroyed by the Calamity. He manages to escapes to the Bastion where he finds another survivor who also happens to be the games narrator. The narrator is brilliant in his game as he narrates depending on your actions, often commenting on your actions as well as telling the games story.
The gameplay is quire good as well you roaming through different levels which form in real time as you walkthrough them fighting the various creatures the game throws at you. The combat manages to be quite varied as you unlock a ot of different weapons and abilities throughout the game which are also upgradeable. The game also has some replay value with a NewGame+ mode.
It'd be hard not to mention the brilliant soundtrack which really is one of the best soundtracks you'll find in a game. It is worth buying the soundtrack as well since it is that good.
There aren't really any bad points for me other than my initial playthrough felt a little too easy but the game does have a device that allows you to increase the challenge for a greater reward so there is something there for people who want a tougher challenge.
This really is a game everyone should try. It's a 9.5/10 from me.

In a culumination of over a decade of revisions, insane characters, rockin' music and killer style, what sits before you is an easy contender for one of the greatest fighting games ever.
+R is the result of four immediately preceding games in the XX series, coming with 25 extremely individual and complex characters, matched only by a fighitng system which encourages the very essence of its titular character's main trait: freedom. Guilty Gear is freedom in that if you can imagine it, with practice and understanding, you can probably do it. The game allows for some of the greatest flexibility in any game, and you'll derive as much enjoyment from discovering its nuances as you will beating opponents senseless and rocking out doing so.
This is the game that got me playing fighting games, made me appreciate game design, and made me appreciate Queen. Without question, this is a game for the ages. Buy it.
