Until not too long ago, I didn't think well of the Tales games. All that I had seen or heard about it, all that I had played myself – it all seemed very underwhelming to me. Stereotypical characters, cliché stories and button-mashy combat – everything about the series just screamed „average“ to me. That was until I played Tales of Berseria.
Where Berseria absolutely shines is the characters. An honor-bound warrior chasing his own personal nemesis, a garish, teasing witch who may be wiser than she lets on, a young boy discovering the meaning of the self and of being alive, an exorcist struggling to find her own way to improve the world, an art-loving, unlucky pirate on a rescue mission, and a loving sister who's lost everything and is hell-bent on revenge – that's the party at the heart of the plot. But their personalities and the dynamics between them run so much deeper than brief descriptions like these could ever hope to cover. The same is true for the story. There is no black and white in Tales of Berseria – no good and evil. Instead, it clashes different sets of morality and shades of gray against each other. It poses important questions like: Do the needs of the many outweigh those of the individual? Do the means always justify the end?  How do we deal with the imperfections of humanity? What does it mean to be alive? And, perhaps most importantly, why is it that birds fly? Instead of just raising these questions, though, the game actually provides multiple answers from different angles.
The game offers you less freedom in terms of progression, however. Berseria is rather linear until around the 30 hour mark, when it opens up a bit and starts presenting some side quests for you to tackle. That being said, the intriguing plot and the excellently written dialog keep you invested so thoroughly that you almost don't want to divert from the main mission. No matter which language option you choose – English or Japanese – both settings offer a great cast of voice actors and well performed lines. The quality of the music meanders between pretty good and mediocre – with only a couple of standout tracks. But when these pieces do play they are especially powerful and add a lot of emotional weight to certain scenes. From an artistic point of view, Tales of Berseria feels like a well thought-out, complete package with a lot of highlights and virtually no low points. Some of the world's unique terminology can be confusing at first, but implicit explanations arise naturally from dialogs, and soon enough you'll get a clear picture of everything important. This age-old conflict between chaos and order is, on all fronts, competently to expertly presented and rides a perfect wave of both predictability and surprise.
However, Berseria stumbles somewhat in terms of certain gameplay elements – especially when it comes to the equipment system. The game borrows from Final Fantasy IX and other RPGs in that every piece of gear comes with a unique skill that characters can learn permanently if they wear it for a certain amount of fights. In the case of Final Fantasy IX, characters learn active and passive abilities with clearly visible effects. But in Berseria, the term “skills” refers to small attribute increases, like enhanced fire damage, that just lack impact. The characters grow stronger at such an incremental rate that no learned skill has any immediately perceivable effect. Changing out your old equipment for new one is important in the long run but never really feels rewarding. That being said, once you're familiar with the menu, going through the motions becomes second nature. Changing gear and the long-term benefits associated with the process may not be a highlight in itself, but it does serve as a nice breather between story parts and combat. What's baffling, on the other hand, is the enhance feature, that let's you upgrade your gear pieces to increase damage or damage reduction among other things. When you're constantly swapping old equipment for newer and better one, especially if it teaches you new skills, there is little incentive to spend materials for upgrades. And indeed the game is easily beatable without enhancing any items – even on higher difficulty settings. To a certain extent, Berseria is an example of disjointed systems that don't seem to have any synergy and feel like an afterthought more than anything. Luckily, they don't present much of a barrier. Learning equipment skills is low maintenance and enhancing can be ignored altogether.
Where the developers clearly did have a well-defined concept, however, is the combat. The real-time action battles are admittedly somewhat button-mashy in nature, but there is a distinct layer of strategy that involves clever resource management. It's important to know when to use a special or super move – so-called break souls techniques and mystic artes – and when to build up resources or switch characters instead. Making the right decisions let's you unload seemingly never-ending combos on your foes; choosing wrong can get you in trouble quickly. Using the right elemental attacks against your enemies is also of some importance, but unless you're playing on the highest two difficulty settings, you can always come back from mistakes without too much effort. Should you want to challenge yourself though, the game offers nice incentives to ramp up the difficulty, such as increased item drop rates. The combat is simple enough to be intuitive and easy to pick up but offers just enough depth not to bore you. Thanks to pre-definable strategy settings, the AI-controlled characters do a good job of not getting themselves killed too quickly, although the game doesn't quite offer as many options as you'd like on that front. Every once and again you'll see a party member acting strangely, but the same can be said of enemies as well.
Tales of Berseria is a long adventure, netting you over 60 hours of playtime even if you only dabble in the side quests. Between cooking, mini games and naval expeditions, there's a lot to keep you busy – if you decide to partake in these activities. Cooking is quite useful, since meals completely restore your party's health and provide a neat little buff for your next battle. Mini games and the automatic, timed expeditions, that you can check in on every 20 to 30 minutes are less essential and can easily be ignored. But they do offer nice rewards. Among the best of them are new outfits and accessories that you start unlocking very early on. I probably spent hours dressing my characters in different styles ranging from totally ridiculous to illegally cool.
The technology behind the Tales series has hardly ever been state of the art. Berseria, too, is limping behind the current generation of consoles and games in terms of graphics. Muddy textures, low shadow resolutions and frequent pop-ins are a constant reminder that Namco Bandai is not dishing out the hugest budget for their long-running RPG series. But despite technological shortcomings, there is a certain charm to the visuals. The graphics may not be impressive in the conventional way, but they are quite pretty from an artistic point of view. There's a lot of color in the different environments, enemies come in all shapes and sizes, spell effects look gorgeous, and the anime-styled characters are surprisingly well animated and expressive. Clearly there's a lot of passion and vision put into the art direction of the game. It's just a joy to look at.
Tales of Berseria is not the best RPG ever made. Some of its gameplay mechanics aren't exactly well designed and feel inconsequential or unrewarding as a result. But the quality of the writing is on a level that few games in the genre ever achieve – whether it be the intriguing and thought-provoking plot or the multi-layered characters. Solid combat and a great artistic vision make this an easy to recommend action RPG.

Summary:
This game is good. No its great! But not perfect. The graphics though great for a game from 1998, havent aged well at all, and playing at 1080p makes most textures very blurry. The shooting part (Since this game is a First person Shooter) Isnt very good at all. I rarelt saw my bullets hit any of the enemies even with my crosshair on them. The shooting is pretty terrible. But thats not what the game is about. The game is more about thinking than shooting, and you'll find yourself solving puzzles to progress. Some puzzles are good, but most of them will leave you running around like an idiot until you realize what to do. But Even with that the game is still really good.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is pretty good, but the shooting cant go pass unchecked. The shooting isnt very good, and is downright annoying and very frusterating. But even with that the pacing is fantastic and youll be addicted, Trust me! (8.5/10)
Presentation:
The presentation in this game is absolutely fantastic! The intro does an amazing job at immersing you into the world and learning about the story. Though it can be a bit Slow... (9.5/10)
Graphics:
Honestly Graphics havent aged well. For what was a game from 1998, this game wouldve looked amazing for its time. But now it looks crummy. There are multiple points were the textures overlap. Im not saying graphics are everything, but they can be a visual disturbance at times. (7.5/10)
Sound:
Sound is good. Just good because the barely isnt much sound. Music only settles in certain parts of the game, creating a creepy and mysterious atmosphere. It fits the games theme perfectly! Its pretty amazing! Ofcourse, Sound effects are good too, but i noticed some gun sounds to be too loud, and some enemy sounds are very annoying. (8/10)
Overall Score:
In all honest ill give this game an 8.5/10, It was a great game for its time, but alot of its faults are overlooked like the shooting and graphics which havent aged so well. But the presentation, level design, and pacing are fantastic, and is a blast to play.

Thumbs up for what it is. Was not exactly what I was expecting, but I am still enjoying it. This is not a hardcore management/simulation game, so know that before buying. To me, it feels more like an arcade game with a light management twist on it.
Pros:
- Lots of time to be sunk into this
- Can be played when you only have a half hour or so (low single sitting commitment)
- Quite a good looking game
- While you don't directly drive the car, the "skills" present a highly engaging play style that doesn't have you just "kicking back and waiting"
- When you are against bots, they seem to have a nice range of skill
Cons:
- Low level of content (currently)
- Have not seen more than 2 players in a race thus far
- A bit too casual for a management, or a simulation, game (not sure which it wants to be, but leans towards casual for either category)
- Have run quite a few races and only seen 2 of 5 tracks, making the content level feel even lower right now
- Based on income rate and car cost, your "team" looks like it will be a single car/driver for longer than many would be willing to play the game (assuming you even can get another car - looks like you can)
- No apparent way to "party" with someone
- You don't know which track you will be racing ahead of time (randomly selected when you join a race) so you have to setup your car in the garage to be an overall setup
- Pre-race setup consists of just choosing your tire type (3 basic choices, no fine adjustments)
- In-game pit options are fuel refill level and tire type (again, no fine adjustments)
Other Thoughts:
- Price might seem a bit high right now with the lower amount of content. I am assuming that more will come. Regardless of the low content right now, if you can get into the game, I could see a very good hours/$ return.
- A few small issues/bugs, but not bad for an early access and quite a lot better than many other games on early access (and even full release for that matter).
- The in-race management is where you spend most of your time. Front office stuff takes a back seat in terms of time spent in game, and front office complexity is quite low.

It's difficult to say exactly what makes Sleeping Dogs such an enjoyable game as there isn't one original concept to be found within virtual Hong Kong. Originality notwithstanding, each aspect of the game from the gripping story to the exhilirating hand-to-hand combat to the tight sleek driving controls come together to form one of the more polished contemporary free-roaming experiences you've yet to see.

JetDogs Studios has found its perfect cash cow with the 12 Labours of Hercules series, and they are determined to milk it. And since the series has created its own standard for time management games, who can blame them?
The third instalment is yet another simple but very polished example of the exact same recipe. And it's a good recipe, well worth the asking price for fans of the genre. The mechanics are solid, if unchanged, and the many and varied levels are decently designed. Plus, it's technically impeccable in its simplicity and understands its core audience. With a clean UI, clean and bright graphics, decent music and sound effects, a non-offensive overarching narrative that doesn't take itself seriously and is totally skippable, simple puzzle mini-games that aren't trying to be more than a breather in-between levels, lots of achievements, 3 difficulty levels and tons of content to keep you occupied for hours, it still ranks amongst the best time management games of this type out there.
Unfortunately, as good as it may be, the recipe is starting to get a bit stale. Girl Power simply has nothing new to say; if you have played the first two games, this is one of the same, just a little less interesting, less well balanced and less inspired.
Yes, the levels are well enough designed. They just aren't as clever, fun and innovative as in the first two games.  I also didn't much like how the difficulty was scaled this time around. Ignoring the aptly named relaxed mode, I finished the game in casual mode feeling mildly disappointed at the lack of challenge. Then I started again in expert mode, which ramps up the challenge by a lot and is initially very exciting. However, the excitement ended about half way through, when I realised that too often getting a gold star wasn't going to be the fun process of coming up with a valid strategy, but repetition after repetition in order to learn it by heart. So none of the modes felt as satisfying to me as I had hoped.
Again, this is a solid casual time management game, that offers many hours of play with no technical or UI hassle and at a good price. It's just not as great as fans of the series were expecting.

Truly one of the greatest gifts you can give to a video game historian or someone who's just interested in retro gaming. This is a compilation of Atari arcade games including Asteroids, Centipede, and Missile Command and Atari 2600 games including Adventure, Combat, and Yars' Revenge. The selection of games Code Mystics chose for the game is amazing, even though the compilation is missing my favorite retro Atari game, Food Fight (Which I guess is kind of an unpopular opinion). Oh well, the literal ONE HUNDRED Atari games included in this package makes up more than enough for it. So I did the math and it turns out that since the package is $20.00 and there are 100 games in it, you'd be paying $0.20 for each game. Wow, talk about a bargain. Anyway, every game in here is remastered with different graphics and/or sound effects, most likely to incorporate the online play feature. No, your eyes are not deceiving you. I said online play. (Too bad literally no one I know owns this game.) Though since some games have different aesthetics, when I play games I grew up with like Black Widow and Red Baron with different sound effects instead of the nostalgic sound effects, it's just not the same. But they're still really, really enjoyable. And now for the biggest gripe with arcade compilations: The trackball execution. Since the mouse can be used as the trackball, it works really well. Now I can finally play Crystal Castles the way it was intended without going at the speed of light due to how fast you move with the Xbox 360 controller left stick. And even if there's a couple of games in the compilation you dislike, there's bound to be at least half of the games in the compilation that you enjoy. Really, buy it now as a gift or for yourself.

This is coming from someone who's played very few point-and-click games so I'll say upfront that I might not have the best idea of what makes a game in this genre good or bad.
This game is best classified as an atmospheric mystery with just a bit of horror mixed in. You're dropped into gameplay right after launching and given no direction at all whatsoever. It quickly becomes clear that the only thing you'll be doing in the game is clicking on objects in a cabin and listening to the protagonist's commentary, all while slowly unraveling the mystery of what happened between him and his wife.
While I do give the game props for quality voice acting and for creating a memorable atmosphere, I can't say I ever sympathized with the protagonist all that much to really be drawn into the experience. So much of the commentary boils down to "I miss my wife" and just feelings of anger and remorse that you tire of clicking on objects since you pretty much have a good idea of what the protagonist will say. We're not given too much context throughout this brief adventure (I beat the game in 35 minutes), so it would've been nice if perhaps more effort had gone into telling actual stories about the objects in the cabin to really flesh out the two characters better.
In terms of progression (because there is an actual end; you don't just click on things ad nauseum), I'll just say that there are a few objects that are inaccessible at first and must be revisited after finding other objects before they can be fully interacted with. Again, the game gives you no direction at all and I can see this being a frustrating point for some players.
Considering this is a free game-and a very short one at that-I'd go ahead and recommend it. The gameplay isn't very special, the characters aren't too relatable, and the story payoff is neither horrible nor memorable. That being said, there are certainly far worse ways to spend 30 minutes to an hour of your life.

OK, let's get things clear out of the way. If you want to buy this game solely for online mode, forget about it. It's not that GGXXAC+R's netcode is bad or anything (it's actually quite decent). Fighting games are meant to be played with friends, face-to-face. It's way more fun to play with a bunch of guys, sitting behind the screen, cheering for the underdog,screaming when something dope happen etc you know what I mean. Plus, network delay is one of the main reason I dont bother with playing online anymore. It just doesnt feel right at all when you're used to playing with delay-free situation (this is what gamer usually aim for regardless of what game they play). However. spending a bit of time with online mode isnt so bad. But still, I'm not recommend playing on online mode.
So, if you're not buying this game because of the online mode, why should you buy it then? Well, for starter, It's GUILTY GEAR ffs, the game  that havent released a new version on PC for like 10 years. New story to be discovered. Believe me when I say this, but GGXXAC+R's story is absolutely awesome (yeah, I kinda went through the whole story mode when there was a GGXXAC PS2 rom on PCSX2)
What's more to add? Arcade mode's got enhanced with the addition to the hidden Order-Sol Boss (that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is really hard to chew), Boss I-no's got a quite few tweak herself with the addition of disabling Instant Kill, making it more challenging
Survival mode is quite cool as well, you have to ability to power-up your character after defeating each boss. Still. no save function. But hey, it's survival mode. Why do you even need a save function for?
Saving the best for last, we have the major gameplay update. More balance than the previous versions, more mechanics to vastly improve the "every-situation-has-an-answer" property, namely throw break, slashback (this one is quite hard to use effectively though). Then we have 2 new characters (A.B.A and Order-Sol) and 2 re-balanced character that was consider OP and was ban from every Tournament (yes, I'm talking about Kliff and Justice)
TL;DR: 10/10 would buy for the game's content

The current pinnacle of the Guilty Gear series finally arrives on Steam and in a fairly well port. Easily the most well-balanced entry of the series and sports the largest cast as well coming in at 25 combatants. For gameplay modes it sports Arcade, story, vs, team vs, mission, survival, training, & online. There is also a gallery in which you can view at atwork and other content you have unlock while playing.
The online play is touchy subject of this title as it can be really good or really bad entirely based on the distance from other players. For example the online feels next to perfect playing against my friend who lives about 40 minutes away by car but playing random people online, it can show some seriously bad input lag. It should also be noted there is no spectating or lobbies for that matter if that was something which interested you.
As for the port, it runs a lot smoother than the steam store page would lead you to expect with the high recommend specs, so much so i'd guess the real recommended specs are much lower. The only serious port issue i've encountered at this time is no way in-game to exit the game, but that is said to be on a 'To-Do' list. Its also nice that they throw in the OST for the game as an added bonus (though it should be noted certain shared tracks in the game itself are in the included Guilty Gear XX #Reload OST instead of this one, so view this more like an OST expansion).
I really recommend this game as the ideal starting point if you want to get into Guilty Gear, though it should be noted Guilty Gear does have a learning curve, so don't expect good results running up blind against a seasoned player. At $14.99, you will get your money's worth on content.

You  already know what you're getting into, and you also know if you're going to like it or not. So, if you enjoy these, i recommend Berseria as well. It's a good entry to the franchise, despite some of the gameplay aspect being streamlined, or "dumbed down" a little bit to make the game more accessible to new players. Better character cast and storyline makes up for them pretty well.
You might be looking at this, and thinking to yourself "what the hell is this game". Tales games are almost a genre in themselves at this point, every game follows a certain formula (with some changes every time) that some of the people will enjoy, and some other will not. I'l ltry to explain what you're getting yourself into:
As every main Tales game, Berseria is a JRPG focused almost entirely on the gameplay, with the highlight always being the insanely fun combat system (which is the major reason people enjoy the series). Looking at the screenshots you might see a lot of exposition and cutscenes but don't be fooled, what you'll be doing for the majority of the game is dungeon crawling, with light puzzle elements, and beating the crap out of A LOT of various monsters. Anything that happens outside of it is there only to be a breather to the player, and an excuse for your characters to keep doing what they're doing. In the case of Berseria we actually got a pretty flavorful cast of (mostly) interesting characters, with a story that, while being a standard revenge plot, is surprisingly competent compared to what we usually get. But don't go in expecting an overworld straight out of Witcher 3, this game is played for it's gameplay. You won't find fancy storyline, great dialogues or complicated characters, it's all there to be a distraction. And this is actually a part of what we sign up for as the fans of the franchise, without all the silly dialogue, over the top moments, corny one liners, the game would just not be the same, it just wouldn't work if the game took itself seriously all the time.
Enough about story and characters, let's talk about the meat of all Tales games, COMBAT. This time around we got introduced to a streamlined, four button combo system (fully customizable) which will make skill managment and making perfect combos much easier for begginers. Essentialy your character can chain up to 4 moves into a combo (this number changes depending on various factors) , and each one of the four buttons represents a different skill that will be executed during a part of that combo. That gives you 16 skills you can put on those buttons, in whatever order you like, you can even change your setup mid-fight if you want, neat huh? Well, that's just the tip of the iceberg. Each of the skills can be put into 3 categories, which changes what stat it uses for scaling. Eeach one of them has different elemental and monster properties, making it effective against different kind of enemies, which is essential knowledge if you want to be effective. Each skill places the character and the enemy in a different position, making some other skills better suited to follow certain combos. Skills have different costs, which must be considered so your character doesn't run out of fuel mid-combo and get destroyed by the enemy follow up. There are special burst skills that will let you do a powerful move, that will allow to chain combos together into ridiculous lenghts if used correctly. Skills have status aliments, that will help you extend your combos when applied to the enemy. Guarding changes your attack properties, dodging at a perfect time will give you opportunity to extend your combos. There are six playable characters (4 max in a party), each one of them has different and expansive moveset, and special abilities that make their playstyle different...
There is way too many things about the combat system to explain on paper. If you think that's WAY too complicated, don't leave yet!
about all this is that the combat is only as complicated as you want it. If you look at all this and thin kto yourself "this is way too much, I don't get half of this, I just want to kick♥♥♥♥♥" as you wish, just set the difficulty to normal or casual, and kick the crap out of the monsters using your favourite characters and skills. But if you enjoy a challenge, want test your mettle and master every aspect of the advanced combat system of a Tales game, you can crank the difficulty up, and make the most optimal combos, character builds, and combinations you can! The game provides good tutorials that explain the game mechanics very well, and it paces those tutorials so you don't get too overwhelmed by the knowledge.
Aside from the comabt, you got the typical gameplay elements of a JRPG, things like: equimpent upgrading, minigames, and such. Nothing to write home about, but good additions nonetheless.
At this point you probably already know if you want to play Berseria or not, so I'll leave the rest for Your judgement. Have fun!

Until not too long ago, I didn't think well of the Tales games. All that I had seen or heard about it, all that I had played myself – it all seemed very underwhelming to me. Stereotypical characters, cliché stories and button-mashy combat – everything about the series just screamed „average“ to me. That was until I played Tales of Berseria.
Where Berseria absolutely shines is the characters. An honor-bound warrior chasing his own personal nemesis, a garish, teasing witch who may be wiser than she lets on, a young boy discovering the meaning of the self and of being alive, an exorcist struggling to find her own way to improve the world, an art-loving, unlucky pirate on a rescue mission, and a loving sister who's lost everything and is hell-bent on revenge – that's the party at the heart of the plot. But their personalities and the dynamics between them run so much deeper than brief descriptions like these could ever hope to cover. The same is true for the story. There is no black and white in Tales of Berseria – no good and evil. Instead, it clashes different sets of morality and shades of gray against each other. It poses important questions like: Do the needs of the many outweigh those of the individual? Do the means always justify the end?  How do we deal with the imperfections of humanity? What does it mean to be alive? And, perhaps most importantly, why is it that birds fly? Instead of just raising these questions, though, the game actually provides multiple answers from different angles.
The game offers you less freedom in terms of progression, however. Berseria is rather linear until around the 30 hour mark, when it opens up a bit and starts presenting some side quests for you to tackle. That being said, the intriguing plot and the excellently written dialog keep you invested so thoroughly that you almost don't want to divert from the main mission. No matter which language option you choose – English or Japanese – both settings offer a great cast of voice actors and well performed lines. The quality of the music meanders between pretty good and mediocre – with only a couple of standout tracks. But when these pieces do play they are especially powerful and add a lot of emotional weight to certain scenes. From an artistic point of view, Tales of Berseria feels like a well thought-out, complete package with a lot of highlights and virtually no low points. Some of the world's unique terminology can be confusing at first, but implicit explanations arise naturally from dialogs, and soon enough you'll get a clear picture of everything important. This age-old conflict between chaos and order is, on all fronts, competently to expertly presented and rides a perfect wave of both predictability and surprise.
However, Berseria stumbles somewhat in terms of certain gameplay elements – especially when it comes to the equipment system. The game borrows from Final Fantasy IX and other RPGs in that every piece of gear comes with a unique skill that characters can learn permanently if they wear it for a certain amount of fights. In the case of Final Fantasy IX, characters learn active and passive abilities with clearly visible effects. But in Berseria, the term “skills” refers to small attribute increases, like enhanced fire damage, that just lack impact. The characters grow stronger at such an incremental rate that no learned skill has any immediately perceivable effect. Changing out your old equipment for new one is important in the long run but never really feels rewarding. That being said, once you're familiar with the menu, going through the motions becomes second nature. Changing gear and the long-term benefits associated with the process may not be a highlight in itself, but it does serve as a nice breather between story parts and combat. What's baffling, on the other hand, is the enhance feature, that let's you upgrade your gear pieces to increase damage or damage reduction among other things. When you're constantly swapping old equipment for newer and better one, especially if it teaches you new skills, there is little incentive to spend materials for upgrades. And indeed the game is easily beatable without enhancing any items – even on higher difficulty settings. To a certain extent, Berseria is an example of disjointed systems that don't seem to have any synergy and feel like an afterthought more than anything. Luckily, they don't present much of a barrier. Learning equipment skills is low maintenance and enhancing can be ignored altogether.
Where the developers clearly did have a well-defined concept, however, is the combat. The real-time action battles are admittedly somewhat button-mashy in nature, but there is a distinct layer of strategy that involves clever resource management. It's important to know when to use a special or super move – so-called break souls techniques and mystic artes – and when to build up resources or switch characters instead. Making the right decisions let's you unload seemingly never-ending combos on your foes; choosing wrong can get you in trouble quickly. Using the right elemental attacks against your enemies is also of some importance, but unless you're playing on the highest two difficulty settings, you can always come back from mistakes without too much effort. Should you want to challenge yourself though, the game offers nice incentives to ramp up the difficulty, such as increased item drop rates. The combat is simple enough to be intuitive and easy to pick up but offers just enough depth not to bore you. Thanks to pre-definable strategy settings, the AI-controlled characters do a good job of not getting themselves killed too quickly, although the game doesn't quite offer as many options as you'd like on that front. Every once and again you'll see a party member acting strangely, but the same can be said of enemies as well.
Tales of Berseria is a long adventure, netting you over 60 hours of playtime even if you only dabble in the side quests. Between cooking, mini games and naval expeditions, there's a lot to keep you busy – if you decide to partake in these activities. Cooking is quite useful, since meals completely restore your party's health and provide a neat little buff for your next battle. Mini games and the automatic, timed expeditions, that you can check in on every 20 to 30 minutes are less essential and can easily be ignored. But they do offer nice rewards. Among the best of them are new outfits and accessories that you start unlocking very early on. I probably spent hours dressing my characters in different styles ranging from totally ridiculous to illegally cool.
The technology behind the Tales series has hardly ever been state of the art. Berseria, too, is limping behind the current generation of consoles and games in terms of graphics. Muddy textures, low shadow resolutions and frequent pop-ins are a constant reminder that Namco Bandai is not dishing out the hugest budget for their long-running RPG series. But despite technological shortcomings, there is a certain charm to the visuals. The graphics may not be impressive in the conventional way, but they are quite pretty from an artistic point of view. There's a lot of color in the different environments, enemies come in all shapes and sizes, spell effects look gorgeous, and the anime-styled characters are surprisingly well animated and expressive. Clearly there's a lot of passion and vision put into the art direction of the game. It's just a joy to look at.
Tales of Berseria is not the best RPG ever made. Some of its gameplay mechanics aren't exactly well designed and feel inconsequential or unrewarding as a result. But the quality of the writing is on a level that few games in the genre ever achieve – whether it be the intriguing and thought-provoking plot or the multi-layered characters. Solid combat and a great artistic vision make this an easy to recommend action RPG.

Are you searching for meaning in life? Tired of pondering the intricacies of the greater universe unfathomable?
"A Kiss For The Petals" or Sono Hanabira is the answer. It is the shining beacon of respite in a world without enough yuri. When you may have troubled yourself as to life's mundane purpose, you smile, knowing that you must trouble yourself no longer, for it is done, and Sono Hanabira is on Steam.
Notes:
This was originally a mobile/iPhone supplementary game in the Sono Hanabira series, and this is clearly an experimental English license. Fans will be supporting this release wildly for further localizations, and for newcomers, it may seem a bit overblown. This is not a long visual novel, nor is it entirely representative of Sono Hanabira as a whole. With that said...
"What's with 'Sono Hanabira?'"
For long-time fans of the series, this is the seventeenth game, and one of two that are 'all-ages' (the other being Hanahira, for those of you interested in continuing your adventure into Sono Hanabira while staying within the 'all-ages space). Sono Hanabira started as a doujin nukige (doujin: amateur work by a small group of individuals; nukige: visual novel where the plot is only around to allow for 'plot') that was very well received for its tone, atmosphere, and high-quality character designs.
"Finally, yuri done right!"

A core cast of couples was developed, and multiple releases furthered the story between each of them. The success was too much to ignore, and after ten doujin releases, the company 'Yurin Yurin' was founded and it became a professional endeavour. "St. Michael's Girl's School - Maidens of Michael" was released as a full length visual novel that connected, expanded, and meaningfully explored the characters in a way that previous entries didn't have room for. A shorter sequel was released, focusing on the new couple Risa and Miya (the ones featured in this game!), as were wholly original ventures (such as ones focusing on a post-high school Nursing School) and even a "New Generations" series re-boot with an entirely new cast, as 'Yurin Yurin' was replaced as developers by 'St. Michael's Girl's Academy' (again, a company founded entirely for this venture).
At this point, fans are dying to play Sono Hanabira in its wholly professional and full length visual novel glory, but, it has far outpaced the fan translators and official English licensing and releases are wanted. So, with everything we've got, fans support Sono Hanabira in its fullest with this game! With enough support, the more lengthy games will be licensed, and the age of yuri can be heralded!

My review on Trove. First off, I just started playing it so I don't know what it used to be or things that have changed. I only know what it is in its current state in Jan 2017.
I started playing it on the xbox one, then my daughter wanted to play and we both started playing on PC. I'm not an MMO expert but have played a handful of them in my 30 years of gaming including a couple free to play MMOs. So my review is on PC after 130 hours of playing. I'm not really fond of pixel type graphics but something about this grabbed me and I'll get to that shortly
Trove has charm, it’s like Minecraft in a way, but has a lot better combat.  The similarities to Minecraft are small though. You can tear up the land with your “laser”, collect blocks, and use blocks to build whatever you want. It goes a little further by allowing you to place multiple blocks at once with one click, though it’s super sensitive. You can build wherever you want, but I haven’t seen anyone build anywhere besides their cornerstone. The cornerstone is a flat block that you can build your house on using blocks you mine or craft. If you find another flat block, you spawn the exact same house you built earlier. The cornerstone is like your own little hub where you can build forges, workbenches, personal chests, and other types of items to help you craft. These all stay in your house once you build them there.  Other than building and farming materials, that’s all there really is in common with Minecraft.
The premise behind the game is running dungeons. And the first thing I noticed on my first dungeon is how small they are. They can be soloed or ran with friends. You can complete dungeons in 10 seconds if you know how. There are numerous types of dungeons but all types are similar. Fly into the dungeon, kill the boss at the end, collect the loot, and leave through the portal. Easy. The game actually has you complete certain amount of dungeons in a time frame to collect items. After the tutorial, you start in the hub world and go through different portals to higher difficulties. As you level up, you can go through higher portals and collect better loot.
Here is what I like and don’t like. There are a good amount of classes, however you have to either craft them or buy them with credits you purchase with real money. You do get a starter class in the beginning for free and you can get a class coin that allows you to unlock a second toon.  I wouldn’t worry about having all the classes in the beginning because you can switch to another class and play them as a trial until level 5. After that, they don’t level anymore. If you like them you can unlock them later. I like that the classes only have 3 skills and a passive. Unlike WoW you can have over 50 or more. Only three skills isn’t bad as there is still depth on using them at certain times. The game is grindy after level 12 or so and you’ll start needing more valuable items to craft better things. There aren’t any quests per say from NPCs but you’ll figure out to just run dungeons or collect certain ore to craft items or sell on the market. There are NPCs that sell stuff, but it feels like it’s more for end game users as I didn’t find any use for some of the items they sell and they’re expensive for starting out with nothing. I tems:  There are hundreds of items that you’ll have no idea what they’re for until later. Mainly used for crafting new items or upgrading current items.
The game can be a lot of fun, but then after you’re done grinding, or gathering the stuff that you need, you’ll just end up logging off until you get a wild hair to play again. This isn’t a bad game at all. I’ve ran into a few bugs but they aren’t game breaking.  Items can be expensive for new players. You can buy stuff with in-game currency (flux) or credits that you pay for with real money.  However, it is possible to never buy a thing with money however it can take you 4 times as long to accumulate. You can even farm enough flux to buy 30 day patron coins that is like having a subscription. Subscription benefits are okay but you don’t need them.  But they do offer increased XP gain and that’s nice as you’ll take hours and hours to level up once.
You will find that after you’ve done 100 dungeons, collected tons of ore, and still haven’t gotten any stronger, that’s when the game feels grindy. You can either pay for items to help boost you up or log off and return to the grind later.  Loot collecting is fun and item levels (that I’ve seen)  on weapons and gear only go to level 10 meaning you have to be level 10 to use them.  After 130 hours I have two toons in the high teens and as of right now the level cap is 30.  You can level your mastery to like 300 or something and get rewards after each level.  Mastery stays the same for all your toons, but the character level starts at 1 each new one you unlock.  Another good thing is that everything you collect is shared for all your toons including your inventory, personal chest, mounts, dragons ect. The only thing that changes is your toon and their weapons. So once you get a high level toon and want to try a new one, all that grinding and stuff you’ve accumulated stays in your inventory and your chest for your new toon to use.  You can trade a lot of items with other players or the “auction house” to earn flux but some items cannot be traded. And you can only buy from the auction house crafting items. No weapons or armor. Everything is simplified but there is still some depth to playing.
After so many hours, I’m barely scratching the surface. There are shadow towers, epic bosses that spawn, and tons of items to collect. Drops are rare and remind me of Diablo 2 with drop rarity. The game is about efficiently looting and farming to get your good item or rare drop.
If you don’t mind the grind, not quest related grinding, but grinding for items you need, then this game is a lot of fun but tapers down after a few hours of gameplay. Others may disagree because they have tons of toons and club houses and all that crap. But I’m speaking to the new player. I don’t even have a club house yet.  This game is recommended to play, it’s simple but yet satisfying. I wouldn’t say this is pay to win, but pay to advance, pay to quit the grinding.

Not all demons must be evil, and not all heroes must be good.
An unforgettable experience. Emotional story, great characters and an aggressive battle system that doesn't get boring. Worth it even at full price.
The English voice acting, visual effects, special moves are all good. The enemies are mostly diverse, although there are some that are similar/reused/recoloured like most RPGs.
The various systems (battle mechanics, equipment upgrading, etc) are all good and there are plenty, but they are all straight forward and easy to understand. Some other games complicate things to the point you end up not caring about them or taking advantage of them. The only system I didn't use much was the ability to switch control of party members during battle, since most of the time I just controlled the main character Velvet. But it's nice that I had the option to play the other characters if I wanted something different.
The characters are each unique in their own right, and grow and develop over the course of the game. Each character is memorable and cool/interesting in their own way, and the conversations between party members help to reveal their thoughts, beliefs and their past. Sometimes you'll laugh as they banter among themselves, and other times you'll feel sad hearing about what they have been through in their life.
If I was to fault anything, I would probably say the music. Although the music did seem to fit the game/scenario, some of it was decent, even a few battle themes were quite good, but in general the music wasn't that memorable.
When the game was first released, there was an issue with the AI of your party members where sometimes they wouldn't fight much and kind of just walk around (apparently the PS4 version didnt have this issue). It wasn't that noticeable if you were busy beating everything up yourself, but this was fixed in an update and they play well now.
It took me around 160 hours to complete while playing on the highest difficulty, including the end game content and optional side quests, although I missed some collectibles which are really just for completion/achievements. Side quests aren't missable, but many of them don't open up until near the end of the game, so you can enjoy the story and worry about them later. That play time does include a lot of level grinding though (due to playing on highest difficulty). On normal without doing the extra stuff, I would estimate 70 hours or less.
Overall the game is a must play for any JRPG fan.

It's been a long while since I have touched a Tales game--last time I did was with Xillia on the PS3, so you could imagine my surprise when this turned out to be handled excellently in terms of both gameplay, and story direction. I can assuredely say it is nothing short of a heartwarming, and beautiful experience.
For starters, I was hardly expecting such a fluid combat-system that actually felt satisfying and made grinding feel like much less of a haslle. The Soul-Break system, which is the system which accomadates sort of 'action-points' for combat, support, etc., is a massive break from the norm of this series. There is something insanely satisfying about successful chainings of combos, and obtaining a mastery in said system after a mere few hours within the game. When parred with a large level cap (200), and acquiring  fairly wide arrange of possibilities for combos/modes of utilzing characters/their equipment, this game becomes intricate, and increasingly intense (presuming you scale the difficulty as you level, as well). The gripes I had with this, and the progression of acquiring 'bonus' features to combat along the way (simply through continuing to trek through areas, fighting sub-bosses in said areas, and progressing story consequently) were minimal. The tutorialization for how it works, is somewhat off-puting and lasts through the introductory-segment of the game (I'd estimate a maximum of 45 minutes, with a few other mini-tutorials for player-characters sprinkled throughout the subsequent formation of the party). Aside from these limitations, it's simple to discern that this is a substantial improvement over previous iterations of Tales, or for many round of the mill RPGs in general. Dare I say, it seems like it would be the least polarizing aspect of this game.
But what I was primarily vested in when the first trailers for this game aired/new information began being relayed out was related to story, and progression of characters. Now Berseria exists as a prequel to Tales of Zestria, which is known for more than a few, how should I say... shortcomings in both departments. Berseria, I am pleased to say after a full-playthrough of everything offered (as far as story-developments which aren't tertiary, or minor go, that is), is a complete inverse of this. The optional 'skits', or dialogues between major or minor characters allow for a substantial amount of details pertaining to the world, and this existing periphreally to main-story cutscenes reinforces much of the plot, main themes, quests, dialogue in/out of battle which accompany it. Additionally: there is variety amongst the company you playthrough the story with; the way each 'handle' in terms of playstyles; none of which necessarily fitting into a singular character-typing, and in how they are assimilated into company with the protagonist (through 'chancing' upon them, arriving at similar trains of thought, etc.), all of which contribute to an excellent 'sum of all parts' for enjoyment of the story and characters.
The upward-slope in budget is also seriously apparent in regards to these two aspects, and my only qualms with both [story and writing] consisted of: certain 'turns of phrase', or dialogue, being mistranslated (meaning, there were instances where certain information would have to be omitted from my understanding of what was being conveyed through lines, or causing puzzlement in terms of how exactly I'm suppose to feel), and some issues with pacing. The former had just few enough instances of this occuring, so that it, truthfully, couldn't be considered a major detracting factor (should not hinder the writing's ability to make you feel things); the latter is mainly due to segments of plot having to, quite rapidly, accelerate/decelerate tension, or create time to understand the motives of the protagonist, Velvet, or the other main party-members. I could name several moments that were somewhat jarring shifts in how quickly/slowly plot progressed, yet cannot say they were crucial proponents to the main-plot at all. There were a plethora of moments I laughed, reflected, or moped all the same, which I suppose is what ultimately counts.
In terms of world, and dungeons, I'd comment that Berseria has a world which is colourful, vivid, and diverse to a great degree. Dungeons have these very same qualities through the secondary half of the game, yet I found myself holding some issues with how empty the starting stages were. I mean, both are plenty spacious, and filled with more than a fair amount of interesting tid-bits about where you journey, goings-on in the Midgand Empire, etc, yet the design for some of the first dungeons you will come across seem bare-bones, samey, even generic after a few reoccurences of designs almost repeating. This is made all the more unfortunate because the later instances feature design-schemes which are far more vivid, or atleast unique to view.
But, I'll retire from this longwinded rant to simply say you're in for a wholesome experience if you're a Tales fan (fair amount of light nods outside of main story to games aside from Zestria), or a newcomer to the series alike. I am not one accustomed to praising Bandai, as I'm sure is true of many, but there may be merit to doing so for the dev-team responsible for this game, after seeing so many aspects of it working, well, splendidly. So far, aside from P5, this is probably my top contender for favourite game that's come out of 2017 as of late--and that's me saying this while Berseria is amidst many other games which have overshadowed it. I truly love this game.

In A Kiss for Petals - Remembering How We Met, what seems at first to be a regular yuri VN in actuality has the two protagonists Risa and Miya present an interesting take on the position of Cartesian Duality, in contrast to the earlier Aristotelian rejection of Forms. This Visual Novel functions as in essence a prequel exploring the backstories of the two primary characters, a juncture where they were unfamiliar with one another. This unaccustomed disposition the two take establishes the analogue to Cartesian Duality, as outlined in the Meditations of Descartes.
In this past instance where the two principal characters are recondite to each other, the comparison is established as a degree of separation is seen between the two. Just as they are separate, two very different characters with Miya the intellect as the mind and Risa the epicurean as the body, so too then are the mind and body, a distinction between the the bodily substance, res extensa and the thinking immaterial yet definite substance, res cogitans.
However, as the two character become closer, there is a dramatic shift to a more Spinozan philosophy as outlined in Ethics. Just as Spinoza follows Descartes, so too is this represented by the growing attraction between the two characters, leading to their relationship. The couple is thus as a single thing, but with differing properties. Countering Descartes, the whole is as such and we can not draw a distinction between in terms of interaction. For Spinoza, there is no thinking substance and no extended substance, only the one substance, represented as the couple.
“We say that they all form one body or individual, which is distinguished from the rest by this union of the bodies.”
-Baruch Spinoza

A Kiss For The Petals franchise, Remembering How We Met is a great chapter for those who are new to the series as it tells the brand new story of Risa and Miya romance while looking back on the history of their time in St. Michael Girl's School. A long look back at Risa and Miya relationship, telling the tale of how they first met and came to be lovers it follows Risa and Miya’s storyline from Sono Hanabira ni Kuchizuke o - Michael no Otome-tachi (correct me if i am wrong)
The story starts off with Risa suddenly feeling nostalgia. It was this very uniform she was wearing on her first day at St. Michael’s. The day she met her future girlfriend Miya.
As Risa starts to look back this will be a story that shows Risa and Miya’s first encounter, where they were initially antagonistic toward each other as both are smart in different ways.
Risa is studious and works hard for her achievements while Miya seeks the freedom to pursue her own interests, bcause of her innate intelligence making class a bore for her, as it all started with Risa just trying to get Miya to come to class...
How did love manage to blossom between them? Find out as they recount the tale in a sweet loving and charming fashion.
- The CGs of this game are very pleasant to look at and the art style is very "charming" with the use of bright colors to depict the mood and environment.
- The music sets the mood for every situation, depicting playfulness, happiness and many more. While dialogue and voice acting are both well done. Ending credit music are pleasing to listen to.
there is one problem which i found is that the "applause" sound does not fit into the visual novel at all in. Eg. The scene where Miya presented her plans for the tea party and it was perfect, the applause at that scene does not fit in at all.
For those who are new to the franchise, this series is a must follow for every fan of yuri. As it focuses on relationships between two girls who fall in love with each other, A Kiss For The Petals stays true to the romance between two women. Though adult scenes are plentiful, this series is charming, and have natural development of relationships as the heroines go on dates, try to steal moments alone to express their love, and bond with each other in a very tender fashion.
To sum up i would recommend this visual novel to anyone who are fans of this genre, Yuri. This visual novel will last 3 - 4 hours.

Great retro game package. Classic Atari arcade games from back in the day as they were... back in the day. Missile Command, Pong, Asteroids, Asteroids Deluxe, Black Widow, Red Baron, Crystal Castles, Centipede, Millipede, Tempest, Gravitar, Lunar Lander, Super Breakout, and more.  You can play the games with the cabinet art or without. Configurable controls for movement and firing button(s) were easy to set.  I had no problem configuring any of the controls to what I felt was comfortable for my style of playing.
Another part of the game includes an emulator for the old Atari 2600 Game console.  There are too many games included in the repository of games to start naming them off but they have everything from Asteroids to Warlords. Well almost everything as I didn't find E.T.. The emulator feels like you are playing those old emulated games on the old Atari 2600. They did a great job bringing those old games back to life for a new era. These are not the old games redone. These are the old games with the OLD graphics from an Atari 2600 (blocky... 8 or 16 bit... retro).
The Atari Vault game package also includes some nostolgia box art, original game manuals from the cartridge games and old arcade cabinet art for each of the games offered. Nice touch for those retro game enthusiasts like myself (especially if you have a Rasberry Pi or Steam Box arcade project going and you're looking for the perfect art for the cabinet or whatever).
The graphics for the games themsleves are EXACTLY the way they were in the old games or at least so close I couldn't tell the difference. I felt like I was standing at a cabinet instead of my PC.
I highly recommend Atari Vault for any gamer who appreciates classic Atari.  Many nicely done classic arcade games in one package from an era when Atari first hit the market and having a pocket of quarters was the way to play video games.
The package would have gotten a full 10 except there were two games not included... "Battlezone" and "Star Wars".  Two cabinet style games that were from the old vector graphic days of Atari and I would have liked to have seen those games included. There was also no E.T. game in the 2600 Emulator. Petty I know... but I find the probability of them doing a DLC package to include the games they missed... very low and they probably should have just included them if they hadn't planned on future DLC. . If they do indeed do a DLC addon package for this... I will revise to a full 10 on my review.

If you hate reading, it's kung-fu GTA with better story missions but less content overall.  Otherwise, keep reading.
GTA with street chases and martial arts.  You don't have to spend hours getting an apartment and car.  Plot is a bit better than standard fare for crime simulator free-roam game.  Voice acting is very good.  Fighting is fun and of course a bit repetitive but deep enough to be satisfying.  Lots of little minigames and whatnot.  Multi-venue Level-based upgrade system with dual-tree progression; one venue is based on finding collectibles, another is on sidequests, and two more are kind of merit based; one increases when you defeat your enemies in more technical ways, the other decreases when you cause damage or kill innocents on missions.  They are not mutually exclusive, and the latter can be increased with side missions.
I haven't played a GTA since Vice City and by comparison this was a lot more focused.  On the other hand, there was less variety (no golf carts, for instance.)  This is a blessing in disguise; although many of the different systems are not what I'd call incredibly polished, they're also quite servicible which is not the case when you have, say, a helicopter minigame.
The world is open and big but there's not a heck of a lot to do in it until the game decides to give you side missions, in which case it's a bit of a hike.  It's trying to be faithful to Hong Kong, which makes it just about the right size, but it's still a smidge big for the content.  There's a save/load system, but props to the developers for having it be nearly completely redundant due to the constant auto-saving.
Ending is pretty bad, story-wise.  Things that were already really ridiculous are taken to a level of absurdity that can only be called "cartoonish".  It's a fun end to the romp, though.  I thought it was going to stuff morality down our throat or give us a really contrived choice-based ending but it settled on just a semi-contrived one.
In summary: This is a very good game that only has committed the sin of being a GTA-clone in the era of GTA-clones.  It has enough to differentiate it, but if you hate GTA you'll hate this.  If you liked or were indifferent to GTA, maybe give this a shot.

Bastion is one of the most original titles I've played in quite some time. From the charming graphics to the smooth vibes of the narrator perfectly blended with a magical soundtrack, and the 10-12 hours of action-packed exploration and combat, Bastion is like kicking back with your favorite interactive storybook.

I really, REALLY liked it. The atmosphere and soundtrack were top-notch and the story, at first, seemed really cliche, but towards the end got really cool, pulling out a completely unexpected ending that, get this, actually makes sense! It's easy to tell the makers of this game wanted to do something completely fresh and original and they succeeded brilliantly. It, at first, gives off a nostalgic, gentle feel that quickly turns to uneasiness and discomfort, then to a dark tenseness that envelops the setting. The color scheme remains the same throughout, but as atmosphere builds and soundtracks darken, everything looks more oppressive, dark, and tense. Very well done. This is one of the few games that really touches me emotionally: seeing something beautiful and ideal wither and die before your eyes is one of the hardest things to see for me and people who find that emotionally depressing or at least touching will very much appreciate this. Another thing I noticed: items you look at in the beginning take on a completely different meaning in the end, which is something I really enjoyed. Very very very good. Recommended completely to anyone who appreciates a good story, a good atmosphere, or a hella good soundtrack, even if it isn't the longest thing in the world...

Where to begin?
This game is probably the best early access game on the market. Not to mention, it's really fun.
PROS:
- Pirates
- Cannons
- Putting holes in ships with said cannons
- Server-based lobbies
- Boarding enemy ships, slaying the entire crew, stealing their supplies, and taking their tickets
- CCCCHHHHHHAAAAAAARRRRRRRRRRGGGGGEEEE!!!!
- Physics of cannonballs are realistic. They have trajectory.
- Requires teamwork. There's no such thing as being a lone wolf
- The games doesn't take itself seriously. When you're a Brit and heal yourself, you whip out a teacup (with tea) and a saucer. When you take a sip, you stick out your pinky. Either that, or you take a long pull from a bottle of rum.
- The guns take forever to reload. So when you grapple an enemy ship there's a huge exchange of murder while everyone unloads their single-fire weapons into each other, then everyone goes ham using weapons that range from cutlasses to broken rum bottles.
- The sailor banter is ridiculous
- There's a bleed mechanic
- Grapeshot + spawnroom = mass homicide
- Grappling enemy ships is a last-man-standing fight. When the first person dies it starts a 2 minute timer before everyone respawns. So things can go really well for you, or really bad for you
- You have to make shots count, so you can't fire willy-nilly. You're using muskets, flintlock pistols, and cannons; you only get one shot before you have to spend some time reloading
- When you get shot in the head the screen goes black, all game audio is cut, and some white text appears in the center of the screen informing you that you have, in fact, been domed.
- You can get headshots with cannons
- Ragdoll physics are great. You'll either turn into a pile of red jelly, or be sent into orbit when hit with a cannonball
- Weather effects can certainly make fights a lot more interesting. They range from clear, to fog, to snow, to thunderstorms, and rain. For example, during a thunderstorm you won't be able to clearly see enemy ships until they're almost on top of you, which makes for very interesting panic volleys. During low visibility weather the lanterns on ships will be on so that no one is truly invisible due to weather. There's also night and day
- You can mutiny the captain (basically kick him out of the captain position)
- Galleons. With lots of guns
- Your ship can catch fire, and panic ensues (put it out with buckets of water found on deck)
- It's $20 for lots of fun and free updates
- Repairing sails with hammers
- There's only a few maps, which is essentially open ocean to open ocean with rocks and sandbars
- The maps are huge
- Lots of different approaches to combat. Wanna grapple ships and sink them? Maybe snipe ships with your cannons at their extreme range? Or maybe ram the hell out of all the enemy ships you see? Or play it loose and dangerous with close-quarters ship battles. Lots of different options
CONS:
- There's no party system, so you and your buddies will have to spam-click the side you want to be on and hope that you can get in together. If you don't get on the same team, then it's fun anyway to fill your friends up with lead.
- Graphics aren't super awesome, but it's still pretty anyway
- Sometimes you'll get crew memebers without mics. That's a major pain, especially if it's the captain.
- You have to commit suicide if you're ship sinks (resulting in a counted death, obviously) if you're still alive when it sinks. But I suppose it's possible to quickly swim onto a nearby friendly ship, or if the enemy ship is low in the water you can jump on and take as many of those scallywags with you to Davy Jones' Locker. Either way, it would be nice to have a spawn mechanic that automatically places you back on your ship if no ships are nearby
- Sometimes the lobbies can be laggy, but that's more on the side of the owner of the server. Usually it straightens itself out in a few minutes when everyone is done connecting and whatnot
- Sometimes I feel like the maps are a little too big, but the more I play the more I realize it's more for preparation and to reduce spawn sinking. You travel a large distance pretty fast anyway
- There's this weird zooming lense effect that happens when you're not looking directly at a target with swivel guns that makes the target look closer than it is when you're not looking directly at it. Minor bug though
If you're thinking about getting it, just do it. You'll be happy, the pirates will be happy, and the rumbling of cannons will continue.

If you've ever played one of those hidden role party games like warewolf, mafia, coup, the resistance, etc, then you understand what this game is all about. Admitedly, you do loose some of the fun of being in a live room with your friends and seeing the facial expressions and whatnot but do not let that stop you from trying this one out. What it looses from not being an in-person party game, it gains in other aspects that cannot be pulled off in person.
Unlike warewolf, you are not totally out if you get killed. For instance, one role can resurrect a dead person, another role can talk to the dead people. Their is even a spy that can see any wispers as well as the mafia conversations at night. You can play the role of a sheriff or investigator to gather intel on who might be a bad guy. You could be a jailor and interrogate someone each night. You could even play a neutral role such as a jester who wins if they convince everyone to try and lynch them or an arsonist who's goal is to douse everyone in gasoline and burn them all.
The game does have a bit of a learning curve to learn the ins and outs of each role but the wiki page helps with that quite a bit and is a highly recommended resource. Their is a fairly active community so getting loaded into matches is never very difficult and aside from the occasional offensive player names and people who drop out of the game, most players tend to play the game as intended. Bluffing does play a key role in this and as you get better at the game you will learn what to look for and how to act to avoid giving up too much information.
If deduction and bluffing are your thing, definitely check this game out. It's worth your time and you'll find it one of those "just one more round" type of games. A load of fun to be had.

I wish there were a neutral recommendation option for this game.
The good- this game has a unique take on the turn based combat formula. Permadeath for any character makes you care about your teammates health more than other games. The fact that you can almost never heal adequately in this game (generally 10-20% max most of the time) creates this odd endurance dynamic that I've not seen in a game like this before. And the game is lengthy, you'll get a great amount of play time out of it, repetitious as it may be.
The bad- this game is comprised of two things, combat and a menu. AND THE MENU IS ATROCIOUS. And, it's even worse with a controller, to the point where it's non-functional at times with things like your cursor disappearing, and being unable to drag an upgrade item onto a weapon to upgrade it, instead of clicking on person to edit their job, or anything on the right page, if you want to keep the list of people up for easy navigation, you have to back out, switch pages, then select the items you want to choose from... It's a mess. The controller support should really just give you control of the mouse with the analog stick, it would have been much better. The combat is repetitive, though the bosses break it up. You get stuck going to specific areas on missions, and those areas only give you certain types of resources, so you can end up never getting materials needed to make items. When your main character dies and you have to restart, the alternate classes you unlock with achievements don't actually give you an edge, they just rearrange stats. Guns and gear don't make enough of an impact to justify how many materials they require to make. When you go on a date with a character, you lose the ability to equip things to them, because they leave camp at the start of the day, so suddenly you're doing a two person mission with someone who has no equipment, despite having rifles available at the camp. The writing is laughably juvenile, just forcing its way through every zombie cliche. And the more people you have in your home base, the more micro-manage-you have to get every day, exchanging equipment between characters, choosing their jobs (which again, with a controller is an exercise in tedium...). To the point where, I'm not even going to beat this game. I played a good amount of time in it, but 33 days in, it's just no fun anymore since I've seen all the enemies the game has to offer, and the menu system is just a chore at this point...
...All this and still a positive review?
It's dumb fun. It's functional. And there's plenty of content. Everything works, even if just awkward. And if nothing else, it's worth experiencing for the "no healing items, plus permadeath" dynamic. For the amount of time they put into it, and the amount of effort the developers have put into it, it's worth $15... I just won't be coming back to it  (Already played 20+ hours) unless they streamline the menu system/assigning jobs system.

Half-Life is a first person shooter gamer developed by Valve Software on the GoldSrc engine. It follows the exploits of physicist Gordon Freeman after he accidentally jumpstarts the end of the world because he was late to work. Sort of.
So Half-Life is another one of those games that people hold on their shoulders and parade as a masterpiece. Like Psychonauts, or the following Half-Lives, people call it out for its great writing and clever gameplay and the like. For Psychonauts, I really did agree with the praise, it's a genuinely good game. For Half-Life 2, I thought the hype was slightly heavy handed, but I still really like it. Half-Life 1 is different.
The thing about Half-Life is, there are certain things that really totally gell with me and certain things that don't. I like how it feels like a B-Movie crossbred with Lovecraftian Eldritch style horror. I like how they took a lot of risks with what they could get away with in a "Shooter" game, like puzzles and prolonged "Nah who even needs guns" scenes. I like that guy who's all like "Why oh why do we have to wear these RIDICULOUS ties?!" he's fantastic. I like to imagine the scientist who teleports you in the lambda complex, up on the balcony, is the disgruntled tie guy. I picture him fighting tooth and nail just like Gordon did to get to the Lambda complex after the cascade.
I actually like almost all of the gameplay decisions. I think the platforming bits are overly critiqued, I quite liked them. I also thought the Xen portion was absolutely lovely, it's a great and stressful culmination of the previous 10-ish hours of gameplay, (at least that's how long it took me to beat it but I was taking my time and this was a first time playthrough). I also liked the final boss, I thought he was gleefully terrifying looking and I like how the final setpeice takes some level of exploration and a degree of critical thinking for your surroundings.
Wasn't a big fan of those floaty brain enemies that shooting homing balls of yellow glowing dust, what were they supposed to be doing? Also thought the pacing, which is commonly revered as incredibly solid, could have used some work. Often times fights and set-peices lost their "UMPH" idk what it is. A guy shows up and then I shoot him and then he dies and then I move on. The canned running and dying animations don't help with this weird sensation either. It sort of feels like Gordon is kinda drifting around in a hazy dreamlike state of zappy noises and radiochatter overset by staticy low quality 90's game noises. That being said the weapons are punchy and the AI is challenging...it's good action, for sure, but something about it rubs me the wrong way.
Really great level design though. It really flows nicely and the puzzles are non-intrusive and make logical sense. They don't feel like puzzles half the time and that's appreciated. Something feels a lot grittier about the "one step at a time" storytelling here too, moreso than it even would in the sequels which often get lost in their more fantastic sensibilities. I also loved the tone of the story, B-Movie horror underset by lovecraftian demons from another dimension. Brilliant. I love how the scientists have the ramble scene at the end and theres a mid-point climax with the portal and they explain the nonsense science to you all straightlaced and stiffly, the game doesn't drop the b-movie edge even at the end. It's great. I love it.
In the end, Half-Life is a surprisingly good game. If you're like me and can easily look past shoddy graphic-capabilities and appreciate great graphics utilization than you'll probably agree that the game has actually aged pretty well, too. It's also dirt cheap so there's no excuse not to get it.

Eh. It's okay.
Okay, being serious now, I really really really liked this game, as you can see by my play time. I want to preface this by saying I didn't hate Zestiria, but I do know that Zestiria had a lot of problems such as the plot, characters, gameplay (armatization), and world. Berseria fixes a lot of these.
The story is very engaging and I love the main party. It feels good to play and follow characters that are not a bunch of goody two-shoes or at least will get their hands dirty. All of the party members have their own motivations for being there and you are reminded time and again that these people are working together only because their interests align. If you only like to play games where the cast is altruistic then I don't reccomend you get this. Some people complain that one or two party members are not well integrated to the main plot very well and are pretty much along for the ride, though I don't mind this since I like their personalities.
The story definitely has direction, unlike Zestiria which I felt what I was doing was pretty aimless a lot of the time. Tales games usually don't have the best plots anyway, though Berseria's is definitely up there. If I remember correctly only one thing isn't really explained, but they do lampshade it. While Berseria's story is good, it is very linear. A lot of the time you can't go back to areas you have been until certain points in the game and you don't get complete freedom until right before the very last dungeon.
Armatization is no more so enemy stats aren't balanced around that anymore. You don't have to keep two members in the party and the camera is greatly improved from Zestiria. Berseria gives you more freedom with combos by allowing you to customize what move goes in what order which really helps with getting weakness combos (hitting all of the enemy's weaknesses). The only issue I have with this is that you usually change your button mappings when you enter a new area to fight the new enemy types so you change them pretty often. It'd be nice if you could be able to save some favorite settings but that's just me. If you don't want to change your combos all the time, you can just map a certain element to a string of buttons, though that can get a little boring. Also, the beginning of the game feels lackluster because you do not have as many artes. As you get more as you level up it starts to feel better. Also, in my opinion, Rokurou is really bad in the beginning of the game, so you may want to wait if you're interested in playing him.
In game dungeons are still like Zestiria's which is really bad. They're all linear, disintersing, and the most complex puzzle is just pressing a button and lighting a torch.
I enjoyed Tales of Berseria a lot. If you're looking for a good story with good characters then I really reccomend you get this. If you're hesitant after playing Zestiria, they've fixed a lot of the issues, though one or two things can still be felt. Overall I give it an 8/10.
