Wow - I was skeptical at first but this game was so damn good. It's basically a murder/mystery RPG with a great story told in an inventive way that let's you gradually piece together the plot in layers as well as from various perspectives. The way it's implemented embellishes an already well-written story and keeps your attention the entire time.
You wake up as a ghost without any knowledge of yourself, and need to figure out who you are as well as who on the cruise ship murdered you. You work towards these goals by possessing the suspects (crew and passengers) to take control over their bodies and investigate them. While possessing someone, you open up new dialog possibilties with other characters - and also gain a special skill that's unique to each character such as being able to peek in door keyholes or read people's emotional state. You can only possess people after learning personal/private details about them so you need to find ways to accomplish that during the investigation since it's critical to progressing the story. There's also two different levels of possession which makes things even more interesting by adding another dimension to the concept. Between the dialog choices from all possessed suspects' story threads and special skills, you come to understand/experience the plot in additive layers of detail from different perspectives. I really enjoyed playing multiple storylines and watching how they weave together while collectively manipulating the suspects through  forced interaction with possession. It comes together seamlessly as such a unique experience.
I can't believe this game is only $5. I played through it in about 7 hours or so and there's still a few more endings to see. I really enjoyed the graphics and the music was awesome too. Overall the entire game felt well polished in every way. The only complaints that I had, which didn't bother me at all really, are: a) can only have one save file which can be annoying with multiple endings, and b) collision detection between characters at times was a bit sticky.

The third game in the 12 Labours of Hercules series still doesn’t bother telling a story, and sadly it also forgot to try and improve game play. It’s a good time management game, but doesn’t live up to the predecessors.
12 Labours of Hercules III: Girl Power is slowly falling into a common problem with time management series: it is running out of ideas.
The core mechanics are naturally untouched: you command a few servants who gather three types of resources used to clear the large amount of obstacles in your way. The mythological helpers return, but their role is much more limited; each stage is almost purely servant management.
This wouldn’t be that bad if the level layout would provide adequate challenge, but they are a little too gimmicky and uninspired. Game play is also slowed down by limiting the available servants on most levels to 2-3, which puts the difficulty somewhere between the first two games. Except for the bonus stages. Those are time management hell incarnate.
The series was never really big on story, and that didn't change: this time Hercules gets kidnapped and his wife Megara is on the rescue. This means no more Herc-only obstacles; they are replaced by food bushes only Megara can activate, further reducing the variety in level mechanics.
Girl Power is still a fun game, but it is showing that the series is getting tired at this point and needs new ideas.

I generally like to explain something about the game so: Wall of text incoming!
JRPGs.
Half the time they are so weird u wonder why ppl play them, but the other half they are as awesome as Tales of Berseria.
Vengeance, Emotion versus Reason, Birds and apples.
Those are the themes of Berseria, and while Revenge stories are as common as love stories the devs have found a way to make sure Berseria does't fall in the standard cliche plotholes while also keeping u pining to find out how it will end all the time.
The story follows Velvet Crowe, a tomboyish girl who cares alot about her little brother Laphicet(who came up with this name??) and her brother in law Arthur, an exorcist who saved both of them when the whole town turned into demons years ago but cost the life of Velvet's sister.
Their uneventful life comes to an end when Arthur decides to  sacrifice Laphi in some twisted attempt to save the world from Daemons while Velvet only tries to save her brother and gets thrown in as well only to come back as a Therion, a demon-eating demon who only wants 1 thing, to kill arthur for what he did.
This is where the game really begins, and it does not dissapoint.
3 years after the Laphi's death Velvets been thrown into prison to feed on demons untill someone gives her a chance to escape the prison together with some others while finding out that Arthur(now Arthorius) has been declared the world's savior and has an army of exorcists at his beck and call now...
The game's Combat system needs some getting used to but once u have it in the fingers u can make it as easy or complicated as u want by building your own combo's for each character.
The game also features as Switch blast system that allows u to explosively switch in a character that u had put on standby, wich reminded me alot of the Mortal combat games.
The game has alot of nice area's with alot of different settings, from snowy tundra's to tropical seas, u will be giong all over Midgard in your quest for revenge.
Only downside of them is that the dungeons look very bland and that any puzzles in them are so simple its almost an insult to call them that...
The outside area's look great though with lots of plantlife and nice lighting effects to make it nice to walk trough.
Towns on the other hand look rather simple(a few exeptions nonwithstanding) with most of the game's NPC's having the same faces making it feel like u are talking with the same persons most of the time....
It also does't help that for much of the story or sidequests u will be revisiting almost every location in the game more then a few times.
But the main story and the characters more then make up for any faults the game has, the story is long and has more then a few plot twists in it but what really makes it fun to watch are how its all told,either trough cutscenes,full anime parts or trough "skits" moving comic-like scenes where the characters debate about their adventures,with alot of comedy spread through it as well and also showing the really great character growth they all are giong trough.
Many of these skits are optional, but i recommend u watch them all :)
I think what made me really like this game is the fact that there are no heroes in the game, Velvet is willing to kill anyone who stands in her way, and does't care if she has to destroy a town or two along the way to get it, or if its a dragon or a god she has to kill..
Thankfully she lightens a little up halfway trough but still, this is anything but a standard story thanks to the weird set of characters.
wich are Velvet, the vengefull bro-con sister, Rokerou, a cheerfull samurai demon, Magilou, selfproclaimed witch and the weirdest character u have ever seen, Laphicet the 2nd, a Malak Velvet named after her brother who's trying to find his place in the world after Velvet dragged him with her.Eizen, a malak Pirate cursed with eternal bad luck and Elaneor, a exorcist who gets forced to travel with the group and seems intent to do the right thing, even if she has a hard time figuring out what that is...
There are alot of nods to other Tales games(mainly Zestiria since this is that game's prequel) but even if u don't know one of those(like me) u will enjoy yourself immensely with it, even more so since the game has a game+ mode that lets u replay it with almost everything u unlocked in your 1st playtrough unlocked from the start, wich is a nice thing couse many of the optional bosses u can kill(code red monsters) unlock parts of the game, like new difficulties or allow skills to trigger more if u play on a certain difficulty, wich is something u can recommend since it makes combat much more exiting.
for example, i tried intermediate diff and suddenly the fights were alot tougher and more tactical but i also got more loot, this has to do with the fact that u get graded for each battle, the longer u do combo's and the faster enemies go down the more xp and loot u get,something that becomes critical in the later stages of the game.
As for scores, i give it this:
story 11/10. Been a long time a game grabbed me like this one did!
graphics:8/10. its nice but u can see its a port and thats a shame.
combat 9/10. great with alot of depth altrough it can become dull if done to much.
sidecontent 10/10. alot of mini games and costumes to keep everything from getting to onesided and gives u a reason to unlock it all!
The game has DLC content but this is just cosmetic stuff to dress them differently, i would personally not buy it since the game already has plenty of stuff u can unlock if u want to see them in something else just by playing the game, from swimsuits to alternate costumes to teddybear stuff :)
Anyway, just go play this game, u won't be dissapointed!

This is an interesting turn-based combat game in a typical zombie environment.
It looks very simplistic and repetitive —and it is indeed—, but it also provides some satisfaction while you progress.
It also has some "roguelike" elements in the way that there are random missions and loot, and even the survivors you find are not always the same and in the same order in each game.
It also features perma-death for your buddy characters and for you. However you can receive medals while completing achievements and you can use those ones when restarting the game to make your character a little bit more powerful with each death.
The game also comes with 3 different difficulty levels. Some menus are a little bit clunky, but nothing game breaking if you got a bit of patience.
The game is divided in 2 sections:
*First you have to manage your campment wasting the resources you have, assign tasks to your survivors (some have to hunt for food, others guard to protect the campment from hostility during the night, others craft new items and ammo, others make healing items, etc). The good part is you can specialize each survivor to have a different rol (you can make one good in melee and hunting, another one good for make medicine items and using pistols, etc). You will need food for every character and some materials too, so you will have to plan ahead a bit. You will also read some lines about the future missions and different events that can happen involving your survivors.
You will then also assign up to 3 of them to the daily missions. In this section you can also improve the skills and stats of your survivors if they leveled up before, gear them up and thats it. You select one of your missions and go for it.
*In the daily mission you will go outside with your chosen characters and fight zombies and punks in a —sometimes annoying— sucession of combats. Between each of them, there is a possibility for a random event in which some of your main skills will be test it (with a random roll) and you can get food, items, ammo, or some other resources, or you can be attacked too or damaged if you fail the roll. You will receive some exp and prizes if you finish your quests too.
When back at the camp, you will see what happen there, and a new day will start.
Ah, and there are a few different endings, depending on what you are able to do.
And pretty much that's it, it's a game that is not for everyone but I find the mix very enjoyable and immersive. It's not a masterpiece but if you like these kind of games you should give it a try.

.

Personal Rating: Well structured zombie surviving simulator.
Classic Rating: ★★★★☆
Dead Age is a surviving simulator with many of the features you can find in other same-genre games, like "Zafehouse: Diares" or "Dead in Bermuda".
The base concept is to survive until a given goal is reached. You do that with the help of other survivors and you must manage your relationship with them.
There are different daily tasks to accomplish, alone or with any of the other people in camp: either you explore to find resources (food, ammo, materials, clothes, etc) or you stay in camp and craft items, stay on guard, go hunting for food. You'll also get timed missions alongside your daily routine: those are assigned to you by other party members.
You'll have to fight zombies, punks, beasts and scavengers too. The combat mechanics are quite easy if you're into TBS games, but ammo is scarce and there are also waves/hordes of zombies to deal with. Game's not a walk in the park, but it all gets easier from the second playthrough and the next ones: in fact you get to upgrade your skills every time you begin a new game, with previously earned medals. Last but not least, Dead Age has a nice RPG element added to the mix: every time you fight enemies and complete quests, you get XP. When you and other characters level up, they can use earned point to upgrade combat and/or job skills.
I liked this game quite a lot, only had one issue:
I'm not sure why graphical requirements are so high. There's only the battle arena in 3D with some visual effects and yet the framerate gets very low. My HW is old but I'm running games at 1080p, 30 FPS (e.g. TF2) and I don't get why 2 silly animations should bring down my GPU so easily; you know, I'm running this at minimum details, 720p... Don't think I'm asking too much.
So, if you like this game's genre, you should probably play or "get and play" Dead Age. It's been bundled, you could maybe trade for it, if 15€ are too much... they honestly are in my opinion; it was gifted to me by a friend.

Oh, boy where to start with this one? I guess I should clear some things up first.  Now I know a lot of people have valid complaints about these games and Tall Tales themselves. Some of the vaild complaints I just. For one since I don't play a lot of games when they first come out, the whole eposiodic nature of there series doesn't affect me as much. Since by the time I pick up the first one in one of the series the second and even sometimes the third one is already out. Second since I don't play the games when they first come out I have the luxary of waiting for a discount. So the price complaint doesn't affect me as much either. Finally I know the choices aren't as impactful when you go back and play the game a second time, or even some cases the first time. The game was able to suck me in an make me care about the characters so I was able to push that out of my mind. Okay now on to the game itself.
The Walking Dead is a point and click adventure game. This time instead of using puzzles to advance the story. You make choices and depending on what you choose. These choices determine wethere or not someone dies, until it doesn't. See this is the most fustrating part of this game for. The game spent so much time getting me invested in the character and the world. Through the pastel but gritty look of the character and the enviorments, the diagloue tree, and the particular situations the game puts you into. Yet it fails to deliver on true choice.  The weird thing is I'm not made, just disappointed. This game had so much promise and squarned it. Through I guess that can't be to surprising we've seen bigger games with bigger budgets fall into the same trap. The only games I know of, and I know that hit the head with this are Witcher 2 and 3. I know there are probably otheres, but those are the only ones that come to mind. I do recommend this game, just keep your expections low and your mind open, even if the game doesn't.

This is a seemingly unpopulair oppinion, other reviews considered, but if you are considering buying this, I recommend you read this to see if you still feel like it afterwards - if so, then you should buy it.
TLDR: The 'game' is more like a movie; your choices doesn't matter; Not much 'gaming' is involved.
If you can get all episodes for under 5€ combined (and you're a fan of Walking Dead) then consider it. Other than that, I wouldn't recommend this.
Full:
While it is a fairly entertaining story, it really doesn't deliver what it promises.
I was quite far into the game when I decided to make a different choice, to see if it would change anything. It didn't.
I wondered if it was just in this specific scenario, or in general, so I changed all my decisions to see the difference.
Nothing was different. Your choices doesn't matter at all, they merely change a bit of the dialogue.
What they state in
"A tailored game experience – Live with the profound and lasting consequences of the decisions that you make in each episode. Your actions and choices will affect how your story plays out across the entire series."
is so close to bending the truth, that I would call it lying. Your dialogue change, but the story does not.
I have avoided "Telltale" games ever since.
So if you still want to explore the story, being aware that your actions doesn't have direct impact; that not much is required from you and; you'll be watching a story more than playing a game, then you should buy this (Though I strongly recommend getting it on sale) :-)
- Otherwise, don't waste your money.
Thanks for reading, hope it was worth your while :-)

100 games, but they are mostly ones we have seen before in other collections.
The presentatoon is slick and pleasing with 3D rendered boxes and cabinets looking sharper tha n ever before.
The online multi-player is what wil lset this title apart from any previous ones.  Dozens of the game can be played online, and it really breathes new life into old classics.  Games like Combat! Outlaw, Surround,  Bowling, Basketball, and even 3D Tic Tac Toe feel new and vibrant when playing against online foes.  I have not enjoyed these games this much in 30 years.
There are few bugs though.  Some games offer multiplayer whre there is no multi-player to be had (i.e. Basic Math). Also, games exit out abruptly and don't let you see the final score.  This is espcially apparent in mutli-player games where there is no option to rematch or replay, and the game ends before you can even see who won.  However, even with this issue,s it's a great package and shows a lot of promise if Atari can keep it going.
For an update/DLC/version 2.0 I'd suggest adding any Lynx games Atari has the rights for, as the Comlynx games would play well here.  Also, any classic 8-bit Computer games would be nice, including Star Raiders, Caverns Of Mars, etc. Ditto for 5200 and 7800 games.    Also, 2-player cpin-ops like X's and o's Atari football would be awesome to play online.

Why Am I Dead At Sea is a "background discovery" game as I'm calling it in this review, the game's premise is that you're on a boat, having a cruise, but, there's a catch, you've been murdered.
You play as a wisp, who can talk to this kid name Paulo, and you can possess many characters, with varying secrets, backstories, and charicterastics, varying your playthrough. You use this mechanic to find out who murdered you, how, and why. This mechanic is handled very well, actually, as like this : say, you possess Person (A), and talk to Person (B), about something like what they ate for dinner, and then possessed Person (B), and talked to Person (A) about what they had for dinner, you would know, because you previously communicated before, but, If you then leave Person (B)'s body, and possess Person (C)'s body, and talk to Person (A), about what they had for dinner, you would not know, unless you found out, because you learnt that in Person (A)'s/Person (B)'s body, meaning you would have to find it out again, if you have the option to.
The mystery solving is very intriguing and you have continious questing for "Who did it?" and your bond with characters build up, and up, you could be controlling your murderer, or not, who knows? who, if anyone, told them to do it?
The puzzle solving is very good, but annoying at times, and you may have to check a walkthrough at some times, but it is inevitably pleasing when you complete a hard to beat puzzle.
Great game for a cheap price, many endings to change things up a little.

A good departure from the low effort Tales games of recent years. Yes, Xilla 1, Xilla 2, and Zestiria were terrible- cookie cutter characters in a heroic save the world because you're good guys plots are boring. Berseria takes notes from Vesperia's story in that it actually has one. The characters act in accordance with their desires, not just "save the world because you're the main characters" sort of nonsense. It's a good change of pace. (Side note, Berseria is connected to Zestiria story wise, but in the same way that Zelda games are connected lore wise- yes, if you know the underlying story you get some interesting insights, but Zestiria is truly a terrible Tales game and there's no reason to play that before Berseria or vice versa)
The combat is enjoyable and fast paced, although can bog down if you burn through your souls and can't recover any. The characters are varied and enjoyable, but the AI is still rock stupid; don't expect any backlining from the AI if you decide to main a caster, they are no help. There's no rock-paper-scissor nonsense like there was in Zestiria, there's no attack chaining slowing combat like in Xillia, it's just pure action.
Overall, the game is pretty good. If you're a fan of Tales games, you'll find this one in your top five, if not top three. If you're a JRPG fan, there are certainly waifus to be had here. If you just enjoy seeing the world burn, well, have I got news for you... It's a good game and worth your time if just to see where the story will go.

Disappointing execution of some classic games.  The biggest issue is, sigh, as always, controls for the trackball and rotary dial games like Tempest, Warlords, Centipede, etc.  It's simple, right?  Map the mouse to act as a trackball or dial?  It shouldn't be that hard.  It ISN'T that hard, seeing as how many other pieces of software manage to do this just fine.  But not Atari Vault.  Either the mouse can't be set to be sensitive enough to make the game playable (even at the highest sensitivity setting) or it just flat-out doesn't work.
That said, the joystick games work just fine, either mapped to a keyboard or with a variety of gamepads.  Even there, though, you cannot turn v-sync on and so most games exerpience "tearing".  Just really lazy execution here.  The in-menu extras like manuals and PR documents are cool, but are scanned in low-res and sometimes aren't even legible.  The overall presentation is slick enough, but there wasn't enough attention paid to detail and the result is that this product feels slapped together as just another lazy appeal to nostalgia.
When will game companies give us an alternative to legally questionable means of playing these classic games?  And I don't mean packages thrown together with a few games (or even 100, which is still a fraction of the number of games available for the Atari 2600 alone), but a truly viable commercial option for playing classic games?  If you were hoping Atari Vault would be the first one, no dice.  Save your $20 and stick with alternative options - you know what they are.

I did not expect that.
This might be one of the best indie games I have ever played.
In this game, you are a ghost trying to piece together your own murder case.
You do so by taking over the passengers and talking to each other.
Getting a whim of their personalities allows you to follow them around (you control their movement, but you can't relay information that you know through them).
After getting to know them intimately, you can finally possess them and speak through their mouths, relaying that information that you've pieced together through other characters and exploring the ship.
This game throws a lot of twists into the story. Some bigger, some smaller.
Some fairly predictable.
It keeps you interested throughout. It's a game that you can't really put down until you finish it.
Something that I really enjoyed was the Mindreading mechanic.
It doesn't really advance the plot (which is sad, cause that would've been kinda cool), but god is it aesthetic.
The cat one is probably my favourite.
This game features multiple endings based on the evidence that you collect throughout your journey.
I recommend not looking at guides on how to get them until you finished the game once (don't worry, you can't really miss evidence until the very end. If you save, you can collect the rest of it before entering the finale).
Sometimes it can get kind of frustrating, in which case, look at a guide or keep trying.
The soundtrack is very memorable since its mostly tied to the characters. This gives every track a personal feel to it and it also helps giving life to the characters themselves. The melodies reflect their personalities.
The graphics have a very earthbound feel to them. They're fantastic for a pixel-art game.
The longer you play, the more do you get a feel for the ship, It's rooms, the character's usual hideouts.
One gripe I have with this game is that every character has his/her own special ability.
They really do range from kinda-, no - sorta-, nah, maybe important? to completely useless.
For example, one character's ability is to see what other people have in their pockets.
Yeah. It's never used.
It's kinda sad actually. It could've been used for some cool evidence collecting.
Like, what if you look into someone's pocket and you find the protagonist's handkerchief in there?
Then you could point it out and they'd get all nervous, which could then later be used as evidence.
That's just an example. Not sure how you make the "take pills which make you run faster but also muddle up the screen" ability useful in collecting evidence. It just feels like a tacked on feature, which is sad. It could've been a pretty cool mechanic to be honest.
I've encountered one bug where Donnovan wouldn't meet me in his room and I'd be locked out. If that happens to you, just talk to him again and wait until he goes back to his room.
Now I'll get into spoilers, DON'T GO PAST HERE IF YOU HAVEN'T FINISHED THE GAME.
THE GAME IS FAIRLY CHEAP AND QUITE AN AMAZING JOURNEY.

After the release of Quake in 1996, Valve decided to heavily modify the Quake engine, in 1998, to create, the title we all love today, known as Half-Life. Of course for an older game, the GoldSource engine isn't all that great compared to games we see today bult on Unity, Unreal Engine, Source, ect. However for a game that's nearly 20 years old, the engine suprisingly still works well enough for a good gameplay expirence.
In Half-Life you take the role of the scientist, MIT granduate, and hero known as Gordon Freeman. One thing made Half-Life what it is today, is the fact that the games protagonist, Gordon Freeman, never said a word, even when being spoken too by other characters. Because of this the player would expect to not truley feel like a hero with a voice. However this is completly wrong. In Half-Life you are the voice of Gordon Freeman. You still feel likes and dislikes towards certains characters and the more the player continues into the game, the more the player will find himself getting attached to the main character. However, the other character's in the game, or at least the half that can speak, don't show much of any emotion besides fear and discomfort. Realisticlly speaking this would be understandable with the current situation the character's are expirencing, how there's no character that want's to fight to be free, while another just want's to hide and cry in the corner.
Gameplay wise, the mechanics are great, controls are simple, and level design is well thought out. Due to this game being released nearly 20 years ago I cannot make a firm judgment on the graphics, compared to most modern games today, which is why i'm not going to give the graphic's and visuals a rating. Other than that, one problem that i've had with level design is the reuse of model's and textures on almost every single level. There are only a few different scientist models and only two security guard models. With 6 - 10 hours of gameplay, you will constantly see the same character that just died ten minutes ago.
The music gives a perfect vibe to the current situation in the story. It keep's the mood growing and still keep's that uniqe Half-Life style that all the other games have. No complaint's here, well done.
Lastly, i'd like to talk about the extremly large modding oppertunities and community this game has. For anyone looking for a place to start to get into creating mod's, i'd recommend this game before anything else. Like all other Valve games, it has easy to explore game files, and a slightly less complex way of creating maps. Even if your not into modding, there are great and uniqe mod's being released to play, every week. For a game made in 1998, this community is very active, not only with mod's but also on internet forums such as reddit and entire blogs deticated to this game. If this is not a sign that this is a game that will keep you entirtained, even after you beat the main campaign, I don't know what is.
tl;dr
Characters - 8/10
Story - 9.5/10
Gameplay - 9/10
Controls - 10/10
Music - 10/10
This is a game that will make you enjoy your time playing, as well as make you want to keep playing even after you've beat the main campaign. I would highly recommend this to any type of gamer.

Most of the other Atari collections have come up short, but this one seems to be comprehensive, and done with attention to detail. For instance, you select the different games by rotating through a lineup of either the arcade cabinets or video game boxes, both being historically accurate. There's also included scans of the instructions, and nice touches like being able to select between a modern options menu, and one that looks like the Atari 2600 switches (nice bit of nostalgia).
If there's any downside, it's that this doesn't really capture the range & quality of the Atari 2600 library, but in all fairness, that's due to the fact that these are all games made by Atari, rather than 3rd party licensed games like ones from Activision (which was an *entirely* different kind of company back then). I'm obviously not faulting them for this, but I am naturally inclined to want to play those games now. That said, the game selection is really the best that Atari had to offer, and it's a fantastic lineup.
It was easy to get sucked in by the gameplay of classic arcade titles such as Centapede & Asteroids. It goes to show the appeal that action-arcade games had back in the 70's & 80's of very short, but fast paced intensity that uses a risk vs. reward system to encourage your skill level to determine your score. Speaking of which, there are leaderboards, both local & worldwide, so you can see how terrible your skills of deterriated from age... Or maybe that's just me. Either way, this is a collection heavy on the nostalgia put together in a nice package. Worth picking up!

A very interesting Zombie Survival simulation game.
Features your usual resource management, strategy, turn-based combat and an interesting catastrophic theme.
This feels like playing a board game - reminds me of Chainsaw Warrior, but with 3D animations.
Thumbs up:
1. Undead/living dead/zombie apocalypse theme.
2. High replayability - while the general plot and characters remain mostly the same, everytime you start a new profile, all the events occur differently and influence the game in a different way.
3. Characters build relationships - this creates an interesting plot.
4. I'm a fan of resource management and planning games.
5. The variety of items; and the flow of character development, traits, skills and attributes is very well achieved overall.
I could revisit the "inflation" of damage and hit points (instead of having 500 HP and suffering damage ranges from 30 - 50, you could just set 50 HP and get damage ranges of 3-5).
Thumbs down:
1. Combat gets extremely repetitive, it would be great to be able to configure an automatic combat behavior for characters for quick-combat (a simple criteria, such as attack weakest or strongest...and which skill/weapon to use)
2. Using a cool non-standard font on titles is fine, but not for the entire game - it just looks terrible - simple Arial or Times New Roman would have done the job, clearer, lighter and serious.
3. All female characters that arrive to camp try to hit on you - it would be nice to handle *other* kind of relationship not just flirting and wink. It would be nice to have a more flow of survivors - some that just leave the camp when their "personal goals" are not achieved.
4. The game gets extremely hard sometimes - everything costs and sometimes you don't seem to find what you need easily (which I think it's the point of the game)...so...in this game you'll lose many times.
Reminds me of Darkest Dungeon.
5. Some animations are not suitable and could be GREATLY enhanced to truly express what is going on with the character. Also, some other animations look quite silly or stupid.
Ex. When any of your characters gets "stunned" it feels like the character is standing, while being unconscious.
This can be greatly improved.
6. The overall feeling of the User Interface is solid. However, it can get very confusing.
I think that you should hide/show some action buttons as they are needed.
7. Some of the quests are crucial, and will end the game if not taken or fulfilled. I feel it would be more interesting to let the game flow with whatever consequences came from those events. For example - losing specific survivors or "moving" your camp.
Overall, I loved the game concept and idea.

As someone who hasn´t played this game in his childhood and isn´t driven by nostalgia I am really really impressed by this game. The best things Half-Life has to offer is its great level design, its fun, different and rememberable weapons and the variety of enemies and aliens you fight against. The voice acting and the few bugs that occur at some points are probably the only things I can criticise about this game. The enemy soldiers sound like kids roleplaying spys on a super-duper secret mission that comment everything they do by screaming it out loudly which is absolutely hillarious.
To prevent bugs from screwing over your game it is advised to save every 5 minutes or so to be on the safe side. (Quick safe and quick load are a great way for doing so effctively)
The story is very well done and I love its connection through the two DLCs where you get to see other perspectives on what happend at Black Mesa facility and around it. All in all, whatever you want to criticise about it, you have to remember that this game is from 1998 where FPS standarts weren´t that high. In my opinion it is by far the best story-driven FPS of that time.
I can definitely see why people like this game and the DLCs so much because if you´re willing to pay attention to the story and you know how the physics in these games work you´ll get ~15 hours of playtime you won´t regret investing in.

Take your time. There are many secret areas to discover that contain extra ammo, health packs or new weapons you would´t receive otherwise (That also goes for breaking all breakable boxes). Meleeing dead bodies lets you obliterate them at sonic speed which is really fun. My favourite weapon is the double-barreled shotgun which lets you shoot two bullets at the same time when right-clicking, it´s really strong at close range. To take as much profit from the game(s) I recommend you buying the Half-Life Collection at Steam Sale for 4 bucks.

Not done yet, but so far I've really enjoyed Dead Age! Definitely worth what I paid for it (which I think was a little under $10 on a sale?).
Once I've put some more hours in I might write a more in-depth review, but for now I'll keep it brief.
It's a zombie survival game with survivor management similar to many others (think State of Decay, Dead State, Z-RPGs of whatever kind). You start out with just your character (which they irritatingly, for me at least, refer to as 'you,' even though they let you name that, but that's an aside) but quickly assimilate into a group. You're presented with many opportunities of risk and reward, and can customize each survivor that comes into your party as they level up. The combat is turn-based, capped out (under most circumstances) at 3 v 3. The one complaint I have is the writing is pretty bland. If the gameplay devs of this team could get together with the writers of Dead State...well, they could just shut up and take my money.
In any event, if you are fan of Z-RPGs and Zombie Survival Settlement management style games, I think you may enjoy this one.
EDIT: Having beaten the game once, I would still recommend it. There are mechanics that are clunky, but overall it is a fun game, and the medal system upon finishing a game (whether you win or lose) is generous and interesting enough that I'll probably go back and play it again sometime.

It's a pretty basic JRPG game using RPG Maker as the engine.
If that alone bothers you, you've probably already made up your mind about this game.
It does use many stock assets, but the dungeons are nicely laid out.
My only complaint is that some of the icons don't really match the item they're associated with.
It's a little short but priced accordingly.
The story is a little simplistic but solid and consistent with the intended theme of the game.
There is no branching quests and only two optional dungeons.
Personally I wish the back story of the other main characters were fleshed out a little more.
(What did Killian do to be pursued?)
The combat doesn't have as much "grind" as some JRPG games.
There is an interesting mechanic in the game, involving changing cloths to achieve various tasks.
One moment you may be dressing as a peasant to sneak past the guards, another you may be wearing a tribal outfit to pay respect to their chief. In dungeons and caves you have to wear your "Adventure Cloths" to jump and push large objects around.
This was a clever thing to put in the game.
Overall, not a bad game if you like JRPGs and don't mind the RPG Maker factor.

I played through the entire game 3-player co-op in a single sitting.  This was a lot more fun than I expected!  The levels are challenging and nearly all of them take multiple attempts to complete.  There's a campaign of 25 levels, plus and endless mode, procedural-generated levels mode, and a player vs player mode.  The campaign is definitely the best aspect, but the other modes are pretty fun too.
Your goal is to release a prisoner on each level and escort the prisoner to the exit.  This objective can be brutally difficult to accomplish, but it's loads of fun!  Guards and exploding spider robots patrol the levels, and they have fantastic aim.  You'll need to dodge often to avoid their attacks, then quickly aim to kill them before they shoot again.  Friendly fire is possible, and we actually had quite a bit of enjoyment from accidentally shooting each other in every single level.  Sometimes your friends just get in the way.  Fortunately you respawn after 3 seconds, and you only lose if all players are dead simultaneously (or if the prisoner is killed).
The game recommends using a controller, but keyboard and mouse makes aiming so much easier (movement is a bit harder).
I do not recommend playing solo.  More players is definitely better.  Not only will the difficulty on solo be (nearly) impossibly difficult, it's just way more fun to play with people.

Tales of Berseria is probably the richest of the modern 'Tales of' games. Not only it succeeds in improving the mechanics of the previous games, but also it introduces an interesting new mood to the series: this isn't a story about heroes; instead, it's a story about the villains, who seek revenge and will not stop even if their deeds are to break the order of the world.
Telling the story of a group of underdogs is thrilling, and the rather darker mood it brings to the series gives a fresh feeling, however, the main quality of a story isn't always about what it tells, but how it tells, and Berseria has that quality. The story is very well-written from start to end, and the characters are captivating, making you laugh and have fun even in the darkest hours. The story takes places in the distant past of Zestiria's events, so there is no need to have played it to get to this game, however, for those who did play it, it is really joyful to constantly notice the little details relating to Zestiria's past, showing not just funny curiosities, but doing an exellent job in explaining the origin of many events that latter happen in Zestiria.
The combat greatly improved over the previous games, and it's safe to say it has one of the best mechanics of the series. The possibility of switching characters at any time in the middle of the battles gives fluidity to the combat, and along with a more simple skill management, the system seems more intuitive than ever before.
The item improvement system was very criticized in Zestiria for being too complex, an issue that was solved in Berseria. This game has a rather simple equipment mastery system, which is really easy to grasp and to use, not demanding an insane amount of grinding to harness the best out of your equipment.
Finally, this is a great game, and, personally, one of the best games of the 'Tales of' series, going up the shelf together with Symphonia and Abyss. Not only recommended for the fans of the series, but for anyone who happens to be looking for a good JRPG.

This game was frustrating, rage inducing, madness but a total blast. It's up to 4 player local co-op. I played with my 8 year old son and we had a great time beating all the campaign levels. It was a tough challenge when your enemies have perfect aim and you die with one hit. You have one basic enemy who will shoot arrows back at you and then you have a crap bomb that will chase you down and explode. On top of those you have land mines and exploding barrels. When enemies die you get money that you can use to unlock 4 different types of arrows. When you use a different arrow the enemy will use the same one so take that into account.
There are 3 other modes to play through that will add more replayability and challenge. There's Gladiator mode which is a survival style mode where you fight through waves of enemies and each wave it adds more enemies, Rogue mode is a timed mode where you need to get the key, kill all the enemies, save the princess and get to the exit in time. You can gain a little more time with the enemies you kill. Each level is randomly generated so it gives you a lot to play through. The last mode is Arena where you just fight your friends. We didn't try it since it was just the two of us but with 4 players I bet it could be a blast,
At $5 this game is well worth the money. I highly recommend giving it a go specially if you have some friends to do some local co-op.

Why Am I Dead At Sea takes a simple concept (of what is essentially a point and click adventure minus clicking) and alters many core elements to make the game stand out among others in its genre. However, these were core elements for good reason, and the changes cause problems that are uncommon and jarring for the genre. But whatever the verdict, it's a unique ride all the way.
The main draw to Why Am I Dead At Sea is its story. Without spoiling it, the basic premise is that the protagonist is a ghost (assumedly recently dead) trying to sort out, well, why it's dead at sea. This transforms the narrative into a murder mystery with a twist, as you can posses and manipulate the various characters during their own investigations. I personally love this mechanic. Instead of using a pointer, you'll control the ghost with a controller or in my case the keyboard. This makes the game significantly more interesting, since each character has a different ability, so once you unlock a new character you'll be able to explore the ship more efficiently (at least in most cases). Overall, this mechanic is the best part of the game. It makes playing the game more interesting than clicking and scrolling through text, it works well with the setting and tone of the game, and it combines some of the better parts of a first person and omniscent perspective without any narrative hiccups.
Speaking of the narrative, it does it's job well for a story rich game. The game is paced well, and has a great climax that will lead to one of the multiple endings. As far as the actual writing goes, you can learn a lot (I'd say a little too much) about characters and the mystery simply by reading the dialogue (which takes up most of the game). The characters are diverse, likable, and relatable, and the dialogue is well written. There are also a few missables that answer some questions that the main story never does.  And to top it all off, most of the characters' simple designs work with the visual style without seeming too basic. After all of this, it sounds like a perfect game, but unfortunately this isn't the case.
My first problem in the game is that many of the mechanics are buggy. It's surprisingly easy to get stuck on a single pixel or clip through a wall, and since the game has manual saving, this can lead to loss of progress. I'd advise avoiding walls when you can (
). To be fair, I only experienced issues twice in my two full playthroughs, but as both instances led to lost progress, I resent both of them.
Secondly the narrative progression has some small issues due to the game mechanics. In most adventure games you'll expect a certain ammount of trial and error, but this game makes it much worse. Because each character is different, certain actions will only cause progression if done with a specific character. There is a speech bubble that will appear over a characters head when they have something to say to whoever you're controlling, but because you can only control characters one at a time (and the NPCs won't stay put while unpossesed), you may have to check each character, with every other character multiple times in order to progress. There is one chapter in which you must talk to one character with three different characters in order to progress to the next chapter. For this reason, I found myself possessing characters en masse and trapping them all in the observation room so I could check for new dialogue without having to walk back and forth between rooms. And what I discovered by using this strategy during my second playthrough was easily the most disappointing part of the game.
Now, the following contains pretty blunt spoilers. It does not contain any details that would spoil the plot, but this information will likely ruin the climax and any multiple playthroughs for you. In my case, ignorance was bliss, so I'd recommend skipping this part if you haven't played the game yet. However if you do intend to 100% the game, the following information is important.

If you've made it to the end of this review, I'd simply like to specify that I do think Why Am I Dead At Sea is a good game. If you like this kind of game you'll definitely enjoy it, and if you don't it will likely change your mind. But in my case, I feel like I went in too deep (again) and ruined what was a fun experience for me by overthinking and overplaying it. If you're just looking for something new to play, I'd say go for it. If you intend 100% the game, or follow in my footsteps, approach with caution and reasonable expectations.

Original review:
The game currently offers terrible value.
They delayed the story mode of the game to summer and the character-stories that are in the game last 5 minutes each with ca. 3 fights and a few still-images. Seriously. There is currently no arcade mode. Or challenges. The tutorial is nothing but a button-check and explains nothing about the mechanics of the game. The movelists do not list any framedata and do not mention all properties of a move (such as armor or projectile invincibility).
The game also lacks polish. You can see glaring clipping problems with almost every model. Hair and chainst go through their own body. The game is not well optimized and you need to edit .ini files to tweak the game properly. There are no advanced graphics options. NO REBINDABLE KEYS! The game also does not support all peripherals that it should and even for PC fightsticks, you may need to install a work-around. The main menu is also a joke. There is tons of dead space and 20% of the actual menu is taken up by an image. If you are using a controller, you have to make your way around that image to get to the option you want. You cannot spontanuously decide which character to pick, you have to pick it beroe even starting the match-search.
If you can see past all of that and only care for online, the game has some terrible disconnection problems currently. The worst part of that is that you can't even waste your time with the story mode because you won't be able to earn fightmoney, the in-game currency while offline. So you lose out on currency which you could later spend on characters. Oh, the online store is also still unavailable.
IF you can connect to the server, you won't be happy with the lobby system which currently only supports 2 players, making a lobby almost pointless.
The downtime between matches is way too long. When it finds a game, you will be taken through SEVERAL loading screens, from the overly long "Match Found" to black to the character select (where won't selevt your fighter, you need to do that in the menu beforehand lol) to white and THEN to the match. After the match, you have to watch an animation and then wait for every point to be added to each profile. Then black, then back to the menu. It is insane.
Now, for those who keep bringing up the argument that we should ignore offline content and not expect a story from a fighting game, please check the other games of the genre released within the last few years.
MKX may have been a disappointment in many respects but it still has tons of content. Hours of cinematic story, daily/weekly/monthly towers with unique modifiers, the crypt, arcade, challenges like Test Your Might and party modes like Test Your Luck.It even had more online modes like King of the Hill.
Guilty Gear Xrd has an expansive tutorial which does not only explain buttons and the basics of fighting games but teaches you every mechanic in the game. It even introduces option selects in the tutorial. That game also has tons of offline content such as a story for every character AND a story-mode. It also has Trials etc.
Fanboys will say "But SFV will build up on this!"
Killer Instinct which will also come to PC with crossplatform play released with little content initially BUT it didn't ask for full price, it was only 20 bucks! And that game fullfilled that promise later on with a MUCH lower investment on the consumer side.
At this stage of the game's lifespan, I CANNOT recommend it. At all. If offers virtually nothing for the full pricetag and it is obvious Capcop rushed this game out so it will be present for Capcom Cup.
They shipped an incomplete game and want to make you believe that we should be thankful the rest will be free. We already payed for all that content, they simply delayed it and shipped an Early Access version of the full game.

If you're a fan of murder mysteries, supernatural themes, or like character driven games with lots of text, I highly recommend this game. Heck, even if you're not a huge fan of those things I still would probably recommend this game! In Why Am I Dead At Sea, you explore a strange cruise ship as a murdered soul, learning bits about the passengers and crew members and piecing together the mysteries behind them, your murder, and the ship itself. I enjoyed possessing people and searching the ship, trying to find new info that would help move the narrative along, but if you're not into a lot of walking and talking that might get old quick. There are a lot of secrets in this game however, many of which are tied to the original flash game Why Am I Dead (which isn't necessary to play before this game), and I liked searching the ship for all of the achievements.

My only warnings about this game besides what I mentioned above would be some of the themes and potential glitches in this game. Despite it’s fairly harmless appearance, Why Am I Dead At Sea has heavy themes and language that might surprise you if you’re not prepared, so if that isn’t your cup of tea, consider yourself warned. I have also seen complaints of glitches around, but I never experienced any during my own playthrough.

If any of the above has piqued your interest, Why Am I Dead At Sea is definitely worth the price, especially if you buy it on sale. I believe a game with the thought, story, and soul of Why Am I Dead At Sea is easily worth 5 bucks!

Finally, after YEARS of complaints, they fixed the game.
Scroll down for TLDR.
Long story: When you first made an account for this game, you didn't need an email, just like how runescape used to be where you had an email, but didn't need it to log in ever unless you needed to buy membership or submit a ticket, etc, etc.
So when the new studio took over and made it so steam users who had already played the game, had amassed fortunes, gotten tons of high tier items, even owned a guild like me and my friends, unable to play, I didn't take another glance and I watched as the thumbs down reviews came flooding in. Reason we couldn't play was because we had to sync our steam account... to our email used for our account on the game when re registered. Hint hint if you didn't remember everything above, we didn't need an email to register an account. Therefore we couldn't log in ever again.
It's been YEARS, and as I stated above, they FINALLY got it so you can be synced to the game correctly.
So here's the good and the bad part of the review.
Good:
-Simple but challenging
-Permadeath system is fun still and makes you evaluate risk vs reward
-You don't NEED to buy anything from the market, you can earn most of it through effort in game.
Bad:
-Graphics, of course, but it's still fun.
-P2P/P2W heavy. This is the WORST game for F2P in existance. You have to use real money for bank slots. Enough said.
-Did I say P2P/P2W heavy already?
-Gets very repetitive after unlocking all classes.
-No clear guide in game as to obtaining higher tier items.
TLDR: Needed an email to play in 2014-15, you didn't need one in 2013 when it started, steam users couldn't play ever again, now they can.
All in all, I enjoyed this game alot when I played with my friends, or when joining up with an "Exp Train" and I'd definitely recommend you to try it at least. If the pay to play/win gets too much for you, it's a free game, just dip out and come back whenever.
My rating? Eh, 6/10, the new company really ♥♥♥♥ed over everything, least it's not Maplestory... *shivers*

Okay, before I start this review I have but two things to say:
-I have very little hours on this account, as this is my alt account, that was made for Csgo.
-This review goes a lot off of my personal experiences with this game.
Ahh, RotMG... This game kinda brings me a sense of nostalgia... This nostalgia brings on a lot of mixed feelings; I've had some of my best laughs, met new mates and plain and simple, had something to come back to when I was bored.
However, I also have bad experiences with this game such as the permanent death feature - don't get me wrong this doesn't make the game it's self bad, it's just not for me personally - which has made some of the angriest and most regretful moments of my gaming life.
There's also the pay to win path that I followed for a short while before realising, "WAIT! I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥and keep dying, why am I spending money on crap I'm gonna lose in 2 days?". To be fair I DID know that you could get all these items playing legit, but my low level newbie self didn't know how damned easy it was! Like seriously, $12 or something to get a dagger that one, I'm never going to use and two, would take about 1/2 hour of farming to obtain. So yeah, if you are going to play this game, avoid all the equipment shops in the nexus at all costs ;c;
Heres one that I've never really seen anyone but myself complain about; the classes are extremely unbalanced. People only ever play knight, warrior, wizard and possibly a dbow archer, with higher level players - unlike myself - having maxed every class, and still choosing to play these characters. Why? WELL, let me explain...
Now, I'm pretty sure the original devs of RotMG, Wild Shadow Studios, never intended the game to be like WoW with full on raids and♥♥♥♥♥♥ However, I'm pretty sure they wanted a teamwork element. These teamwork elements do not exist for multiple reasons:
-The two classes that have the highest defence in the game, also have some of the highest dps... WTF?!
-Kabam added pets which attack enemies, but most importantly; heal, rendering the weaker defence healing classes USELESS!
-Private loot. In other words, the classes with the highest dps - which again apart from wizard, have the HIGHEST defence in the game!? - are the only ones to get drops.
-Some of the classes are utterly usless to the player, let alone a whole team.
It's because of these reasons that people only play high dps classes which are practically invincible, destroying the whole concept of teamwork.
Finally, there's the player base. I remember when I was a newb I had a 3/8 come up to me and give me some hydra skin armor. I didn't know what it was worth at the time and i was playing knight, so I couldn't wear it anyway, and my friend offered me a crossbow - a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥item - for this hydra skin - a legendary item to a newb - and being the newbie I was I accepted - the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ XD. Despite looking back fondly on stories like these, people who create stories and friendships in this game no longer exist. Ever since a RotMG YouTuber by the name of Kalle quit the game - the first real major game figure to leave - the whole veteran community left. By that time I was a mid level player, stranded in a waste land of guildless people keeping to themselves and not talking to anyone. As a result, me and my mates slowley started to quit the game.
In other words - the friendly community is practically dead ;c;
Overall, I did enjoy and make memories on this game, but that was back in the golden days of early 2013. It's the 3/1/2016 as I am writing this - happy late new year everyone! - and I jumped into the game a few weeks ago to see if any of my guildies still played. To my (sarcastic) surprise, the guild was disbanded. I was left a PM on the RotMG forum:
"G'day Eoghann how've you been? How's school been or whatever?
You know what, I'll cut to it. We've disbanded as a guild due to the sheer lack of enjoyable community. Most of us are moving onto WoW and we were wonding if you'd like to join us? If so, contact me here: *nopenopenopenopenopenope*
~Regards, *nopenopenope*"

Town of Salem is an adaptation of the classic party games, such as mafia and werewolf.
Before the start of a round, all players choose a name that they will be playing as for that game, which can result in some interesting interactions and even roleplays, missing the point of the game, but still being fun.

Basically, there are 7-15 players that are all assigned certain roles, that are all part of 3 factions: Town, Mafia or Neutral.
All Town roles have the goal of "lynch all evildoers", while all Mafia roles have the goal of "kill anyone that will not submit into the mafia". Neutral roles, however, all have their own goals. Some neutral roles are, for example: Jester, Serial Killer, Arsonist, Executioner, Survivor, etc. The game can be won by all Town roles, all Mafia roles or individual neutral roles.
For example, if 2 mafia members and a witch(neutral) are still alive, the mafia wins with the witch. Even thought the screen comes up with 'Mafia wins.', The witch still counts as a winner. All roles have a list of roles/factions they can win with. Certain roles can win with anyone, as long as they complete their objective (Survivor, Executioner, etc.).
The most annoying part of the game, however, are 'cheaters', that use skype or multiple accounts/profiles to play in a single game. Now, a lot of people do play with friends and use skype, but that, however, doesn't instantly mean they are cheating, as long as they do not exchange information that can ruin the game for other people. Thankfully, there is a report button.
In the end, you should definetly buy this game. If you want to try it out, there is a free version that you can play on
, which is identical, except you can't use your steam account to login, and you get 1300 TP ( the currency which can be used to by decorations and stuff). Now, go ahead and support blankmediagames and buy Town of Salem.

Another old style rpg from Warfare finds our heroine (Princess Calliope), her bodyguard, a mercenary, and a bohemian outcast forming a party to save the world from destruction by an ancient monster(s) that awaken every 1,000 years to destroy humankind.
All the details as to what is happening are laid out in this straightforward tale that takes you to the far corners of this ancient kingdom. Along the way, there will be battles with assorted monsters, secets to discover, exploration to do, lots of items to find or buy, and numerous problems to solve.
Old style 16-bit rpg experience that is very nicely done.
All these games, for me, are perpetuated by the story, and this one is clever with a lot of humor.
The art is nicely done, particularly in the battle scenes.
Music is very good ---- fits what is going on.
NPCs offer just the right amount of help, and add to the exposition (and humor) of the tale.
As I indicated, there is lots of exploring to do, and you can search carefully or speed along as you prefer.
There is a system of buttons that is used that increase various stats as you go ---- get the "lucky" buttons for everyone.
It's a solid game that fans of the old 16-bit rpgs should look into for sure.

I played through this game to the end, largely because it was pretty short. It wasn't bad or anything, but I honestly wouldn't recommend it to others.
Story - It's not complicated, and it is more or less complete, but it still felt a bit lacking. There's even a bit of info thrown out at one point that begged for at least a side quest, but then it's quickly forgotten and never mentioned again.
No Side Quests - Not a single one as far as I could tell. There were 3 optional dungeons, but they had no story or quest content whatsoever. Just a bunch of enemies, winding paths, and treasure chests. One of them has multiple floors leading you to a room with a door, and then . . . nothing. Just another regular battle and a few treasure chests.
Crappy Maps - They're just not good. Towns make horrible use of space. A lot of doors can't be entered, and the ones that do seem to be at random and lead to, at most, some unimportant NPC dialogue. This game really does not reward exploration. And the various dungeons are just narrow branching corridors with enemies and treasure chests almost never contain anything of value. There's like 2 puzzles in the game, and only barely. One of the optional dungeons has a ladder leading up, but you can't actually climb it. That same floor has an entire section that you can only see from a distance with enemies and treasure chests that you can't actually reach. I scoured everywhere on all of the floors you can visit, and nothing.
Underutilized Features - You can switch outfits on the fly, and some of them have special abilities tied to them, and/or they change the way certain NPCs react to you. Except that for the most part they don't, and only 1 outfit has abilities you'll use in more than 1 dungeon. Speaking of NPC dialogue . . .
NPCs Never Change - There are a few event-related exceptions, but for the most part NPCs have one thing that they say/do throughout the entire game. That girl who's pretending to sleep on her lawn? No matter where in the game you are or what outfit you're wearing, nothing changes. Those tribesmen who tell you to go away? Even after you do the quest that makes you officially a friend of the tribe . . . they still want you to go away. Even if you wear the outfit you wear the outfit the chief himself gave you.
The Ending(no spoilers) - Basically, the ending sequence begins, takes a couple minutes to get through, and then it's over. And most of that time is spent on some NPC rather than, y'know, the characters you adventured with through most of the game. You don't really feel rewarded for completing the game.
It's functional. It's not overly challenging. It has a more or less complete story. But everything about it screams that it's a half-baked effort. If you just want something that scratches the itch and that you can finish in maybe 6 to 8 hours, you could do worse. But don't say I told you to get it, because I didn't. It's not total crap, but it's well below average. So . . . 3 out of 10? I think that's fair.

Cons.

which he needed absolutely no help with.

This is a seemingly unpopulair oppinion, other reviews considered, but if you are considering buying this, I recommend you read this to see if you still feel like it afterwards - if so, then you should buy it.
TLDR: The 'game' is more like a movie; your choices doesn't matter; Not much 'gaming' is involved.
If you can get all episodes for under 5€ combined (and you're a fan of Walking Dead) then consider it. Other than that, I wouldn't recommend this.
Full:
While it is a fairly entertaining story, it really doesn't deliver what it promises.
I was quite far into the game when I decided to make a different choice, to see if it would change anything. It didn't.
I wondered if it was just in this specific scenario, or in general, so I changed all my decisions to see the difference.
Nothing was different. Your choices doesn't matter at all, they merely change a bit of the dialogue.
What they state in
"A tailored game experience – Live with the profound and lasting consequences of the decisions that you make in each episode. Your actions and choices will affect how your story plays out across the entire series."
is so close to bending the truth, that I would call it lying. Your dialogue change, but the story does not.
I have avoided "Telltale" games ever since.
So if you still want to explore the story, being aware that your actions doesn't have direct impact; that not much is required from you and; you'll be watching a story more than playing a game, then you should buy this (Though I strongly recommend getting it on sale) :-)
- Otherwise, don't waste your money.
Thanks for reading, hope it was worth your while :-)

I buy alot of cheap games here on steam. Most of the time they've got little good pieces but are overall pretty bad. But every now and again, I find a real gem hidden in all that dross, and this was one of them. Low production value, a number of minor non-gamebreaking bugs, but superb mystery and characters. Honestly, I found that this game captured all the things I liked about the Nonary Games (albeit in a different format and without escape sequences.)
The game takes the form of an overhead RPGmaker style game (without combat), like corpse-party or mad-father. You play as a ghost who can possess characters to some degree and read minds, but not work outside the context of that character's norm. A few characters have special abilities (technically they all do, but most of them are abilities like 'i change the background music' or 'I made amusing and silly flavor-text announcements over the PA' or 'I take a pill to walk faster'). So that means most of the game is instigating conversations between different people, although there are a few "figure out how to get the key" moments. In any case, swapping characters is a great mechanism for allowing you to investigate the story from different angles. As you get to know certain characters better, you get higher degrees of control over them, and so in some situations you need to learn more about each character to advance the plot.
There is a hint system as well, although it was disabled at the end of the game when I really needed it. It offers both vague suggestions that give you a rough idea of where to look, but you can press for more specific ones. I did the specific one once, and the result was almost as explicit as a walkthrough "try taking this character and talking to this other character to open up more dialog options, then return with a different character and they'll react differently." I liked that because it ensured you never got really stuck, but again, it is disabled at the end and I ended up getting stuck once, although I did feel like the specific ones were a bit too easy.
This game is a murder mystery, and an excellent one at that. Multiple people are working in different directions, without knowing the entire story. Everyone has their secrets, and almost noone is who they initially appear to be. It creates a complex and intricate situation to unravel. The game does an excellent job of dropping just the right hints and the right pieces to keep things interesting without giving away too much.
The ending takes place with a big confrontation between all the characters, a little like you'd expect from an Agatha Christie novel. Except instead of a detective putting together all the pieces of the mystery, that role falls to the player. So you take control of each character to get them to reveal their piece of the puzzle, and try to reveal the whole mystery. I'll admit, I missed a few pieces the first time, so the game ended with parts of the mystery unsolved. I'm not sure how many endings there are, but apparently there's more than one. I need to go through a second time to see if I can figure out the rest of it.
The character development is one of the best things about this game. There are numerous characters, all with their own backstory and motives. Some are innocent. Some, not so much. Everyone's hiding something though, and as you sort through the evidence you come to understand the characters and get attached to them in their own way. Their interactions are complex and dynamic. Manipulative and dishonest at times as well (at least if I didn't misinterpret any pieces of the mystery)
There are lots of problems with the game too. The character sprites are good, but everything else is kind of bland. The music is simplistic and obnoxious, and I ended up turning off the sound about a half hour after I started the game each time. The characters were said to each have special abilities, but I'd say maybe half at least of them were useless. Also, the story can get caught at times, and your only way to continue is cycle through each of the characters and they've all talked to each other and exhausted all dialog options, which is a pain. The scenery never changes either. There's maybe two dozen rooms, most of which are tiny, and they get kinda old by the end.
Also there are alot of bugs... nothing game-breaking, but just annoyance kind of stuff. The biggest one I saw was when you tried to enter a room, but another character was blocking the door in the other room. You'd enter and get pushed back out, or end up inside a wall. Also, sometimes you'd click on a door and it wouldn't react at all. Normally you'd get a "door's locked" or "I shouldn't go in" message, but sometimes you got nothing. There was an ability for the ghost to scan who he could control, and it lagged horribly whenever I used it. Also the game wanted to restart every time I exited it, so I could only close it by rapidly jamming alt-f4. Nothing gamebreaking, but obnoxious.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game. If you like mysteries with strong characters anyway. It's got alot of little bad things, but the overall game is so great. The game took me about 7 hours on my first playthough, although may have left it idling a few times while I got dinner ready, and I'm not sure how much that inflated it. Still, it's much more length than I usually get out of a cheap game like this. The characters and mystery were masterfully executed.
I will certainly keep an eye on this developer. If they can produce more stories with such great characters and plotlines, especially if they can add a little more polish, we might be looking at some real masterpieces in the future.

This game boils down to clicking lots of things as fast as possible. There's little need to strategize, just click anything that's green. Once in a while you'll click your power ups, but that's about it. It sits in a space between a pure clicker game and a casual time management game and unfortunately ends up doing neither in a way that satisfied me. Here's the thing though... certain people really seem to like it and there's a demo, so check it out for yourself or watch my playthrough. I also have a breakdown of pros and cons below the video.
From the perspective of a clicker game:
+ It's more than just "click this one thing"... it's has an interesting (perhaps even novel) mechanic (watch a couple minutes of the video to see it in action)
+ The price is right. It's a mobile port for sure, but at least it has a mobile price.
- In a pure clicker the fun is in optimizing to get maximum clickage... there's no optimization that resonated with me. Any optimization in what I clicked felt wholly unimportant.
- No purchasable upgrades... it's nice to get something for the grind other than three stars.
From the perspective of a time management game:
+ no pros
- No need for strategy, mastery, or optimization... it's just too shallow to even qualify as a proper time management game, IMO.

I love this game. The name, honestly is pretty dull and the art is barebones but what makes up for all of this is an excellent murder mystery wrapped up in flawed and interesting characters.
One of my favorite choices design-wise is a character named Paulo. He's completely isolated from all the action and therefore I never felt pressure when talking to him. Paulo gives a little backstory but what I especially loved what that he exists as essentially an in-game walkthrough. Paulo will rarely give straight answers, but he will point you to what characters/ areas of the game you need to focus on to complete the story. He's a great crutch for players (like me), who frequently struggle to solve these types of games but he doesn't take the fun out of solving the mystery. He does what Contradiction's chief tried to do, but he fills his role much better because of how we are introduced to Lewis. Such a simple character that gives the player a lot of leeway in how they want to approach the game!
Another thing i liked: i got the feeling the game had a lot of respect for the player. There's a point in chapter two where one of the main riddles of the game could have been solved with context clues in the dialog, but the answer is never spoken out loud until chapter three. However, at the end of chapter two the game gives dialog options to the player as if the mystery had already been revealed. This showed me the game had faith that the player was working the mystery on their own and didn't need obvious plot points to be outlined to them.
Noteworthy: The game gets dark, but it's not really edgy like a lot of games are now. This is a personal thing, but I hate games that try to be edgy, pushing things sexual harassment and gruesome murders in the gameplay and forcing the player to watch. Not that the game strays from those topics, but i appreciated the tact shown when handling sensitive subjects.
There are a ton of choices in the game, but never does the player have an actual impact on the story. While you can approach the story in a nonlinear fashion by following different leads and characters, the narrative is ultimately linear and events happen in a fixed sequence. I appreciate this, because it meant for things like dialog are almost always repeatable. This is a very pleasant change for someone whose always worried about missing an option, even if it's a little disorientating when you give conflicting answers to one question.
Now with all that said, I did have several issues (mostly technical) that would have made me quit the average title. These include:
-having to completely restart my game because the first mate got stuck inside an invisible wall. Easily the biggest issue
-Almost all the controls for gameplay are with keyboard, but in the audio menu you can only escape using the mouse?
-the name, while descriptive, is pretty dull. If it wasn't on sale I’d never look into this game.
-unskippable cutscenes
-there is no auto-eject out of conversations. Honestly this one is super nitpicky, but i hate accidently starting conversations and having to mash through 4 textboxes
+-to that point there is also no button to progress a conversation other than 'k,' or whatever you remap it to. This means if you mash 'k' too fast you can accidently conversation you might accidently start it again. Having another button to progress the conversation that doesn't start a new one would be nice.
-sometimes crewmen back block doors. I see no reason why collision with other passengers is needed, especially with this sort of drawback
-The ending feels really messy. SPOILERS: The best ending comes out in a clever and logical way, but it's attachment to 4 other endings makes it an extremely painful trial and error bonanza (if you don't give up and grab the walkthrough like i did). Moreover, the entire game is designed so that you can also go back and redo events, and nothing you can do is permanent. Having major elements of the story locked away behind optional activities at the very end feels cheap as hell, mostly because it only happens once in the entire game. Considering the games linearity up the that point, it might have made more sense to have only one or two endings.
All that icky stuff aside, love the game and will definitely be looking for other stuff the dev has made :D
