A very good example of the casual  time-management (CTM) game genre.
If you've played the other two games in the series this one will hold little in the way of surprises for you.  Really the only difference is that you are playing as Hercules' wife, Megara, in her efforts to save her husband and their dog (of the three headed variety) from a grabby tentacle sea monster.  If you are looking for a game that faithfully inserts the player into the plot of a classic Greek myth you might want to seek elsewhere.
If you're not hung up on  classical literacy accuracy or the ability to play as a male protagonist, and you like low stress play experience that CTM's game typically provide, this game won't disappoint.  The levels typically take 3 to 5 minutes to complete, at least at the lower levels that I played.  The pace is quick, with very little downtime waiting for resources to  mature to the point that you can harvest them.  The goals are clear, so you don't spend time wondering what the heck you're supposed to be working towards.  You can spend some brainpower trying to find the best way to manage your resources to get the told time or to beat the top of the scoreboard, but with an untimed relaxed mode there is no need to do this if you don't feel like it.  I do like that you can change the difficulty at any time,  from untimed, normal play, and hard, then back again if you feel like it.   The storyline is coherent and engaging as long as you accept that it is based on Greek Mythology in the way the Disney's Haunted Mansion ride is based on the study of spiritualism.    The graphics are bright and cartoonly peppy as befitting a game of this sort.  And the music is easily mutable, which is how I play all my games, so perhaps I am not the best reviewer to talk about that aspect.
This doesn't have the depth of Skyrim or the viseral thrill ride quality of Farcry 4, but it really doesn't have to.  It's a cute, fun little timewaster, much like my kitty who try to "help" me tie my shoelaces.
8/10 For games of this type, not all computer games ever made.

This game is absolutely worth your time if you like ghosts, murder mysteries, or story-driven games, and it's a steal even at the regular price. It's a bit on the shorter side, but the multiple endings, engrossing story, and rich details make it worth at least one replay.
This isn't the only game where you play a murder victim back from the dead (with Ghost Trick being another great example), but Why Am I Dead At Sea executes the concept masterfully. The mechanics change as the player gains a better understanding of their former identity and the people around them, tying together narrative and gameplay in a way that feels satisfying and natural. All the characters have multiple layers, and their interactions are realistic and well-written. Also, I loved the way the human mind was handled. Reading someone's mind displays some abstract visuals that give you a glimpse of their general attitude, with snippets of text floating by as their surface thoughts. It's not a huge deal, but it does a great job of making the mind feel dynamic and real. Much more creative than just having a line or two of inner monologue. Also, interaction between characters is well-written and engaging, even in cutscenes when the player isn't at the wheel. For the most part, the things a posessed character is willing to say will tell you as much as the answer you get in return. Also, even within the same ending, characters will act a bit differently depending on what you made them say earlier in the game. Otherwise, the story is mostly linear before a certain point, although some things don't need to be done in a certain order. This gives the player a nice sense of flexibility.
There were a couple of issues I had, though. First of all, the last stretch of the game is a bit difficult to navigate. The pacing of the story doesn't suffer much, but there's a relative lack of guidance and some of the things you need to do are accomplished in an unintuitive way. Throughout the game, it can be difficult to figure out what to do, but this issue becomes more pronounced as the game goes on. A more astute player might have less trouble juggling all the information they have, but sometimes it's hard to tell which character needs to talk to who, especially near the end. Also, while the endings are mostly satisfying, I felt like a couple of characters could use a little more focus, or at least acknowledgement. Those issues, in my opinion, are still far outweighed by the strength of the characters and the excitement of unraveling the story.
In conclusion, Why Am I Dead At Sea is a thrilling experience, packed to the brim with complex characters and unique mechanics. An excellent mystery and a great game.

To be completely honest, Serena left me with a "wut?" feel at the end. But that's because the ending sequence is triggered far too quickly after the various "checkpoints" of sorts have been cleared. I missed a bunch of important storytelling pointers as a result. So you've been warned: take the game slow and easy; look around carefully. Don't panic like I did.
And don't hit escape. It exits the game. You can finish it in an hour or so anyway.
After catching up on what I'd missed out, I have to say Serena is dark, creepy... and inspiring. It truly leaves an impression. You'll be thinking about it for hours, days, maybe weeks after playing. It's like an poem wrapped up in an unnerving game on romance and... well, life. Trust me, it's deeper than it sounds.
+ Amazing & immersive atmosphere.
+ Visual storytelling in the details!
+ Developers crammed in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of characterization and backstory in such a small space.
+ Intriguing characters.
+ Just... what the hell... happened?! The mystery is there, and keeps you going.
- Ending sequence can be triggered far too quickly if player follows the hints; they'll miss out on important storytelling pointers that make the OOMPH happen.
- Pointers might spaz at certain parts (most notably armoire for me) and you'll have to move it to a precise spot to get out.
A list of controls might be helpful; hitting escape to exit was an unpleasant surprise. Also, you can apparently press spacebar to see the interactable objects - didn't know that. All in all, an amazing experience for a game that is free. Looking forward to Asylum!

Okay, before I start this review I have but two things to say:
-I have very little hours on this account, as this is my alt account, that was made for Csgo.
-This review goes a lot off of my personal experiences with this game.
Ahh, RotMG... This game kinda brings me a sense of nostalgia... This nostalgia brings on a lot of mixed feelings; I've had some of my best laughs, met new mates and plain and simple, had something to come back to when I was bored.
However, I also have bad experiences with this game such as the permanent death feature - don't get me wrong this doesn't make the game it's self bad, it's just not for me personally - which has made some of the angriest and most regretful moments of my gaming life.
There's also the pay to win path that I followed for a short while before realising, "WAIT! I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥and keep dying, why am I spending money on crap I'm gonna lose in 2 days?". To be fair I DID know that you could get all these items playing legit, but my low level newbie self didn't know how damned easy it was! Like seriously, $12 or something to get a dagger that one, I'm never going to use and two, would take about 1/2 hour of farming to obtain. So yeah, if you are going to play this game, avoid all the equipment shops in the nexus at all costs ;c;
Heres one that I've never really seen anyone but myself complain about; the classes are extremely unbalanced. People only ever play knight, warrior, wizard and possibly a dbow archer, with higher level players - unlike myself - having maxed every class, and still choosing to play these characters. Why? WELL, let me explain...
Now, I'm pretty sure the original devs of RotMG, Wild Shadow Studios, never intended the game to be like WoW with full on raids and♥♥♥♥♥♥ However, I'm pretty sure they wanted a teamwork element. These teamwork elements do not exist for multiple reasons:

Deflinitely one for those with the nostaliga of gaming in the 80's.  The claim of 100 games is a little loose, but that said still good value for money.
A lot of the games port well to the PC and the controller (I think a game controller is pretty much a must have), but unfortunately a few port very badly.
Back in the day you had analogue controllers with dials on them to adjust bat position in games like pong and breakout.  Unfortunately this doesn't translate well to a modern controller and the speed sensitivity is terrible.  There's a few games of this style on the compilation and they fall into one of two categories, either the bat moves so slow it's unplayable, or the bat moves so fast, it's unplayable.
Moving past that you'll find some true gems, a few versions of asteroids, some truly unique arcade hits like Gravitar and Black Widow as well as yes another version of asteroids called space wars (we got colours).  Classics like Crystal Castle port very well and are pretty much as addictive today as they were.
So in short, do all games port well?  NO.
Is there enough that it's worth the money?  YES in my opinion as I'm a fan of many of these games from the 70's and 80's.
You'll need to be patient, you'll need to learn how to play the games but they're still great fun the mechanics in many of them are sound and there's something soulful in playing the predescessor to modern RPG's, Adventure.

Originally at the start you are presented with 5 landscapes Forest day and night, Highway day and night and camp. There's really nothing much to do at camp other than meet people who request you to be there and it's basically just a single paged background. As for the other two area's you will be greeted with the minimum of 20 backgrounds with each battle being split up by scavenging goods or a rather limited visual novel. Day landscapes will often present you with two enemies at each battle scene and the night time ones while presenting you with the same backgrounds at night will require you to confront 3 enemies on each battle page. At the end of each 20 paged battle scene there will be a Boss which you will be required to defeat. The longer you survive, eventually you will be greeted with three more landscapes, city day and night and finally Desert. With the same mechanics basically being involved just enemies with higher health points.
The objective of the game is to help a group of survivalists last 42 days. As more and more join your party, you get to delegate which 1 or 2 of them join your party to complete tasks, while the others you assign to jobs to basically shield the camp and hunt for food.
Each mission you successfully complete will help you to level your party up and each mission will give you time to scavenge for materials that allow you to shop or delegate people to be crafters so that they are able to create weapons, ammunition and clothes
The battle perspectives are easy to master, you seriously won’t break a sweat. You can win the entire game just by levelling up melee weapons and forget everything else.
Unfortunately, more than likely, you'll only begin to understand how to craft, travel and delegate jobs, through trial and error as one of your party succumb to a walking sausage roll. Needless to say, without your guidance your team is as intuitive in defending itself as much as a fluffy pillow is.
Animation and graphics make the apocalypse look sexy and the musical soundtrack perfectly fitted the Armageddon scene. The story board was to keep it simple just like the game itself was, but there were interesting secrets to discover as your forced to identify a traitor in your group, the secret brother and sister relationships that some had, what happens if you take away a certain persons weapon and finally even the secret bio weapon at the end of the game.
You might need to repeat the same exact process which consists of 42 days to achieve 100% completion since there are lot of achievements that you will not be able to get in parallel with others if you play it once. In addition that there are more than 1 ending that could happen.

It's easier to figure out what Town of Salem is by reading the wiki and then playing it, so I'm not going to go super deep into that.
Once I got a hang (heh) for it though, I found Normal mode extremely boring and predictable.  Being able to know all available roles in the specific instance of the game you are playing gives Town too many advantages to pinpoint who is
Town; all that the Mafia, SK, Arso, WW, and Witch can do is pray they off enough Town to deny them majority voting power in the first two or three nights.
The solution to this is All Any, a mode that has (almost) no restrictions on roles and doesn't advertise how many of which role or faction: the role list is simply 15 Any's.  The complexity of the game from that point is practically infinite, because now the game is truly one of bluffing, counterbluffing, stealthily determining roles and factions, forming alliances that may coincide with your faction or not, and hoping you survive to the end (and most likely you won't, but someone's gotta die on night one and you have as good a chance as anyone else).
Town of Salem reminds me a lot like poker.  You know all the cards in the deck, but you don't know the hands that have been dealt except your own.  Eventually, as time goes on, clues will hint at the other player's hands.  Sometimes you get dealt a pair but you swap out two trash cards and are dealt two cards that turn your pair into a full house that fundamentally transforms the game.  Sometimes the game plays out exactly like it looks, a stomp for one side or another.  Sometimes people who should carry the game for you are complete idiots; sometimes you have a great role and get roleblocked AND slaughtered by three people night 1.  It's a brilliant combination of luck, skill, game knowledge, and deception that make the game a classic for me.
So yes, you should
out with this game.

Really enjoyed this. Not really a fan of the TV show, but I've had a blast playing this game. Really well-executed gripping moments, great characters, and a charming art style.
As expected, the game centers around a small group of characters who are trying to survive the zombie apocalypse, having to deal with not only the undead walkers, but also bandits and heated disagreements between one another, which at times lead to explosive conflicts. The game especially focuses the most on the father-daughter type relationship between Lee, the main character, and Clementine, an 8-year old girl he meets at the start whose parents have succumbed prior to the start of the game. Their relationship is very deep, emotional, and was pulled off very well, making you care for both characters.
There are many difficult decisions presented throughout all 5 episodes, whether it is having to choose which of the two characters who are in danger to save, choosing to mercy kill someone or not, deciding which character to side with in arguments inside the group whilst losing trust with the other character, and so on.
As with most Telltale games, there are quick-time events present every now and again, requiring you to act quickly. Most, aside from maybe 1 which comes to mind, are pretty easy enough so not to be offputting for those players who hate QTEs (like myself). A few catch you off by surprise, but the game saves very frequently between the cutscenes, so even if you die, you only lose like 10 seconds of progress.
A very touching story overall. Between this game and Wolf Among Us, I think Telltale has become one of my favourite developers. Not sure why I've not gotten into these games earlier. Even if most choices in them lead along a linear story path and have little effect on the outcome, the stories themselves are crafted so well that they simply absorb you into their world. I'm sure going to be checking out season 2 of this and other Telltale games in the near future.

This game has halfway decent potential, but very frustrating and fundamental flaws in the game design make it ultimately unenjoyable. However, fans of the genre may find the game worthwhile despite its flaws if bought on sale.
You can almost never do what you want to in the game; at any given time you have 1-3 timed quests that must be completed on short notice or face a steep penalty. This means that there is no free roam: instead of exploring the areas you want to, or collecting the resources you want, you spend 95% of your time going where the game forces you to or resting up to regain the health needed to do another timed quest you didn't ask for.
The writing and plot are honestly excrutiatingly painful. You have no choice on how to respond to quest developments; your character spouts the most eye-rolling lines like 'I will do whatever it takes to protect them' to random survivors you just met. In a game that is supposed to be about tough choices in grim times your character is an annoying white knight whose reactions are as dumb as his dialogue is painfully unconvincing.
Characters quickly become useless. Once you collect 6-7, the rest literally do nothing but require food and provide more timed quests.
Some quests appear to be bugged or poorly designed: I failed two important quests simply because the game did not spawn enough of a type of zombie I had to kill, and later after killing enough of the desired type I simply failed the quest anyway.
Ultimately the reason why I give this game a negative review is the following:
The player is rarely free to do what they want in the game
Plot and dialogue are truly painful and unconvincing
Although this game has potential and the hard work of the developers is obvious, the developers really need to rethink the player experience hard in their future work.

The general concept of the game is already well presented, so let's just skip to the pros and cons:
Pros:
- The characters are memorable.  They vary in depth, but most of them have multiple levels that make them interesting to discover.
- The story is above average.  There is a nice sense of progression -- although the fact that it will have twists is obvious, what those twists are isn't always.
Neutral:
- The majority of the game is the conversational aspect.  There are very few puzzles, and what puzzles there are are pretty simple.
Cons:
- A game-breaking bug where characters can get stuck in place and unable to move, requiring you to edit the save file to continue.   You're advised to keep multiple saves.
- The plot runs on a script, regardless of your choices.  If you figure something out before you're supposed to, you can't do anything about it until the plot catches up.  Towards the end, you may know exactly what you need to do, but get stymied because you can't figure out the series of actions the game is expecting to advance the plot.
- The game begins to fall apart, mechanically, towards the end.  Actions that were able to be done earlier in the game cannot be repeated even though there's been no change, some actions (like attempting to open a locked door) no longer give any feedback at all, etc.
- Sometimes keystrokes are dropped, especially during conversations.  This is doubly annoying because you don't want to accidentally overpress the key either, or you'll inadvertently skip things.
All in all, I enjoyed the first 75% or so of the game, but the last quarter just got downright frustrating, which unfortunately left a bad aftertaste.  Still, I got several hours of enjoyment out of it, making it worth the $5 going price, much less the the $2 I actually paid for it, so it still ends up with a positive rating.

As much as it pains me to say this. You should give Street Fighter V a few months before buying it. Right now with a pitful amount of modes and online matchmaking that takes way longer than it should considering it has cross platform play. It has nothing to offer for it's caual players or its hardcore players.
Let's get the visual argument out of the way. I think it looks fine runing on the max preset, I like the art direction for this one and the added detail to the fighters make them look better than before. However saying that there have been a number of complaints regarding optimization and in a fighting game optimization is critical. I have not had any optimization issues however the complaints are still there and it's important that they do not go unacknowledged. Also quick compliment to the soundtrack, I have always loved the soundtrack to the Street Fighter games and this is no acception.
Gameplay wise I believe this to be a very solid entry. With the foccus attacks gone there is a heavy emphasis on ensuring that every hit matters. The introduction of the V-gage allows charcters to feel a little more diverse thanks to it's three different uses. The V-trigger  will effect the characters moves or abilities in some way, the V-Skill is a special move that the player can activate, and the V-reversal counter attack. How the V-gage works is the more damage you take, the more it will fill, it's essientally works the same as the Ultra combo meter without the Ultra combo its self and with more applications. Along with the Critical arts meter(think the Super meter from Street Fighter 4) the game's mechanics are similar to 4 while still doing enough differently to feel new.
With solid gameplay and a nice art style what else does the game have .... and thats where the game trips up. The game has very little to offer in terms of gameplay. In terms of offline modes it has Survival, a 5 one round story mode for each of the characters and a fairly basic training mode. That's it no battling the CPU, no arcade mode or no combo trials(it's coming in march but it's not out now so it doesnt count). Normally I would be fine with out these because I bought it to play online and when it works it works really well the netcode had been greatly improvved from street fighter 4 in my very little success finding a game. however the online mode is broken at the time of writing. You need to be online for any progress to count in any of the modes and connecting is still a pain the♥♥♥♥♥and when you do connect you can be disconected mid match or in the worst case scenario win a round and have the server not register the win at all feeling like you just wasted your time. I get that the cross platform play probably has something to do with this(and it is a very nice touch for the PC guys) however considering how many betas this game had it's unforgiveable.
All in all don't buy this game. As one of the few franschises I would call myself a fan of, it hurts but it needs to be said. The online isn't working for the hardcore players and there is a disturbing lack of offline content for the casual players. It offers nothing for everyone. While being able to buy new fighters with in game money is a nice touch, a working game would be even beter.

As far as negatives go, there are some minor gameplay gripes. I can't speak for everyone (and obviously I don't), but in my personal playthrough, I very rarely felt like I was just randomly guessing at what to do. Very few games provide, and reward players for following, clues as successfully as this game, and if you feel like you're fresh out of leads, you can always talk to Paulo. THAT is the point where I think this criticism is valid, as the game hits a bit of a lul, not only because of the absence of Paulo, but also because it takes a long time before a visual change in the ship, which kinda makes you wonder when a major change in the story is gonna come, as well as making the gameplay feel a little monotonous. Overall, if I had to sum up this game in a number, I'd give it like an 8/10 (Really goooooood maaaaaaaan)

Sleeping Dogs is pretty much every other open-world game you've played, only this one is about the only one to get driving right and not much else. Instead, Sleeping Dogs is just a big pile of boring, but I guess I should have known that given that it has the word "sleeping" in its name.
The combat system isn't quite as robust or complex as anyone's ever really let on. Most of the time you'll simply be waiting on enemies to attack you so you can perform a one-button auto-counter. The upgrade skill trees offer nothing all that exciting or effective. When the game introduces guns (and forces them on you for mission completion) they're about the worst thing this side of Deadly Premonition and only lead to aggravation. The game also has a terrible habit of forcing minigames on you without ever explaining how they work or what you're supposed to do, often leading to dropped missions.
Other than that, Sleeping Dogs has all the standard fare, boring after 10 hours nonsense you've seen in every other open-world game. Dumb collectibles that mean nothing, dumb races that mean nothing, and dumb missions that never offer anything special or interesting, and lots of mission breaking bugs that will require you to start entire missions all over again because NPCs bug out or waypoints don't activate.
Best to stick with something like Saints Row: The Third, because even if it's just as boring, at least it has style and spectacle.

This is what I've been looking for, for a long, long time.
Lemme just make this short, as there are 100 of these games, that everything feels so spot on.
GRAPHICS: As I boot up the game, I'm treated to an organized menu of game right from the getgo. Each game is represented by a Cabinet, complete with the original art that you would find right on the real thing. Getting into a game of Black widow to check out the graphics of one of the games, It looks exactly like how I remember it from the good ol' arcade down memory lane. You can clearly see what represents what, and best thing is: It all runs clearly on your computer screen. I ran this on a plasma screen TV, and there was no quality loss on the resolution. For other things, you also getbonus Art from the original covers, and even the Manuals for the games for newcomers, Or if you're like me, for Nostalgia-driven Nerds. Loved looking through them then, and I still love looking at them now.
SOUND: Just like I was stuck with awe at the menu, the theme for it is fantastic. Something I will never get annoyed with. Going into black widow again, the sounds are spot on. All those beeps and blips from the good ol' days are back again, and they sound fantastic. Nothing to complain about!
Gameplay: Now here's the Shining Jewel on the Golden Crown: The Multiplayer Capabilities, and the Leaderboards. The Leaderboards are just what you expect: They show all the top scores out of your friends, AND in the world. Wanna be the best? Better get crackin' at those Top scores! There's 100+ of these games, so you're in for hours of fun and hard work! And the biggest, and greatest change, is that you don't even need to be at your friends house in order to whoop him at that game of Warlords! Yup, there's ONLINE MULTIPLAYER. Me and a buddy both got the collection and tried a game of Asteroids to see the lag issue, and I can safely say there were no problems on either end. It's seamless, and it works perfectly.
Controllers are no problem, either! like using a Mouse and Keyboard? GO ahead! Xbox One controller? No problem! I spent a few minutes testing a bunch of controllers I had, including the Keyboard, Mouse, Xbone controller, A U-TRAK Arcade Trackball for Missile Command (Just for that authenticity, and my Very own USB Arcade stick, and ALL WORKED FLAWLESSLY. No input lag, not even on the trackball which I was worried about the most!
OVERALL: Guys, even if you're a Gaming Veteran like me, or even a gamer starting fresh and new, this has fun to be had. It's One hell of a collection that I myself, am glad Atari brought over.

A bastion is an angular structure projecting outward from the curtain wall of an artillery fortification. The fully developed bastion consists of two faces and two flanks with fire from the flanks being able to protect the curtain wall and also the adjacent bastions.It is one element in the style of fortification dominant from the mid 16th to mid 19th centuries. Bastion fortifications offered a greater degree of passive resistance and more scope for ranged defense in the age of gunpowder artillery compared with the medieval fortifications they replaced.Contents  Bastions differ from medieval towers in a number of respects. Bastions are lower than towers and are normally of similar height to the adjacent curtain wall. The height of towers, although making them difficult to scale, also made them easy for artillery to destroy. A bastion would normally have a ditch in front, the opposite side of which would be built up above the natural level then slope away gradually. This glacis shielded most of the bastion from the attacker's cannon while the distance from the base of the ditch to the top of the bastion meant it was still difficult to scale.In contrast to typical late medieval towers, bastions (apart from early examples) were flat sided rather than curved. This eliminated dead ground making it possible for the defenders to fire upon any point directly in front of the bastion.Bastions also cover a larger area than most towers. This allowed more cannon to be mounted and provided enough space for the crews to operate them.Although surviving examples of bastions are usually faced with masonry, unlike the wall of a tower, this was just a retaining wall. Cannon balls were expected to pass through this and be absorbed by a greater thickness of hard-packed earth or rubble behind. Having been a gamer across almost every genre since the 90s, it's rare to come across an experience that inspires. Blackwake provides that experience. I might be a special case, having always been captivated by the unique nature of the throes of naval combat in the Age of Sail. Whether you've been a tall-ship nut your whole life or not, the type of experience that Blackwake generates is not easily found elsewhere these days.
Your first ten levels or so will be spent getting your wits about you and learning how to handle the stress. The next ten levels will be all about perfecting your skillset. Levels 21-30 will lead to an increasing irritation with your public-server shipmates who have just joined the game and haven't learned any of those lessons yet. That's not to mention the usual continent of trolls and genuine ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that populate the public servers. The real future of this game is (or should be) squad-based or potentially faction-based warfare, in which highly-skilled crews pit themselves against similarly inclined opponents. Whether or not this type of thing is in Blackwake's future remains to be seen, but I'm extremely excited to see how the development progresses.
In the meantime, you owe it to yourself to spend a few hours on a boat in Blackwake. Bounce around to different servers and different boats, and I can guarantee that there will be a mixture of jovial, exciting, tense, and even tragic situations that you'll encounter.

MY REVIEW WILL BE FOR THE GAME PRICED AT $5
In light of the fact most reviews for this game have been negative (due mostly to developer abandonment) I had extremely low expectations for this game.  I should note that I was able to purchase this game for $5 with a steam sale.   Now after playing the game for over 10 hours I have decided this game needed some perspective.
WHY DID I VOTE THIS DOWN?
Simply because I believe it is overpriced at $20 for the content and quality (or lack thereof) of content you receive.  Simple put, this game has been abandoned by it's developers, it's not complete and is therefore not worth more than $5.   The rest of my review is for a $5 game.
OVERPRICED GAME
As I have already stated, since the developers seem done improving this game,  I don't believe the game is worth more than $5 in its current state. The main reason is its age.  This is a dated game with minimal features compared with today's standards in games. If you can get at a low cost, it's probably worth it.
WILL YOU LIKE THIS GAME?
I think it mostly depends on you. Everyone is different so it depends on what types of games you enjoy playing.  If you find yourself still interested after you have read this review AND can get it for a low price, I would recommend it.

THE GAME'S GOT NOSTALGIC CHARM:
If you have ever played Police Quest from the 1990's, this game reminds me of an open world, updated version of that with some tweaks.  I enjoy the old 1990's sim style games which this game vastly improves upon.  For me this game is a simpler form of Police Quest III: The Kindred without the story-line or the updated vehicle abilities.   For me, Nostalgia is the biggest reason for why this game is fun to play and definitely worth my time.
GRAPHICS:
The graphics are NOT the latest and the greatest but it gets the job done, especially if you like nostalgia police sim games.   The sounds of the police car siren are great and the lighting options are nice!  I have found the game as a whole a relaxing break from the usual high energy, fast paced shootout style games of today.  In this game, you are given the choice of patrolling at leisure which involves random police procedures and also given choices to participate or ignore missions and calls as they occur.
SOME GAME TWEAKING/MODDING IS POSSIBLE:
What many reviewers have failed to note is that this game can be tweaked (ability to change in game costs, money, levels etc.) in the source file folder which makes this game slightly better  (and playable) especially if you like messing with settings.  Many of the annoying game limitations (such as time on duty and off) and other event/callouts settings can be altered!
KNOWN GAME PROBLEMS AND THINGS TO BE AWARE OF:
Be aware that there some noticeable graphical bugs in the game although  I haven't experienced any complete game crashes yet.

The AI car speed is too slow (30mph) and vehicle steering mechanics are not very good especially if compared with modern driving games.
Cars will get stuck at intersections causing wrecks, your personal car can lock up if you try to use the siren/lights and sometimes people will appear to respond until a correct procedural order is followed according the game requirements.  In my experience this didn't occur often but it can become frustrating trying to get someone to get out of their car or to get them to stop their car.
MORE ITEMS OF INTEREST AND ENHANCEMENTS THAT WOULD IMPROVE THE GAME:
Sometimes an AI person will shoot at you but since aiming  can be difficult you will be shot.    A better aiming system could be implemented (a further aiming shooting ability) would help with this.
The actual game city is quite small and bland (no people actually inside the buildings).  The city could be expanded or even have multiple cities which would make this game greater.
It is worth noting that there is quite a bit of terrain to cover now.
The police station cannot really be entered.  Entering a police station and exploring it would make this game even better.
The game doesn't have fast travel capabilities as modern games do (unless you use the taxi off duty only).
The map could be integrated instead of broken up into sections.
AI driving needs improvement.
There should be other police cars, more random AI traffic and less people walking around.
Ability to customize character (skin color, person, clothes,uniform) would enhance the game even more.
There should be a police backup option.
Full Xbox controller support TOGETHER WITH the keyboard would help.  (Although there are ways around this through third party controller apps)
There are many more possible improvements for Enforcer but as it stands as a low budget Indie game I have enjoyed what it offers at the $5 price point.

So I discovered this game about a year ago and for about...8 or 9 months, I played it daily. I was actually addicted.
I have a far healthier relationship with this game now, and I believe I am better qualified to talk about it and its flaws.
This is without question my second most played game on Steam beating out other games like Skyrim, Mass Effect, Garry's Mod, Civ 5, Borderlands 2, Crusader Kings 2... the only thing I have played more is Team Fortress 2.
Town of Salem is a 15-player version of Mafia/Werewolf. It pits multiple teams and factions against each other to determine the victor, and unlike some of the more common versions of Mafia that you might play in real life with friends, EVERYONE has a specific power to get information, remove information or more generally influence the game.  There is no one who is "just a Townie" and that is perhaps my favorite part on this take of the game.
The second big twist is that there can be multiple bad guys who are competing against each other.  It's not always just "large group of innocents who don't know who everyone is Vs. small group of bad guys who know who everyone is."
All of the different roles make any given game different from any other, but I've found that most of the fun in the game depends on the other players. A single jerk can utterly ruin a game as they deliberately draw attention away from gameplay and force the townies to waste time policing them instead of playing the game - this is made complicated by the fact that there are roles like the Jester and Executioner that take advantage of such behavior!  Or a faction like Town, Mafia or Vampires can be utterly cripples beyond any hope of winning if a lot of players leave the game at once.  There are penalities to discourage such behavior but that doesn't always make a difference.
All of this being said, you may wonder why such a variable game that is dependant on other people not being horrible wastes-of-space is getting a recommendation from me.
Well, what other game can you win as a Serial Killer named "Cannot Lie" when you tell everyone from the get-go exactly what you're going to do, when you're going to do it...and they think you're just a really good Jester?
Only in Salem.

Theres nothing found or gained or learned here, just "I need off this island, ciao"

Adewale is not a typical short sword and pistol assassin, this guy prefers a blunderbuss that can kill squads of baddies and a machete that looks like it could lop down a tree with one swipe. Long story short, don't buy it unless it's on sale for say... 5 or less dollars, underneath all the pretty colors and the aesthetics there really isnt much to this game, but for people who love the series or played rouge and black flag and want to learn more about adewale, it can be fun. Angry Arrows is a small game made by independent developer Daniel Davis. You play as an archer who is sent to enemy camp where hostage is held, to kill all hostiles and save the
captive.
Controls are made with focus on being precise, and the game reacts properly, without any delay. You can move, roll and shoot (to any selected direction). Controls reminds me of another indie game, Titan Souls (though there you could use only one arrow, Angry Arrows allows you to spam as many arrows as you want).
Difficulty of the game is set pretty high and requires a patient player. If you can get angry and tilted pretty fast, this isn't a worthwhile pick for you. There aren't any checkpoints, each level (though they are not long) requires to be beaten without dying. There aren't any lives - one shot, one kill, and that applies to both player and the enemy NPCs.
But the NPCs aren't everything to make your playthrough harder, there are also mines, explosive barrels and, mainly, fast annoying spider mines. They like to jump on your head, but trust me, you won't like it.
There are four modes in the game - campaign (25 levels), endless arena, rogue (procedurally generated levels) and multiplayer arena. Game as a whole is perfectly polished (for a cheap game made by yet unknown developer), everything works great - responsiveness, menu screens, gamepad compatibility.
Angry Arrows is a great game for those who want to play something small but difficult, and is also great example many poor indie developers should check, as they could learn something about making the cheap game polished (say hello to Digital Homicide).

Tales of Berseria is a mediocre JRPG.
I'm new to the Tales of series, but far from being one to the JRPG genre as a whole. I love old school RPGs and JRPGs too, so I have absolutely no problem with "old" features that can enrich the gameplay in a meaningful way if well balanced. Tales of Berseria, as mentioned, is the first in the series that I've tried with good intention, having seen the other titles via gameplay trailers and friends playing them live; I wanted to experience a good story with antiheroes, or even straight up villains.
But.
Tales of Berseria puts the word "boring" before the word "cliché" and then, in between the two, has some fickle sparkles of creativity which is immediately suppressed by "plot convenience".
The first two hours are, for the most part, a good setup: a girl named Velvet, the main protagonist, gets thrown in a well and emerges as a demon with a huge crimson arm that devours blood and demonic power from other demons. Her brother gets sacrificed to a god that must be awaken in order to cleanse the world and... well, you get the idea, it is the usual plot. Not long passes and Velvet is freed from the prison her captors put her in, and then ... revenge! Or so you may think. At first, I thought it would be similar to the Count of Montecristo, which is one of the greatest stories of revenge and villainy of all time. Sadly, this is a typical japaense anime disguised as a JRPG. Some have compared it to Final Fantasy VI, but I consider it to be an insult.
The main villains are a joke; the classic motivation of "destroying everything to prevent evil and suffering" has so been done before that I'm not even willing to suspend my disbelief for this. IF you decide to go this route, then you'd better have a superior cast of villains and heroes to support it, with rich personalities and backstory. Both are lacking in this game. One of the greatest villains, which uses powerful illusions to deceive the party, is constantly revealing himself to the player only to take away precious items crucial to the plot from him and then disappears speaking mysteriously, this is a common narrative device that is used many times during the advance of the plot, which results in basic patterns such as "villain casts illusion, illusion is broken, villain mocks the party and takes away item, party chases him". The second pattern most used by the game to advane the plot is "random event pops up, in the middle of this event, we discover a device to keep the plot going", like that one time when the party stopped in the middle of the ocean with fishing rods and no clear objective only for them to retrieve an ancient pot with that ONE AND ONLY piece of extremely rare metal to forge a sword from. Or when they retrieved a book that was a copy of the ultimate guide to the rituals and weaknesses of the final boss, left for them to find mere seconds after the villain took the same (original) book away from them. And wouldnt you know it, one of my party members had the power to get rid of malevolence all along but it never came about before the last 5 hours of the game, not even a hint. It is stuff like this, plot devices and deus ex machinas of this magnitude and stupidity\convenience that really makes me drop any sense of immersion. To make it worse, the flow of the plot suddenly stops and resumes to have you run around the same locations and talk for some time with your party members, which have almost nothing to say that is useful or characteristic. There are moments when you feel like the party has a good connection, some of your companions are legitimately cool to look at and hear from, but their time in the spotlight is short lived and their most prominent interactions are comedic. Also Velvet's costume. Seriously, if you want to have a supposed "mature" view on things, for the love of all that is decent, keep her breasts covered. It is incredibly distracting when the camera is pointing at her chest and 80 percent of her goods are exposed for no reason whatsoever. You could have done that to Magilou which is a character that has the kind of personality adapt to this treatment, but not the main heroine with such a dark tone and backstory.
The best part of the game is definitely the combat system. It is cool to look at, easy to manage, very fast paced and engrossing in the most chaotic battles. Controlling Velvet is a pleasure for close combat fanatics and Magilou, the best ranged sorcerer ever created, is not only fun but also encourages a somewhat strategic approach.
The AI is not bad, certainly more competent than most RPGs when it comes to resource management on the fly, it does what you tell it to do, doesnt go overboard with combos, and can be customized entirely spell by spell.
Of course, if such a versatile and fun combat system was used in better locations and with a more powerful score, that would have been much better; the scenarios are bland, boring, repetitive, with low resolution textures made slightly more plastic and cartoon-like thanks to normal maps applied to them, low resolution as well. You have your average village carved in a mountain, your forests and autumn trees, villages in the middle of nowhere, plains, castles, city docks... the usual quasi-medieval stock fantasy stuff. Nothing original was put in there, and you have to visit each location multiple times as your travels resume inside the same places over and over again. The "world" map is a joke, two islands and a couple of plains with the imperial capital near two villages, that's the extent of what you'll see apart from the few towns that you can only enter at specific points in the plot and serve no purpose. The citizens inside have nothing to say except one or two lines, also not useful. As for costumes, the weird mixture of medieval themed armoured guards and civilians and 18th century pirates \ naval crew is as generic and poorly thought out as it gets, especially considering that nobody wears a tricorne, pirates only.
Oh, but you can play as the villains right? Wrong, so very wrong. The game adivertises itself as a more mature story of villainy, but of course that's all thrown out the window the second you realize that the party is "evil" only by words. Nothing of what they say gets accomplished, nobody gets killed, there is no blood ever, not even a cut. All the "evil deeds" they claim to be responsible of are just evil from the point of view of the common citizenry. They did nothing meaningful aside from gathering a bunch of powerful demons in a single place and change some maritime trade routes so that a major city gets in trouble. That's it. That's the extent of their villainy. The only characters that actually get killed are legitimate bosses with clearly evil intents. There is no chance for the player to question his own morality.
What's worst, is that members of the party are constantly bragging about how evil they are. 10 minutes pass, and there's a character talking about their deeds and how terrible their actions are... The villainous nature of the protagonists is equivalent to a 5 year old playing evil king.  Oh, and in the end, the story goes full on hero mode with the last couple of hours defining the good nature of the party.
I did appreciate some of the final moments and the middle point of the adventure though, in particular when the heroine reaches the typical breaking point and has to face reality and make her resolve, and the way the developers treated the final moment between the heroine and her supporting character, with "I forgive you" as a culminating touch spoken at the right time and with the right tone. But ultimately, it wasnt enough.
All in all, considering it was a very "standard" experience with next to nothing original, I'd give it a 6\10. Not worth it at this price, 20$ at most.

TL;DR A brilliant game ruined by bad executive decisions
Fallout 3 and 4 have both been beautifully entertaining games, even though story wise, I still prefer Fallout 3. Fallout 4 itself is good and there is plenty to love and hours among hours to kill in play time, which has been covered in detail in other reviews.
One thing which has always made Bethesda games great, is the modding capabilities of the engine and the small army of skilled modders working individually or in groups to add anything between small and big changes to the game. Bethesda had tried once before to introduce paid mods in an attempt to monetize these modders works and has failed because of the community resistance. While I clearly understand that some mods are so excellent and vast that they could well work as a full game expansion and people would want their favourite modders rewarded for their hard work, its important to understand that this is not what is happening here. Bethesda is outsourcing development to external contractors, and selling small bits for premium prices. I sincerely doubt that the hourly salary for those modders would match what Bethesda would have to pay if they'd develop the same content in house. While this is a smart business move, I don't believe for a second its in the interest of modders or customers in the long run.
Its easy to dismiss the thousands of negative reviews in response to this, as "review bombing of angry <insert favourite gamer insult here>" and it may be true for a fraction of them. But if you scroll through them and see the playtime hours of many of these reviews, you'll see that you are looking at players who often have hundreds of hours and are obviously still playing and caring enough years after the release (and most other players have moved on) to actually write these reviews. In other words, you are actually looking at the most loyal part of the customer base of this game, the people who still have it installed after all this time, often with hundreds of mods and they are exactly the customers Bethesda now tries to sell mods to. Clearly, this is a reaction of having a something forced upon players which they don't want (after all we can't deactivate or uninstall creation club) and since there are little other options for players to make their voice heard, giving a thumbs down to indicate one doesn't like what is being done with ones favourite game, is a legitimate option.

I was going into this with high expectations, given the overwhelmingly positive rating here, and as of now (6 hours in) I have uninstalled the game due to pure boredom. I'm writing this because I'm not too happy, that this complete letdown of a game costed more than $60 of my money. Note: I have not played any previous tales games.
Clearly, I have not experienced the whole story, but if someone has to sit through over 6 hours of generic crap to get to good stuff, obviously there is a problem. Lets get to the details-
Characters: Snore. A goody-two-shoes goes pure vengeance edgelord. She's not even an extreme-edgelord, just like an android with 1 emotion programmed into her brain. Okay, but where's the depth? Not just with the main heroine, but everyone. The kid that looks like her dead lil'bro, generic emotionless character that regains "humanity" over time. Never seen that before, eh? No, it's♥♥♥♥♥♥♥everywhere. The "good" guys, waving around their justice and honor, we've seen all this before. COME ON. There's just nothing new, and no depth so far. These characters all feel fake as hell, unrelatable. They feel like pure "anime" escapist nonsense, shocker eh? I saw reviews saying the game's themes were dark/twisted and that really attracted me to buying it, but no, they're not dark, they're your generic tragic backstories that some of your more emotional friends might cry over and tell you how sad things are. I'd call this sort of "dark" storytelling a "cheap-dark", if you know what I mean. You clearly haven't seen real dark stuff if you call this stuff dark. This is for kids. You might like that, but not me.
Voice Acting: Main character's voice is pure monotone, puts me to sleep. Other girl characters are sqeaky anime voices, cringe. Some of the male VA are okay, but nothing stood out for me.
Plot: Snore. Banter is lengthy, pointless, and boring. Just dull. Skip skip skip. Good vs evil but evil turns out not so evil, what a shocker. Boring. You got your classic "few vs many" and plot armor to the max. Everyone is asking main character for help etc because plot destiny. Unrealistic. I'd let this slide if the game didn't market itself so much as a plot-focused game.
Costumes: Completely immersion-breaking costumes. Ripped bikinis and animal onesies. You're telling me you want to tell a dark storyline with this sort of outfits? No. Once again, this game is for kids.
Combat: I'm sure many people love it, I just don't understand it, and apparently I didn't need to either. I just button-mashed and spammed R from time to time, totally worked. Maybe it's because it's early on, but yeah. I had 0 desire to learn the complex battle system because the story is boring.
Music: Cannot remember a single tune in the game. generic.
Environments: This may be unfair to this game, but coming from games like Witcher 3, Dragon Age inquisition, Mass Effect, etc, this was just bad in comparison. Most grounds were just flat, including the nature areas. Characters stood out from their enviornments like sore thumbs, implying it didn't feel like they belonged there, and that constantly reminded me that this was a game, completely immersion-breaking for a game with such heavy emphasis on plot.
Dungeons: Complete waste of time. Grind grind grind. Every area in the dungeon look the same. Which door goes where again? Oh you're lost, tough. Why don't we do some no-brainer puzzles that just makes you walk more in the meantime? Great! No.
Positive: Say whaa? Yeah there are some good stuff. Like.... ...... .. . . the... colours? Some areas' art direction was nice.
Overall, it feels like yet another inbred JRPG game out of an industry that stopped experimenting. Generic escapist stuff, highly un-realistic. Nobody talks the way they do in the game in real life. Unrelatable, simplistic, 1-dimensional characters with "cheap-dark" themes. More waifu bait.

Serena is a very interesting take on the horror genre. It relies on a story telling element rather than fear tactics to induce the player in its setting. Depending on how you play it, you can beat the game in as little as 10 minutes, but on average you'll spend about 30 minutes to an hour playing though the story. The only bone I have to pick with this game is the fact that it literally throughs you in blind and clueless leaving you to do tons of searching around for triggers that progress the story. That being said, the story makes up for the searching. As the story goes on, your attitude towards Serena changes dramatically and it eventually leads to an incredible ending. Overall, if you like adventure/horror games and have an hour to kill, there is no reason not to play this game.

Freedom Cry is a great DLC and I recommend it to those who both enjoy Black Flag and appreciate Adewale. If all you care about is Edward, then maybe stay away from this.
+ Adewale is a fantastic character to play as. He also seems to be perhaps the most sensible Assassin that you get to play as, having a better understanding of the Creed and how decisions should reflect it...although maybe it's just more noticeable because he's contrasted with Edward, who doesn't really get it for a very long time.
+ I actually enjoyed being "limited" to the blunderbuss and machete as main weapons. The machete fits perfectly with Ade anyway, but the blunderbuss was a nice touch, even though I preferred the version that was better at range than spread.
+ I am very glad that you are able to simply sail around to take down ships and raid plantations as in the main game, so even if the story doesn't appeal to you, you can still have an enjoyable time wreaking havoc, freeing slaves, and upgrading the Experto Crede.
- The relative shortness of this DLC (which is understandable, so I don't count it as a negative).
- Aside from finishing the storyline fairly quickly, the liberation goals seemed to be set very low. I finished those before the story was over, so now that I've finished the story, there's not much to keep me playing, aside from trying to get 100% synchronization (which isn't too difficult when you don't have to complete all of the constraints in one playthrough).
- The fact that several of Ade's objectives, albeit optional, were geared toward being stealthy and/or non-violent, which I don't really feel suits his character. Especially in the setting, as a rather heavily-geared black man should stand out a lot more than someone like Edward would. While that can be used as justification for having Ade have more of a stealth emphasis, I would have liked for the game to have him just embrace that issue and put himself out there, daring people to challenge him.
- No sea shanties. At all. Disappointing.

Burnout: Paradise was one of the first games I had for PlayStation 3. It's been years since I have traded it in, and decided it was worth another try. Got it on the 2013 Summer Sale and booted it up immediately. For a game made in 2009, the graphics are brilliant and the racing and crash physics are next to none. In this installment, EA introduced a freeroam mode, which you use to get to the indeividual events, and it works well. The problem is, there is an extreme lack of menus. Everything is done in-game by driving through junkyards, gas stations, repair shops, and paint booths - an awesome novelty for the first hour or so. After a while, it gets extremely annoying. Another downside is that everything just seems a but juvenile; there is little to no customization and the pre-designed paint schemes are enough to make any car enthusiest vomit.
All of the bad stuff aside, Burnout: Paradise is a brilliant buy if you kind find it on sale. The driving works well, like has been expected from the long-running series, and the gameplay is fun for a good few hours. If you're expecting a driving simulator like Gran Turismo or DiRT, you are looking in the wrong place, but if you're looking for an over-the-top action racing game, Paradise will not disappoint.

Really enjoyed this. Not really a fan of the TV show, but I've had a blast playing this game. Really well-executed gripping moments, great characters, and a charming art style.
As expected, the game centers around a small group of characters who are trying to survive the zombie apocalypse, having to deal with not only the undead walkers, but also bandits and heated disagreements between one another, which at times lead to explosive conflicts. The game especially focuses the most on the father-daughter type relationship between Lee, the main character, and Clementine, an 8-year old girl he meets at the start whose parents have succumbed prior to the start of the game. Their relationship is very deep, emotional, and was pulled off very well, making you care for both characters.
There are many difficult decisions presented throughout all 5 episodes, whether it is having to choose which of the two characters who are in danger to save, choosing to mercy kill someone or not, deciding which character to side with in arguments inside the group whilst losing trust with the other character, and so on.
As with most Telltale games, there are quick-time events present every now and again, requiring you to act quickly. Most, aside from maybe 1 which comes to mind, are pretty easy enough so not to be offputting for those players who hate QTEs (like myself). A few catch you off by surprise, but the game saves very frequently between the cutscenes, so even if you die, you only lose like 10 seconds of progress.
A very touching story overall. Between this game and Wolf Among Us, I think Telltale has become one of my favourite developers. Not sure why I've not gotten into these games earlier. Even if most choices in them lead along a linear story path and have little effect on the outcome, the stories themselves are crafted so well that they simply absorb you into their world. I'm sure going to be checking out season 2 of this and other Telltale games in the near future.

text:
Oh boy, reliving the feels trip.
I very much love deep, story-driven games, with TWDG being one of my favourites. You play as Lee, and while playing as Lee, you must make some very hard choices that can affect how your play through plays out. Choices may help, while some others may kill your allies. But the main focus isn't just Lee; there is another character, and her name is Clementine. To make this simple; this game shows why children make apocolyptic worlds more sad. They aren't meant to see all of this. All of what is happening in this story.
The comic-book style art in the game is very appealing, and it suits it well. Pretty much all the charcters are well written, but I'm kind of sad that some were either not touched upon again by leaving the group throughout the series, or just killed off. (Can apply for S2 as well.) The soundtrack that is used for this game is beautiful as well, and sets the scene amazingly. There is so much sympathy in this game, and parts will definitely make you cry. Prepare for a feels trip.
TL;DR: Get ready for a feels trip kiddos, grab your tissues and make sure there aren't any onion cutting ninjas in your room.

All things considered, this is a good story. I say "story" rather than "game" because I think there's this notion going around that a video game has to have gameplay. This doesn't. You interact with the world and the characters through a set of mechanics, but it's more a storytelling device than a game.
There were things I didn't like. The supernatural angle didn't end up being particularly relevant. It only provided a way within the context of the story for the player to interact with the world. I'd have like to see it taken further. There are a couple of optional scenes in which the player character uses their ghostly powers to help a character conquer their personal demons from within. I wanted to see more of that, but then the game ended.
If you've played Capcom's
- and you should - I'd compare this game to it as shorter, less interesting, with a less satisfying ending. But it is more grounded, which can be seen as a good thing, depending on whether you think the supernatural element clashes or not.
All that said, if you ever have an urge for a murder mystery thriller story with a supernatural framing device, this game is what you're looking for.

This was my 9th 'Tales of' game series that i have played so far and this is one of the most I enjoyed playing the Tales series following Tales of the Abyss, Graces F and Xillia 2. Here are my 'Free Spoiler' review.
Graphic wise,  Bandai Namco are still using the water painting style graphic which was used in the previous titles such as Xillia, Xillia2 and Zestiria. Another thing that worth mentioning  is the character models which now have slightly better animations also with better particles around the map.
Gameplay and combat wise is now all about coordinating and conserve our actions to a better strategy to have  better chance of defeating the enemy. The combat is more or less like Graces F and Zestiria where basic atack is unavailable but instead we are given sets of multiple artes to choose to combo it  together. What is unique about Berseria is that the game lets us arrange our artes to our own preferrence which is unavailable in Zestiria and this allows us to make combos that we like.
If you are hoping that the game will have a great dungeon and exploration then you won't find it here as the game is somewhat a begginer friendly. Almost 70% of the dungeon in this game have the same layout, the only differences is the enviroment and the pathways (This can be apply to the monsters as well). Comparing Berseria's dungeon and Zestiria's I would say that Zestiria had better dungeon as Zestiria had more challenging puzzles with better music as well.
Overall I really recommend this game, the game was very fun especially if you are looking for good JRPG.

You're playing as Lee Everett, a teacher who was on his way to jail when the apocalypse break. You're on your way to jail because you killed a guy that was cheating with your wife. But, the trip didn't go too well. Your car struck a walker then fell off a cliff. You were running away from the forest to find a safe place, which leads you to a house, an empty one. That house is Clementine's. She's an 8 years old girl who was hiding in her Treehouse, waiting for her parents to come back after a trip to Savannah (which they never will). You brought the girl with you because she won't be safe alone in that treehouse. But that is only the beginning of an 12 hours long playable movie.

UPDATE 2- 10/18/16. It was a pretty rough season... but Capcom came through with the content. A form of dailies has been added to help boost FM and the DLC cast is pretty solid. Extra Battle and Arcade Mode are still on the way- but Season 2 shows promise. Back to positive.
Street Fighter V is not just simply the next entry in the Street Fighter series, it's the beginning of a service by Capcom... a point many have failed to recognize. From the very first announcement trailer with footage of tournaments and die hard fans... they sent the message for us to
.
What does that mean? Well in the fighting game world... to get better takes work and research. If you've made it this far into reading my review without thumbing down... you're the right kind of person so far. This game isn't going to let you equip a gem that does a combo for you... or blocks for you... or thinks for you... your wins and losses are all on
That's where research comes in... you might notice I have over 60 hours logged into the beta. There's people who spent way more time- and youtube is jam packed with content on how this game works from those people.  The only way to succeed in this game is to educate yourself and practice.
If that's what you're looking for... this is exactly what this game is. There's minimum story at launch, and beating on a CPU punching bag is designed to be just as boring as possible. They want you to go online... take a licking... learn from it... and come back stronger. There's also online leagues designed to match you with opponents on your level- so it won't feel impossible for a total beginner to make any progress. Combos and inputs have also been simplified to help new players.
The biggest improvement by far is the netcode, leaps and bounds above anything Capcom has put out previously. It's a terrible feeling when you lose because of lag- that's almost non-existent in this game when playing on a wired connection with the right filters.
Now as to my title and SFV being a service. Capcom has provided a roadmap for this entire year and everything that's being added to the game. Take a look over the
.
From now until September a steady stream of modes, characters, costumes, and stages will be added to the game- free of charge to those willing to just put the time in to unlock stuff. 2017 content has also been confirmed with the hopes it will go for at least seven years like Street Fighter 4.
So there you have it... you're a smart guy/gal. Make your informed decision... you can either rage quit now, or

Best Tales game in years.
The battle system is easy to learn and hard to master. I never had much experience playing as any of the other characters apart from in passing as I mained velvet and loved her fighting style. In battle you'll have up to 5 points, which determine how long your combos are, or can tactically be spent one by one to go nuts and temporarily extend your combos as well as give them one of many tasty finishers. If you do it at the wrong time you can potentially find yourself screwed with only a 2 move combo, but if you can keep things moving, deal a lot of damage and reclaim points through stuns then you can keep an almost endless combo going. It's a great risk-reward system that never got old throughout the game, and get expanded upon with increasing movesets and passive traits which you unlock as you level up, progress through the story, and pursue side quests.
I wont go into much detail about the story, as that's the main draw for this series and I'd hate to spoil. All I will say is that if you're familiar with Tales already then expect more top tier stuff but this time with a much darker tone than in previous titles. The story and characters in this game are night and day in terms of quality compared to Zestiria. The story had me hooked and on the edge of my seat throughout. Since it takes place in the past within the same world, it does a lot to call back (forward?) to Zestiria, which does a lot to expand upon the lore introduced with that game. I would say playing Zestiria beforehand is a MUST, as there are a myriad of callbacks and references to the game, and a lot of the themes and plot elements play off of what Zestiria did.
The characters all feel very fleshed out and likeable. They all have their own goals and dreams which get fully explored as the narrative progresses and expanded upon nicely in some late/post game side quests, which is quite the contrast when compared to its predecessor.
My only gripes I have with the game are pretty minor.
First, a lot of the dungeon design is pretty uninspired. Expect to walk through a lot of similarly shaped, yet differently coloured corridoors and rooms as you progress through the game. Some more effort in this department wouldn't have been a bad idea, though it didn't really do much to take away from the overall experience as the story and the battle system kept things from getting dull for the most part.
Second, I'm not a fan of the Katz chest side quest which requires you to hunt down collectable shiny balls throughout the entire game. For the most part the game feels pretty balanced here. Provided you're not just rushing the story and take time to explore each environment then you almost always have enough orbs to open the next chest, but as I got into the last third of the game I found myself having to backtrack and run through previous areas in order to collect enough to keep up with new chests. This was frustrating as almost every time I ran into this issue it was leading up to, or just following a big story moment. I found it annoying to feel obligated to back track on myself at key points so I could stay afloat.
Having said that, the katz chests are merely an optional extra thing that just unlocks a few sidequests and gives you fashion options. Also none of the chests are missable, so there would be nothing stopping you coming back and finishing it off another time.
Overall I felt like this game was one of the strongest in the series. An excellent return to form after the somewhat lacking Tales of Zestiria, that easily contends Tales of Vesperiphonilia for that number 1 slot.

Rpg where you take up the role of a random kid who wakes up in a beautiful yet crumbling world.  You are only guided by a voice telling you to go to the Bastion which is a safe heaven from the world that is currently falling apart.  The story is amazing and gives you surprises throughout that you were not expecting.  You travel from land mass to land mass finding items to put the bastion back together again.  In addition to just the story there are arena's and weapon challenges.  A feature that I enjoyed is that during the ending you could make choices that would effect the ending of the game and how the story ends, allowing for re-playability to find out what happens if you choose the other option.  Once you do beat the game there is also a new game plus which allows you to start the game over but you get to keep all your weapons and XP.  Game difficulty isn't too hard and you are given two more tries if you go down.
The game has gorgeous art, some of the best I have seen.  It's colorful and bright yet the artist also did a good job during the bleak parts of the story where your surrounding areas get gray.  The music is great music.  It definitely has this folk-rock and bluesy feel to it.  It fits well with the story and goes great with when you are fighting against monsters.  Throughout the game the story is told by a narrator.  A narrator with quite a sexy voice.  It's definitely nice to listen to.
This game is a steal at the price and has become one of my favorite games.  I recommend it to anyone.  You don't need to be a RPG fan to like this game.  The story telling is just that good.

Come to relive the classics, stick around for 3D Tic Tac Toe and Video Pinball!
No course in the history of video games would be complete without this collection of games.  As you play each game you'll recognize bits and pieces that helped shape the games we play today.  Personally, as an old fart gamer, I remember each and every one of these.  I played them all for hours on end.  I know for you young pups it's hard to understand how anyone could spend hours playing most of these games but in their time they were the most awesome games ever!!
So what do you get for your hard earned money here.  Well you get 100 classic Atari games.  A handful of them are Arcade versions but the greater majority of them are Atari 2600 games.  Controls are a bit funky but they were with that Atari joystick that we had to keep taking apart and fixing all the time too.  There's certainly some standout games like Asteroids, Centipede, Missile Command, Tempest, and Crystal Castles.  There's some seriously retro ones for you game historians that want to say you've played the earliest of games like Pong, Breakout, Outlaw, and Combat.  Then there's a host of ones that have been forgotten Yar's Revenge, Sword Quest, and Haunted House.  I think there's literally something for everyone in this package, if you like seriously retro games.
Trouble is, most of them you'll end up playing long enough to remember the game or see what it was like, then never play it again because the new games have so much more shiny lights.  There are however a handful of games on here that might keep you coming back.  3D Tic Tac Toe is an awesome game in concept.  When I told my 20 year old son about it (he'd never even heard of it) and explained how to win he asked why nobody ever picked up that game again and remade it.  For all you pinball fans out there you have to try Video Pinball.  I think it was one of the very first video versions of pinball ever.  I remember literally sitting for hours playing the same game.  If memory serves me correctly I maxed out the score once.  BTW pro-tip on that one, you can nudge the table and it's helps, a lot......  Checkers, Chess, and Combat might be fun to play online or locally with friends.
At the end of the day it really depends on who you are and what your gaming tastes are when determining if you should get this one or not.  If modern graphics and depth of gameplay are super important to you then I'd say don't get this.  If you hate grinding or repetitive gameplay then you probably shouldn't get this.  However, if you love retro games, seeing where your modern games started from, or are an old fart like me that wants to relive a little of the old days of gaming this is a great gem and should be in your collection.  Personally, I love it and recommend it.  Your mileage may vary.

On the other, controls felt awkward and caused a lot of deaths, in most situations the game tries to take you by surprise and it often feals it gets cheap kills (if yore low on HP, you may die from falls that are scripted, if you dont have grenades in some ares youre screwed, etc), some of the weapon functionality isnt explained, for example, only at the end I realised that if the laser sight is on the rockets will mimick your movements when launched (Lord, that was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥, how some other weapons worked I didnt understand at all. The game creates an environment where you will get killed a lot unless you know the layout of the missions and know well how to use controls and weapons. Being careful, attentive and having good reflexes will often be not enough if youre playing this for the first time, there is often little room to maneuver on the spot. Its basically challenging you to play it again. Thing is, there is not much incentive in this day and age to play it again once you beat the story.
Even though this game made me frustrated quite often, I will give it a positive review, considering its a 20 years old game and, what was the deciding factor for me, I really liked the end credits music after you finish the game. )))
All in all, it is a good game.
But be warned, you should only get this in the bundle with the rest of the franchise and on sale. The price is way to big for todays standards.
And note, if youre not good at FPS, the frustration from the levels may overweigh the enjoyment of everything else. I havent played FPS games from the 90's, but there is a reason people say "difficulty like in the old shooters". (even though I dislike this kind of difficulty.)
