Best Tales game in years.
The battle system is easy to learn and hard to master. I never had much experience playing as any of the other characters apart from in passing as I mained velvet and loved her fighting style. In battle you'll have up to 5 points, which determine how long your combos are, or can tactically be spent one by one to go nuts and temporarily extend your combos as well as give them one of many tasty finishers. If you do it at the wrong time you can potentially find yourself screwed with only a 2 move combo, but if you can keep things moving, deal a lot of damage and reclaim points through stuns then you can keep an almost endless combo going. It's a great risk-reward system that never got old throughout the game, and get expanded upon with increasing movesets and passive traits which you unlock as you level up, progress through the story, and pursue side quests.
I wont go into much detail about the story, as that's the main draw for this series and I'd hate to spoil. All I will say is that if you're familiar with Tales already then expect more top tier stuff but this time with a much darker tone than in previous titles. The story and characters in this game are night and day in terms of quality compared to Zestiria. The story had me hooked and on the edge of my seat throughout. Since it takes place in the past within the same world, it does a lot to call back (forward?) to Zestiria, which does a lot to expand upon the lore introduced with that game. I would say playing Zestiria beforehand is a MUST, as there are a myriad of callbacks and references to the game, and a lot of the themes and plot elements play off of what Zestiria did.
The characters all feel very fleshed out and likeable. They all have their own goals and dreams which get fully explored as the narrative progresses and expanded upon nicely in some late/post game side quests, which is quite the contrast when compared to its predecessor.
My only gripes I have with the game are pretty minor.
First, a lot of the dungeon design is pretty uninspired. Expect to walk through a lot of similarly shaped, yet differently coloured corridoors and rooms as you progress through the game. Some more effort in this department wouldn't have been a bad idea, though it didn't really do much to take away from the overall experience as the story and the battle system kept things from getting dull for the most part.
Second, I'm not a fan of the Katz chest side quest which requires you to hunt down collectable shiny balls throughout the entire game. For the most part the game feels pretty balanced here. Provided you're not just rushing the story and take time to explore each environment then you almost always have enough orbs to open the next chest, but as I got into the last third of the game I found myself having to backtrack and run through previous areas in order to collect enough to keep up with new chests. This was frustrating as almost every time I ran into this issue it was leading up to, or just following a big story moment. I found it annoying to feel obligated to back track on myself at key points so I could stay afloat.
Having said that, the katz chests are merely an optional extra thing that just unlocks a few sidequests and gives you fashion options. Also none of the chests are missable, so there would be nothing stopping you coming back and finishing it off another time.
Overall I felt like this game was one of the strongest in the series. An excellent return to form after the somewhat lacking Tales of Zestiria, that easily contends Tales of Vesperiphonilia for that number 1 slot.

Wew..buckle yourself up for a long♥♥♥♥♥review!
When I picked this game on a whim for thirty dollars and after the sorefest that was Tales of Zestiria and the inferior Tales of Symphonia PS3 port, I came expecting to play through yet again another forgettable game riddled with a frustrating camera, capped framerates, and a boring, sluggish storyline with stupid as hell characters. However, through my time with playing Tales of Berseria, it slowly became one of my favorite Tales game (even on par with Vesperia), eventually one of my favorite JRPGs.
Hell, I'd even go as far to say that Tales of Berseria is one of the best JRPGs available on Steam. And it is absolutely the best Tales series PC port so far.
If you aren't familiar with the Tales series at all, it's one of the few JRPG games that feature a real-time combat system (unlike Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest games). It still stays in JRPG land, so it's not an action RPG (Dark Souls or Nioh). That said, Berseria has easily one of the more responsive and fast-paced combat system in the Tales franchise.
Now say if you're just like I was in the beginning of the game and just mindlessly buttonmash spam attacks one after another until your thumbs go numb, you would say this game is a bit easy. And yes, I'd have to agree, the game gets pretty easy and actually boring when you mindlessly mash buttons to go through the game. You eventually get so bored of getting into enemy encounters and combat, you’d just skip 'em all together.
However, Berseria has several difficulty levels, and unless you are playing on the super baby-tier difficulties and plan on staying there, the game punishes you for mashing away by increasing enemy stats, aggressiveness, and changing their movesets.
It’s nice to have some challenge as always, but prepare for the worse when you reach that boss that'll keep stun locking you into a corner. It’s important to know the game’s mechanics before turning up the difficulty and you should never jump into the hardest difficulties at the start. Oh, and I never used a walkthrough at all, so you’ll probably won’t need it either.
As for the AI for your party members, they can be iffy. Sometimes they can be very functional, Magilou and Laphicet can deal some massive DPS, Eizen and Rokurou give some good starting combos, and Eleanor can hybrid DPS and combos. Or they can stand around, do absolutely nothing, run around like headless chickens and eventually get K.O’d or stun locked to death.
Also, unlike previous Tales games, you cannot assign items for your party members, so enjoy not getting revived at all while the party’s designated healer/reviver gets stun locked/spell locked into cornerhell.
But whatever, no one never plays Tales games only for the gameplay! What Tales fans really care about are the characters and the story!
Set a thousand years before the events of Tales of Zestiria, Tales of Berseria is a prequel taking place in the same world. And don’t worry, playing Tales of Zestiria beforehand isn’t a requirement to fully enjoy Berseria. You will miss some Zestiria references here and there, but nothing that hampers the story of Berseria.
The main protagonist is Velvet Crowe, a young, easygoing village girl who witnessed her young brother coldly sacrificed for greater good, received a demonic transformation, and imprisoned for three years only feeding on demons like herself; who is now hellbent in getting vengeance against the person who murdered her brother. Her brother-in-law, who has risen through the ranks of the Abbey and has become a shining beacon of hope, where the entire world praises him for saving humanity with Advent, the event of slaying Velvet's brother. She states again and again, no matter the circumstances, that she will kill anyone that stands in her way against the person who betrayed her and her brother until she has killed him herself. Even if that means being seen as a horrible, monstrous villain working against the good of mankind.
For once, this is the first time that a Tales game has featured such an edgy protagonist, who acts more of an anti-hero more than anything along with the other party members in Berseria. Oh, and the rest of cast is easily the best Tales cast probably since Vesperia. They're likable and entertaining to say the least and won't be breaking out into arguments friggin’ every minute or into “friendship is strength!” crap like nearly all Tales games have.
Overall, it’s a rather emotional story and time and time you’ll find the game’s overarching theme of emotional reasoning vs. logical reasoning shown to you. Of course, you might find Velvet’s unnecessary edgelordness insufferable, but hey, her character does improve. Eventually...
The voice acting (at least in English dub), is stellar and surprisingly good. Sadly, no big names like Troy Baker this time, but Velvet’s voice actor really hits the nail on the head with her performance as Velvet (I’ve always pictured her as the chick who voices the high-pitched, annoying Compa from the Neptunia games). And don’t let me wrong, the rest of the cast did a great job as well. Especially the main antagonist, whose pretty much Noctis from FFXV.
Of course, Berseria isn’t perfect by any means, I’ve still had my share of problems with it.
For example, one of the major flaws (screw flaws, this is a huge♥♥♥♥♥problem) in this game is how linear the dungeons are in this game. Many of the dungeons in this game consist of loooonnngg♥♥♥♥♥hallways and corridors. Not to mention, even after getting a movement boosting hoverboard halfway through the game, the dungeons’ hallways and corridors become even lonnngeeerrr to go through. WHY. Previous Tales games had much more interesting dungeons and level design than most of the ones in Berseria.
The game does have some fast travel to the major cities and ports to prevent you from running everywhere, but dungeons can be painful to play through, especially toward the end of the game.
I also felt like the game’s world could have been bigger, seeing how this is my 5th Tales game I’ve played, the areas could have been more expansive, open, detailed, and numerous. The monster arenas are also disappointing too; they aren’t nearly as challenging or as difficult as previous Tales games have always been.
Graphics feel kind of old for this time and age, I mean Zestiria barely got passed by with its’ average♥♥♥♥♥JRPG graphics and that released nearly two years ago.
I think it’s time to invest in a new graphics engine Bamco, no? And time to ditch the PlayStation 3 in Japan so don't hold back the graphical development of these games? This is my review of
, I mean
, one last try...Tales of Berseria! (Seriously, a master swordsmen weilding a two-handed sword with his left arm NAMED Artorias?)
As you can tell the creators of Berseria have taken some inspiration from the works of Kentaro Miura and Hidetaka Miyazaki but as Pablo Picasso says "Good artists copy; great artists steal." And in this endeavor the creators of Berseria have made one of the best stories in a tales game, rivaling even Symphonias. The deviation from "We are the good guys thus we save the world" was a much needed change and even more compelling considering it is a prequel to Zestiria. This connection sets up LOTS of world building that gave me a strange sense of giddiness as I understood some of the obscure references. In its own funny way that almost makes Zestiria worth playing, just to better understand the story and to be fully immersed.
Now the main reason most anyone plays a Tales game is for the gameplay and boy have you come to the right place. The new controls are intuitive but like a cranky old man I am not one for change. At first this was a bit of a gripe I had with the game, it felt a little stiff if you're coming off any of the predecessors but I vouch for it now that I have completed the game by saying it is a much superior control scheme. Instead of having two of your buttons (most of the time Y or X) being unused in combat half the time, ALL the main buttons are now used for combat which adds the possibility to string a wide variety of combos. The port this time around was also done fantastically, smooth FPS, cut scenes don't sound like garbled trash and everything looks nice (for a xbox/PS4 port). I am not a computer whiz but anyone with an inkling of experience of game ports knows that Zestiria was a baaaaad. Also instead of having the really boring Armatization like in Zestiria, the each character uses different abilities called "Break Souls" which are actually really fun, unlike Zestiria where Armatization
have been really fun but was extreamly dull.  The only real complaint I had with the game was that I didn't care much for the Martial and Hidden arts that Velvet used, they felt too flashy and sometimes were hard to land hits properly on enemies but its a minor complaint.
The Tales series has a tendency to have lackluster endings imo but Berseria wraps up in a very neat way, leaving you with the feeling that the creators really knew what they wanted to say by its overall presentation and climatic ending. If you a fan of the Tales Series or if you enjoyed Zestiria even a little, buy this.
TLDR: Is good game, should get.

I highly reccomend you beat Zestiria before you play this game.
What I liked about the game:
Almost everything in the Asgard universe is connected chronologially and this I mean from Tales of Phantasia, Symphonia 1 and 2, and Zestiria. Your ship also picks up notable items from other games as well as treasures. Tales of Zestiria is chronologically after Berseria and has soooo much to do with this game that a lot of times I found myself Googling to see if  "blank" was in Zestiria. 2/3s of the time it was in Zestiria be renamed a bit. A lot of the plot holes that there were in Zestiria, Berseria used as story and origin pretty much and personally it made me appreciate Zestiria's story a lot more when I stopped playing that. Berseria's form of plot basically mind-blows you by giving you tons and tons of plot-hole fillers to make an original game.
Gameplay-wise this time you don't need to leave a "Free Run" skill to freely run around the combat plane, instead of CP skills they use Ventites which is in their own sense the same thing, only you have to hunt down those tough dark-purple monsters to get them. (Called Code-Reds.) Their unique combat trait is the soul system which basically replaces MP or Mana. So in other words you won't be seeing any gels that replenishs MP like Orange or Pineapple Gels.
What I didn't like about the game:
Finding the Cameo Battle was harder than it should've been.
I found the weapon enhancement feature to be unnesnessarily snowballing with weapons in my bag the weapons each get different random skills but you can't choose which to keep and you just leave them in your bag and you try to master each weapon proficiency. But then you eventually need to dismantle some to get more materials to enhance them to catch up with your level otherwise those weapons will be useless. Overall I think ther random skills thing is not needed. I rather just have one of each weapon and enhance them. Dismantle duplicates, etc. Personally I liked Zestiria's weaps because it's more simplified like that. Just equip and you had your skillset.
I didn't like the Katz orb collecting. While playing the game you have to constantly collect Katz orbs.  Personally I just want to run normally.

Plotholes that are in the game:
Since this is basically a game between Zestiria and Berseria there's one thing that's still left out. Why Malak was renamed to Seraphim in the future.
Overall this game I feel has taken the crown of best Tales game so far despite my gripes about it, it's a must by if you have played Zestiria. If you haven't played it you should first before you play this to have a fuller experience.

If you like side scrollers, but always wanted to go beyond the limited worlds or levels they present, this might be your ticket.
Starbound is a 2d side-scrolling action/adventure/building game. You've probably seen this style before with it's older cousin Terraria, and comparisons between the two are almost unavoidable. Starbound however, takes things a bit further by adding in a bit more "story", as well as a variety of randomly generated worlds to explore (More than you can count!), and even randomly generated weapons and creatures!
The devs have already crammed a LOT of game into this package. Despite being an early access title, you'd easily forget that while playing. This feels like the real deal. To top it off, the devs are continually updating and adding more content, as it's still early access, and they aren't done yet.
If you like sidescrollers, you'll probably like this game. If you like building/creative games, you'll probably like this game. If you like exploring unknown worlds that no player has ever touched before, you'll probably like this game. If you liked Terraria, you'll probably like this game a lot.
The only real complaint I can muster against the game at this point is that despite all of the random gen things, there is a pretty high degree of "sameness" to the game after a while.
Overall though, it's a delightful romp through colorful worlds done in a 2d platformer style. Add in a few buddies and play multiplayer and it's even better!

Fallout 4 is a continuation of the Fallout series, and many of the story beats from earlier editions (most particularly Fallout 3) are picked up and expanded on here. The core plotline (find/save missing son) is more or less a MacGuffin, in that it serves as a jumping-off point for exploration which is really where the game is strong — there are a ton of locations, both with and without map markers, and these range from the frustrating (what, I kill my way through a horde of ferals just for a bottlecap and a couple of tin cans, for real?!?!) to the blind-sidingly rewarding (hot dang, I just opens up this crate and I gots me a Gauss Rifle!!!!) via all points between. There's missions, sure, but exploration is 90% of the game.
Missions, yes, many of these are the usual go there, do that, bring stuff back, kill that guy formula fodder — if you've never played an RPG before you won't recognize these tropes but, honestly, there's only so much scope in terms of objectives a game can provide, and as I've yet to find an RPG with entirely new concepts in the quest department I'm not going to hold this against Fallout 4. Moreover, some of the quests have formulaic bones but are nonetheless entertaining  — the USS Constitution quest is a great example of this, as it's a great off-the-wall diversion from the more gritty stuff the main quest throws at you.
Morality is big in this game, too, in the sense that you can choose how moral (or otherwise) you want to be. Where this is most obvious is in the factional squabbles — who do you help, and who do you make enemies with? Are the Brotherhood of Steel more noble than the Institute, or they simulacra of each other, and the Minutemen occupy the moral high ground? These are questions you must answer yourself, and the game doesn't brow-beat you into siding with one faction or another (seriously, you can sack off any of the faction storylines if that's what you want to do).
Graphically this game is odd, in that while the world has been beautifully realized, there's a psuedo-cartoony feel to proceedings that, for me, works well but that I completely understand is off-putting for others. Some elements work better than others with this artistic approach, and the weapon meshes are especially good  — there's a strong, cohesive aesthetic to the various guns that really helps engender a sense of place and setting.
The music is a real high point for me (not the radio, the ambient stuff) as it works to thematically link each of the games in the series, while forging new groung unique to the Boston setting of Fallout 4 — for example, there are phrases lifted from Irish folk music alongside eerie synth refrains that call to mind the Metallic Monks theme from the original Fallout, or odd chants that clearly reference the Aroyo theme from Fallout 2.
The game system is more bare-bones than previous installments, and this is a marmite aspect of gameplay (love it/hate it) — there's no skills system at all, with a perks system replacing them wholesale. For me, this works extremely well — in first person, you have more engaging gameplay in that you don't have to constantly second-guess which skills you might need to advance your character along the lines you wish to pursue without making the game impossibly challenging as you've neglected something that later turns out to be crucial. I don't miss that at all. And combat is improved, to my mind, especially gunplay as you no longer have the inexplicable sudeen critical misses from your maxed-out, high end sniper that absolutely isn't going to miss a sitting duck, no matter what the unforgiving RPG system says... The game feels more like Borderlands or Rage in terms of combat, which is no bad thing, and I enjoy the gameplay more than I did Fallout 3 or New Vegas (the isometric gameplay of the earlier games is so different that a comparison can't be drawn).
An aspect I don't much like is the settlement system, but for many I suspect this would be a major plus — if you choose to engage with this aspect, you have a whole resource management and strategic defense gameplay that is entirely unique to Fallout 4. Or, if you're like me, you could go with the bare minimum and spend all your time doing something more fun (like slaughtering a masive quarry full of those pesky raiders, damn their eyes).
Overall, Bethesda have crafted a vast and yet sometimes surprisingly subtle game, packed with content and appealing in diverse ways to a diverse player base. It's a quality product, a satisfying experience, and I have no hesitation in recommending you play it.

Why yes, I
played Atari today.
And it was amazing.
As a collection, it's a great value. Contained within the Vault are faithful emulations of the original Atari arcade games, such as Asteroids, Centipede, Missile Command, and my personal favorite, Tempest. It even introduced me to a few I'd never had the chance to play, before -- Crystal Castles, Black Widow, Liberator, and Major Havoc are great fun, and I'm happy to have had the chance to try them out. Heck, even the original Pong arcade cabinet is here.
Then you have a selection of perfectly-emulated Atari 2600 games, complete with 3D models of the original boxes and scans of the original manuals, to boot. (Even the aforementioned arcade games are represented with 3D recreations of their cabinets, too!) Many of them play best with multiple people, and thankfully, Atari Vault gives you the option for not only local multiplayer, but online multiplayer as well, on top of high score leaderboards.
Controls for each game are fully customizable, from a gamepad to a keyboard. Which is great, considering that a few of these games used to be controlled with a trackball or paddle. I used a Steam Controller for most of these games, and the touch-sensitive circle pads actually worked really well for paddle controller stuff. I found it could be somewhat over-sensitive at times, requiring me to adjust the settings a lot, but it wasn't a terrible inconvenience or anything. And -- I'm not sure if this is a bug or what, but -- on a few games in particular, pressing a button that is normally bound to an action (fire, special action, etc) causes it to open the game menu AND perform the action. That proved to be rather annoying, but it only happened a couple of times to me.
As for the overall game selection? Good, for the most part. While there's a few stinkers in there -- mostly a few of those sports games, painfully-boring "learning games" intended for very young children, and I'm not sure why an intriguing but nigh-unplayable prototype of Tempest for the 2600 is stuffed in there, but yep it's there too -- a lot of them are good, simple fun, which offsets the bad. Warlords is a blast, Yars' Revenge is a classic, Millipede is great fun, and Asteroids... well, it's Asteroids. It's hard to screw up Asteroids. The arcade versions of some 2600 games are obviously the superior version, but I like playing both of them, just to take note of and enjoy the differences. Though it's definitely missing a few 2600 games I would have liked to see (no Jungle Hunt? Battlezone? Berzerk, even?), it's a great collection on its own, even if most of the better 2600 games were produced by other companies or based on licensed properties.
Criticisms? Well... emulation quality is fine, sound is okay, the menus and options are fairly easy to navigate... I suppose some of the manual scans are a bit on the fuzzy, low-res side, so it makes them kinda hard to read at times. And the "soundtrack" isn't very prevalent anywhere except the menus, where you are bound to spend essentially 5% of your overall playtime in. It sounds fine, if a little forgettable. Maybe an option to include tunes (or your own personal songs) during gameplay would be welcome? (I for one like to play the Tempest 2000 soundtrack while I'm playing Tempest, but that's just me.) These aren't serious or grating issues for me, though.
Now, despite my glowing praise, I would have to say my recommendation is "conditional", in a sense.
By all means, these games are classics, and I believe it's important to preserve and remember them. Reintroducing these titles to the newer generation is also something I enjoy the prospect of. But, well... if you aren't nostalgic for these games, then you should be aware that these are from a very different period of videogame history. These games are very simple, both in concept and design. Reading the manual is usually required. They may confuse and frustrate you as easily as they can inspire and entertain. They can potentially offer hours upon hours of enjoyment, or you can play them for five minutes and get bored. Yet, at twenty dollars for a hundred games, there's not much risk involved. Why not give it a try? Set a few high scores while you're at it, too.
TL;DR, a great collection of Atari classics and an excellent value to boot. You really can't go wrong.

How do I put this without spoiling anything at all?
Well, let met start from the top: Serena is story driven. Heavily story driven. A first person explorer, you play a nameless man in a cabin trying to piece together memories of his relationship with his supposed wife, the titular Serena. To do that, you must explore and click on items and objects in the tiny cabin.
The game is simply an interactive horror mystery novel and seems simplistic, but the writing is of a calibre alongside Poe and Lovecraft. Josh Mandel delivers a brilliant performance as the protagonist, and the story will grip you to the very, very end. There's simply no reason to not play this game and experience its story. It's enough to give one chills, and plenty to make one ponder.

I'm very critical when it comes to this type of indie game, but the writing in this one is actually very good. Perhaps most importantly for me, the dialogue writing feels fresh and interesting. The story keeps your curiosity piqued, and your brain working on figuring out the mystery. It's good stuff.
It gets off to a really good start that's almost immediately very engaging and dramatic (in no small part due to the soundtrack), and its characters feel surprisingly nuanced.
You get access to various unusual abilities that you can use while exploring or during conversations, and it meshes really well with the story (even if some are more useful than others. But I don't really see that as a flaw.)
Lots of things about this game work really well, but it does have a few pretty significant problems:
I've had to restart the game multiple times before I was able to finish it due to various technical problems, the most common of which is that some characters will get stuck before they reach their destination, and can never get unstuck.
Another odd issue i got was that the game's save files seemingly deleted themselves overnight.
It's very easy to get stuck not knowing what flag you haven't tripped so you can move on to the next thing. But the game dialogue is also oddly structured, which hurts the game's pacing.
Often, you seemingly need to "talk to everyone about everything", but the dialogue trees are oddly designed in that choices don't "stick". You can say every possible choice by just repeating a certain dialogue tree path.
If you haven't exhausted all your dialogue with a character, there's a "..." icon, but it doesn't go away before you've made every possible choice.
So the problem is the character you're controlling has to be a total weirdo who starts multiple identical conversations about the same topic by saying the exact same thing at first, and then ends it by, for example, stating wildly different opinions each time, say, 4 or 5 times, to the same character. This doesn't make sense in the narrative of the game, and stands out especially because the game is well written.
It seems to me that the game is signalling that exhausting all of these dialogue options and thus removing the "..." icon from every character is required to progress - but I'm honestly not sure how that really works. It's entirely unclear as you're playing, and becomes especially apparent if you (like me) end up playing the game multiple times.
Skill and effort went into crafting this story, and I recommend this game to people who enjoy a good mystery.
If you can find a way to back-up your save files, then you might want to do that in case a character gets stuck, or the saves decide to disappear like mine. Or just beat it in one sitting.
I found it quite enjoyable despite having seen perhaps the worst of its flaws.

Just finished Half Life and wanted to write a review. Wow, Im deeply divided on this.
On the one hand the level design was pretty nice, the story ineteresting, environments good, graphics are alright, sound is ok, but soundtrack isnt anything special though.
On the other, controls felt awkward and caused a lot of deaths, in most situations the game tries to take you by surprise and it often feals it gets cheap kills (if yore low on HP, you may die from falls that are scripted, if you dont have grenades in some ares youre screwed, etc), some of the weapon functionality isnt explained, for example, only at the end I realised that if the laser sight is on the rockets will mimick your movements when launched (Lord, that was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥, how some other weapons worked I didnt understand at all. The game creates an environment where you will get killed a lot unless you know the layout of the missions and know well how to use controls and weapons. Being careful, attentive and having good reflexes will often be not enough if youre playing this for the first time, there is often little room to maneuver on the spot. Its basically challenging you to play it again. Thing is, there is not much incentive in this day and age to play it again once you beat the story.
Even though this game made me frustrated quite often, I will give it a positive review, considering its a 20 years old game and, what was the deciding factor for me, I really liked the end credits music after you finish the game. )))
All in all, it is a good game.
But be warned, you should only get this in the bundle with the rest of the franchise and on sale. The price is way to big for todays standards.
And note, if youre not good at FPS, the frustration from the levels may overweigh the enjoyment of everything else. I havent played FPS games from the 90's, but there is a reason people say "difficulty like in the old shooters". (even though I dislike this kind of difficulty.)

Adewale is a black former slave from the old English-French-American triangle-trades where the blacks were used as slave to pick cotton, and different plants for plantage owners. Like 70% of the gameplay is to free slaves, and a bit is the old piracy from AC:IV where you steer another pirate ship just like in AC:IV but with Adewale as the captain onboard. It's some real fun if you didn't have enough of AC:IV. And myself, I miss AC:IV after finishing it because I feel that something more besides the campaign mode would be much appreciated. There was a time, about a year ago, this game wasn't actively updated by the developers. It sat untouched for nearly a year, with things like body temperature and hunger to manage. Realistic, yes. Fun? Not as much as it could have been.
Fast forward to now, and you can (and probably WILL) make your own settlement. Fish-folk, deadly plant-people, hyper-advanced monkeys and wingless birds living in a settlement run by a collection of plasma with guns.
The music is fantastic. Curtis Schweitzer deserves much more credit for this than he does, it's some of the most gorgeous music I've heard in a video game in a very long time. The scenery is fantastic, and the universe feels endless. There's so much to explore- planets that are 90% water, planets that have long since frozen over, and more await you in the expanses of space.
If you've been on the fence about Starbound, I implore you- try it. It's one of my favorite games, and it's only getting better.

All in all this game is amazing, and for the price it is at you shouldn't even hesitate to buy this game immediatly!

In Angry Arrows, you take upon the role of Legolas who has to battle hordes of Uruk-hai to rescue Princess Zelda from  the Legend of Zelda series in an alternate timeline in which she no longer wears a dress and has brown hair. Despite no longer being blonde, Zelda has gotten significantly more stupid: the alternate dimension has stripped her of her Triforce of Wisdom, leaving her with only two apparent skills: getting kidnapped and catching arrows with her face.
In this timeline, the wizard Saruman has improved the Uruks originally created by Sauron: he made them green and also very good at shooting long bows. Also, he invented suicide bomber spiders or something; he can do that, he's a wizard, you know.
Anyways, in this quest to rescue Princess Zelda twenty-five times, Legolas can rescue Zelda alone or with up to three other companions: Link, Hawkeye, or Red the Green Arrow on the same machine with local co-op. However, Legolas works alone, which is why I worked through the campaign by myself without any other person's help. And no other reason.
Besides rescuing Princess Zelda, you can also play as Garrett that guy from Thief and be in a sneaky forest in a randomly generated time trials kind of game thing, or you can also play as some guy who fights orcs in a gladitorial arena. I've considered Tales games to basically be the vanilla ice cream of JRPGs for the better part of a decade now. Although they never sunk to Compile Heart's level of literally copy-pasting entire dungeons into three consecutive games, Namco Bandai wasn't terribly interested in surprising anyone who'd played one of their games before - whether it was the general theme of the power of friendship or such bizarrely specific elements as a character that coudln't cook, Tales was basically just reskinning itself every few years. It never produced a bad game, but most of the positive memories I have of the recent series are from laughing at it rather than with it.
Berseria, thankfully, changes that. It's still a long way from competing for #1 JRPG, but it's the first time in ages that I felt like Namco really tried. They've made a genuinely entertaining cast and world, and even more remarkably, a plot that's largely unique, I can actually recommend Berseria for its story, and that's not something I thought I'd be saying about a Tales game ever again.
That said, longstanding series issues remain. The dungeons are filled with wholly unnecessary stretches of nothing and "puzzles" that mostly consist of running to every end of said nothingness. Despite all-around improvements in the writing, some lines are still comically heavy-handed. The soundtrack is completely forgettable. The combat system is clumsily explained across basically the entire length of the game. And so on. Berseria is absolutely still entertaining despite these issues, but they're enough to prevent it from being truly great.
Essential if you've ever enjoyed a Tales game, and strongly recommended to JRPG fans in general. Here's hoping Namco Bandai's newfound creativity isn't just a one-off.

Normally I don't bother with reviews, but for Street Fighter 5 I felt like I had to. This game has launched in such a sorry state that it has to be mentioned as many times as possible.
What Capcom is trying to sell you here is a broken, bare boned game, along with a promise of future content updates for 60$. Standard and expected modes are missing here. Arcade mode, Vs. CPU, a proper tutorial mode, etc. About 75% of the game is "coming soon".
What's included in the package is Online mode, Local VS, Training, Survival, and Character Stories.
- Character stories are mini stories that feature poor quality illustrations, and anywhere from 2-4 single round fights. The fights are the same every time, and the A.I. does little more than just stand there as a punching bag. For clearing a characters story, you unlock the ability to purchase an alternate costume for the character in the store. The store however is not available and is "coming soon". You should just automatically unlock the costumes, and it's even more insulting that you don't when most characters are fighting in the story mode wearing the alt.
- Survival mode is exactly what it sounds like. You go through a number of opponents depending on difficulty. You can also spend or gamble points off your score to help you advance, which is cool. For completing the each difficulty of survival you can unlock character colors. However, It can be a frustrating experience with how unstable the game and servers are at this time. Disconnects are frequent, and if it happens you're automatically taken back to the main screen and all progress is lost.
The rest of the modes are pretty standard affair and need no explanation. It would have been nice to have a proper tutorial mode though, which is absent. They have a mini tutorial when you first start the game, which consists of just a quick explanation of what each button does and how to move your character forward, really basic things like that. It also tells you how to use v-trigger ability, but has no explanation beyond that. Nothing is explained really. It's like they expect you to know everything already, or you will search out community forums just to learn basics. Proper character tutorials and combo training, etc. needed to be included.
Graphically the game is average. I'm running on max settings, and the game holds a locked 60 frames per second with no issue. The characters and effects look nice, and are animated well. The same can't be said for the stages and backgrounds however. The quality is poor and they're noticeably blurry.
Another visual issue I instantly noticed was the physics. Particularly the breast physics. Breasts jiggle on the character select screen on the 2P side only. Why the 1P side isn't working is a very noticeable eye sore. Jiggle is just as inconsistent and head scratching while fighting as well. For example, a character like Laura should have very noticeable jiggle in both of her costumes, but she has little to none. Rainbow Mika has little to none. Cammy has none. These characters should all have very noticeable jiggle with their outfits. Meanwhile, Chun-li in her cop outfit is jiggling around like crazy, when in reality it should be more subtle in that outfit. The level of jiggle should be dependant on the costume. Little details like that are important. Especially when you have costumes that draw attention to the characters breasts. I like those kinds of costumes very much, but make sure you get the breast physics on point.  Give Team Ninja's boob guy a call if you need help!
The number of control options is also a big problem. Out of box compatibility is for X-Input devices only right now, so controller and arcade stick options are extremely limited without jumping through hoops. Keyboard keybinds can't be changed either for people who enjoy that.
Also in my short time playing I've encountered a soft lock where the game went completely unresponsive, numerous disconnects, and even an error message after closing the game. This too much for < 3 hours of gametime. Seems like the game could be buggy and unstable.
Just to leave on a positive note, the fighting itself is fun, as is the varied and unique 16-man roster. I personally only play as female characters in fighting games, and the girls here don't disappoint. There is a lot of sex appeal and fanservice, which I love. So big thumbs up for that, but they still need to get in touch with Team Ninja or something and get those jiggle physics on point.
As for my recommendation, I can't in good conscience recommend this game. I'd highly recommend waiting till June so all the game modes are added in, and all the other fixes have hopefully arrived, before even considering a purchase. Personally I would have requested a refund if I hadn't bought from GMG.

Some games are over so quickly that it takes a while for their impact to sink in. "Serena" affected me like that, in that I'm still not sure if I should recommend it. There were plenty of things I liked about it: the slow, quiet way the story progressed, the dark and almost claustrophobic feeling of the room in which it takes place, the fact that examining an object further along in the story produces a different response. The voice acting was effective, too, even if it felt a little Tommy Wiseau at times. But would I suggest that *other* people play this?
Yes, if want to question your own sanity.
There's no action here, no puzzles, no extrinsic reward for playing. But there's something about it that strikes close to home. You can go into your living room every day of your life, and then one day, you'll be in "that mood" and remember that the chair in the corner is the one you and your long gone partner used to cuddle in, and you'll cry your eyes out and not know why. That's the nature of memory sometimes, and that's at the core of "Serena". For the protagonist, it takes the entire game to put those memories into place.
When I had beaten the game, I thought, "That's it?" I originally pegged it as having "surface depth", the sort that artsy game developers use to make people immediately go, "Oh, wow, that game gave me soooo many feels!" I hate the obviousness of that approach. So despite how much I liked the atmosphere, I held off on giving it a "thumbs up". But now that I've had time to soak in the experience of playing "Serena", I DO recommend it. The depth is in applying the lessons about memory to your own life -- what things have *you* forgotten that might have changed your life? Did they change you in ways that you're not aware? Can you still learn from your own past, or is it too late?
I realize that interpretation is entirely a reflection of how I see the world, and may not be what anyone else gets out of "Serena". If you enjoy self-reflection after playing a small, quiet, uneventful game, please give this one a go. It might make you sad, it might bore you to tears, but for the chance you might get something valuable out of this, it's well worth the download.

TL;DR: Remember Spacebase DF-9? Pretty much the same thing here. The game is badly optimized, blatantly unfinished, and the developers have abandoned it completely. It is not worth its full price, and I cannot recommend it.
---
Alright, I've tried to stave off writing this review for roughly a year and a half, in hopes the developers would fix the game's bugs (which, in my opinion, should have been done before full release) and work towards giving us more content. Unfortunately, it seems they have abandoned the game, hence the missing blog page,
and
I will attempt to write a 'fair' review, however.
-Despite the warnings, you can stay on duty forever. I've found that stress and sleep affect nothing, just make sure your hunger bar doesn't drop too low or your officer will stand still and pant for a few seconds.
-You are able to choose between seven different police vehicles, and you can customize them (albeit the customization is lacking).
-You have four vehicles available to purchase for driving while off-duty to avoid the great sin of driving your police vehicle while off-duty despite being the only officer in the city.
-To drive off the monotony of pulling over impaired and speeding drivers and ticketing cars for parking violations, you can receive calls from dispatch and either accept or refuse them. They give you a reason to use the siren, at least.
-Technically, the game delivered on everything it stated in its 'features', barring the amount of missions.
-None of
vehicles are roadworthy. It takes a second or two for the wheels to straighten after fully turning, and for some reason your vehicle engages the warp drive when accelerating above 30 miles per hour. Additionally, the officer physically cannot depress the brake pedal fully, and holding it down for too long, despite still moving forward, will shift the car into reverse and hit the gas.
-The vehicle physics are horrible. Upon colliding with an object, be it a building or a car, no speed will be lost. This can lead to multiple additional collisions as your officer attempts to slow down with the defective brake pedal. The vehicles can climb close to 90 degree slopes, though, so great job to the manufacturers there.
-Nobody knows how to drive. None of the drivers in town can maintain their lanes while making a turn. Additionally, there is a loop near the city where a traffic jam will form every day either because a semi cannot make the left turn into the city without hitting a traffic light, or two drivers collide and, due to the collective inability to reverse, are forever stuck. Any driver you pull over will make two consecutive near 90 degree turns while slamming on the brakes, most of the time leading you to either ramming them or passing them. Fleeing drivers will also slam on the brakes after you collide three times, causing the same problem.
-The pathfinding (or lack thereof) is terrible. The pedestrians in the game are on rails, which often lead them directly into parked cars or a building. Fleeing suspects will proceed directly away from the player on the nearest rail, or to the nearest rail if not already on a rail. This can lead them to shooting directly up a mountain, as, like in vehicles, forward speed is never decreased. Movement can only be blocked by vehicles and buildings.
-Fleeing suspects are a nuisance. Fleeing vehicles usually lead to high damage to your police vehicle. Fleeing suspects run at the same speed or faster than your officer, making chasing them on foot rarely worth it. In addition...
-Your officer forgets how to run. When pulling out any of their equipment, your officer will revert back to walking speed. In addition, your officer will only make a brisk jog at max when aiming their weapon, leading to great difficulty when attempting to tase a fleeing suspect.
-Sometimes, after going off duty and returning to duty, the dispatcher decides to quit, and you will no longer receive any calls.
-Weather and tire smoke tanks your FPS.
-Many police vehicles have clipping issues with both your officer and any arrested suspect.
-Some zones don't have gas stations.
There are probably many more cons I could list here, but it's 2:05 in the morning and I'm too tired to think of anything else the developers left broken or unfinished.
-Play on realistic mode. You can be given up to three calls at a time, so it gives you stuff to do. The permadeath really doesn't matter.
-Don't worry about your reputation. The game only ends if you manage to get -1000. So feel free to uphold the law differently.
-The SMG keeps you alive a lot better than the pistol.
-Suburbs usually gives you drug-related or burglary calls. Lake usually gives you assault or kidnapping calls. The rest are fairly balanced.
So yeah. That's my review. I'm going to go pass out in a pile of blankets now.

There are interesting concepts and good gameplay mechanics here, and it's an interesting fusion of RPG and management sim, but it fails to do either very well. There are basically two parts of the game; the first is going out to fight zombies and find supplies, the second is managing your base.
The combat is fairly standard turn-based rpg with basic attack options. Character progression slowly strengthens your character and unlocks new abilities, with a strong emphasis on "slowly". Equipment is very uninspired; just 3 different tiers of most items in the game without any unique abilities or qualities. There's nothing really wrong with the combat, other than it being so dull and basic that there's nothing this game offers combatwise that many other RPGs do much better
The base management showed promise but ended up being very dull. At 3 hours in I had more survivors than I knew what to do with and very few raw materials, so the decion-making was obvious given a lack of choices. Again, the management portion of the game really fell flat for me.
I played on the normal difficulty there was never really any sense of urgency or threat, severely weakening the impact of the permnanent death aspect of the game since I never really felt under threat or close to dying. The UI also has a lot of room for improvement and was immediately offputting to me, but I ended up getting used to it.  I found myself bored around two hours in, but stuck with it for another hour because I was hoping it improve, but the next hour was similar slow-paced grinding and I had to stop.

After following the developement of this game for over one year I was lucky and had the chance to back it.
While following the developement of the game I rised many expectations very high. After my first hours of playing each of them had been confirmed.
Now after nearly 90 hours of alpha testing and further 20 of Early Access I have new friends all around the world, know (more or less) what it means having an entire crew to captain and also to be responsible of and had so much fun like only few other games gave me.
The strong team based character of Blackwake, makes it a very social video game, in which it matters more being well coordinated with the rest of the crew rather than being singularly skilled. This makes it a game for everyone who likes to feel the power that good teamplay could give one. No special ability or skill is required to play this game (you don't have to be a tactics expert nor to be a great FPS player), the two main keys of Blackwake are listening and talking, short: communication is everything!
People who are real lone warriors and prefer playing on their own, rather than being part of a team, will have not much fun playing BW, everyone else will feel the drill of good teamwork from the very beginning on.

Let's say you had all the time in the world to read every single review for Half-Life, and then you realize much of those reviews are positive and are usually saying the same thing other reviews have said. Remember that all these reviews are coming from all types of people and opinion differs, yet this game has manage to make the majority love it.
That's one of Half-Life's accomplishments. Along side making a dude who trash talks Microsoft and looks like Michael Moore into the most recognizable business men in the game industry, making Steam the #1 online service to play video games on PC
and giving a future for Valve and the rest of the gaming world to enjoy.
Half-Life takes it's story from other works of Si-fi, with aliens and a science experiment gone too far. This sounds so cliché, yet the way Half-Life does it makes it fun. There's other si-fi shooter back in the 90's no doubt, but Half-Life never breaks immersion (aside loading) and puts you HEV boots of Gordon Freeman. You'll find whatever went wrong, and when you do, I'll be damned if you aren't surprised
This game never breaks immersion (aside loading times) 'cause your hands are never off the keyboard and Mouse, you are always running and shooting. Not because you know you'll die if you don't, 'cause you feel like you need to. The amount of enemies in this game is huge! You have 8 alien types with different abilities and speeds. Some can shoot, some can bite, and some will slash. Then there's the army who can take a shotgun blast standing and eates a bowl of nailes for breakfast, without milk. There's Black Ops chicks who do crazy moves you'd see in Ninja Gaiden who were the hardest of them all! Luckly for you, you carry an arsenal, some work better than others. In short, combat is tight.
If you like those 90's FPS sound effects, and don't mind dumb voice acting, then you'll love this! Although it sounds crappy in today's standers, it's not that bad, and it's surely not enough to break immersion. The music on the other hand is amazing! You get pumped up when you reach a new part of the game and the music changes while enemies come at you. I'd say it's good enough to blast in your car, so bust out the AUX cord.
This game looks like hell, but with the HD pack, it like putting a little bit of salt. But looks shouldn't be a problem since the gameplay works so well, plus graphics are not a problem unless you're a 13 year little kid who bashes 90's game for looking bad while still playing Minecraft. For me, it's the way 90's games were made, you had to work with limitations, and if you did a good job, then you earned it.
As a man, if this game was a woman, I would marry. Then I buy the best house for her, and if I really have to, I'd rob a bank to afford it. If you're a girl, then just think of this game as your dream boat who's a vampire and is into some BDSM stuff.
But in all seriousness this game was amazing enough to do a lot in the gaming world. We have this game to thank for just even reading this review alone. Consider getting this game whenever you got the time, and usually it's only a dollar during the sales, so that's just great enough time to get it.

Even if that isn't the case, however, there seems to be plenty to do with what I have now, and I still have several other beginning jobs to unlock.
The zombies all have different abilities and stats based on what they were when they were alive, which I think is a pretty neat idea. Battles aren't difficult, but they slowly start to weaken your party over time after back to back fights, which I think makes it more 'realistic' in a sense.

Assassin’s Creed Freedom Cry is a standalone game that follows the same pattern as its predecessor did, Black Flag, but this time the main protagonist was a secondary character on the previous title, Adéwalé, being an assassin and many years after the ending of Black Flag, we found ourselves stranded on Port-au-Prince, with no ship and no crew, we must struggle to find our way out of there, though now his motivations are focused on the liberation of slaves that suffer greatly in the new world.
1735 is the year and Adéwalé is now an Assassin, embracing the creed’s beliefs and struggle, he finds himself stranded in Port-au-Prince. But after many years of piracy he decides now is time to put the Creed’s name to a good use and begin a new fight and the liberation of slaves, helping the resistance called The Maroons for independence and dignity, Adéwalé and his skills turn out to be of great help to the resistance. Before leaving, he helps building a new hope for the slaves.
The game mechanics don’t change that much compared to Black Flag, though some new load-out for a new assassin is required as per usual, for Adéwalé we have now some powerful weapons like the blunderbuss and machete, while the blunderbuss is a one-shot gun, its power doesn’t have match, it is a slow weapon but once you have multiple enemies facing you, one blow will kill most of them, if not all, making it a death fest every time you pull the trigger.
On the other hand, the machete is kind of new to us, we have mostly used swords before, but Adéwalé with machete in hand makes him, perhaps the most brutal and relentless fighter of all assassins in my opinion, he is just a beast and the killing animations are proof of it, a good tool for a great and skilled killer.
Many other things remain the same, there are not many differences, smoke bombs, the rope dart and the poison and sleep darts are kept, a small addition were the firecrackers that will help you with guards at some point in the story, besides that, the game remains almost the same.
Naval combat is the same as well, and the map is very limited, but makes sense, this game is not that long and the exploration is restricted to some few islands and locations.
The interesting part of this game is and will always be slavery, our struggle is focused on the liberation of slaves, there are plantations in different parts of the map which can be raided and liberated, this will help you unlock new items and missions and also bring new people to the resistance, also during naval combat you will encounter enemy ships carrying many ore slaves, this ships cannot be attacked but they will always have protection. In the main city, small groups of slaves can be liberated as well, either from punishment, caging or auctions.
There are not many things to say on this point, it looks the same as Black Flag, equally beautiful, so if you want to know more, read my Black Flag review.
The sound remains identical to Black Flag as well, voices are full of passion and the accents are great. On the music side, we have some new sounds and tunes that are related to the culture, some sort of African like melodies with chants in French, this makes the atmosphere of the game and the slavery theme. Awesome.
While ACFC remains bug free and found no issues in-game, I really believe that some few things could have been different to my taste. For example, after liberating plantations, a good idea would have been to destroy at some point certain plantations, setting them on fire or destroying the crops, making them a waste of time to rebuild, this came to my mind after seeing how many times x plantation had a new owner after a few minutes, making it an endless loop of liberation, makes sense, yes, slaves were a profitable business back then and at some point someone will bring more and more, but stopping them once and for all would have been more satisfying in the end.
ACFC is a good game on its own, it doesn’t have the same spectrum as previous titles and the character is not developed in depth, but that is not a problem when it comes to action and the brutal way we kill enemies. There are some scenes that truly show how slavery was back in that time, it was terrible and at some point you can see how the life of the slaves was regarded as disposable by the masters and the empires. There are heartbreaking moments to say the least.
All in all, it was an enjoyable game, with more pros than cons, new tools and weapons and a very satisfying gameplay, Adéwalé is a killing machine!

I've considered Tales games to basically be the vanilla ice cream of JRPGs for the better part of a decade now. Although they never sunk to Compile Heart's level of literally copy-pasting entire dungeons into three consecutive games, Namco Bandai wasn't terribly interested in surprising anyone who'd played one of their games before - whether it was the general theme of the power of friendship or such bizarrely specific elements as a character that coudln't cook, Tales was basically just reskinning itself every few years. It never produced a bad game, but most of the positive memories I have of the recent series are from laughing at it rather than with it.
Berseria, thankfully, changes that. It's still a long way from competing for #1 JRPG, but it's the first time in ages that I felt like Namco really tried. They've made a genuinely entertaining cast and world, and even more remarkably, a plot that's largely unique, I can actually recommend Berseria for its story, and that's not something I thought I'd be saying about a Tales game ever again.
That said, longstanding series issues remain. The dungeons are filled with wholly unnecessary stretches of nothing and "puzzles" that mostly consist of running to every end of said nothingness. Despite all-around improvements in the writing, some lines are still comically heavy-handed. The soundtrack is completely forgettable. The combat system is clumsily explained across basically the entire length of the game. And so on. Berseria is absolutely still entertaining despite these issues, but they're enough to prevent it from being truly great.
Essential if you've ever enjoyed a Tales game, and strongly recommended to JRPG fans in general. Here's hoping Namco Bandai's newfound creativity isn't just a one-off.

is a murder mystery adventure game where you play a ghost with the ability to possess each of her potential murderers and lead them to find clues against one another in order to figure out whoddunit. A great concept, excellent execution, fun world design that rewards exploration with insight, just a wonderful and memorable gaming experience.
I am so into these games that offer unique modes of storytelling, I mean, it's a brilliant solution to a concept I've always hated in games: dead-eyed, slack-jawed NPCs who sit around waiting for you to do every little thing. You're ostensibly playing one entity, but really this game has more in common with "split the party" type horror games like
or
where you play different people caught in the vortex of one event, each with their own fully realized personalities and desires. The care that has been put into constructing the characters is really what makes the game so great. Each character has unique music that plays when possessing them, a unique mindscape that can be peeked into, a unique placement in the societal incubator that is the setting, and each has different methods of talking to the other characters and dealing with the world they're situated in. In order to possess them, the game asks that you understand them, and thus witness them through the eyes of the people around them and then ultimately through their own.
What results is a game that feels very empathic, very alive, where both the player and the characters seem to have so much agency towards pushing the story forward and solving the mystery. This ties into the existential crises of nearly all the characters, which range from poverty to surviving the suicide of a loved one to facing their own imminent deaths, the game offers several discussions on time and moving forward, overcoming traumas and spending whatever time you are given meaningfully and not just keeping your head down and doing the bare minimum to achieve comfort.
And the mystery is good! And more importantly, it's something you can figure out with the clues you're given even before you get to the final judgement, though how to organize those clues into evidence is harder than it initially seems.
Now, I did face a little bugginess, but nothing game ruining. Also I would have liked everyone to have different colored text boxes or something, it gets confusing in group scenarios. Otherwise... its-a goooood.

This game is very story driven, all characters have their own individual personalities, and it's an emotionally-challenging game. And I'll define how well-driven.
Your choices matter for how this story goes. The protagonist you control and the choices you make will define how characters will think of your protagonist.
Your choices and actions will carry from Episode to Episode, which is a rarity... unless you're talking Tell Tale Games.

Such a neat little casual mystery game. As the title implies, this game's universe revolves around a journey at sea on what seems to be a particularly small cruise ship.
You - as the player - are handed control over a spirit. And that spirit is an energetic remnant of what was once a human being, who unfortunately died under strange circumstances.
The fun thing about controlling this spirit, is the ability to float through doors. And that inevitably means you get to take peeks behind closed doors... in spaces that hold secrets.
Yes... secrets. We're here to uncover secrets. One obvious secret revolving around the protagonist's demise.
But there's more... mhmm, a couple of subplots that tie in beautifully with the main plot.
So, on this ship there's a lot of moving from one cabin to another on different floors (which unfortunately has the process feeling repetitive and even dreadful at some point, but because the story takes place on a tiny cruise ship; it's kind of fun and doable, thanks to speedy movement of the spirit).
This spirit has no memory of what happened, where, when or how it occurred (which is very distressing & confusing to this little residual ball of energy), but of course we are here to do something about that, ey!
And the way this is done, is by first being informed of the spirit's death, thru a very young passenger on board (i.e. Paulo) who is capable of tapping into the paranormal (and thus, communicating with spirits).
His guidance jumpstarts the exploration process and makes it easier to grasp what's going on and what to do.
He explains the process of possession/mind control, and encourages you to test the process on a cat which happens to be in his cabine at that time.
Concerning possession; the game logic goes as following; the most insecure passengers of the whole lot are to be possessed first - which is simply figured out thru trial-and-error -  and via them you get to know the stronger minded folks (and thus possess them afterwards).
The more you know about someone, the easier it becomes to manipulate them (i.e. their insecurities weaken their aura so-to-speak, and allows for easier 'entry' in their body).
There is a basic possession mode & a full possession mode.
In order to unlock 'full possession' (which in this game, equals the unlocking of specific dialogue lines - which are required in order to progress and find out what really happened - one has to become acquainted fully with all passengers on board.
And this is where a lot of running is done, because you're required to possess each and every one of them to get answers, progress and finish the game.
The one thing that really stuck with me (after finishing up) was the music and the graphics. And heck, even the plot.
The plot was nice. It was good enough and it made sense.
A really cool thing they did in this game is the ability to see inside the passengers minds.
What you get to see is a graphical representation of what their mind looks like (this is done thru clever use of colour, music and specific phrases, which reflect their thoughts & demeanor).
This really adds to the atmosphere of the game.
Each character has their own theme music (which plays when they're possessed + in their cabins) and this really helps grasping their personalities.
On top of this, when the characters converse, their personality is emphasized thru sound & pace (as the dialogue appears on screen).
So even though, there's no voice acting present, it IS possible to 'feel' what the characters are like, because of the smart application of sound & tempo in regard to dialogue.
How this works is; as the words appear on screen, sound is played for every letter that pops up.
I thought that was really awesome. It made a difference. This is a feature I had come across before in games (especially of the RPG type), and it simply works well for this game.
This is a game I would so replay if they ever decided to remake it in an upgraded version :).

A fun, engaging, and well-thought mystery aboard a small ship.
You're dead, and you don't know why, how, or even who you were/are. You're stuck on a cruise ship with a motley assortment of passengers and crew. Everyone is weird. Everyone is suspicious.
Luckily, you can partially possess people and move them around the ship to uncover clues about your death. When you control a fellow seafarer, you not only get to abuse the relationships they have with other people on board, but you get access to a unique skill that can help you move around or talk.
This was a real lucky find for me. I love games like this, especially when they have a "fishbowl" setting. Getting to know the passengers is easy and fun. Learning the truth behind the whole setup is rewarding.
PROS:
-Good story
-Well-writen
-Interesting characters
-Fun mechanics
-Creative ideas
-Easy to learn
-Quick intro (straight into the action)
-Multiple conclusions
CONS:
-Rough around the edges
-Semi-buggy (nothing broke for me)
-Some ideas were under-utilized (unique character actions, etc.)
-Characters at the beginning get neglected at the end
-Mediocre audio
I've seen this is a spiritual sequel, although I never played the first. The one real flaw in this game is that as you play it, something inside you knows it could be better. There's a lot of potential here, either in a completely re-polished version or just another sequel in the same vein. Still, I HAVE to recommend this. It's a fun way to tell a story and it shouldn't be passed up.
PLAYER SKILLS REQUIRED:
-Interest in reading
-Interest in mystery
-Tolerance of trial and error

A simple click sets off a warhead, creating a circular wave of destruction. The explosions are reminiscent to those familiar with ‘Missile Command.’ Perfect timing in launching these warheads creates a chain reaction, blowing up an entire rotating planetary system’s cities or at least that’s the goal. You’ll be wise to plan your shots as eradicating a planetary system with a single warhead, garners the collection of triangular gems. These gems are use to acquire power-ups and presumably, save your species.
While this mayhem and destruction can be overall enthralling, Destructamundo became a chore halfway through. Level progression stalls if you do not collect the necessary resources to gain the power-ups as certain levels cannot be completed without said power-up. This back tracking through previous levels seems forced as, in most cases, the player may not be able to clear the necessary levels with a singular warhead. Not only that but collecting the triangular gems seemed random or broken. Swinging the mouse after clicking a gem seemed to be the most effective in collecting gems en masse. A single click would only net you a single gem or a small surrounding cluster. Mind you, you only receive one click, leaving all the uncollected gems floating lonely in space. The banter between your alien higher-up in the beginning of each level, while light-hearted, can leave you confused. The dialog tends to be strange one offs at the attempt at humor. A chuckle can be heard now and then but the humor inside adds little.

Bastion was produced by Supergiant Games, a modest team of seven people, back in 2011. It follows the story of the player's character, known simply as "The Kid", waking up after a mysterious global disaster called "The Calamity". You are guided by a man's voice, and instructed to head to the titular Bastion for safety.
Bastion's gameplay is akin to an action-RPG. The player controls his character in an isometric world, using the mouse and keyboard (or Xbox controller) to move throughout and interact with his surroundings. Bastion features a large variety of weapons for the player to use, from a simple hammer to a small mortar cannon. The player uses two weapons of his choosing, each with it's own unique mechanics and upgrades. The player fights through levels in a fairly linear fashion, gaining experience points and eventually leveling up. Where Bastion's leveling up differs from a typical RPG is the benefits of gaining levels: Leveling up in Bastion only grants the player one additional point of life- a fairly insignificant bonus. However, in addition to this, you also gain an extra "Spirit" slot. These spirits, chosen from the Bastion's distillery, grant the player special effects, often with conditions on their usage. One such spirit, known as "Werewhiskey", causes the player to always score critical hits on their enemies, but only works when the player's life points are critically low. Another one, Leechade, causes the player's attacks to leech life points from enemies, but severely reduces the effectiveness of the life-restoring tonics you find along your journey.
Overall Bastion's gameplay is extremely enjoyable, but is also fairly easy. The games tries to compensate for this by the inclusion of a shrine, in which the player can opt to make the game more difficult in exchange for increased money and experience gains. These difficulty increases come in the form of special bonuses granted to the enemies, ranging from regenerating health to a chance to reflect the player's attacks back at them. While this seems like an elegant solution to complaints about the game's difficulty, many of the difficulty modifiers result in the gameplay becoming more tedious without actually making the game significantly harder.
Bastion's soundtrack features a great variety of musical motifs, drawing from Western, Folk, Blues, and many others. These tracks are all highly memorable, and musical are often synced amazingly well with the events of the game, with the music picking up as a battle grows more tense, or cutting dramatically to punctuate a big plot reveal. One of the most memorable songs from the game is the one that plays over the credits, combining parts of each character's own theme to make a song that is nigh-unforgettable:
However, the music is not the only striking part of Bastion's soundtrack. Bastion features a narration of the game's events from the point of view of Rucks, another character within the game. Rucks, voiced by Logan Cunningham, reacts to your actions as you progress through a level – sometimes delving into the history of a location within the game, or other times directly addressing something the player did. For instance, in the introductory level, falling off a ledge prompts Rucks to say: "And then The Kid fell to his death. Just kiddin'!" The narration is filled with interesting little touches such as these, as well as glimpses into Rucks' own backstory and personality, as he tells The Kid's story. Finally, the narration also greatly enhances the atmosphere of the game at times. When you enter what remains of The Hanging Gardens, you find the ashen husks of people. As you walk down the path, Rucks recounts the names and professions of the people you pass, punctuating each sentence with a sorrowful "...he didn't make it."
Pictured: The Kid, standing in what remains of Caelondia's Hanging Gardens. Nordy the bird boy... didn't make it.
Pictured: The Kid, fighting Queen Anne, a massive creature known as an "Anklegator."
Bastion's graphics are, simply put, fantastic. They capture the mood of the scene beautifully, without getting boring. In the first screenshot above, the player is meant to feel that they are in a desolate place. You meet very few enemies, and instead find what remains of the people who did not survive. While the scene is dark, there is still a nice range of color, without which the scene would become boring quickly. The second screenshot takes place in the Roathus Lagoon, home of the dreaded Anklegator, Queen Anne. The lagoon also houses a wide variety of colorful plants and animals. Additionally, as you progress through the lagoon, the rain starts to pick up, which is represented with a murky filter over the scene. Despite this, it is still easy to make out all the various colors of the lagoon. Little touches like these are what makes Bastion's graphics truly spectacular.
Close to the end of the game, The Kid makes a long journey on foot to collect an important item for the Bastion. This journey takes seven days' time within the game, but is represented by giving the player a few small levels to play through, each with a caption to show how far along he is, jumping forward from day one, to three, and then to seven. At the start of this journey, there's a light rain, turning to heavy rain and finally snow as The Kid approaches his goal, travelling through a wide variety of terrains along the way. The use of differing weather and terrain give the impression that this has been a long journey without having to show the entirety of it.
Bastion features a New Game+ mode, allowing the player to play through the game again from the beginning, but keeping all of the thing they unlocked in the previous playthrough. While this feature is by no means a bad addition, it serves to make an already easy game even easier by giving you access to your fully-upgraded weapons from the start of the game.  The narration is actually a big motivator for repeat playthroughs- you can stumble across interesting comments from Rucks that you missed on your initial pass through the game. However, small pieces of flavor text coupled with a rather hit-or-miss system for adjusting difficulty mean Bastion's replay value leaves something to be desired.
Overall, I feel that Bastion is a must-own game for any gamer. Between it's spectacular presentation and highly memorable soundtrack and story, Bastion is a game that is sure to leave a lasting impression.

After following the developement of this game for over one year I was lucky and had the chance to back it.
While following the developement of the game I rised many expectations very high. After my first hours of playing each of them had been confirmed.
Now after nearly 90 hours of alpha testing and further 20 of Early Access I have new friends all around the world, know (more or less) what it means having an entire crew to captain and also to be responsible of and had so much fun like only few other games gave me.
The strong team based character of Blackwake, makes it a very social video game, in which it matters more being well coordinated with the rest of the crew rather than being singularly skilled. This makes it a game for everyone who likes to feel the power that good teamplay could give one. No special ability or skill is required to play this game (you don't have to be a tactics expert nor to be a great FPS player), the two main keys of Blackwake are listening and talking, short: communication is everything!
People who are real lone warriors and prefer playing on their own, rather than being part of a team, will have not much fun playing BW, everyone else will feel the drill of good teamwork from the very beginning on.
I could write a lot about this game and how much I missed one like this before. Just a few more notes:
- people playing are (mostly) friendly, they help and explain with devotion.
- the learning curve is very steep and even steeper after watching one or two gameplays (reccomend The Alboe Show).
- BW is an immeasurable ton of fun.
- the many different things one could do on a ship and the speed with which one has to adapt to each different situation make sure one never gets bored by the dynamic of the game.
Last but not least (I thought about this a lot and I'm still wondering how amazing it is):
Blackwake has been created by just two (2!!!!) persons!!!
Thank you for the magnificent idea and for the great effort you put into developing Blackwake!
