TL;DR A brilliant game ruined by bad executive decisions
Fallout 3 and 4 have both been beautifully entertaining games, even though story wise, I still prefer Fallout 3. Fallout 4 itself is good and there is plenty to love and hours among hours to kill in play time, which has been covered in detail in other reviews.
One thing which has always made Bethesda games great, is the modding capabilities of the engine and the small army of skilled modders working individually or in groups to add anything between small and big changes to the game. Bethesda had tried once before to introduce paid mods in an attempt to monetize these modders works and has failed because of the community resistance. While I clearly understand that some mods are so excellent and vast that they could well work as a full game expansion and people would want their favourite modders rewarded for their hard work, its important to understand that this is not what is happening here. Bethesda is outsourcing development to external contractors, and selling small bits for premium prices. I sincerely doubt that the hourly salary for those modders would match what Bethesda would have to pay if they'd develop the same content in house. While this is a smart business move, I don't believe for a second its in the interest of modders or customers in the long run.
Its easy to dismiss the thousands of negative reviews in response to this, as "review bombing of angry <insert favourite gamer insult here>" and it may be true for a fraction of them. But if you scroll through them and see the playtime hours of many of these reviews, you'll see that you are looking at players who often have hundreds of hours and are obviously still playing and caring enough years after the release (and most other players have moved on) to actually write these reviews. In other words, you are actually looking at the most loyal part of the customer base of this game, the people who still have it installed after all this time, often with hundreds of mods and they are exactly the customers Bethesda now tries to sell mods to. Clearly, this is a reaction of having a something forced upon players which they don't want (after all we can't deactivate or uninstall creation club) and since there are little other options for players to make their voice heard, giving a thumbs down to indicate one doesn't like what is being done with ones favourite game, is a legitimate option.

While the game is unique and super fun, I yet would still recommend to wait, though i only played for a bit, I noticed several things that are still missing, and knowing the early access way of games, I'd keep the money in the wallet, but just in case , I wouldn't rush to buy it. However it is still a great game and super fun !

Half-Life is one of if not the most iconic video game series there is. In the first installment you play as Gordon Freeman a Human test subject that is on the run after an experiment goes wrong. Do not be fooled by its age as even to this day it has some of the best physics and story a game has to offer.
Pros:
-Massive array of weapons allowing for the user to make decisions on what one is the best for that certain situation
-Multiple enemies including Human and Alien types all with there own fighting styles for the player to counter
-Indepth story with many different easter eggs for the user to experiance
-Options to change the model you play as well as the mark you make on surfaces in the game
-Advanced physics engine that still to this day is one of the best
-Allows the player to interact with the enviroment
-Option to play stealthy in certain situations allowing for hidden areas to be found
-Due to its age it can run on any system made in the past 10 years with ease
Cons:
-Small amount of NPC models meaning that many of the allies you encounter have the same voices and appearances
-Can be hard to understand at some points due to no objective being displayed to the player
-Sometimes the player can glitch into certain objects leaving them with no other option that to reload an older save
Overall
Overall i would say that this is one of the best games i have ever played in terms of story and player interaction. Therefore i would rate this game a solid 10/10 and encourage anyone to give it a try even if they are sceptical about it due to its age!

Sleeping Dogs, i.e. "True Crime Hong Kong", is a third-person GTA style free-roamer set in Hong Kong. You play an undercover cop infiltrating the triad known as Song On Yee, and you will swear blood oaths with various triad members, as you understand they are just people like you, yet you will need to bring them to justic at some point. As the story progresses, you will do whatever needs to be done to stay undercover, even if it means eliminating witnessses, kill a few innocents, all for the greater good, perhaps. As the dividing line between good and evil blur, you will find out perhaps not all is as simple as you thought things to be.
The various areas of Hong Kong have been simplified but the flavor had been retained. It is big enough to hold races, and various races are already available in the game (with more available via DLC). There are dozens of different vehicles in various classes, plus motorcycles, and if you don't want to run around all day taxis are always avaialble. And there are always tons of things to do (until you manage to do all of them). There are food stands that gives you a boost in various areas, clothing stores to buy outfits (some gives you bonus), car shops to "buy" cars, as well as missions such as clean up a gang near a certain hotspot by beating them up, hack the camera nearby, then call in the cops when a mastermind come along. There are also special crime solving missions that have you chase down leads or car stealing missions where the "dealer" want a particular model of car "obtained". Add that to "collectibles" (found all around town, several different types), and over a dozen DLCs that adds more outfits, more missions, more weapons, and more vehicles, and you have a total experience.
The game doesn't skimp on combat either. Most combat is melee involving various forms of kung fu, and you will either fight barehand or with weapon (from cleaver to knife, tire iron to lead pipe) There are a few improvised weapon as well (ever tried... fish?)  There are guns avaiable for certain missions, but they are NOT that popular. in HK. You will learn more moves as you go along.
All in all, Sleeping Dogs is GTA in Hong Kong with a TON of options, and it will take you dozens of hours to complete, and you can even challenge other players on the Rockstar "social" web to establish records and such. And the makers are still pumping out the occasional DLC. Just buy them while they're on sale, and enjoy them.

The game consists of managing your people and camp as you try to scavenge from 1 of the 4 areas (well 2 but at day or night and there is a camp but you can only do story stuff there) 3 more get added later (city day/night and desert). you can try to do all 20 random parts to an area to fight the boss or leave when you want or when you run low on supplies. each part consist of a fight and sometimes you find something to search. fights can be just a few zombies/punks, 2-3 wave fights or just having wondering survivors help you for a fight.
STRADIGIES AND GAME INFO
when you play i suggest focusing on one 1 ranged weapon per person (if they have points in one go with it) and melee (since you'll be using melee when you run out of bullets) also focus on 1 of the 4 jobs (these give bonuses in fights too) but doont do both on the same people. if you can spar it take 1 in engineering (for a molly or up to 3 for a spike trap) and 3 in medic for a combat heal. you'll want to have 3-4 main fighters who focus on a weapon and melee and only put a few states in your job so you can do something (hunting most likely or guard to help your main guard. these 2 are most helpful at low levels). then the rest focus on jobs you'll NEED 1 guard and they should be an ok fighter (your guard(s) can get into fight. if this happens all people on guard will be in the fight). make 1 dedicated crafter (not only will they make better gear but it will be of higher levels) then you can decide if you want a dedicated medical person and hunting can be done with 1 point though you'll get more food with more points.
weapons and usefulness
=Melee: you'll be using them when your low on ammo so fighters should have a few points in this. this also gives you strength. =you'll want anyone you take scavenging to have points in this as you'll only use ammo when you have extra or for harder fights like past area 10, military, bosses and maybe punks. if you don't max it go for the 2nd to last ability because it give you 2 hits and the one before this one is a knockdown=
=shotgun: not overly strong but this is good against groups or just 1 enemy. this also gives you focus. =go for the 2nd ability right off then the others when you can, it hits all enemies and the one after has knockdown.=
=handgun: its ok but its main use is in disabling your target and the strongest attack hits 3 times (for 3 ammo). this also gives you focus. =i only use this if the character has high states in it or i have very few people using them but if you have it its best to max it out for the 3shot move but the 2nd ability is very good also since it stuns=
=assault rifle: this is really good BUT you'll burn ammo fast as all but the lowest attack will eat ammo per shot and the later abilities can do 3, 5, or 7 shots as is consumes that much ammo. this also gives you focus. =the first attack hits 3 times for 1 ammo but the 3rd and last abilities shoot 5/7 random shots with a chance to hit any enemy. its good to at lest go for the the 3rd skill for the 5shot move=
=engineering: this is used to use mollies and traps in fights. traps are placed in front of a character and hits any one attacking them in melee range. (you need engineering supplies equipt to use). this also gives you intelligence. =its good to take 1 point in this for a molly and 3 points gives you a spike trap but only go more if you can spar the points=
=medic: this is for healing and removing status effects or even add positive effect to allies. (need medical supplies equipt to use). this also gives you constitution/hp. =its good to take 3 points in this for the heal but if you can spar the points the 4th skill cures negative effects.=
one more thing about combat: some of the strong abilities take more actions so you can use the 1point medic ability to get action 2 points + 50% defence for 2 turns or just use the first attack that takes 0 points and you can use your 2 point attack the next turn.
jobs and fighting bonuses
=survival: This lets you hunt for food or make ammo but is also helps with hunting events in the forest and adds crit when fighting.
=crafts: This lets you make better weapons and clothing and also helps your defense in fights.
=medical: This lets you make med kits and syringes to boost states or heal in combat but also helps with medical events and will also add to your resistances.
=cunning: This is for guarding the camp and you'll need to train at lest one to max to stop invasions from zombies and then punks this one also helps with lockpicking events and adds to your block in combat.

This review is for those who actually have played Assassins Creed Black Flag. If you do not have it I suggest you buy it at a sale because the main game will be cheaper than the dlc since the price is only slightly higher but the overall content is more aswell.
I own Assassins Creed on XBox 360 and the game simply is breathtaking with the easy to learn gameplay, the open world features and the good and atmospheric music. The story however was a little short and Freedom Cry as a dlc is of course even shorter. Most players suggest an average gametime of only 4-6 hours. However it took me about 20 Hours to discover all the places unlock everything and tried the minigames like fishing. (They are the same as in Black Flag though)
Adewale has his own combat style and uses a machete. Like Kennway he can use firearms, ropedarts, poisoned darts etc. The overall gameplay is the same as in Black Flag but the story is set 20 years later. (I wont say much about it since i dont want to spoiler and it depends on your taste if you will enjoy it or not).
The map is not very big, i am guessing less than 25% of Black Flags overall map but the locations have their own appearance and are detailed.
I did not encounter any notable bugs but I was a bit dissappointed that Adewales ship is a repainted Jackdaw.
The ship however cannot be upgraded as much as the Jackdaw.
A new element in the game is as already mentioned Adewales own combat style and the ability to free slaves either by boarding slave ships or by killing the overseers at the plantations. Some of the overseers have become very hostile and will attack you instantly. If you are spotted on the plantations, the overseers are going to kill your maroonfellows so you should really take care.
The plantations sooner or later always get new owners so you can replay this part. The game also can be continued after the story has come to an end just like in Black Flag.
If you enjoyed Black Flag and want some more story related content or discover some more West Indies locations I really recommend this but dont expect a lot of new content. Also keep an eye out for a decent sale, I suggest maybe 3-5 dollars is a good price.

Just beat the game today, and have to say, I was pleasantly surprised. Like a lot of reviewers, I was immediately drawn to its Earthbound-style graphics, and expected a lighthearted indie romp through a ship. That compairson shatters within the first five minutes of gameplay, though. The 90's nostalgia and surreal charm of Earthbound are nowhwere to be found. Instead, you find yourself on a third-rate ship, among its cynical inhabitants. You've been murdered, and a telepathic boy named Pablo has pulled your soul back into the land of the living. He explains that in your current state, you can't open doors or speak to people, and must possess a living person to talk and search for clues.
And that's the basic premise of the game: possess people and puppeteer them into revealing conversations. The more conversations and clues you amass, the more leverage you have over the ship's occupants, and the more you understand about who you were and what's at stake. In general, it plays like a lot of early 90's point-and-click games, trying different dialogue combinations with different characters. Some might find that frustrating, but I honestly found it a highlight. I miss old games like that.  If you get too frustrated, though, Pablo offers hints throughout most of the game (usually two hints per section, a "where should I go" style hint, and a "complete this part for me" style one).
Sadly, these hints fall away where they're needed most, in the fourth act of the game. Up until that point, there's a sort of internal logic that can point you in the right direction. By act four, though, your choices are too broad, and there's no rhyme or reason for the interaction combos you need to pick. After reading a walkthrough, I understood why the choices I made were necessary for the story, but still thought "I never would've realized that I should possess this character and speak to this character after doing this not-very-obvious thing." You lose sight of why characters are motivated to act the way they do, basically.
That said, I still enjoyed the story quite a bit. It was a solid, unpredictable muder-mystery with a interesting game mechanic. The music never felt out of place, and a lot of thought given to the personality and backstory of each character, even down to how they speak to one person versus another. Overall, I'd recommend this to anyone that wants to hear a good story, even if the last parts can be a bit frustrating.

is an underrated gem created by Peltast Software just a year ago. Aside being an incredibly well weaved murder/mystery, it is a unique game that presents the rare opportunity of taking a glimpse on the human nature and the perpetual failure to communicate with one another, keeping unintended secrets while failing to hide things that they intended to hide to begin with. Through associations of the language and the mind, we are to investigate a horrifying affair. You should remember that you can only discover what people do care about the most by taking note on what they do not care about.
Our story starts with a brutal murder; a soul is snatched away from its mortal body before its time. We start as the fragment of this soul, as a piece rendered out of personality due to shock and we remember not a thing about our former mortal identity. Who were we? What happened? Who killed us? With all these ominous questions at mind, we awaken. A young boy medium seemingly managed to help us manifest at the last minute, thus our scarred consciousness has taken form in the cruise ship he's been travelling in as a ghost. We are to wander around, listen to passengers and the crew, and influence their actions by possessing them in hopes of revealing the vile businesses going on in this ship to reach some kind of closure.
The game manages to present a unique atmosphere with a limited environment. We are in an old cruise ship with 3 floors: the residential floor for passengers, the residential floor for the crew and the deck, alongside utilities and recreational areas. Graphics-wise, it's nothing exceptional, but these limited areas are well used in both in display and story purposes, harboring countless unique details that you may investigate and discover. All characters have their own background music, dominating the game according to your interactions with them - and with your ability of taking a glimpse to their minds, you'll gather uneasy clues about their goals and pasts.
We are given unique gameplay dynamics and a well written story. All characters involved has complicated personalities, various conflicting motives and secrets to keep depending on their situations. With all parameters involved,
may be interpreted as an Agatha Christie novel with supernatural undertone. You are welcome to possess people if you are to grasp a basic understanding about their personalities and motives only - and still then you can only present subconscious suggestions to manipulate their actions. They cannot talk about a subject they have no idea about to begin with! For the full control of people, you should first reveal the fundamental drive that each of them possess. Only then, you can completely control their actions and speak through their mouths. Each character has a unique ability that could become useful in your investigation, including your ghost self. By revealing details of your own past and personality, you are to gradually gather your former self and memories, presenting grander abilities with stronger manifestations. As the story progresses, you'll find yourself in a web of intrigue, lies and misconceptions.
This whole experience takes 5 chapters to wrap up - 4 investigation chapters and one conclusion chapter - and contains 5 different endings according to your ability to conclude the interrelation of all happenings during the last chapter, presenting you genuine replayability. All said and done,
is a noteworthy experience and a thrilling story with more than decent narrative and personality depictions. Enjoy!

The game engine is quite optimized, I was able to play at absolute max settings and did not suffer any lag whatsoever, way better than I expected.  For that alone, and the next-gen graphics, it is a recommendation from me.
The story mode is extremely poor quality, indie studios could do a better job.  But maybe that was not a focus for them.
The multiplayer works.  Everyone bashes the game's multiplay but actually I played a few matches and I found it flawless.  I know, it's not a lot of data to go by, but after playing ONLY laggy matches in MKX I expected this to have input lag as well but in fact I found that the opponent was able to respond to my every action.  I never noticed a single hitch and in fact it is superior to Dead or Alive's multiplayer by a long shot.
The gameplay itself, well, I've never really been  a big Street Fighter fan before.  I'm not sure how broad the move set is normally, but maybe this is just normal.  Each character has like, 10 to 12 moves?  Is that normal?  I found it to be a bit shallow in that regard, comparing it to Dead or Alive's 100+ moves per character.  Even though it is not that deep, the moves are easy enough to pull off and I assume you could still become that much more experienced by knowing what to execute at the correct time and reading your opponent is the key to this game, instead of having to know a whole lot of moves.
I see most people are complaining about the lack of certain fight stick support.  Same with keyboard support.  So this AAA release is far from perfect, it does not seem like they thought of every aspect and polished it up, instead it seems to have solid actual fighting with little extra added on.
So what I'm trying to get at is, it's not a horrible game, but it is a great fighting game with superb graphics.  Don't expect more.
edit: the server disconnection issues are really annoying.  borderline horrible.  but usually the volume of players drops by 90% after the first 3-4 weeks of a game's release so if this gets smoothened out, I don't see it being an issue later.  really rough launch though.

I've played Fallout 4 for hours now, and I absolutely love this game! When I first started, I had no idea what I was doing.
I had never played a fallout game before, so I had no idea what I was supposed to be picking up and throw away.
After an hour or two I started getting the hang of it.
You can join a few factions to make an impact on the world
Join the minutemen, a group of civilian soldiers who's ready to stand together and protect each other
Join the railroad and you'll be tasked with saving synths all secret agent style
Join the brotherhood of steel and you'll know what it feels like to be a scum of the earth
You can customize your guns, make them exactly how you want them
And you can build your own settlements!
The building system isn't as good as Bethesda claims it to be, I'd recommend mods there..
And companions!
You can actually romance companions in this game! Not just wear a necklace and boom you guys are married, like in Skyrim.
In Fallout 4, you have to earn their love, dragon age style!
You can romance humans, synths and even a ghoul!

2 years ago, when this launched, I jumped on it and played through it like I would have with any Fallout releases. I did finish the game, but walked away hugely disappointed and uninspired. This particular wasteland felt flat and boring. The characters didn't inspire, and the story was so weak that it copied a shocking amount of the ending from Fallout 3 beat for beat. This weekend, in a fit of ennui, I reinstalled it to give it another chance. Maybe I'd missed something, maybe... no. It's just as weak as it had been before. Or maybe that's intended. Maybe it's supposed to be a painful, boring grind, like some sort of artistic statement on the joyless futility of life. Perhaps that's giving it way too much credit.
Amazingly, it's also now buggier than I remember: it still has the problem where textures pop in multiple *minutes* after they should have on a GTX1080, and new and weird distant placeholder textures don't disappear when you get close after all. But all the hits were back, like dog getting stuck on random outcroppings. Good times.
It would be needless hyperbole to say something dumb like "wow this really wrecked Fallout for me", but boy did it put a dent in in my fandom. I don't even feel a need to care about this content creation thing. Why bother?

Bastion is one of the best games of the current era.  It borrows ideas and elements from various genres, but only just enough.  The combat system challenges you more and more, but never becomes overly complex, and it allows the player room to experiment with different combinations of weapons, special abilities, and tonics (which affect things like your chance to crit, chances to continue, damage dealt, et cetera).  The combat is also balanced very nicely.  It takes hints from RPGs by giving you chances to crit with various weapons and displays the damage in numbers above the enemies' heads, but it also incorporates a health bar system that's easy to understand; this leads to both ways giving you accurate measurements of your progress.  Combined with chances to crit (displayed in yellow numbers), the game doesn't bog you down with any typical stats (strength, dexterity/agility, et cetera).  What it gives you is the chance to upgrade your weapons in simple ways (25% more damage, +10% chance to crit, +100% crit damage) that can completely alter how you approach specific levels.  The numbers are also kept simple.  You'll typically deal between 40-80 damage, and more depending on the weapon's ability to crit.  But you'll never ork to break a certain threshold with minute details.
The isometric (top-down, at an angle) approach is reminiscent of adventure games as well as RPGs.  The angle and controls keep the action fast at points while technical at others, but it never feels unrewarding.  Some levels are tough and the angles can throw you off here and there, but there aren't any troubling spots.
The game is also very self-conscious.  There are several levels where you don't get a new weapon, but in most levels you'll either acquire a ranged or melee weapon.  This in turn opens up a challenge later to complete, which will give you items to further upgrade
items you've acquired.  Thus giving you more insentive to return to challenges later on.  Even when you acquire a new weapon, you typically have to use it immediately, but the game will place arsenals for you to change back to another weapon in the same level.  This way it forces you to try new weapons and learn just how they work while still giving you the chance shortly to play as you see fit.
And that's really the overall tone.  Bastion gives you the freedom to approach the game and each individual level as you wish.  It never arbitrarily levels your ability to fight or progress beyond the simple conventions of combat.  In fact, it gives you alternate ways to approach each situation - each just as great as any other.
If you're going to own only one game, it's probably Bastion.

I noticed a huge influx of negative reviews for this game ever since Bethesda introduced paid mods. Let me get a few things straight: Are you required to partake in these paid mods? NO. Does it at all take away from the experience of the game? NO. Does it mean you can no longer use free mods from sites like Nexus Mods? NO.
All of these negative reviews COMPLETELY ignore the fact that overall, Fallout 4 is an excellent game and is one of my favourite games of all time. I think that they're rather unfair as they have nothing to do with what Fallout 4 is like, and are focused exclusively on the paid mods (which I do disagree with, for the record). This review will be about the actual game itself, and not about the paid mods. If you're interested in the game, you should ignore those reviews.
Fallout 4 is a huge game. Even just the base game, with no DLCs or mods. The open world is huge and really detailed, it seems like there is thought about each location's back story. There are tons of locations to explore, all full of loot. Perks are really good and useful, levelling up is not difficult and if you're into the type of game, it will likely have you playing for hours.
I've got a couple hundred hours in the game and I've by no means explored all of the game's features and locations. My first 40 hours were just me building my settlement, which is a cool feature to have. You put together buildings using materials you've collected around the world. In previous titles like Fallout 3, New Vegas and Skyrim, there was all kinds of useless junk that you could pick up. In Fallout 4, everything is now useful, because it can be broken down into various materials for use in creating stuff for your settlement.
Companions, while there are fewer than in other games like Skyrim, have much more personality to them, in addition to their own voice actors (generic NPCs aside, Bethesda seems to have hired many more voice actors than in previous titles so there's much more diversity in voices). Each companion has their own backstory, set of likes and dislikes and personality. It really makes them feel a lot more real than in previous games. Unfortunately, conversation in the game is a bit limited, only ever having four options to choose from in any given dialogue option, but now the player character is voiced.
With the way the game now handles conversations between you and other NPCs, it feels more cinematic and lively than before. The game's main story is quite interesting too, and there are many other quests with interesting stories to complete as well.
Character customization is superior to past Fallout titles. For starters, it's much easier to make an attractive looking character than in Fallout 3 and New Vegas. Sculpting your character's face is similar to The Sims 4. Not quite as intuitive or fluid as that in The Sims 4, but similar nonetheless. Also, customizing your character's clothing is far more detailed than in Fallout 3 and New Vegas. There are more items and more ways to customize what you're already wearing.
Combat has also been hugely improved over Fallout 3 and New Vegas. While I love Fallout 3 and New Vegas and still play both quite often, Fallout 4's combat system is just so much better. For starters, the way you use guns is really good, on the same level as other big, triple A first person shooters. Playing the game in third person is also pretty good too, and if you prefer third person, you won't have to switch to first person if you need to shoot a gun. You also no longer have to switch from your gun to a grenade. You can have a gun and a grenade equipped at the same time, and by holding the Alt key, you'll throw a grenade without putting away your gun. Also, by simply tapping the Alt key, you can do a quick melee attack in case an enemy gets too close.
This point is more of a personal opinion. One thing I miss from Fallout 3 and New Vegas is the darker, bleaker, grimmer feeling of the world. In Fallout 3 particularly, the game world is really dark and grim and quite unnerving at times. While there are parts of Fallout 4 that are creepy and grim, the game world is much brighter, much more colourful and actually seems more lively. I actually loved how Fallout 3's world seems so dead, and how it made me feel like "this place was once so important, so busy and so active, and now it's all gone". Fallout 4's world actually kind of gives me a feeling of "hope for the future".
Fallout 4's intro and prologue, on the other hand, are awesome. Without spoiling everything, it does an excellent job of setting the stage for the game, and always gets my heart going whenever I go through the sequence again.
Overall, Fallout 4 is an excellent game and improves on absolutely everything from past games. Fans who stick to the Fallout games before Fallout 3 might have a different opinion, but I love Fallout 4 and if you love open world games, RPGs, or first person/third person shooters, you'll probably love Fallout 4 too. I highly recommend this game.

I loved the original Xcom and Terror from the Deep so naturally I played the hell out of Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within. I bought Xcom 2 when it came out but don't have many hours on PC (mostly played on Xbox) but have managed to complete it on Rookie level. I would recommend this game but it's not as easy to pick up as EU or EW. The first time I played I never lost a mission but hadn't figured out that making contact was kind of the same as putting satellites in the sky in the first game, so the Avatar project marched on until the 20 day countdown and I searched online for some kind of tutorial. After that the next playthrough I finished it (Rookie level) and am now working through veteran. Some things to note for anyone new to the game (I'm still learning but this is what I picked up):
- Your starting troops are imbeciles. You can stand them next to an alien, put the gun barrel in the aliens mouth (or another orifice) and they quite often still miss. Grenades will save your sanity. They may destroy loot drops but at least they will stop you swearing out loud as much as the random number generator leads you to do.
- the layout for the Avenger will make your job easier, or harder if you get it wrong. I generally start with Guerilla School (to increase squad size) in top right, a power relay in the top middle, advance warfare centre top left (heal troops faster). Then a resistance comms room 2nd row down on left or right hand side, a workshop in the middle of second row and power relay in the other 2nd row slot. The rooms up side and below of the workshop can be manned by gremlins which frees up engineers for other rooms. Next row have another Comms room under the workshop and the other slots fill as needed (power relays). For the rooms with shielded power conduits I generally stick PSI training and another resistance comms.
- The game DOES get easier, generally when your characters are Major or Colonel level. Even then the random number generator can be a joke, leading you to regularly miss 80s and 90 percent shots. The aliens seem not to miss anywhere near as much. Getting close, flanking etc all helps, but if the dice aren't rolling your way... well... :( Put it this way. Much of the time, if you were as unlucky in real life as this game makes you feel, you'd fall down the stairs, call the ambulance, be electrocuted by your phone, have your head bashed into when the paramedics get there and open your door on you, then they'll drop you on the way to ambulance which will then crash on the way to the hospital. After you finally get to the hospital it would be struck by a meteor from space. I can't remember a game in recent memory that has made me swear like this one has.
- Fan Fire. Your Colonel sharpshooter/Gunslinger with plasma pistol, lightning hands and fan fire can really help when chopping Sectopods down to size. Get two, and they'll drop a Sectopod in one turn, especially if you shred it first with a grenadier and let the guys at it with pistols.
- Stick with it. Honestly, the game is basically great but with a horrendous learning curve. I thought having finished EU and EW and played the originals back in the day would make things easier but I had to start from scratch. Overwatch everyone apart from the last guy in your squad THEN attack with them from concelament.  Sorry to those who know this but I found out the painful way (squad wiped numerous times on first mission - turns out my son had put the game on the hardest setting... grrrr... but still my tactics were charge in and kill. They don't work in early game).
- The Xbox version is bugged, glitchy, freezes and corrupts save games. Having seen a few reviews it seems the PC version has similar problems. I'll play it through and see, but the basic rule is to save, save save. Save the game whenever you achieve anything of use/note. Sure, you may say 'that's cheating' but the game may well crap out on you and you lose your hard earned progress.
If you haven't played XCom before, go buy Enemy Unknown and/or Enemy Within on Steam Sale. If you have played that before and want to play the next chapter, buy this but be prepared to swear, rage quit and uninstall the game. A lot. Frustrating is about the least offensive word I can use to describe it sometimes.
For some reason I like it, even with its quirks and WTF moments. Overall I'd say it was 7/10. I'd rate the original Enemy Unknown/Within 9/10.

Pros:
-	Nice graphics
-	Interesting game mechanisms, even if it stays behind the original XCOM games, especially with respect to base management.
-	It is XCOM!
Cons:

This is the kind of video game where players either fall in love with the art & narration style and the absurdity, or you cannot see anything more than just a random collection of strange and quick puzzles.
Despite what many would think, ‘The Franz Kafka Videogame’ is not an adaptation of Kafka’s works but more like a game that feels like as if a contemporary Kafka created it. His trademark surrealism saturates through every layer, from plot to puzzle design.
From a technical aspect, this one is exactly like mif2000’s previous video game project,
: a touchscreen-friendly puzzle game that relies solely on interacting with scene elements. Its unique selling point is the so outlandishly Kafka-like solutions that would make even early 90s adventure games look sane in comparison.
Some players will absolutely love this surreal approach, while others will see nothing more than a bunch of disjointed and short puzzles. Therefore, definitely buy this if you enjoy pure weirdness, but if you do not, then it is unlikely you will find any entertainment value here.

Do I ever try and like this game...
There are a great many issues that are hard to overlook and a great many subtle nuances I keep trying to convince myself are worthwhile canceling out the problems, but ultimately I can't...I just can't.
On first playthrough I was excited about the artstyle and potential subject matter... and upon delving in I was even more pleased with the small pieces of detail and pastice that are probably lost to most; be that the Scheele green walls, the SS Blumfeld (the elderly bachelor), and I did get so many giggles from the vulture wine advert; but so much of it was just so shallow and of no substance and concequence.   The more I tried to prove that was not the case to myself the more I found quotes and disclamers from the sources proving my wimsy wrong.
The kill screen bug and latin quotes first keyed me off... should a developer be telling us to err is human, should they be showing us a totally out of context broken coding screen... because they most definitely should not be telling us that it is better to never start a quest than have to concede...and that is what they said and how I felt. I was happy I played it, but it was not a proud happy and felt a little dirty thereafter.
The Strinberg style dream within a dream; and very obvious homage to David Lynch's "waiting room" give a little credence to my desire for this to be a complex causality and hope the puzzle's seeming brute force or superficaility were me missing something which would become self evident after discovering the outcome; but after looking harder and harder, i just couldn't find them... andI don't just mean inside the game.
The idea seemed to be utilize surealism to be a kafkaesque non-sequiter but not alegorical as kafka himself did. The reflection puzzles were a little rough in having to jump to the correct term with no primer; while the number puzzles were overly easy but had seemingly no significance as to why the numbers were chosen. And I am sorry; using in game oration to explain there is no rhyme or reason does not forgive such tie in/continuity issues.  Had the planetary model been something significant... like the actual alignment from his birth, or a famous date, or the location of the "Kafka" (3412) asteroid rather than the "America" asteroid it may have made some sence and been redeeming.
For the most part this game was a string of somewhat properly translated dialogs very superficially skirting deeper philosophical ideals of clandestine intent and nihilist purpose; blocked by very easy puzzles that change in difficulty based on their involvement with the story; the more integrated ones are absolutely a breaze, while the ones that apparently no rhyme nor reason are absolutely murder.
This can be seen when completing the erudite achievement.  some hints are absolutely obvious, vague to the point wondering why even bother, while the harder ones, just plain give you the answer because there is aparently no logical hint to be had.
To cut short; had this game been longer, had this game delved into the philosophical underpinnings that it started to (even if they were not inline with most of Kafka's own intents), or had this game had contnuity with puzzles and they have been more enjoyable/challenging I could in good faith recomend this game.  But as it stands it is a cute aesthetic of a game, that was made around a handful of somewhat amusing puzzles, trying to tie them in together with a very rudimentary (if not just wikipedia'd) knowledge of passing Kafka trivium, of which seems to only have been used because of the idea of his work was thought to be sureal for sureality's sake rather than a deeply disturbed alienation it was meant to convey originally. It was frustrating, and i am not sad i threw down a couple bucks, but I am kind of embarased I did so just to fulfil some idea of intelectual stimulation rather than looking at a lets play or something of the sort before hand and realizing this was not the droid i was looking for. I guess it is kind of like having a book on your shelf of an author you have not read, and probably won't read, purely to impress someone who may come over and see it who would extrapolate ideas of who you are based on a ... well, not actually lie.

Why Am I Dead at Sea is an adventure mystery game, wherein you play the role of a ghost who has no recollection of who they are, how they died, or why they were killed. Throughout the game, you are set upon the task of finding out the answer to each of these enigmas, and in doing so you will also learn much about the passengers and crew aboard the ship. I've been waiting almost a year to finally play this title, so needless to say I was hoping that I wouldn't be disappointed; I definitely got a lot more than I expected out of this experience.
The game plays out like an incredibly gripping novel, and at any point it's overwhelmingly difficult to put it dow for even the briefest moment. You will want to continue playing through until the end, so that you can unravel the questions that were roused from the beginning. You will initially start off by getting to casually know the people aboard the vessel, but as you progress throughout the four chapters you will get to know their most intimate details and innermost thoughts. The character building, and the relationships that are formed between them, are key points to the success of Why Am I Dead at Sea; many of the details that you will learn later on in the game, and especially what lies in wait at the end, will have many players on the Feels train, headed full speed towards Feelsville.
So as you may be able to determine, the title relies heavily on dialogue. That being said, the actual gameplay is minimal; as a ghost, you are able to possess the other people on the ship, as well as use their unique special abilities. These special abilities range from extremely beneficial, such as Donnovan who can highlight interactive objects, to utterly useless, like Darryl who can walk faster but at the disadvantage of having the screen become disoriented. Needless to say, you probably will not utilize of most of these special abilities, despite possessing the characters multiple times. To fully understand the story, and to uncover your "true" self as the ghost, you will talk to everyone around the ship at least once on every chapter, and at some point you will also be tasked to investigate every room aboard the liner. These are not incredibly daunting or time consuming tasks, as the boat only has three floors and ten passengers.
Once you get to know a character completely, you are then free to fully possess them; doing so enables new dialogue options to appear at certain stages of the game. Once you reach the end of the fourth and final chapter, you then proceed on to unlock an array of different endings. While the endings are somewhat diversified, there is in fact one true ending in the mix; however, you are still left to piece together, yourself, many of the riddles that the game presents. This is a nice change of pace, versus games that feel the need to explain their outcome in excruciating detail; it also leaves an air of mystery to the title, and one that is open to interpretation.
As a final note, I will say that the soundtrack by Bill Kiley is an absolute masterpiece. I never found myself getting tired of the amazing retro, Sega Genesis styled bytes that were infiltrating my ears; from the downright creepy, to the dubstep influenced, to the upbeat. The only gripe that I do have is that each letter of dialogue makes a sound, and it overtakes the background tracks. These sounds, however, can be easily bypassed by pressing the action key; although it would be nice to have the option to turn it off completely. It's also worth noting that if you enjoy retro soundtracks, the one for this game can be downloaded for free, or pay what you want, at Bill's Bandcamp page.
Why Am I Dead at Sea is one of the best mystery games on Steam at this point, and it's unfortunate that it's severely underrated and often bypassed. As of now, this will be the 55th review for this game. The depth of the characters is really where this game shines, without that element, Why Am I Dead at Sea would not be the diamond in the rough that it is. The only way that the experience could've been improved was if the ship was a little larger, and the story a little longer. With talking to everyone, obtaining all of the endings, and earning all of the achievements, I clocked in at a little under 5 hours. Since the time that I initially posted this review, this title has seen a significant price drop, and the current price of $5.49 CAD is very fair for the amount of content that you get. If you can nab it on sale, it's one hell of a steal for a must-play title.

Feature-wise, the game is lacking and clearly unfinished. But we knew this. At least, those of us paying attention to previews and updates over the past year did. The community asked for this game to be released early with an emphasis on online functionality so it could be debuted and played in the Capcom Tour Cup. They got that.
Server issues on launch day? It's more rare to find a game that DOESN'T have server issues on launch day. Wait a few days and let it get hammered out. it will be fixed and life will go on.
Single-player modes will be added in the coming months. Is the game overpriced for what it is right now? Yes. I won't argue with you there. But if you look around the internet (not that many of you know how to do this; else you would have known what the game would and would not be launching with) you can find it for considerably less. The choice is yours.
Mechanic-wise, the game is amazing. The controls are tight, fights are fast-paced and offense-oriented. V-triggers provide a great element of strategy that never really makes-or-breaks a match, but definitely can help counter some moves and throw an opponent off balance.
My only true complaint is the lack of D-input support at launch. I'm aware this was noted beforehand, but... This is such an easy thing to include, and it really excludes a lot of people who have fightsticks and controllers they want to use with the game. It will be added eventually, yes, and of course there's Xmodder in the interim, but I just see no reason why this couldn't have been implemented at the get-go. Especially for the highly competitive tournament crowd, which the current release was catered to.
If anything, the game probably should be listed under "Early Access," since that is indeed a category it currently falls into. The game is by no means complete. But that does not mean it is "bad." Should you wait? Probably, if the upcoming features are your focus. But I really can't stress enough that everything SFV launched and did not launch with was already highlighted before today, by Capcom.
Not educating yourself is no excuse to throw a tantrum.

I recently started picking up Visual Novels again, and this is by far one of the best currently available on Steam, for the
:
The art is certainly amazing; the characters don't appear too cute or overly sexualized (like some other games on Steam here ehem...); the art has obviously been influenced by Anime. Hence, if you don't like this, don't buy this game.
In addition to that, the soundtrack is OK. It's not played in a loop and I actually enjoyed listening to the OST. Don't expect Hatsune Miku or JPop, the music is really fine
The text aims to create the impression of an actual novel. There's not just one sentence per "page" displayed, the pages are filled with actual paragraphs, which is definitely a plus since the developers really put  their thoughts into their game. You may need to take breaks though since you may not be used to the font. I certainly needed to get used to reading that much on a screen again (old fashioned me, IKR)
The story is very good for a VN, it will get you hooked with some nice cliffhangers here and there, and it is not too predictable which seems to be a common problem among some titles on Steam here. A lot of details have been added and every choice usually adds a different junk of dialogue. I was suprised since the developers really did their home work and researched historical facts and added ancient tales not related to Japan. The plot is somewhat serious, and this is certainly not a comic version. Expect daily lives of college students and Sci/Fi. It was definitely interesting to me.
Also, the game has a very nice feature some other games seriously lack: choices. I'm mentioning this because a lot of games have been tagged with "choices", but the choices don't change the overall play style. In this game, you can get slightly different outcomes depending on your choices (dialogue) and these choices also influence what the characters say while the story itself is mostly linear. In addition, you can get different endings which heavily influence some of the content. You'll need to read carefully.
But what's most important are the loveable characters who have been equipped with a lot of personal and emotional details. The characters appear real, very real, and depending on your choices, they can show surprising development. Don't just pick your favourite yet, they'll surprise you.
The game does not offer voice acting, you need to actually read the lines, so if you are used to LISTENING, you may be disappointed. The FONT is tiny and may prove difficult to read, whereas some achievements are a bit too easy to guess in my opinion (if you're an achievement hunter that may annoy you)

This is the 2nd of 4 Last Heroes games, and, with a few minor changes in style, moves the story of Amelia's search for her heritage to the land of Odaro where the exploration, the battles, the searches, and the discoveries continue.
This one is a bit longer than the first as Amelia and Roland (from the first game) team up with Leon and Sofia to track down the evildoers of a group called Illion in the hopes of putting a stop to their plans, and to discover more clues about Amelia's parents.
So, in the classic rpg style, you are on an adventure that takes you to many locales that require investigating, fighting monsters, and meeting various characters that all build the story.
There are some changes here that enhance the game play, most notably that the enemies respawn so you can level up more. And by the leveling, more skills are acquired. There are also more treasures to find, and there are some side quests involved.
The artwork, especially of the enemies, is good, and the music is nice with a pleasant variety.
So, do you need to play the first one to enjoy this one? Not really, but I would advise playing them in order for the cohesion of the long range story ---- and, at the low price for both ---- why not?
All in all, if you are a fan of these classic games, this one will keep you entertained for hours, and is a good addition to the series. Recommended for sure.

Street Fighter is fun. It's not about uber high level competition fighting. First and formost the series has been about providing an engaging but comprehensive platform for single or versus play at all levels. I have owned so many itterations of the series across multiple systems dating back to SF2 World Warrior pack in with my SNES. But honestly I'm a below avg player. The last time i played competitively against human players regularly was local play of SF3 on the Dreamcast. These days its mainly CPU play in Ultra SFIV or the Alpha series on PSP.
I dont have the time, the patience or the passion to put hundreds of hours into one game anymore. Especially one that has argueably the highest learning curve for even casual online play. There's just too many great games being released on a weekly basis. I buy SF games for that 1-2 hour session every now and then. A quick breeze through Arcade mode with a random character or maybe a 100 Kumite on a long flight. Fun not frustration.
So that said SFV. Is it really as bad as people are making out. In a word no. But its certainly not what longtime fans have come to expect from the series. And by that I mean a robust single player experience with well programmed tiered AI. And a pletora of fun and diverse game modes to keep things fresh. What we have right now is akin to something like single player in CS:GO. A means to an end which is to understand the most remedial of concepts and play online. An after thought to meet a release window. And that annoys me.
Can you imagine a first time SF player transitioning to MP after completing story mode? They'ed be lucky to win one round out of 100 matches. Even with over 20 years of playing this game at least a few hours every month. I could only manage to win 4/10 ranked matches. And thats early on a Tuesday morning the day of launch. By this time next week I doubth I could even achieve that. And thats fine by me. I dont play the game to be uber elite. I play the game to enjoy it. So as of right now I feel its fair to say SFV is not a fun game for a rather significant portion of the series fans.
If Capcom cared at all they would have marketed and released a MP only preview version of this game. With no mention of SP. But they got greedy and decided to just ship it as the complete product with a random press release about adding additional SP content later. Knowing full well the majority of players would be none the wiser until first boot. Thats video games today. Its get it out the door, fix it later. Or in alot of cases don't bother.
And what makes me sick to my stomach is the uncomprehendable backing of this disgraceful practice by a sizeable margin of modern gamers. Whether its fanboys, buyer's remorse or just plain trolling. Gamers in their droves are publically backing these devs and making this the norm. I hate to say it but it seems to be generational. Back in the day SF would have gotten critically and publically panned across the board. Now its "knock 0.5 off the score" and justified public outcry has to compete with equally supported enablers.
So in my opinion whether you play 50 hours of SF a week or 2 hours a month. You still shouldn't buy this game.

Bastion is a beautifully-crafted indie platformer, which sets itself apart from the rest with its constant variety and unique gameplay.
You play as The Kid, who wakes up suddenly as the world around him is ending. They call it the “Calamity”, which basically results in the ground around him falling apart. Under the Kid’s feet, blocks of land rise up to settle beneath him, which is the main way for getting around throughout the game. He sets off for the Bastion; a large homely mechanism floating in the sky, which was where everyone was to meet when the world ends.
Lucky it was there!
You initially only find one old man there, Rucks. He slots himself in as the gruff narrator of the tale, speaking in metaphors and eloquence, detailing your actions at every turn, and providing the backstory as you go. The narrator is essentially the centrepiece to the story, which is what most of the praise for this game (mine included) aims at.
As you hop from area to area, you find more unique weapons. You can equip two at a time, which leads to an incredible amount of variety in your attacks (which Rucks comments on each time you leave the armoury). This is where much of the fun is; the gameplay itself. Each area, you can try a different combination of weapons, and not grow bored of it. Especially when you throw in a secret skill slot, which has limited uses, but opens up for even more variety.
The soundtrack is amazing, and sets the tone for each cut scene and level you come across. The world itself looks like an oil-painted artpiece, yet at each point you know what your objective is, and pick out what is harmless scenery, and what is potentially life threatening.
The story itself flows nicely, and even brings about a couple of choices in the final moments. These choices have real emotional weight, and what you choose will depend on the kind of person you are.
As an indie game enthusiast, this is one that must be in your Library.

TL;DR A brilliant game ruined by bad executive decisions
Fallout 3 and 4 have both been beautifully entertaining games, even though story wise, I still prefer Fallout 3. Fallout 4 itself is good and there is plenty to love and hours among hours to kill in play time, which has been covered in detail in other reviews.
One thing which has always made Bethesda games great, is the modding capabilities of the engine and the small army of skilled modders working individually or in groups to add anything between small and big changes to the game. Bethesda had tried once before to introduce paid mods in an attempt to monetize these modders works and has failed because of the community resistance. While I clearly understand that some mods are so excellent and vast that they could well work as a full game expansion and people would want their favourite modders rewarded for their hard work, its important to understand that this is not what is happening here. Bethesda is outsourcing development to external contractors, and selling small bits for premium prices. I sincerely doubt that the hourly salary for those modders would match what Bethesda would have to pay if they'd develop the same content in house. While this is a smart business move, I don't believe for a second its in the interest of modders or customers in the long run.
Its easy to dismiss the thousands of negative reviews in response to this, as "review bombing of angry <insert favourite gamer insult here>" and it may be true for a fraction of them. But if you scroll through them and see the playtime hours of many of these reviews, you'll see that you are looking at players who often have hundreds of hours and are obviously still playing and caring enough years after the release (and most other players have moved on) to actually write these reviews. In other words, you are actually looking at the most loyal part of the customer base of this game, the people who still have it installed after all this time, often with hundreds of mods and they are exactly the customers Bethesda now tries to sell mods to. Clearly, this is a reaction of having a something forced upon players which they don't want (after all we can't deactivate or uninstall creation club) and since there are little other options for players to make their voice heard, giving a thumbs down to indicate one doesn't like what is being done with ones favourite game, is a legitimate option.

Originally released as five episodes starting in April and ending in November 2012, The Walking Dead: The Game casts us as Lee Everett, a convicted murderer on his way to the big house. However, before Mr. Everett can trade his denim shirt for an orange jumpsuit, the zombie apocalypse breaks out and gives Lee new goals in life: namely, surviving at all costs and protecting a little girl named Clementine.
It is these two goals that make The Walking Dead: The Game the juggernaut that it is. See, The Walking Dead is an adventure game, but it’s not the kind of adventure game you’ve come to expect. Sure, you’ll need to figure out how to get a radio working and how to distract walkers here and there, but the real draw here is a “choose your own adventure.”
As you play through the five episodes, the big moments come when you choose how Lee responds to situations and what he says in conversations with his fellow survivors. Choices and dialogue pop up on screen with timers, and you have seconds to pick exactly what you’re going to do or say. Whereas previous adventure games from developer Telltale Games would let you run through every possible line of dialogue, that isn’t the case here. In The Walking Dead, you choose, and the game moves on – adapting its story to each decision.
This is what makes The Walking Dead so special. You and I are tasked with the same goal of protecting Clem, but the way we do it might be completely different. I might choose to befriend someone you hate, and you might choose to leave someone I took. I might shoot my mouth off in anger, but you might keep your cool; either way, the group will remember that and the dynamic will change. The decisions you’re making in the moment have ripples that go throughout the entire adventure. When you get to Episode 5, the things you have and haven’t done – the choices you haven’t thought about since Episode 1 – are going to come up.
Will our endings be completely different? No. The Walking Dead: The Game is telling us the same story and thus taking us to the same conclusion, but it allows us to experience it in different ways. I’ve heard some naysayers refer to this as “the illusion of choice” -- as in what we’re doing or saying really doesn’t matter because it all nets out relatively the same -- but that’s selling the journey short. The Walking Dead: The Game is like a coloring book: we each have the same black and white sketch, but it’s up to us to fill it in as we see fit. The relationships I’ve built, the emotions I’ve felt, the choices I’ve made – that’s what makes The Walking Dead: The Game so endearing.
Part of that connection comes from excellent writing from the Telltale staff that manages to be funny, tense and scary at the right moments, amazing voice acting from Lee and Clementine, and a visual style that’s pulled from the comic book world the game is set in and that never manages to get boring. There’s this perfect storm here that manages to create such believable characters and set us in their world.
When it comes to actually playing The Walking Dead: The Game, Telltale whipped up a new adventure control scheme. Like I said, for choices, text pops up and you have to jump on it, but for controlling Lee, one stick controls the character and the other controls an onscreen reticle you can use to interact with objects and people. When the action gets going and you need to shoot zombies or fight off walkers, it can be jarring to use the reticle stick to line up shots, but that’s part of the fun – the game catches you off guard with things and you have to scramble to the foreign control in order to survive.
What holds The Walking Dead: The Game back from being a masterpiece are technical hiccups that have been well documented throughout the episodic adventure and are common Telltale stumbles. Scenes freeze as the next one loads, gameplay slows down as the game tries to process intense action, and save files inexplicably disappear. These are disappointing, but in the end, experiencing The Walking Dead: The Game is well worth any technical blemish you might have to sit through.
While we have not encountered these problems, some owners of the Xbox 360 disc version of the game and Xbox 360 units without hard drives have reported stutter/playback issues. For information on how to fix that, see Telltale's support page.

I immensly enjoyed OG X-COM (including TFTD) and the first remake, but XCOM 2 only has glimpses of brilliance and ultimately I cannot recommend it.
There are many reasons I came to this conclusion.
1.) The combat missions are intentionally disjointed and this forces huge imbalances between your forces and the enemy. I understand that you are the resistence and this is part of the theme of this game, however having 'special' enemies (such as a certain enemy that gets a free turn everytime one of your soliders takes an action) really breaks the underlying mechanics and rules of the game world without extending that same mechanic to the player to counter act. Add this with scripted events (move to part A on the map and four mechs pop out of no where) that make combat more frustrating and annoying than ever before.
2.) There are still timed missions in 2017 (boo, Firaxis, you should know better).
3.) Resources and time. There isn't any time to build upgrades or mine resources before you're thrown in the thick of it. Which sounds like a real situation for a rebellion, except for the fact that all these artifical rules are imposed on your campaign (for example: you can't fly over to 'random base A' because you don't have enough 'intel points').
Additionally, you literally have to manage multiple resources at a time and have a working strategy already in mind so that you don't get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you within the first two months. I don't know about you, but my precognition mental powers aren't what they used to be, so it's literally ALL ABOUT LUCK of the draw when it comes to resources.
4.) The story is cool but I find myself not really caring about the any of the characters or the main plot line because I'm so focused on a million different other things that literally have to be done for you to continue playing the game. The urgency is artifical and feels artifical, which really brakes the immersion for me.
I can't stress how unfun this is, it is so much work, it literally feels like a job.
In closing: what happened to this being a simulation first and a turn based game second? This new XCOM francise has really devolved into the iPhone of turn based games. It's carefully crafted to restrict access/prograss by artifical means and dumbs down most of the simulation elements that made XCOM popular to begin with. For these reasons, I cannot recommend this game to anyone.

Quick pros and cons for this game:
Pros:
* A lovable cast of playable characters.
* Fun combat with each party member feeling unique and actually have an impact on the battle.
* Interesting side quests which flesh out characters in the game and give you a better understanding behind some things in this game and in Tales of Zestiria as well. (Sort of remind me of Xenoblade Chronicles side quests)
* The hardest difficulty is a real challenge and is rewarding! (I recommend playing the game on the more harder difficulties)
* Weapons and armour take a while to become redundant and have their pros/cons; adding a layer of strategy. (For example one weapon is good against Undead while another is good against Beasts)
* Skits galore! (Personally I think some of the skits in the game are the one of the best in the Tales series)
* Decent post-game (Not the best but good enough)
Cons:
* Most villains in the game were bland and boring with a few exceptions
* Character customization has been a step down compared to other Tales games like Tales of Xillia 2
* Not much in-game costumes and the good ones are DLC
* Most areas in the game are really simple and generic.
* Lots of going back and forth in this game (Although its not so bad when you get the option to fast travel)
* During combat some skills make the battles a bit choppy (Usually seen while using Velvet and her Soul Break)
In short if you're familiar with the Tales Series, Tales of Berseria is a Tales game that's definitely worth giving a shot especially if you played Zestiria. As a JRPG, it's not the most strategic and intense JRPG out there but it's a nice relaxing one that I recommend trying.

I strongly dislike this game, for reasons i don't quite understand.
Somehow it annoys me immensly that almost all missions have a timer, forcing me to advance very fast to complete the mission. Even the missions that don't have a timer almost invariably involves som sort of infinite-spawn mechanism forcing me to advance to avoid beeing overrun.
On the strategic map, it's almost the same situaion. No matter what you are doing with the Avenger random missions will pop op on intervals, most of them urgent and/or time sensitive. This forces you to run the missions ASAP or miss them, suffering the associated penalty. No waiting 4 hours for research to complete or half a day for your best soldier to heal.
These factors makes me feel like I'm constantly rushing through everything in the game, both combat and strategic decisions. Does it create a sense of urgency: Yes. Does it make the game more challenging: Yes. Does it make the game more fun to play: No - not for me at least. I detest the feeling of beeing rushed, especially when playing a turnbased game. That's just wierd and unnecessary.
Also, I think the game looses a lot of appeal by gimmicking through combat with the aliens. You're 75% through the game  before the game stops throwing new wierd abilites at you. This leaves you constantly scrambling to figure out how to deal with the new enemies - but only for the first playthrough. In my mind, the makes the first playthrough very demanding and any succeeding playthrough dull. It's hard to explain properly, but there is something annoying about the games pace and/or mode of introducing new enemies.
Perhaps it is because the storytelling isn't gluing the missions together in a coherent whole, that the rushing and the constant stream of new outlandish abilities feels so off. The story telling consists mostly of poorly voice-acted cutscenes and your XO screaming at you/the operatives to hurry up. (See above why I dislike the latter.) It doesn't help either that the stoy makes no sense at all.
While I do enjoy the customisations available, it makes zero sense for you to be unable to duct-tape two magazines together before the enemy drops them. Come on: We're flying a high-jacked spaceship around; mouting scopes, replacing triggers and rigging magazines on rifles shouldn't be outside our reach.
Perhaps that is it then: The story and most of the mechanics makes no sense and gameplay consists mostly of ham-acted cutscenes and voicemessages telling you to hurry the f*** up.

One of the worst games I have probably played in the past year. Easily the most "meta" point-and-click puzzle game of all time, and it's horrible for it. Extremely shallow and short.
The game just throws random passing references about Franz Kafka but isn't really much about him or his themes. It just brings up certain details or pieces of his work, like Metamorphosis, but does not make anything sensible about all of this. The whole experience is just random absurdity for the hell of it, and it's not even "fun" absurdity.
The plotline is almost non-existent, as said above. The dialogue is just awkward and boring, and in fact takes up probably 50% of the game time or more, given how slow it progresses, and you having to click specific bubbles as they pop up across the screen.
The other 50% of the game is a collection of "puzzles," but I'd even say half of those are not real puzzles. A good chunk of them simply involve randomly clicking around the screen until you find something you can interact with that might not seem obvious, then bashing in multiple attempts to get some event to occur.
Very rarely are the puzzles intuitive, and most don't give you a sense of accomplishment or an "Aha!" moment, but more so make you wonder "What the hell was the developer thinking?" Just because the game is acting like it's focused on Kafka doesn't make any of this better.
Earlier I said it is short, and I
mean it. The first attempt took me less than 1 hour, and I decided to rush through it again to see how much actual "content" exists. If I immediately canceled most of the dialogue as it showed up, it only took ~20-25 minutes to get through the entire game again!
Honestly, I think the developers are selling this over the art style and some fake sense of dedication to Kafka, when really there's almost nothing worthwhile in this creation.
A great game, more people need to play it though. It lasts about 5-6 hours total. Anyways, great game, and you should check it out.

Now this is a hidden gem. "Why am I Dead At Sea" is a wonderful narrative-based game that desperately needs more love. Its influences are clear; Mother 3's art style, Phoenix Wright's murder mysteries and Ghost Trick's possession mechanic..., yet it still manages to stand on its own as a unique and immensely gripping adventure, with plenty of brooding atmosphere to spare. These small 2D characters have more dimension to them than most from AAA releases; they're broken in sympathetic and often relatable ways, and the methods used to convey them show how effective games can be for storytelling.
I do strongly recommend the game despite some faults; a few story details weren't elaborated on as much as I would've liked, even after the 'true' ending. Progression can be a little tedious or obtuse at times, mainly due to having to exhaust dialogue options with every character combination. Also, I did come across a couple of game breaking glitches (usually getting stuck somewhere with the cat), not to mention issues with music cutting out. Hopefully these can be resolved, not deal-breaking due to frequent saves but still something to be aware of.
If you look at the game's Steamspy sales, its sales numbers are criminally low. Let's change that folks! If anything that you've read on this page sounds appealing to you, I can't recommend "Why am I Dead at Sea" enough.
