The thing about puzzle adventures is that the player and the creator have to "click", sharing a common logic. There's nothing more satisfying than moving to a new location in an adventure game and having something weird pop up at you, feeling that warm rush of a eureka moment. Catching the end of the line that needs to be unravelled, discovering a discrepancy, and consequently solving a puzzle is incredibly satisfying.
Unfortunately, none of this happened with me and TFKV. Almost every single puzzle felt esoteric in a bad way, offering zero clue as to how to move forward and zero satisfaction upon solving, demanding trial and error at best or just waiting for a hint to pop at worst. Heck, in some cases I used both hints and they helped me none! (Like in the WWI puzzle, where I quickly realized that shapes meant letters, but had no clue as to what word I was supposed to spell.) I get it that the puzzles in TFKV are supposed to make one think out of the box, but to me, they ended up being just... random.
"Random" is perhaps
word to describe TFKV. The game tries very very hard to throw surreal imagery at you, but, while the visuals are very lovely and well-executed, I'm not sure how placing a level in the Black Lodge is supposed to make the game more interesting. I mean, yeah, I've seen Twin Peaks too... so? What was the point of this reference?
And, of course, the Franz Kafka aspect. Going in, you have to keep in mind that TFKV is colorful, light-hearted, and has a dog sidekick. Any references to Franz Kafka's work are purely superficial and pop-cultural. Is this a bad thing? Not necessarily—there's nothing wrong with shifting genres.
Just keep in mind that this puzzle adventure game about Franz Kafka has very esoteric puzzles and has little to do with Franz Kafka,

Very innovative gameplay, in the sense that even though the battles are fought in 3D hack n' slash style, the most important of elements of traditional JRPG 2D strategizing are preserved in quite ingenious ways. Difficulty choices would satisfy players looking for different challenging levels, and the robust collection and leveling up system goes above and beyond just collecting equipments and leveling the characters up.
The protagonist (and her group) has decent characterization, and the story quality rise above the industry average. However, there are several problems with the story and characters that might not meet your first impression of the game just from the PV. The single biggest problem that I find is simply that all the important antagonists are cliched, lacking rounded substance that make them compelling, making the opposition to the protagonist team quite dull. Other problems include a somewhat cliched story if you look at the bigger picture and a relative weak depiction of the grimdark-ness throughout the story. Though to be fair, there were some cut scenes moments that move emotions.
Tales of Berseria is an excellent game where its RPG element is concerned. Diehard and casual RPG players will enjoy it alike, in different ways that are enabled by its game system. Although it certainly does have a decent story to boast of, story-telling quality alone won't make it stand beside RPG "greats" such as Trails of the Sky. Spend $50 on this game only if you think you are going to enjoy the vast amount of gameplay to a certain degree. Do not buy this if you hate RPG and are only here for the story.

There is a loose storyline here, but you don't realise there is one until the end. It's a series of single-screen scenes that start off with some speech-bubble dialog followed by clicking stuff to solve a puzzle, of which there are a good variety. Some you can use logic to solve, others trial/error/repetition, others benefit from simply clicking around the screen until something happens. After each few levels there are screens with bits of storyline and artwork without any puzzle, I guess you'd call them intervals. That's all there is to it really, it's a straightforward game with very little to explain.
There's not much in the way of options menu, it looks like a mobile game. You can switch from window to fullscreen (goes to full 1920x1200), toggle sound (no volume control) and there's a nice marquee-style level overview with pictures scrolling past. You can replay from any point.
The scenes are strange and imaginative, with Monty Pythonesque puzzle animations. It's not sophisticated but interesting to look at, nonetheless. Music and sound effects are sparse, but again, enjoyable when they do appear.
There are a few very easy puzzles but most are easy/medium difficulty. There's a 3-stage hint system, each increasingly-obvious hint appears after a 3 minute countdown so you won't have any trouble progressing. There's no general timer for the levels, it's a casual game.
I often see Steam reviewers complaining that a game is too short and I think to myself "that's a bit harsh, there's enough to satisfy", but in this case I have to put my foot down. There are 20 or so levels that I'm sure could be speed-run in well under 30 minutes. There's no replay value once you know the solutions, unless you want to be a stickler and get the final achievement, as there will always be one missing - complete with all hints or complete with none. It's a shame because this silly price spoils my otherwise whole-hearted recommendation.
12 achievements, all easy to get apart from the last one (see above). 6 trading cards, Windows-only and no Steam Cloud.
The puzzles are fun and I enjoyed the surreal scenes and artwork, but it's over before you know it. The price is outrageous. I would certainly recommend it in a sale though.

DEAD AGE
*NOTE: Game has been significantly patched since this review was first published*
PUBLISHER – Headup Games
DEVELOPER – Silent Dreams
GENRE - Roguelike
THE BASICS:
Dead Age is a Roguelike RPG with turn-based combat  (this a revision of a review started when it was in Early-Access/Alpha). Permadeath applies to you and to all of your allies, and healing items are often hard to come by; ditto ammo and other needed supplies. Your team only heals a small amount each night, so you will have to decide whether it's worth it to press on to the next area in search of, say, bandages to make more Medkits with, knowing that you could lose someone for good. Of course, this being a Roguelike, you might also end up finding a place for your current battle party (up to three members) to rest up to full...that is, of course, unless they're interrupted by some inconsiderate undead. You never know. Meanwhile, the guard you posted back at camp is dealing with a raiding party of punks in leather jackets and praying that your hunter you sent out in search of food will make it back in one piece.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
The nation – and perhaps, the world – has fallen victim to your standard everyday zombie-type apocalypse, complete with spreading The Infection via biting live victims. The government, if it's still out there, is out of contact; all you have is a bloody club and a pistol with half a clip of ammo remaining. As a Roguelike, you never know if you'll come across half a dozen clips over a day's time, or none whatsoever (hint: it'll almost always be the latter)
CONTROLS:
Mouse and/or keyboard. Blessedly simple combat mechanics – choose Melee, Firearms, Engineer (traps and bombs), Medic (buffs and heals), or Backpack, then choose your action from the menu that pops up in its place. Simple, quick, and straightforward. No manual saving; the game saves at the start of each Day, and if your main character dies, that's it. You start over again, with bonuses from special Tokens applied to future runs; you earn the Tokens for special achievements in-game.
GRAPHICS:
Surprisingly detailed. Decent animation; a huge amount of detail has been paid to the backgrounds. In most any area, the BG's alone are worth checking out  just for themselves. Highway areas have burned-out hulks of cars scattered about, with their former occupants lurching out on the far side of the meridian. An overpass has damaged highway signs and the ever-looming zombie hordes eyeing you from a distance. Wooded areas are reasonably creepy, and have the occasional zombie chowing down on a victim a few feet beyond where you're fighting (complete with appropriately icky sound FX). And so on, and so on. Interstitial, static drawings that appear after many fights – indicating a decision you'll need to make – are quite well-drawn, and fit in well with the overall aesthetic of the game.
SOUND:
Little actual music aside from stings when something important happens. Instead, that effort has gone into ambient audio effects – the sound of an undead pedestrian calmly ripping the meat off of a nearby corpse; the groans and moans of a horde in the background as you fight some shotgun-wielding punks; howls of huge dire wolves in the distance, waiting for their chance to take a bite out of you. Hits feel (and sound) “meaty,” and have impact. Very well done!
OVERALL:
Has some rough edges, but shows a great deal of promise. Plenty of potential to expand and improve, but it already has a solid foundation. Enemy variety is better than expected – generic zombies, buffer zombies, healers, summoners, powerhouses that can either buff themselves, or get stronger based on how many of their allies are still up. You get the idea. Living human enemies such as Punks are also in the game, and often present more of a challenge. Their AI seems to be a bit more sophisticated – e.g., their Engineer might drop a bear trap (causes a fair amount of damage if you use a melee attack) in front of their AK-47 user, who will then drop into a stance that counters your ranged attacks for a few rounds. They also have more visual variety, and could be wearing anything from a t-shirt and jeans to a Bojack horsehead mask.
Tips:
Give everybody at least one point each in Melee (even if they're a “gun bunny” type) and  one in Medicine. The former, so you can conserve ammo early on, and the latter, so they can use Combat Readiness to buff up their own defense, or to simply skip a turn if you want. This comes in handy for those times when an enemy is using something like that “bear trap & ranged counterstance” combo I mentioned earlier.
Also, give 'em all a point in either Survival, so they can contribute to hunting for Rations; or Cunning, so they can help as Guards, if you've nothing else for them to do back at camp. An Engineer with bear traps and high Cunning makes for a superb guard.
Load up your main character on Cunning so he can have an easier time picking locks on car trunks and sealed containers on the road – which happens quite often.

First, its the resource management aspect, as for me this was the most painful. Look, I get it, this is a post-apocolypic world and resources by all means should be scarce, but this is also a game and it shouldn't be so frustrating just to keep the colony fed, let alone go hunting for everything else.
The next problem is the combat mechanic, as it gets stale and repetitive very quickly. It feels more of a mechanic from the 90's than for a modern game. Again, I do realize this is not a AAA game and I can't expect FF15 level complexity, but it gets stale when you regularly end up using the exact same attack over and over.
Progression is another big mis-step in my view. While charachter progression itself seems fine, the difficulty curve doesn't flow with it and often I end up hitting walls, especially given that the first problem I mentioned comes into play. I found myself using almost the same equiptment hours into the game that I started off with.
Lastly, and for some the biggest issue is the story. It felt very empty and I found myself just scrolling though it to get back to the game itself. Nothing about it really grabbed me unfortunately.
Give the game a pass, the market has lots of other zombie games to look out for.

I've read a lot of these review claiming the game hasn't changed significantly in years. These people obviously haven't played the game in years. What began as, essentially, 'Terraria in Space' has really grown into it's own, especially in this past year. This is not just some survival sandbox game, but an intergalactic exploration game with an incredible amount of content. You could play for hundreds of hours and still not discover everything this game has to offer, and they aren't even done with it yet.
As I said, Star Bound is a voxel based exploration sandbox that has you beginning as a survivor of some cataclysm that differs based on race. You find yourself aboard your now derelict space craft/life boat orbiting a rather peaceful world. Initially, you only have a bottom tier weapon (a sword for everyone except the Starkid race who begin with a gun), a flashlight, matter manipulator and a couple other things.
Your first goal is to repair your ship's drive core so you can make your way to a nearby space station. From there, you gather the needed resources to repair the hyperdrive to unlock the ability to travel to other star systems.
The game play itself is quite a bit like Terraria, though combat is quite a bit more in depth. Not only do you have the standard melee weapons, complete with elemental effects, you also have various firearms, each type also having different ammo types making for a mind boggling variety of weapon possibilities. Then you also have Tech Staffs, to become a kind of space wizard. I've only ever had a couple of these, but the are incredibly fun.
Then you have the crafting. The crafting in Star Bound is incredibly vast, almost needlessly so. There are countless different decorative items that can be crafted, though many you need to find blueprints for. Best of all, with the recent Colonies update, those decorative items have a real, useful purpose. The better the items, the more money you make for renting out houses you've made, and the types of items used determine the type of resident. If you want a Glitch colony, build using Glitch furniture.
The best thing about this game, though, is the developers. I've never seen a game in which the developers take such avid interest in community feedback, even hiring certain mod authors that have created incredibly popular, well made mods. These guys show what early access is supposed to be.
Between the already vast game, the constant updates, and the incredibly helpful and attentive developers, this is by far the best early access game on Steam.

AC: Freedom Cry
Short, standalone story with simple premise, but featuring two strong characters that have some quite good conversations in between the missions and are the best thing about this DLC. Other than that, it's very similar to AC4, taking most of the features, often simplifing them, since it's on much smaller scale, and unfortunately bearing all the problems AC games have.
And the bugs! Oh god, the glitches. I've never seen something like this (haven't played Unity yet) - enemies suddenly spawning from their dead comrades (and instantly raising alarm), friendly AI falling down from ladders and killing themselves, invisible enemies that appear on minimap, the good old "I just wanted to jump over that wall, not walk on it", just to name few that were the most memorable, but I kid you not, when this DLC breaks, it breaks hard. I do not remember having such a hard time with AC4 or any previous AC.
Still, even without the bugs, the experience is very limited and other than the story, the exploration is so bare bone that it honestly isn't worth it, you won't find anything different from AC4, where pretty much everything is more fleshed out, so I can only recommend this for the story and when on sale, not for it's regular asking price.

Why Am I Dead At Sea locks on to a pretty solid formula and adds a murderous flair to it. Story driven games like To the Moon and Last Word are classic examples of narrative over action. You don't need flashy graphics and explosions to make a good game. Dead At Sea captures this in natural style with its supernatural themes. From the moment you begin to play, your immediately entranced. You are given the powers of possession and to read minds and set loose aboard a vessel with a unique ensemble of characters. Someone aboard the vessel is your murderer. Can you find out who? Through conversation, puzzles, and a little bit of trickery. You will guide your ghastly visage in a tale that takes many twists and turns. With multiple endings adding even more layers of complexity to the story. Graphically the game is akin to a darker Earthbound style of avatars. It feels like an RPGMaker style game but is different and unique enough that I appreciate. The music is used quite effectively as the tone of the game shifts. As you possess different characters, enter different rooms, or read minds. I liked this quite a bit. The music gave personality to each of the characters and scenes.
In all it was very difficult to find anything really wrong with the game. It's bug free and plays well. The only problem I found was that the momentum of the game was hard to maintain. With little direction given to the player as to what to do next. The goals were sometimes obscure and confusing. Only being made clear by constantly running back to your guide. This caused the game to drag a bit. As I constantly kept having to find the target I needed to possess over and over as they move about the ship. This lead to some frustrating moments. Nonetheless Why Am I Dead At Sea is a fantastic story and a example of how to do story driven game.

40 hours in, and I can safely say I get the gist of this game. For those who like open ended RPG's, understand that this is first a foremost, a JRPG. There are no decisions to be made here. You are along for the ride, and sadly, that means the game can get very linear. The true meat of the game is not in the story (which is excellent, if hard to understand at times) but in the customization of the protaganists gear, fashion look, and combat. People who enjoy min/maximization will be overjoyed with this one, as you can spend a great deal of time figuring out what works, what will get you better combos, better DPS, and so on.
It should be noted that the combat itself is a hugely complex system that the game spends about 30 hours just explaining. So there is a natural learning curve to it. For most players though, simply button mashing will suffice, especially on lower difficulties where the enemies are pretty much made of glass. I had to bump the difficulty up to Hard simply to break the tedium, since most of the trash mob fights get repetitive and samey and even on Normal difficulty are brain dead punching bags.
All in all, a solid JRPG. Its not the second coming of christ, but its a good product that you can sink hours into, if you are a fan of the genre.

As much as I love Tales games, this one turned out only okay at best due to the extremely poor combat (some of the worst AI I have seen explained further on). I only recommend it because it is still decent for the story, and worth at least a single play through.
Berseria should have been released before Zestiria as there are a few small bits that aren't a surprise if you have played through Zestiria, and it almost makes it a bit confusing as the characters find out about something you already know (that, or almost annoying to watch). If you haven't played Zestiria, play Berseria before that is my advice.
I loved the combat in Zestiria and its engaging directional attacks, flashy effects, and rather difficult fights that would take up to 20 minutes of spamming the water bow just to win. In here, there is very little flash minus some of the spells. The fights are mostly easy to where you can just spam a single skill in almost every fight (Magilou's Spirit Drop). The Soul Break system is fun and makes comboing fun so it isn't hard to go on a spamming spree with that Spirit Drop skill and go from 200 dmg a hit to 2000. However, that is where the enjoyment stops due to the abysmal AI of your characters.
This might be a non-issue on the 2 lowest difficulties, but it becomes a problem on hard+. So what is the problem with the AI? They are more of a liability. Each character seems to have a major flaw that relates to thier prime purpose.
-For Laphi, instead of spamming heals, he will run around the field over half of the battle time while the others die. His only redemption he is actually able to dodge/block properly.
-For characters like Velvet/Rokurou, they tend to just jump back into a large enemy attack despite having been out of it before, or they just stand there and take it despite having 2-3 seconds to have moved. Just as annoying is when they randomly stand on the field and do nothing for 5-10 seconds easily and an enemy comes along and just kills them while they refuse to dodge.
-I did not use Eizen/Eleanor much but they have similar issues.
Basically, you can't at all rely on your characters AI, which makes the highest difficulties hard as it quickly becomes a fight of you + Laphi vs enemies as they just keep dieing by the first easily avoidable attack. If that all isn't annoying enough, the enemy AI seems to really love to chase down the character you are using. If you are using Magilou, this gets tedious as it is tough to even get a spell off. On top of all of that, bosses tend to guard most of your hits so it becomes a boring and drawn out fight.
There are only 2 tough story bosses which have a huge increase in difficulty over others. They are so harsh against your characters that there is no chance on hard+ unless you spent a ton of extra time leveling. Even then, I am not sure this would help your AI much, that, and being on par with the enemy would make it no different than playing at a lower difficulty at your level anyway. Most other fights consist of boring spamming of a single button or 2. I enjoy the Tales games for the combat, and coming of Zestiria which is the first game I would NG+ because of how fun its combat is, there definitely won't be a NG+ here for me. Quite the opposite really, the combat is just so watered down with such poor AI from your allies.
This component is interesting as you can essentially pick what gear you want, then find a version with good bonuses on it, and then upgrade it up to +10. You won't be bursting through gear here constantly, you may change versions about 3x on each slot, pending the playstyle you choose for the character. Once you are happy with an item, you upgrade it. Upgrading gets pretty hard at the higher ranks as the items are hard to obtain or come from the end game zones. On another note, you won't have a Gald shortage unless you buy the unnecessary consumables for 50k+.
In terms of characters, the cast isn't as exciting as Zestiria either. Magilou should have been the main character as I find she is the only one that shines, in terms of her comedy, and her outfit. Everyone else just was average at best. Velvet is worth going into detail over. She is not a great main character. They gave her a personality that is more male than the males. The lack of emotion for the most part and her coldness really don't make her exciting or stand out. Sure she is on about vengeance and whatnot, but this just doesn't work well for the star of the show. It is hard to connect or feel any sort of attachment, she ultimately is just annoying more than anything. Considering this was the first female lead in a Tales game, it may as well have been a guy. Without spoiling anything, she shines a bit more at the end and the very start, but the other 95% of the story she just doesn't shine like a main character. Her combat is decently fun and her soul breaks are fun to play, but other than that, it just didn't work for me.
Magilou was the saving character for the cast. Her dialogue is always entertaining and she is really fun to play (and overpowered compared to the rest in my view). From her outfit, to her spells and dialogue she made it worth playing.
The geoboards (think of a snowboard) is a great addition and helps with traveling a lot. No more running everywhere on foot. Combine this with the warp points, and exploration or going back isn't painful at all. Another new addition is these Class 4 Zones which is like a mini arena where you fight waves of certain themed enemies. Not hard, but a fun while it lasts (briefly). The other entertaining piece is the minigames. There are several, such as sliding puzzles, card games, playing a waiter, and a few more. Doing these give Tales Coins which you can buy fashion with or enhancement items. The last new thing worth pointing out is "Katz Spirits". You use these to open Katz Chests around the world. Later on you won't have enough spirits to open each chest you come by, so I recommend just waiting to farm them till you are near the end of the game (the zone with a huge amount of them will be extremely obvious).
Overall, I looked forward to this game for some time like any Tales game. Sadly, I feel let down this time by what seems like a step backwards in exciting combat combined with an extremely poor ally AI. Worth a play through once for any Tales fan, but can't say anything much better than that unfortunately. Hopefully the next Tales game will have better AI programmed and less single button spamming combat.
Personal experience score: 6.2/10
Story: 9/10 - A dark themed story about a girls vengeance consuming her to get her revenge, no matter the cost. It was quite entertaining and possibly the only real redeeming component for this Tales game. If you played Zestiria, the theme is somewhat familiar.
Sound: 5/10 - The soundtrack feels bland for a lot of the game. Some of the tough areas are nice, but it just wasn't all that exciting
Graphics: 8.5/10 - The anime graphics you would expect from a Tales game. However, after around 2 hours there is a micro stutter that requires restarting the game to fix. It gets very obvious to see so its an annoyance. Also on the videos there is a pixelated strip across the bottom of the screen.
Controls: 8/10 - Easy to use and all, but the controls weren't as fun as in Zestiria where directions determined the skill. This is a lot more basic and boring where you just mash one button endlessly for your strongest skill
Game Length: 10/10 - Exactly what you would expect for a Tales game. On hard difficulty it will take around 60 hours if you plan to do most of the content and after story content. Obviously far less if on an easier difficulty.

This was my second Tales game, Zestiria being my first last year.
I think Berseria is a superior game to Zestiria in almost every way.
I enjoyed the combat and didn't really get tired of it, although I only played on Normal difficulty, so I was able to spam my way through most of it without putting much thought into it. For stronger enemies or bosses I switched up my attacks to target their weaknesses and was able to do so without many problems, though a few were just a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
The story was nice, although maybe a bit slow.
The upgrade and mastery systems are nice, but I was able to get away with just switching to any gear I hadn't mastered yet, without any real regards for the stats. Maybe this was because I was "only" playing on Normal, but it didn't bother me very much.
Cooking and Expeditions were alright but didn't really feel necessary. Though, again, that might be because the game wasn't really hard and on higher difficulties these systems are more important.
There are tons of minigames in the world and most a pretty nice. Mug Match is pretty crappy on higher difficulty, but since the only reward are coins this game doesn't really matter (many other games give costumes as rewards). The fishing minigame is just random and during my playthrough I found <10 of the best bait, so I have no idea how you're really supposed to get all the rare fish.
One negative point are the animations. During cutscenes they are really stiff and there isn't much variation, so I started noticing the same poses over and over. The arms of the female character are almost always at an angle, away from the body, to avoid clipping into the costumes but they just look weird. During combat or running around in the world this either didn't happen or it wasn't noticable.
Overall I really enjoyed the game but I can't see myself ever going back to it for some post-game stuff or NG+

TALES OF BERSERIA - TALES IS GREAT AGAIN ! MAGILOU BEST GIRL !
TLDR : game is great. If you're a fan buy it already !!!!! If you never played a tales game then this is a great place to start. as a fan of the series I can say that this game is worthy of it.
NOW time for the huge♥♥♥♥♥in-depth review.
Berseria is the latest entry in the tales of series. I will be comparing it to the previous entry in the series i.e. tales of zestiria and especially more so since this game is a prequel to zestiria although it takes place roughly 500-600 years before that game.
THE GOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOD
berseria follows a group of misfits and not so good people. our main character is velvet crowe. the story of this game isn't like most other tales games. the team did a lot of work to try and make this non standard cliched animu stuff thus going for a more dark tone in the story with more mature tone.  Excellent job at breaking the mould. where zestiria went so hard into the mould that itself was the standard jrpg anime story with goody two shoes trying to save the world, this game is about velvet seeking revenge for his dead brother laphi who was murdered by her brother in law. Of course all the other characters have their own motivations and reasons for joining her but I wont spoil any further.
Characters are not your young teen anime stereotypes, they are rather mature and not your typical good guys. infact the whole crew is all antiheroes especially velvet herself. i would even go as far as to say this may be the most likable cast of all the tales game to date. each with their own motivations and struggles that you will see and help them overcome. gone are the bland and boring characters from zestiria. everyone here is interesting in their own way and relateble. this particular is very good because tales games are very character focused
there are occassional skits that show character interaction building and developing character or telling you world details
the game does an excellent job of world building. all the npcs always have something to say about the current state of the world and after major events in the story change the circumstances of the world, you can expect the npcs to have all new dialogue. to top that off some npcs are voiced and are present to give you important details.
the games new combat system is great. its has plenty of mechanics for the general party as well as for individual characters. but nothing too much that may overwhelm you. so play all characters as they appear and by the end you should have one you like and have mastered fully. i would also like to point out that although the combat in zestiria wasnt bad by any means this new system is far superior to the one in zestiria.
MINIGAMES ARE BAAAAAAAACK !!!! after so long too :D i spent an entire 4 hours playing fishing and being a waiter/waitress. these arent necessary by any means but are there simply to add more content to this already amazing game. playing minigames earns you tales coins which you may use to buy accessories for your character or items that you can use in battle or during exploration or for crafting.
theres so much in this game i can spend hours writing about it all but you should find out for yourself. from crafting and enhancing items to minigames to sidequests( OF COURSE ! ) optional dungeons and much mooore.
another amazing thing about the game is difficulty. on simple difficulty you arent expected to understand elemental weaknesses and strengths and enemies have lower hp but you arent rewarded as well. as you go to normal and moderate the elemental weaknesses and strength come into play and enemies have much higher hp but you are rewarded pretty well. above moderate is when things start to get interesting. some enemy moves are only used in harder modes and the power of healing items/spells gets reduced. you are rewarded excellently on higher difficulties. another addition to higher difficulties is DIRE FOES. really strong enemies that will appear during battle starting from moderate. the chances of them appearing increases as the difficulty increase and trust me they are hard. i personally got rekt by 2 a few times before i finally managed to kill it.

If you choose a title like that, you have to expect some people to be disappointed. Live by the sword. Probably if you call your game, say,
, people are less likely to say, "What does it have to do with Shakespeare, and where's the drama, the wit, the masterful use of the language?" It's more or less understood that the game just borrows the archetypal characters and situations and recycles them purely for amusement. That is really what FK does as well; strong writing or memorable characters are not what this game excels at.
FK is a puzzle game consisting of single-screen levels. There are 22 levels, although I may have miscounted by one or two. Some of the puzzles are Goblins-like -- or Amanita-like, which to me is the same thing -- where essentially you need to figure out the required sequence of clicks through the on-screen hotspots. Others are based around a single puzzle idea, where you just need to "see" the solution. And no, the game won't make you solve logic puzzles with convoluted rules or push sliding crates.
The whole shtick of the game is that its events and puzzles have their logic, but it's a surreal logic. That is, you're not left wondering why the puzzle solution worked at all, and the game is actually fairer with its puzzles than Hamlet was, but it's always Franz Kafka: Unexpected Juxtapositions (TM). This isn't going to appeal to everyone, but I think it makes for some very entertaining puzzles.

What a bizarre game. And most likely not in a good way. It's hard to approach a game that does not appeal to you more than by name, and it is of no interest of mine to solely go into something writing about weaknesses or confused game-design.
The perfect word for this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization. Making Kafka into some goofy ground upon which to build an edifice of superficial references coupled with Latin phrases with uncertain relevance to both the game and to Kafka. While interesting at times, they served little purpose.
To me, Kafka could never be a cartoon. The tone of Kafka does not easily traverse mediums, I'd say it is a futile endeavor. But at the same time I admire the attempt, nothing else considered. It's a light Kafka game, it doesn't go into the emotional or philosophical depth of Kafka, instead it operates under the commonly referenced aspects of him, and connects Kafka's stories to a general clichéd tropes. While Kafka sometimes gets close such things as detective stories, he never quite crosses the line to the all too familiar stories or frameworks that make stories. Kafka always transcends commonality, and the normative. He revels in the outer limits of it, you could say.
This game, however, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥izes Kafka, in my mind. Not a single hint of the atmosphere gleaned from Kafka as such can be found in this game. It is whimsical, in tone-deaf a sense. While it is pleasant in itself, it is not Kafka, and it is not what I bought the game for. Kafka can be funny, but never silly. Never quite absurd in a way that isn't also reflective of something real.
I do not understand this game and how it relates to Kafka as I know him. And maybe that is indicative of my peculiar way of viewing this author, but that is my impression, regardless.
It's an entirely separate story covered in a veneer of Kafka, but everything internal to that veneer is not Kafka, it is a themed puzzle game.
So what about the puzzles? Not many of them were logical. And a lot were solved by randomly clicking objects. Unfortunately that makes for a very unsatisfying experience. Some were variations on older types of puzzles with clever twists, which made it somewhat interesting, the random clicking was coupled with classical puzzle designs. It had its moments, certainly, but was never quite impressive or felt worth the money paid, which is something I rarely criticize a game for.
I suppose certain moments of Kafka was cited and made into a visual for the game, which was in a way delightful. But there was no attempt at all to made a holistic experience that made congruent any of Kafka's stories and the game mechanics. I am really puzzled about the positive tone of this game, and the art design. Is this how the game creator interpreted and visualized Kafka? If so, there is no way to really argue with that, other than to say that you, or I, don't see how any imagery in Kafka could ever be close to what was presented here.
If this was not a supposed Kafka-game, I would have very little to say about it. There is nothing too awful, nothing too excitingly good. The art-style is in itself interesting and fairly cute, and would be perhaps good for any other game like of this kind, that is, a somewhat streamlined puzzle experience.
One concrete criticism would be that the timer for the hints can be too long in relation to the time it takes to exhaust all the immediately available options. So you can click everything, and test everything intuitively, before you get a hint. This results in sometimes minutes of dead time, that could be filled with or mitigated by trying the same things over and over, but how would this be purposeful in any way? The hints are optional to begin with, so why have a timer on them? What integrity is there in logic puzzles not necessarily based in logic or any available knowledge.
Maybe a game like this should be supported simply due to its literary relation. But even that is unclear. The more “failures” in efforts like this, the less I want to see games try to engage with other mediums. Games are good at things that literature isn't, and that movies generally aren't. Maybe games should focus on those things, instead of trying to sloppily appropriate well-known names from other mediums to artificially increase sales.
But perhaps you, dear reader, will find joy in a game like this. Maybe the references will be enough as a novel little engagement with Kafka in a different medium. It was cute, in a sense. But in what world is Kafka cute? It's fairly nonsensical, it's confusing, but perhaps worth supporting and trying for yourself. It stands on its own in how it creates surrealist scenes that are somewhat amusing. It's just the name Kafka that makes this game into a failure, to me. There is nothing “Kafkaesque” about the game, no congruence with gameplay and atmosphere or anything relating to Kafka. Nothing evokes despair or existential uncertainty, nothing adds to Kafka as an author of the minor literature. It's a theme park with Kafka as the theme. It's the failed interpretation of Kafka, that ends in him being whimsically absurd, as opposed to using absurdity to exaggerate and elucidate the real and at times abhorrent and frightening circumstances of sociality and society.
Maybe I am too serious about Kafka. I am not well. Perhaps it is best to leave it there. I am just writing for the sake of writing anyway.

I noticed a huge influx of negative reviews for this game ever since Bethesda introduced paid mods. Let me get a few things straight: Are you required to partake in these paid mods? NO. Does it at all take away from the experience of the game? NO. Does it mean you can no longer use free mods from sites like Nexus Mods? NO.
All of these negative reviews COMPLETELY ignore the fact that overall, Fallout 4 is an excellent game and is one of my favourite games of all time. I think that they're rather unfair as they have nothing to do with what Fallout 4 is like, and are focused exclusively on the paid mods (which I do disagree with, for the record). This review will be about the actual game itself, and not about the paid mods. If you're interested in the game, you should ignore those reviews.
Fallout 4 is a huge game. Even just the base game, with no DLCs or mods. The open world is huge and really detailed, it seems like there is thought about each location's back story. There are tons of locations to explore, all full of loot. Perks are really good and useful, levelling up is not difficult and if you're into the type of game, it will likely have you playing for hours.
I've got a couple hundred hours in the game and I've by no means explored all of the game's features and locations. My first 40 hours were just me building my settlement, which is a cool feature to have. You put together buildings using materials you've collected around the world. In previous titles like Fallout 3, New Vegas and Skyrim, there was all kinds of useless junk that you could pick up. In Fallout 4, everything is now useful, because it can be broken down into various materials for use in creating stuff for your settlement.
Companions, while there are fewer than in other games like Skyrim, have much more personality to them, in addition to their own voice actors (generic NPCs aside, Bethesda seems to have hired many more voice actors than in previous titles so there's much more diversity in voices). Each companion has their own backstory, set of likes and dislikes and personality. It really makes them feel a lot more real than in previous games. Unfortunately, conversation in the game is a bit limited, only ever having four options to choose from in any given dialogue option, but now the player character is voiced.
With the way the game now handles conversations between you and other NPCs, it feels more cinematic and lively than before. The game's main story is quite interesting too, and there are many other quests with interesting stories to complete as well.
Character customization is superior to past Fallout titles. For starters, it's much easier to make an attractive looking character than in Fallout 3 and New Vegas. Sculpting your character's face is similar to The Sims 4. Not quite as intuitive or fluid as that in The Sims 4, but similar nonetheless. Also, customizing your character's clothing is far more detailed than in Fallout 3 and New Vegas. There are more items and more ways to customize what you're already wearing.
Combat has also been hugely improved over Fallout 3 and New Vegas. While I love Fallout 3 and New Vegas and still play both quite often, Fallout 4's combat system is just so much better. For starters, the way you use guns is really good, on the same level as other big, triple A first person shooters. Playing the game in third person is also pretty good too, and if you prefer third person, you won't have to switch to first person if you need to shoot a gun. You also no longer have to switch from your gun to a grenade. You can have a gun and a grenade equipped at the same time, and by holding the Alt key, you'll throw a grenade without putting away your gun. Also, by simply tapping the Alt key, you can do a quick melee attack in case an enemy gets too close.
This point is more of a personal opinion. One thing I miss from Fallout 3 and New Vegas is the darker, bleaker, grimmer feeling of the world. In Fallout 3 particularly, the game world is really dark and grim and quite unnerving at times. While there are parts of Fallout 4 that are creepy and grim, the game world is much brighter, much more colourful and actually seems more lively. I actually loved how Fallout 3's world seems so dead, and how it made me feel like "this place was once so important, so busy and so active, and now it's all gone". Fallout 4's world actually kind of gives me a feeling of "hope for the future".
Fallout 4's intro and prologue, on the other hand, are awesome. Without spoiling everything, it does an excellent job of setting the stage for the game, and always gets my heart going whenever I go through the sequence again.
Overall, Fallout 4 is an excellent game and improves on absolutely everything from past games. Fans who stick to the Fallout games before Fallout 3 might have a different opinion, but I love Fallout 4 and if you love open world games, RPGs, or first person/third person shooters, you'll probably love Fallout 4 too. I highly recommend this game.

Town of Salem is a mafia-esque game by BlankMediaGames.  To properly explain this game, I'll first have to explain "mafia".  Mafia is a party-based game that is a real life game, not a video game.  Basically, it involved a group of innocent people trying to find the mafia.  The mafia could kill at the night phase, and during the day phase, the innocents could lynch a suspected mafia.  Depending on who you play with, or what rules you play by, the game can vary, and have added roles, but that is the game at it's core: a deception-based party game.  Town of Salem takes the core concept of Mafia and expands on it by a ten-fold.  Tons of different roles, 3 technical core teams, and different game modes.  So, is Town of Salem worth a try?  In my opinion, definitely.  Here's why.
First, let us talk about the graphics.  Graphics are nothing to gawk about, for sure, but you aren't looking at a 60$ Call of Duty: Kevin Spacey.  It is a 5$ game on Steam, free if you play the  web browser version.  And for it's asking price, it is a decent looking game, with an interesting art direction.  There isn't much to say about graphics, they are decent looking, with a definite influence all throughout.  Nothing looks stand-offish or out of place.  Overall, they are good graphics, and if you are looking for great graphics, you're in the wrong place.
Sound design is pretty good, the little sound effects sound nice, like the clicking, and the  soundtrack really puts you  on edge when performing a risky move at night.  Overall, sound design is great, I love it.
In terms of gameplay, Town of Salem has all the right cards.  It basically performs like Mafia, except a lot better, and has an addictive quality to it.  There is no voice chat, which is for the  best, to be honest.  People would spam it anyways.  In terms of the roles, they all perform and function on an overall equal playing field, they all feel balanced, except for a few exceptions.  Some classes outperform others, usually by a lot.  For example, Medium, a class that talks to the dead, and Lookout, a person who watches someone every night to see if anyone visits them, sometimes feel underwhelming.  You won’t feel like you are helping the town when you are the Medium and all of the dead Town members quit.  It sometimes feels like you are not contributing to the success of the town, while the Investigator is getting baddies hung.  Sometimes these roles will get useful information, which can get a Mafia member or Serial Killer hung, but they feel less important than the higher up roles.  I feel like it’s intentional, but you can’t help but sigh when you get the Lookout role.  But, besides that, I enjoyed the gameplay, it is definitely a very strong part of this game.
Now, I want to bring up the community, as it is an important part of this game.  The community?  Absolute garbage.  A lot of people spam, a lot of people are racist, some people make sexist jokes, and it’s a damn shame, because this game deserves better community.  Now, I’m not calling out every Town of Salem player, because some of them are good-willed, kind people who play the game properly.  But they are basically the one percent.  The ninety-nine percent consists of racist, sexist, offensive gamers, and they do it just because no one knows who they are.  This game needs a clean up, because a major turn off is the toxic community.
Back to the game itself, the interface in-game is pretty good, everything is neat and organized, and you can close a tab if it is useless to you, or if it is getting in the way.  Overall, the interface is very sleek, and that’s appreciable.
Before I give my final verdict, I want to talk a little bit about the developers.  The developers are probably the coolest developers any game could have.  They communicate with the community, they respond quickly and kindly to people’s questions and  criticisms, and they really care about their game.  I have never seen a development team so dedicated to a game.  It is a true rarity in today’s gaming market, and for all the hard effort they put into their game, and the community, I definitely feel like they need a shoutout on this review, and a real acknowledgement to the fact that they are great people and developers.  They aren’t trying to siphon money from your wallet, like many other devs, everything in the game that you can pay for in the game is cosmetic, and really, supports the devs.  I would much rather give 20$ to these devs than give 20$ to a P2W company, or a scumbag company.  I could recommend this game just for the devs, and I could keep going on and on about the devs, and how awesome they are, but I need to wrap up this review.
Overall, I enjoyed my overly-long stay with Town of Salem.  Is it worth your time?  Yes.  Like I said, the developers are great, and the game is great itself.  The only aspect to be wary about is the community, like I said, there are the nice players, and there are the sour players.  Besides that, I definitely recommend this game, you get a great game and non-pessimistic developers, what could be better?

Dead Age took me by surprise. There wasn't a single moment of my playing this game that I doubted I hadn't landed a gold mine in a pile of endless Zombie Steam game garbage we constantly see hit the platform. One hour became two. Two became two dozen. During the July 4th weekend, I plunged headlong into this strategic turn-based RPG with reckless abandon. Was the story-line griping? Not really. Did it have great voice acting? Zilch. Huge open world exploration? Nada. What did it have? A deep layer of tactical combat that I haven't seen in a Zombie game ever.
Inside the game, there is a light story-line and a sprinkling of decision making that does matter. Also, the only time you hit a save state is when you finish a day. Otherwise, game over man(RIP Bill Paxton). With a dash of roguelike, decisions making a difference and medals that unlock to give you other class arch-types to choose from, Dead Age pulls off replayability well. Overall, this was a very pleasant experience and if you are a fan of the genre of zombies or turn-based strategy done right, then Dead Age definitely deserves a look.

This trumped – down, Black Flag spin – off can easily be described in four words: Pure, unadulterated, machete mayhem. Freedom Cry suffers from the same issues that all these little filler titles in the series face. It is small in scale, meaning that from the grandiose Black Flag Caribbean, you now get to basically explore a rather small Port-au-Prince, some plantations and beaches and a single wreck. It is less polished, with a fast and easy story whose completion comes rather swiftly and without much diversity. Lastly, the characters don’t give off the same attraction as in the main titles of the series.
The above is not to say that Freedom Cry doesn’t have its good aspects. The weapon and upgrade acquisition mechanics have been simplified, to the extent where they liberate the player from grinding money to acquire a new weapon or a ship upgrade, taking a menial task of a player’s shoulders and allowing for more slave – freeing. Which, slave – freeing, is done with ample use of your machete and blunderbuss, adding to this loose yet deadly feeling of the title. There is a liberating feeling on just hacking and scatter-shooting your way through the streets, while at the same time freeing the unfortunate slaves paraded about. Adewale is also pretty cool as a character, though he lacks an adequate support cast.
The controls are the same as in Black Flag, so if you’ve been there, you can jump right in here. There is also some nice music and signing, appropriate for the culture of the people ferried in as slaves to the plantations, which gives a nice feeling of change to the previously known Europe-based musical scores. The game remains definitively easy though, with almost nothing to offer in terms of difficulty, challenge and replayability.
Freedom Cry is by no means a bad game. It is just too small and limited in scope for me to be able to recommend it as a purchase to someone, as not playing it doesn’t really deprive you of anything.

So, I've been following this game ever since I saw the trailer; something about the Earthbound inspired environments really caught my eye.  It's not a clone by any means; Earthbound was a true turn-based RPG while this is a more puzzle-y narrative-driven adventure with a supernatural twist.
The good:
-Great pixel graphics and environments
-Great character work; each person has a different personality, motives, secrets and strengths
-These differences are more interesting when you possess them in order to find out what happened to you
-Diving into people's minds was executed very well
-I really got invested in wanting to find out what makes these people tick and what happened to me
-The music in the game is fun and true to their retro roots
-Tons of unique dialogue to trigger depending on who you are
-Great throwbacks to Earthbound
Cons:
-Not a wide variety of music to hear; can get a little repetitive as you walk around
-Some of the puzzles are difficult to figure out (Who needs to do what and where? Etc.) which leads to some extra wandering around
-Can be difficult to tell who is talking when you are learning who is who; dialogue boxes could have been positioned more over the person talking instead of centered on the screen
-Which there was more interactivity with mind-reading (A mini-game to learn secrets would have been cool, or literally explore their mind (Like Alundra on PSX?) and unlock secrets that way.)
Disclosure: I was provided a complimentary advanced copy by the developer for review purposes and I was not compensated any other way. All opinions are my own.

This game is absolutely fun! Working as a crew is an absolute must. The Galleon is alot of fun as 13 players work together on a ship with 2 decks. Shooting cannons goes like this: Theres ammo crates next to each cannon. You put powder in the cannon first, then the ammo (Ball, Grape, Grapple) use the ramrod, push, then aim the cannon and fire. You are doing all this while under fire of other enemy ships. When your ship gets hit, its really intense. Crew mates getting killed, wood splinters going everywhere, large explosions. If there are a bunch of holes in your ship from enemy cannons the crew has to repair these holes as fast as they can for the hull starts to flood with water. If you dont fix and empty the water in time then you sink.
On the top deck you have to worry about sail repairs or fire. There are water buckets at the ready to put the fires out. Watching your crew mates catch on fire running around screaming is quite humorous and adds to the intensity of the battle. If the ships sails are damaged then you have to climb up the masts and repair them. Ramming your ship into the enemy is also a thing which damages the nose of the ship. If the nose is damaged you'll sit there unable to move while under fire. So the pressure of fixing the ship as fast as you can while being circle by enemy sloops is super intense.
And of course to my favorite part! Boarding enemy ships. You have a variety of weapons to choose from. Different rifles, side arms, swords, grenades. I personally enjoy grenades as you throw them over to the enemy ships or into their bottom decks. To board you can either ram a ship and have crew mates jump over, or you can have a proper boarding action using grapple. When you hook the enemy ship, the ships start being pulled together. Now the enemy can cut the grapple or get away. But most choose to stay and fight. You need to kill everyone on the other ship in a time to win the fight and the boat to sink. If you dont kill everyone in time then they all respawn and the melee continues. There is something satisfying about the chaos of boarding. Musket or flintlock smoke, swords, grenades going off. The boarding action is pretty intense.
Over all this game is in alpha stage but the gameplay is so fun that I hardly notice bugs or graphic glitches etc. Try it out and give them your support!

While AI: Rampage is well-polished for the price, some of its important features are unfortunately botched. Still, it does enough things right that it remains enjoyable and true to what is advertised.
As one would hope after reading the game's title*, enemy behavior is on point. Robots chase you aggressively. Their hearing is acute and they have long sight lines, which are reliably blocked by objects. Pathfinding seems excellent. Passive movement is randomized but slow. All-around solid AI, no complaints from me here.
The player v.s. robot speed balance is good, as is the noise level for footsteps and gunshots. Combined with the aforementioned AI, this makes for enjoyable and tactical gameplay overall.
Detailed textures and lighting give the "2-D" levels a surprisingly realistic look. Performance seems very smooth and stable as well (although this isn't saying much, since my PC is high-end).
The directional sound takes some getting used too, but it really adds to the realism. Wind, aircraft, and stomping robots all sound great and contribute to a nice soundscape/atmosphere**. The game sounds very good in my stereo headphones.
+   Very high difficulty, generally for good reason (more on this later...)
+   Player weapon/abilities give the player cool options besides pure hiding/running.
+   The concept of spawning from bunkers and bringing supplies to them works well.
+   Movement feels smooth, controls are generally responsive. (more on this later...)
+   The "human survivor of a robot apocalypse" theme works in the game's favor.
+   Short loading times: little delay between starting the game and playing.
+   It's only two dollars!
Strangely, the WASD controls are linked to the direction you aim. So, depending on which way your character is pointed (determined by the mouse), pressing "w" could make you move down the screen while "a" would make you move right. This is disorienting for a top-down view game and contributes too much to the learning curve.
There are currently*** three levels, each with a day/night version. They are big, and will surely take a long time to complete (I have yet to beat one, despite playing mostly on easy), but the lack of variety may make that achievement less satisfying.
First, each level's "border" actually only applies to the player and their visibility. There are robots beyond that border who may enter at random positions and times. This is clearly cheap for the walking robots. Also, the levels themselves have vast open areas and very few hiding spots. Altogether, this makes the current levels unfairly hard on high difficulty, preventing the AI from shining.
-   It's sometimes hard to tell which objects block line of sight.
-   The laser gun robot looks too similar to the melee robot.
-   Wait time for entering the bunker is stupidly long.
-   Nuclear wind can cause cheap deaths.
-   The robots don't look as good as the environment.
-   The splash screens are very ugly.
And after all those cons, my review is still a "Recommended". For two dollars, you get stealth gameplay with tactical depth, along with some serious production values. Just don't expect it to be easy to get into, and prepare to retry the same levels a bunch.

Town of Salem is a mafia-esque game by BlankMediaGames.  To properly explain this game, I'll first have to explain "mafia".  Mafia is a party-based game that is a real life game, not a video game.  Basically, it involved a group of innocent people trying to find the mafia.  The mafia could kill at the night phase, and during the day phase, the innocents could lynch a suspected mafia.  Depending on who you play with, or what rules you play by, the game can vary, and have added roles, but that is the game at it's core: a deception-based party game.  Town of Salem takes the core concept of Mafia and expands on it by a ten-fold.  Tons of different roles, 3 technical core teams, and different game modes.  So, is Town of Salem worth a try?  In my opinion, definitely.  Here's why.
First, let us talk about the graphics.  Graphics are nothing to gawk about, for sure, but you aren't looking at a 60$ Call of Duty: Kevin Spacey.  It is a 5$ game on Steam, free if you play the  web browser version.  And for it's asking price, it is a decent looking game, with an interesting art direction.  There isn't much to say about graphics, they are decent looking, with a definite influence all throughout.  Nothing looks stand-offish or out of place.  Overall, they are good graphics, and if you are looking for great graphics, you're in the wrong place.
Sound design is pretty good, the little sound effects sound nice, like the clicking, and the  soundtrack really puts you  on edge when performing a risky move at night.  Overall, sound design is great, I love it.
In terms of gameplay, Town of Salem has all the right cards.  It basically performs like Mafia, except a lot better, and has an addictive quality to it.  There is no voice chat, which is for the  best, to be honest.  People would spam it anyways.  In terms of the roles, they all perform and function on an overall equal playing field, they all feel balanced, except for a few exceptions.  Some classes outperform others, usually by a lot.  For example, Medium, a class that talks to the dead, and Lookout, a person who watches someone every night to see if anyone visits them, sometimes feel underwhelming.  You won’t feel like you are helping the town when you are the Medium and all of the dead Town members quit.  It sometimes feels like you are not contributing to the success of the town, while the Investigator is getting baddies hung.  Sometimes these roles will get useful information, which can get a Mafia member or Serial Killer hung, but they feel less important than the higher up roles.  I feel like it’s intentional, but you can’t help but sigh when you get the Lookout role.  But, besides that, I enjoyed the gameplay, it is definitely a very strong part of this game.
Now, I want to bring up the community, as it is an important part of this game.  The community?  Absolute garbage.  A lot of people spam, a lot of people are racist, some people make sexist jokes, and it’s a damn shame, because this game deserves better community.  Now, I’m not calling out every Town of Salem player, because some of them are good-willed, kind people who play the game properly.  But they are basically the one percent.  The ninety-nine percent consists of racist, sexist, offensive gamers, and they do it just because no one knows who they are.  This game needs a clean up, because a major turn off is the toxic community.
Back to the game itself, the interface in-game is pretty good, everything is neat and organized, and you can close a tab if it is useless to you, or if it is getting in the way.  Overall, the interface is very sleek, and that’s appreciable.
Before I give my final verdict, I want to talk a little bit about the developers.  The developers are probably the coolest developers any game could have.  They communicate with the community, they respond quickly and kindly to people’s questions and  criticisms, and they really care about their game.  I have never seen a development team so dedicated to a game.  It is a true rarity in today’s gaming market, and for all the hard effort they put into their game, and the community, I definitely feel like they need a shoutout on this review, and a real acknowledgement to the fact that they are great people and developers.  They aren’t trying to siphon money from your wallet, like many other devs, everything in the game that you can pay for in the game is cosmetic, and really, supports the devs.  I would much rather give 20$ to these devs than give 20$ to a P2W company, or a scumbag company.  I could recommend this game just for the devs, and I could keep going on and on about the devs, and how awesome they are, but I need to wrap up this review.
Overall, I enjoyed my overly-long stay with Town of Salem.  Is it worth your time?  Yes.  Like I said, the developers are great, and the game is great itself.  The only aspect to be wary about is the community, like I said, there are the nice players, and there are the sour players.  Besides that, I definitely recommend this game, you get a great game and non-pessimistic developers, what could be better?

Combat in Starbound is unique and filled with action, a ton of different weapons await you.
You'll find everything ranging from swords to bows and fist weapons, even energy wands.
There's also the huge and diverse modding community, hundreds of diverse mods await you if you feel adventurous, the addition of the workshop made it even easier to get these mods.
Get this game if you love to explore hundreds of diverse worlds, building, and fun combat.
This game is best enjoyed with a group of friends, but it's still fun if you want to explore the stars alone.

Like Terraria, but Better.
Like Terraria, Starbound is a 2-D explorative worldbuilding sandbox game
however
Unlike Terraria, which has unclear goals, nonlinear boss progression, and a very small and limiting world, Starbound has the opposite, Clear Goals, Linear Boss progression, and an infinite universe to explore.
And Starbound is still early access.
Pros:
Craploads of items
Each race has entirely seperate armor skins for all 6 tiers (7 races x 6 tiers(will be 10 at release) = 52 armor sets)
Very rewarding exploration with dungeons and colonies all over
Awesome Musical Instruments in-game
Multiplayer (i haven't played it, but i imagine it works fine)
Over 200 pieces of armor and clothing with optional cosmetic slots if you don't like it's appearence, including back items
Matter Manipulator Tool - Manipulates anything that matters, works as infinite Pick/Axe/Shovel at the cost of being slower than actual pickaxes. Can also easily gather and move liquid once upgraded some.
Cons:
Crafting system is not robust enough with basic furniture crafting, relies too much on random chest drops for blueprints
Almost impossible to find armors for other races without multiplayer because even colonies only usually have 1 set
Early game can be painfully slow if you aren't very lucky or efficient at digging
Game isn't very long yet, maybe 15-20 hours to reach Tier 6 gear and defeat the boss
Overall I highly recommend it, it's only going to get better from here. I enjoy Starbound more than Minecraft and Terraria, which combined I have over 2k hours into, don't let my steam hours fool you, i played offline for a few hundred on my main Floran character.

I look down at the reviews and see a lot of whiners.
This game has so much to offer. I'm 40 hours into the game and i'm still discovering new things! I've only done two of the boss fights and I know there's much more to come.
This game is constantly throwing new, interesting environments at you that you can explore freely and at your own leisure. I've found underground, trap-laden crypts on desert worlds, i've found ruins and buried treasure at the very bottom of the sea floor on ocean worlds, i've found colonies on forest worlds, abandoned camp sites and mining digs full of loot. There are some world types I haven't even been to yet, and I can't wait to find out what they have to offer. There are even challenge doors you can find underground which feature both platforming and combat challenges, with a nice reward for completion.
Some people say the enemy types become carbon copies of eachother. They must be getting pretty unlucky, because i've had a healthy amount of variety so far. I've fought strange monsters that sling vomit on you investigating a distress call from a mining dig gone wrong, i've fought a penguin in a ♥♥♥♥ing UFO, creatures that slam the ground to create shockwaves, giant fish that want to skewer you and creatures that can fire lightning out of some unspeakable orafice on their heads.
The incentive to keep playing is helped massively by the many things you can concentrate on upgrading. You have your ship, your armour, your weapons, your house, your matter manipulator, your furnace, your workbench and so on. There's so much to do, and so many things to want, need and eventully have.
Others have said the game hangs or crashes on startup. Never happened to me once, and i'm playing the game on an ASUS N55SL ( gaming laptop ) with distinctly mediocre specifications. That could be because the game was very recently updated, and they fixed the problem. All I know is, I have had no issues with the game as of yet.
The people posting negative reviews have a lot more playtime of the game than I do, but to be honest, I don't think i'd enjoy many games after sinking 500-1000 hours into them. The only game i've played that much is CS:GO, and that's because it's a competitive shooter and a personal hobby, and still, I can feel a little jaded playing that game sometimes.
To summarise, i'm still on my first playthrough of this game and so far I have yet to experience a dull moment. I'm enjoying the missions, the exploration, the incentives to continue playing and upgrade my equipment. I'm enjoying expanding my property empire, making each new building with a different theme and interior design. I'm enjoying the combat, and the variety of different effects that your weapons can have. If you're into character customization, there's plenty of that too. I might not be an expert or a long-time player, but in my 40 hours i've had more fun in this game than I have in Minecraft and Terraria combined.

A solid turn-based Zombie Survival where managing your camp is as important as venturing out for resources.  Along the way you'll encounter more survivors which may or may not join your camp.  Any that do increase your camp's need for rations.  It's a good idea to associate each of your survivors with designated tasks/traits.  One might focus soley on hunting for ration procurement, another might find themselves the blacksmith of the camp, using tools and materials for ammunition production.  These jobs are issued before the end of each day -- or before traveling with your party of three -- and provide a little strategic element back home while your party ventures out in search of additional survivors or supplies.  The hardcore/roguelike rpg mechanic is interesting, where progress is only saved from one day to the next. Should your main character die, it's game over with the exception of a medal system.  Medals allow you to develop certain attributes for the next playthrough.  Random quest chains, survivors, events, supplies, and so on give each playthrough a different twist and add to the replayability.
While the mechanics and overall graphics and sound design are appealing, the music quickly becomes repetitive.  It doesn't help that it was also mixed in mono, as you might find with mobile games.
It's recommended that you mute the music, and head over to youtube for 1-6+hr dark ambient audio from the likes of cryo chamber, jonnie13black, Robert Rich, and others.  You'll bring the atmosphere up from a 2.5 to a solid 9.

Nothing comes as close to the perfect definition of "improvement" as Burnout Paradise.
That's what Criterion has always been good at: building off their previous accomplishments to bring you something even better. Little tweaks, here and there. Enough to say, "Hey, this is brilliant! Why didn't they think of this sooner?"
Burnout 2 added Crash Mode.
Burnout 3 added takedowns (and nothing was ever the same!).
Revenge took what 3 had and multiplied it five-fold.
Dominator took a dump.
Paradise... it did something drastic. It took everything we knew, brought it out of its soggy cardboard box, shook it around, and then put it in a new storage tote (referring to the open world).
And it worked perfectly. That's the kicker! They could have botched a number of things along the way! But the simple fact that they pulled it off and excelled brought Paradise to a summit.
Perhaps that's the reason Criterion pulled away from the series. Maybe, just maybe, their ability to improve ran out here.
Maybe they thought they couldn't do any better than this, so why even try?
If that's the case, Criterion: great job. We love you.

The story is really simple: a man who doesn't remember anything about his wife Serena and he lives all alone in the house that they lived together in the past. All the game is inside this little house where pointing and clicking every single object inside the house you are able to rebuild all the story between the protagonist and Serena (and of course i will not reveal the final).
As a horror game it was in my opinion little bit aseptic: you can see the circle of the feelings of the protagonist (love-anger-disperation-depression) but i think are not really good connected to each other and as a player i wasn't able to feel the connections between them inside my mind. The only moment where i can found a connection is only when you are pointing and clicking some objects (with a particular order) without trasport the player FOR REAL into the deeps of the protagonist's mind.
About the graphic and the music nothing to say: i think they were good.
Graphic design is dark but simple and related with the atmosphere of the house. The same thing is for the music: easy going and good with the atmosphere of the game. But nothing to be surprised or something that said to you "oh wow! This is great! Make me feels distressed as the protagonist!".
The gameplay as a point-and-click is really simple, and it was a good choice for a product like this but it wasn't good to do the scripts on the screen, because every time you click the same object for the scripts, these overlap to each other (and in few cases, even the voice, but maybe it was a problem of my speed of the laptop's processor).
This game is a sort of fifty/fifty, not good but even not to bad, i think the developers have done the right choice to put "Serena" as a free-to-play and also is a really short game (i've finished it in 20 mins or something like that) so if you want waste some time with a cute "horror" game, this is a good title.

Disappointing.
That is the word I would use to describe the release of Street Fighter V, which while boasting a strong core game, is essentially another phase of Beta testing that costs full price.
Amongst the many issues and lack of features, Capcom's failure to support a large number of common previous generation fight sticks is nearly inexcusable. Many recently released games of the genre support any Windows-recognized device that can register inputs, but perhaps the decision to incorporate XInput as their means to handle input devices is the real culprit here.
Don't be fooled by "Full Controller Support" as a feature of this game; do your research and make sure your device will work with this game before you regret it.
Either way, the fact of the matter is that Street Fighter largely does not support many PS3/Xbox360 supported fight sticks, so you can either choose to shovel out some more money for a new stick or use a 3rd-party application of dubious reputation such as XPadder, MotionJoy, or Joy2Key.
As an aside here, hilariously the game uses XInput display assets for all of the buttons (e.g. X, Y, A, B as seen on an XBox controller) despite the release being exclusive to PS4 and PC.
Besides this, Street Fighter V is also lacking basic support for multi-player lobbies, instead limiting the "Player Slots" to "1" which nearly defeats the purpose of lobbies altogether.
Speaking of online features, connectivity remains shoddy for the time being, though Day-1 PC releases are prone to similar issues. Street Fighter V is no different than many of the AA or AAA game releases we're probably used to in terms of server stability until Capcom works with their networking teams to resolve them. Take this as you will, but don't expect strong connectivity between friends and other players for a while.
Meanwhile the game is lacking a number of features that make this release feel utterly bare-bones, including a lack of an Arcade Mode, no "Versus CPU" mode (though somewhat mitigated by being able to set Training Dummies to complete rounds), no Challenge or Trial Mode (to be added in a later update), and a very lacking "Story" Mode that contains a handful of Best-of-One rounds against about 3 opponents in total. The Store is also another "to be added later" feature which is baffling considering the amount of content that Capcom has and will be preparing to offer up to users on a "Freemium" model.
Did we mention bugs? Training Mode doesn't save your game settings, so enjoy having to set "After First Hit" every time you want to work on combos on a training dummy. Hopefully you didn't need to change the game's in-game language either, because you'll need to set that through an INI file on your system. If you prefer (or have no choice) to use a keyboard as your controller, get used to the pre-set controls because you can't re-bind the keyboard keys for any action in the game. Then you can note the numerous launch, login, application freeze, and otherwise game-breaking technical issues that have been reported on 15 pages (as of this review) through the game's official Steam Support page. One of the more ridiculous and yet somehow common issues reported thus far is that WACOM tablets connected to PCs appear to cause input and game stability issues, resulting in player being unable to type in any fields in-game and in worst-case scenarios encountering game crashes without any error reporting.
I don't think I've mentioned anything good about the game so far, so to be fair it is important to note that Street Fighter V, when you actually get it to work and play without any graphical, technical, or input issues, is an incredibly fun and diverse fighter with a great cast of returning and new characters all of whom feel unique and familiar at the same time. While some may say that Street Fighter V seems more inclined to be friendly for beginner or intermediate players of the genre, time will tell. Regardless, the actual meat of the game is very refreshing.
Graphically the game is excellent, boasting another nice take on the visual design that began with Street Fighter 4 with distinct and noticeable cues on special moves with a lot of flair. The sound design may be the standout factor here, where every hit, block, special move, and cheesy-voiced-lines sound on point and impactful. Drowning out the music when performing a Critical Art is a small but significant decision that brings an air of effectiveness to the action itself.
I really want to like this game, but I also want it to work, not just for me but for the people and community that also want to play the game. Unfortunately getting past all of the chaff to find the actual wheat that Street Fighter should boast about is such an exhausting process. This feels like a game that needed another few months of development to be an actual, full-priced release.
