Bastion is an excellent mix of hack'n'slash action and light RPG elements. You're plunged immediately into the story, which seems to have started at the end of another. As "the Kid", you must recover the lost fragments of the world and restore the Bastion while unraveling the mysteries within. The gameplay is fun and satisfying, with a massive hammer being your first toy to play with. More weapons with different abilities are collected along the way and you can even upgrade them with materials you find as well. Most importantly and possibly famously as well, the entire game is narrated by an old man called "the Stranger". This narration is adapted dynamically to what happens to the Kid, so every playthrough is tailored to the player's style. I can't imagine not owning this little gem, especially since it's on Steam!

Sometimes it can be a bit too tryhard - you will lose count of how many times certain characters remind you of their so called evilness. One wonders if this is an issue with translation, though.
There are many optional skits to delve into character building or interact with NPC's and for the best part they add to the game. But - sometimes it feels like a little too much. I like pointless banter, especially when it builds character, but I feel some of it was either poorly translated or just plan went overboard. That said, the dove scene should win some kind of steam award.
Velvet makes for a great main character - it can be easy to be put off her given the oversexualised outfit - especeially if you're a feminist, like me. It's worth ignoring it this time, because underneath the pointless fan service is a well crafted character with a lot of depth and progression to work through. You can change her outfit too, but sadly there's no "fixed" version of her main attire - a real shame as half nudity aside I like the overall design.
The English dubs in this game aren't so bad, in fact Velvet and Magilou are so good I prefer them to the jap audio. Eizen is great, too - though rokoru sounds a bit like he has a constantly blocked nose which is a shame. The overall soundtrack is perfect, but some later battle tunes are nowhere as good as the former. Thankfully there's an in game mechanic to pick your soundtrack, and you can also tweak volume sliders if you're unable to hear the music over the constant battle chatter.
The in game graphics are a bit dated, but they do the job well and the anime cut scenes are above par in terms of animation etc.
Overall it's a great game and I enjoyed the solid 80+ hours. I am half tempted to play through NG+ but so little time...

While not a perfect game, the combat system is a bit unwieldy, the default outfits for some of the women are ridiculous, the sidequests aren't great, the core of Berseria is diamond. The characters are well-written, their personal story arcs are believable and engrossing, and the combat is fun, once you've got the hang of it.
It's also lovely to have a game that takes a mature look at revenge, freedom, existentialism, and morality. The game deliberately avoids simplifying these topics or providing easy answers, while still ultimately settling on one side, providing both complexity and narrative cohesion.
The English translation and voice work is lovely (a few of the English VAs are odd choices, but Artorias, for one, sounds even better in English than he does in Japanese), I've had zero issues with the PC port (no crashes, no controller bugs, nothing), and just all in all this is an excellent game that is well-worth investing in.
Also, don't worry if you haven't played Zesteria. While Berseria is a prequel, I went into it with very little knowledge of Zesteria (I'd played a bit of it, and gave it up as aimless and lacking focus a few hours in) and understood everything just fine.

This may seem like old news and no one is even looking at this game anymore. But, I've had this game for almost 5 years, being the first PC game I've ever gotten. I remember playing through this game millions of times making the smallest different choices from my original playthrough, explaing my record of 67 hours. But, I would find that high of a record not too common, unless you're a tiny little lad with only one PC game to play. And I might be very soft with this game considering it's the most memorable game in my life, and I still remember every single choice to this day. Enough with my personal experience, let me tell you about The Walking Dead.
So I'm guessing many of you are looking at this game because you've heard about the release of The Walking Dead Season 3, and you looked at a trailer and now want to catch up. And if you haven't heard all the complaining towards TellTale from fans, then let me point it out. The game doesn't change the future of your playthrough, and the game doesn't care how you play it. No matter what, the outcome is always the same. But, if you cut that aside like I did, then you'll have a wonderful time. Your choices only change what happens at that present moment, which brings in my 67 hours. I won't explain the story either because I'd recomend not looking into spoilers or even previews.
Playing through all of The Walking Dead games, including the first 2 episodes of Season 3, I will say Season 1 is the best. It's the most pure and original, with great emotional and amazing characters. And so far, I think Season 3 is a let down. So if you like Season 1, move onto Season 2, which I found very enjoyful as well. If you really like that one, then move onto Season 3 if you're really into the game. Season 3 isn't bad, it just isn't the same. I also have to point out that the game's gameplay is fine. It's just an involement of QTE's and walking around talking to people and picking up items.
So, let me just say this. Buy the game already! What are you waiting for? I swear you will find much enjoyment to this game and you'll always remember it. From the very sad and emotional moments, to the intense action moments. I loved this game to death, and I think you will to.

For a text review, continue below-
The Walking Dead is a point and click adventure game released FIVE years ago. I know, I’m late. But with 10,000 persons still playing this every week, the game is far from dead. I thought I’d take a look at this game that while linear and single player can retain such a player base after five years.
What I found surprised the hell out of me. I don’t know what I was expecting, but I found one of the most emotionally captivating storylines in a videogame I have found in...I don’t even know how long. Seriously, if you play games for stories, this game has one, a damn good one at that. And if you don’t cry by the end of it? Then you’re dead inside. With an array of different well-developed if narrow-personalitied characters there is so much to get attached to. And considering the game is based off of the same comics that the TV show is based off of, you can guess that there is going to be some moments of loss and emotional grieving. I could go on endlessly about how amazing the story is. But to the dismay of those that love this game, there are a few flaws we have to go over to make this a serious review. The story alone as a pro is enough to sell millions of copies of this game (Which it has), but there are flaws that are going to even out the final score of this game.
The first thing I want to mention is a general misconception with the game. It seems to be advertised and spoken about like some sort of thrilling choose your own adventure game. It’s not. It’s a point and click adventure game like I said. Half of your time may be spent watching the story progress with the occasional choice that isn’t flavor dialogue, but the other half is spent walking around in sometimes the most horrible camera angles I’ve ever seen looking for prompts and actions you can take to y’know...get yourself the hell out of this point and click stuff and get to the story, the only thing anyone ever talks about with this game. The point and click portion is not bad, in fact it’s cool if you enjoy the point and click genre, but if you’re in it for the story, the vagueness of what you have to do and lack of direction can get mildly annoying. Also, there’s a lot of quick time events in this game where if you fail you die or someone else story-critical dies and then you have to go back checkpoint...those were...unexpected for a game like this. I’ll let you all decide how you feel about that.
Now this next thing can be considered a pro or a con really. The writing of dialogue in The Walking Dead is on par with that of some emotional hollywood experience. From a creative writing perspective what this basically means is that it’s GREAT at evoking emotion and getting you attached...but the actual quality of what’s written for these characters to say? It doesn’t sound like realistic conversation and doesn’t even sound like good on-paper conversation material. If you like generic hollywood writing with zero depth but maximum emotional captivity? You’ll love it. If you wanted a bit more realism and depth to the way characters interact with each other? You won’t.
The graphics are alright. They’re exactly what you’d expect from this company in 2012 and maybe more than I expected from this genre from my previous experiences with it? More of a pro than a con unless you’re someone that NEEDS graphics. The con here is the animations. The animations are bad, which makes sense for this genre. It’s worst with the facial expressions. Some of the expressions characters make are hilariously disgusting and ugly at how failed of an attempt they are to mimic real life expressions and reactions.
The sounds that are there are good. They’re impactful and realistic. They help add to the immersion of the game and reinforce what happens in the story. The sounds during the point and click portions of the game though? There could have been more ambience as everything seems rather empty when you’re not pushing through a storyline in this game.
And now my BIGGEST gripe with this game which I have saved for last for those of you that are willing to make it past my lesser critiquing of this overwhelmingly positively received game. My biggest gripe is this. “The game series adapts to the choices you make. The story is tailored by how you play.” This is the biggest lie I have read all year. The game lets you make choices sure, but it certainly doesn’t adapt for more than a few minutes to any of them. If someone was supposed to die and you don’t let them die or kill them yourself? The game does it for you in every single occasion. That’s why by the end? And this might be a slight spoiler so I’ll leave out specifics- Every single person will find themselves with the SAME exact group of companions give or take one very uninteresting side-character. There are end-of-episode screens that show you your choices compared to the choices other made and reactions in-game to the choices you’ve made plenty of times. But none of them matter because there’s no consequences for any of them. Even if you do what the game considers the right thing? It will still punish you for doing the wrong thing if that’s what the writers have decided should be the choice you should have picked. The point I’m trying to make is that this story never diverges for longer than one conversation. This is not a dynamic choose your own adventure game. This is a linear story that tries to give you the illusion that you have a say in anything that happens at all, which you don’t.
Now that being said. Assuming you aren’t already writing a hate comment or haven’t already disliked this and left because, “♥♥♥♥ this guy he doesn’t know what he’s talking about. This game is amazing.”. I STILL LOVE THIS GAME. I am so happy I played this game and I can’t wait to play The Walking Dead Season 2. That being said, there’s a lot of design choices that hold this back from being a perfect game. I still recommend it, and I’m going to have to give it a 7/10. 8/10 is too generous for everything that’s wrong with it. 6/10 is too harsh for everything that’s right with it. This is quite simply a good game. And in my 10 point review score that’s what a seven means. “Good, but with plenty of room to improve.”. If you want a really damn good interactive story to follow? Get this game. You’ll love it, I did. Just make sure you’re willing to look past all the flaws that the game has that I had to learn the hard way.
Now as any of you who have watched or read any of my previous reviews know I like take on a very, “Is it worth the price” mentality at the end. Full price? $25? For a 10-11 hour game for completionists and a much shorter game for those that are rushing through the story? With a $5 DLC tacked onto the side to bridge the gap between this game and it’s sequel? With zero replayability to the story due to the linear nature and how your choices don’t matter? No. Don’t get it at full price. Wait for a sale.

The Walking Dead is second best TellTale game I've ever played. The Second best only because I liked the season 2 a bit more which is probably because season 1 made me emotionally attached ;)
Your character is called Lee and he has to make many difficult choices. He can choose to tell the truth or lie to protect himself and people he cares about. Especially kids make choices not easy at all. Very often you are forced to decide between two options and none of them feels like a victory. People will die, of course. It's zombie apocalypse after all. There is time pressure  so you might regret hesitating or choosing the wrong option just because you missed  one important word when reading all options in hurry.
The story is very interesting, exciting, brutal and dramatic, full of twists and surprises. Every character in  the game is very unpredictable. I remember when I was just about to like someone and side with that person, he/she suddenly did something very stupid and all the sympathy was gone. You never know what is happening inside of each of them so you never get to feel like you have a full control of any situations.
Combat/Action parts are quite fun but can be stressful. You need to react fast and aim very often or search for an item which could help you. If you fail because you hesitate for too long, it will usually not happen again. It's not a very difficult game.
Graphics are not impressive at all. Background textures look quite terrible but honestly who cares about a visual quality when the narrative and sounds take your breathe away, right?
Warning: The game can make you feel very sad and emotional. That's very rare I would say. There are not that many games which made my eyes wet and made me drop some tears. If your heart is not like an ice cube you will love The Walking Dead!
100% recommended! Go and get this game + season 2! NOW ;)

This is by no means a bad game, but for me personally it was a thumbs down. The heart and soul of the game is grinding, which is not something I'm fond of unless there's some other payout (e.g. character development, story arc, etc). What narrative does exist is thin (to be generous) and silly. Some might find the boring charicatures somewhat endearing, but I couldn't help but roll my eyes at the handful of lines of dialogue you have to click through for each new survivor you add to your base. I only put in ~5 hours, but in that time I failed to encounter a single meaningul decision, which I find a crutial element to these type of squad-centric base management games. You just assign survivors to jobs each day, and then send out a crew to scavenge, which involves extremely repetitive battles ad nauseum, with an unhealthy dose of RNG involved.
I did like the aesthetic of the game for an indie production, but the game itself lacks heart. There's definitely a framework in place for a good game to exist, but nothing in it captivated me enough to suffer through the endless grind. If there were a neutral steam option, I'd probably lean towards that, since I can see the appeal to a certain subset of gamer looking for something ultra light in terms of strategy, story, etc, and just want to kill time clicking the same buttons over and over for little pellets of RNG-dopamine goodness. It's simple and vapid, with a somewhat charming aesthetic, and sometimes that's all someone wants in a game, but that's not me, so my review has to go negative.

A catastrophe in the desert of New Mexico could imply the end of humanity. As a consequence of an experiment that went dreadfully wrong, dimensial tears create a wormhole into our world. A foreign dimension: "Xen", gets merged with ours and subsequently aliens invade the Black Mesa facility, kickstarting a trans-dimensional cataclysm.
from some of its contemporaries is its thoroughly developed storyline. It's not told through cutscenes - the game is seamless without intermission - instead you have to take notice of your surroundings. By interacting with fellow scientists you will be told valuable information and further objectives, and overhearing radios will grant you greater insight into the antagonists' cause. Somehow, Valve manages to make the narrative immersive and riveting - without detracting from the action.
  As you expect from any shooter post Doom, a plethora of weapons are at your disposal. Some more fitting for a theoretical physicist, such as the "Tau Cannon", an impressive craftsmanship fueled by Uranium. But when ammo is scarce and you have to finagle, the iconic crowbar could be a feasible, if a somewhat more primitive, option.
  In the later stages of the game Freeman leaves Black Mesa and enters Xen, where he confronts and slays the invasion's mastermind, thereby putting the alien assault to a halt. These missions proved substantially more difficult, even for a battle-hardened player, yet the quintessential remains the same. The strenuous ending makes the reward greater however, and upon beating the game you are greeted by a satisfactory endscene - the mysterious G-Man himself congratulates you on your heroic actions.
, Half-Life's graphical and innovative feats have since long lost its grandeur, today taken for granted. Still, released in late 1998, Half-Life remains relevant and on par with present day releases, retaining its immense replay value.

I can't recommend XCOM2 while XCOM:Enemy Unknown exists and is just better in almost every single way.
Firstly, while I don't usually care about pacing in a video game, the pacing in XCOM2 is just flat out terrible. You have high-octane missions with a time limit, which a) doesn't fit in with XCOM's tactical, methodical combat style, and b) doesn't make sense in the majority of situations when your squad enters in f*cking stealth mode. Why are the ayy lmao's trying to blow up their own ♥♥♥♥ again? You COULD argue that the ayy lmaos know you are in the general vicinity, but then they're just casually strolling around in those stealh missions, so...
The pacing gets so much worse in the campaign map. In XCOM:EU  you could just manage your base at clicks of your mouse, then scan for♥♥♥♥♥♥to happen. It was fine, it suited the style of the game, and the base management was actually an enjoyable aspect of the game.
But in 2, to do any side quests (which shouldn't even be in the game, they're terrible and just waste time while f*cking you about for resources that you should get from missions instead), you have to fly to a location and scan it. It's time consuming (IRL) and more often than not, you get interrupted by a dark event mission or some other sh*t. I can't fathom why they added this to the game other than to pad out the campaign.
Combat is worse in general. The AI positions themselves terribly and makes questionable decisions that I never saw in XCOM:EU except on the 'easy' difficulty, but 'compensate' for that by having stupidly OP abilities that they can spam. Additionally, the combat ramps up ridiclously quickly, with you finding high tier aliens early and in great numbers. Most annoying of all is the Lancer spam, which means if they stun one of your dudes, they're out of the fight unless you expend a single use ability by your support to bring them back. That's just one example of the stupid OP abilities the ayy lmaos throw around, and it's EARLY IN THE GAME when you face those f*cks. More frustrating sh*t comes along later too. It might make more sense that the ayy lmaos have their big guns around from the start since they're in charge of the earth this time, but it makes for an incredibly unfair game, ESPECIALLY since your scientists seemed to have forgotten all the OP tech you had lying around in XCOM:EU.
Combat itself is incredibly un-smooth. The camera spends ages on revealed aliens and their moves for no reason whatsoever, whenever there's a voice over you are FORCED to sit there and listen to it while they blab on about how civilians are being killed or whatever the f*ck bradford is complaining about this time, and FPS stuttering is common.
All in all this game is a resounding "eh." They missed the mark on combat, making XCOM into a fast-paced, high-octane game when it's supposed to be a slow, methodical tactical turn based game. The pacing is atrocious, the game difficulty ramps up ridiculously quickly, which would be fine except the stupid Avatar Project is looming over the horizon and you can, in the long run, do nothing about.
Just go get XCOM:EU instead.

You let out a cry of freedom as you return
home from work, dead tired.
It’s bad enough you’ve been juggling school
and a part-time job at the bookstore, in
addition to your growing relationship with
the beautiful Goth in the class, _Summer-Rain_.
She’s been arguing with you lately.
Logging in to Steam once more after dragging
your feet from the bath, you see a game
that you don’t seem to remember:

Assassin’s Creed: Freedom Cry.

You vaguely recall that it focused on the
supporting character, Adewale; from the
fourth title in the series, Black Flag, and it
was originally marketed as DLC before
becoming a standalone title.
Shrugging, you buy and soon install the game.
You try not to think about the things you
had to put up with throughout the week
in the back of your head; that idiot boss
you hate but you need your job more,
the school projects getting more mentally
demanding and _ Summer-Rain_ arguing
with you over a misunderstanding.
Whether you’re a returning player from
Black Flag or someone entirely new with
no knowledge of the series, Freedom Cry’s
story is the main draw of the game, being
simple, accessable and without any obvious
baggage from the previous games.

Freedom Cry’s cast is limited to revolving
around only four characters; Adewale himself,
his person-of-interest; the beautiful Bastienne
Josephe, the local Madame of the Brothel in
Port-Au-Prince, the evil Governeur De Fayet
and the stoic Augustin Dieufort, leader of the
Maroon Rebellion.

Most of Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag is on
display at its finest here. The activities like
whaling for animal skins and crafting materials
return in a smaller capacity, the naval combat
and free-running are top-notch as ever and
the graphics can bring an underequipped
PC to ruin.

You find yourself giggling as you see your idiot
boss in the villainous Governeur De Fayet, and
you relish how satisfying it is to go around
freeing your brothers in chains while you kill
Slavers and soldiers who oppress and bully.

Each mission or small side-quest you complete
brings you closer to the real-world, so you can
resume your responsibilities without the urge to
take a machete into your boss’s face or kill your
classmates for not doing enough in your group
projects.
Freedom Cry’s ending makes you pick up
the phone to apologize to _Summer-Rain_.
She asks what brought about this change of
heart. You tell her about Freedom Cry.
How you bought a game of prejudice, which
was also with a means to fight it and the effort
it came with to fight such things like prejudice,
racism and slavery.
How you bought newfound gratitude for your
life and things you have. The things you took
for granted, and the things you had taken for
granted.
The people you had taken for granted.
She responds, dabbing her eyes.
“Let’s not fight... Not when we can play
games like the one you just finished.”
You answer while smiling on the other end.
“You’re right, Summer. Let Freedom Cry.”

A short, pleasant addition to one of the best games, if not the best, in the Assassin's Creed franchise, Black Flag. This expansion is quite short (I logged 6.8h), but has great voice acting, great graphics, and mostly the same great gameplay from the base game. In addition to the standard assassin gear (smoke bombs, sleep and berzerk darts, dual hidden blades), Adewale has more powerful moves (a brutal machete and a room-clearing blunderbuss), but he often must refrain from using them in order to save the lives of captives and slaves. At sea, it's much the same: slave ships are escorted. They don't fight themselves, and if you damage them while fighting the escorts, it will cost lives you might otherwise have saved.
The explorable area is much smaller than Black Flag, which is understandable, but I felt like some of the smaller islands were copies of each other. Secrets and collectibles generally require little or not effort to find, though they aren't as often visible on the mini-map as they were in Black Flag. The side missions to free slaves and gain rebels are great at first, feeling both thematic and rewarding, but they become a bit tedious, as they repeat endlessly in dense but small Port au Prince. Clearing the plantations is rewarding and fun, but there aren't many plantation types, so you'll see copies. Some plot points feel like they could have been expanded too. There's good material and potential that perhaps should have been its own full game, like Rogue.
Recommended with reservation. Play Black Flag, and if you want more, here it is. It runs great and looks great and is just different enough, and fun enough, to be worth those few hours.

Assassins Creed Freedom Cry is effectively a 3 – 6 hour long DLC (I finished it closer to 3 even with finding collectables though) and for what it’s marketed as, it’s very good.
The game puts you in the shoes of Adewale (who from what I’ve played of ACIV:BF is a main character) and a heavy chunk of the game is aimed at freeing slaves and helping the faction on the island accomplishing this. Most of the main story and missions are completed around this island, but for a 3-6 hour DLC, the actual explore able map is fairly large, and ship combat also plays a part when completing a few of the objectives. The ship combat is as it was in ACIV – fun but extremely repetitive at times (though I prefer the sword combat to ships anyway).
Outside of missions and a few collectables though, there’s not an awful lot to do. In the 4 hours I played, I achieved 90% completion, with the other 10% being collectables I missed on one of the islands as I didn’t have a “need” to explore it. There are side objectives on missions and such to flesh out the replay ability a bit, and some of these objectives take a bit of thinking and time to achieve – but bar Uplay achievements there’s no need to accomplish them unless you’re a completionist.
And yes, there is Uplay integration and you need Uplay running and installed to play the game – doesn’t bother me in the slightest as I’ve never had issues, but I know for some Uplay is an issue.
Not at all, unless you really enjoyed Black Flag, though at that point
you probably would have bought this as the DLC with the game.

Lack of content could be forgiven. Lack of polish cannot.
Why not to buy this game:
- Barebones keyboard support: cannot bind keys to your liking (only a limited selection of keys is available), can't play 2 players on one keyboard, can't check the key bindings (keyboard keys are always displayed as XOne controller buttons)
- No D-input devices support. If your controller is not X360/XOne you'll have to work around with joy2key and binding buttons to keyboard keys
- No Steam UI support (cannot invite or join game, very clunky and slow to navigate ingame menus have to be used instead)
- Menus/load screens (such as characters facing off before match) may drop to 30 fps even if your rig can run the match at stable 60. Game speed is relative to framerate, so if it drops to 30 you'll experience slow motion. This occurs on PCs that match recommended specs
-Console crossplay is nigh impossible (tested PC to PC - 10/10 connection, PC - PS4 on the same connection - unplayable)
-Invites to player lobbies often outright do not work (no response or "lobby does not exist" message)
Aside from that general issues:
- Barely any SP content
- No option to decline matches (if you get paired with someone who lags you just have to suck it up and play even though you know you won't enjoy the match)
- Characters models are detailed, but very unpolished (horrible hair clippings, even on character select screen and numerous cloth physics errors)

Well, I won't go into lots of detail, many have done so before.  Apart from Swordgate, this game is 100% epic.  Sure, the combat is maybe a bit easy, and strategy isn't really important (I've not played New Game+ yet... I suspect it might be more important here...), it's the story that keeps you playing.
While some characters are never fully explored or even understood (Magilu for one), they are all unique and excellently portrayed.  The character development for Velvet and Phi are absolutely the stars of the show, and will keep you wanting more right up till the end.
The previous Tales games are great, but this is the first time in the series that we have 'proper' Anime quality visuals, without the childlike look - and I think it make the game so much more appealing.
Dungeons are disappointing, seemingly there to space out the actual story, but also to give room for the skits you get as you travel.
If you like games with great combat, skill, and like to just skip the 'boring story bits' - do not buy this game.  You will dislike it completely.  It's not for you.
Combat and katz orb collecting aside, this is a must have game for anyone who likes JRPG's with great story.  If you like Final Fantasy games, I highly recommend this, mainly for the excellent anti-hero story.

I do have to say though, if you have a low specification computer, GTA4 might not be the game for you, but check out the minimum specs to see if you qualify to play it.

This may seem like old news and no one is even looking at this game anymore. But, I've had this game for almost 5 years, being the first PC game I've ever gotten. I remember playing through this game millions of times making the smallest different choices from my original playthrough, explaing my record of 67 hours. But, I would find that high of a record not too common, unless you're a tiny little lad with only one PC game to play. And I might be very soft with this game considering it's the most memorable game in my life, and I still remember every single choice to this day. Enough with my personal experience, let me tell you about The Walking Dead.
So I'm guessing many of you are looking at this game because you've heard about the release of The Walking Dead Season 3, and you looked at a trailer and now want to catch up. And if you haven't heard all the complaining towards TellTale from fans, then let me point it out. The game doesn't change the future of your playthrough, and the game doesn't care how you play it. No matter what, the outcome is always the same. But, if you cut that aside like I did, then you'll have a wonderful time. Your choices only change what happens at that present moment, which brings in my 67 hours. I won't explain the story either because I'd recomend not looking into spoilers or even previews.
Playing through all of The Walking Dead games, including the first 2 episodes of Season 3, I will say Season 1 is the best. It's the most pure and original, with great emotional and amazing characters. And so far, I think Season 3 is a let down. So if you like Season 1, move onto Season 2, which I found very enjoyful as well. If you really like that one, then move onto Season 3 if you're really into the game. Season 3 isn't bad, it just isn't the same. I also have to point out that the game's gameplay is fine. It's just an involement of QTE's and walking around talking to people and picking up items.
So, let me just say this. Buy the game already! What are you waiting for? I swear you will find much enjoyment to this game and you'll always remember it. From the very sad and emotional moments, to the intense action moments. I loved this game to death, and I think you will to.

I had heard quite a bit of pleasantly-surprised hype about this game. Apparently everyone expected something that sucked, due to the game's storied past - it was originally a True Crime game? So when it went on sale I decided to pick it up for myself. You've probably played this game in one form or another, it's a GTA-alike sandbox game, only this time, it's heavily Chinese-influenced, set in Hong Kong. The setting is probably the best part of this game, it's both well-fleshed out and novel, and the game seems to sport more of a "living" environment than the sometimes sterile underpopulated cities of other GTAlikes. That said there are only a few mission types, and they tend to repeat themselves over and over. The game starts with a parkour chase-scene, and you do chase-scene after chase-scene, after chase-scene. You'll hate them by the end of the game. What is interesting is the game's combat- there are few guns, at least initially, and you dispatch most enemies with a well fleshed out kung-fu system. The story missions carry the plot, though without much pacing. It's a rags-to-riches criminal tale with a twist, you're an uncover cop, trying to move up in the mob. Things kind of meander along until it just suddenly ends- they could have easily cut the story in half. There's a ton of padding in the form of side missions, but those are nearly always more repetitive than refreshing. I'd place the game higher than the GTA-series, but it's not nearly as good as Saints Row. Pleased I picked it up on sale, if you're interested, you should too.

The Walking Dead is a point and click adventure game released FIVE years ago. I know, I’m late. But with 10,000 persons still playing this every week, the game is far from dead. I thought I’d take a look at this game that while linear and single player can retain such a player base after five years.
What I found surprised the hell out of me. I don’t know what I was expecting, but I found one of the most emotionally captivating storylines in a videogame I have found in...I don’t even know how long. Seriously, if you play games for stories, this game has one, a damn good one at that. And if you don’t cry by the end of it? Then you’re dead inside. With an array of different well-developed if narrow-personalitied characters there is so much to get attached to. And considering the game is based off of the same comics that the TV show is based off of, you can guess that there is going to be some moments of loss and emotional grieving. I could go on endlessly about how amazing the story is. But to the dismay of those that love this game, there are a few flaws we have to go over to make this a serious review. The story alone as a pro is enough to sell millions of copies of this game (Which it has), but there are flaws that are going to even out the final score of this game.
The first thing I want to mention is a general misconception with the game. It seems to be advertised and spoken about like some sort of thrilling choose your own adventure game. It’s not. It’s a point and click adventure game like I said. Half of your time may be spent watching the story progress with the occasional choice that isn’t flavor dialogue, but the other half is spent walking around in sometimes the most horrible camera angles I’ve ever seen looking for prompts and actions you can take to y’know...get yourself the hell out of this point and click stuff and get to the story, the only thing anyone ever talks about with this game. The point and click portion is not bad, in fact it’s cool if you enjoy the point and click genre, but if you’re in it for the story, the vagueness of what you have to do and lack of direction can get mildly annoying. Also, there’s a lot of quick time events in this game where if you fail you die or someone else story-critical dies and then you have to go back checkpoint...those were...unexpected for a game like this. I’ll let you all decide how you feel about that.
Now this next thing can be considered a pro or a con really. The writing of dialogue in The Walking Dead is on par with that of some emotional hollywood experience. From a creative writing perspective what this basically means is that it’s GREAT at evoking emotion and getting you attached...but the actual quality of what’s written for these characters to say? It doesn’t sound like realistic conversation and doesn’t even sound like good on-paper conversation material. If you like generic hollywood writing with zero depth but maximum emotional captivity? You’ll love it. If you wanted a bit more realism and depth to the way characters interact with each other? You won’t.
The graphics are alright. They’re exactly what you’d expect from this company in 2012 and maybe more than I expected from this genre from my previous experiences with it? More of a pro than a con unless you’re someone that NEEDS graphics. The con here is the animations. The animations are bad, which makes sense for this genre. It’s worst with the facial expressions. Some of the expressions characters make are hilariously disgusting and ugly at how failed of an attempt they are to mimic real life expressions and reactions.
The sounds that are there are good. They’re impactful and realistic. They help add to the immersion of the game and reinforce what happens in the story. The sounds during the point and click portions of the game though? There could have been more ambience as everything seems rather empty when you’re not pushing through a storyline in this game.
And now my BIGGEST gripe with this game which I have saved for last for those of you that are willing to make it past my lesser critiquing of this overwhelmingly positively received game. My biggest gripe is this. “The game series adapts to the choices you make. The story is tailored by how you play.” This is the biggest lie I have read all year. The game lets you make choices sure, but it certainly doesn’t adapt for more than a few minutes to any of them. If someone was supposed to die and you don’t let them die or kill them yourself? The game does it for you in every single occasion. That’s why by the end? And this might be a slight spoiler so I’ll leave out specifics- Every single person will find themselves with the SAME exact group of companions give or take one very uninteresting side-character. There are end-of-episode screens that show you your choices compared to the choices other made and reactions in-game to the choices you’ve made plenty of times. But none of them matter because there’s no consequences for any of them. Even if you do what the game considers the right thing? It will still punish you for doing the wrong thing if that’s what the writers have decided should be the choice you should have picked. The point I’m trying to make is that this story never diverges for longer than one conversation. This is not a dynamic choose your own adventure game. This is a linear story that tries to give you the illusion that you have a say in anything that happens at all, which you don’t.
Now that being said. Assuming you aren’t already writing a hate comment or haven’t already disliked this and left because, “♥♥♥♥ this guy he doesn’t know what he’s talking about. This game is amazing.”. I STILL LOVE THIS GAME. I am so happy I played this game and I can’t wait to play The Walking Dead Season 2. That being said, there’s a lot of design choices that hold this back from being a perfect game. I still recommend it, and I’m going to have to give it a 7/10. 8/10 is too generous for everything that’s wrong with it. 6/10 is too harsh for everything that’s right with it. This is quite simply a good game. And in my 10 point review score that’s what a seven means. “Good, but with plenty of room to improve.”. If you want a really damn good interactive story to follow? Get this game. You’ll love it, I did. Just make sure you’re willing to look past all the flaws that the game has that I had to learn the hard way.
Now as any of you who have watched or read any of my previous reviews know I like take on a very, “Is it worth the price” mentality at the end. Full price? $25? For a 10-11 hour game for completionists and a much shorter game for those that are rushing through the story? With a $5 DLC tacked onto the side to bridge the gap between this game and it’s sequel? With zero replayability to the story due to the linear nature and how your choices don’t matter? No. Don’t get it at full price. Wait for a sale.

The Walking Dead is second best TellTale game I've ever played. The Second best only because I liked the season 2 a bit more which is probably because season 1 made me emotionally attached ;)
Your character is called Lee and he has to make many difficult choices. He can choose to tell the truth or lie to protect himself and people he cares about. The story is very interesting, exciting, brutal and dramatic, full of twists and surprises. Every character in  the game is very unpredictable. I remember when I was just about to like someone and side with that person, he/she suddenly did something very stupid and all the sympathy was gone. You never know what is happening inside of each of them so you never get to feel like you have a full control of any situations.
Combat/Action parts are quite fun but can be stressful. You need to react fast and aim very often or search for an item which could help you. If you fail because you hesitate for too long, it will usually not happen again. It's not a very difficult game.
Graphics are not impressive at all. Background textures look quite terrible but honestly who cares about a visual quality when the narrative and sounds take your breathe away, right?
Warning: The game can make you feel very sad and emotional. That's very rare I would say. There are not that many games which made my eyes wet and made me drop some tears. If your heart is not like an ice cube you will love The Walking Dead!
100% recommended! Go and get this game + season 2! NOW ;)

I can't recommend XCOM2 while XCOM:Enemy Unknown exists and is just better in almost every single way.
Firstly, while I don't usually care about pacing in a video game, the pacing in XCOM2 is just flat out terrible. You have high-octane missions with a time limit, which a) doesn't fit in with XCOM's tactical, methodical combat style, and b) doesn't make sense in the majority of situations when your squad enters in f*cking stealth mode. Why are the ayy lmao's trying to blow up their own ♥♥♥♥ again? You COULD argue that the ayy lmaos know you are in the general vicinity, but then they're just casually strolling around in those stealh missions, so...
The pacing gets so much worse in the campaign map. In XCOM:EU  you could just manage your base at clicks of your mouse, then scan for♥♥♥♥♥♥to happen. It was fine, it suited the style of the game, and the base management was actually an enjoyable aspect of the game.
But in 2, to do any side quests (which shouldn't even be in the game, they're terrible and just waste time while f*cking you about for resources that you should get from missions instead), you have to fly to a location and scan it. It's time consuming (IRL) and more often than not, you get interrupted by a dark event mission or some other sh*t. I can't fathom why they added this to the game other than to pad out the campaign.
Combat is worse in general. The AI positions themselves terribly and makes questionable decisions that I never saw in XCOM:EU except on the 'easy' difficulty, but 'compensate' for that by having stupidly OP abilities that they can spam. Additionally, the combat ramps up ridiclously quickly, with you finding high tier aliens early and in great numbers. Most annoying of all is the Lancer spam, which means if they stun one of your dudes, they're out of the fight unless you expend a single use ability by your support to bring them back. That's just one example of the stupid OP abilities the ayy lmaos throw around, and it's EARLY IN THE GAME when you face those f*cks. More frustrating sh*t comes along later too. It might make more sense that the ayy lmaos have their big guns around from the start since they're in charge of the earth this time, but it makes for an incredibly unfair game, ESPECIALLY since your scientists seemed to have forgotten all the OP tech you had lying around in XCOM:EU.
Combat itself is incredibly un-smooth. The camera spends ages on revealed aliens and their moves for no reason whatsoever, whenever there's a voice over you are FORCED to sit there and listen to it while they blab on about how civilians are being killed or whatever the f*ck bradford is complaining about this time, and FPS stuttering is common.
All in all this game is a resounding "eh." They missed the mark on combat, making XCOM into a fast-paced, high-octane game when it's supposed to be a slow, methodical tactical turn based game. The pacing is atrocious, the game difficulty ramps up ridiculously quickly, which would be fine except the stupid Avatar Project is looming over the horizon and you can, in the long run, do nothing about.
Just go get XCOM:EU instead.

A catastrophe in the desert of New Mexico could imply the end of humanity. As a consequence of an experiment that went dreadfully wrong, dimensial tears create a wormhole into our world. A foreign dimension: "Xen", gets merged with ours and subsequently aliens invade the Black Mesa facility, kickstarting a trans-dimensional cataclysm.
from some of its contemporaries is its thoroughly developed storyline. It's not told through cutscenes - the game is seamless without intermission - instead you have to take notice of your surroundings. By interacting with fellow scientists you will be told valuable information and further objectives, and overhearing radios will grant you greater insight into the antagonists' cause. Somehow, Valve manages to make the narrative immersive and riveting - without detracting from the action.
  As you expect from any shooter post Doom, a plethora of weapons are at your disposal. Some more fitting for a theoretical physicist, such as the "Tau Cannon", an impressive craftsmanship fueled by Uranium. But when ammo is scarce and you have to finagle, the iconic crowbar could be a feasible, if a somewhat more primitive, option.
  In the later stages of the game Freeman leaves Black Mesa and enters Xen, where he confronts and slays the invasion's mastermind, thereby putting the alien assault to a halt. These missions proved substantially more difficult, even for a battle-hardened player, yet the quintessential remains the same. The strenuous ending makes the reward greater however, and upon beating the game you are greeted by a satisfactory endscene - the mysterious G-Man himself congratulates you on your heroic actions.
, Half-Life's graphical and innovative feats have since long lost its grandeur, today taken for granted. Still, released in late 1998, Half-Life remains relevant and on par with present day releases, retaining its immense replay value.

Astronaut Simulator is definitely not for everyone.
=======
CONS:
- Hard to control: takes a LOT of practice; easy to press the wrong key and botch everything.
- Frustration level = MAXIMUM OVERLOAD
- Looping audio for missions: gets a tad annoying when you have to repeat the mission so many times.
PROS:
+ Good atmosphere: visuals are good, and the aesthetic is on-point
+ True to life: Using the N2 to control your movement in space is right-on.
+ Very precise
Do I recommend?
Well... yes. It's a very good game to give a go at, but I wouldn't say it's for everyone.
It can be extremely frustrating trying to get through the very first level (if you can), as you have to really try to control the precise movements of the astronaut. Small movements are important (very few button presses to release N2), and taking your time is crucial. It's very easy to screw up, so make sure you're pressing the right button, or you may go into a panicked frenzy of button pressing that jetisons you off into the darkest regions of the nether that is space..!
...
Don't buy it if you can't handle a good challenge, or don't have a lot of time to spare in getting really good at pretending to be an astronaut.

If you combine the naval combat from Assassin's Creed 4 with team-deathmatch from Mount & Blade, you get Blackwake.
Pros:
Excellent teamwork-based gameplay concept similar to Guns of Icarus - multiplayer crews fighting against enemy multi-crewed ships. Teamwork is essential.
Good graphics (but higher settings require powerful PCs)
Big servers with up to 54 players across 6 ships (up to 13 players per ship).
Ramming and boarding enemy ships is a lot of fun.
Funny ingame voice commands that perfectly capture the pirate or navy vibe.
Game and netcode runs more stable than any ubisoft release.
Cons:
Game made on indie budget.
Lack of controls against team-killers and trolls (when friendly fire is on)
There are some bugs and the odd CTD, but not too much.
Some of the controls are a bit awkward, but you get used to it.
How much fun you have depends a lot on how mature and compitent your crew is.
Skill curve is a bit shallow compared to Guns of Icarus, but still deep enough.
Combat usually feels a bit laggy, but its ok.
No bots and no single-player / training mode.
Overall a great multiplayer game, recommended!

Very disappointed. In Xcom the fun for me was all about the slow advance, covering all the angles, making sure that when the aliens appeared I was in the right place to take them down. Imagine the Colonial Marines entering the base at the start of Aliens; that was Xcom for me. Sure there were terror missions, where you had to save people asap, but they were the exception.
Xcom 2 is the total opposite. Time and again you are given a ridiculously low number of turns in which to complete your missions, making you push into enemy territory at break-neck speed, against enemies who outnumber you 2 to 1, have better armour, and better weapons.
Even the 'terror missions' are annoying, because there are aliens disguised as humans, so just rescuing them is not enough, you have to be careful not to overextend, and in the meantime evryone dies.
Then there are ridiculous bosses like the King snake, who moves twice a turn, can disable your troops with one attack, has way too much health and armour, and then does a disappearing trick as soon as its health starts getting low; and all the while in every single mission, Bradford is trolling you about what a terrible mess you are making of it all!
Your troops are dumb; if you accidently don't get your lines right, they will happily run into fire and burn to death. On one mission. my troops had to use a lift to stop a baddy, but my sniper was suddenly cut off from the rest of the squad by a big influx of enemies. She was standing next to the plane, but no, I wasn't allowed to get back on board; I had to fight all the baddies solo cos those that had used the lift were no longer able to take part. Stupid!
The way I found to cheese the game was have 2 stealthers, 2 snipers and an expendable newbie, so that even in a hot LZ I could still sneak up on enemies and just shoot them to pieces at long range with squad sight.
I think the character models are just bad, with unrealistic faces and way too many whacky transmogs. Chen's daughter is highly irritating, too.
I played 30 hours before deciding I just didn't want to play any more. Bradford, you are such a critic, lets see you do a better job, my friend, cos I'm out of here.

Ever since Steam recommended this game to me it's claimed a portion of my daily life.
It's a game that reminded me of Mitadake High (Pyrce High I think it's called now over on the BYOND webiste) except better mechanics and a helluva lot more orgainzed. There's light role playing to figure out who's who, who should be hung or killed and the ability to take notes, all in the name of trying to win the game. Whether you're Mafia, a Townie, or some non-denominational bad or good guy, The whole goal of the game is achieve your objective and win the game. That could mean tricking people into lynching you, setting people on fire, survive the whole game without dying, or a myriad of other objects as there are tons of roles.
You don't get to pick your role. It's randomly chosen for you. You're given a box that tells you what it means, what you can do, and how to win the game. The best part of this game, is you don't always have to be alive to win. For instance, if you are aligned to win with Town and you die but Town survives, then you also have won the game.
"But I don't wanna sit around and watch a game I'm not playing." I might hear you say. But what if I told you that sometimes there's a Medium that can talk to the "dead" and you can give them info to help the living people win? But sometimes the Medium's Curse is strong and they get killed first night. So that can suck if you know exactly who killed you but you can't tell anyone.
This game is definitely a must have in my book. It's less complicated then it sounds and totally addictive. If you like RPG elements, sprinkled with a board game atmosphere and Whodunit mysteries, give this game a shot.

This game is good, however there are a few things I am not particularly pleased with.
Let's start with the good stuff though.
I like the whole infinite universe, As you never run out of things to explore, thins to have, things to make, and thus, this game is a good time killer and it is fun while you are doing said time killing.
I also like the randomly generating structures and towns, for when you run out of steam while exploring, why not do a favor or buy something?
The architecture on the buildings is really nice, and putting that to your own example is just one of the things that you can do while building mass super-structures on barren and uninhabited worlds.
Or lush and habitated worlds. Both work.
I like the questline so far. I just wish they would make it more interesting with more easter eggs in unexpected places. I really like the Apex and Erchius missions, Where you got to flip the switches and translate ancient runes to find hidden awnsers in the storyline.
I would like to have a Novakid artifact though. Who knows what the quest would be?
I also like the infinite amount of weapons and weapon combinations. For example, I gave my friend a poison shotgun that shoots grenades full of bubbling, searing, you guessed it, poison.
Speaking of friends, this game has AMAZING join support. Picture this. You're on your singleplayer world, in the middle of butchering some small, poor, alien creature who was in the wrong place at the wrong time. Then, all of a sudden, your friend joins your game, zooms across the universe 80X faster than the speed of light, and beams onto your planet and helps you murder the helpless alien. Easy.
But, sadly, it cannot all be sunshine and rainbows.
Every game has flaws, and Starbound has quite a few of them.
To start off, my friend spoke of a time when Starbound was not questline at all. the universe lay out before you, easy to get fuel, and easy to travel. Each new planet offered an exciting new challenge. Every boss in the game was optional to fight.
Now, I didn't really play Starbound at that time, although I had it. My friend kept on ranting and raving about how good it was, and I believed him. Just wasn't as good at the game as he was.
Now, I know this story is true not just because my friend is trustworthy, but because everybody else speaks about how good Starbound was at that time. So if the majority of "old timers" say it was better at that time, then i'll say it too.
That being said, I like Starbound the way it is, but I have one major, personal blow to my heart that they did in the 1.0 update.
They removed the lore.
Well, mostly. They removed the lore and added new lore, but its just not the same.
I never really pay too much attention to lore, but pre 1.0 Starbound changed that for me forever.
The Starbound lore, you could look at it any way and it would turn out perfect. Not exactly happy lore, but perfect.
In FNAF, there was so much lore there was no room for a story. In Teraria, there's probably lost of potential for story but there is no lore or backstory. In short, lore and story depend on each other.
So far the only game besides pre 1.0 Starbound that has perfect lore that I have seen is Undertale. (Maybe, just maybe Skyrim)
IN SHORT, good game, please re-add the good lore in a way that fits with the current lore, and add more types of planets and weapons. 8.5/10
I recommend it. I really do, but I would say wait until a steam sale. If you do believe they are going to re-add the lore and more interesting stuff, then you can buy it off sale. Its a good game.

If you combine the naval combat from Assassin's Creed 4 with team-deathmatch from Mount & Blade, you get Blackwake.
Pros:
Excellent teamwork-based gameplay concept similar to Guns of Icarus - multiplayer crews fighting against enemy multi-crewed ships. Teamwork is essential.
Good graphics (but higher settings require powerful PCs)
Big servers with up to 54 players across 6 ships (up to 13 players per ship).
Ramming and boarding enemy ships is a lot of fun.
Funny ingame voice commands that perfectly capture the pirate or navy vibe.
Game and netcode runs more stable than any ubisoft release.
Cons:
Game made on indie budget.
Lack of controls against team-killers and trolls (when friendly fire is on)
There are some bugs and the odd CTD, but not too much.
Some of the controls are a bit awkward, but you get used to it.
How much fun you have depends a lot on how mature and compitent your crew is.
Skill curve is a bit shallow compared to Guns of Icarus, but still deep enough.
Combat usually feels a bit laggy, but its ok.
No bots and no single-player / training mode.
Overall a great multiplayer game, recommended!

DISLIKE

Ever since Steam recommended this game to me it's claimed a portion of my daily life.
It's a game that reminded me of Mitadake High (Pyrce High I think it's called now over on the BYOND webiste) except better mechanics and a helluva lot more orgainzed. There's light role playing to figure out who's who, who should be hung or killed and the ability to take notes, all in the name of trying to win the game. Whether you're Mafia, a Townie, or some non-denominational bad or good guy, The whole goal of the game is achieve your objective and win the game. That could mean tricking people into lynching you, setting people on fire, survive the whole game without dying, or a myriad of other objects as there are tons of roles.
You don't get to pick your role. It's randomly chosen for you. You're given a box that tells you what it means, what you can do, and how to win the game. The best part of this game, is you don't always have to be alive to win. For instance, if you are aligned to win with Town and you die but Town survives, then you also have won the game.
"But I don't wanna sit around and watch a game I'm not playing." I might hear you say. But what if I told you that sometimes there's a Medium that can talk to the "dead" and you can give them info to help the living people win? But sometimes the Medium's Curse is strong and they get killed first night. So that can suck if you know exactly who killed you but you can't tell anyone.
This game is definitely a must have in my book. It's less complicated then it sounds and totally addictive. If you like RPG elements, sprinkled with a board game atmosphere and Whodunit mysteries, give this game a shot.
P.S. If you don't want to buy it, it is free to play here:
Though if you do buy it on Steam, apparently there are perks such as, there are faster loading times, $5 worth of town coins if you're into stylizing, the ability to unlock acheivements that give you more coins, and better compatibility with operating Systems.

TL;DR - It is a perfectly competent puzzle platformer with a fairly one note joke.
All hail Lord Gaben! Our savior and deliver us unto Half Life 3 so that we may be more holy in its graces. For those of you NOT in the know. Gaben is a meme about Gabe Newell, the founder of Steam. Rolled up into that are things like the PC Master race, console peasants and various other hilarious memetic hilarity. This game is based on the idea that Gabe is the heroic King of Game Sales kingdom which he protects from the evils of corporations. You play as a little, short, and fat stylized version of Gabe Newell who wears a crown, glasses and as far as I can tell, a pope hat.
Artistic style
The art style of the game is simple, pixel graphics, but it works in this setting. The bright, sometimes garish colors keep the mood light and the game friendly. Every time you smash into a baddie you get a large text announcement as well as a voice saying Ultra Kill or Rampage. It makes killing the baddies actually feel pretty good. The game is broken up into several areas, Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter Sales, as well as peasant land and Brexit. Hardee har har. While that is reasonably topical at the moment, I don’t imagine it will have the same staying power as Gaben which has persisted since the rise of Steam.
Gameplay
On the gameplay front, there are two strings to the games bow. First you have the bad guys that you must kill. Don’t let them being baddies fool you though. They cannot harm Gaben, they don’t move, and are really just checkpoints that you must clear in order to get to the pile of steam sales and money that is at the end of every level. Secondly, there is the edge of the screen. This is generally the thing that will kill you. And you will be killed, A LOT. If you leave the screen you die. This becomes a massive problem very early in the game. The camera tends to center on Gaben. However, when you are close to the top, bottom or sides of the screen and there is no more level beyond that, the camera stops centering and you end up with Gaben squashed into the side. This is a problem, because of the way the dude controls.
Controls
Controlling Gaben is an exercise in frustration and rage. He has a simple click and pull jumping mechanic and that is it. If you are familiar with the arrow shooting games, or any of a million mobile Pool games, you will recognize the mechanic. You pull back, he jumps. When you click, time slows down to enable you to direct Gaben. The problem lies in the edges of the screen, as I mentioned. Several spots in the game will require you to navigate near the bottom of the screen, but because it is the edge of the screen, you have a VERY limited space in which to pull back. This results in wasted moves, and often, just dying because you cannot get him to go the right way. Additionally, determining which way Gaben will go based on the direction you pull is an exercise in complex guessing. Sometimes Gaben will barely move, sometimes he flies off the screen like he had just bounced off of a trampoline full of scorpions. While this adds difficulty, it doesn’t feel good.
The game feels best, when you are slow-mo flying over an enemy’s head and shift direction midair to smash into him. Gabe’s little blue sword (I think) flashes out in slow mo and you get the big text saying FIRST BLOOD, or whatever it is at that moment.
Music
I struggled mightily with the music. Each area of the game has a different theme song. Now I realize old school games got away with having a very limited selection of music, and to this game’s credit, the music on offer is chinsy and cute and serves to reinforce the bright colors and style of the game. However, given that one might conceivably play the same level for a while and the same area for an hour depending on difficulty (Some will definitely take longer than that), having the same song repeated over and over and over is just infuriating. I would be extremely happy if each level within an area had a different tune.
Difficulty
I will admit it. I did not beat this game. I wanted to get my review up before the release and to be honest, I don’t think I have it in me to beat this game. Not in the current state. The controls, the way the camera locks and the music all combined to drive me away after about 23 levels.
Final grade
Bright, bouncy, colorful and full of “jokes”, Gaben Kingdom delivers on its promise of puzzle platforming with Gabe Newell. Does it do anything significant with that premise? I don’t know. Any time you take a one-line joke or meme and turn it into a full-fledged game, and make no mistake, this game has a lot of content, you run the risk of people playing for a bit and then stopping. I think I would have liked to see some more cut scenes. Maybe more jokes to help divide up the gameplay. As it is, if you are bored and like the idea of a quite difficult puzzle platforming experience, then you could give this game a whirl. If you are looking for hilarious Gaben memes, and jokes, might I suggest using Google image search?
Thanks for watching. Gaben Kingdom is available on Steam on the 12th of May. Make sure you like and subscribe and leave a comment. I always respond .

Yeah, I recommend this game. And I've enjoyed all the other games before it. There's a strange line of thought these days that says; Everything new is bad.
But why is that?
I have over 1,000 hours on Fallout New Vegas, and that's just on the computer. I've also spent an ungodly amount of time on my Playstation 3. The same can be said about Fallout 3. I quickly became a fan of the series, and was dying for the arriveal of Fallout 4. Without any kind of hesitantion, I had pre-ordered for my Playstion 4 and played through it over the entire game, collecting the new gear, making the new guns, getting all the trophies, and went into great lengths in building several settlements that were basically small military bases, spending several hundred hours into the game (And that's not mentioning the other things either).
A year or two later, I upgraded my computer and bought Fallout 4 as soon as I could when it went up for sale (30-ish dollars at the time.) First thing I did was mod the crap out of the game. Dowloaded dozens of things I really did not need, and lost the ability to get achivements. I didn't care that much since I had already (tehnically) collected all of them. Sure, I didn't go the extra mile in building my settlements this time, or searched every location like before, but running it without lag and enjoyed more of the eye candy, I was able to get pretty far into the game once again. Unfortnately, I went back to my Playstation to complete some loose ends on the DLC (Which is all pretty great in my opinion). By then, I was completely spoiled by my high stats and upgraded weapons, so returning to my lesser character was a bit of a downer. Not mention, I had probably hit the 1,000 hour mark once again, finally burning myself out on it just after completing around 90% on the DLC's trophies. . .
. . .I realized one thing though. . .I really, really, really liked the game. I mean...I REALLY liked the game. in fact, I liked it as much as the other ones.
But why? Everyone else had mixed feelings about it. Fans of the series, just like myself went as far to say that they HATED it.
Well, I think that's because I approached FO4 with mindset that allowed me enjoy the game for what it was. . .
. . .I entered Fallout 4 expecting it to be nothing like the other games. I didn't want a reskin of Fallout 3 or New Vegas. I wanted it to be different from the others, completely different! I did this partly for defending myself against a chance of disapointment, however, I already knew that Fallout 4 was going to be drastically conflicting from the other games to begin with.
If you have spent as many hours as I have in the earlier games, you'll probably notice that just looking around isn't like it was in the others. In the first 20 minutes, I knew I wasn't playing any of the other RPG Fallout's, but that wasn't a bad thing. I got exactly what I wanted. A game that was benchmarking the next generation of both engine, and pace.
And before you get angry for this approach, think if Fallout 3 / New Vegas were like the orginal games. Nothing had moved on, it just had a different story, some better graphics, same  gameplay. Not too good, right? Fallout HAD to move on -- it has to make a path for whatever *could* be next.
Listen, do not enter Fallout 4 expecting it to be the last two games of the series. Instead enter it expecting the generation of the series instead. It isn't perfect, and now there are paid mods now...But, keep in mind, I was able to have 1,000+ hours in the vanilla game on a CONSOLE. You'll manage just fine a computer.

I will keep this review short as I do not support steam's reviewing setup because it doesn't not allow for a balanced judgement. Which amazes me. I would imagine that customers are key and allowing customers to express their opinion would be important, both towards other customers and towards game developers. Instead steam seems most reluctant to allow customers a voice.
I judge  Dead Age to be neither good nor bad. Thumbs up and down do not capture my review.
Dead Age is a game set in a zombie-apocalyptic world and is about you running a group of survivors. This has you run a base at the one hand and a mission crew on the other. It is a heavily scripted game with a predetermined setup.  I found myself forced along a fixed path and this both annoyed me and gave  me a challenge.
The game confronts you at times with though choices and making the wrong choice will abruptly end the game.  This annoyed me to no end. Bad choices should not be punished by instant dead of everyone involved. It should offer you thougher choices.
While at the one hand the game is scripted and set along a specific track, much else is random. Combat, finding things, attacks on your homebase and much else is random.  This makes you a victim of randomness versus scripted challenges..
The upshot it that the only recourse for a series of  random generated disasters is to reload. As the game forces you into one save game: you can't go back unless you do some copy and pasting of the game save games to undo some previous bad randomness.
I do not understand the desire of gamedevelopers to force one savegame games on customers.  Why not let a customers(= players) decide for themselves? It is like determing that a player might not powerplay and game designers therefore prevent it.
I like a challenge so I play hard often, some like an easy victory(like a friend of mine) and they play easy or casual. To each their own.
I will not elaborate on other issues, except that the game favors certain skills over others. after a while you find out that some are just not worth the limited amount of experience points. This makes some skills and weapons redundant. Limiting replayability more.
My biggest gripe at this game is that it forces into decisions at the spur of the moment and then throws randomness at you for the outcome. This makes you feel that all your careful playing is wasted by randomness. Even when carefully planning. Reloading the game changes the randomness. One trip might be hard, the next easy.

Tales of Berseria is a JRPG in the highly-acclaimed Tales series. Even though the series' last few entries have had some missteps, ToB has come along to remind us all that the people who develop these games still give a damn. Is it a great Tales game? Oh, yes, absolutely. It might even be the best Tales game in the series, taking that spot in my personal scorebook from Abyss (bearing in mind that I've never played Vesperia).
"Okay", you say, "but I've never played a Tales game. All of these names mean nothing to me! Do I already have to be a fan of the series to enjoy this one?" Not at all. This game is very approachable for anyone who's enjoyed a JRPG and/or likes RPGs with flashy, action combat systems. Heck, I'd say if you like anime in general, you wouldn't go wrong.
I don't even know where to start with this wonderful game.
I'm going to keep this simple and avoid spoiling anything. The story in this game is great, held together by entertaining characters, the unique (at least, as far as JRPGs go) motivations of the protagonists, and excellent Japanese voice-acting (I can't speak for the dub, but it exists). There's a lot of cutscenes and talking, something else the Tales series is well known for, in that there are many 'skits' where the characters in the party will interact and talk about various things. It's all very well written. You'll cry, I'll laugh, emotions will touch the rafters!
Bear in mind, this is a japanese game, so there are going to be a few anime tropes here and there. As long as you can accept that, you'll be satisfied, or better, by what you get here.
This is a JRPG, so a lot of the game is going to spend talking to NPCs, watching cutscenes, listening to skits, and when you're not doing that, exploring dungeons and fighting enemies. Dungeons aren't especially interesting, mostly being linear with chests and items scattered around, and mountains of enemies to fight through. Some have unique twists but they're straight-forward for the most part.
Where this game really excels is the 'battle' part. There's about half a dozen characters that'll be in your party. Each one of them has a unique gimmick and will learn a lot of special moves called 'artes'. You beat enemies down by stringing these artes into combos. They will also learn Break Souls, which are more limited special attacks that have more unique effects. For example, one character learns a 'counter' Break Soul, where a well-timed press of R2 will negate an attack that hits them and damage the enemy who launched it instead. All characters will eventually learn 'mystic artes', which are very flashy finishing moves that have cutscenes tied to them. You can control any character you want at any time, and they are all varied enough to keep you entertained for a long time.
There's also minigames everywhere. Some are good, some are meh. My favorite one are the Character Cards, which is basically a Tales-themed version of Hanafuda Koi-Koi cards. The effort put in is very much appreciated.
I have some minor complaints. Two of the progression systems do not flow well together at all; Master Skills and the upgrade system. Master skills are special bonuses gained by using equipment over time. Generally, you'll want to use an item until you get its master skill, and then afterwards, use a new item that you haven't mastered yet. This is fine and it's enjoyable to switch around and get new goodies.
However, the upgrade system is the opposite. You gain materials by breaking down items or by finding them randomly on the ground. You then use these materials to upgrade your equipment, increasing its stats and its enhancement skills, meaning you're encouraged to upgrade and use the same items over time, meaning you won't be learning new master skills. Using upgraded items is pretty much mandatory on the higher difficulties if you want to stand any chance against bosses.
The upgrade system itself is a bit of a pain in the butt, too. Since you're trying to upgrade 5 items for each character, the materials you get by normally playing don't go very far. Eventually, you will probably have to grind for them. Thankfully, this is easy, because the game mercifully gives you side areas with arenas that give you a lot of items, and you can just turn on auto-battle and AFK if you really want to. However, for the higher upgrade levels you'll be required to use materials that can only be obtained by breaking down equipment that has been upgraded to certain levels. So you get your items, break them down for materials, upgrade some more extras a little bit to get the next tier of materials, and so on.
If that sounds annoying, it's because it is, but is probably only really necessary if you crank up the difficulty as high as possible, meaning you know what you're getting into. The difficulty can be adjusted at any time without penalty, so there's no dead-end if you get frustrated. Overall, this part of the game could have been done better, but it doesn't ruin it by any means.

Then came the Creation Club update. I waitied for the mods to be updated and they still won't work after a reinstallation. It looks like free mods from outside sources are no longer welcome.
I paid for this game after the brilliance that was New Vegas, which is honestly probably my favorite game of all time. Obsidian should be given back their franchise because Bethesda's attempts at making Fallout games are like an awkward fan fiction. I bought the Far Harbor DLC and found it rather mediocre. Nuka-World was a bit better, but still in the end didn't add much. At least, I thought, the modding community could help resolve these shortcomings, as they have in the past, right?
I've since uninstalled the game and no longer plan to buy any Bethesda products in the future. If Bethesda has so little respect for their customer base, I'll be making sure to tell everyone I know to avoid buying Bethesda products in the future as well.

I really want to give this game a positive review, because I've had some real fun with it, but in it's current state, this is not worth the price.
The movement is awkard and stiff, much worse than the Isle. Jumping seems to respond very poorly, and is delayed as hell.
Hitboxes are HORRENDOUS, and this is one of the biggest problems with dinosaur games in general. I'm assuming this has something to do with the awkard body shape compared to something humanoid, but it is just so frustrating to have the tip of your tail clip against a crocodile's mouth and then have your character drop dead instantly.
The environments are beautiful, and the models are incredible, however the very poor optimization almost completely kills it. I have a beast of a PC and I am experiencing the entire range of texture imperfections, clipping/flashing shadows, blurry visuals, etc. And there is next to nothing in the way of graphics settings, so trying to fix the graphical errors is out of the question.
So with all that being said, do I recommend Saurian? No. I would personally suggest that you wait until it has more work put into it. The ideas are incredible, and I can see the skelton for a truly amazing game. But between the stiff controls, and poor optimization, it simply isn't worth the price tag now.
Although before you write it off, I must say that there is a very passionate and devoted dev team behind it, who have continued to be very honest about their limitations, and have kept up with their promises. If anything, keep an eye on this project, because I suspect great things will come from it.
TL;DR Game is buggy and stiff right now, wait for refinement, but keep it in your mind.
