So Town of Salem...So much to say about this game, all positive, yet so hard to put it into words. First off, there is definitely a learning curve in terms of learning the roles and what they do. As a general explanation to the game there are three sides or factions if you want to think of it that way. There's the town members, technically the good guys who want to hang and kill all the evil doers in their town. Then there's the mafia, the bad guys who's goal is to kill all town members either through trickery during the day or murder during the night. And finally there's the neutrals, roles that are sometimes evil and have to win on their own or maybe they have their own, specific role of their own and in general, can win with anyone. Within these three factions are a large selection of roles, all of which you will be randomly given each game. With each game you get coins that you can spend on character skins, house skins, town skins, death animations, etc. After 50 games of either Classic mode games or custom games you can play Ranked games which are much more challenging and generally filled with more people who know what they are doing. It's a game of deception and lying and causing chaos, depending on your role. And it is beyond fun as hell. 10/10. :)

Honestly, for a game that was made in 1998, this game still holds up today. A game for valve that would quickly blow up in popularity, and again when releasing a sequel six years later with Half Life 2. Unfortunately, of course I have to mention the fact that Half Life 3 was never released for it's scheduled time, and at this time, most people have given up on the story ever being finished in the Half Life series. But, back to this particular game, the one that started it all. The visuals and mechanics are revolutionary for the time it was released, and you can tell some features of this game have influenced many other games after it, whether it be valve themselves or other studios. The most brilliant part is the story. From start to finish, the player is indulged in the story to see what's going to happen, and to also figure out how G-Man plays into the story. It's 2017, and I enjoyed it more than some modern-day titles of the same category, and the sequel seems to outdo this one! So I definitely recommend playing this series, although with a lack of Half Life 3 ever being developed, you'll be held on to that cliffhanger most likely, forever.

One of the Best Tales to date.
Warning: I will be bringing up ToZ here most of the time since it is one of the latest that can be used as a comparison.
This is from someone who is a big fan of the franchise and played the previous games.
After the disaster that is Tales of Zestiria (TBH, watch the anime. Much better!), i somehow lost the desire to buy another one. I initially plan to pirate it just to get  but after the good "promotional" episode 6 & 7 of the Season 1 of Tales of Zestiria the X and a positive reception of the game, i was sold into buying the game.
Initial Review:
Technical - Miles ahead of ToZ. I have some lag spikes in ToZ while ToB is very smooth. Camera positioning is one of the things that i liked in this one and previous Tales titles (Abyss, Vesperia, Symphonia and Xillia) while some is in 2D. ToZ camera is somewhat awkwardly placed especially during battle and some un-necessary background interference like trees hinder you while this one is just perfect. Might have different opinions from others.
Gameplay - Very good. They introduced a new battle system which is one of the best to date systems of Tales series. Might got repetitive for some but for fans of the series then this isn't really a problem. Equipment Mastery is pretty straightforward. Btw, I hate Armatization (I want to form my own team and play who i want to main!)
Story - Berseria takes place approx. 1000 years before the Zestiria so they are somewhat connected but either both games can be played without the experience of any of the two. This title took a somewhat dark tone unlike some of the typical Tales games which i don't really have a problem too. Last dark scene that i could recall is some "mass death" and "corpse back to life" shenanigans scene in ToA (which also a very good title)
Characters - All lovable and i love that all of them have different personal agenda. Typically, people will party up because they believe in the same bla bla bla bla but here? We have a therion, an exorcist, a war deamon, a malakhim, a witch and a pirate. Don't forget to read the skits! They are hilarious especially when they are fighting each other since they have different ideals. There are also sidequests which will develop those characters so be sure to check them.
Enjoyment - I really liked it because of the characters. BECAUSE OF THEM! Yes, they are the main charm of the series for me. Gameplay is good but unless you are playing on Hard~Chaos then it is fairly easy (especially for tales fans). If not for them then i might haven't finished this yet since that's the case for me.
All in all, this is a good series and i assure that it is worth all the penny spent. It might have flaws (DLC is somewhat expensive) but with a very good character interaction, likeable characters and stellar story-telling then you will surely enjoy it.

Okay, so I managed to finish this game. I tried using a Rock Candy controller first but cursor aiming was too hard, so I used a mouse and keyboard which was okay. This game is a flash game which I usually try to avoid, which is hard to without any tag for flash-based. Anyhow, how to rate this game.
Graphically, the animations are loose joint kind, like there seems to be strings holding up characters.  Not alot of bright colors, which for a military type game is normal, and at 1080p textures and outlines are slightly dull. Backgrounds are the slightly blurred effect type-for an off in the distance effect.
Gameplay, is going to depend on finding a good controller or mouse and keyboard. My keyboard is the normal big desktop kind; it has very squishy keys with slippery surfaces.  Anyhow, the main character has a floaty jump, and its height is affected by various factors: like unsteady ground or surfaces, carrying heavy guns, riding mech, jumping direction, springy objects like floatsom on water and tree branches and low ceiling of courese etc.  Aiming cursor is a big yellowish triangle, It is still easy to lose track of said cursor because the whole screen is targetable-not at the same time of course. But there is an particles gun that can pass through certain walls and objects and can target multiple enemies in a straight line. Besides riding a big Wolf that can squish slash enemies, there are mechs: grappling hook mech which grabs and throws barrels and light debris. Gun mech with sword and another combination mech with missiles. Enemies include standard unarmored to armored soldiers, mech riders, dragons that shoot, grab and or use a knife tail, wolves, fire-spewing balloons etc. Physics allow using barrels, rocks, snow, and expanding goo jars for defense, offense or for climbing. So there is lots of fun to be had experimenting there for fun of strategy.
Bosses are good variety, flying grabbers, wild girl robot with elemental and gun weapons, and Mace the last boss. The last boss took me about 15 hours, but I kept getting stuck in debris or knocked off the edges. Finally, managed to get some pointers online, but I was lucky and memorization helped with getting ready for last boss phases.
Decent game, and perhaps original, well, original from my experiences with these run and gun games. Game is short if the last boss does not phase you.
If I had to make improvement suggestions I say: 1) make custom cursor color available-the last boss was same color as cursor. 2) on last boss the main character's waist to feet are cut off by camera and also when jumping off elevated stands the bottom of screen is cut off.
I had alot of trouble with the debris piling up, sometimes getting hit by a barrel and flying off ledge. I finally just managed to quickly learn how to aim ahead of the giant enemy last boss and take off health quickly, especially at the beginning phase, still debris could help by blocking homing missles so its up to player preference.

I'm a fan of the Tales series and have been since Symphonia. I've tried most of what's come out since then. Recently I put together my thoughts and figured out that my favorite is probably a toss up between Vesperia and Abyss, though after 70+ hours with this latest entry I'm pleased to say that there might be a third to the top spot tie.
The story opens in a way that feels like they learned a lot from Zesteria's good and bad, giving you some humble beginnings that feel like they actually round out the main character, Velvet, as an actual character. Hell, they even toss in a somewhat unique looking NPC to your starter village as your friend rather than just giving them a generic design and pretending that you care so much about Villager 23.
This is followed up by a second part of the prologue where it's dripping with edge to the point of ridiculousness and might give you Vietnam flashbacks to FFXIII's Lightning if you were unfortunate enough to play that, but thankfully Velvet gets rounded out once more cast members show up. Here you get a rough look at the combat that kinda plays out the opposite of Zesteria, making you build up a pool of "stamina" as fights go on rather than having to manage to keep it topped off (That said it does still make you figure out a risk/reward system that's satisfying once you master it).
Both sides of the prologue set the tone for your villain/antihero protagonist adventure and it feels properly paced with the occasional snag from there on out. Once the rhythm of combat kicks in, and you dig deeper into the equipment system that constantly feeds you some measure of progress, the whole thing is smooth sailing as you embark on your revenge-fueled saga, slowly becoming the villain of the world whose heroes are much less heroic than they appear.
However it's not this oppressively grimdark slog, nor does it fully break from the Tales series's usual tone of adventuring around with an oddball cast, managing to balance the two tones in a way that makes the tragedies you stumble across hit harder, and lighter moments more fun (especially the sidequests, which usually seem to take whatever emotional direction they're going for and ramp it up more than the main plot).
What I really want to say though is that Tales of Berseria had me hooked to this game alone for 2 weeks and I actually started working through the EX Dungeon rather than moving on to another game. Given that the last couple games I slowly burned out on, that's saying something. There's room to grow here, yes, but this feels like a return to form and I don't regret dropping my money or my time on this game.
Oh and if you played Zesteria through to a point, even if you didn't see the ending, there's some plot threads here and there that retroactively improved my experience with that game.
The Positives:
-The plot and characters had me hooked
-Once the sidequests show up, they're great. Also the game doesn't require you to have a guide open to tell you when they're available since they show up on the map (ah, painful memories)
-Very light on Grind (outside of post-endgame bonus fights)
-Return of a lot of good mechanics (customizable fashion, cooking, etc.) and the equipment system from Zesteria is gone
-Dialogue skipping doesn't seem to interfere with animations anymore
-Animations aren't cutting edge but seem a lot less wooden than Zesteria's (I mean the transitions in Zesteria were beautiful, but two character talking to one another occasionally looked like puppetry)
-Very stable for me (during fights it could slow down during more effect heavy stuff, but usually I was locked into the animation of a heavy hitting attack. I hesitate to call it frame rate issue since it only seemed to be when I was hitting and not enemies)
The Negatives:
-The game has a lot of linear areas
-the sidequests are absent for a lot more of the story than I'd like
-combat has a weird learning curve to it that made me initially hate it much more than i should have
-there aren't a huge amount of costumes that aren't DLC
-a couple characters start off as somewhat grating in their own ways
-normal mode can be a tad easy at points
-towards the end, the game has a bit of a problem of plot to dungeon ratio (though thankfully leveling on normal difficulty is generous enough that you don't have to fight every enemy after a certain point and stay at a proper level)
Mixed:
-I had exactly one crash in the game. However, it was right after I beat the bonus boss fight with two level 126 characters vs my party of 70ish characters. I got through with an all-divide and abuse of items and fought uphill for that and it was physically painful. Funny part: the characters were talking in the skit about avoiding certain creatures from then on out of fear that they could inadvertantly end the world. The moment there was an abrupt ending to one of their sentences, the crash happened, so it couldn't have been timed better if it were a joke that didn't erase my progress.

It seems that Intrusion 2 try to be a clone of Metal Slug series with the addition of a physical engine. However, the physical effects finally realised destroy the feeling of Metal Slug completely. The control is quite strange and often does not respond in the way it supposed to be (or in other words, as in most normal 2D action/shooter games). It is very annoying that some small object may block your path or prevent you from picking up an item.
Another major problem is the shaking of the screen is so furious that it may cause dizziness.
In addition, the controller support of this game is not very satisfacotry, since you cannot re-define the buttons and jumping is assigned to pushing left stick up and button C at the same time, with the former one easily leading to mistakes in contrl and difficulties in continuous jumps.
The other aspects, such as graphics, BGM, sound effects, enemy design, are generally bland.
Therefore, I won't recommend this game unless you really love 2D action/shooter games but don't have anything else to play.

Gameplay - average at best
Story - the reason you would/should buy this game.
About 5 years after initial release, I think the story (and "Choose your own adventure" mixed with "Walking Dead") is done excellently; enough to warrant purchase.  But.  And this is a big But.  If you've played other (perhaps more recent) similar TellTale (or even Life is Strange) kind of games, you won't find a whole lot really new/innovative.  You'll still wander through an area trying to find the right dialogue path to take to get your desired outcome(s) - or find the right size/shape "peg" to fill a problem's "hole" with.
There's enough choices of dialogue (and characters & paths to choose) that there's a smattering of endings that can resolve the story - so there is potential for replayability to see how a different route goes - but it feels  untapped.  There's a sense of "finality" that comes after it all regardless of your choices that makes it kind of hard to go back through and change them.
The DLC available is a nice sampling of what this kind of story system can "build up" to with a motley of characters - and origin stories with them - but it feels oddly disjointed with little/no connection to the main 5 episode game.
Overall - Its story holds up despite the ~5 years.  Other elements not so much.  Feeling generous and don't own it, go for full price.  On sale and don't own it, buy it.  DLC optional either way, it doesn't change much.

People need to calm down. Yes the dialogue only has 4 options, but 90% of all dialogue in the other Fallout games had 3 to 4 options. The dialogue is my biggest complaint, but It's not that big a of a deal in retrospect. My other complaint is that quests often have 1 ending, I would love to choose from several endings but I do not expect this for every quest.
The Game is beautiful, it's got a great feel to it and I love the way the world is set up. The dirt may be a boring brown but you find that the Post/Pre-War buildings have a nice color scheme and It makes the game that much more nice looking. As for people who are underwhelmed by the map, C'mon? If you want to be underwhelmed look at New Vegas. The City was an empty pile with 50% of the buildings being unenterable. It had a total of 6 nice looking buildings, That was it!
The Power Armor makes you feel like an absolute BEAST! I don't mind that they gave me a Minigun and Power Armor in the first 20 mins of the game because the Armor is in bad shape to start with (and after killing a Death Claw it's in worse shape) and after killing everything in that mission I only had 21 shots left on the gun. I droped it because who wants to carry around a useless (and heavy) weapon. The people who are questioning the use of Power Armor in the first 20 mins should take into consideration that it's a way of giving you an incentive to find, craft, and customize your own set(s). In Fallout New Vegas I never bothered with Power Armor because I already had some cool cowboy stuff, and it didn't do that much for me anyways. Not to mention that it looked pretty bad too.
I don't mind the Perk system because they were always the best part about leveling up anyways. I like looking at all the options that are placed before me and planning out my character before I even hit level 5. For this reason alone, I do not agree with the people claiming that "Fallout 4 is not an RPG" off of the grounds that dialogue choice is limited. You get to make your character look the way you want, fight the way you want, join the factions you want, and so on. You get to create a character who is individual to you, just because he/she can't say exactly what you want to say doesn't mean that the game is not an RPG.
Now that I'm done defending the game from common criticism lets talk about what the game did exceptionally well at. The game has amazing sound design, I'll be walking along and all of a sudden I'll hear far off shots. The fact that I can tell what guns are being used, how many people are shooting at eachother and how far off they are from me speaks valumes for the game's sounds. This skill comes in handy more times then you might think.
Another thing That I like is the looting system. The game feels so much more seemless now that I don't have to look through body after body to find nothing useful. Instead I am given a nice UI that tells me exactly whats is available to loot. I can also choose to go into a more indepth UI if I want to.
Character/Enemy design looks and feels great. Ghouls look and act far more "feral". Mole rats have a nice little add on with the ability to go underground and pop out at you. Your Dog now has the ability to pin people down so you can shoot them (Team work is actually a thing now!) and I am overall impressed with how far they came from the "Run at the enemy and block your friend" companions from Fallout and the Elderscrolls games alike.
Finnally, You can have lasting change in a Fallout game. The fact that you can build your own settlment, is the largest change in a Fallout game since the destruction of Megaton. It adds just as much content as being able to say something new, and I like the change. The next related topic is the crafting system, which is extensive. Build what you want were you want. it's a great feeling and I love it.
Cons:
- "I wanna say something else!"
- "Put the gun, on your back!" (Gun randomly appears when you have to use it)
- Lack of Quest endings choices
- Repetative Quests (Like some Skyrim Quests)
Pros:
- Looks Great
- Sounds Great
- (Seemless) Feels great!
- SOOO much crafting
- Lasting impression on the world!
This Game IS an RPG, and it stands strong on it's own. I like it! :)

This is perhaps the last racing game of its kind from Criterion.  One of the unique aspect to Burnout Paradise was how the developers implemented multi-monitor support to the game.  Back then, such a thing was possible using Matrox's TripleHead2Go.  Now both nvidia and AMD implement multi-monitor using their video cards and without the need for an external device like TH2G.
Still, Burnout Paradise is likely the last of its kind when it comes to being the best arcade-style racing game on the PC platform that truly differentiated itself from its console counterpart.  Since then, Criterion has gone on to make Need for Speed games under the EA empire.  Sadly, the games they put out weren't the same nor did they stood out.  But that's another issue altogether.
Even if you do not have 3 monitors to play this game, it's still a fun game.  Buy it up.  Install it.  And get driving.

It's basically Time Limits: The Game.
Both in the campaign and in a lot of (if not most) missions. You'll have a ton of things to look at and do, but everything on the map is on a timer. And then while you're going to one thing you'll have timed events or missions that expire that the game tells you you shouldn't ignore or something bad might happen. Your time is basically spent rushing from one place to the next. Rush to the next supply cache, then before you finish getting it (because it takes several in-game days), rush to a mission before its timer expires, then in the mission rush to finish before the turn timer hits zero, then rush to make contact with a region, but before that finishes rush to help out someone before that mission timer expires. And so on.
If you love racing against the clock while being given only a vague idea of how to best prepare yourself for the various story missions that the game implies are super urgent, then this might be the game for you.
To sum up the combat: In one mission, my experienced sharpshooter missed a large stationary object (a turret) with an aimed shot from a sniper rifle, meanwhile a close-range assault soldier took it out from further away with a shotgun.

I am a fan of Assassin's Creed series and I played most of them.
Freedom Cry is the first AC game I have played on my PC (all previous were on X360) but still using the same X360 controller so I was very used to AC mechanics.
I have Black Flag and I have completed it like the previous ones with 100% synchronization so my approach is rather not a casual gamer one.
Maybe the good stuff first:
- Naval battles - they are quite enjoyable and still give a lot of fun.
... and for me that was it.
The stuff that was annoying:
- Glitches ... a lot of them ... some minor, some heavy, some crashes. For e.g. in one of the missions I was talking to some salesman and listening to his explanations and also observing a queue to fish stand next to mine. Well it was quite impressive cause 6 people who bought fish from this guy they just ... disappeared. Yeah just after trade was done, every one of them got deleted from Animus. As you watched them. Another example. During fights it is very likely that you will get badly synchronized enemies, whose bodies react to your punches or combos being few meteres to the side of your grab or machete slice. Final example is ships and enemies spawning from thin air just because you were too quick to get somewhere before the game was able to load it. For 14 hours I played Freedome Cry bugs presence was way to often (12 hours extra was logged by steam when I left my computer running with AC opened doing some other stuff).
- Respawn time of slave liberation events. It did'nt matter that I just rescued some convoy or stopped the punishmet on poor slave souls ... nope turn around went few steps the othere way and bam we have another convoy to rescue. Very annoying when you try to do story missions with all that auctions and running slaves crossing your path every 50-100 metres. Very badly thought out.
- Saturation of ships sailing thru quite small naval area that you are limited to. Do not be surprised that in every moment of your sea escapade there will be at least 2-5 ships in your view range. Quite crowdy to be honest even after 15 ships plunder series that I made after game completition.

I was among the priviledged few Sailors to work aboard the S.S. Auschwitz, and captained her smaller, sister ship, the S.S. Treblinka. A fine, 13-crew ship, the Auschwitz works just beautifully when the crew listens and the captain knows what he's talking about. If captain and crew work together, the machines have never been so well oiled, and while the ship may become holy (hole-y?), we can repair it.
Of course, if the captain is a bag, and the crew is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, then it's not as well working and the ship will probably sink.
Pros:
-Democratic system for choosing captain
-Captain names and colors ship
-Ship names can be inappropriate, and as a result, sailor morale isn't crushed by the iron fist of moderation.
-Extreme emphasis on VoIP talk, with dedicated keys for Squad (whole boat), Faction (whole team, all pirates or all Navy), proximity (for battle charging the enemy ships and plundering the boot- I mean crew), and all (rarely used and doesn't really have any purpose in my eyes, though still handy to have). It seems like overkill, but it's definitely worth it, and you use 3 of the 4 VoIP keys a fair bit.
-Novel game that promotes fun playing, teamwork, less trashtalk of the other team (at least, not to their faces, though there is usually little time to do it; though, on the S.S. Auschwitz and its counterpart, we found time). It also encourages ♥♥♥♥♥♥ pirate accents, which is beautiful.
Cons:
-Some 11 year olds
-If captain and crew don't work well together for whatever reason, you get ♥♥♥♥ing decimated
-English voices (from British Navy) sound like they're all gay and just feel unnatural
-Need a mic to play: basically no way to play without a mic, or very difficult. You simply *cannot* type fast enough to communicate effectively.
-Small ships seem underpowered, and are easy to sink with holes that are hard to repair. No cover available on small ships. Teamwork is absolutely required on the hoys.
-Can be hard to repair sails, especially on small ships, as if you fall in the water, you're done for, as cap'n won't come about to pick up your sorry rear.
Overall: 5/7, will continue to support and plunder. Yar m80

SFV is a huge disappointment so far. I wasn't expecting a 30+ character roster out of the blocks, but there's no reason for it to be missing basic features present in SFIV. There's no arcade mode for starters - no individual endings for characters. The "Story" mode is a pathetic substitute, four single rounds with static drawn art in between (no animation) - should be called "Prologue" mode instead perhaps.
Vs lacks ability to play CPU or set unlimited time for some reason. There are posts in the forums showing workarounds but DInput/keyboard support is missing too.
The game is also extremely buggy - frequent disconnections from server, DX errors on quitting. The game scales extremely poorly on lower end machines too (read: unplayable). A disconnection, by the way, during a single player mode like survival kicks you back to the menu. Too bad if you've just spent an hour and are 40 rounds into a 50 round survival. Let alone the 100 survival (which REQUIRES you be connected for the rewards available).
Some things are stored on the Capcom servers and some aren't - and with no Steam cloud support, yep you guessed it, it's back to the GFWL SFIV days - you need to manually sync your gamesaves to keep scores/unlocks and so on the same between computers. Because apparently Capcom believes you'd only ever play on one machine.
From a technical standpoint, I don't like the V trigger system. They've moved several specials to the V system too. So going between SFIV and SFV is a bit jarring with the same characters. This adaption and learning curve is no problem for pros but for more casual gamers, they might not like learning a new moveset for the same characters.
A graphically upgraded SFIV built with the same love and care and respect for players would have been immensely better. Even the graphical upgrade is not a huge boon. Background animations for example play at 30 FPS and look out of place. And the, ahem, inconsistent character physics brought on by kneejerk censorship means some characters body parts move realistically, and some look like they are hewn from granite.
Capcom have really dropped the ball on this game, as many reviews are showing. Save yourself the money and go back to USFIV. Or just wait a year until hopefully this game is something like it should have actually been at launch and be priced at what it's actually worth.

This game has the best story and storytelling I have ever seen in a videogame. By LONG and by FAR. The excellent art style, music and controls provide a solid arcade-ey foundation on which to build one of the most well-crafted and immersive experiences of this decade. The game has a delightfully rustic feel to it, sandwiched somewhere between Western, Fantasy and Post-Apocalypse. And then there's the narrator. My God, the narrator. His voice is like ear sex. I'm not even kidding. I could listen to him narrate my game all day long, and he does a damn good job of it. His voice pulls together the entire theme of the game, finalizing the Western overtones.
The art style and visual execution oozes with charm and effort, setting an excellent stage for the world you play through. It's like the world only exists if you've passed through it. The ground rises up beneath your feet as if pointing the way. You don't stop to wonder why. It creates an EXTREMELY appealing atmosphere.
The music is like... acoustic frontier trip hop. It's like Bluegrass combined with Techno, with expert composition. You have to hear it to understand what I mean.
The story is immersive and draws you in, constantly making you WANT to know more. What the heck happened to the world? What was the Calamity? What caused it? Why did it happen? What are all these creatures? Do they have feelings too? Where did they come from?
And the best part is, you don't have to read freakin' in-game books or sit through a boring NPC lecture to learn anything. The narrator tells the story as you play.
This game also features a very cool upgrade system for your weaponry and innate abilities, and every upgrade makes a HUGE difference instead of a tiny and inconsequential one.
Bastion is like a good book, transformed into a game. I reccomend turning the lights off, closing your door, putting on some headphones and losing yourself. Make sure no one bothers you.

Tales of Berseria is one of the stronger entries in the Tales series, especially recently, but some serious caveats prevent it from being all that it could be. Its chief strength is in its cast and acting, with the truly ragtag and ethically ambiguous group surrounding Velvet being a huge improvement over the black and white moralism of Zestiria. Its personality, though, isn't enough to cover some core gameplay and pacing issues. A chief example is its combat system, which even on the Chaos difficulty can be a mindless button masher. While you can control any of the characters, all with diverse styles, the most effective way out of any battle will always be to spam attacks while Velvet's Soul Gauge recharges, fire off a Mystic Arte, then rinse and repeat until the field is cleared.
One area the game does not improve upon its predecessor in any way is in dungeon design, all of which are bloated, sprawling, and generic, with puzzles that can only be described as brainless. These are often a matter of lighting torches directly in front of a locked door, or worse, traveling to the other side of the map to collect a key item, and then backtracking to drop it in the correct place. It's this habit of cutting corners that has characterized recent entries in the series, and while Berseria may be an improvement on a game like Xilia 1, it's still not what it should be, and certainly not of the caliber the Tales series promises.
The character banter and skits Tales is famous for return in full force in Berseria, but the 457 sequences interrupting a game that is only 45 hours in length can seem excessive and tedious. If taken at a more measured pace this isn't an issue, but after playing a while you may find yourself skipping through more than you're actually pausing to enjoy. Tedious is also an apt descriptor for the game's final act, which quickly moves from being a stirring story of revenge to a thinly veiled JRPG trope of collecting the seven special items before the final dungeon. It's problems like these that are especially frustrating, as they seriously compromise what could have been an excellent game. Given the huge improvement the Zestiria anime has over the game, one's left wondering whether Berseria would have been better off getting the same treatment.

After 3 days and noticeable improvements to the servers, I figured it's time to update my review and make a note of what others are complaining about.
To many, this is an unfinished copy of the game and you wouldn't be wrong to believe that, it's unfortunate to see it release without some staple features of the series (Trials, Arcade, etc).
However I must say that there has been plenty of posts in gaming news and social media expressing the fact that the contents of the game will be more barebones at release to have the game ready for the Capcom Pro Tournament, and so players should have been more critical as to whether or not they should buy this game.
I figure I would summarize some of the issues people have been experiencing from my readings on the community hub and over other sites relating to discussion of the game, if any of this would deter you from purchasing the game in its current state, that's your decision to make.
- The game (currently) contains minimal single player content (Training, Local PvP versus, the Pre-Story episodes and Survival) and is more geared towards the online aspect and getting people prepared for the Capcom Pro Tournament.
- Although I previously stated the servers have been improved, this is not to say they're not perfected, this can be jarring when you are trying to complete a Survival run and are cut off at your feet because you disconnnect from the game servers.
- Some people have expressed their concerns about having a smaller roster than Street Fighter 4, with this game currently having only 16 characters on release and another 6 coming as DLC which can be obtained free (Costing 100,000 Fight Money each).
- Funnily enough although this game is exclusive to the PS4 and PC, the game does not currently support Playstation hardware (Controllers, Fight Sticks, Fight Pads, etc) and contains support and button prompts for XBOX controllers. This is coupled with the fact that people choosing to play with the Keyboard cannot currently customize their controls, these two facts are rather concerning and have been acknolwedged by Capcom who is aiming to amend this issue in the first update, as for now you will just have to use a third party program to get your controller to work.
If you can stomach that and are looking for a really solid fighting game, I would personally reccomend it. A lot of the new and returning characters feel fantastic with the games larger windows for combo links. There is also less of an emphasis on charge mechanics which may have intimidated newcomers, which could be seen as a pro or a con for certain players. The new netcode for the game is amazing to experience when playing against someone with a good connection and is currently the best I've experienced (I unfortunately won't be seeing MKX's new netcode any time soon :(  ).
There is a really good game to be found here which may have potentially had its reputation tarnished by a terrible launch, with the teams at capcom aiming to give us something new with PC - PS4 crossplay (which mind you also works really well and gives players a larger pool of opponents).
As future updates roll out I would like to encourage players to consider changing their reviews once the game has fixed any issues they may have had with the game at launch.
Thank you for reading and I hope you take what I have tried to convey here to heart and take your time with deciding if this is the game for you.

Usually, I try to review the game per se, without referencing too much to the other chapters of the same saga. However, I feel compelled to take a different route this time, focusing more on its role as a 'Tales of' game.
But maybe you, dear reader, are looking for a JRPG and you don't know anything about the saga... So I'll give you a straight and brief answer right away: it's an AWESOME game. It has all good elements of roleplay games (vivid worlds full of lore, great characters heavily developed, an epic adventure full of emotions, drama and humor) combined with a fun fast-paced real-time fighting system, deep yet simple.
9/10
Now, to address my fellow fans of the 'Tales of' games. Before Berseria, I played (and reviewed here on Steam) Zestiria and I was a bit disappointed. Don't get me wrong, it wasn't a bad game, but it felt like they tried to change too many things in just one go, resulting into a messy execution. They totally learned their lessons with Berseria, improving basically everything I didn't like from the previous game. The result?
Tales of Berseria is one of the best chapters of the saga, with a strong story and great characters. The combat system regains the flexibility and the customization that were lost in Zestiria; not only that, but it adds mechanics peculiar to specific party members, creating depth and encouraging the player to change frequently the one that's directly controlled. Some of them are a bit hard to master, but since you can leave them in any moment to the CPU's care it's not a real issue. Honestly, it's the game I've spent less time using the main character than any other 'Tales of' game. As in Zestiria, you don't have a MP bar, but an Action bar, that refills over time during the fights and refills completely at the end of the battle, allowing to go all out rather than saving on your Artes.
The world map, as it happened in Zestiria, doesn't exist anymore, it's just a series of interconnected areas, some big (like plains, snow fields, beaches, roads), some small (dungeons and cities): you don't have flying vehicles like Symphonia, Abyss or Vesperia to mention a few. However I realize this is the direction they chose with the games (since, as I said, it was already in Zestiria) and I can't really complain: I believe it's actually better this way, allowing to introduce big and suggestive landscapes; it was still worth mentioning it.
The story is a bit darker than usual and it's very well written: still, you can expect character interactions and skits to brighten up your travel. The characters are GREAT and they get serious development, as per series standard. Also, as an added bonus, Berseria is a prequel to Zestiria, but like 1000 years before, so you are not required to play both of them to know what's going on, but if you did, you'll find many interesting elements of lore and extra character backgrounds (with all the emotional consequences... I'm looking at you Eizen).
The only negative element I found in Berseria is the crafting system: it requires lots of farming and patience, asking the player to improve a piece of equipment up to a certain point using crafting resources only to break it to gain new types of resources based on how much you previously improved it. Also, you rarely have the resources to improve the newest weapons and armors, so you have to decide to either stick to your improved equipments or have something new that has a negative impact on your character (the more improved equipments you have, the more your character receives bonuses). Honestly, it sucks out the excitment of getting a new blade or a new suit of armor. Still, it's a bit more accessible than the one in Zestiria, so it's a small step in the right direction. Also, every piece of equipment has a passive ability that you can 'learn' by fighting: once you mastered it, you'll keep that ability (that can even be a permanent stat boost) even if you disequip that piece of equipment. This helps improving the characters over time, along with the standard level advancement.
In the end, it's a really great chapter for the 'Tales of' saga and I strongly recommend it.
Final votation: 'Almost Vesperia'

I've played and completed various games from

series and I can say that this is one of the better ones at least compared to the newer games. This series has had its highs and lows, and like many big franchises, can have predictable storylines and unexciting gameplay loops. That being said I have really enjoyed playing this game.
The plot deviates from the standard right-versus-wrong story, choosing to be much more dark, violent, and haunting. Despite this you still feel sympathy for the protagonist's cause for revenge. The introductory parts of the game were very engaging in the story.
The characters, as per many
games, were a colourful band of characters. These characters have fleshed out backstories and interactions that do not deviate from the main plot too much. You really get the sense of the bonds within the party.
The combat is, in my opinion, fluid and dynamic; always keeping me on my toes. Chaining combos through the use of the Velvet's martial artes, stabbing attacks, and powerful break souls is intergral to success, and the soul gauge system keeps the fights going.
The crafting system has been improved from
allowing for the dismantling of weapons to improve weapons, rather than needing to combine two of the same weapon.
Lastly, the music is outstanding for lack of a better term. The opening song is lovely and there is a certain piano track which I simply adore.
As a fan of JRPGs, I would highly reccomend this game to anyone looking for a fresh story and overall great experience

I'm going to just throw this out there in the hopes that it helps someone else make an informed decision before buying this. Keep in mind that I started this early access a little late, so I have less to gripe about than most people.
I honestly am unsure if I recommend this game or not. At its core, I love it. It's amazing, and I was hooked right away on the character creation menu. I'm coming from hundreds of hours in Terraria, and I know this is a genre I love. And I did. I got to around 20 hours and realised the pacing was... off. I wanted to set up a super base on one of the many uninhabited planets scattered across the universe. I chose my planet, the blocks I wanted to use, and got to work. I built around 20 blocks and a singular door with all of my life savings. Every penny. I then understood that building was terribly imbalanced if I wanted to use anything other than wood and stone. This made me start following the Chucklefish Starbound blog, hoping that there would be news of changes that would fix a bunch of my concerns (and there were way more than just building prices.).
So I sat there. And watched, day after day, as tiny bits of graphical updates and furniture sets were added to the nightly build of the game. Not a single core mechanic in desperate need of a fix was changed, but tiny ambient animals were added in. The game still lags when there are too many light sources or NPCs, but at least plants now have to be watered instead of growing on their own. It just seems like the devs are using their time for little things that should be added in post-beta, while they neglect things that should be top of the priority list.
But I keep playing it. I can build pretty much anything if I spawn items in (not sure if that even counts as an accomplishment, but whatever), and I love it that you can spawn NPCs to populate the villages you construct (as opposed to Terraria's 20-ish NPC count). I see that the possibilities are endless, and the are infinite planets to build on. It keeps me busy, but it feels like that shouldn't be the only thing keeping me interested in a 15 dollar game, especially when Terraria is 10 dollars at maximum.
So as of this writing, even with a new Stable update around the corner, I suggest those who value their money steer clear. If you feel like blowing 15 bucks, go for it, it's probably a lot more worth it still than games that are much more expensive. I'll probably have to come back and revise this is the next few months (fingers crossed that the game actually changes in that time), but I wouldn't wait up for it.

Yeah, I recommend this game. And I've enjoyed all the other games before it. There's a strange line of thought these days that says; Everything new is bad.
But why is that?
I have over 1,000 hours on Fallout New Vegas, and that's just on the computer. I've also spent an ungodly amount of time on my Playstation 3. The same can be said about Fallout 3. I quickly became a fan of the series, and was dying for the arriveal of Fallout 4. Without any kind of hesitantion, I had pre-ordered for my Playstion 4 and played through it over the entire game, collecting the new gear, making the new guns, getting all the trophies, and went into great lengths in building several settlements that were basically small military bases, spending several hundred hours into the game (And that's not mentioning the other things either).
A year or two later, I upgraded my computer and bought Fallout 4 as soon as I could when it went up for sale (30-ish dollars at the time.) First thing I did was mod the crap out of the game. Dowloaded dozens of things I really did not need, and lost the ability to get achivements. I didn't care that much since I had already (tehnically) collected all of them. Sure, I didn't go the extra mile in building my settlements this time, or searched every location like before, but running it without lag and enjoyed more of the eye candy, I was able to get pretty far into the game once again. Unfortnately, I went back to my Playstation to complete some loose ends on the DLC (Which is all pretty great in my opinion). By then, I was completely spoiled by my high stats and upgraded weapons, so returning to my lesser character was a bit of a downer. Not mention, I had probably hit the 1,000 hour mark once again, finally burning myself out on it just after completing around 90% on the DLC's trophies. . .
. . .I realized one thing though. . .I really, really, really liked the game. I mean...I REALLY liked the game. in fact, I liked it as much as the other ones.
But why? Everyone else had mixed feelings about it. Fans of the series, just like myself went as far to say that they HATED it.
Well, I think that's because I approached FO4 with mindset that allowed me enjoy the game for what it was. . .
. . .I entered Fallout 4 expecting it to be nothing like the other games. I didn't want a reskin of Fallout 3 or New Vegas. I wanted it to be different from the others, completely different! I did this partly for defending myself against a chance of disapointment, however, I already knew that Fallout 4 was going to be drastically conflicting from the other games to begin with.
If you have spent as many hours as I have in the earlier games, you'll probably notice that just looking around isn't like it was in the others. In the first 20 minutes, I knew I wasn't playing any of the other RPG Fallout's, but that wasn't a bad thing. I got exactly what I wanted. A game that was benchmarking the next generation of both engine, and pace.
And before you get angry for this approach, think if Fallout 3 / New Vegas were like the orginal games. Nothing had moved on, it just had a different story, some better graphics, same  gameplay. Not too good, right? Fallout HAD to move on -- it has to make a path for whatever *could* be next.
Listen, do not enter Fallout 4 expecting it to be the last two games of the series. Instead enter it expecting the generation of the series instead. It isn't perfect, and now there are paid mods now...But, keep in mind, I was able to have 1,000+ hours in the vanilla game on a CONSOLE. You'll manage just fine a computer.

Honestly, for a game that was made in 1998, this game still holds up today. A game for valve that would quickly blow up in popularity, and again when releasing a sequel six years later with Half Life 2. Unfortunately, of course I have to mention the fact that Half Life 3 was never released for it's scheduled time, and at this time, most people have given up on the story ever being finished in the Half Life series. But, back to this particular game, the one that started it all. The visuals and mechanics are revolutionary for the time it was released, and you can tell some features of this game have influenced many other games after it, whether it be valve themselves or other studios. The most brilliant part is the story. From start to finish, the player is indulged in the story to see what's going to happen, and to also figure out how G-Man plays into the story. It's 2017, and I enjoyed it more than some modern-day titles of the same category, and the sequel seems to outdo this one! So I definitely recommend playing this series, although with a lack of Half Life 3 ever being developed, you'll be held on to that cliffhanger most likely, forever.

Just for reference, this review is coming from someone who put 50 hours into Terraria.
I really want to love this game, but it lacks an element that makes you want to come back and play it. It lacks reward for the infinite grinding that you must do to progress, and it lacks the means to motivate you to take advantage of most of the game's features. I personally think that the spaceship is what ruins the game. It is extremely overpowered and needs to be a resource that the player has to work for to use. Why would I bother with any planets when I can just fly around infinitely? Planets are simply resource depots at this point in the game.
Motivation. That's what the game needs. Incentive and reward. The game needs to be meaningful and have reward for the toil of the players.
But not too much toil, or it becomes frustrating and pointless. Balance it out, and this game will be good. For this reason, I recommend picking it up some time when it goes on sale. It was good fun for the many hours that I put into it, and I feel that it will be a great game when (or if) it becomes fully fleshed out.

I've put about 15 hours into this game and I'd give it a healthy thumbs up. It's a fun little simulator and is well worth the $15 price tag if you like such things. Once you get the game figured out it doesn't have quite the depth or replay value of Prison Architect, but I certainly enjoyed my playthrough.
Pros:
* Over the first few years in the sim, the game mechanics evolve a good bit, keeping you on your toes.
* It allows some fun, nostalgic combinations and amusing anecdotes.
* It's simple to pick up and doen't require spreadsheets/calculators to keep ahead of the curve.
Cons:
* The tutorial covers just the very basics. Some other (important) aspects are not explained and can cause repeated failure with no clue as to why. (Just fiddle with stuff until it works)
* Some aspects of the interface are clunky, though none are really deep enough for this to be a huge issue.
* Towards the 'end game' (if there is such a thing) it gets a bit repetitive, but it took me probably 8-10 hours to get to that point.
* There isn't much variety in music, so I turned that off after the first hour or so.
Liked the gameplay and the story. (Though main story was a bit short) Lots of replayability and mods available.

It's not very often that I go ahead and impulse buy games on Steam on full price. But in the case of Dead Age, something about it struck a chord with me so I took a chance on it. I don't regret my purchase for a minute. On the surface, it looks like your generic zombie survival game. But if you dig deep enough, you find a lot more.
There are two aspects to the game. First off, you manage your camp. There's no base building, or even taking care of specific buildings in this game. Managing your base is all about what jobs you assign to survivors. You can assign people to craft ammo, weapons, armor, or medical supplies, hunt for food or guard the base. The way the game is set up, every time you progress, one day passes, so you need to choose what you craft carefully, make sure your base is properly defended so you don't lose resources, and make sure you have all the proper resources stocked.
The effectiveness of these jobs are governed by a set of four skills. Survival improves ammo crafting and hunting, Crafts improves the making of guns and armor, Medicine improves crafting of medical supplies, and Cunning improves effectivesness as a guard. The higher the level in these skills, the better that person can do the job. But these also give you bonuses to your other stats such as defense and critical hits, which takes me to the other aspect of the game, which is the combat.
After you figure out what you're doing at the base, it's time to head out and scavenge for supplies. There's not really a map, but instead several locations to choose from, and times of day for each one. Primarly you'll explore a Highway at day or night, the Woods at day or night, and later on 'The City', either in the day or at night. The time of day and location determines what enemies you face, and also what supplies you'll find. Whether you need rations for food, leather clothing for crafting, or weapon materials for your new gun, you should choose your location well.
Your scavenging runs consist of travel through 20 'areas' in all locations. Each area is a randomly generated encounter with zombies. One very nice touch about this game is how they approached the zombies. You have so many types, such as zombified nuns, nurses, cheerleaders, soldiers, scientists, prisoners, and more. Each one can use different abilities, some are immune to certain attacks, and some can even heal and buff other zombies. After each area you can choose to progress or retreat, but regardless of what you do, when you're done, one day passes. In between each of the areas, you get random events, usually a chance to loot something, with an extra battle usually the result of a failure in investigating or unlocking something. Your various skills can have an impact on these random events as well.
Like the skills for the various job, combat has several trees as well. You have one for melee weapons, dedicated ones for pistols, shotguns, and assault rifles, one for healing and buffs, and one for engineering. The enginneering one is my favorite as it allows you to throw molotov cocktails and put bear traps down to damage anyone melee attacking you. As you increase these skills, you gain bonuses to associated attributes (strength for melee, perception for ranged, etc). You also gain additional skills, such as melee knockdown, shotgun spread fire, etc. You can easily specialize all your characters in this way.
The combat itself is Final Fantasy, JRPG-styled, in that it is turn based, and things usually resolve immediately once selected. In long stretches it can be a little tedious, but you can definately have some fun with it if you're smart. If you're well equipped, you can get to Area 20 and face a boss. You usually don't get anything special from the boss, experience aside, but being able to push all the way to the last area is always satisfying in my opinion.
One things that adds a lot of replay value is the rogue-lite elements it has. As you complete the achievements, such as "Kill X Enemies" or "Craft X Items", etc, you earn medals. When you finish the game, or more likely die, you can invest these medals into a special skill tree for your save file. You can give yourself extra bonuses this way, such as an upgraded starting weapon, more resources, higher skill ranks, and the ability to start off with different inventories and skill sets. At first, your only choice is for your main character to be a Student, with no specialites whatsoever. As you invest your medeals, you can start off as a soldier who specializes in Assault Rigles, a Bodyguard who specialises in Shotguns, an Engineer or a Medic (self-explanatory).
In addition, things happen different each time you play. For instance on my winning playthrough, one of the survivors named Jennifer joined me rather late, around the 25th day or day. When I started over after this, she was the first survivor to join. You may recruit Hank, and he'll ask you to find his wife, Lydia. You may find Lydia and she'll ask you to go find Hank. The survivor named Bill may wander into your camp or maybe you'll have to find him. In fact despite having 43 hours in as of this writing, consisting of two failed attempts and the one success, I still haven't encountered two of the survivors. There are also six endings, three failures and three successes (although I unlocked two of the successful endings at the same time).
All in all Dead Age is an awesome RPG, with lots of replay value and lots of fun. If there's anything bad, it's that the graphics are nothing special and the music, while catchy, is not memorable. But don't let this distract you from your experience. Pick it up and go create your own story and have a blast doing so.

Saurian... Where do I begin. This was a near-personal game to me as I connected with it so well. As you may have gathered from my profile picture alone, I love dinosaurs, and this was right up my alley.
Though in EA and very, very buggy as of the time of this review ( 30/11/2017) It still proved some great content and a realistic view into the life of Dakotaraptor. (More playables added soon: In order: Pachycephalosaurus, Triceratops, Tyrannosaurus rex then Ankylosaurus and Anzu)
Positives:
-Feels great, every minute movement and turn (Except Jumping, ocassionally) just feels amazing.
-Animation, Everything in this game is animated beautifully, the turns, jumps and idle just blend perfectly with the environment and background.
-Graphics, AMAZING! For an indie game with a relatively small team, Saurian looks F*cking gorgeous. Everything from the smallest leaf to the Tyrannosaurus rex had countless hours to make it perfect. Couple that with some pretty great lighting and it looks amazing on the higher end settings.
-Unique gameplay elements, I as of writing this, have only played Dakotaraptor, but even in that, it has elements like biting the throat for a faster kill, a risky but worthwhile hunting tactic, scents which, in a unique way, tell you so much about what's around, predator and prey, as well as not causing massive frame drops in other games it's featured in (The Isle, particularly, also pretty good game, if not grindy), and RPR (Raptor Prey Restraint). RPR is a basically a juvenile to super-adult way to pounce on an animal, pin them down or grapple onto them, and start eating them alive. While not unique to Saurian, Primal Carnage comes to mind, it's never been taken to this extreme before. It's a very difficult maneuver for animals larger or stronger then you, but if you perfect it you have a way to hunt basically anything within reason. There's also species based sight and hearing senses. Sight is a cone that in some animals, like Tyrannosaurus, lets them see large animals from almost literally across the map if it's flat terrain, but doesn't let large animals see smaller ones, and hearing, which is a radius aroudn the whole animal, also depending on what it is.
-AI Behavior, AI behavior is a very controverstial thing in Saurian. It's very buggy currently in game, but when it works, it WORKS! The animals behave and react very well to stimuli in the environment, but some pathing issues lead us to the negatives...
Negatives:
-AI Behavior, Two main issues arise when using the AI, Pathing issues caused by some map changes, making some animals (noticably your Dakotaraptor parents) run into trees or have general issues getting around, like getting stuck in water, and the hitboxes. Some animals (Paleosinawa v Dakotaraptor Subadult and Adult for instance) just seem not to be able to hunt certain animals. This can be very frustrating when dependant on your parents, and in some ways even affect you in your later gameplay.
-Jumping. Jumping as of now is VERY VEEEERY buggy. It's also very hard to predict where you're going to land, as for juveniles and hatchlings it's a tiny jump, but for subadults and Adults, you can suddenly leap across mountains. It can also lag out and do a double-jump, the first a tiny one where you land, then you basically get slingshotted forward, throwing you off.
-Frame Drops, While actively being optomised all the time, something about this game just kills frames. Keep in mind I only have a mid-tier rig but it can still run most things very well, but for some reason even on medium graphics I get major lag drops when in heavily forested areas and sometimes just randomly. This impacts your success rate in RPR, as well as many other things.
In conclusion, I do believe the game is good enough to get a recommend from me. Just prepare for some EA bugs and fps ♥♥♥♥♥torms from time to time.

TL/DR: Great game with some flaws. 9/10
Let me start off by saying that I am an absolute strategy game scrub, so this is from the perspective of a guy who has basically never played strategy games.
So, it was halloween sale, and I noticed an extra 30$ in my steam wallet that I just didnt know what to spend on. I came across XCOM 2 and decided to give it a try, knowing I could always refund it if I didn't enjoy it.
The first few hours were rough, and I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked even on easiest difficulty (yes, I'm bad, I know.)
I was on the brink of refunding it, but I decided to give it a second chance. That night, I played XCOM for 4 hours straight.
Even as a strategy game scrub, this game pulled me in. Its full of adrenaline fuelled moments, but it is as exciting as it is frustrating. I absolutely reccomend this game, but it does have some slight annoyances, or as some people might see them; flaws.
The gameplay is exhilarating and addicting, mixing turn based strategy combat with fully destructable environments, with an element of RNG thrown it. Its an absolute blast fighting your way through a horde of aliens, or infiltrating an alien stronghold. The main issue I have with this is the RNG. While it can be exciting and fun, it can also be extremely frustrating. The precentage to hit numbers sometimes seem off, like 95% hit shots missing way too often. However, it may just be that I'm extremely unlucky.
Another part of the game is the base management part, mainly the ship portion of the game. All of that is mechanically sound, and good, but pretty straightforward.
The main downside to this game, is it constantly forces you to act, not letting you take a more laid back approach. Without spoiling anything, there is essentially a constantly growing threat meter that you must keep in check. I have no idea what happens when the meter maxes out, but I assume it's bad.
The game's graphics look quite nice, and you can run it on max @ 1080p on most midrange rigs.
Overall, the gameplay is fun, but there are some flaws. However, do not let that discourage you from getting the game, as out of the few strategy games I have played, this one is by far the most fun.

The character development is very well made, you feel the pain of the characters, you care for them and you will remember them for your whole life. You are constantly in communication with the other members of your survivors group. You have the abillity to build firendships, make a enemies or trust people who will betray you.

Berseria is at least a little better than Zestiria was, but still not at all what the Tales series used to be.
The good:
- The battle system isn't a mess like it was in Zestiria.
- Character development and interactions are great, as with all Tales games.
- The story and characters are more interesting than recent titles.
The bad:
- You are constantly walking into cutscenes and talky bits with no warning, that you also can't pause.
- Treasure chests are pointless. They just give you the same generic equipment that enemies drop or random consumables.
- The equipment system is incredibly boring and gives you no sense of progression. Getting a higher rarity level of equipment doesn't mean you'll actually use it so you are stuck with "low level" equipment that's still better than stuff you get near the end of the game. They also expect you to grind materials for upgrading. Many of the weapons models are just recolors as well. Very lazy.
- Remember when you could earn actual costumes that you don't have to pay extra money for, that weren't just recolors or the same default outfit with just the jacket off? I do.
Play Vesperia, Abyss, or even Legendia if you want to see what an actual good Tales game looks like. It makes me sad that Tales, like so many other series nowadays that used to be great suffer from a lack of ambition and even take steps backwards.

The early game is very hard, then it gradually ramps down to just "hard" over the course of the campaign, but with frequent difficulty spikes to a point that it becomes frustrating. While the funny 95% = miss shenanigans still happen occasionally, they definitely have (or at least feel like they have) been toned down. The story is also stronger this time around and the variety of play much more interesting.
At the time of writing this, if you could only buy one XCOM game I'd say that it would have to be this one.

Freedom Cry is a bit of stand-alone DLC for AC4. You play as Adewale, your ship Quartermaster from AC4 turned Assassin. Who sets out on a quest of his own to liberate slaves in the Carribean.
Freedom Cry does a lot to try and be different than AC4. For starters the game is more stealth focused. For much of the game you're liberating slaves from plantations by eliminating their overseers. And the player gets rewarded with new tools, upgrades and weapons for freeing more slaves. However if the player caught they begin to murder the slaves before you can free them. This creates an incentive to play as stealthily as possible and as a result there's significantly less of a combat focus. This was clearly intentional and you tend to only use your blowgun and hidden blades.
As a result Freedom Cry feels significantly more like a stealth action game than any of the previous Assassin Creed games. And it's to it's credit. The only real gripes I have with it are the story is a bit lacking compared to AC4 and it doesn't take you that long to complete. It is priced pretty reasonably though and it's a blast to try and complete 100%.
I highly recommend Freedom Cry. It complements AC4 nicely, and its more focused stealth gameplay is a welcome change.

Realm of the Mad God is the first ever free to play Bullet Hell MMO. Team up with dozens of players and battle through the Realm of the Mad God, Oryx. With a retro 8-bit style, Realm is an evolution of traditional MMO gameplay. A dozen classes and hundreds of items to discover means Realm is easy to play but difficult to master. Players can jump in Realm for 5 minutes or stay online for hours because there is nothing to install or download.
Key Features
Action combat! No turn-based battles here, only skilled running and gunning.
Epic boss battles. Navigate demented waves of bullets from nasty demons.
True cooperative play. All experience is shared and you win by playing together.
Great 8-bit art: Retro styling straight from the 8-bit era.
Over a dozen unique character classes. Play as a powerful wizard, a clever mystic, a brawling warrior.
Loot! Hundreds of weapons, potions, armors, and rings.
PermaDeath. Dying well means something in Realm. Earn fame if you survive for long enough and kill enough monsters.
Sheep. The sheep say 'Baa.'

Not many games that i play make me want to go out and write a review, but for Blackwake, different story.
First game I played i was genuinly in awe... The sound of cannons in the distance, watching cannon balls wiz by from near misses and the utter chaos of trying to maintain the ship whilst in battles. The pure excitement of watching the nose of your ship steadily get closer to the enemy ship while you hold your sword waiting for that crunch of wood before boarding ..
Blackwake is the first game in a long time that makes players TALK! With out communication, you wont get to far. You must load cannons, repair damages done to the ship, pump water out of your hull, refill supplies, repair shredded sails, put out fires and more. All of this must be done while working with your captain, who will be shouting commands on which side to fire, what ammo type to use, priorty repairs and more.
Now being a captain... The joys and the horrors! If your going to be captain, you must have a mic, if you dont... prepare for mutiny! If you dont call out which side you are facing your ship for volley in time... your crew will miss or not fire at all. Ship is sinking fast? You need to tell your crew to leave cannons and focus on repairs and pump water. Everything you decide to do and the communication with your crew will result in victory or failure when captain, so lead carefully!
If you are looking for a game that heavily relies on teamwork and communication, then this will be the game for you. I highly recommend this game because of this, if your a lone wolf... not for you.

=> October/2016:
It's unbelievable that Capcom did a rootkit, potentially exposing everyone to massive security problems. They show no sense of responsibility. For me personally it's sad to be a fan of a franchise where its parent company and its employees seem irresponsible.
I confirmed myself that the 1-sided lag is real. While one player gets a smooth experience, the other get lots of rollbacks. This is really unfair. And most incompetent from the netcode creators. I don't see people stick playing a game with a bad online experience, which is unfortunate.
Let's cross fingers and hope that Capcom will fix the netcode, like the Mortal Kombat X creators did, where they improved their netcode.
=> September/2016:
This is probably my last update for a while. I tried to like this game, but I couldn't. The netcode is so garbage that ruins all the experience. The servers are garbage too. Also, this game favors mostly a extremely aggressive type of player, and this is not my kind of game. If you are a balanced or defensive player, this game is definitely not for you.
But this game is still in its infancy, perhaps it will get good someday. Probably I will be watching to see what happens.
=> August/2016:
Game has had some improvement, but still maintains flaws.
Improvements:
- Netcode has improved a bit, but still leaves to be desired. Only usable at 5 bar connections. Sometimes 5 bar connections give rollbacks and teleports, but they shouldn't happen (not all 5 bar connections are really 5 bar, the connection quality metering is not reliable).
- Matchmaking now do its job properly, matching with players close to your skill. But sometimes takes too much time to find players, and I don't think it's a lack of players problem.
- Game now has more content, enough to satisfy many people.
Flaws that persist:
- Unstable servers, often the battle results are not displayed properly. Although it seems the results are uploaded 90% of the time. Yes, that are times where results aren't computed.
- Input lag is still high (8 frames).
- Rage quitting is not punished properly yet and is still a problem.
- Keyboard and some sticks still aren't supported. Come on Capcom... seriously?
- Game still doesn't remember the battle request and training mode settings.
- Graphics has lots of clipping. Come on Capcom... seriously, again?
As a final note, the season pass has shown itself a terrible deal. It's not a real season pass (that should've given all the DLC), it gives roughly half of the available DLC for the season.
=> May/2016:
Sad that the game didn't get what it deserved. My cons list is bigger than before.
- Servers are still unstable, sometimes data isn't loaded.
- After further experimenting, found that netcode is garbage, even with 4 or 5 bar connections. I hate the rollbacks and teleports, along with the sound cuts. It's common on 5 bar connections to have animation frame skipping, which mess up the moves timing.
- Input lag is high.
- Rage quitting is still not properly punished.
- Keyboard and some sticks still aren't supported. That's some extreme lazyness on the board.
- Game still doesn't remember the battle request and training mode settings.
- Graphics has lots of clipping. Super ugly.
- Matchmaking is unoptimized, keeps matching with the same person and matches tiers/leagues that are too far away, for example Ultra Gold vs Silver. Also, still gives 1 bar connection opponents even if you chose 5 bar.
=> Feb/2016:
I was always a SF fan, since SF2. It's sad that this game hadn't the launch it deserved:
- Unstable servers
- Unreliable matchmaking (1 bar connections regardless of chosen settings)
- No keyboard support
- No support for all fighting sticks
- Game doesn't remember some settings (battle request and training mode)
- Rage quitting is not punished (with points withdrawal, for example)
Some of these alone make the game unplayable for a lot of people.
Make no mistake, though: this game is good. But what are nice graphics, awesome sound, interesting mechanics good for if you can't play the game properly? As for the netcode, it could be better: it is good at 4 or 5 bar connections, but not good below that.
Hope the game RISE UP to what it really deserves. Until then I can't recommend it, sadly.

I'm going to just throw this out there in the hopes that it helps someone else make an informed decision before buying this. Keep in mind that I started this early access a little late, so I have less to gripe about than most people.
I honestly am unsure if I recommend this game or not. At its core, I love it. It's amazing, and I was hooked right away on the character creation menu. I'm coming from hundreds of hours in Terraria, and I know this is a genre I love. And I did. I got to around 20 hours and realised the pacing was... off. I wanted to set up a super base on one of the many uninhabited planets scattered across the universe. I chose my planet, the blocks I wanted to use, and got to work. I built around 20 blocks and a singular door with all of my life savings. Every penny. I then understood that building was terribly imbalanced if I wanted to use anything other than wood and stone. This made me start following the Chucklefish Starbound blog, hoping that there would be news of changes that would fix a bunch of my concerns (and there were way more than just building prices.).
So I sat there. And watched, day after day, as tiny bits of graphical updates and furniture sets were added to the nightly build of the game. Not a single core mechanic in desperate need of a fix was changed, but tiny ambient animals were added in. The game still lags when there are too many light sources or NPCs, but at least plants now have to be watered instead of growing on their own. It just seems like the devs are using their time for little things that should be added in post-beta, while they neglect things that should be top of the priority list.
But I keep playing it. I can build pretty much anything if I spawn items in (not sure if that even counts as an accomplishment, but whatever), and I love it that you can spawn NPCs to populate the villages you construct (as opposed to Terraria's 20-ish NPC count). I see that the possibilities are endless, and the are infinite planets to build on. It keeps me busy, but it feels like that shouldn't be the only thing keeping me interested in a 15 dollar game, especially when Terraria is 10 dollars at maximum.
So as of this writing, even with a new Stable update around the corner, I suggest those who value their money steer clear. If you feel like blowing 15 bucks, go for it, it's probably a lot more worth it still than games that are much more expensive. I'll probably have to come back and revise this is the next few months (fingers crossed that the game actually changes in that time), but I wouldn't wait up for it.

This is basically a sort of space-invaders meets physics chaos type of game. You stand on top of buildings and drop poop on unsuspecting passersby. That might sound like it could get dull, and the game does have a lifespan, but there's a surprising amount to be discovered. There is a huge amount of different trick shots and animations to discover. Certain characters react to the poop differently and you can bounce the poop off of awnings. If you poop on a certain number of people, you unlock little perks, such as more people walking around, or alternate poop weapons. As you only have a finite number of poops per session, you have to replay the level a few times to unlock things. The alternate poop weapons are pretty powerful and allow you to really begin upping your score, but they sacrifice accuracy, so specific outcomes might be harder to predict. Even though you unlock things through the number of people you poop on, the true goal is to get the highest score you can. The fact that you have to replay the levels to achieve the number of people pooped on does lengthen the game, but it does make the early stages a bit slow, and the game truly hits its stride when you've got the maximum people walking around. That said, it is important to start slowly so you can learn each area, so it's not too bad of a progression.
The game's biggest asset is its charm. The graphical style is cute and hilarious. I love the weird, springy-haired guy who drops the poop, and the random citizens are equally memorable. I love the sound it makes when you poop. The visual style on the menus is clean and slick looking. The ragdoll physics add to the chaos in so many ways that even the developer might not have foreseen. One time I pooped on a guy and he ran out into the street and got hit by a car, only to have his body flung over the buildings. There were several moments where I had genuine, gut laughter from either the physics, the animations, or some secret thing that the game snuck into a level. It's crude stuff, but the game never feels mean-spirited and it lets you in on the joke. On that level, I definitely reccomend this game for its entertainment value.
The game's biggest failings are in its technical merits. The framerate is choppy and the game feels a bit unoptimized. My PC can max out most games at 60fps, so I should have no problem running a game like this. It does seem to smooth out after playing for a few rounds, but there's no reason for a game like this to lag. The other big issue is that there is not controller support. You have to aim with WASD and this feels a bit too clunky and imprecise to always get the exact shot I'm going for. Most of the time it's not too much of an issue, but it does hold the game back a bit. In a game like this where movement is part of the challenge, it would probably be too easy if you could aim with the mouse, but I think analogue stick movement would be the perfect middleground. I also think the camera on the New York level might benefit from being pulled out a bit, as when you try to aim into the extreme foreground, you can't see where you're actually aiming. The China level does rectify this however.
isn't perfect, but for 89 cents it is a funny and charming way to kill a few minutes. The game's biggest issues seem like they could easily be solved with a patch or two, and I hope the developer will keep working on this. It has issues, but I like it.
