Just for reference, this review is coming from someone who put 50 hours into Terraria.
I really want to love this game, but it lacks an element that makes you want to come back and play it. It lacks reward for the infinite grinding that you must do to progress, and it lacks the means to motivate you to take advantage of most of the game's features. I personally think that the spaceship is what ruins the game. It is extremely overpowered and needs to be a resource that the player has to work for to use. Why would I bother with any planets when I can just fly around infinitely? Planets are simply resource depots at this point in the game.
Motivation. That's what the game needs. Incentive and reward. The game needs to be meaningful and have reward for the toil of the players.
But not too much toil, or it becomes frustrating and pointless. Balance it out, and this game will be good. For this reason, I recommend picking it up some time when it goes on sale. It was good fun for the many hours that I put into it, and I feel that it will be a great game when (or if) it becomes fully fleshed out.

Sandbox racers are kind of rare, and Burnout Paradise is arguably the best one out there. It's pretty interesting in that you're not given much context when you start: you just pick your car and DRIVE. But soon you're introduced to events and missions in the world that, when completed, level up your license. Completing enough missions and leveling high enough unlocks new cars. Some of these cars can only be obtained by wrecking them in the open world. It's my favorite mechanic in the game, but it could be handled better. You can only wreck cars recieved from missions, but there are still a million NPC cars on the roads that have their own physics from the wreckable cars, like NOT BEING ABLE TO WRECK THEM. It's weird. The system would be improved upon if almost every car in the world was a unique, racing, destructable vehicle, and crashing them resulted in recieving the car.
Take yourself down to Paradise City and pick this up.

This is a game specifically designed for people that watched Hong Kong action movies in the 90s and 2000s.
It's also the most clever twist on the open-world genre I've seen since GTA3. It most games of that genre, you are free to cause chaos and mayhem all the time. (I'm talking every GTA, Just Cause, Prototype, Saint's Row, etc.) It makes the tone a bit strange, if you want to play anything other than a psychopathic killer. Kudos to Saint's Row for playing with that idea, and I sneer at Rockstar for the tone-deaf plot of GTA5.
Anyway, in Sleeping Dogs, you're an undercover cop. Thus you must simultaneously keep in with the Triad by committing appropriate violence and theft, while at the same time doing what you can to minimize civilian casualties and property damage. This, together with the best plot I've yet encountered in an open-world game, makes this the pick of the breed. It's even pretty good for a console port, with hi-resolution textures available for download, and the default keybindings are, for the most part, quite sensible.
This is a great game. You should play it.

I purchased this one on sale and got a very safisfying 80+ hours out of it!  (I don't normally use a lot of exclamation marks in my reviews, except ironically.  That one represented pure surprise.)
It's not brain surgery: the crafting is really simplistic and the combat is less strategic than, say, Final Fantasy 1.  It's riddled with typos.  The interface is strange and not particularly intuitive.
The plot seems to be that a zombie virus has trashed the USA, particularly ravaging the stripper community, judging by the number of naughty nurses and cheerleaders who've been infected.  The only people immune to zombie bites are the ones who speak english as a second language.  Probably a brain chemistry thing, I'm guessing.  They have to destroy wave upon wave of zombies who are polite enough to group up in threes at the most, and respect personal space by always keeping five paces between themselves and the un-infected.  Once the zombies are kind enough to shuffle off into the afterlife, they leave behind plausible gifts of cake, concrete and nicely-sorted packages of ammo.  As brain-eaters go, they're very civilized that way.
And yet, despite the silliness, I'll be damned if I could stop playing.  I ran through the game end-to-end four times to see the different completions.  Romanced three different NPC's.  Purposely tanked after 10 hours just to see what it was like to get nuked.  The graphics are gory and gorgeous at the same time.  One of the romance interests is really quite charming, if suicidally silly.
So turn off your brain and pick this game up.  The zombies would just eat it anyway.

This is an early access review.
Starbound is a game thats starts you out in a wrecked ship in the orbit of an unknown planet. Most of the ships systems are broken, but that can be fixed. You quickly begin exploring on the planet below, trying too find resources and special core shards that you need to repair your ship.
The best thing I have noticed in this game is the RNG. The game generates an infinite universe for you to explore, with a handy bookmarking tool so you can return to planets you liked. The monsters are formed from individual base creatures, and colored to match the environment they live in. Then, random limbs and abilities are added, like spider legs, poison breath, or even a multitude of eyes. I have found many a fish-puking armadillo, for example. The weapons that you cna find are also random, so you might get a machine pistol grenade launcher.

Combat is bad, story starts strong but doesn't go anywhere, Level-design is grindy. Skip this one, unless you are starved for a Tales Games.
This review will be aimed at those, allready familiar with Tales-Games, and will contain minor spoilers in the Story section.
:The gameplay dies a death of thousand cuts. You are battling in real-time, on a 3d map, as expected from the newer tales games. New are the so called "SOULS" which limit the amount of attacks you can do, and can be gained and lost through different actions and items. In addition every Character gets some form of special ability which consumes a SOUL but are stronger than normal attacks, and usually allow you to create longer combo-chains. Why should you care about your combo? The damage your characters deal is directly tied to the height of your combo-counter.
The idea is interesting in its core concept, but it has a really big flaw in it's execution: You either completely wipe the floor with your enemies, or you get reduced to hit and run tactics slowly grinding away at your enemies health bar.
You gain Souls by executing combos, and to execute combos you need souls. If your combo count is low, it's more likely that you'll get stunned by an enemy, which in turn will reduce your SOULS and the ability to do combos.
There are some mechanics in place to mitigate this effect, but they will be handed to you fairly late in the game, and they consume BG, which - you guessed it - can be gained by performing attacks with SOULS.
During Boss battles this effect becomes even more severe, as most bosses have some form of hard to dodge attack, that reduces your SOULS.
If this was the only problem of the game, it would have a mediocre battle system, but saddly it isn't.
The controll Scheme seemingly aims to streamline the usual button-mashing battle style that Tales Games are known for. Allowing you to customize pre-set combos to each button, and changing the attack according to which place in the combo you have reached. You can transition seemlessly between each combo, at any point, in theory allowing you to map up to 4 x 4 atacks (4 buttons with four stages for each combo), as well as some non-combo commands.
In practice this controll scheme is just plain counterintuitive. Instead of knowing which attack is assigned to which button, you have to constantly keep track, of exactly where in your combo your are at the moment, to know which atack will be executed by each button press. On top of that, it actually reduced the amount of atacks and abilities you can bind, when compared to the classical tales system (4 buttons + 4x4 button and direction combos). Maybe this system could work, if it wouldn't add further "administrative overhead" to a system that allready hinged heavily on timing, blocking, and how you chained certain attacks.
The final nail in the coffin is the approach to enemy design. Every enemy deals large ammounts of damage, meaning you  largely rely on keeping your enemies staggered by piling on attacks.
Bosses are largely immune to beeing staggered.....
Entire sections had their mood completely ruined, because, what was supposed to be a climatic battle, devolved into a benny hill routine, a I ran away from the bosses "if I hit you once, you will spend the next 2 hours watching me as I stagger you to death"-attacks.
The developers still havn't quite understood that they don't have a overworld map anymore, and they approach their map design with the same design-philosophy as you would design classical JRPG-dungeons, meaning you are in for a marathon session of the less-than-stellar combat. There is little to distract you from the Slay-athon, as nearly all traces of puzzling have been eliminated from the game. Instead of puzzles you get a bunch of fancy buttons (runes, crystals, fancy chalices, ...), each with their own fancy animation, but with little to offer to actual gameplay.
The equipment system is not as absurdely cumbersome as in Zestiria, but you still will spend a unhealthy amount of time staring at your inventory, sorting through the long list of generic generated Loot. If you just thought about just equiping the weapon with the strongest attack value and selling the rest, say hello to the newly added "mastery" and crafting system. Now it's all but required that you learn to like your new job as "Senior Inventory Manager" if you want your weapons to do a decent amount of damage.
The lack of unique or even just interesting items also means that there is little worth to exploring. Gold chests, which - according to the game - contain unique high level loot, will reward your with the same generic items you just got from fighting a random enemy.
There are some non-required mini-games throughout the world, which are decently well implemented... which would be more impressive if they weren't the same kind of minigame that every JRPG since Final Fantasy I used.
Also there is a time-based side-mission - as in: Click the button. Wait 30 Minutes. Receive random reward which you can't influence in any meaningfull way.
If I didn't know better, I'd think that BAMCO played arround with the idea of micro-transactions, but they would never do that, would they now? *sarcasm end*
For those of you that like to play dress-up with their characters, the custom parts are locked behind a collectible currency... which lies pretty much everywhere and makes the world look like a sonic stage... and also respawns whenever you leave the area... and will be needed in such amounts that you will have to revisit a lot of areas...
You know, if one was of a more cynical nature than I am, one could assume that this has something to do with the custome-dlc that was released, but that would be all together to crass now, wouldn't it?
The story is damn shame, and might very well be the source of much of my vitriol concerning this game.

Lets get one thing straight, this game introduces a new kind of game mode which is actually quite refreshing. 4 teams? Genius.
The RPG element where you equip your character in between games is fun - you can either buy items in the shop when not in-game or you can find it during a game. Potions are also limited, which makes for strategic use.
However, there are a few minor problems with this game. And when i say minor, i actually mean this is pay2win or being massochistic till you actually make it.
Let me break it down.
There are 3 free heroes, the other 3 you can buy. The free heroes are far from bad, but the paid ones seem slightly better. Not a very big problem, because you can earn points to unlock said heroes. You earn points by winning or placing 2nd in a game.
Here is the reall kicker, there are different item sets; normal, special and legendary (or something like that). You can either buy them in the shop or find them during your games. The ones you'll really be looking for are the green ones, the legendary items. If you buy those in the shop, black gems instead of gold. (Black Gems are the equivalent of real-life money.) But even if you find something green, you have to transmute it, at the cost of your black gems, to keep it.
Green items are significantly better than other items. Not only give they better bonusses, but when you own a complete set, it'll unlock another skill.
As stated before, if you have what it takes, you can unlock everything for free. And if you have the time and patience, i'm sure you can do it. But. But, if you want to stand a chance to unlock everything, you'll need to end up being 1st or 2nd very very often.
If the games where balanced, this would actually be a fun challenge. But they're not - unless you and your team have legendary gear, you stand no chance of winning, because there's always another team that does.
And there it is, pay2win at its finest; deluding you into trying to do it all for free, only to frustrate you enough to give up and give in.

Below i have prepared a comprehensive early access video review for any scallywag, what be findin themselves adverse ta readin ARRRRRR!!!!
We need to begin with the obvious, this is an early access game and roughly 99.999% of what i type up in this review will change by the middle of next week... but in all honesty these devs update DAILY! All two of them, who don't even occupy the same country, who share their work over the interwebz... who kickstarted their game in the most humble of ways, who... (i'm actually making a point here) didn't rush their f#%$ing game to market for $39.99 or some nonsense like that. Nay my friends, NAY! Graphics: The game looks great, especially the water. The lighting is nice and the weather effects are quite good, the rain especially! The particle effects from cannon smoke to bits of wood and debris all look the part but the clothing and sails seem placeholder to me.

*Edit as of 3/31/2016*
Sf5 finally got its major update, giving us the shop, a new character, trials, some bug fixes and a few new features (bo3 in ranked, 8 slots in lobbies). There's still however, no mention of fixing the fps issues (which I "fixed" by upgrading to Windows 10...) or any other PC specific bugs, is still lacking single player content and still boasts the same f2p-like economic model (4€ for premium costumes, all released one month after release, Capcom definitely learnt something out of SFxT apparently).
The game is definitely in a better state than one month ago though, and is still a blast to play, but you shouldn't probably buy this at full retail price, especially if you were planning on playing it casually in single player.
The game in its current state is a massive disappointment. It is riddled with bugs and issues (it took me an hour and a half to get it "working"), and even then it suffers from frequent random framedrops despite the GPU/CPU being barely used.
Content is abysmal, no arcade mode, no trials, no VS against AI, story mode is ridiculously short, and the artworks used are very hit or miss, sometimes looking completely amateurish. A lot of the unlockable content is also locked from the game like a free-to-play would do (costumes and characters will cost a ridiculous amount of "in-game" money), which I find baffling for a fighting game that retails at full price, and the shop is not even available until march.
Now the gameplay itself is undeniably great, even despite the casualisation of the mechanics which I'm okay with, but the only thing the game offers is basically online VS, which doesn't even work properly as of now.
Hopefully the game will look better in a few months once it gets all of its functionalities and rid of its issues. Until then, the game is far from being worth its $60 pricetag

Not many games that i play make me want to go out and write a review, but for Blackwake, different story.
First game I played i was genuinly in awe... The sound of cannons in the distance, watching cannon balls wiz by from near misses and the utter chaos of trying to maintain the ship whilst in battles. The pure excitement of watching the nose of your ship steadily get closer to the enemy ship while you hold your sword waiting for that crunch of wood before boarding ..
Blackwake is the first game in a long time that makes players TALK! With out communication, you wont get to far. You must load cannons, repair damages done to the ship, pump water out of your hull, refill supplies, repair shredded sails, put out fires and more. All of this must be done while working with your captain, who will be shouting commands on which side to fire, what ammo type to use, priorty repairs and more.
Now being a captain... The joys and the horrors! If your going to be captain, you must have a mic, if you dont... prepare for mutiny! If you dont call out which side you are facing your ship for volley in time... your crew will miss or not fire at all. Ship is sinking fast? You need to tell your crew to leave cannons and focus on repairs and pump water. Everything you decide to do and the communication with your crew will result in victory or failure when captain, so lead carefully!
If you are looking for a game that heavily relies on teamwork and communication, then this will be the game for you. I highly recommend this game because of this, if your a lone wolf... not for you.

This is a game specifically designed for people that watched Hong Kong action movies in the 90s and 2000s.
It's also the most clever twist on the open-world genre I've seen since GTA3. It most games of that genre, you are free to cause chaos and mayhem all the time. (I'm talking every GTA, Just Cause, Prototype, Saint's Row, etc.) It makes the tone a bit strange, if you want to play anything other than a psychopathic killer. Kudos to Saint's Row for playing with that idea, and I sneer at Rockstar for the tone-deaf plot of GTA5.
Anyway, in Sleeping Dogs, you're an undercover cop. Thus you must simultaneously keep in with the Triad by committing appropriate violence and theft, while at the same time doing what you can to minimize civilian casualties and property damage. This, together with the best plot I've yet encountered in an open-world game, makes this the pick of the breed. It's even pretty good for a console port, with hi-resolution textures available for download, and the default keybindings are, for the most part, quite sensible.
This is a great game. You should play it.

This is what I refer to as a "time warp game".  I start playing before bed and find that suddenly it's getting light outside and my wife's alarm clock is going off.  On the same note, I find myself needing two meals for a single gaming session, and if my chair's ergonomics aren't good, I've screwed up my back again by the time I've rushed to the couch to pretend I've been sleeping all that time. If I wasn't self employed I'd be fired by now or forced to quit playing this game.  Not joking!!
Onto the game, then.  For the record, I've currently got 39.8 hours logged in Mad Games Tycoon.  Those hours were put in over the course of the last 9 days alone!  For background, previous to finding this game I played a similar one, Game Dev Tycoon, for a total of 124.2 hours. I've also played Game Corp DX for about 32 hours. I've enjoyed all of these game development tycoons, but if I had to choose only one, THIS game would win.
My draw to this game was seeing that I could build and furnish the offices.  I figured the game itself wouldn't be very good, but perhaps interesting and fun to mess around with for a while.  I was surprised!  It's actually a very good game!  Even after nearly 40 hours of playing, I'm finding entire facets to the game which I hadn't noticed.  The last one was being able to buy shares of other publishers or buy them up altogether.  I've read that once you do that, you can get residual income from them and even direct them to publish games exclusively for your own company's game console. This game has depth!
Pros:
- There are lots of facets to this game, areas you can get into or ignore... it's YOUR company!
--- Examples: (1) become a publisher if you want, or just use already established publishers. You can focus on publishing for other game development studios, taking a cut, or just publish your own stuff for more profit. (2) develop a game console and try to compete in that market, (3) get into MMOs and manage your own servers, (4) invest in other publishers and take a cut of their profits because you're a shareholder. Or buy them out completely and direct them to only publish games for YOUR console to gain more market share! [In my 39.8 hours of playing, between 2 different savegames I've got going, I haven't explored #2, #3 or #4 yet]
- Employees have the right amount of complexity. Not only in skills, but specializations (one genre and one feature/technology boost each, plus their skills)
- Game creation options are diverse with many options
- Building and room management is fun to try to perfect, and you figure out what's best by jumping in and playing.
- If you have two different game development rooms, you can set Room B to assist Room A. They combine into a bigger taskforce, but you can cancel support at any time to persue another sudden need without canceling the game since Room A can still hold onto that project.  Again, this game has depth!
- The background math and factors that affect everything are complex enough to keep the fight for prosperity interesting for a long time.  Once I started looking up ideal slider positions and topic/genre combos, it became easier to survive, but a little less fun.  I'll go back to not using references now that I'm doing pretty well.
-- speaking of references/guides, there's a built in system for figuring out how to better understand what you could have done better.  The Quality Assurance room, which unlocks after producing a game with 50+ bugs, allows you to generate game reports, which show if you got any slider to the ideal spot or the correct genre/subject.
Cons:
- The game allows you to block doorways with furniture, cram desks against other desks to where the staff realistically wouldn't be able to move, or would have to climb over desks to access their chair.  The staff simply *poofs* and teleports to where they need to be.  Possibly a pro because doing this will save walking time.  It's just a little unrealistic.
- Employees never go home or come to work. They permanently stay in the building once hired. There is no time-of-day in Mad Games Tycoon - just weeks which go by visually with an indicator showing 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4 dots, then resetting to 0, which would equal one week.  I guess that means there are 5 workdays per week, yet there are no weekends.
- No Steam Cloud Save. That's why I'm playing two savegames concurrently.  The 2nd is on a computer I take/leave at a friends house for gamenight each week.  I was disappointed I had to start a new game, but I had learned so much that it was quite nice to start again with all my gained knowledge.
- Game updates haven't happened for a while now. The last one was 7 months ago. Before that 5.5 months.  Maybe this is ok because according to outdated guides, when patches come they've added more depth/subjects/content, not just bug fixes.
In the end, this is a wonderful game with some meat to it.  It's addicting and you can lose yourself and all sense of time while playing it.  It's inexpensive at full price, and had I known how much I'd like it, I would have felt fine paying as much as... maybe $10 over full MSRP.  In other words, it's a bargain.  Grab it whether it's on sale or full price!
And... don't tell my wife I fake-sleep on the couch.  ;)

The time has come, I have finished the game in 63 hours in moderate/hard difficulty in a casual setting(did not grind for hours or made the game last longer by stalling...I simply followed the main story/few side quest and that's it), and I have to admit this game goes into my top 3 tales game, just above Abyss and just below Symphonia, let's talk about the main story and what I think about it before getting in to game mechanics/features
Spoilers ahead, will try to keep it at a minimum:
The premise of the Story is quite simple, a young girl (with long girl) has a grudge against her brother in law, and wants to kill him at all cost, no matter what she has to go through to achieve her goal, Velvet Crowe goes through an Adventure around the world searching for the man she wants to kill, Artorius Collbrande, the now head of the exorsists, who wishes to bring peace through "reason".
Our main protagonist turns out to be the antagonist of the story, as she is determined to kill the man who will give peace to the world, in her travels she meets various comrades, Malak Number two, Eizen, Magilou, Rokurou and Eleanor, EVERY SINGLE ♥♥♥♥ING CHARACTER MAKES SENSE...as in, the "characteristic" of this Tales game, which is: "RPG of Discovering Your Own Reasons to Live"
The story is simply amazing, the plot twists are on point, very...VERY few things were expected, the game keeps you at bay until your brain is ready to collapse, overall 9/10 because the story needed a better sense of how the "villains" walk into cities, but no biggie.
As for the mechanics and features of the game:
The battle system is very similar to Zestiria with some twist here and there, personally, I prefer the use of "basic attacks combo + arte chain + finisher" but the thing is that this improved battle system lead the player to freely choose and optimize the skill usage to turn the tide of battle to their favor, I loved it. 9/10 because it could use some more customization and save some buttons and it's hard to master at first.
The equipment mechanics were ♥♥♥♥ing awesome, exactly what I wanted in a tales game, I can't remember if Zestiria had it as well, but if it did, it sure made me re-live that moment, equipment give stats to your character, improving them as you see fit, there's defensive, offensive, disruptive and balanced equipment, beside that, they have a passive skill, that after fighting for a while, will permanently give that bonus to your character, which is PHENOMENAL for character growth and customization. 11/10
NPC interaction was good, then again, I don't care too much about the plebs, just talked to them until they went into that loop of always saying the same and left.
Skits....oh god the Skits....they are a small (no more than three minutes long conversation between the characters of the group) ALWAYS funny, this is something I think it's super Unique to the Tales of Franchise and gives a certain sense of "reality" to the game, since the character will obviously have their chats here and there as they travel, no different from other tales, this game's skits were phenomenal
Let's talk about feels now...this game is FILLED with feels...they are all over the place...sadly, since people new to the franchise won't know, this game is the prequel to Tales of Zestiria, around 100 or 200 years before the events of Zestiria, but it's one of those cases where you need to play the game that happens after, then the one that happens before, people will miss 90% of the feels if they don't play through Zestiria first.
Aaaaaand that's pretty much it, I loved every single second of the game and expect the franchise to keep growing and releasing tales games for PC, because never been too much of a console guy except for Nintendo stuff.

It can be hard to get gems that benefit your character, if you happen to be a class that deals physical damage, you'll probably get a million magic damage gems. Not only that, but you can't even buy other classes with the normal ingame currency anymore, instead you have to now use the premium currency. Enforcer: Police Crime Action is a good basic police simulator.  You are able to do some basic police stuff and you must take care of your player with food and comfort.  However, the game gets really old after a few hours of playing.  You are very limited with what you can do and the map is very unique.  When you enter a new section of the map, the game must load the new section as aposed to just continuing driving.  The bright side to this game is that it is compatiable with Mac users and it is the only realistic police simulator out there for Mac.  However, for PC users, I DO NOT recommend this game.  Instead, I recommend the LSPDFR mod for Grand Theft Auto V.  I know it is a bit pricey for the origional game, but trust me, it is a lot better then Enforcer.  I believe that Enforcer's price should be reduced to about $5.  However, the gameplay is not what makes me so angry.  It is the fact that the community wants to help the game by trying to give the developers ideas to make the game better, but the developers are not listening.  In fact, the developers have abandoned the game.  Everyone knows that this game has huge potential to become a major video game, but the developers have completly abandoned the game.  So do not try to give your ideas to the developers, because they do not care anymore.

Having been introduced to FPS games through Half-Life 2 when I was growing up, I imagined that its predecessor might also  provide another such welcome experience. Alas, it did not. It is not difficult to see what Half Life shares with its descendents, such  as the music, sound-effects, and the way levels change in terms of pace (Think Ravenholm from HL2 followed by the Antlions). But, the simple fact is, even playing on normal difficulty, I found myself getting gibbed more than I could count, and for no reason at all. Some levels were repetitive and quite tedious, to the point where I would either pull up a guide for help, or rework the entire level, something I cannot recall being forced to do in Half Life 2. The important thing is, Half Life isn't all bad, it's not; but it's flaws detract so much from it, that it makes the enjoyable points of the game much less enjoyable. God help whoever choses to play this+ Opposing Force+Blue Shift (Me). Overall Score: 7.5/10

For a game that is almost 2 years old now it feels like it is still in alpha. I tried Starbound when it initally came out but quickly gave up on it because it was so buggy. Coming back to it a year and a half later I figured it would be nice and polished by now.
Nope.
The drops are awful compared to crafting. The best drops for melee weapons has never been more than 60% of the damage of one I crafted. Same deal with armor, the stats are nowhere near as good on defense or energy as the set you can craft. It makes exploring for loot a huge let down. Mining for ore is strangely fun, but that's all the game turns out to be. The boss fights are awkward and clunky. The fourth boss one-shots me with every hit even with the new armor I just made.
A couple of suggestions to make this game better:
-More room in the ship (at least enough to put down all the crafting stations)
-Consolidate crafting stations. There is a lot of redundancy and it is confusing.
-General bug fixes! Examples:
--crafted something and it ate my materials but I didn't have the item
--Fuel is wonky, put in 60 and it gave me 59
--(can't think of more off the top of my head but I ran in to a lot of other little glitches while playing)
-More variance in armors and weapons, better drops in chests
-Ability to sell to merchants (or scrap for crafting mats/pixels)
-Make refining and cooking instant like the other crafting (I don't think anyone wants to watch it tick down from a 100 ore to 0 over the course of several minutes)
-Have pixels tranfer to your balance automatically after refining (and cooking end products go to your inventory, not have to loot it from the crafting menu)
-A coherant and easier multiplayer setting. I don't want to have to join a forum to find someone to play with. Can't we have a matchmaking system?
All in all I can see what they were trying to do with the game and it is a brilliant idea but the execution is too little too late. 4/10

I gotta say, Sleeping Dogs is a great game overall. It has great (optional) graphics, great gameplay, and a fluid combat system. Definitely in the top percentile.

Of course, not every game is perfect. One I had is pretty nit-picky. One car in particular, probably of the faster cars in the game, had handling problems.  Under full steering lock, the suspension would bottom out every quarter of a second or so and cause the car to jiggle and fail to turn. Another problem was the slightly sticky parkour and sprinting. Once the character starts sprinting, it's difficult to stop. While sprinting, turning is limited and world objects start to get into the way. The last thing are the guns, specifically the shotguns. The spread deviates up to 10' when the target is 20' away. They are truly Nuclearneo shotguns.
Otherwise, the game is absolutely wonderful with great gameplay and an excellent story (although I don't usually play games for 'story', so I can't really say). The time has come, I have finished the game in 63 hours in moderate/hard difficulty in a casual setting(did not grind for hours or made the game last longer by stalling...I simply followed the main story/few side quest and that's it), and I have to admit this game goes into my top 3 tales game, just above Abyss and just below Symphonia, let's talk about the main story and what I think about it before getting in to game mechanics/features
Spoilers ahead, will try to keep it at a minimum:
The premise of the Story is quite simple, a young girl (with long girl) has a grudge against her brother in law, and wants to kill him at all cost, no matter what she has to go through to achieve her goal, Velvet Crowe goes through an Adventure around the world searching for the man she wants to kill, Artorius Collbrande, the now head of the exorsists, who wishes to bring peace through "reason".
Our main protagonist turns out to be the antagonist of the story, as she is determined to kill the man who will give peace to the world, in her travels she meets various comrades, Malak Number two, Eizen, Magilou, Rokurou and Eleanor, EVERY SINGLE ♥♥♥♥ING CHARACTER MAKES SENSE...as in, the "characteristic" of this Tales game, which is: "RPG of Discovering Your Own Reasons to Live"
The story is simply amazing, the plot twists are on point, very...VERY few things were expected, the game keeps you at bay until your brain is ready to collapse, overall 9/10 because the story needed a better sense of how the "villains" walk into cities, but no biggie.
As for the mechanics and features of the game:
The battle system is very similar to Zestiria with some twist here and there, personally, I prefer the use of "basic attacks combo + arte chain + finisher" but the thing is that this improved battle system lead the player to freely choose and optimize the skill usage to turn the tide of battle to their favor, I loved it. 9/10 because it could use some more customization and save some buttons and it's hard to master at first.
The equipment mechanics were ♥♥♥♥ing awesome, exactly what I wanted in a tales game, I can't remember if Zestiria had it as well, but if it did, it sure made me re-live that moment, equipment give stats to your character, improving them as you see fit, there's defensive, offensive, disruptive and balanced equipment, beside that, they have a passive skill, that after fighting for a while, will permanently give that bonus to your character, which is PHENOMENAL for character growth and customization. 11/10
NPC interaction was good, then again, I don't care too much about the plebs, just talked to them until they went into that loop of always saying the same and left.
Skits....oh god the Skits....they are a small (no more than three minutes long conversation between the characters of the group) ALWAYS funny, this is something I think it's super Unique to the Tales of Franchise and gives a certain sense of "reality" to the game, since the character will obviously have their chats here and there as they travel, no different from other tales, this game's skits were phenomenal
Let's talk about feels now...this game is FILLED with feels...they are all over the place...sadly, since people new to the franchise won't know, this game is the prequel to Tales of Zestiria, around 100 or 200 years before the events of Zestiria, but it's one of those cases where you need to play the game that happens after, then the one that happens before, people will miss 90% of the feels if they don't play through Zestiria first.
Aaaaaand that's pretty much it, I loved every single second of the game and expect the franchise to keep growing and releasing tales games for PC, because never been too much of a console guy except for Nintendo stuff.

Okay, the year of 2012 really disappointed me on a number of counts. I was feeling quite forlorn that the gaming industry was beginning its downfall and headed towards an influx of cookie cutter games, each with slightly "better graphics" or "one or two new weapons" or "better killstreaks" (You know what game I'm talking about). You know, it sells, so keep doing what sells, right? As horrible as that sounds. Well, to the point, Sleeping Dogs restored my faith. Square Enix really did an awesome job taking up this project when it got scrapped by the guys doing the True Crime series.
This game is like GTA except without so much of the random♥♥♥♥♥♥to do. It's a bit more serious, a bit more mature. The storyline was great - I'm not going to ruin any of it, but it was awesome albeit a bit too fast. It was a game I finished and I felt that I wanted more. The ending left me a little empty because it felt a little rushed, I mean, you could totally make a Sleeping Dogs 2 or something, definitely. Overall though, this game really, really made up for all the disappointments that year (yes, the whole year).
The gameplay is pretty fluid, the fighting can get repetitive after maybe four days straight playing, but it always keeps you on edge. It was very hard to put down. I never found myself bored and, even now, I'll start it up and complete a couple side missions. They really, really did a great job recreating the Hong Kong cityscape and atmosphere. You can't go into most of the buildings, but the world's so big that you won't even want to.
The ONLY thing I think I would've done to make this game better is tweak the story a little bit. Just near the end. Everything came together really quick. This could've been a full on, like, 60 hour game if they wanted to. And just... well, playing this game really beats a lot of the crap dramas you see on TV. THAT's how good it was. I beat the game and for a long time after, I felt really empty because nothing else really matched it. There was a sort of... "What's next?" And that gave this game the move from "good" and "great" to "outstanding".

For me, I can't understand why this game has such a high rating. Even after beating it, I felt nothing happened in the game at all. Unlike past Tales games, the goal is set for you at the very beginning of the game after the prologue and it keeps heading to that goal- past games have had arcs. For instance, with Vesperia it was getting the Aque Blastia and with Abyss, it was freeing Luke from his manor's constraints- the ending of those plot arcs in Ghasfarost and Akzeriuth led neatly into a plot that ended in a fake-out ending before you began the real final plot. I still feel more happened between the start of those games and their midpoint fake-out endings in Zaude and the Absorption Gate than happened in Berseria from the beginning to the final dungeon. The plot is, simply put, very linear and dull compared to past Tales games.
But that's just a small problem compared to how downright detestable the protagonist is. I find Velvet has no redeeming qualities until very late game. Any moment of kindness she displays is swiftly contradicted by her reasoning for saying or doing it or by what she says next (which is usually selfish or heartless if not both). In the prologue, she's an incredibly bland person. The game even CALLS her "plain" and "ordinary" later on. However post-time skip, she's got exactly one personality trait and because of it, she forces the aforementioned problem with the linear plot. By the time she gets a real personality outside revenge, the game is nearly over. They did a similar thing with Yuri from Vesperia but with Yuri, his vigilante schtik was temporary, did not drive the plot, and did not make up his entire character. Due to Velvet's personality, the group lacks any sense of companionship. That is, I do not feel any of them really like each other, apart from Laphicet towards the group (which is reciprocated with Eleanor), and between Eleanor and Rokurou (optionally with Rokurou, as many of their scenes and skits are in sidequests, but he is the one who saves her life in a plot scene, which is more than I can say for most anyone else in the party). I feel most of them are there out of convenience or obligation more than because they want to. Even Jade, Raven, and Zelos warmed up to everyone in the party and grew to genuinely care for them. Furthermore, I don't feel the characters go through much development. Magilou is at least mysterious enough that this isn't a bother.
Now, the smaller things. First off, the rather boring if not awful costumes you can get in-game. I get that DLC is a thing, but there's no reason why the best costumes you get in the game should be the ones they start with. I like the winter costumes for Eizen and Magilou, and I think Velvet's swimsuit (the in-game black one) is all right since it looks like a cute black dress, but frankly, I feel the Normin costumes should have been DLC and not make up the majority of the costumes you can earn. If you are going to go through the trouble of making costumes that change the music, and then allow you to turn the music off, then make different costumes for each music theme, as was done with Eleanor. Second, I like the costume and cooking skits, why have I not seen one yet? I love skits. Third, the menu screen is really boring-looking since it's overly simplistic and also doesn't work with my controller for some reason, I have to use my keyboard. Relating to the costumes, some of the attachments are really disappointing. The right-swept bangs (or either of them really) stick out if only because THAT was the attachment for the Tales of the Abyss reference island, Cheagle Island, in the Expedition game. I was thoroughly excited to finally get the location, and THAT is my prize? Think of the people who really love that game and ask yourself if that's the prize they'd want, when you can get a Repede balloon and a Lloyd doll from the Vesperia and Symphonia islands. The reference islands should all have given you a reference item, not some miscellanious items like animal ears or swimsuit costumes. Those should have been findable in chests in optional dungeons, or been another reward for clearing the Class 4 islands.
Another little thing is that sometimes, the skit subtitles do NOT match with the spoken dialogue, especially in the skits at the end of the game you see doing sidequests (the quest regarding the 29th Code Red Daemon stand out in my memory as being littered with errors).
I also didn't like how most of the Code Red prizes are irrelevant unless you play on a higher mode nor do I like how the higher modes were constructed- the reason I refused to do them was the lack of EXP earned, which the game already doesn't give out a lot of EXP to work with. I hate how "level grinding" is equated with "making games harder". With the aforementioned Code Red enemies giving you absolutely no experience at all (not counting the ones, like the Weighty Witch, who have support in the battle). I also find the second Mystic Artes hard to trigger, since they trigger exactly the same way as the first ones, and the acquesition of gage points to be difficult. Speaking of, I prefer the HP/TP method, not the HP/Soul method. I constantly run out of Souls because it's the only way to attack, since normal attacks have been removed and everything is an arte now. The battle system overall is a little complicated as is weapon enhancement and the Random Skills. There's so much to do in both departments that I can't even be bothered with trying to get Item Collector.
That aside, I didn't totally HATE the game, exactly. But it sure as hell wasn't worth what I paid for it.
I like that costumes are totally separete from the titles now, and that each title does something and tells you what it does.  I like Eleanor, Eizen, Magilou, and Rokurou as characters. I like how many recipes there are. I like most of the characters that aren't in the party. The game itself is gorgeous to look at, and some of the battles are legitimately hard. I liked the references to older Tales games you can find all over the place. I liked some of the sidequests. And I like the way the AIs work in battle. Sometimes they do use resisted artes, but they're not spamming high-cost attacks for nothing and the two spellcasters stay the hell out of battle like good spellcasters. On the downside of things, though (but this isn't much of a complaint), I haven't used Rokurou or Laphicet in battle much at all because Magilou, Eizen, and Eleanor can all heal and have better healing artes than Laphicet. I don't mind not using them, but I do wish I had a reason to. I really like the cutscenes that play after you approach the final boss all the way through the end of the game, but it doesn't fix the game.
Oh, the best part of the game is the AI. They're really competent and actually follow the Strategy settings ridiculously well. I can leave the entire team on Auto and watch the battle while I eat, and nobody in the party dies. Magilou and Laphicet, your mages, stay out of the way and don't use their melee attacks (unlike past mages, where to stop them using their melee moves you'd have to turn them off). Honestly, the only problem is they don't abide by what an enemy is weak to/resists.
I cannot recommend Tales of Berseria unless everything I just talked about doesn't sound a complaint to you. If you want to play a Tales game here on Steam, pick up Symphonia. If you want my overall opinion on the Tales series, check out Abyss, which is my all-time favourite game, period.
I mean, you can see how many hours I've clocked in. I played the entire thing, did sidequests, and I just didn't enjoy it.
Oh, I nearly forgot. One last complaint- every damn enemy drops weapons, so your inventory fills up fast. I wish there were a way to turn that off. NEVER do that again, Namco-Bandai. Only make special enemies drop weapons. This drives me up the wall, since it means I have to spend untold hours it eh shop clearing out my inventory.

I love this game, don't get me wrong, and if you are a bit masochistic, you will love it, too. Without the DLCs the game is absolutely solid! Seriously, don't buy any DLC and you will enjoy the f... out of the game.
BUT, given its long release time already, there are still some bugs I canot just look over and that should have been fixed years ago:
- Stun Troopers attacking through solid walls (them being outside a building, you inside on the other side of the solid wall with no line of sight) or uphill one floor (They must have 3 meter stun weapons)
- Line of sight going through solid walls for the enemy, especially when it comes to different floor levels.
- Enemies taking pot shots at you from the utmost line of sight range and hitting (obviously, otherwise they wouldn't have taken the shot .. AI knows the result before the attempt, I guess), while others, 5 meters away from you will go into ridiculously positioned overwatch stances, where they are sitting ducks.
- Rulers from the DLC being ridiculously overpowered. They can wipe out your whole team with no effort, since they can take an action after each(!) of your actions. A simple reload on your side will cause him to wreak havoc in your ranks. Especially annoying, if he decides to strangle one of your team. Everytime he strangles a team mate, he deals instant damage. If you waste a shot on him to free your strangled mate, he will use his reaction to strangle him again, dealing damage. Try to free him like this with several team members and it will result in his death in the same turn.
All these bugs make playing harder difficulties in iron man mode a mess. Might as well throw a dice at the beginning, before you even start: Result of 6 means you make it through the campaign, 2-5 you don't.

Honestly, this is the WORST MOBA I've ever played and I've played pretty much all of them.  Imagine League of Legends Dominion mode mixed with Diablo 3.  Items are PERMANENT and the matchmaking does not seem to take that into account.  Meaning, if you're starting out in this game, you have close to zero chance of winning since half the other players start with more health and damage than you'll have at max level.
To make matters worse, there are also four consumables that you basically must have to have any chance at victory and the best consumables are for a paid currency.  You do get a small amount of this currency after the game, but unless you placed first (highly unlikely until you've shelled out 500$ or played for 1000 hours) you won't get enough to refresh your consumables. This makes the game go in a horrible spiral of "Lost a match. Either I lose the next one too or drop 5$ for a chance to win. Lost again." and so on.
This game is clearly a money grabbing scheme shrouded with the concept of "well you 'can' just play the game forever and get everything." but that's not realistic when it's nigh impossible to actually contribute to a win without dropping a lot of money.

While I cannot atest to the quality of Assassin's Creed IV, III was an utter mess. Glitchy, buggy, time-wasting and otherwise lost in the sea of AAA checkpoints just to make a sale; Connor deserved a much better game surrounding his wonderfully built world.
This seemed to be the trend with a lot of Ubisoft titles as of late. Stuff the world full of as much nonsense as you can and hope the players get distracted to ignore the flaws. It didn't work in the case of Assassin's Creed III and I have no idea how much superfluous extras there are in IV. With this standalone campaign, though, Ubisoft have finally nailed a perfect balance of missions and pacing.
No longer do you need to trek through mindless set ups and investigations to get to the good stuff. Freedom Cry almost sticks to action 100% of the time, but you do get some small diversions to break up the monotony. Forcing side missions on the player isn't that nice, but the missions are given some extra weight due to the setting and narrative.
As for the plotline, I can't say that I was impressed. I love the idea of a former slave joining the creed and exacting vengeance, but I think IV had more setup for main character, Adewale, that is missing from this. Even the beginning of the game seems like it was already underway before my intervention.
The game also does succumb to being a bit scripted. One of the later missions on a sinking ship would have been exhilerating if there were some actual danger involved. Instead, you simply can wait around until the game tells you to leave and be done with it. Smoke and mirrors was the name of the game with III and I'm sad to see it still being utilized here.
There are also the occassional problems with pathfinding while running and combat getting lost with the camera. I often couldn't tell what I was doing or had a hard time stopping myself from performing one action and ended up failing missions. It can be aggravating when you fail due to no fault of your own, but the extremely generous checkpoints make nearly every mistake moot.
The game is also exceptionally easy. I messed up in a few parts with naval battles, but that was mostly because of my lack of experience with them (I know IV is based around naval encounters). The ship mechanics are vastly improved from III and are actually quite enjoyable. I wouldn't mind getting into more of them.
So overall, Freedom Cry is a nice little diversion from the normal Assassin's Creed experience. It's short length makes it great to plow through in one sitting. It's also a lot more consistent in quality and mission structure than III could ever hope to be.
While it may feel a little undercooked, it still rings true as a beacon of fresh air within this franchise. Hopefully Ubisoft realizes that jamming your game with extraneous missions isn't the best way to garner value for your title.

Sure, I ragged on the graphics and the fact that there can be entire episodes where there is barely any gameplay in this so called game and yeah, sometimes it feels crowbared in just for the sake of having it. Then again that is hardly what we are here for. Rather than being a typical, old school point and click adventure, The Walking Dead is, above all, an interactive drama where the story takes centre stage above all else and the players main involvement is to be the voice of reason, choosing the right thing for the main character to say, or not depending on how you feel. Ultimately, this turns out to be the right level of interactivity given that The Walking Dead aims for a more realistic depiction of a zombie apocalypse where you spend more time divvying up rations than solving convoluted puzzles and this ends up being more immersive than it sounds, especially when everyone has genuinely good reasons for being fed but there isn’t nearly enough to go around. Although the ending is typically more or less the same irrelevant of what choices you took during the game we’re not here for the outcome, we’re here for the ride and man does this game give us one. With characters as well developed as they are and decisions that you question yourself about for days after, of course I’m going to get absorbed. Just do me a favour and never hand me an axe...

This game devoured my weekend. I'm normally in bed by 10:30 and this keep me up until 4am without noticing - it's been years since that has happened.
If you've ever played one of the game develeopment tycoon-type games and wished it were deeper, well this what you were wanting. If you're new to tycoon games, this game allows you to play as shallow as you'd like, and want to do more each play through. I spent hours just doing the reseach and development tasks for other companies, and then learned how to make my own successful game. I've started several new games to learn the other aspects like production and mastering my own games through quality control. There is still so much I haven't even started to explore, like actually producing my own games, making my own consoles, and managing training schedules feels like its own game.
The menu navigation does leave a bit to be desired. You have to get used to flipping through lots of windows and memorizing names and jobs. The group management feature is something you'll need to master, I feel, before you can really enjoy the game and maximize your team's potential. I keep a little notepad beside me, and rename everyone to better help me remember where they should be as I shift everyone around to fill in jobs during training. You can also just hire, and fire, but I really wanted to train my techs as high as I could, and it's paid off.

I’m four and a half hours into XCOM 2, and that’s where I’m calling it quits. I’ve just had my entire squad wiped three missions in a row and there’s now no point continuing. I was playing on ‘Easy’.
I enjoyed the original XCOM and I enjoyed 2012’s XCOM Enemy Unknown, but this is different beast. It’s much, much too hard to actually be enjoyable or entertaining.

I promised myself that I wouldn’t save-scum in this game, I’d play it and see how it goes and that would be my story. But it’s unplayable that way. Reloading a save-game every time one of your soldiers misses a shot or takes damage is the only way to successfully play the game. It feels like the developers are using reloading a save as a crutch so they don’t have to actually balance the difficulty.
We all know the least fun game mechanic is time-pressure and this game is fundamentally based on it. The aliens are working on a secret project and you have to stop them before they complete it. Time-pressure. You start a mission and you have a limited number of turns to complete your objective. Time-pressure. You have to rescue six civilians, they’re on the other side of the map clustered around the enemies who will massacre two or three a turn. Time-pressure.
Even when you aren’t under time-pressure the game heavily stacks the odds against you.
The UI between missions is unintelligible and could use a tutorial of its own.
I have no resources, I don’t know how to get more. I’ve barely done a handful of missions and I only have basic soldiers with low health and assault rifles, but I’m fighting seemingly endless hordes of enemies.
I’m fighting against enemies with more health than my solders, enemies that have better weapons than my soldiers. I’m fighting against Sectoids that can mind control my soldiers and turn them against me, and who can resurrect enemies I’ve already killed. I’m fighting against big robots and snake men, I’m fighting against enemies than can kill, or render my soldiers unconscious with a single hit.
What am I fighting with? Four basic soldiers with assault rifles and tiny health bars. I haven’t had time to research anything better and even if I had I have no resources to buy or build anything with.
This is my rare and precious leisure time and this is supposed to be an entertainment product, but all it’s succeeded in doing is making me angry and unhappy and causing me to shout at my monitor, and I haven’t done that since I last quite Battlefield 1 a year ago.
I’d be happy if the ‘Hard’ difficulty level was pitched like this, because I would never play it to encounter the frustration. But when I choose ‘Easy’ I’m looking for story, some base management and some turn-based strategy, and that isn’t what I’ve got, and I really wish I could get my money back.
Some patches and new fighters will still come, but this is definitely the best Street Fighter since II.

Hy all :D First i want to quote another guy who got me into this game:
"A fun game, that is easy to get the hang of but has some nice depth and some dramatic moments to it. If you have even the remotest fondness for strategy RPGs or the zombie genre, it's a steal on sale."
So yeah since i am a Final Fantasy raised X-Com addict who loves Z-Movies and TV Shows i gave this a shot and i am not dissapointed so far.
This is a solid 5-10$ bucks game that has classic RPG Fights with ur 1-3 guys beating a set of 1-3 zombies sometimes in several waves. You can lvl ur survivors up in combat, crafting or lvl camp support skills like beeing a better guard to protect ur base or lvl up hunting so your guys get more food when going out for a hunt.
You have some cliche quests to solve like save this guy in zone 7 or collect 50 mats and repair a radio tower. While equipping ur main fighters and going out for zombie hunts, you (up to 3 ppl in ur PT) can order the remaining guys in ur base to make ammo, build weapons or armor, hunt for food, make medicines, etc.
You can equip each char with some slots head/body/hands/feet/legs- equip and melee/ranged weapon, ammo and technical ammo and first aid ammo.
The story is ok written and the "random events" make sense in most ways.
You can expect a solid ~10$ experience and upon ur first walktrough you will get rewarded with medals wich you can trade in to upgrade ur main chars stats in ur 2nd walktrough to have a slight headstart. The learning curve is allright - you can date some girls and even have a romance ending with them.
I sorta like the comic book design and drawings, but wish the DEVs would have used more unique char models and drawings.
You cant save the game since it autosaves each new beginning day. So if you dont have time to finish ur 20 zones long dungeon trip you have either leave PC on or you exit game and start the whole day over, wich is kinda meh ;/
What would make this game better in my opinion: More detailed animations in battles - not static camera angle in fights ( give us some zoom ins and zoom outs, the background really is nice done, so we should have a more indepth look in that to get a even better feel while burning zombies down with molotovs) - more unique char models and animations as well as potrait drawings - each zone should have its own soundtrack not just boss fights - can still finetune the balance in perks if resources are available :o 3 x shotgun pretty much lets you zerg trough zones and bosses ;/
General conclusion:
Buy it if you like old RPG elements and Zombie killing with some crafting/hunting for supplies. It is worth 5-10$ and will take some days to finish all achievments and endings. The drawings are nice, the game is clean so far for me, no bugs, no crashes. It has steam cards and achievements (thumbs up). Your man guy can date girls.
Bear in mind the animations are meh and the fighting will get grindy after a while - in late game when more experience with the game you want to try to get to zone 20 in each lvl when possible to beat the boss and get some rare lootz.
For me it was a steal, i enjoyed it but after getting the achievments and seeing all endings i doubt i will come back for a 2nd rush. Nice game tho, thanks for making it :D

Freedom Cry tells the story of Black Flag's Adéwalé, twenty years after the story of Edward Kenway, following Adéwalé in his journey through the West Indies Sea, where he ends up shipwrecked on the coast of Haiti. Making his way into Port-au-Prince he meets up with Bastienne Josèphe, the proprietor of a local brothel and a sympathiser to the Maroons, a faction of freedom fighters made up of liberated slaves. Soon afterwards Adéwalé gets caught up in the events and ends up teaming with the Maroons to free slaves from around the West Indies Sea. As emotional and personal the story is, its length demolishes almost everything the plot wants to uncover, as most missions will be over before you realize it, leaving details aside and focusing only on the main objectives, therefore taking away from the emotional impact the story could've had if we were presented with some background on the slaves and their masters which Adéwalé is supposed to fight blindly. Adéwalé's relationship with Bastienne Josèphe is one of the few things that stands out strong throughout the six hour adventure, as you will find out more about her intentions from one visit to the next one, and by the end of the story form a bond with her that you could only wish would continue for a few more hours.
Being an extension to Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, Freedom Cry plays exactly the same, with a few interesting things added for the best, and a lot of amazing features present in the original game removed for the worst. This is still an open world game, so you can use your ship to travel from one location to another just like you did in Black Flag, but not only is the game limited to the West Indies Sea which is a pretty small portion of the Caribbean, but at the same time that portion feels empty in a way that Black Flag never did, even with its enormous map. There are only three main islands where the main plot will take you and maybe five more where you can find a chest or a secret, but for the most part the seas feel empty, and even in those main islands aside from the objective where the mission takes you and the slave liberation missions there is nothing else to do, something that feels weird to begin with for an Assassin's Creed game. On the bright side, the Blunderbuss and Adéwalé's machete are some great new tools to play around with, at least in the main missions since that's the only occasion you'll get to use them properly.
Freedom Cry was built as an extension to Black Flag, so it uses the same engine and environment, which is only for the best since the original game was a beauty with vast seas, populated lands and unforgiving fleets. In this title, the seas are still there in all their beauty and so are the ships cruising them, but the difference comes when you set sail for land and realize there is nothing else to see there; unlike Black Flag, Freedom Cry has only a few island and even those look similar, as no matter which one you set foot on next, you'll still be greeted by the same slave plantation or empty beach.
With such great audio design and quality in Black Flag, it was impossible to screw it up this time, since most of it is reused in here, which isn't much of a problem since all the effects feel authentic in Adéwalé's story as well. There are a couple new tunes created for Freedom Cry exclusively and those find their spot in Adéwalé's story flawlessly, and thanks to some great voice acting performed by Tristan D. Lalla, Adéwalé's character feels even more authentic than it did before in Black Flag throughout Kenway's story.
Even though this can be purchased as a standalone experience, it is obviously just an extension to Black Flag, but even so playing an Assassin's Creed game where you can barely squeeze six hours of playtime if you're taking your time with the story, completing all the slave liberation missions and looking around for the few islands that hide a chest feels weird since Assassin's Creed was always about exploration and the things you can do on the side, things that are almost non-existent in Freedom Cry.
Freedom Cry wanted to tell a more personal story than the original Black Flag, but unfortunately the limited length of the story, as well as the empty environment in which it takes place makes it fall flawed as important and emotional events will be over before realizing it and for most parts without any explanation or background on Adéwalé's intentions.

For a game built on Flash by a single Russian guy over the course of two years, Intrusion 2 quite the product.
It plays like a crossover between Contra and Metal Slug.  There's not much of a story - you're basically some mercenary with a red scarf sent to a part-forest, part-tundra planet to shoot the crap outta everything, with no narration as to why.  But the old school games never did bother with such details, did they?  It's short (only 6 levels in total), and aside from the achievements you won't have much reason to replay it, but the experience is fun enough to deserve the purchase.  That's about my only complaint, because everything else is just minor gripes.
Each level throws you into over-the-top situations that would feel right at home in some anime or AAA-title setpiece. It's slightly more forgiving, though - there are no limited lives to worry about, no one-hit deaths, checkpoints, and you can save your progress.  It has it's tough spots, but nothing that feels unfair or too frustrating.  The game also has a physics engine, and it's put to good use.  One memorable moment has you traversing a series of floating pontoons over waters infested with large, hostile marine life, while also dealing with enemy soldiers.  Since the pontoons keep bouncing around in the water and react the weight of whatever's on them or any nearby explosions, it's possible to knock enemy guards into the water and see them get eaten up by the wildlife.  And while on land, the physics engine also applie to any crates, barrels, eplosive propane tanks, or uneven boulders lying around, meaning you can easily weaponize the environment in often goofy ways.
Just like in Metal Slug, there's vehicles to use, this time in the form of a couple of mechs to drive, including a giant wolf which you can mount and ride.  And yes, he even chews on enemy soldiers if you let him.

The enemies deserve some mention.  While the typical soldiers you'll be gunning down en-masse aren't anything special, the robotic foes are.  Many of them have limbs and weakspots which can be individually targeted, and will continue flailing around, trying to pursue you even if their legs/tentacles/arms/whatever have been entirely blown off.  The amount of persistence they show is notable as well - once these guys pop up, you'd best try and get rid of them, because they WILL chase you to the end of each level if allowed.
And the final boss?  Well let's just say it's got a reputation for being one of the longest, craziest and overall-awesome final boss fights in recent history for those who've beaten it.  Heck even the prior two boss fights are pretty damned good!
TL;DR?  If you're a fan of old-school sidescrolling shooters, Intrusion 2 is good enough to recommend grabbing even without a Steam Sale going on.

Considering the troubled development of Sleeping Dogs you might have expected it to come out the other end as a bit of a mess but, luckily, it mostly managed to avoid that. Instead, it turned out to be a solid open world action game with with a “good enough” crime drama story and some fun mechanics. My biggest gripes with it are that the camera can be wonky at times and the vehicle physics are...let's say, odd. Driving feels like it should be accompanied by the Benny Hill theme song as it all feels a bit sped up and jerky, although not so much that you can't have good control over vehicles once you get a feel for it. The hand-to-hand combat system isn't particularly complex, but it's probably the most robust of the open world games I've played and helps give it something somewhat unique in a genre that shares a lot of the same core concepts between titles.

The game, the mechanics, and the idea are top notch and are a blast to play. The execution however is dismal. Bugs, audio issues, crashes, terrible interfaces, lag during cutscenes, camera issues, etc -  arnt we past this, especially in a sequel which had the same problems?
You have a wonderful game here based on cover tactics and strategy and then you add timers (both in the tactical missions and in the ship-exploring world game) that remove any ability for you to use tactics and strategy. For example, the end game is on a timer, similar to the first XCom. So losing a man and retraining a rookie becomes extremely difficult.  So you just reoad over and over until RNGesus gives you a hand. But I feel like Im cheating - thats not fun. If its permadeath why does it almost end the game when I lose a man?
If a group of enemies in the fog of war catch you on your flank - reload. If you fail a hack and it gives the enemies a buff - reload. If you rush up to save a civilian and it turns into an alien and attacks you when you have no more turns left - reload. Is this a rogue-like or what?
Yes there are mods - Im just not sure why I need mods to fix the absolute most basic functions in this game.
And yet - I WANT to recommend this game because there is some really fun gameplay. But the bugginess and overall ♥♥♥♥♥♥ UI, crashes and all the other problems mean that I feel like we are being ripped off for a full price game. So I cannot recommend this lest I be contributing to accepting this unoptimized software as acceptable.
But, dont bug me because I have a game to reload.

If you're not in first. Get there.
If you're in first, stay there.
This game doesn't bother you with a clunky HUD and a speedometer, letting you know that you're traveling faster than everyone else, from last place. There's no rear-view mirror, blocking your view of what dangers might lie before you.

Race.
Race Faster.
Win.

TLDR: A sloppy and underwhelming DLC product that does a disservice to both it's subject matter and original game. Buy the base game, Assassins Creed 4: Black Flag, or Assassins Creed: Rogue.
The narrative feels rushed and unfocused, beginning and ending rather abruptly. It starts with your classic AC MacGuffin, then promptly forgets about it; Then touches on themes of slavery but begins to quickly move them to the backround, instead focusing too much of it's narrative on a cartographer mapping the Caribbean that happens to be in Port au Prince (The primary setting of this DLC.) This leads to far too many tail/eavesdrop missions, moreso some of the worst, most frustrating examples in any of the AC games to date. It relies too much on tightly scripted sequences that limit your mobility and/or abilities and mistakes tedium for engagement too often. The main story missions can be completed in under 4 hours.
The freeing of slaves is relegated mostly to narrative-devoid side activities, tied to unlocking upgraded weapons and other optional items, cheapening the poignancy to the point of repetitively farming a statistic. The repetition is not helped by the rapid respawn of prisoners; I could return to the same spot within two minutes to find new caged prisoners, new guards taking the exact same routes, the corpses of their predecessors still laying about.
The game is really at it's best when you are raiding plantations. You free the slaves of the plantation by killing guards. It's just nice having that chance to take it on in your own way, with your full set of skills and the space to use them instead of limiting them like a majority of the main missions. It's always the same objective, Kill 20 guards, and it feels like a wasted opportunity; It could have used more variety to keep it fresh, and without narrative it only serves as a distraction from the underwhelming storyline.
Sailing feels like an afterthought, with a very small map and only a handful of locations to explore, with many of those being little more than beaches with a chest or two on them. After all the sea shanties of AC4, it is very noticeable that Adewale's ship crew is generally silent; it would have been nice if there were a couple of new, theme appropriate songs for them to sing, or just a few of the old ones. There are no treasure maps to find, no forts to destroy, no side assassinations to undertake. Hunting and whaling are pointless as there's nothing to craft. I didn't even notice there were ship upgrades until the second playthrough, the ship's upgraded enough out of the gate to deal with the few ship-to-ship fights. It's also painfully obvious you're always sailing the Jackdaw, the recycled ship model from the main game (AC4 Black Flag.) The ship you're sailing and sinks out of the gate is identical, and then the next one you steal is EXACTLY THE SAME, right down to the decorations, even the three skulls hanging over captains quarters entrance.
The new items border on impractical: The blunderbuss is a shrapnel-spread shotgun that's just as likely to kill the slaves you're trying to free or your crew as you board other ships; The noise-making firecrackers can only be dropped right in front of you and the noise doesn't seem to have much distance. The Machete is a sword, just like any other AC game, albeit with some pretty sweet, brutal animations. The animations are sort of aesthetically flawed since they go on a little long in combos and tend to get cut off as you parry other enemies in groups.
As with other recent series entries, this one suffers from an inconsistent frame rate and animation/scripting bugs that mar it's presentation. I watched a hunter's ship sail up the side of an islands rocky peak and into the air before flipping back into the water. I was caught during tailing/eavesdrop missions because sometimes the target would get caught on something/someone and would do a quick spin on the spot, seeing in all directions at once for a second. Sometimes freeing slaves would spawn guards out of thin air (Maybe not a bug but it happened a lot, it was tedious and annoying.) The frame rate plummets noticeably at seemingly random intervals and occasionally assets will materialise in front of Adewale as he runs through the streets.
Adewale is a potentially interesting and charismatic character and I was hoping to get to know him a bit better, as well as explore a very dark aspect of colonialism that was largely glossed over in AC 3 and 4. Freedom Cry does little to add much dimension to it's protagonist, seems uncomfortable confronting the issues of it's own subject matter, and it's disappointing it failed to approach it with compelling narrative or engaging gameplay.

In short: Bastion is a story driven isometric action game. It mixes strategy and skill to great effect and is quite challenging if it is underestimated. Also, it includes the vocal performance of the highly underrated Logan Cunningham. Other suggestions for those who like this game would be the upcoming Hyperlight Drifter, Lunar Knigts on the DS, and the Boktai series on the GBA. Highly reccomended

Well, I just finished my first playthrough of the game and it excelled in every single thing that I expected from it... Except for one. I HATE the Avatar Project mechanic. Basically when you start the game you're in a constant struggle to not have the Ayy lmaos reach 12 squares on the Avatar project and throughout the game you keep sabotaging their facilities in order to counter them up to a point where you're literally forced to finish the game or else you lose.
I really hate this mechanic, because, unlike the previous game, I can't go ahead and just do missions for fun (even though they're repetitive that's fun for me, shooting down UFOs or getting other random missions y'know), BUT THE THING IS THAT I COULD POSTPONE THE FINAL MISSION TO END MY PLAYTHROUGH FOR WHEN I WANTED TO DO IT.
Doesn't apply to this game though, because when an Avatar Project Facility is created it gains 1 point, if you destroy it you remove the point which sounds alright... BUT, every month aliens have 3 bonuses against you, for example an UFO is hunting you or Enemies have bonus armor or... they instantly add a point or two to the Avatar Project.
You can counter these Dark Events, as they are called, but then you're left with the other two for the whole month, some can be pretty un-fun y'know. So you have to always counter the Bonus points for the Avatar Project and then destroy any facility that appears instantenously if you want to be able to postpone the last mission... AND YET THERE'S ANOTHER BUT.
As with all the RNG in the game, Dark Events have a chance to trigger themselves before you have ANY CHANCE to counter them, so you can basically say "GOD DAMN IT, I HAVE TO END THE GAME NOW OR ELSE I LOSE."
Except for this tidbit, I thoroughly enjoyed the game. Still prefer the previous one though.
