The Burnout series is the pinnacle of the racing game genre. Nothing tops flooring it through a crowded city at several hundred km/h then witnessing a huge crash in slow motion. Burnout Paradise improves upon the franchise in the sandbox like city of Paradise. The visuals are delicious, AI difficult enough to challenge but not to provoke ragequits. The unlockable cars steadily grow in awesomeness, speed, durability and drifting capability.
Rewarding and fun throughout, more so once you acquire a broader knowledge of all the intricacies and shortcuts of the city and highway layout.
The car handling is relatively simple and by this I mean actually drivable, unlike the absolutely abysmal steering of Test Drive Unlimited 2 or Grid.
Paradise is slightly atypical of a Burnout game, replacing set modes for a large world with challenges scattered throughout and an interesting new take on the crash system.
I would definitely recommend this for any racing game fan or car enthusiast.

重启的 xcom 系列到现在有两作加两个大 dlc，牛逼的地方在于他每一次迭代除了横向的内容扩充，都还有很清晰的思路在向更好玩的方向发展，同时能跟之前的系统完美的叠加起来。
xcom enemy unkown 作为系列重启的第一座，应该是定义了新时代的 3d 战棋应该怎么做，以后估计像疯兔这样借用 xcom 玩法的游戏应该还会有，因为这个实在做的太好了。掩体和高低差，可破坏的场景都利用到了 3d 化的优势，战斗系统和数值都很简单但有趣，加上枪枪枪的演出也很容易吸引人。
但 1 代里有一个很严重的问题就是游戏里最优的战术总是龟缩战术：游戏里有战争阴影，发现阴影中的敌人的话，对方会马上进行反应进行一次移动，所以比如在你回合最后一个人遇敌的话就很糟糕，敌人等于是可以免费移动一次然后再攻击；所以对于玩家最优的方式就是大部分人做 overwatch，然后最后一个人往前移动一点点，如果碰到敌人的话，overwatch 的人可以在敌人移动时马上进行攻击。这个是唯一正确的做法，但同时也是很无聊的一个玩法。
后来出的 dlc xcom enemy within 里就很明确的开始尝试解决这个问题，关卡里会有限时销毁的奖励，你需要在指定回合数内去拿到他。这样之前说的最优策略就不太对了，你需要多承担些风险才会有更高的回报。
到了 xcom 2 里面针对这个问题做的更激进，大部分关卡都增加了各种各样类型的计时器，如果回合内没有成功就算失败。这个的确很激进，但游戏也给了你对应的工具，比如很多任务开始的时候玩家小队全部是隐蔽状态，你可以保证第一轮遇敌总有优势。最后结果上，我个人感觉是更刺激了。
在最新出的 xcom 2 war of the chosen 里面，想要解决的问题应该是转到了差异化上。区别于日式战棋，xcom 里的士兵，装备都是平的，即个体之间数值几乎是一样的。之前有一些这方面的尝试，但这次应该是真的是认真的做了这一部分，游戏加了类似英雄单位的士兵，同时也对应的增加了英雄单位的敌人。还添加了特殊武器和装备；普通士兵在职业技能树之外会随机几个技能可以额外点出来，做了羁绊系统感情好的两个人一起出击会有额外技能。这些都是有很明确目的的做差异化。
总体来说，xcom2 加上现在 wotc 的 dlc 应该算是系统较为简单，但足够好玩的策略游戏了。

Was hoping for a contra-esque platformer shooter. This feels more like a low budget freshman attempt from a studio with good ideas but bad execution. The menus are finnicky to navigate with the controller. The aiming with the R analog stick is terrible and oversensitive, meaning you spend half your time trying to get your aim locked onto constant and fast moving targets. It also doesn't help that every enemy can shoot like 6 bullets in an arc at you and be able to anticipate where you go, and since the bullets are huge and all you can do is jump you automatically get hit. Enemies also happent to take about 10 bullets each just to kill 1, and these are the first enemies of the game. They also have wonky hitboxes, and sometimes hitting them doesn't count, and others can roll up or use moveable armor to block shots. Each shot does 1 hit of damage, and in the multiple fire acrs fighting multiple enemies at once you will lose more than 1 , and each health only replenishes 1 little sliver.
The graphics are very pixely and grainy, not looking aesthetically pleasing at all. The same annoying song plays the entire level. If you die at all, since theres very few checkpoints, you need to replay entire large chunks of the level, a lazy tactic done to inflate game length. The platforming is also bad, as your guy feels floaty and unweidly when jumping. Theres no grabbing onto ledges, and many times I feel through the edge of a platform, showing theres hitbox issues. The analog stick moves you, but it also makes you jump and is super finnicky with that, meaning many times you'll jump when you dont wan't to. But in other times, like climbing these annoying ripe ladders, it won't work and you have to use the directional buttons. There clearly is a lot of use of the physics, but it's sometimes more annoying than anything else. Ladders and objects get stuck. Many times it wouldn't let me push something. Other times a dead corpse would get stuck over ammo or a health pickup, or something would fall in the path. Speaking of paths, the levels have no flow or sense of direction, you just randomly fall, go left, go right, go up, and it just seems random and haphazard. Every gun uses ammo and runs out super quickly with how much health guys have and how hard to is to aim, meaning you have to go back to using the weak pistol.
I applaud them for their idea's but the bad physics, finnicky platforming, terrible aiming, bad enemy design, and lack of checkpoints forcing repetition take away what little fun there is to be had. Go buy any of the other actually good platform shooters.

Intrusion 2, developed by Aleksey Abramenko, is a shining example of what is possible when you harness the past with the technological capabilities of the present - doing so in an innovative way which builds upon that rock solid foundation with exciting new ideas and concepts in order to produce a winner.
This single-player side-scrolling platform shooter clearly takes a generous helping of inspiration from the Metal Slug franchise at first glance, both in gameplay & art style, yet does so in a creative manner which makes the whole experience feel so much more impressive than merely being yet another modern-day clone of a popular retro-game, which so many other developers are more than satisfied with doing. But in this particular one, you have an entire physics system in place which tremendously adds to the gameplay dynamic in ways that I never even dreamed possible for a 2D game...in effect unlocking a whole new dimension of limitless possibilities.
Clearly, much thought and consideration was wisely invested in the level design here, because at no point did it feel repetitive nor monotonous to me. Each & every segment of its several carefully crafted levels offered something compelling and unique as far as gameplay goes...and I soon found myself dangling from ropes, grappling, tumbling, nudging giant snowballs over my foes to crush them mercilessly, prancing around in powerful mech suits, riding atop a big bad wolf who also attacks nearby enemies on his very own...and it just goes on and on from there!
Essentially, the genius of it all is that the highly interactive environment is much like a character unto itself here in many ways, because you will be both battling against as well as manipulating it to your advantage while using all of your wits - and doing so in the midst of the traditional slew of both human & robotically enhanced type enemies you'll face (of which there are countless different types to engage with). And they come in dramatically varying sizes as well...including truly massive and epic boss battles that will leave you utterly breathless afterward.
Moving onto its storyline now, not surprisingly it is fairly basic for this type of retro side-scroller: a hostile military corporation conducting forbidden weapon research has taken over a reserve planet and it is your sole duty to conquer this threat. Not exactly deep, but then again you aren't playing this for any other reason than to cause maximum destruction, carnage, and mayhem with the vast assortment of weaponry at your disposal. Speaking of which, I was quite impressed by the gradual introduction of new weapon types as you progressed further into it...and mostly they are seized from your fallen enemies to be used against them. Now that's some sweet justice if you ask me.
One caveat to note here however: this is by no means an easy casual game...in fact it is quite challenging & hardcore in scope...and you'll invariably need to repeat many checkpoints again...and again...and again. This admittedly may frustrate some. But on the flipside of the coin, the sense of accomplishment to be had is equally as intense when you are finally able to properly memorize the enemy patterns and movements...as well as formulate the most optimal strategy for success. In fact, it's downright gratifying once you are able to overcome whatever it may be that is hellishly impeding your progress further into this game. Fortunately there exists 3 difficulty settings present to help you along.
Graphics are fairly on par with 90's arcade games from this genre, and are quite adequate overall. Not hugely impressive by any stretch, but they certainly get the job done, and are pretty much what you'd expect from an idie developer. Although I do feel that they could have had a slightly higher contrast with more vibrant & saturated colours. And on a related note, the character movements & animations could have been a bit faster, as well as being snappier with the controls, where sometimes it felt just a tad sluggish. These certainly aren't major issues, but for the sake of balancing my review I did wish to mention it.
Thankfully Intrusion 2 does include Steam achievements (but no trading cards) which will enhance its replayability to a nice degree, but even without them I could definitely see myself going back and testing out different strategies and approaches for certain situations. Its robust physics system allows for quite a lot of experimentation indeed!
Finally, there is no online co-op present, but fortunately the single-player campaign itself offers several hours of nitty gritty entertainment which will surely be enjoyed by those who are up for its challenge.
It's great to see games reinvent themselves in ways which lift them even higher in the modern era, and this is why I was so enthused about Intrusion 2. It brilliantly captures every single ounce of what made these classics so much darn fun, yet in a way which feels fresh and exciting since more magical ingredients were added in to the recipe...resulting in an even tastier experience. At its very reasonable price-point, I would recommend this gem in a heartbeat to those who are looking for a bit of nostalgia with a modern twist, because make no mistake about it, this one is heaps of fun all around. And from my vantage point, that is always the number one yardstick by which to measure how good a game truly is. So saddle up your inner wolf and go on a prowl for what this one has to offer with your guns'a'blazin!

Not only one of the best RPG's I've played in my life, but quite simply one of the best games I've played in many years.
Having never played a Tales game and never really thought myself much of a JRPG fan, I tried this game out on a whim as it seemed like a good way to pass some time, and after a few hours in, I couldn't stop myself from playing. I haven't finished the game yet but I feel I'm a decent way in now and I hope there is much more to come.
The gameplay is smooth and just feels incredible to play. The combat system is intuitive and contains a fair amount of depth, but is easy enough to understand that it is not overwhelming. I've played a majority of the game on Hard more thus far and that feels like the ideal mix of difficulty and enjoyment. It's not hard and unfair enough that it becomes frustrating, but it provides an adequate amount of challenge that forces you properly prepare and think before every encounter. It's a system that works incredibly well with the rest of the game and is one of many things I love about the game.
Graphically, the game is appealing to look at and there is a significant amount of variety and diversity between every area, every town, and every dungeon both stylistically and aethestically that nothing leaves a stale impression and there is a good amount of detail and care in every region that makes you want to see more of the world.
Pertaining to the story and plot of the game; I will say the story of the game is surprisingly dark, moreso than I was expecting; religion, fratricide, and murder are all prevalent themes throughout the game, it's not overdone that it becomes meaningless and edgy, at least not much, but it certainly gets you thinking from time to time. There are plenty of moments I've found myself completely enveloped in the events that happen throughout the game and plenty more times I've been completely shocked by various twists and turns as well.
However, I believe my favorite aspect of the game is the characters and dialogue. You have a total of six different main party members, each with significantly different backstories, personalities, and goals and they all present themselves extremely well throughout the game so far. There are times I've found myself enjoying their dialogues between each other moreso than any other part of the game.
The perfect mix of world-building, combat, characters, and graphics makes this a game you simply cannot pass up. I still have yet to finish the game, as previously stated, but I can tell this will likely be one of the, if not my favorite game, of this year. It has easily found itself in one of my favorite games of all time.

Tales of Berseria is the best Tales of game since Tales of Vesperia.
This review assumes you have some familiarity with the Tales of series.
Tales of Berseria isn't perfect but it still has one of the most memorable combinations of gameplay, plot, and characters.
Combat
Berseria's combat is very similar to Zestiria with a few changes. Most significant is that combat now has free motion as the default vs moving on lines towards or away from your anyway. This makes fighting slightly more technical. Adding to this is slightly more customization in setting your artes. Like Zestiria, you have a tree of artes but you're able to customize it and switch between branches. It leads to a very thoughtful and fluid combat system. As always, you unlock more artes as you level up.
All four face buttons now map to artes while shoulders control guarding and targetting. Since all arte buttons tie into the arte tree, this makes spell casting not as convenient as it once was. You receive an item that allows you to set artes to each face button from a guarding stance but this not being a default makes it hard to play characters with melee and magic options like Eizen from the get go. Furthermore this only provides four binds which isn't much compared to the library of spells some characters get.
Gone however, is Zestiria's fusion mechanic. Instead the game gives you six unique characters. Each character has Soul Gauge in place of Zestiria's SC. It works mostly the same except that your maximum Soul Gauge increases when you stun an enemy or deal them a status effect. Conversely, it drops if you're stunned or hit with a status effect. At 3 SG or higher, a character can spend a gauge on a Break Soul. These are powerful abilities that are different for every character. Velvet's Therion Arm grants her a stat boost based on what she attacks, a finishing arte at the end of her next full combo, armor until that finishing arte, but also drains her HP until that arte. Rokurou's increases his ability to deal out stuns. Eizen has him launch a fireball that picks up and heavily damaged downed enemies.
It creates an interesting push and pull of building gauge to give you longer combo ability and cashing it in for high damage potential or to avoid losing it to a stun. The one major con of this system is stuns feel random and baseless. I have no real idea when I'm going to stun something or get stunned. On normal difficulty, I had no issue dealing with higher level enemies but would get stunned frequently purely because they were higher level. This is honestly the game's biggest flaw.
With that in mind, I'd recommend playing this game at Intermediate. I'm guessing it's balanced towards that.
Blast Gauge also returns and is used for Mystic Artes and switching out for a benched character.
Gameplay
Berseria clearly uses Zestiria's engine but does away with a lot of the open world feel due to the setting. You travel through the world mostly by ship so open world would have felt odd. The world feels somewhere between Xillia and Zestiria. You travel between large towns, dungeons, and fields on foot in the Zestiria perspective in areas with a bit more to them than many of Xillia's areas. There's space to explore and look around but fields are mostly linear. Towns and dungeons are however large and sprawling.
Travel is generally slow and the game is in no rush to make it faster. You gain spendable items to fast travel but they're not made purchaseable for a while. You gain a runic hoverboard to speed up foot travel but not until roughly half way into the game. It honestly feels okay since the pacing of this does cut down on the tedium of backtracking in a reasonable timeframe. By the end of the game, you can effectively fast travel anywhere extremely fast.
Characters develop in the classic RPG fashion. You gain XP/Levels through fights and equip better equipment as you go. As you level you unlock more moves, making combat more interesting and varied. The equipment system in this game is a massive improvement over Zestiria's mess. It's a much simpler and easy to understand system. Equipment come with two stats they boost, a learnable skill, some passive skills unlocked by enhancing the equipment, and some random skills. The learnable skill is generally the focal point as it stays with your character. The enhancement skills determine what equipment you want to invest in. The random skills seperate equipment of the same namesake.
Dungeons have a bit more space and character to them. Most have unique puzzles and some are even challenging.
Sidequests require some hunting down but once started have their goals marked on the world map. They can be started by talking to people with a ! on the map. Finding them is often the challenge.
Plot
The setting of the plot is that of Zestiria but thousands of years in the past. Here seraphim are called malak and hellions are known as daemons. Berseria manages to do a lot more with the settings than Zestiria does. Zestiria in many ways serves to introduce the setting while Berseria really digs into it.
The characters are all strong and compliment each other well. The main character, Velvet, is a daemon bent on revenge. She has a range of emotion and is challenge throughout the story. Her supporting cast are all similarly great. From the honorable but battle crazy Rokurou, to the principled and worldly Eizen, and the mysterious yet charistmatic Magilou. Everyone contributes to the plot, has development, and is generally engaging. It's apparent from the get go that most of the cast aren't good people. It's a different take for a Tales game and they do a ton with it. They explore these damaged and flawed characters to great depth and use a lot of it as a statement on the setting.
The story itself is great though a bit of a slow starter. The intro has strong punchy moments but they're paced with lulls. It feels like a while before you really get into the game. Once you do the story proceeds pretty strongly. Like all Tales games, it features three story arcs. I won't go into further detail but I greatly enjoyed the story. I'd rate it second only to Tales of the Abyss.
The plot ties in pretty strongly with Zestiria. Playing it is not required but does enhance the experience greatly.
Sound
The sound direction for this game is pretty average. The music is never bad and never detracting but rarely augments anything. It has a bit more of a grunge/metal vibe to it than other games but still features heavy orchestral themes. Voice acting is incredibly strong (I played in English) and I was blown away by a great performance from the entire cast.
Conclusion
Berseria is the best Tales game since Vesperia. Its combat isn't perfect but it is above average and the correct difficulty may make everything feel right. To start, I don't think this is a BAD game per se. Just one that needs more polish and a little better execution in its mechanics. So, we'll start with the good:
- Gives you options in the beginning. Want to build a console right away? You can start researching it right away, which is something I sorely wished for in Game Dev Tycoon
- The ability to set things like what country your company is in and your genre focus in concrete terms.
- A market that seems more alive compared to Game Dev Tycoon. Your competitors are real and are releasing games, engines, consoles, etc.
- Marketing options, like bundling stuff with your games or selling to a market outside of your country
- Ability to build a very large company and take care of your own game production and publishing. This is in the literal sense of building a production line to produce your game, which I loved.
Now for the "bad", which is less making the game bad, and more like a fly in the lotion. Little things that are just irritating enough to keep the game from achieving its potential:
- Lack of instruction and direction. I'm not the hold your hand type, but it really gives you almost no direction after teaching you how to build a room, furnish, and start production on a very basic game. This means that later on in the game when you need to start worrying about things like customer support, you have no context or explanation on how to execute this effectively. This means there's a good chance that a new mechanic or aspect comes in when your company is 15 years old, and since you're completely unprepared, leaves you in a sink or swim scenario with the consequence of having to start over at the cost of several hours.
- No "credit" on older technologies. Want to start working on your first console 25 years in? Better start by researching  8-bit tech. Admittedly, I didn't touch the console aspect as much as I wanted for a reason I'll state next, but I didn't see any reason to require researching a tech from absolute scratch when its been around for two and a half decades.
- On the note of consoles, you have the option to research it right away...kinda. It's incredibly expensive, time-consuming, and the only way to even start is by taking out massive loans and try to work SOME kind of income while squeezing in research. Again, if there was SOME kind of way to learn some of these mechanics outside of "keep failing until you succeed" when it's often not clear what you did wrong.
- Countries have "genre bonuses". though the idea itself isn't bad, its execution is. Want to make primarily RPGs? Better set up shop in China. Why China instead of say... Japan, a country known for its RPGs? Dunno.
- Min-Maxing to the max. When you make a game, put in EVERYTHING when it comes to deciding if you should bundle merch. Releasing just a game with its instructions doesn't mathematically make sense. This leaves many aspects in the game a situation of being able to do things any way you want, but if you don't do it this one way you're wrong. A very similar thing exists for language. If you don't release in every available language every single time, you're mathematically wrong. It only increases your production costs dollar wise, without ever touching on things like needing more time, staff to translate, or where distribution is. Put another way, I develop a game in every language, but I live in China where Chinese is the overwhelming majority. But gotta make sure the German speakers in Germany can get your game. You don't indicate what percentage of games are in what language. And if it's supposed to be implied that your sending your foreign language games to their respective countries, the cost doesn't reflect what it actually takes to breach a foreign market that you've never touched before.
- Game development is nothing but guessing. You just try the sliders in different positions mostly at random until you hit the sweet spot for that genre. At that point it's just a matter of farming as many points as possible during development. Though this is also true for GDT, the difference is that in GDT, you got concrete feedback on what worked and what didn't. After two or three mediocre games in a given genre, you get a pretty good idea. With Mad Games Tycoon, you get almost no tangible feedback. The reviews will say something like "sound was awful," but you don't know if it's because you suddenly fell behind on tech, was the engine, the console choice, or your slider selection.
- The charicatures, art, and music look and sound like they were pirated from a generic click spam phone game
Please don't look at the bulk of the negative compared to the comments on the good. The "bad" aspects are usually localized to specific (but important) aspects, and are bulky because the bad only shows when there is context. If you catch this game on sale, get it. It has its moments, and if you find the one pattern that lets you do well in this game, you can enjoy a little bit of "Zen and the Art of Game Development on Rails." As a pilot game for a new indie company, it's not a bad attempt. I sincerely hope they take the criticisms from this attempt and apply that knowledge to their next game. They have real potential that does show in this game that could make a game shine with a little polish.

So, just figured i'd give a base review. So far i'm only five hours in.
Simply put, this PC port of Tales of Berseria is probably hands down the best PC port we've had of a Tales game to date. With true 60 FPS options, a generous amount of graphics options, and killer optimization, those of you who were teetering due to Zesteria's somewhat mixed release can rest easy: It's up to the quality standard that you're expecting.
For those of you concerned with the one censored scene, just go watch the uncensored cutscene, get it out of your system, and move on with your lives and enjoy the rest of the game for what it is.
But anyways, let's talk about the actual game:
Tales of Berseria is an RPG game, part of a long-standing series known as the *Tales Of:* In this Entry, we follow the story of a young woman named Velvet, whose kind-hearted demeanor was warped somewhere down the line and now her quest for revenge leads her into a myriad of people, and situations in order to attain her goals.
For those of you who are fans of RPG's, in even the most minute of forms: I highly recommend giving this game a shot. If this is your first JRPG, then there's a couple of things you should generally be aware of before rolling into these kind of games:
- The art style is highly focused on Anime-Esque character models.
- The emphasis is mostly on story > gameplay complexity
- You'll notice that some characters are 'Quirky' in some regards. This is pretty normal-faire for the *Tales Of* series.
- Generally, you'll want to play the game in it's native language.
I stress the last point, because generally the Japanese VA's tend to not only be better, but capture the essence of the character in a way that I feel like the creator's imagined them. I'm not saying that English VA's can't be good, but I feel like the Japanese VA market is a lot pickier, and as a result quality tends improve drastically.
----------------------
Visuals:
Easily gets a solid score here. Visuals look crisp, refreshing, and have that signature Tales look that we've come to love and enjoy in recent Tale's Titles. The character designs are all pretty interesting in some way or another. The area's i've wandered into so far have been visually impressive in some manner or another, albeit, some of the dungeon areas begin to feel a little "Same-ish" upon second thought.
You spend just about enough time in an area to grow familiar with it, only to say goodbye to it just as fast so a sense of permanence hasn't been felt yet so far in my five hours of game time. Still though, it's very pretty.
-----------
Combat:
Probably the funnest combat system in a Tales game to date. Break arts add an interesting flavor to combat, and all of the characters so far feel interesting to play in some margin. Combat is done in real-time, and the flow is especially nice in this one. AI has been drastically improved since the last game, and there's a plethora of tactical views/commands you can give to your party to make them stronger.
The basis is that your character's have a "soul" gauge, which acts as a stamina bar of sorts. You can get more "Soul" by either defeating enemies, stunning them, making them suffer a staus effect, or dodging perfectly (which makes a random 'Soul' spawn on the combat field that anyone can pick up.)
The combo systems also a lot easier to manage this time around. Instead of Zesteria's direction-based combat system, we instead get combos that are assigned to the four buttons, and are free to assign artes to them as we see fit. Generally, this means that you'll have combos that are dedicated to taking out a certain enemy type.
Artes have also seen a bit of a change. They're now divided into three types.
Enemies prefer swarm tactics, which makes sense for most of the creatures. It's up to you to both dodge/evade smartly, and counter-attack accordingly. The evasion window is a lot less generous than it was in past tales of games, so a bit more skill is required in this one.
Truthfully though, I highly recommend slamming that difficulty up to max immediately. Moderate felt a little too easy for me, as a tales veteran myself. Newcomers to the series might feel like the combat feels "Slow and dull" until you start getting Velvet's special ability. The other characters open up different playstyles, but I won't lie: For once, I'm pretty satisfied playing as the MC. Unlike Sorey, I find myself enjoying Velvet for her berserker-like playstyle.
--------
Music:
Battle music is good, area music seems to fit every area i've wandered into, so no real complaints. Haven't heard anything that's really stood out to me yet where i'm like: "Gotta find that on youtube later!" though.
No complaints, but not real compliments either on this front.
-----
Story:
So far? I'm only five hours in. What I've gotten out of it so far has me genuinely intrigued though. I feel like a child being lead at the moment, though. One moment it feels like Velvets in control, while the next i'm totally uncertain whose actually leading who.
Some things fall into convenience a little too well for my liking, but I'm definitely loving the grim undertone of the story so far. The small bits of comedy here and there are well-placed, and thankfully, not too overwhelming as to totally make you forget that you're a wanted Daemon, and that you essentially have a rag-tag group of similar people who are also in a situation that makes them have complications of their own.
That being said, the party characters are....a bit flat, admittedly. Maybe i'm at a point in the game where they just feel like odd tag-a-longs, but none of the characters minus Velvet feel very fleshed out at the moment. We'll see how much that improves with time.
--------------
Overall? Yeah, It's worth keeping, just based off this small bit of experience alone. It's been a thrill so far, and here's hoping it'll continue to be a thrill as I keep playing.

The Burnout series is the pinnacle of the racing game genre. Nothing tops flooring it through a crowded city at several hundred km/h then witnessing a huge crash in slow motion. Burnout Paradise improves upon the franchise in the sandbox like city of Paradise. The visuals are delicious, AI difficult enough to challenge but not to provoke ragequits. The unlockable cars steadily grow in awesomeness, speed, durability and drifting capability.
Rewarding and fun throughout, more so once you acquire a broader knowledge of all the intricacies and shortcuts of the city and highway layout.
The car handling is relatively simple and by this I mean actually drivable, unlike the absolutely abysmal steering of Test Drive Unlimited 2 or Grid.
Paradise is slightly atypical of a Burnout game, replacing set modes for a large world with challenges scattered throughout and an interesting new take on the crash system.
I would definitely recommend this for any racing game fan or car enthusiast.

Well, I just finished my first playthrough of the game and it excelled in every single thing that I expected from it... Except for one. I HATE the Avatar Project mechanic. Basically when you start the game you're in a constant struggle to not have the Ayy lmaos reach 12 squares on the Avatar project and throughout the game you keep sabotaging their facilities in order to counter them up to a point where you're literally forced to finish the game or else you lose.
I really hate this mechanic, because, unlike the previous game, I can't go ahead and just do missions for fun (even though they're repetitive that's fun for me, shooting down UFOs or getting other random missions y'know), BUT THE THING IS THAT I COULD POSTPONE THE FINAL MISSION TO END MY PLAYTHROUGH FOR WHEN I WANTED TO DO IT.
Doesn't apply to this game though, because when an Avatar Project Facility is created it gains 1 point, if you destroy it you remove the point which sounds alright... BUT, every month aliens have 3 bonuses against you, for example an UFO is hunting you or Enemies have bonus armor or... they instantly add a point or two to the Avatar Project.
You can counter these Dark Events, as they are called, but then you're left with the other two for the whole month, some can be pretty un-fun y'know. So you have to always counter the Bonus points for the Avatar Project and then destroy any facility that appears instantenously if you want to be able to postpone the last mission... AND YET THERE'S ANOTHER BUT.
As with all the RNG in the game, Dark Events have a chance to trigger themselves before you have ANY CHANCE to counter them, so you can basically say "GOD DAMN IT, I HAVE TO END THE GAME NOW OR ELSE I LOSE."
Except for this tidbit, I thoroughly enjoyed the game. Still prefer the previous one though.

重启的 xcom 系列到现在有两作加两个大 dlc，牛逼的地方在于他每一次迭代除了横向的内容扩充，都还有很清晰的思路在向更好玩的方向发展，同时能跟之前的系统完美的叠加起来。
xcom enemy unkown 作为系列重启的第一座，应该是定义了新时代的 3d 战棋应该怎么做，以后估计像疯兔这样借用 xcom 玩法的游戏应该还会有，因为这个实在做的太好了。掩体和高低差，可破坏的场景都利用到了 3d 化的优势，战斗系统和数值都很简单但有趣，加上枪枪枪的演出也很容易吸引人。
但 1 代里有一个很严重的问题就是游戏里最优的战术总是龟缩战术：游戏里有战争阴影，发现阴影中的敌人的话，对方会马上进行反应进行一次移动，所以比如在你回合最后一个人遇敌的话就很糟糕，敌人等于是可以免费移动一次然后再攻击；所以对于玩家最优的方式就是大部分人做 overwatch，然后最后一个人往前移动一点点，如果碰到敌人的话，overwatch 的人可以在敌人移动时马上进行攻击。这个是唯一正确的做法，但同时也是很无聊的一个玩法。
后来出的 dlc xcom enemy within 里就很明确的开始尝试解决这个问题，关卡里会有限时销毁的奖励，你需要在指定回合数内去拿到他。这样之前说的最优策略就不太对了，你需要多承担些风险才会有更高的回报。
到了 xcom 2 里面针对这个问题做的更激进，大部分关卡都增加了各种各样类型的计时器，如果回合内没有成功就算失败。这个的确很激进，但游戏也给了你对应的工具，比如很多任务开始的时候玩家小队全部是隐蔽状态，你可以保证第一轮遇敌总有优势。最后结果上，我个人感觉是更刺激了。
在最新出的 xcom 2 war of the chosen 里面，想要解决的问题应该是转到了差异化上。区别于日式战棋，xcom 里的士兵，装备都是平的，即个体之间数值几乎是一样的。之前有一些这方面的尝试，但这次应该是真的是认真的做了这一部分，游戏加了类似英雄单位的士兵，同时也对应的增加了英雄单位的敌人。还添加了特殊武器和装备；普通士兵在职业技能树之外会随机几个技能可以额外点出来，做了羁绊系统感情好的两个人一起出击会有额外技能。这些都是有很明确目的的做差异化。
总体来说，xcom2 加上现在 wotc 的 dlc 应该算是系统较为简单，但足够好玩的策略游戏了。

If you're a fan of the more modern video games and like strong mechanics and gameplay alongside a good story, you probably won't enjoy this game like I have. Half-Life isn't as timeless as many fans like to think it is, as the mechanics feel very clunky and the gameplay is pretty sub-par compared to newer generation games. But it's still an all-time favorite among fans since it did have a successful release with an original story, fast-paced gameplay, and all the cool quirks that came along with the whole idea of first person shooters.
Basically stated, Half Life was an 11/10 for its time, way beyond the extraordinary. But to today's standards, not so much.
Recommended for those who want to experience a strong backstory of Gordon Freeman and see why he's so badass, but for those who don't have the attention span to play through the archaic graphics and gameplay, just watch a playthrough video.

Hello everyone! I've got two dinos to adulthood and I have a few things that I would like to point out and maybe recommend the developers to fix or add to the game on the full release, but I would like to talk about the game a bit first. First of all, for the ones that are intrested into trying it out, if you love dinos and you want to control one on your own and survive, this is the game for you. You start out as a baby that is trying to survive by finding prey and avoiding being prey for the big ones. As you age, you get bigger and change! At the beginning, I have to admit I was confused. But as I died a few times I learned good ways to survive and strategies. Find water!! That's what you need most, and stay close to it. If you get lost, sometimes you can be running around and you won't find water. Near water there are birds you can catch and lizards also are plenty near the shores on certain spots. Now, to the actual review. I was so excited and happy to play this game, I really want to see this game fully out. Pros: -Graphics are really nice, the shadows mostly. Very accurate sunlight and moonlight interaction with the environment. -The growing stages are cool to see how you grow up to something stronger and larger! -Other dinos are really nicely designed and sometimes terrifying when you find them. -You have to actualy stalk, but sometimes you're algo stalked. In one time I looked around me and saw nothing when I went to drink water. I turned around a second later to see a T-Rex charging at me from nowhere and I had no idea! Cons: -Some graphical bugs make me sad but I bet most of it will be polished later on. I would like to point out some I would deffinately want improved: *On the Dakotaraptor some of the wing feathers when you see them from behind are just blocky and not refined as a shape. *When you walk through the foilage and bushes, it would be awsome if it moved out of your way. *Talking about foilage and bushes, the reeds and tree tops don't move at all either. Maybe make them move would improve the realistic experience. *The birds when they fly away sometimes it glitches weirdly and just turn all over and it does not look refined at all. *Maybe adding some night lights like fireflies here and there would also look very cool. -Some moves and actions are a bit wonky: *When you want to sit (C) it won't sit down immediately, sometimes it glitches and you have to press it a few times. *The jump action (Space) it's quite delayed which makes the jump on attack hard to calculate. *Sometimes when you get the meat out of the carcass it just rolls to the ground from your mouth and you have to get it again. -Adding more dinos. I know it is said there will be more to play as, but the issue is there should be more dino kinds just as fauna or prey/predators. Right now you only got T-Rexes, some small raptors, more Dakotaraptors, Pachycephalosaurus and Triceratops lurking around, oh and crocodiles (at least I did not find any other). Maybe adding more smaller hervibores and bigger predators to vary would be deffinately nicer. Right now the map is quite empty. -The targeting system is a bit strange too. When you press (E) it focuses your watch and you see hidden lizards or birds but when you run while using (E) it sometimes just goes away quicker, sometimes it won't even work properly. The blue highlight should stay on even if the prey is out of the foilage. (I got a few cases where the lizard ran out of the foilage to open space and using (E) it was not highlighted. ) Since some prey is small you can't really see it properly when you chase it down. Also, other dinos should be highlighted too since it only does highlight now the lizards and birds. -The scaring technique for Dakotaraptors should for my opinion remain as the one you use when on first stage where you spread the wings and tail feathers to intimidate as when you're older you just screech and kick the air. It feels a bit lame and not scary or intimidating at all. Just my opinion tho. -Maybe add the option to zoom in more to see more in detail your dino. It gets close but not close enough. -In one ocation I had to restart the game because when I went to drink water, my water bar just went down instead of rising up and no matter what I did it did not get back even tho it made the animation that I was drinking. -The eating secondary bar goes down quickly, but the first one goes a bit slower. Since you got nothing else to do right now than just wait for you to need water or food, maybe make it go down quicker? There was times when I was just sitting down doing virtualy nothing because you got not much to explore, no many dinos to see around. As mentioned before, right now it is kinda empty.. All of these are just from my point of view. I hope the developers take a look. See you again at the next update or full release.

Half-Life was a game released in 1998, developed and published by Valve Software, and published by Sierra Software as a retail publisher, and Valve Software as a digital publisher. It was Valve's debut product and the first in the Half-Life series.
Dr. Gordon Freeman arrives late for work at 8:47 am in the Black Mesa Research Facility, using the advanced Black Mesa train system that leads through the facility. He arrives at the Anomalous Materials Lab, his workplace, and is informed by the security officer that the scientists have a special experiment today. He then arrives at the Anti-Mass Chamber, where he is instructed that the specimen to be used that day is the rarest and also the most unstable specimen the lab has ever worked with. He is tasked with pushing the specimen into the scanning beam of the Anti-Mass Spectrometer for analysis. However, as soon as the specimen enters the beam, the spectrometer explodes, creating a sudden catastrophe called a "resonance cascade", and opening a portal between Earth and a dimension called Xen.(edited)
What did the others think?
Half-Life was critically acclaimed for it's realistic grpahics (AT THE TIME), seamless narrative and plot, and much more. It won over 50 GOTY awards, and is genuinely considered as one of the greatest games of all time. It revolutionized and influenced FPS games after it's release.
Half Life sold 8 million copies in 2004, and over 9 million in December 2008. It was ported to the PS2 in 2001, and Mac OS X and Linux in 2013. It emerged another sequel, Half-Life 2.
Half-Life is a first-person shooter that requires the player to perform combat tasks and puzzle solving to advance through the game. Unlike most FPS games, Half-Lifes story is entirely shown through scripted sequences. That means the character rarely loses control of Gordon.
The game regularly integrates puzzles, such as navigating a maze of conveyor belts or using nearby boxes to build a small staircase to the next area the player must travel to. Some puzzles involve using the environment to kill an enemy.
For the most part the player battles through the game alone, but is occasionally assisted by non-player characters; specifically security guards and scientists who help the player. and both guards and scientists can assist in reaching new areas and impart relevant plot information.(edited)

I got this for $5 when it was on sale a couple of weeks back. After having played for about six hours, I can honestly say that it wasn't really worth the money, because I'm not sure I was actually having fun at any point. The game bills itself as akin to FTL, which is superficially sort of true but doesn't really hold up in any sustained kind of way because the gameplay is so different between the two. More to the point, FTL is enjoyable to play; this is not.
Why is this game not fun to play? Partly the focus on Final Fantasy-style combat. At a basic level, it's fine mechanically. But very quickly, the fights turn into rinse-and-repeat affairs. Is this enemy immune to KO? If yes, regular attack or breakdown; if not, stun. Attack until dead. Now, on the face of it, not wholly awful, but Dead Age's trick to extending gameplay is to make you do this over, and over, and over, and over again. Quests and progression happens by progressing through areas: the first five destinations all have 20 areas within them, but all that means is that there are 20 fights like what I described above. Is this dull? Yes, it is very, very dull. You'll have some random encounters, but they consist of RNG occurrences to receive loot, or worse, RNG occurrences to get in yet another fight. And if you think you don't need to explore very far, think again: you will frequently be pushed to areas 10 and beyond for quests.
Leveling up is also really unsatisfying, in part because you never really feel like your people have advanced that far. Min-maxing doesn't produce that much apart from the unlockable abilities, but guess what? To have the action points to use them, you have to sit in combat for a while, so it's not like you can attack quickly out of the gate to end fights. Nope, the grindquest will continue.
Is it difficult? Not especially. I played on normal and made it to Day 20 on my first save, and I only quit because I've gotten so bored with the game. Make sure you train one melee fighter and use ammo sparingly, and bam, there's your game. First aid seems pretty useless; it only came up in one boss fight (somehow, the only boss fight I saw in the 20 days), and even then, I would have made it without it.
Item crafting is there, but it's kind of a pain to actually implement. You can turn your excess survivors on jobs like crafting, but the one thing they can't do is farm the raw materials to make stuff for you: if you want materials, you can sell stuff or find them out fighting. For tools, you're farther up a creek because you can only get them by completing quests or finding them out in those areas. The only time you want to keep your survivor home is if he's nursing wounds...but this just worsens the "gonna go out and bash my head on a rock until something interesting comes out of my head" problem this game has.
Part of the selling point as the devs describe it is that you make "difficult decisions." I'd be fascinated to know where they were hiding in my playthrough. Generally, the decision consists of "fight some zombies for somebody," and usually that's not difficult but just dull. Do I feel like being bored some more? If no, then I guess it's a difficult decision. I encountered one thing that might have been described as a difficult decision, when some married woman I saved decided she wanted to get cozy with me and not her husband. I said no, which I guess was supposed to be difficult? Couldn't really see any benefit to saying yes.
In short, I wouldn't recommend this game to people. I have to say, even if you're in love with the FF style format, Halcyon 6 (which I also didn't like, but which was certainly better than this) is a better game.

A fun lil rpg. Certainly got my moneys worth out of it.
Summary of design: A turn based rpg that clearly wants to focus on combat and storytelling. The entire game is played out in phases, the preperation phase for setting people you cant take in your party to doing jobs. (hunting, crafting, guarding. Basic things a group of survivors might need to do,) followed by a combat phase, which is broken up into two parts, One the actual combat, two being the loot and resolution phase, that is sometimes interrupted by random events. This repeats up until you get o the end of the area, (each area has 20 fights,) or you decide to pack it up for the day. Most of the storytelling occurs during missions either in the preperation phase back in your camp, though can occur in the combat phases themselves. (for example, rescuing a survivor will often end in a combat phase with the survivor in tow.)
Graphics: Far better than I have seen from similar indies in the same general genre. It reminds me of playstation 2 esk generation of graphical fidelity. Nothing wrong with them, but I think they could have put a bit more effort into some of the effects. they can seem rather plain in compare.
Storytelling: considering how little content the game actually ends up having, the storytelling takes a front and center stage and sometimes its just not prepared for that much spotlight. the beginning for example has your created character for some reason taking control of a group of survivors with clearly far more qualified people sitting in the camp. I cant say this isnt unexpected, but its a irritating trope none the less. Probably more so simply because the game forces such focus iwth ts design. Its a perfectly fair story so far though.
Combat: the bread and butter of the game really and it doesnt disappoint. each weapon skill has clear uses that easily compliment one another. Further, You find yourself making overall strategic decisons to conserve your ammunition essentially in exchange for hp. If there is one bothersome thing about the combat it is that there is sio much emphasis on this trade. Melee has its role but is certianly not for dealing with a greater amount of the threats you face which i found odd considering the setting.
Game systems: All the rest of the systems are completely functional. Thye are just nothing al lthat special either. Crafting is pretty simplistic, and the other jobs your survivors can do are just trading one resource for another at the end of the day. Hunting for example requires one resource to get 5-7 of another. all other jobs follow this basic idea. There really is no other game system to speak of. other than making a choice or two between, it seems, two mutually exclusive options.
Overall: Honestly if this game was any more expensive I probably couldnt recommend it, but considering the price point it is exactly what you want if you enjoy the setting and genre. the only real stink I could make of it is it does have stiff competition in the same general setting. Keep this in mind if the price is what is attracting you to this one, and not its turn based rpg stylings.

Tales of Berseria is one of the best JRPG's I've played in some time, and definitely the best Tales game I've played in a very long time. I was quite disappointed with several factors of Zestiria (didn't even finish it), but I took a chance on this one and I do not regret it one bit.  It's clear I'm missing some minor subtext by not having finished Zestiria, but it's nothing major and the game is completely playable and enjoyable without having played it.
So why is Berseria so good? First thing is the story. Gone is the, "I'm the savior trying to save the world," cliche story. In it's place, we have a unique story that's quite the opposite. Velvet is basically the embodiment of what everyone in the game's world is afraid of and hates, and she doesn't care. She's on a quest for revenge and she doesn't care who she hurts along the way. It allows for a unique story that you rarely see in RPG's. There's no grand quest to save humanity, and in fact Velvet's agenda basically supports the opposite.
The world feels living as there is lots of dialog that's basically random and relevant to the world, but completely pointless to the story. It helps make the world feel alive. All of the characters are believable, as well, and they are built well throughout the story and optional skits (What Tales game would this be without skits?). That being said, some of the side dialog has some errors. This mostly pertains to the side quests you can do later in the game. Whoever turned the voice overs into text dialog did a bad job. It's always the subtitles too, no error from the VA's. The subtitle makes no sense and doesn't fit the dialog at all. I don't know who proofread it but they did a terrible job.
The combat is very fun. It can be button-mashy, but ultimately that's all about how much effort you want to put into it. I tended to keep specific chains available to me and mixed and matched through those chains to get good combos on whatever enemy I was facing. You can also spend some time crafting combos specific to the area you're in but I didn't do that. It made it more engaging personally to have to swap around between X, Y, A and B to make combos that were effective, rather than putting Weakness Chains into a single button for each enemy. It's pretty much however you want to do it, which makes the combat more engaging and more enjoyable.
The combat system works like this: You have what they call souls, blue diamonds on your portrait. You usually start with 3 in battle. If you use a special Break Soul attack, you lose a soul. If you get hit with a status effect, you also lose a soul. If you dish out a status effect, you get a soul, and if you perfect dodge an attack there's a (pretty high) chance that a soul will appear on the battlefield (that the AI loves to steal from you). You can have a maximum of 5 souls, and the amount of souls dictates how many actions you can take in combat in a single combo. When you stop for a very short while, you get all your actions back, however you also have a Soul Gauge mechanic that makes you unable to actually finish attacks if you have no Soul Gauge (the blue amount on your Souls shows how much you have). This regenerates much slower, but you can attack all you want, even with no SG, if the enemy is incapacitated in some way.
The reliance on Status Effects makes the battle system occasionally RNG based, however you are more likely to dish out status effects when you have low souls and more likely to get status effects when you have high souls, so it typically doesn't take much to get a soul back when you are low.
Although I only really played as Velvet, I have to say that her unique mechanic is really fun, but also makes the game easier than it could be. When you are in her Theronized mode (which you unlock rather early into the game), it negates most status effects you already have and also makes her immune to all status effects while in this mode. You can also ignore the Soul Gauge mechanic entirely, because while Thernoized it doesn't matter at all. It leads to pretty easy abuse to tank most attacks in the game, so long as you have at least three souls (have to have three souls to use it, and it takes a soul as it's her Break Soul attack). But, as overpowered as it can be, it really makes Velvet's playstyle shine throughout the game, and I had a blast playing it because of the Theronize mode.
If you hated Zestiria's equipment skill system, rejoice, because it's gone. It was terrible anyway. What we have now is an equipment system where you can Master equipment and get permanent buffs. Mastering Equipment comes through your Grade from finishing fights (one of the best uses of Grade they've come up with, in my opinion). Gear in general drops in droves, and typically gets a lot of random abilities that can be very useful. The biggest problem? You get A LOT of gear. You can actually hit an equipment inventory cap, and the game just stops giving you gear (by marking them as crossed out in the rewards screen), but never really tells you that's why the items were not obtained and doesn't tell you what the cap is, either, which is frustrating.
The game is ultimately pretty linear, as much as I wish it wasn't. There's about 5-6 optional dungeons, however they're not all that important if you miss them. Since gear is so common, you don't really ever miss anything if you miss chests, which does suck. Additionally, chests respawn which takes some of the joy out of getting gear from them. There are side quests, but they mostly revolve around going to old maps that you've already beaten (or even if you haven't, are brought up in side quests far later than they should be).
One thing I love is how they constantly added new mechanics throughout the game, even up to the final dungeon. They really did a good job pacing upgrades throughout the game, and you always feel like things get changed up at least a little bit.
The biggest problem I have with the game is the Katz Souls and Chests. After the prologue, you start seeing these floating orbs on every map, called Katz Souls. You gather these to open Katz Chests, which contain Katz. Katz either give you absolutely nothing, or fashion items. At first, this system seems fine, although unrewarding. However, as you progress into the game (I'd say by the half-way point), you start getting chests that require A TON of souls while the rate of obtaining souls hasn't really increased all that much. I ended up leaving four chests in an area that the game didn't let me go back to until the end of the game, at which point I had to leave another 5-6 chests, and that's just from the ones I found. When I beat the game, I was still 10+ chests behind with no souls. This means I'd have to farm souls for hours, for absolutely no reason. What a waste of time! The amount of souls you get compared to how many you need is just completely disproportionate, and very frustrating. Either I need to spend hours farming areas for only souls, or I need to just ignore them, and I don't want to do either. I suspect I left one or two I forgot about and the game cut off the area completely, too, which just makes things worse. I hate this system, and hope they either do it better next time or leave it out completely.
Overall, the game is a lot of fun. I typically want my JRPG's to last at least 20 hours for $60. This game took me over 60 hours just to beat, and outside of a few minor things I enjoyed the entire thing. If you like JRPG's, get it. It's absolutely worth every penny.

Well, after multiple hours of trying to get the game to connect, it's a fun game. The actual play is very good, with enough changes to make it feel considerably different from IV. I had long since before accepted that Capcom was mostly out of ideas, hence the art style looks like IV (but more polished), and much of the music is (again) remixes of SF2. That's fine. What I can't forgive is the terrible online play. IF you manage to connect, you'll be annoyed by the experience of trying to find a lobby or match. Which you have to do, because for some asinine reason they decided to omit an Arcade Mode for you to play in while leaving Fight Request On. Your only one-player options are Story and Survival Modes, both of which seemingly have no real difficulty settings for AI skill. Which means your one-player experience is beating up on a very, very weak and not-fun CPU. As a further insult, on the many cases where it fails to connect, the game reminds you that you can't get Experience or Fight Money in offline mode, and hence, nothing you do will mean anything. You would think that after the super-extensive Beta testing of this game, they might have all this figured out by launch, but you'd be wrong. Game developers making sure the game they've already been paid for is functional at launch is Old Economy thinking. That said, the game is pretty, and, when it works, is actually fun. The problem is this: do you want to spend 10 minutes screwing around and waiting for the server to connect every time you want 90 seconds of play? Overall Tales of Berseria gets a whole hearted recommendation from me.

Town of Salem is in a weird place for me. I really enjoy the game, and can reccomend it, but... that reccomendation comes at a risk.
Town of Salem is a much smoother version of a popular forum game,  in this game, 15 people are randomly given roles in their town. Usually three Mafia, tasked with killing all the townies, Townfolk, tasked to kill the Mafia and the random killers, and random killers, tasked with being the last ones alive. The town can vote to lynch a person each day, trying to find killers, and the Mafia can kill a person each night. Each player's role gives them a little power over other players, knowledge, killing, blocking roles, etc, and use of these is the focus you'll need to be rid of the other teams. Bluffing, tricking, killing, all important, and make the game part social, part mechanic, and part mob mentality. That's a very quick summary, I know, bu that's the gist.
I really enjoyed it, you have know how to use what little knowledge you're given to be effecitve, and convince and work with other players to achieve a goal, or trick them into forwarding your goals. The human element shines, but it's also it's weakest part. Players disconnect if not given the role they want, or just randomly, making your job all the harder. Bickering, in fighting, and rage occur quickly in the emotion driven game. Sometimes you're randomly killed night one and are left a ghost for the rest of the game.
Games don't last very long though, and blocking jerks is easy, so getting into a fresh game with hopefully decent players isn't hard. If you can take that, I reccomend it, if not, there's always getting ten friends together and playing the forum version.

Tales of Berseria follows the story of the main female lead Velvet Crowe.
It is not your typical story of "lets save world" and instead it places the lead character in a quest for vengeance.
Graphics: 8/10
It appears to use the same engine as the previous game (Zesteria) so it is similar to that if you played it before. The textures are not highly detailed but the artistic style and choice of colors are pleasing to look at.
+Supports up to 4k resolution (upscaled though)
+60 FPS
Story: 9/10
Velvet will do whatever it takes and use any tool at her disposal to achieve her goal. Due to the nature of this goal ahead of you it sets a darker tone from previous entries in the franchise which helps make it stand out. This change in story is a nice change of pace. You will encounter other characters that join you since your goal crosses path with theirs and they are all unique and likable in their own way.
Sound: 7/10
English voice cast is superb with exception of a few more minor characters.
Sound effects are standard tales of and within what'd you expect.
Music is acceptable but only a few select tracks stand out and not as good as previous entry Zesteria.
Gameplay: 9/10
Excellent and fun.
It uses an action realtime 3d free motion battle system and can lock onto an enemy and switch targets.
The new combat system introduced with this game assigns all four face buttons on your controller (A, B, X, Y) as combo string buttons which you can press in any combination there of multiple times. You can customize what attack skill (artes) are assigned on which button and your characters will learn more attack skills as you progress. Also you can assign an additional 4 attack skills to the face buttons by pressing L1 first. Getting familiar with attack skills and which order to use them will help you create your own combos.
Additionally introduced is the SG gauge (Soul Gauge) which determines how many attacks you can do in a row. When the gauge is lit up your attacks have a higher chance of landing hits on the enemies but when it is depleted or in the red you can still attack but the enemy has a high chance to guard.
Some attacks can stun, poison, paralyze enemies and those are key to earning more SG to continue your combo strings.
Beware that the enemy can use this system against you and chip away your SG when you take damage by being stunned etc.
Defensively you can guard to avoid being stunned and reduce damage. Evasion is also an option and if you do a perferct evade you take no damage and high chance of an enemy dropping an SG point to collect.
Breaksoul is another offensive ability available at the cost of 1 SG spoint and requires minimum of 3 SG. This attack skill breaks through enemy guard and grants your character a unique property temporarily. Each character has their own unique skill tied to Breaksoul - Velvet = Beast Arm and gains new abilities, new movesets . Eleanor = Hits the enemy into the air, Rokuro can counter enemies etc.
There is 1 more guage to keep track of called the "BG" or Blast gauge which lets you the following:
1. ) Tag in moves are also available at the cost of 1 BG which lets you do tag attacks with characters in realtime and bring it the benched characters quickly into battle and boost your combo options.
2.) Mystics arts (very flashy special finishing moves to a combo) are the second use for the BG gauage, you need a minimum of 3 BG and there is higher level mystic artes to unlock as you progress.
All the characters are very unique in their gameplay and movesets which keeps things fresh as you can switch between anytime during battle. Mastering how to make best use of each character will help you get the most of the game and overcome the challenges.
+Variable difficulty settings that can be changed anytime (harder difficulties above "Hard" are unlockable as well)
+There is 3 settings for  battle that you can choose -
1.) Auto -AI will play character automically
2.) Semi-Auto -the character will home in on the enemy you locked onto when you attack.
3.) Manual - Highly recommened choice for more advance players who want to get the most out. the combat system as     this allows you to manually aim which directions your attacks will go.
Lastly Minigames: There are several minigames like a card game, combo challenge , balloon popping and others that are nice side distraction that earn you points to purchase additional costumes and items in the game.
-Minor con: Cosmetic DLC is expensive, purchaseble item pack DLC probably makes the game too easy.
+There is new game plus mode and post game content .
Combat, story and characters and replay value easily 80+ hours of game content.
Final verict: Excellent, must play for Jrpg fans.

Num momento onde os jogos sandbox já são carne de vaca e senso comum, Sleeping Dogs tenta injentar mecânicas novas no gênero e se tornar um dos melhores jogos do gênero. Será que consegue?
No jogo, Wei Shen, policial infiltrado, trabalha para as tríades de Hong Kong. A dualidade tríade e polícia que o personagem vive é tratada muito pouco na trama.
Há mecânicas de aprimoramento da habilidade do personagem relacionado a isso; upgrades que vão sendo desbloqueados na medida que vai jogando. Dois medidores, nas quest principais, que possiblitam essa evolução das habilidades.
O medidor de pontos de tríade e outro de policial. Se você é sanguinário, violento e até ás vezes criativo com a forma de lidar com os inimigos você recebe pontos nesse medidor. Por outro lado,  caso você seja imprudente, destruidor, assassino de inocentes, ladrão e até atrapalhado você perde pontos de policial. Essa dualidade é interessantíssima. Pena que é só aplicada nas missões principais. Deveria ser aplicada em todas as missões.
A questão da dualidade de ser policial e gangster, ao mesmo tempo,  nem é desenvolvida plenamente na trama. O jogo seria muito mais interessante caso a história principal fosse guiada por suas escolhas, para que lado o jogador fosse. E um final da mesma forma. Infelizmente a trama não é das melhores. Ainda bem que o jogo tem outros elementos positivos.
Os colecionáveis do jogo são todos relacionados ao jogo e não são gratuitos. Pegá-los pode ajudar mais tarde. E eles ficam visíveis conforme você vai progredindo no jogo. Dessa forma toda aquele parte de ficar vagando a esmo perdido e sem saber o que fazer não acontece quase nunca. A sinalizaçao do jogo é outro ponto forte, dificilmente você vai errar o caminho.
Outro ponto positivo são as batalhas. O jogo é todo baseado em lutas. Seja com armas de fogo ou sem, a ação é bem feita e bem executada, resultando numa mecânica de batalha simplificada e intuitiva. O único porém fica pela câmera que atrapalha ás vezes.
Sleeping Dogs não é o sandbox do ano. Não é o melhor sandbox de todos os tempos. Talvez nem seja o melhor jogo do mês do seu lançamento. Mas há um caminho de evolução que o jogo pode criar. Lembre-se, ninguém admira GTA I, mas sim o GTA III. Será que veremos acontecer com Sleeping Dogs?

If your interested in a good revenge story with a cast of interesting characters and good gameplay, I highly recommend Tales of Berseria!
I like RPGs and JRPGs mostly for the story and gameplay, primarily the story.  I don't quite remember what my first Tales series game was, but I do remember the first one that really impressed me, and that was Vesperia ( minus Carol ).  I recently bought and beat ToZestiria which was, except for the music, pretty bad overall ( especially the story which seemed to be aiming for cringiest Tales game of the year, and I got the feeling they rushed the ending...  while some of that can be blamed on trying not to spoil Berseria's story... the writing was pretty horrible. )
Tales of Berseria really shines in character and story ( for an RPG ) and I have definitely been waiting for a game like this for awhile.  I have also played the Legend of Heroes:  Trails in the Sky ( FC and SC ) as well as LoH: Trails of Cold Steel ( I & II ).  I mention those games because they also shine in the story and immersion department.  Since I have played those 4 games I have been really wanting a good story driven game and Berseria really fit the bill.  This, more than anything, is why I hope you give Berseria a try ( there is a demo ) and I hope you enjoy the experience.  ToBerseria really restored my belief in the Tales of games again!  So what are you waiting for, go play it!!
So I realized later that I did not really touch on the gameplay.  Sorry, that was partly because if you have played one "Tales of" game the gameplay is mostly the same ( with improvements and tweaks to the standard action oriented gameplay ).  However they have added Break Souls to this iteration and combat can be very fluid if you take advantage of the Break Soul system... however in the early stages of the game sometimes it can be difficult to get souls even if you abuse weakness, sidestep, and block properly leaving you under 3 souls and kind of hosed until you get more.  Normally I go through a Tales game on normal or hard (depending on the game) until my second playthrough on Nightmare/Chaos.  In Berseria, once I unlocked Chaos, I stayed on Chaos for the rest of the game... this might mean the combat is too easy or I am just a Tales vet at this point.  I think the combat could have been harder because there was only one "Boss" mob that was actually difficult that I just had to find gear with reflect skills on them in order to beat.  However in my second playthrough I have had alot of fun playing all the different characters and I think I really like Magilou and Rokurou's combat styles as well.
So overall I enjoyed the gameplay and you can play the demo to get a feel for the combat ( it is late game enough to give you the full feel of what combat will be like for most of the game ).
Graphics and sound were both good overall ( for a Tales game ).  They are similair to Zestiria but strangely I liked the music in Zestiria more than Berseria.
So... play the game/demo already!  :P
P.S.  On a side note, if you have not yet played Trails in the Sky or Trails of Cold Steel yet I recommend trying them too.  Trails in the Sky is more of an old school RPG but it has real heart, story, and charm.  Once you get past the older graphics its a really good game that would be a shame to miss out on just because of the graphics.  Trails of Cold Steel is unfortunately not on Steam but you can get it on PS Vita or PS3/4 I believe and the graphics are much better but its more of a JRPG with a social aspect.  Enjoy!~

Bastion is a good game, has excellent music, plays like a dungeon crawler, and has a great story that you can complete in maybe 5-6 hours.
you play as one character known simply as “the kid”, the kid is trying to collect shards to bring back the Bastion. The Bastion was a place everyone agreed to meet if there was an emergency. Through great story telling, a great narrator and many twists and turns in this puzzle-piece-world you find yourself sitting back and enjoying a story being told with some good natured humor as well.
The game has extraordinarily good music, a video game itself needs to have good music, or else it takes away from the experience, but bastion has very suitable music and a soundtrack that I personally wouldn’t mind downloading.
You can swing a hammer, shoot a bow, poke with a stick, go click-happy with double revolver pistols and many other choices of weapons and combinations. Pick your favorite weapons; upgrade them at the forge to make yourself into one lethal mean killing machine.
I tend to play video games like I’m in a race to complete them, so I have played through the game’s story about 4 times now gathering achievements. In addition to playing through that many times, it took me only 21 hours. (Such as 02/12/14)
The achievements themselves aren’t overwhelmingly challenging, which is good sometimes you just want a relaxing game, if you’re going for a 100% completed game, this one is very doable, look up the guides for the harder achievements, and prepare yourself for a some-what challenging experience
I consider price by how much time I’ve put into a game, how enjoyable it was, and if it’s replayable. Full price for Bastion is 14.99 at this time. I would suggest waiting for a 50% or 75% sale before purchasing. But I would highly recommend this game to anyone who’s looking for something new to play.

I liked Tales of Zesteria, but it had a lot of flaws, from the narrative being disjointed to the world being underdeveloped, to the combat just not quite feeling right. Tales of Berseria fixes all of those to provide an excellent followup to an OK game and a great game in its own right. The world is fleshed out tremendously and given a few sly nods to other games, the narrative feels much more focused while still managing to build on the foundation of Zesteria to provide a stronger whole, and the combat is great, which a much better camera and a focus on four party members being in action at all times again.
The plot is also a breath of fresh air, focusing on what is essentially the villians as they tear through the world. The Tales series has always been pretty good at writing compelling antagonists, and this party is fun, mostly because they're all jerks in some way. The writing's quick witted and sharp, and even though there were a few typos and obvious mistranslations (Zero Impact Vest is an attack name, the voice actress just calls out "Zero Impact") I noticed along the way, they never got in the way of my enjoyment of the game. People that are more apt to notice and focus on errors  will probably find that a bit more irritating, so that is at least something to keep in mind.
Overall, though, the game was just fun. There are tons of nods to the entire rest of the series through the optional minigames, on top of the nods that are part of the main plot, which as a long time fan, I appreciated, it has a stronger plot and better attention paid to detail than the last few games, and the battle system is one of the best the series has ever produced. I enjoyed digging into this game, and will probably get into the post game for a while afterwards.
