This game is over-rated. I can say that comfortably now that I have finished it, having also played and beaten Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within.
To those who have played EU and EW I can convey that in terms of how good the vanilla game is, it's between the previous two. Enemy Unknown was a good game riddled with game-breaking bugs and and plagued by serious balance/difficulty issues (the game was unfairly hard, plain and simple). The expansion fixed EVERYTHING wrong with the original game. It fixed the ragdoll-enemies-shooting-through-the-sky and the numerous hard-crashes. It fixed the balance, making the game a lot more fun and giving you a lot more watercooler moments as your carefully crafted soldiers were an even match for even the new enemy units which were more awesome than infuriating.
The start of Xcom 2 has you thinking it's going to be the greatest strategy game ever. A great premise, a continuation and deepening of the previous story, and a cool new base gets you all excited. Unfortunately that's when the letdowns start. The new base mechanics,a nd especially those needed to survive the brutal early difficulty spike are not readily apparent even if you've played previous Xcom games. The balance of the game early on is clearly completely broken. Early on, enemies can ONE HIT KILL your entire squad, and you'll routinely face more than four at once while you only have four soldiers, each enemy requiring two hits to kill (if your hits even connect, which they won't on the higher difficulties). Add in timers on missions AND timers on the world map that give you mission game over if you don't foolishly rush into danger AND expand your map at a break-neck pace, and you have a game that yes, is COMPLETELY BROKEN if you don't make a mad rush to complete your objectives in exactly the right order (med kits are useless when enemies one-hit kill your soldiers, and if you don't have enough Intel you can't establish contacts, without contacts you can't perform missions that increase the game over timer, without the right weapons and armor upgrades missions to increase the game over timer are impossible).
The game DOES get better if you manage to survive this gauntlet, but at that point you are 75-80% through all your upgrades and tech trees (honestly my playthorugh was a mad dash to get upgrades as fast as humanly possible just so my soldiers would stop dying). You SHOULD be doing the story missions as you go along to progress the story, but since completing them unleashes new enemies that will probably wipe out your squad, you're far better off doing them last (again a broken mechanic).
The new enemies are interesting, and the new gameplay/weapons additions are fun, but honestly the lack of balance means that you won't gets to experience either much. If you don't kill the powerful enemies before they have a chance to even attack once, you will likely lose the entire mission (if you don't have a weapon/armor advantage new enemies will kill your entire squad in a SINGLE TURN). Likewise, while you CAN do cool things with your new unit types, the early-game weakness of low-level units like Rangers mean that most people will use them sparingly or not at all. Enemy HP and armor are so high even compared to the most powerful weapons and gernade radius that removes armor is so small that by the time you unlock cool poweres like Serial for Snipers and Reaper for Rangers the difficulty in setting up a situtation where they are actually useful makes them much less useful than you'd think.
Enemy Unknown had robot soldiers you could use in the vanilla game that could save your bacon in the ridiculously hard long story missions where you were sure to lose multiple soldiers (better to sacrifice a few expensive but unthinking robots than hard-trained soldiers). Enemy Within had genetic modifications for soldiers and mechanized soldiers that were heroic super-soldiers and walking fortresses respectively.
Xcom 2 has...uh...soldiers with some cool new abilities (hacking, remote healing, swords, powered weapons, specialized armor and weapons) that seem cool on the surface, but in actual usage are more annoying than fun. Your scope upgrades are mostly minimal in effectiveness. The really cool weapon abilities (except missed shot damage and free reloads) have such a low chance that they effectively never do anything at all (never ONCE saw an instant kill from a weapon mod). You can lose modded weapons, powered weapons, and special utility items, armor, and weapons if your soldiers die. And to make matters even worse, while you had a good chance of bleeding out instead of dying in EU and EW, in this game I NEVER had a soldier in danger of bleeding out until the final, FINAL mission. No bleeding out. They ALWAYS died. Broken, broken, broken.
Now a lot of these problems are mitigated in DLC (it adds robot units, special weapons with single-soldier equip that actually make the game fun), but these should have been part of the woefully unbalanced base game.
Add to that no controller support (Xcom Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within both had controller support on PC), TERRIBLE performance for a turn-based strategy game, and lots of bugs, and you have a rather mediocre sequel (especially considering that the game, like Enemy Unknonw/Within, has a somewhat weak ending).
My suggestion? Buy this one on sale, install some mods to make the game more balanced, buy the console version if you want controller support. But if you want the best possible experience wait for the expansion to be on the cheap or play Enemy Within instead (it's a much better game).

I would not recommend this game at all. There are too many things that skew the balance of the game. Not only that, this game is pay-to-win. You have 2 12-player maps, Dragons' Lair and Garden of Heroes, where you are divided into teams of 3 to complete a winning objective.
In Dragons' Lair, you have to collect 12 gold chests. I couldn't play this one as there weren't enough players.
In Garden of Heroes, you have to be the first to 30,000 gold. You capture Gold Towers, kill heroes and creeps and find gold chests to get the 30,000 gold.
Forbes Consult Ltd/Elyland (This is the developer) didn't really make a quality game. It was more of a Diablo grinder in the hope that you would get addicted and spend cash to improve your hero. I rate Elyland very lowly as a game developer.
PROS
1. Good First Effort
It looked good until I played it.
2. Graphics
Nice hero models.
CONS
1. Pay To Win
I captured screenshots of the exchange rate and it was totally ridiculous.
2. Item Shop Level
To get higher level items, you have to upgrade your shop level. You'll start off at Shop Level 2 and it can keep on going higher. You have to get more Prestige to upgrade your shop. This skews the advantage to players who have a higher shop and better items.
3. Abilities
Only 3 spells to press QWE. The ultimate is hidden and has to be unlocked by finding artifact items and transmuting them. This is extremely horrible.
4. Inventory System
Similar to Diablo's slot system where you have a torso, weapons, head, neck and feet slots. I liked it at first since I thought it wasn't going to affect gameplay and was purely cosmetic. However, that wasn't the case.
Your items give you stats, similar to Diablo, and since they can be bought with cash, you can buy an advantage. Thus, proof of pay-to-win.
NEUTRAL
1. Heroes
Only 6 heroes at the moment. First 3 are free, others are DLC. Okay to view, but they are very generic and bland. The mage looked interesting though.

I’ve been waiting for a game like this for a long, long time. The market needs a good open world, scientifically accurate, dinosaur survival game. There’s nothing wrong with the concept, and I’m glad that finally a serious project is underway to realize this long overlooked idea.
The title of the game, the store presentation, the desktop icon, and even the main menu all look professionally done. Beyond the main menu and into the main game, the early access state of the project hits you like a truck!
I don’t think there’s a single finished aspect of the game – and I mean this is a bare bones project that has just barely lifted off the ground. The art, sound, and graphic design all lack a general direction at this point. Everything is just thrown together to more-or-less demo the skills of its developers and to test the feasibility of this project. I’ve been hyped for this title since its inception, but this has been a sobering reminder of what to expect from an indie title versus a full production.
That said I would be remiss if I didn’t mention that this is by far the most disappointing purchase I’ve so far experienced on Steam in its current state.
The presentation suggests a game full of imagination, creativity, adventure, and survival. This is an ambitious project that nobody so far has been able to realize, but the product so far could not be further from what the store presentation suggests.
The cover art suggests an action packed, thrilling adventure 66 million years in the making. From hatchling to adult hood, you walk every step as one of your favorite dinosaurs in a scientifically accurate prehistoric open world. Interact with advanced A.I dinosaurs, marvel at their science derived dinosaur models, and be astounded by this rigorously researched world…
… Or not.
The A.I is literally on par with the failed Jurassic Park: Trespasser project. Within my 8 minutes of gameplay, I saw a T-Rex manically walking in circles in a knee high swamp. I saw a full grown raptor walking directly into a tree, determined to phase through it. I did eventually kill a fellow hatchling raptor, which most likely would have rolled over and died on its own if the coding was there. Long story short, I saw enough examples of the A.I. in the starting area to be disappointed. It was then I wished the game was an MMO.
The dinosaur models, while they may be accurate to the most recent scientific iteration, still simply lack imagination. So does the open world environment in general. There’s no artistic flare to draw you in… the world as it exists today just lacks creativity. Just because something is “scientific” doesn’t mean it can’t be awesome. I urge the developers to take SOME liberties with their art/sound design. As it is today, there is no direction here, and it makes for an awkward and disappointing experience.
Now I’m left wondering, because I’ve seen no direction in the development thus far, will this project actually pan out? Or will it be added to the heap of indie titles that merely served as a cash grab? There’s still much to be decided.

Before you click the 'not helpful' button, especially if you've played the game, please read my full review.
I actually like this game a lot, but that doesn't mean it's without flaws.
Some of them are amusing, some of them are annoying, none of them are game breaking.
That said...
Thanks, Indie Devs, for making a game with permadeath and the following gameplay features:
-Awkward interface.
-Fixed save points, so the game saves, then throws a bunch more crap at you to deal with before you can quit. Meaning you have to deal with it all again next time you play.
-Bosses that you have to kill more than once, because apparently the first time it didn't take.
-Sudden shortages of otherwise common resources in timed Fetch or Kill missions.
-Maxed levelling of attacks only to face waves of enemies against which they are permanently 'ineffective'.
-Inability to self-apply first aid in combat. In fact, a pointless differentiation between in-combat and out-of-combat heals so that you can't use one in the other, for some unknowable reason.
-Environmental encounters that work in your favour maybe 20% of the time.
-Incidents that cost you one of the best team members you have (and all their gear) for no reason, because reasons.
-Every group member uses a ration a day, unless you want them to actually do anything, at which point they use two.
-Ruinous economic model, I'm surprised the shopkeeper can't be robbed, shot in the head and chucked in a ditch.
-Weird crafting system (hint: 'brass' is not ammunition casings, it's a quality of ammo- brass/steel/gold).
-Speeling errorors everryware.
-Party members wearing nothing but flip flops and a beanie hat are considered well-dressed.
-A levelling system that's just on the wrong side of fair-ish.
-Repetitive combat, especially against Vagrant class zombies, who are basically immune or resistant to everything, even before they get the chance to block.
-Apparently it's just as time consuming to make a combat shotgun as it is a club with metal strips nailed to it.
-Head Nurse's 'shadow shield' ability is supposed to sacrifice some of her remaining hitpoints, but doesn't.
-Enemies that can use advanced abilities in the first round while you're still 'charging up' so you can do something more than an 'ineffective 24 point' attack vs. a 240 point Suit that summons more zombies every single time he's hit but not killed.
-Quests to get to stage 15 and 20 of a journey, that mutilate your party by stage 15 then say 'you get to rest now' and ask if you'd like to try to continue to stage 20, without making it clear that you're actually fully healed until AFTER you decide.
The list goes on. But overall, the game's a blast. It'd work well as a mobile game too (not a criticism, just an observation).*
You just have to remember that it's the sort of game to play when you just feel like a few hours of semi-repetitive tasks while sliding into a drunken stupor because it's better than doing the dishes.
About an hour after writing this I was having a look at the publisher's website, apparently this is going mobile anyway. Hopefully the devs will fix the multiple glaring issues with the game.

Awesome idea, with great potential. I mean, as a baby dakotaraptor I was zipping in between the legs of a massive triceratops, just for fun--how cool is that! You'll be wandering around looking for food, only to encounter a t-rex doing the same thing...except for it, you're the food.
Pros:
--Great graphics
--Movement feels very natural, very fluid
--Good fps; seems reasonably optimized (for my system, at least)
--Very immersive, feels like you're really a dinosaur
--Good survival experience--you never feel truly safe
Cons:
--Right now, the combat is weird because every dino (no matter how large or small) seems able to kill you in 1-2 hits, whereas it takes you like 20. Not sure if it's a problem with hitboxes, or if it's intentional--but it gets annoying.
--You can go a long time without encountering any food, especially when you're young. This can lead to being near starving to death. Again, not sure if it's intentional.
--Occasional crashes. This doesn't really bother me that much, since it's still in development, and saving is easy.
--No narrative; your goal is just to survive. It might be better to have another option than 'survival mode', one with a story to provide focus (like, an asteroid or ice age, for example). Otherwise, the game will eventually get boring unless you constantly add new, varied dinos.
I think the main thing the game needs is an improvement to combat--no more instant deaths, but a bitter drawn-out battle of tooth and claw. That would make it an amazing experience.
Generally I don't invest in early access games--but the potential here is so incredible I feel it's worth the price.

This game used to be fun when it first came out. I enjoyed it greatly; simple, fast-paced, challenging enough on your own but fun and exciting when you're with a large enough swarm of people. I wanted to redownload the game for some more of that fun, and to check out all of the new updates I've missed. Sadly, the game doesn't even let me log on.
I created an account to Kabam Games. Nothing. I verified my email. Nothing. I tried resetting the game, the computer, changing to different servers... Nothing. I keep getting one of two problems: 1.) A box pops up telling me to re-sign in but the sign in box doesn't work, and there is no box to close the window, or 2.) when trying to play my character I immediately get a "Loading error; retrying" message and end up right back at the character select screen. I also sent a support ticket for these problems, but no response.
The game can be fun, if you actually get a chance to move past the log in screen, but it may be dying all the same.

It's really not that bad. Let's just get that out of the way. Now, on to the review.
This game needs some tlc for sure. The car physics aren't that great. They work, but don't expect GTA or Forza handling.
The interface suffers from some flaws such as some wonky dialog boxes to choose actions, some odd "loading" type screens when taking certain actions that remove a car or an object from the world (such as towing a car or calling an ambulance) and interfacing with cars, drivers and suspects lacks useful feedback beyond a text message at the top of the screen. Some visual feedback would be nice, such as seeing missing/expired plates and/or defective equipment on the cars prior to a dialog-box based inspection once the car is stopped. It's a usuable system, but a complete overhaul to make it more intuitive and user-friendly would be a welcome change.
The career system is lacking. I've yet to see any difference in the "ranks" beyond unlocking a new vehicle type. It would be nice to see it fleshed out more. Having to go "off duty" to reduce your stress level is an interesting idea, but lacks any depth beyond refilling a meter. Some more direct interaction would help it. The station serves little purpose except to drop off prisoners and request a "warrant" but I have yet to figure out what that even does.
There's a currency in the game which is earned by working and can be spent on furnishing for your home (again, not a bad idea, just needs some work to makeit interesting.) Beyond appearances, everything seems to give the same stat boosts. Take the TV for example. The cheap and the middle priced TV both give an equal amount of stress reduction, negating the point of buying the more expensive TV. The other part which makes no sense at all is you have to pay for your own gas and vehicle repairs. I could understand repairs to a point, as you should be punished somehow for wrecking a squad car, but fuel? That makes no sense. Require fill-ups, sure. But no cop pays for fuel from his own pocket.
The controls are functional, but again need thought out a little better. For instance, when ordering a suspect to stop, you have to use the "C" key. If you have your gun out, in order to fire, you first have to "aim" with a right click. I would remove the "aim" portion (since you should already be aiming if your gun is out) and bind the command function to the right click, so you can give orders quickly and still be prepared to shoot. Again, not a big issue, just an annoyance.
So what is good about this game? All of it. It's a hell of a concept, with many underlying systems which make it all work well together. It's not perfect and it's a buggy mess, but it does have a certain allure and charm. The different styles of cruisers are really cool. Thee are several customization options once rank 3 is unlocked, including rims, paint scheme, lightbar type, and colors of each side on the lightbar. Once again, it needs more, but it really is a cool start.
The missions can be repetative, but the constant stress of responding to a call and not knowing what you're walking into is really well captured. Sometimes it ends in a gunfight, sometimes they run then turn and shoot at you, and sometimes they just surrender or you really have to work at identifying which person is the right suspect. Again, it has it's flaws, but has potential. The biggest complaint I have is that there is always a suspect somewhere when given a call. It would be nice to occasionally find out no crime was actually comitted, but that would require a much more in-depth investigation system which I doubt this game would be capable of pulling off.
Sometimes drivers pull over, sometimes a chase ensues, sometimes they bail and run on foot. Again, you never know what you will get. I can't commend this game well enough at mixing in the unknown to every contact with a car or suspect. It really is a good mix and keeps the game entertaining.
If you want a perfect, AAA game with minimal bugs, tons of content, and bleeding edge graphics, then skip this title. However, if you enjoy finding hidden gems that might be a little rough around the edges, then definately give this one a shot. Have realistic expectations of what teh game is and is not and you will find it really enjoyable.
Also, if you have younger children that are always fascinated with police, fire and ambulance vehicle every time they see one, then play this with them. There is no gorey bloody deaths, and while there is the occasional shootout, you still have to call an ambulance for the "bad guy" and be the good guy. For some with small children, it can be a good option instead of GTA and stealing cop cars.

Half-Life was a game released in 1998, developed and published by Valve Software, and published by Sierra Software as a retail publisher, and Valve Software as a digital publisher. It was Valve's debut product and the first in the Half-Life series.
Dr. Gordon Freeman arrives late for work at 8:47 am in the Black Mesa Research Facility, using the advanced Black Mesa train system that leads through the facility. He arrives at the Anomalous Materials Lab, his workplace, and is informed by the security officer that the scientists have a special experiment today. He then arrives at the Anti-Mass Chamber, where he is instructed that the specimen to be used that day is the rarest and also the most unstable specimen the lab has ever worked with. He is tasked with pushing the specimen into the scanning beam of the Anti-Mass Spectrometer for analysis. However, as soon as the specimen enters the beam, the spectrometer explodes, creating a sudden catastrophe called a "resonance cascade", and opening a portal between Earth and a dimension called Xen.(edited)
What did the others think?
Half-Life was critically acclaimed for it's realistic grpahics (AT THE TIME), seamless narrative and plot, and much more. It won over 50 GOTY awards, and is genuinely considered as one of the greatest games of all time. It revolutionized and influenced FPS games after it's release.
Half Life sold 8 million copies in 2004, and over 9 million in December 2008. It was ported to the PS2 in 2001, and Mac OS X and Linux in 2013. It emerged another sequel, Half-Life 2.
Half-Life is a first-person shooter that requires the player to perform combat tasks and puzzle solving to advance through the game. Unlike most FPS games, Half-Lifes story is entirely shown through scripted sequences. That means the character rarely loses control of Gordon.
The game regularly integrates puzzles, such as navigating a maze of conveyor belts or using nearby boxes to build a small staircase to the next area the player must travel to. Some puzzles involve using the environment to kill an enemy.
For the most part the player battles through the game alone, but is occasionally assisted by non-player characters; specifically security guards and scientists who help the player. and both guards and scientists can assist in reaching new areas and impart relevant plot information.(edited)

I liked Tales of Zesteria, but it had a lot of flaws, from the narrative being disjointed to the world being underdeveloped, to the combat just not quite feeling right. Tales of Berseria fixes all of those to provide an excellent followup to an OK game and a great game in its own right. The world is fleshed out tremendously and given a few sly nods to other games, the narrative feels much more focused while still managing to build on the foundation of Zesteria to provide a stronger whole, and the combat is great, which a much better camera and a focus on four party members being in action at all times again.
The plot is also a breath of fresh air, focusing on what is essentially the villians as they tear through the world. The Tales series has always been pretty good at writing compelling antagonists, and this party is fun, mostly because they're all jerks in some way. The writing's quick witted and sharp, and even though there were a few typos and obvious mistranslations (Zero Impact Vest is an attack name, the voice actress just calls out "Zero Impact") I noticed along the way, they never got in the way of my enjoyment of the game. People that are more apt to notice and focus on errors  will probably find that a bit more irritating, so that is at least something to keep in mind.
Overall, though, the game was just fun. There are tons of nods to the entire rest of the series through the optional minigames, on top of the nods that are part of the main plot, which as a long time fan, I appreciated, it has a stronger plot and better attention paid to detail than the last few games, and the battle system is one of the best the series has ever produced. I enjoyed digging into this game, and will probably get into the post game for a while afterwards.

Num momento onde os jogos sandbox já são carne de vaca e senso comum, Sleeping Dogs tenta injentar mecânicas novas no gênero e se tornar um dos melhores jogos do gênero. Será que consegue?
No jogo, Wei Shen, policial infiltrado, trabalha para as tríades de Hong Kong. A dualidade tríade e polícia que o personagem vive é tratada muito pouco na trama.
Há mecânicas de aprimoramento da habilidade do personagem relacionado a isso; upgrades que vão sendo desbloqueados na medida que vai jogando. Dois medidores, nas quest principais, que possiblitam essa evolução das habilidades.
O medidor de pontos de tríade e outro de policial. Se você é sanguinário, violento e até ás vezes criativo com a forma de lidar com os inimigos você recebe pontos nesse medidor. Por outro lado,  caso você seja imprudente, destruidor, assassino de inocentes, ladrão e até atrapalhado você perde pontos de policial. Essa dualidade é interessantíssima. Pena que é só aplicada nas missões principais. Deveria ser aplicada em todas as missões.
A questão da dualidade de ser policial e gangster, ao mesmo tempo,  nem é desenvolvida plenamente na trama. O jogo seria muito mais interessante caso a história principal fosse guiada por suas escolhas, para que lado o jogador fosse. E um final da mesma forma. Infelizmente a trama não é das melhores. Ainda bem que o jogo tem outros elementos positivos.
Os colecionáveis do jogo são todos relacionados ao jogo e não são gratuitos. Pegá-los pode ajudar mais tarde. E eles ficam visíveis conforme você vai progredindo no jogo. Dessa forma toda aquele parte de ficar vagando a esmo perdido e sem saber o que fazer não acontece quase nunca. A sinalizaçao do jogo é outro ponto forte, dificilmente você vai errar o caminho.
Outro ponto positivo são as batalhas. O jogo é todo baseado em lutas. Seja com armas de fogo ou sem, a ação é bem feita e bem executada, resultando numa mecânica de batalha simplificada e intuitiva. O único porém fica pela câmera que atrapalha ás vezes.
Sleeping Dogs não é o sandbox do ano. Não é o melhor sandbox de todos os tempos. Talvez nem seja o melhor jogo do mês do seu lançamento. Mas há um caminho de evolução que o jogo pode criar. Lembre-se, ninguém admira GTA I, mas sim o GTA III. Será que veremos acontecer com Sleeping Dogs?

A game, thats deceptively not about cute white dog-girls that sleep frequently. And is actually about a undercover cop whos working with a Triad gang, that surprisingly has little focus on the use of a gun. Though can be compared to GTA and Saints Row in what you do for free roaming, Sleeping Dogs (or Sleeping Wans, as i keep getting it called) has a deep, and actually solid combat system, that doesnt rely heavily on chest high walls, or who has the best gun. Its more heavily focused on hand-to-hand combat, offering a near-Rock-paper-scissors aspect to who to attack with what to disable, and then encourages follow-ups after the blow is made. Added to this combat system, is the advertised environmental use. From slide-grate-doors, to "Conveniently" open fuse boxes (Even a Jon-woo styled fish tank), Everything (be it highlighted for use or not) is your useage. Added to this, is a quite solid and well programmed driving aspect, that accurately portrays the traffic habits of Hong Kong. Seriously, they drive like ♥♥♥♥ing lunatics, and wount hesitate to run you over if your in the way. And also applies the tractional differences of the rain on their specifically textured roads, which is slicker than usual. The story itself, has enough depth to keep me interested in it for extensive periods, and almost gives you a bond with the organization your working for over the police. I could go into detail, but I would be spoiling it for the potential buyers. As for the sound track, well, you definately have some local flavor, added to Roadrunner's own sponsored bands added to it, leaving you with more than enough of a reason to play with the game's music on for some reason. Be it Dj Kentaro's own work, some international Death Metal, or locally composed music (that isnt the steriotypical chinese music, mostly), you have the formula for a very enjoyable game, that shows fighting with fists, is oftentimes more manlier than guns, with a taste of good Jon-Woo style action and chase scenes, foot and wheel. Long story short, Its a worth while buy, and is a big change from the drive and fight games that are popular to this day, and offers a less steriotypical story with it.

There is a lot of micromanagement and busywork in this game. You will spend most of your time building rooms, putting crap into these rooms, hiring employees and moving these employees around.
The actual game development part of it all is very basic, and essentially boils down to "get as many employees with good stats as possible, put them into a large room, and have them all work on a game". There is again some micromanaging involved to match employees with correct game types, but on a large scale this is completely inconsequential because it all comes down to collecting as many "points" as possible during development - the more points a game has, the better the game, the better the sales.
There is some added complication in that you have to match the game types to the correct topics, but once you've figured them out or stumbled on a couple of winning formulas (Football Sports games, Fantasy RPG games, Space Arcade games etc.) you may well just repeat these over and over.
This is fun if you want to kill a couple of hours here and there, but if you are playing for longer than say 2-3 hours, the game becomes just too repetitive. There is simply no real variety to the gameplay, no overall strategic decisions to make beyond "how much money do I have to hire more people and build more rooms to make even bigger games".
And there is no real interactivity to the game development itself. You just sit there and wait until your guys have accumulated enough points so you can release the game and make money.
tl;dr: Game had some potential, but never rises beyond being a simple time killer for a few hours.

Alright so after playing this game since open beta I've decided to give it a review. I will change it depending on the game's state. But as of right now, it's a positive one.
The devs are often talked of as greedy, and the game is talked of as Pay To Win, but neither are true. The developers are in more than enough contact with the community, they constantly update the game with new content, cosmetics, and mounts. While there isn't a "Set" endgame, there is a cap for mastery and levelling of a single character.
That being said, the game is playable. OH SO BLISSFULLY PLAYABLE. Even after you're max mastery and levelled up and everything, you've still got a lot to do, fun to be had, adventures to be made.
The game's economy is live and well, despite so many sellers of the same item on a global market. NOTE: AS OF THE GET CRAFTY UPDATE, EVERYTHING CAN BE OBTAINED BY PLAYING THE GAME NORMALLY. That's right folks, they removed a massive paywall that many had been complaining about, and added an even bigger grind.
And on that note, the grind in this game is MASSIVE. It's comparable to a hardcore MMO. This game may seem child-friendly and colourful, but it's LONG and TEDIOUS.
Everything can be bought with in game currency should you have enough time to grind for it, and the mindset of anything that isn't a baby-brained quitter.
That being said, some things like GEMS and RINGS are heavily based on RNG.
So get lucky, score big, and have some serious fun.
Just buy it. I don't care if you don't like cars, or racing games, or awesome crash physics. Do yourself a favor. Thank me later.

This is definitely a labor of love, with the upsides and downsides that go along with it.  As is made very clear (perhaps too many times) it's developed by one person, and parts of the game do feel like "it's my game so I can do what I want with it".  Call it a hunch.
Some of those things being that I have to -earn- basic functionality like speeding up the game and zooming into the battlefield via certain upgrades to my "hard drive".  It sounds cute, but... seriously?  The introduction was very shaky and almost off-putting, with it just giving you lines and lines of text, complex UI and hotkeys, and indicators to click this-now do that-now click here, and go through the motions just so you've done them, like a cheap mobile app.  Something like slowly introducing mechanics bit by bit in the first moments of a level would fit this much better, not literal youtube videos comprised of (assumedly) the developer playing and commentating the intros.  Which, by the way, you can speed up and zoom in in the tutorial, then it's taken away for reasons.
It took what felt like 30-45 minutes to really adapt to the game and its interface and understanding all of the mechanics, which in reality are really simple, but they're explained so abruptly it's hard to take it all in.  When I finally felt comfortable actually playing the damn thing, soon enough it already felt kind of shallow, slow, and babying, with these extremely simple first levels, and the notion that the entire rest of the game isn't going to get much more intricate.  Another hunch is that he thought the UI and controls were so alien that he wanted the most absolute tender beginning to not scare people away.
So, a quick recap - the introduction and general pacing is a mess, the game feels shallow, and your linear upgrades are locked behind exponentially more expensive upgrades which just take playtime.  Thing is, there's upsides to the "labor of love"-ness.
Once you sort of abandon your own pre-existing notions and instead walk in the developer's shoes in such a game like this, you start to see some of the design decisions.  Things start to click, to flow together, and fall in place, and while I'm still not really sure it's much deeper than I'm imagining, it feels a lot more entertaining to play - especially if my hopes for what is in store fall into place.  The abstract keybindings feel less strange, the global aiming and prediction... could still use a re-imagining but it's less terrible after a bit, the usage of weapons and towers become more clear, that kind of thing.
The music and the aesthetic are about the only charismatic things in this game, which I guess in my case were enough to keep me invested until I figured the rest of the project out.  The presentation as a whole is very inviting.  The inoffensive and energetic EDM, the shading, colors, and menus, the minor voice overs, the animations of pretty much everthing fits nice and looks nice, the clean UI, and so on.
Bottom line:  it's very alien, but it's interesting and filled with heart and effort.  I realize this is as much "review" as it is just my thoughts on it as a project.

I have played enough of this game (its early access so basically not much of it) so i have decided to write a review.
Here are the pros. Saurian is a highly realistic dinosaur survival simulator that takes place in the hell creek formation during the late cretaceous. Unlike the community freakshow of a game called "the isle", Saurian has no shrinkwrapping, realistic creatures and enviroment, mostly good community(il explain why in a sec), and performs really well. (I have a GTX 1070 and i get no lag at all) while the isle has an incredibly toxic community, corrupt, rude developers, and is itself a poorly optimized game.Most of the dinosaurs have feathers also unlike the scaly bipedal lizards from the isle. Only one dinosaur is playable so far (Dakotaraptor) but there is more to come.So far as dakotaraptor its easy to hunt and kill certain prey aswell as still provide a challenge. If saurian's community doesnt decay like the isle's, then this game has a good future.
The community is good for the most part, but you do get the occasional furry and isle player in it (cringy ms paint and furry artwork is an example).
Now here are the cons: The thing i dont like most about this game is that not everything will be playable in the full release ie crocodiles, pterosaurs, edmontosaurus (not fully sure why its called anatosaurus. i know its synonymous but whats wrong with calling it good ol edmontosaurus?) gallimimus, etc. I do understand that smaller creatures will mean that they will require higher textures (an easy fix for this is to zoom out the third person) and that pterosaurs but i dont really understand the others. Devs have explained that crocodiles have low metabolisms and edmontosaurus are migratory species, but in my perspective i just see that as they dont want to put in the extra work to make those playable.
I think it would still be realistic if they ignored the crocodile's metabolisms(the day cycle is shorter than irl anyways) and the edmontosaurus's migrational pattern. I think they might just be going a little overboard with this realism.
Another big dissapointment in my opinion is that this game runs on Unity. This makes it hard for modders to modify stuff in the game for others to enjoy. so far a workshop isnt confirmed. I personally prefer Unreal Engine myself since its highly versatile compared to unity.
Though the dinosaurs are really realistic, i do have an issue with the mouths of Dakotaraptor and tyrannosaurus. (Tyrannosaurus is getting a new model) There isnt really proof that theropods, let alone tyrannosaurus, had lips, infact theres more proof that tyrannosaurs had no lips or atleast partial lip covering.
Theropods would really need lips to protect their teeth if they are constantly replacing them. also the skin on the snouts dont look avian or dinosaurian at all. They look smooth and scaleless and always wet as if they are more mammal than dinosaur(most mammals like dogs have wet noses and thats what dakotaraptor's snout looks like all over, a wet dog nose).
I have also had a bad experience with one developer/moderator (i dont remember x.x) in discord taking a joke image too seriously then banning me from the discord (i left before i got banned because i was tired of bringing myself down to an immature and rediculous level) but since the other developers and mods have been nice to me aswell as the community im going to let this one slide. Though I am a bit alienated by the Saurian developers because they seem to be friends with the developers of the isle(isle devs are notorious for being corrupt and mean to their playerbase)
So overall, I recommend this game. Devs are nice for the most part, game has alot of potential despite having certain flaws, and there will be multiplayer added. My own advice is to not get yourself involved in the forums or discord(especially if you have a dark sense of humor) since this is an early access game.

It plays a bit like a top-down Sanctum in that, the player shooting baddies is key to surviving, although the shooting itself is vaguely reminiscent of Atom Zombie Shooter or, if you prefer, the special powers in Sol Survivor.
The main problem which however soured me off the game, is its committing one of the cardinal sins of game design: the player is given a lot (can't say all for sure) of the upgrades to play the, belabored, tutorial levels, then stripped of them and thrown into the actual game. Additionally, all of the weapons have sort of a ballistic effect, in that the ammo takes time to reach the ground: crucially, the tutorial teaches the timings for the fully-upgraded weapons, then dialing it all the way back so even the basic 'sniper' shot (or basic/shortest reload time) takes what feels like an incredible long time to get to the ground, turning a mechanic that already wasn't all that enjoyable in the first place, into sheer frustration when trying to hit fast-moving targets. In fact, it does seem the developer may be aware of some parts of this issue, having released
aiming to make the game easier, whereas I feel, after the update, it's not so much that the game is hard per se, but rather, assuming the shot timing is fully intentional, that the way the weapons are introduced is hardly the best: a difficulty curve is almost invariably about offering just enough challenge to make the player get better while at the same time making them feel good about themselves, this game has it backwards.
The whole design seems pretty elaborate, with many different units and building types; maybe too elaborate, and I would say front-loaded, making the introduction feeling rushed and sort of confusing, especially in comparison to the studied difficulty curve and pace, and essential design, of classics of the genre like Defense Grid.
I also feel the computer metaphor is quite strained and doesn't really work all that well: the main currency is called RAM, and it's gained by shooting baddies and in other ways, like ...connecting to databases and building production towers ...huh ? And lost by having the baddies reach the OS (?); I'm afraid it doesn't make a terrible lot of sense to me: at some point even 'medic' units are introduced - how do medics fit in this self-proclaimed "VR" world?
Nevertheless, mechanically, there may be a decent enough game in there, but I'll never know because the way it is designed lost me before I could find it.

I enjoy the game itself but I can't in good conscience give it a high rating. There are two main points that I personally can't get over.
1: 2 years after the release of the game it is still full of bugs and crashes. I am playing the game on a machine that's a little bit over the minimum requirements with an SSD as well and the game runs smoothly. Crashes occur when loading or transitioning from area to area usually and I find it distasteful. Another weird thing is sometimes when you open up the game for the first time in that day some of the NPCs are glitched or bugged and you get stuck in conversation with them or other similar situations so you need to restart the game.
2: Season Pass + Cration Club. Personally I think this is a kick in the nards for players who purchased the season pass thinking they will have access to all the conent (as stated in the SP description) but no ... Creation club haves you pay for mods in a singleplayer game! Hooray! (Sacrasm). Because of this I am having conflicting thoughts on actually purchasing the SP to get Nuka World, Far Harbor and all the workshop DLCs as the Cration Club makes me feel like that's all I will get with the SP from now on.
Conclusion: As mentioned earlier, 2 years after release but the game is still full of bugs. I find it unprofessional and sad that I have to install a MOD to fix most games bugs and lose the ability to earn Achievements. I know Achievements aren't that much of a deal but it is the principle itself, can't have both at the same time, clean game + achievements. Adding to the cesspool is the Creation Club (CC) which gives you the impression that you will no longer get free content from here on and you will have to pay for them through the CC. We have yet to see a big DLC come through the CC but it makes you think. These two points just are a no go for me personally and I consider that Bethesda, for what a big corporation they are as a developer and publisher at the same time, have made some really unprofessional and underhanded decisions. I recommend the game itself but not to actually purchase all the content.

Don't like my review? Here's a recipe for Fish and Chips:
Ingredients
For the fries:
1 gallon safflower oil
4 large Russet potatoes
Kosher salt
For the batter:
2 cups flour
1 tablespoon baking powder
1 teaspoon kosher salt
1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper
Dash Old Bay Seasoning
1 bottle brown beer, cold
1 1/2 pounds firm-fleshed whitefish (tilapia, pollock, cod), cut into 1-ounce strips
Cornstarch, for dredging
Let's Start!
Heat oven to 200 degrees F.
Heat the safflower oil in a 5-quart Dutch oven over high heat until it reaches 320 degrees.
Using a V-slicer with a wide blade, slice the potatoes with the skin on. Place in a large bowl with cold water.
In a bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, salt, cayenne pepper, and Old Bay seasoning. Whisk in the beer until the batter is completely smooth and free of any lumps. Refrigerate for 15 minutes. Note: The batter can be made up to 1 hour ahead of time.
Drain potatoes thoroughly, removing any excess water. When oil reaches 320 degrees, submerge the potatoes in the oil. Working in small batches, fry for 2 to 3 minutes until they are pale and floppy. Remove from oil, drain, and cool to room temperature.
Increase the temperature of the oil to 375 degrees. Re-immerse fries and cook until crisp and golden brown, about 2 to 3 minutes. Remove and drain on roasting rack. Season with kosher salt while hot and hold in the oven.
Allow oil to return to 350 degrees. Lightly dredge fish strips in cornstarch. Working in small batches, dip the fish into batter and immerse into hot oil. When the batter is set, turn the pieces of fish over and cook until golden brown, about 2 minutes. Drain the fish on the roasting rack. Serve with malt vinegar.

I love Xcom EU and EW, played and beat them both. I felt that those games were the perfect level of difficult, but fun. I play a lot of turn based strategy games, many of them roguelikes. I've put about 40 hours into this game and I all i have to say is that it should be called XCOM enemy overwhelming.
I've had multiple playthroughs, In some I've actually gotten pretty far along, but I always wind up getting ground into dust. 2-3 missions in they already start throwing the higher tier aliens at you, and in staggering numbers. Mathimatically speaking, when you have 6-8 enemies on screen, all with enough hitpoints to absorb 1-2 hits without dying even if you had a 100% chance to hit, its mathimatically impossible to down enough of them to keep your troops alive. Couple that with the 8-10 turns that they give you to complete the missions before you autofail, and the fact that you are usually escourting a civilian with 3 hitpoints and... well, you get the idea.
It's a shame, really. The character customization is amazing, the individual unit talent trees are fun and interesting, and I love the idea of flying around a stolen alien vessel as home base. The fact of the matter, however, is that the game is unplayably hard. I came to the reviews to see if other people had the same experience as I did, and apparently that isn't the case.  So I'm sure I'm going to be told to get good or whatever, or maybe i need to spend a few hours watching tutorial videos on youtube, but based on what I've seen playing the game, I'm really not sure it's even possible to win.
I was really excited for the release of this game, even shelled out the $60 to buy it when it first came out last year, which i suppose is fine since its still $60, amazingly. I would however like to get to a point where i can actually progress and see the story, but I play it for 4-6 hours at a time, fail miserably, and wind up shelving it for months because of how frustrating it is.
IMO save your money, wait till it goes on sale for cheap. You're only going to get to play the first 5-6 hours of the game anyway.

The run-and-gun genre was a staple for arcades and home consoles in the late 1980s and throughout the 1990s, with classic series like Contra and Metal Slug. The run-and-gun genre was essentially a combination of the approach to player movement found in side-scrolling platformers with the blistering frenzy of the shoot-em-up genre. Fast-paced action, destruction and carnage, huge boss fights, and epic set pieces were all standard parts of the run-and-gun. Intrusion 2 returns to these sensibilities, but combines them with a physics-based design. As a physics-based game, objects tumble and fall over each other, bend under weight, or are pushed back by gun fire. Everything interacts, and the result is quite intriguing. By combining the relentless action of the run-and-gun with physics-based interactions, Intrusion 2 is wildly chaotic, and extremely fun. You can take out enemies by shooting them, but you can also tumble a rock onto them, or blast apart the structure they are standing on. It's more open-ended then your typical run-and-gun, and this adds a layer of unpredictability that perfectly compliments the emphasis on action-packed craziness. Also, it's a weird example of a side-scrolling game that is actually better played with keyboard and mouse, as it's mouse-oriented targeting system is refreshingly accurate. At the same time, Intrusion 2 is just as relentless and explosive as any Contra or Metal Slug game. Ride and shoot on the back of a massive wolf that can leap over buildings, or snowboard down a mountain while robotic serpent dragons explode out of the ground, Intrusion 2 has the over-the-top action-movie aesthetic that is classic to the run-and-gun genre.
If you want a short, furious, overwhelming action game to play, Intrusion 2 is a pretty great pick. It's distinctive, but with a classic run-and-gun feel.

I've thrown myself into the world of Berseria, not expecting much. I thought it to be nothing more than a shallow game with a titular main character (and I mean titular as in breasts.)
I bought this for full price, and kept myself reserved for a little while, knowing the steam refund policy.
I was vastly amazed by the quality of this game. It opens with beautifully animated anime-style graphics, then dives you right into the world years later with high quality, 3D anime graphics.
Not once did I feel a scene was run over because of budget, my only real concerns were few nitpicky details.
I'll break it down for you.
First of all, the tutorials and menus can give you *subtle* spoilers on the game. (Example:
There are a few inconsistencies in the translations. A lot of the tutorials will call the same thing by 2 - 3 different names and can be a little bit hard to follow. (Example: Approaching an enemy behind is labeled something along the lines of "advantageous approach" or "favorable approach" within a paragraph of eachother.)
The animations in the cutscenes are beautifully done, but some feel a little stiff, like when a character turns around, they use the player-controlled animation so it looks a bit unnatural.
The combat isn't really the meat-and-potatoes of Tales of Berseria, and can become a bit tedious later on when it's like 3 AM and you have to work today but the story so damn gripping.
All-in-all, if you're looking for a serious story that will make you question your own moral standings, I really reccomend this game, even at 50 USD.

Freedom Cry is a short but sweet extra chapter of AC4: Black Flag that brings in just enough new interesting features to make it worth the price. You play as Adewale, Edward Kenway's Ex-First Mate. Most of the game is centered around freeing slaves, and the mid sized area you get to play around with is full of respawning side-missions to do like taking an injured to a safe spot set up by the maroon rebellion or saving a half dozen slaves being auctioned off with force or simplying buying them then letting them go free. Your main area is Port de Prince, a town full of activity, but after an hour of fooling around you will know the town like the back of your hand and done anything there is to do. You get a new ship at the start of the game, and I was happy to see Ubisoft made us a totally new slice of the Carribbean to explore, though another 2 hours and you'll have done literally everything. The bright side is there is a few awesome side missions to play. My favorite is the Plantation missions because of the different techniques to employ in getting the slaves out safely. Start a massive riot and hope to god you and the slaves overpower the overseers or thin the heard steath style until the enemy has only a few men left then swarm them. (It's basically warehouse missions from black flag but once the alarm is triggered you have to act fast because the overseers are outnumbere 4 to 1 by slaves so they start killing them right away after the alarm is trigggered) There are also slave ships which are heavily escorted but carry around 100 slaves but can't be damaged at all before borded (obviously). Adewale is a pretty cool guy but they don't really flesh him out beyond he's has to get back to the brotherhood eventually but he refuses to leave until the rebellion is strong enough to stand without him. The new weapons he gets to use are a nice refreshment though. His main weapons is a machete, and its a brutal weapon that gets the blood flying and seems to always get stuck in the bodies of slavemasters. The second and best new weapon is the blunderbluss, which adds a whole new element of gameplay, because now you can take out a concentrated group of soldiers with one shot. Overall a good game though just barely worth the asking price.

Surprisingly fun - a lot of the negative reviews are quite misleading, possibly becuase they did not play enough to find all of the game's features.  The game stands out as unique in the MOBA genre by having 4 teams rather than 2, and it works quite well.  The game is designed around this 4 team system rather than having it thrown on just to make the game different, which means that the win conditions, map, and pacing of the game aren't as similar to standard MOBAs as you might expect.  Rather than winning by destroying a structure as in most MOBAs, your team needs to be the first to collect 30,000 gold.  Games are quite fast, lasting 15-20 minutes on average, and are fast paced all the way through.
In this game's case, it makes more sense to talk about the problems that the game has before talking about what it does right, as of some of the features available lessen the impact of many of the problems.
CONS
1. Pay to win
A lot of the "p2w" features such as legendaries are earnable in-game, so think of those as pay to progress faster.  Better potion packs are purchasable with the premium currency, though you can get them in other ways and they are quite cheap.  The skins, however, provide a direct stat boost and are only purchasable with real money.  This is by far the worst part of the game; think of the game in its current state as a free trial where you have to pay $10 for a skin to get the full experience.  You cannot use the premium currency for these, you have to buy them through steam.  Hopefully a system is put in place to earn skins, even if it takes 100+ games.
2. Poor tutorial
The tutorial is far shorter than it should be, and fails to cover all of the game's basics.  The game does have a wiki that has more information on how to play, but that should be in the tutorial to begin with.  Some pieces of information are even missing on the wiki, meaning that they cannot be found by searching online at the moment.  This is hopefully going to be changed seeing as the game is in early access, though.
3. No matchmaking system
There is no MMR.  Everyone gets matched together, regardless of skill level.  This is a forgivable flaw, since it allows for great queue times despite the small playerbase, but if the game ever gets a large playerbase then it will become a more glaring problem.
4. Lack of custom game support
Currently, you can only play games through matchmaking, and teams are limited to 3 players.  If you have a large group of friends playing the game, the only hope is to queue up in separate groups and hope to be put in the same game - the game would certainly benefit from having custom games for large groups of friends/stream viewers.
PROS
1. Extremely well executed 4 team gameplay
No other MOBA does this, at least not well.  Golden rush's 4 team system leads to a much faster pace than standard MOBAs.  Teams will often make temporary alliances against the first place team, and fights at the objectives can have as many as 12 players involved in an all-out brawl.  Split-second decision making is heavily rewarded, as catching another team out of position can secure you their tower or an ace if done properly.  The game is simply fun to play, which is what really matters.
2. Premium currency can be earned in-game
Being in the top 100 at the end of a month gives you some premium currency, though the rewards are heavily skewed towards the top few getting a lifetime's supply and the rest getting relatively little.  You can get it in modest quantities from the daily reward (I've been given 300, $3 worth, in just under 2 weeks of daily spins).  You'll earn quite a bit of premium currency from essences. (purchasable for the standard currency of gold, essences can give you legendary gear, ~50-200 premium currency, temporary or permanent buffs, and potion sets)  Last but certainly not least, you can earn it just by winning games.  A win nets you 15, second place gives 10, and third gives 5.  You'll need just under 1500 for a full set of legendary gear, which is easily attainable without paying.
3. Gear sets lend variation to the endgame
Think of your equipment in this game as runes/masteries in league of legends.  They provide some flat stat increases in addition to special buffs such as -ressurection time or -damage taken from towers.  Legendary sets provide an ability on top of that, such as cc removal or cooldown reset.  Each class has 3 legendary abilities to choose from, and they will have a significant degree of impact on the game, much like summoner spells in league.  Since the gear is all attainable without paying, players will eventually be on an even playing field in that department.  Paying simply allows you to get this gear faster.
4. Well designed bots
Teammates disconnect at the start of a game?  No problem, the bots that they get replaced with have you covered.  This game has some solid AI, and the bots can even be controlled with pings to an extent.  While it would be nice to be able to micro the bot abilities as dota lets you do with disconnected players, the bots are sufficient as is.  I've won a couple games where both of my teammates disconnected at the start simply because the bots can be commanded to go to objectives where necessary and have decent enough AI in a fight to survive, provided you give them a few commands.
5. Short matches
The matches, lasting only 15-20 minutes, are a welcome break from the hour+ timesink that many other MOBAs can be.
All in all, golden rush is actually a lot of fun.  I'd strongly recommend playing with a group of friends, as co-ordination is quite important.  Try it out in spite of the mixed reviews - you'll be plesantly surprised at how well-made the game is.

If you like GTA, the previous True Crime games, or John Woo movies, you should check this out. You can still feel the seams where this game was stitched together, but they are a lot harder to see than in its predecessors. Overall it’s a very fun game worth the sale price, even if the DLC will bump you right back up to the sticker cost. Here are the four main elements of the game ranked by personal preference:
Fighting - Like the Arkham games you prioritize targets then use strike and counter timing to put them down. Strategic use of environmental attacks can really tilt things in your favor too. Good melee weapons aren’t abundant, break quickly, and aren’t overly powerful, but I’m actually fine with that. I suggest upgrading the strike combos first, then the counters, and finish with melee weapons. Some of the outfits will change your fighting style which is cool too.
Movement - The parkour isn’t quite up to Assassin’s Creed quality, but it’s decent. Sprint and vault should never be on the same key though. There were more than a few instances where I got screwed over because the game deciding that I wanted to jump off a building instead of throw the enemy I was pummeling. In general the critical mission boundaries aren’t marked and that gets very frustrating.
Gunplay - Cover based shooting with blind fire, realistic gun accuracy (except the garbage SMGs), location damage, and you go into slow-mo when you leap over barricades. Guns are rare and firefights tend to be reasonable in length and frequency. On paper it sounds perfect, yet I can’t help but feel underwhelmed. If you ever need to shoot at a vehicle, just hit the tire, and watch it somersault through the air. It takes the challenge out of vehicular combat, but at least it looks cool as hell.
Vehicles - Driving with the keyboard could use some improvement but is manageable, at least until you try to do the races. If the game’s ability to switch between Keyboard+Mouse and X360 controller actually worked it wouldn’t have been an issue at all. You can tell that the guys that did the driving had previously worked on some NFS games, probably Underground since the game literally cheats by spawning oncoming traffic at inopportune moments. This is even more apparent on the motorcycles where getting ejected from the bike forfeits the race. It sucks that you can’t set the default color for the cars you buy, but you get every color for a car when you unlock it. One trick I learned was to use the “ramming” ability in cars to take corners better. I do like that you can hijack another vehicle while moving by leaping onto it. My biggest wish was that you could call a cab, but at least you have a valet that will deliver a car to you.
A recommendation to new players: complete the “date” missions ASAP, they are even easier than the women (giggidy) and give you awesome rewards, like collectibles showing up on your map.

Coming into this game, I expected a mediocre GTA clone set in Hong Kong. Now, having played about 12 hours or 30% of the whole game, I feel that I like this more than I liked Dishonored.
The story is the best I've seen for any open-world action/crime game. Wei Shen is an undercover cop who is tasked with taking down the Triads of Hong Kong from within, attempting to balance loyalty to the law and playing the part of a gang member. As the story progresses, you get to know more about certain characters that would be considered the "bad guys" and morality in this game is no longer black and white. Having not finished it yet, it will be interesting to see whether Wei forsakes his duty as a cop or brings down the house on the criminals.
The game has an immense focus on melee combat and it plays almost identical to Arkham Asylum, but it doesn't straight out copy it. You level up your combos and abilities which was soemthing Arkham didn't really focus on. You can also grapple enemies and unleash "environmental kills" and use an air conditioner as a blender for some guy's head. You can use butcher knives, tire irons, and a few other melee weapons to kill, but after 10 strikes the weapons "break", so when you actually find one, you know that you'll need to still rely on your fists. As for guns, they are rare and powerful. VERY rare. I had to wait maybe 3 hours to get my hands on a pistol. However, though they are few and far between, the gunfights are most enjoyable. Cars play a big role in the game, and the driving is superb, though not perfect. The ramming mechanic is unrealistic but fun and certain vehicles (any truck) feels clunky. Also, there is no inventory system. You can not sheathe weapons or carry multiple guns. Typically, you can never take a weapon into free-roam from a mission, which reminds me: The game never gets tedious. The missions are plentiful and enjoyable, though some (like the Drug Busts) have the exact same structure (though a different environment) and tend to get a little repetetive, but not boring.
The graphics are amazing and I never thought I'd say it, but China is beautiful. The high-resolution texture pack is not that better than the base game, but it's better nonetheless. One thing I don't like, is that on Extreme Anti-Aliasing, the game hovers at about 30 frames per second, but on Ultra AA, the game hovers at 90. LOL WUT?
All in all, this game is fabulous. I don't understand why it wasn't hyped up or ranked up with games like Dishonored, Borderlands, and Far Cry 3. This truly was the most underrated title of 2012, and it closely ties with Dishonored for my game of the year.

EDIT BASED ON THE NOVEMBER 16TH UPDATE:
The game is still rough around the edges and I can't quite recommend this game to those who aren't intrested in helping further the game's development, or really like scientific accuracy.
With that being said I think with more polish and fixes this game could become one of the best dinosaur games on the market. I truly feel that this game represents something important for dinosaur media as a whole. It pretty common in modern media to show dinosaurs as movie monsters more akin to Godzilla than actual animals. This game manages to harness the feelings of awe and wonder that dinosaurs inherantly evoke, while at the same time presenting them as actual organisms.  In Saurian you aren't just another scaly killing machine, you are just anotehr creature trying its damnest to survive in an unforgiving but beautiful world. The world of Saurian isn't made beautiful by cutting edge graphics, its made beautiful by the elegic atmosphere of its vigourusly accurate ecosystem. The accuracy of this game isn't just a scientific statement, its a very effective aethetic choice.
However I'm afraid I still need to temper this review with some bugs I've continued to run across.
Although the scent ability for the Dakotarpator works much better now, there are still certain animals which don't appear on it at all. Crocodillians and Tyrannosaurs for me do not leave a scent trail nor are they highlighted. This is especially a problem in low light where I can just not see a Crocodillian in the grass and then get chomped by nothing, even though it was only a few feet in front of me and I was smelling the air.
Animals no longer seem to swim indefinetly nor do they run around in circles but just seem to stop reacting at certain points. Pachycephalasaurs sometimes will just stand in place, and one time I ran into an archeoraptor and it just stood there doing nothing while I chomped on it half a dozen times.
The raptor prey restraint seems to work better, but it is still pretty difficult to actually latch onto your prey. However I haven't been shot up 100 meters in the air yet so this mechanic is progressively getting better.

I love Xcom EU and EW, played and beat them both. I felt that those games were the perfect level of difficult, but fun. I play a lot of turn based strategy games, many of them roguelikes. I've put about 40 hours into this game and I all i have to say is that it should be called XCOM enemy overwhelming.
I've had multiple playthroughs, In some I've actually gotten pretty far along, but I always wind up getting ground into dust. 2-3 missions in they already start throwing the higher tier aliens at you, and in staggering numbers. Mathimatically speaking, when you have 6-8 enemies on screen, all with enough hitpoints to absorb 1-2 hits without dying even if you had a 100% chance to hit, its mathimatically impossible to down enough of them to keep your troops alive. Couple that with the 8-10 turns that they give you to complete the missions before you autofail, and the fact that you are usually escourting a civilian with 3 hitpoints and... well, you get the idea.
It's a shame, really. The character customization is amazing, the individual unit talent trees are fun and interesting, and I love the idea of flying around a stolen alien vessel as home base. The fact of the matter, however, is that the game is unplayably hard. I came to the reviews to see if other people had the same experience as I did, and apparently that isn't the case.  So I'm sure I'm going to be told to get good or whatever, or maybe i need to spend a few hours watching tutorial videos on youtube, but based on what I've seen playing the game, I'm really not sure it's even possible to win.
I was really excited for the release of this game, even shelled out the $60 to buy it when it first came out last year, which i suppose is fine since its still $60, amazingly. I would however like to get to a point where i can actually progress and see the story, but I play it for 4-6 hours at a time, fail miserably, and wind up shelving it for months because of how frustrating it is.
IMO save your money, wait till it goes on sale for cheap. You're only going to get to play the first 5-6 hours of the game anyway.

Tales of Berseria so far has been a super solid game.
The characters have a lot going on and aren't super distilled tropes like I remember Zestiria's being. They're also kind of a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and I really love it. They are genuinely an interesting cast that even in the span of like 8 hours has seen some growth. I'm genuinely surprised by the characters in small moments. I expect the tough lookin' Eizen to be kind of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but he ends up being a super cool guy. Or Rokuro to be kinda boring and angry, but he's instead really cut loose most of the time and has fun moments. Velvet slowly changes from a huge edgelord to slowly actually giving a damn about her team little by little.
The combat so far has been somewhat easy to blow through if you just mash, but getting fancy with it yields a ton of fun possibilities.
The music ranges from alright to good. I really like the battle theme.
The story is less about "save the world" and being all grand and epic and more of a set of personal stories with the main goal of getting revenge, which I enjoy a lot more. It also seems to take cues from the classic Berserk series, which isn't surprising in retrospect considering the name...
The game also looks pretty good. It reuses some assets from Zestiria, which is kind of a bummer, but everything else looks pretty nice. It also has some decent graphics options and runs at a smooth 60fps for me like 99% of the time.
The first hours might need some powering through, but once you get all the basic mechanics unlocked and are set free (about the time you get off the boat in the snow zone) to go around a bit more, then it opens up from there.
Strongly recommended if you like RPGs with an action combat system! It's a strong title, and apparently long time "Tales of" fans are digging it, too, so that's something.

Freedom Cry is the main DLC content for Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag and follows the efforts of Adewale, Edward Kenway's former quartermaster and now an Assassin, to aid the Maroon slaves rebellion around the town of Port'au'Prince.
Compared to the main game, Freedom Cry's main novelity as a DLC are the liberation side quest, which involves completing random events around the map in order to free slaves and obtain more rebels on the protagonist's side. Clearing these events becomes mandatory later on due to some main missions being unlocked only after a certain quota of slaves has been achieved. There are also some plantations the player can raid to further boost the rebels rank.
Aside from these events, Freedom Cry doesn't offer much new content or mechanics, fancing itself as just a smaller version of Black Flag which can be cleared in under four hours. It's also worth mentioning that the naval features are barely used in the DLC at all, due to the far smaller overall map and the main missions taking place mainly in Port'au'Prince.
What makes Freedom Cry worth a shot from any player from the Assassin's Creed series is the compelling story, which sets it quite apart from Edward's adventure and manages to be both engaging and rather touching

Addictive like you wouldn't believe. Realm of the Mad God provides a unique and refreshing take on the free to play MMO genre. It's got a charming 8-bit graphics style, a perma-death feature, and loads of fun content. That's right when you die in Realm of the Mad God you're dead for good. It's not actually a bad thing, sure you lose all of your gear and your character progress, but you never feel like the game is over for you. With numerous classes death gives you a fresh start to try something new. The gameplay is simple but addictive. You basically just run around and shoot everything in a large open world. As you gain levels you can fight tougher monsters and get better gear. There's no PVP, but rather the game encourages you to team up with people to take on the games more difficult monsters. The beauty of it is that you don't have to team up with other people if you don't want to. You can very well be a lone wolf, but the game is easier if you team up with others. The best part of this game is that you can play the game any way you want to. You can choose if you want to max out one character class, or you can stick with the class just long enough to unlock another one. You can play for hours at a time or just in short bursts. It's simple, addictive, and very accessible. The only real complaint I have is the lack of friendly players. So far most of the people I've come across are only interested in talking to you if you have something to offer them. In the end though I'm completely addicted to Realm of the Mad God. It's tons of fun and truly free to play outside of micro-transactions. So if your looking for a fun experience and are strapped for cash, or just love fun games, check of Realm of the Mad God.

I'll be happy to change my rating when Capcom irons out all the wrinkles, but in its current state, it still feels like a beta.

To start off:
The creator of the game is a amazingly kind guy who's a huge inspiration to anybody interested in the games development industry. Genuinely, if you have a issue - you can contact him and he'll help you none-stop until the issue is fixed. He'll go out of his way for you, if that doesn't have you sold, read on!
First off, the game is very unique in the way it works. From how you gather points to update things, to how you kill the enemies. The thought of a top-down shooter mixed with Tower-Defence and a tiny hint of RTS is a amazing idea and I'm excited to see more of the developers games.
The developers attempts at a mixture of visual styles; ranging from some cell-shaded, to the clear abstract style definately gives the game a very unique look; the geometric enemies make it very easy for the player to see where they're heading and is definately a positive for the game.
Furthermore, the unique sense that the game goes for somehow helps you get immersed in the game. The attempt at a story is room for huge props considering the game could have easily went without any explaination at all - you're just there to kill stuff and that's it. No; the developer is clearly dedicated and for the things that he does, deserves far more than just £3.99. At such a modest price - how could you not buy the game?
TL;DR:
The game is good, buy it.
You're better off playing Dota 2, Smite or League of Legends.  Although the concept is great, the execution isn't.

I'm going to repeat most of what
has stated, since I wholeheartedly agree.
I'm writing my own review, however, to bring down the ratio of positive to negative reviews, since I feel a bit deceived after buying a game that is apparently well received, but has some serious issues.
This game tries to combine the genre of tower defense with some sort of top-down shooting and a tiny bit of RTS.
The idea is nice, but it falls flat on it's face by how the game is balanced and tweaked.
You have to defend your core structure from spawning enemies that simply will try to walk towards it. If an enemy touches your core, you lose your life. You win a stage by completing three objectives, which are in the vain of "destroy 50 enemies".
The tower defense part consists of three types of towers. One passive resource gathering tower, and two offensive towers. The offensive towers are split up into a long range single-target tower and a short range splash damage tower.
The top down shooter is the most engaging part of the gameplay. It allows you to shoot bullets and missiles from the sky that hit the ground after a delay. This makes timing your shots a crucial aspect.
The final part is the extremely barebones RTS part. You gain resources that allow you to shoot (which requires ammunition) and buy towers. There are points on the map that you can take over with a special unit that allows you to get a resource bonus. These resources have to be safely transported though, akin to how harvesters worked in Command and Conquer.
Now to the actual plaguing issue of the game.
The tutorial gives you unlocked higher-tier weapons and tower upgrades to play with, but once you get to the actual game, you are left with peashooters. The game doesn't compensate for your lack of firepower in the first stages by giving you less enemies. You now have to deal with slowly moving hordes of enemies that you have to kill using weapons that reload slow and do little damage, and by using towers that also have to reload a long time between shots.
I had to turn the difficulty to the lowest level to be able to survive any stage. Attempting or successfully finishing a stage rewards you with points that you can spend towards unlocking better weapons. Having some sort of fun seems to behind a grindwall.
There are a handful of level packs (around 7 if I remember correctly). The levels contain multiple stages, with the only change between them being the objectives given. The layout is identical and so seem the timing of enemy spawns.
So what you end up with is a neat idea packed into horrid balancing.
It is genuinely impressive that this game was made by a single person, since it looks well, sounds nice and has a decent idea behind it. The author likes to really remind you of this fact, however. Showing it in the starting screen, in it's company name and in half of his posts on the game page.
All that it needed was some playtesting and tweaking. But it seems like instead of publishing a good game the first time around, we live in a time where developers can just keep trying things with the thought of being able to patch anything in the back of their minds.
I rather had waited and played this game in a more fun state, than the current product.
This game is really great, tons of fun, I highly recommend it. Def worth paying for it, if you haven't already got it.

The Walking Dead is amazing, especially for story driven fans like me. I wish the sequels could match S1's level of awesomeness.
