is something I believe I have never seen before, part tower defense and part real time orbital shooter makes it one of the most interesting tower defense games I’ve played in recent times.
The theme of the game is rather interesting, you are tasked with defending a computer system against waves of malicious software. The maps are layout fit perfectly this theme, with spawn points for the enemies being USB ports and having different types of enemies that you can kill, including neutral creeps that grant you resoruces in the form of “cookies”.
Aesthetically speaking, I’m a huge fan of these simplistic visuals and the “digital” look to them and the different tracks of eletronic music are also rather pleasant to listen to. That said, if you get stuck on a level for a while they can get quite irritating because the music just goes on a loop.
The game lets you choose 1 out of 3 different difficulty modes with the most challenging one being “Normal”, ironic isn’t it? After playing through a couple of the first few levels I was forced to choose a lower difficulty level in order to proceed because the game was too hard on me on the “Normal” difficulty. This allowed me to return back to normal later on because, as you play you’ll gain a specific currency that you can then use to upgrade your turrets and abilities. The amount of currency that you get per level depends on the difficulty you’re playing on and if you complete or not certain sets of 3 tasks (3 tasks = 1 challenge = 1 challenge per level) that you have in each level.
You’ll also increase your rank the higher difficulty you play on, but rank serves only as a metric and has no real impact in the outcome of the game, at least thats how I perceive it. There are a total of 49 challenges (147 challenges) and while there are only 3 weapons/abilities that you can use at any given time but their upgrades amount for a total of 21 different types of weapons. Still, they’re pretty much variants of a machine gun, rocket and a meteor attacks. In that sense, there is only 3 different towers that you can place but they also have 21 variants. You’ve got a production tower, a close range and a long range tower. Nonetheless I didn’t really find myself using towers that much, other than the production towers, when compared with other Tower Defense games and that is why I say that this is more of a top down orbital shooter than it is a Tower Defense.
On each level you’ll have to prevent the enemy creeps from reaching your nodes. You may also send units to key points in order to gain resources (RAM) and use that to buy new towers or to use your weapons, which cost a certain amount of RAM per use. The level design is probably one of the weakest points of the game for me. Levels are flat and usually the only obstacles between the enemy entry points and your OS (Operative System) are these square structures that force the enemies to go around them. Usually you can only place your offensive turrets in an area given to you on each level. Other than that, you can use your offensive anytime and anywhere you want, provided that you have the RAM for it.

Artificial Defense is an interesting, strange beast. Interesting because it combines 3 types of games in one and strange, well... it was all done by one guy: programming, graphics, music - all of them from one guy and all of them at a high level of polish. That by itself is enough to warrant you to try it out as it does feel like the game is the labour of someone who is a developer but first and foremost also a gamer.
The main aim of the game is to save your OS from becoming corrupted by external sources. These sources generate invaders which try to reach your OS and corrupt it. By preventing them, both directly and indirectly, from reaching your OS and by buying time via various ways, you try to prevent the corruption from reaching your OS before you do what is known as a shutdown, i.e. you close the map and get your points. The game does not force you to do so, however and you can keep raking up points, if you are capable of doing so :P So how do the 3 mechanics fit together? Well you can directly fire and shoot (top-down) on the invaders in order to stop them. You have 3 main weapons available and each can be upgraded in between missions to increase their damage and other attributes. (This reminded me of how I used to shoot rats while playing Theme Hospital.) You can also build towers which generate resources or stop enemies passively as they flow by them. These also can be upgraded in-between missions to become more effective. Finally you can capture certain points on the map (ala Z, if anyone of you remember that game) which can be used to generate resources passively for you to use. These can be recaptured by the enemy if you are not careful! Each of the 3 mechanics require resources to be spent, but all 3 give you a way to generate resources. If you shoot what are known as cookies you gain resources, if you build a resource tower, they passively generate resources, if you capture certain points on the map they give you resources. There are a million other small things I could mention but there is depth in every part of the game.
For the negatives: I found the learning curve quite steep initially until I played a bit and discovered how it all works. After contacting the developer he has assured me that my concerns are currently being addressed in an update he is working on at the current moment. Fantastic as it would be a shame to see such a nice game not become popular because of its inherent depth in mechanics!
If you are a tower-defense fan and you like to try something different rather than the usual build tower, wait until level finishes, I would recommend trying this game. At it's current price I think it's very worthwhile and you would be supporting an indie developer to continue doing what they like doing: making great games.

First Impressions:
At first I thought "Oh no, I'm not prepared, what do I do when I get a role that's hard to have?",
but after a few moments of utter anxiety I decided to just jump in:
I joined a Classic, Classic Game, and the game gave me the role of the Sheriff.
I kept quiet mostly, I didn't see anyone suspicious. Also I noticed you could leave a message on death,
thus I simply filled in everything I found, everyone who was innocent.
And I didn't die. At the end of the game, only 3 of us were left. And the Serial Killer was trying to blame me.
I revealed my role and luckily the other townie believed me.
We won because the only other townie trusted me.
The Second Game threw me right into the Serial Killer role. I managed to kill 5 people without even popping up in the suggestions then someone just declared to "Randomly lynch" me. I was still happy, I mean, I learned from that.
The Third Game I was a vigilante. I didn't do anything and we won in the end by luck mostly.
The fourth game I was an executioner. They killed my target in the night though, so I ended up as a jester. Then I was killed in the night aswell.  The fifth game directly spawned me as a jester and I was killed in the night but it was fun.
The sixth game then spawned me as a Veteran... and I wasted my 3 alerts cause half the nights, nobody would get killed.
The seventh and my last game so far, then introduced me to the role of the jailor.
I didn't last very long, got killed in night two, missed the icon to take someone with me in night one.
I still enjoyed it very much.
The people I met were surprisingly mature and also had a decent spelling, something you can barely see in some communities and not once did I feel unskilled or scared of failure.
Failure is fun, it's amazing to see how it all plays out.
And I don't really have any complaints either.
Every role is explained by some boxes on screen,
there was no time where I thought "Oh gosh, what am I doing?"
The nights nobody attacked anyone made the game longer, sure,
but those few minutes? Oh Please! I'm very patient.
If you're a fan of tabletop games that are like this game,
e.g. One Night - Ultimate Werewolf, I can recommend this very much.
It may seem silly but that sort of Tabletop game is something you need at the very least
6 people to play and have it be fun. Here?
you can avoid the player count entirely because it's online!
Now that I think about it, I do have one complaint.
I can't seem to stop playing. Heh~!

Sound: Nice Menu OST, but a tad loud, crank it down to 1% Volume and it'll be alright.

Ok now after a 100hrs of play (yeah I know my stat says 130 or so but thats because I left the PC on with the game during weekends to avoid booting it up) I can finally write my review of this game, as an introduction statement I can confirm this game is FEELINGS above REASON and a LOVE story convered in a DARK velvet. Here are my facts of the game:
PRO
-World: Vast and enormous is the world of Berseria, the game itself requires more than 80hrs to cover it all (50% more than the last entry), enemies roaming around from evil to just in hunting you down.
-Battle: the battle system has evolved compared to Zestiria it really resembles the name Berseria (berserk), it still holds some parameters that avoid you hack n slash all the time but it is way faster and more satisfactory than ever before. No camera issues this time around.
-Story: at first I thought the game had a simple story, just this guy against this other but after 1/3 of the game, the story starts to give plot twist and plot twist, it makes me remember Symphonia in that sense. Truly depth for a tales game and entertaining enough for you to continue playing without care of anything else.
-Characters: the strongest key point of the tales games are the characters, and this game doesnt disappoint in that regard. The characters in Berseria make the best and strongest key factor in this game, they are memorable, they have personality, they evolve, they progress, they grow, everything you want in an RPG from a character this game has it.
-Graphics: the game looks as awesome and even better than the previous game and its less demanding than the previous game, they truly make a great port of this game I really need to applaud Namco for this.
-Quests: at first the amount of quests are small, like really few, but as the game progress more quests starting popping up to the point that they are so many that it will take you additional hours to complete (hence the additional 20hrs it took me).
-Difficulty: START IN HARD MODE! REALLY! The game is EASIER than other Tales I have played. Other harder difficulties will be unlocked (yes unlocked, not paid) after you finish certain quests, and when you do increase the difficulty. Otherwise the game will start to feel very easy towards the middle part of the game and forth.
-Leveling up: Harder difficulties will make you level up, well, harder (duh) but the benefit is that enemies will drop items more often,  these items have "skills" equipped in them that you will inherit when you fulfill the progress bar based on your GRADE in the fights (the better you fight the faster you progress in inheriting the equip skills). This skills go from more stats to something like making more damage in certain circumstances or enemies. This help you compense your lack of level in harder difficulties.
-Grinding: I know what you are thinking "Grinding is a PRO?! What is wrong with you?!" hear me out, grinding is FUN in this game. How so? In harder difficulties and the more grade you receive in the area, you are prompt to have a visit from a DIRE FOE at the end of one of your fights, which is a strong foe that will give you strong equip items. This FOE will appear once again when you fulfill this conditions in the same area, but the second time it will be stronger, and so the third, the fourth time and so forth. You see why grinding now is fun? Also grinding will help you grow your level faster in Cooking since it is triggered at the end of each battle. You dont want to grind? Sure its your decision but remember the harder the game the less EXP you will receive and the only thing to back you up are the equip skills you will receive.
-NO DLC Story : yes thats a plus meaning the whole story is packed here.
-AI: the AI is better in this game compared to other tales games, it also helps that the combat system is more fluid and faster, in the hardest battles I felt backed up by my partners most of the time contraty to me being watching over them.
-Side quests: the side quests, most of them in fact, are entertaining since they push the character growth, at first they may not look meaningful but as the game progress they will.
-Skits: Villians + Sadistic + Humor = TONS of laughs.
-Music: the music is varied, touching, amazing, memorable and the classic Berseria tune stuck with me even after playing. If possible I want to purchase the OST.
PLUS:
-If you have played Zestiria you are in for a ride. You will know more deeply the world, where everything comes from, the references, even care more deeply for the characters since they have (or will have since Berseria is a prequel) a relationship with the Zestiria characters. Same goes for the locations you will see. Having played Zestiria before Berseria made my interest go thru the roof and my hype while playing beyond control, these weeks I didnt do anything other than play and work (let that sink in).
CONS:
-Dungeons: the dungeons are not so as dungeons they are lineal dungeons or big hallways, floor puzzling at best but just that, not memorable and some are more lengthly than I would like them to be. Some of them I was half thru and I thought "when does this end!? I want to continue the story come on!".
-Lack of customization: compared to Zestiria, there is no customization in this game. Yes you can still custom the equipment of each character but the equip skills compared to Zestiria can be shared between the characters by simply, well, sharing the equip, so at the end if all your characters rotate with the equips you find all of them will have the same equip skills (see where I am going?). There are other tid bits you could customize in Zestiria that in Berseria is not possible, it feels like a drawback even if that made the game simpler and more focused on the other important key points.
CONS: (PERSONAL)
-Costumes: this is a bad thing for me since one thing I like from the tales games are the costumes, alternative versions of the default one, swimsuits, weird other costumes, and this game have just so few ones its kind of sad for me.
Final score: 85-90/100. Highly recommended.

My Grand Replay of all things Fallout has come to its conclusion. Maybe my daughter will one day wonder how dad managed to play hundreds of hours of video games around the time she was born. Or maybe Steam will be long dead by 2030. This kind of peek into one's parents' past is unprecedented if you think about it. Pretty soon 2000s kids will start scrolling through the detailed life log that is the Facebook feed of their parents, asking all sorts of questions : )
Fallout 4 has it's flaws. It is clearly a sibling of Fallout 3, yet again featuring a far too lifelike (as in boring) depiction of an East Coast city. Thankfully we were spared the generic metro tunnels, which makes post apocalyptic Boston a tad bit better than post apocalyptic D.C., but it still doesn't hold a candle to New Vegas or even New Reno. The Institute has been in the works for longer at Bethesda and is therefore more fleshed out than the Enclave of F3, but again pales compared to Caesar's Legion or The Master.
This time around we've sadly been deprived of the 'consequences slides' at the end of the game and the dumbed down family friendliness of Bethesda's newer RPGs is digging it's roots ever deeper. Of the DLCs, Far Harbor was cliche but good, the rest I wouldn't recommend buying at their individual price points. There's going to be a GotY edition pretty soon so that won't really be a problem. Nuka World surprises positively with its amount of content, but forces you to either end everything prematurely or suddenly become the bad guy. As a completionist you have to become evil. The other DLCs might as well not have been.
Objectively though, there are few games that are better than Fallout 4. Lots to explore, good story, interesting companions, satisfying combat. You can spend a hundred hours on the settlement building part of the game alone. They've made the Brotherhood a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s for a change, so there's a creative twist for you. Maxed out, the graphics are exquisite. Upgrading weapons is interesting enough, if heavy on the adhesive stockpiling : )
Fortunately I'm the kind of guy who likes canon playthroughs so the Creation Club BS, while disappointing, really doesn't ruffle my feathers all that much.

As it has been before, it stayed an unrivalled classic. Since its release, Half-Life has become a massive phenomenon and inspiration for many games to come.
How does it play today? I'd say if you don't mind playing older games on your computer, albeit a powerhouse or one with aged specs, then this game is an absolute must-have. Many even consider the original Half-Life to be a better game than the acclaimed masterpiece sequel Half-Life 2, which is a very important statement, considering Half-Life 2 is a game nearing perfection in every way possible.
Gameplay is fast and easy to adjust to, Storyline is impressive, especially for a basic FPS shooter - this is one of the most convoluted, interesting storylines that I have followed, and the legendary arc does start in the first game, therefore it's very important not to miss out. Graphics, as dated as they are, are very smooth, even moreso in the Source remake. Vast selection of guns, and a very long playtime for an FPS. Appreciating classics does help when revisiting this experience, as it has dated a solid bit since it came out almost 2 decades ago, but if it is bothersome to play such an old game then I suggest buying Black Mesa (the fan-made remake made official on Steam), or waiting for Black Mesa to officially finish their second part of the game and buy the finished game when it comes out (which is presumably in the next year).
To give it a grade is hard, because I did grow up on this timeless classic, so I will probably just put it into 2 grades:
For those who have never played Half-Life I suggest bouncing on the Black Mesa train, but this game will come down to an 8/10 -- whereas for me this game has been and will always stay a solid 10/10. If you want to revisit this game for the nostalgia factor, as so many people I imagine have played this when they were growing up, this is an amazing experience regardless.

Intro:
After nearly a year of below par games, both indie and AAA, Blackwake is really a game to behold.  Despite the lack of content, I have been able to put in over 20 hours in two days with the pure excitement and engagement that no other game with a lack of content can provide.  This is also not to mention the waves of free updates to come that will provide even more play time.  This team of two developers knew what they and the players wanted, and did not fail to provide.
Content (at the time of this review):
-  battles with up to 6 ships on each server, with 2 different kinds of ships, galleons and hoys
-  realistic cannon reloading and firing
-  great team communication mechanics
-  teamwork based gameplay
-  ship roles to help the crew (unofficial roles ranging from suppliers to sail repairers)
-  amazing ship combat mechanics
-  melee and ranged player combat
-  ship boarding
-  few others I may have missed
Pros:
-  Great combat mechanics, both ship and player
-  Fails to get boring
-  Encourages good teamwork and communication skills
-  Very few bugs despite what others are saying
-  Plans for large content updates
Cons:
-  Slight lack of customization, but will probably be added soon
-  Few bugs that can get annoying at times
-  (personal problem)  If you have a friend that's a great captain, it's difficult to join back on the ship next round because the server floods their ship next time, a party system would be appreciated.

For future reference I'm going to update this review as time goes on.
As it stands right now, Saurian is a very unique game and an amazing achievement. There exists few other games that want to tackle a realistic dinosaur survival. Otherwise just wait until it gets updated more to your liking because currently only the Dakotaraptor is playable as I write this review.
However, since writing it they have already patched some major bugs and added a new dinosaur. All of this happened in one day's time. I hope to see some great things from this game. If you've beaten Black Flag and want more, this will mostly do the trick. Set 13-15 years after AC4, Adewale has risen from Kenway's right-hand man, to a full-fledged Assassin/Captain. After an intense opening scene, he finds himself washed ashore and caught in the midst of a civil struggle. It's time to free some slaves, hence the subtitle of the game. There are many different scenarios in which you can free said slaves. Some will be locked in a cage, and you have to kill the guard carrying the key. Others will be working on plantations, in which you must eliminate a certain number of guards to free them.
Freeing as many slaves as possible actually grants you bonuses, and sometimes even needed to advance the story. The bonuses range from free restocks on ammunition, to even new weapons. With slaves pratically all over the place ready to be liberated, achieving these bonuses doesn't exactly take a long time.
As you'd expect, Freedom Cry does have naval content, including it's own (DLC sized) open-world map. Attacking and boarding other ships for goods is still relevant, but nowhere near as much as Black Flag. A lot of the locations to discover are unfortunately pretty dull. There's several islands which consist of only a small beach and one chest to open, then you're done there. I'm not sure why Ubisoft even bothered, as it's probably the most disappointing part of FC. Still, just sailing the open sea remains a joy to behold. No sea shanties (pirate songs), however.
Just like Black Flag, Freedom Cry is GORGEOUS. It's a shame that sometimes some information is still present on your screen, even with the HUD options turned "all off", because I love taking clean screenshots. Even so, it's such a beautiful game to behold, especially the water. You'll catch yourself just staring at the visuals and remember there's a game to play.
I was surprised with the length of FC. I expected to be done in about 3-4 hours, but my save file clocks-in at almost 9 hours. That's including all side-content. Not a bad chunk of time for a piece of something that's stand-alone DLC. So, if you want a demo of Black Flag, this is the closest you'll get of that experience. Granted, Black Flag is obviously the fuller experience, but I do recommend buying this if you're wondering what it's like.
I am pleased with the time I spent with Freedom Cry. A lovely slice of Assassin/Pirate content to keep one's interest for a decent amount of time.

One of the best Tales games there is, coming from a veteran of the series.  There was a lot of weight riding on the shoulders of Berseria coming into launch, particularly with how poorly Zestiria was received, and this game easily handled it.
Characters: The highlight of this game.  The dialogue is engaging, emotional, and really pulls you into the journey that each individual person is embarking on, main character or otherwise.
Story: Also a significant strong point of this game.  Intense story that pulls you in from the inciting incident, until the closing line.  Not the most innovative story, but the journey is fantastically well made.
Combat:  The combat is fun, but Velvet is op.  I had to crank up the difficulty just to feel some tiny amount of challenge when fighting enemies.  Just be careful when turning it up too high or you might unsuspectingly meet your end when a dire foe pops up.  Try the other characters, they're all fun.
Dungeons: This is where I'd take off points if I were going to.  The old twisting/unique dungeon designs of abyss/vesperia are a thing of the past.  Basically every single dungeon design in this game is a grid format with a different skin.  I think the only time I saw any deviation of the format was in the very final dungeon, which was a headache to go through.  Definitely not something to prevent me from enjoying the game in the slightest, but just be aware that they will eventually feel repetitive.
TL;DR: Buy it.  The story and characters alone make this game completely worth it in my opinion.  I even liked it so much it made me want to go back and give Zestiria another shot...

This is the best "Tales of" game I've played, bar none, and it takes its place in the upper echelon of JRPGs for my money.
Much less of the "hope and friendship" spiel that pervades the series.  Far darker, far more attuned to the consequences of the party's actions, and for once we're given pretty believable motivations for a party to stick together.  Perhaps the best iteration of the battle system (Vesperia might compete on this and main character).   One of the most entertaining casts of the series (if only the fire and earth seraphs from Zestiria joined this cast.....).  The gear system is a little grindier than I might like (upgrade materials can be a pain) but the permenance of learned skills is very nice.
The graphics are pretty enough, though the environments generally fail to be stunning (Aball is a noted exception).  There's a ton of optional content although most of it is backloaded.    The one disappointing aspect of the game is the music, which is on the whole a letdown after Zestiria.  Still, there are good themes.

As a fan of fighting games in general, this game (so far) has been very dissapointing.
Even though I get into fighting games becuase of the gameplay, I chose SF since the eraly days of IV because of the interesting characters. As such, if you want a great offline/single player experience, this game wil in fact dissapoint you.
I know they wanted to focus on the story later and use what we have here as "story mode" to be more of an introduction, but it also fails to meet the purpose, to get new palyers interested. Heck, I know SF story and lore and most of the character interactions and battles where very nonsensical and out of nowhere. Plus, battles in story mode are maximum 3 rounds, and I say rounds becuase there is only one per match with infinite time and the A.I. is so bad that it barely puts up a fight. You will be getting easy Perfects.
But going into the online, I have not managed to connect to the servers, and that also means that everything you do offline without being connected does not register for progress in your game profile as you gain in game currency (fight money) and experience, but again only if connected to the servers.
I would only recommend this to people trying to get into a brad new game for the online play, but even that is toufh as many seem to have trouble connecting. Lacking in the single player department, rushed art from Bengus, battles are not real battles and the little stories are also very terribly performed. They could have been better if they took actual effort in them. And the voice acting for some instances is unberable for most of the cast, but with some exceptions like Dhalsim, but the majority is in the quality of Shonen Anime stereotype.

This game is one of the best teamwork games I've ever played, but it needs a lot of improvements. In short, I will give it a 8/10.
pros:
GAME-EXPERIENCES
Almost every one in this game is delicated in their roles like captain and sailors, that is the most important point of this game. I've met a good captain, Jack Sparrow style. He even lined us up and gave us a lecture. Well, that's exactly what we come for, the feeling of being sailors. You have to prepare a microphone if you want to enjoy this game or you can hardly get involved to the whole team.
GAME-TYPES
An FPS, yes it is. But not like the others. You die after getting shot. You keep bleeding until death if you are hurt. You fire one shot then unleash your blade because it takes a while to reload. These are far more different than other FPS like Counter-Strike.
GOOD SERVERS
I use VPN to connect other servers and i've never got disconnected or "WALK IN THE AIR" like some games even though my ping is kind of high sometimes.
cons:
ROLE-PLAYING
I've got to realize that the one of the most importance is the captain. Other people can be even replaced by AI because their jobs are quite simple. The developers should find some ways to keep sailors busy or "UNIQUE".
GAMEPLAYS
3 warships VS 3 warships is far from enough! We need more like 6v6! 10 vs 10!
We want more kinds of ships!
We want more kinds of sea areas!
We want more game modes!
We want more methods to invade or destroy other ships!
BUGS
People running in the water, people walking in the sky.
MELEE WEAPONS
You feel nothing when you hit your enemy with your sword. I miss the feeling of slashing in Left 4 dead 2. Acutually the developer says that it will be improved.
SUPPORTS
The support of controllers are really not friendly to controller users like me. And languages, more languages should be supported like Chinese and French.

I knew nothing about this game other than a recomendation that it was amazing and that I should play it now when I first booted up Bastion, and I was not disapointed. While the gameplay itself seems simple at first, like a traditional hack-and-slash, it quickly becomes a fairly deep experience. Enforcer is a simulator game for being a police officer. You work every day and do missions that dispatch gives you, check for drunk drivers check for expired licence plates and such. From time to time you get a "special" crime such as murder robery and assault.
The game it self is not bad, i personaly enjoyed it. But ofcourse it is not perfect and there is room for improvement.
The physics engine isnt really doing its job well but tbh it kinda ads to the fun. The 20 € they ask for the game is a tad to much and i simply do not belive the game it self is worth that much
but if the game dev's improve some parts of it i would definitly recomend this. I have gotten this game in a giveaway and i am happy with it.
The +'s of the game :
The feeling of driving around as a police officer is really good. You can advance your carrer by doing good things. Ofcourse you can write tickets to the people who did nothing wrong but you get penalized which i really like, since it removes the "being a cop like in GTA" feeling. You can see your actions give good or bad results. There are several "maps" or well, area's inside of the mountain town you are working in and that gives it some diversity. You can get better police cars and you can even have some sorth of a customization when it comes to your police (and the civilan car you can own later in the game (its costly))
Some other features i enjoyed in this game were the fact that you can use comply to make people listen to you, its not one of those meh youre just a cop, you actualy have some respect and authorty as a police officer. There are ofcourse moments where the perp's run away by foot or by car and you have to chase them which adds to the game's action.
Id like to add that the graphics in this game is relativly ok and that it doesnt really kill the good vibe the game has.
The -'s of the game :
Like ive said in the upper part of this review the physics engine is a bit dull, if it happens that you are parked on the sidewalk people will walk all over your car, if you accidentily run someone over you will just slide underneeth them.
Another thing i find bothersome is the "roadblock" with the traffic cones simply stop the car, there is no riding around them and such which i belive would improve the game a ton.
And maybe a bit more variaty in the missions we get since, stoping 20 cars is ok but still. Im sure that higher rank cops dont do that :)
All in all i would recomend this game to people, maybe not for 20 but i do belive that you should grab it if you find it on sale. The 12 hours i have on this game (atm) have been speent by enjoying in the game, and not really being bothered by it.
Also to finish this game isnt for everybody, so do watch the trailers, and do follow it. Since i belive with effort from the dev's this can become a really good Police Simulator.

Wow. I suppose that's the best word to describe my thoughts on this game. Finally, a tower defense game that innovates! And it's actually quite good!
So, let me clarify something - calling this a "tower defense" game is actually kind of horribly incorrect. It's more of an orbital shooter with a bit of TD and RTS sprinkled in the mix. I had initially thought I'd be placing towers and whatnot like usual, but instead the towers are merely an option the game includes to simply help you out.
See, Artificial Defense is what some people have called an "orbital shooter", like I mentioned earlier. I've never really heard this term before, but it makes sense - one of your two methods available of killing the little nasty creeps invading your computer system (the setting of the game) is to rain down bullets, rockets, and bombs onto the little buggers. It's pretty interesting, and definitely makes the game seem more RTS-like than anything.
Yet, there's also aspects of the tower defense genre of course. This means that you need to place production buildings to acquire RAM, which allows you to then either fire projectiles at the enemies yourself, since that costs RAM, or you can place either long range or short range towers. The long range towers have to reload, but their range is obviously a bit larger than the short range tower, which fires quicker but has a much smaller range than its counterpart.
The weird thing is though that for the most part I found myself rarely using offensive towers. Instead, I preferred to rush production buildings and just fire away myself at the creeps. This is because the game isn't really about lasting as long as you can, though that option is available to you. Instead, the game's progression system focuses on completing a set of 3 objectives that are specific to each level. These can include just simply killing a set number of foes or something weirder like sending out some little blobs of your own to "conquer" a building on the playing field. And here's where the game becomes a little too chaotic for more casual RTS players like me: juggling the 3 objectives while simultaneously trying to survive can be a bit daunting for inexperienced players in the genre. Yet, the game does include 3 difficulty settings in case things become too hard.
Thankfully, even though the 49 levels become harder as you progress, especially with the new enemies introduced every 7 levels or so, there's also a shop where upgrades for your weaponry, towers, or system itself can be bought. So, a really difficult level can be made a bit easier by buying new rockets for example. The interesting bit about the shop is that new upgrades aren't necessarily the best option for every level since older upgrades may actually be better depending on the situation. This creates a great extra layer of strategy in some cases and it's a nice touch that older upgrades can still be equipped.
In terms of the basics, that's pretty much it. The graphics aren't incredible but they're functional and fit the theme of the game (since it takes place in a computer). What did impress me however is the music - it manages to be energetic and engaging while not being overbearing or annoying. It's some kind of electronic stuff, but I enjoyed it (can you tell that I'm a musical genius who just knows all the correct terminology?).
Artificial Defense is something unique for its genre(s?), and that's one of the key factors I personally look at when deciding if I'm interested in a game or not. It's more of a RTS than a tower defense game, but for fans of either genre, it's a fantastic title to check out. Plus, it's made by one guy!

If you're looking for a single-player tower defence game with firable "artillery" skills, Artificial Defense packs a hearty punch. Straightforward and clean mechanics, with session-to-session persistence allow the user to buy upgrades over multiple levels. The levels are diverse and challenging, involving varied objectives that keep the experience fresh. The thematic choice of defending a computer system is a unique and interesting twist on the genre  providing a consistent and interesting world to play in. Though not core to any mechanics, the soundtrack is great too!
Overall an impressive game for a one-man team that offers a challening and engaging experience!

Just in 20 mins, I has changed my idea on this product from a negative to a positve, because I find what makes me so disgusted is the experience of such life, the opinions on the life held by THOSE, and the actions and comments THEY took and made to THIS story.
Some people may hold such kind of ideas: it doesn't matter even if this game is bad, because it is so cheap and has only 1-hour playing. My opinion is: save your money for another product you feel more interested and save your life once you feel bored if you had decided to have a try,
There are hundreds of ideas on what a game is and what a game should be. I have read an article referring this product as 'a poem of self expression'. If so, the question would changed to 'what a poem is' and 'FOR WHICH the self-expression is' (so what).
These are my concerns if we don't follow a traditional viewpoint of video game. And, I can hardly share any resonance coming from those 'thump ups' under this product. Or to be honest, I dislike the feeling evaporated from such resonance. The only reason for me to write this comment rather than to simply leave it alone is: Many positive ideas echoing here, and this may imply the need for a sound representive of people to speak out.
Now, let me consider this as a game, then there are two points I believe should be developed more: the narrative and the gameplay (more precisely, the interaction).
Obviously, the flow of a story should be smooth so that audiences can dive into the virtual world. It should be the reason why many people replying positively that most of them find themselves somewhere during playing. However, this game doesn't keep the pace with its story due to the fact that the narrator here is a combination based on speech (instead of text-reading) and interwoven with interaction with players.
In other words, the interaction doesn't work well to enhance the story-telling, this product could be published as:
a visual novel or galgame with moe moe paintings, or
a sound book without any pics and interaction, or
a click-game (not a puzzle one) as mentioned in the game description.
So what's the necessarity for putting these media together if they don't improve the final experience? The only answer I could find is:
. That's the reason why someone said it is a game which the people who like it would like it so deep while the other might not dislike it any more. It could be argued that
is essential to like this game.
I think I should stop here because it seems it is the story this product's heart, not the gameplaly.

As much as i love XCOM mechanically, this game has its fair share of problems.
For starters: No mods other than a stuttering fix installed and the mod "Stop Wasting My Time." I am not complaining about the combat; the RNG cheats in your favor and all the whining about difficulty is unwarranted and covered in other reviews.
>Bugs, bugs, bugs. Can't squash them! Everything from opening a door.. only for it not to open, to failing a 100% hacking chance (lol), AI clipping into a building and getting stuck, and the camera locking and staring at something for minutes at a time, save data not carrying through loads properly.. really ruins the experience.
>Frontloaded content, bad pacing. The game has a timer you have to beat the game by. No big deal, other than it's not cohesive to the sheer amount of things that crop up to do. It wouldn't be so bad if it weren't along the lines of "scan for 7 days, 4 events pop up to interrupt you." This is only further compunded if you own any of the narrative/story DLCs, as there will be more events to deal with. There are also in-mission timers, of which the concept itself does not bother me, but the timer length itself does. Some missions, you will be forced to rush a unit recklessly to an objective, only to trigger a group of aliens and watch them be killed. It won't always be the case, but for players that hate throwing caution in the wind, this game will punish them for playing a certain way.
>Poor optimisation. It doesn't matter if you have a beast of a PC; there WILL be graphical issues, stuttering, audio desyncing, etc even with mods and tweaks to help fix it. Even the cutscenes sometimes fail to play properly.
>Getting to the point! This game has lots of stupid delays, which only makes the point above feel even worse. Ordered a unit to fire? Watch them do nothing for 2 seconds before they do. Ordered a movement? Delay. Camera switches to enemies? Watch it linger for 3-5 seconds for no reason afterwards. just pulled a sweet flank and watched someone dump a s***load of critical damage into an enemy? Okay, they'll die 2 seconds after getting hit. It's absolutely annoying and while there is a community made mod to help with it there are still some delays they could not deal with without breaking something or causing issues. It would not be a big deal if it weren't happening consistently.
Really, for a $60 game with $40 major DLC and everal other sets of content expansions, it's inexcusable. Count on mods and console comamnds to slap a bunch of baind aids over the glaring issues. Don't pay full price.

I don't usually go for games in early access, but my friend pointed out Saurian to me and I was intrigued. As an early access game and a proof of concept, it nails that right down. But in its current state, it is very poorly optimised and even on my relatively decent PC I could only get 10 FPS on the lowest graphics settings.
But the concept is definitely there. You play as a baby dinosaur (in the early access version you only have one dinosaur species to pick) and your goal is to survive. It is not easy. This is hardcore survival if ever I've seen it. Plus it's dinosaurs. How can you not want to play as a dinosaur?
In its early access stage it's a bit difficult for me to recommend it in its current form but I'm going to go ahead and give it a recommendation because so far it looks very promising and I'm excited to see where the developers go from here with it!

Oh boy, Capcom. Now let me get this out of the way. From a technical standpoint this game is fine. I get a solid 1080p 60fps at high settings with my gtx 960 with no frame drops. -fight money and exp can't be earned offline through story and survival meaning that if the servers are down (like they are at the time of this review then you shouldn't even bother with either mode)
-The story is extremely short even by fighting game standards. All characters stories can be completed in 40 minutes.
-no spectator mode
-only two player lobbies
-no cpu vs cpu in versus mode as well as no player vs cpu battles outside of survival for the latter.
The game is great and fun to play but I would hold out until march or June when it has more updates. Once Capcom adds more content I'll change my review but until then hold off.

The gameplay itself is enjoyable, the visuals are pleasing and the collection one can build is quite appealing to me, this game has severe problems
--Firstly: The grind is insane, normally you're carried through a story whilst grinding away your levels, here there's no lore whatsoever to try and pull you through, instead you just wonder the wasteland and attack any dungeon you find
--Second: While the gameplay is pleasant it is so insanely repetitive, often times MMOs will have varying mechanics, enemies that have a trick to beating them etc, here it's entirely holding down LMB while occasionally using your other 2 abilities, I say 2 because you always start with your ultimate and that's on cooldown for too long.
--Third: The server is garbage, it doesn't matter what I do, how much troubleshooting I attempt or how many times I've contacted Trion, I can not get this game to run under 230ping with severe rubberbanding, even in the low times! I find myself standing still and suddenly being flung across the bossroom to realise I've lost half my health by standing in fire I wasn't aware of. Walking or gliding to another location is even worst as I'm constantly swung back and forth as though I were a ping pong ball and ultimately it is so infuriating the game is as good as unplayable, this issue isn't just me either, it seems to be an extremely common problem that Trion seems to have no desire to fix.
TL;DR: The game is fun though the grind is dull, however it's current server's state renders it so frustrating I would consider it unplayable, unless you wish to roleplay a tennis ball I don't recommend this game, not until they make serious improvements to their internet service and servers

I'll start my review by saying this: Starbound has been in early access for 2 years. Starbound recieved over 2 MILLION dollars from preorders. This is absolutely unacceptable.
Starbound is a 2-D sandbox game similar to Terraria. You dig, fight, and explore in order to get better equipment and armor. When starting the game, you have a lot of different choices when it comes to making your character. There are seven different races to choose from, each one fairly customizable. Each race has their own armor sets, ships, and they even say different things about objects in the enviroment. This is one of Starbound's very few charms.
Once you leave your ship, you'll find yourself in a randomly generated planet. You're able to fight the local fauna and mine for coal and ores, and perhaps even find cities full of one of the races you were presented upon making a character. This is fun at first! There seems like there's a lot to do.
However, once you begin travelling to different planets, the illusion wears off. The majority of these planets you explore are pretty much the same formula, but with something slightly different slapped on. Yes, the trees might look different, and the water might be a different color, but overall, it's the same experience. Dig for ores, kill some stuff, upgrade your armor and weapons, move on.
This becomes very dull, very fast. Killing the very few bosses in the game becomes more of a chore rather than something you actually want to do, exploring is tedious because you've seen it all before, and digging for ores is ultimately boring. Starbound just doesn't do this formula right like Terraria and Minecraft do.
This game has it's moments, but for a game that raised over 2 million dollars in preorders, it's utterly unacceptable. Terraria is a much better game that costs less, has a load of more content, and actually has worthwhile updates. Starbound is a scam; don't fall for it.

3 out of 5:  This game is mere steps from being an incredibly deep masterpiece, but fumbles at the goal line.
The game is about the same level of fun as Game Dev Tycoon, which, while fun, will eventually be disappointing after a while if you want a deeper tycoon experience. There are some improvements, but in the end, it boils down to basically discovering the "correct" slider positions for the games you are developing.  Additionally, there are some things that just don't seem very obvious to a new player.  Like console development.  It's there, you can blow tons of money on components, but nothing really explains what you are supposed to do with it to actually get it going.  So it doesn't look like you can, out of the gate, start working on your own console and the game doesn't really give you any starting options to allow it.
The most frustrating aspect of the game for me is the way in which things are unlocked.  My big gripe was Game Dev Tycoon was that it was overly simplified in its presentation of game dev history.  This game had such promise with the sheer amount of platforms and options.  But the research mechanic seems very shallow, and things are gated for no real reason.  Specialty rooms are gated behind what are basically milestones or achievements, which means no quality assurance until you make a game with exactly 50 bugs or more, for example.  Not being able to research sound options when everyone is complaining about lackluster sound in your games is weird, especially when the sound options are locked way past where they should given the current year.
Ultimately, pick it up if it is on sale or something, or if you absolutely loved Game Dev Tycoon and want a sidegrade to that game.  If you want something that is a vast improvement over previous similar games, save yourself the disappointment.  This is close, very close, but not quite there yet.

I usually start reviewing indie games with a "for an indie game" mindset, but here it was not necessary. Not to mention I didn't even know that the game was made by a single indie dev, not at the beginning at least. Impressive to say the least.
Well, let's stick to the "official-ish" format and write this review piece by piece.
Graphics - Well chosen theme, clean and easy on the eyes.
The game features a rather minimalistic graphical style which is no surprise for indie games but while many of such games go for the "retro" feel, this baby embraces a clean, pristine look, with a futuristic aftertaste. The well chosen theme with said style produces an aesthetic which is both pleasing to the eyes and free of any clutter while still provides ample visual feedback of your feats. My biggest problem was the tutorial popup window being in my way, but even that was only a minor annoyance (and when you are reading you are not playing anyways so...).
Audio - Nothing extra, but perfectly fine for the role.
I didn't expect much from this department to be honest so it was a pleasant surprise to find it to be fine. Sure, can't expect an astounding musical orgy, nor a cast of world-famous voice actors, but with the game's story/theme there was no need for anything like that. There is barely any voice within the game apart from a few announcements but seeing as it's not story driven, I couldn't care less. As for the music, it has the same feel as Frozen Synapse had, but still generic enough to not get annoying over time (in case of FS while I liked the music, it was so easy to recognize that it became annoying to hear it so many times).
Story - Nonexistent.
The game's story is... well, nonexistent. This baby is 100% about gameplay, has a pretense to it but that's about it. And nobody misses said story.
Gameplay - Challenging and light.
Surprisingly enough the game features a gameplay style where one can just sit down and enjoy a bit of action, a mix of strategy and ballistic shooting gallery, interactive towerdefense. Sitting down, playing a little on one of the maps can be a pretty good recreational activity without any need to overly stress about anything. The implemented progression system allows you to progress even with such minimal effort.
On the other hand, those that take the game more seriously are in for a treat. Completing all the objectives, covering the enemy entry points, hitting those fast moving cookies for that little bit extra money (ram), etc. can speed up progression compared to the less stressful path and provide ample challenge to those that require more than what current mainstream games usually offer.
With the "easy to play, hard to master" approach and the more and more painful challenges/objectives emsire that the game stays relatively fresh and complex even if someone decides to keep playing on the very same map, over and over again for some reason.
Overall - Fun little baby and looks the part too. I'm interested if the dev behind it will continue on this path or maybe even with this very game. My main concern with such games that they make it painfully apparent that something is very wrong with the mainstream (AA+) gaming industry as indie games are generally much better in nearly every single aspect than the "big names".
I love this game. I am excited for the future of this game. This game is education made into entertainment.

ARTIFICIAL DEFENSE is classified on Steam as an action indie strategy game that was recently published onto Steam by Thiemo Bolder and ONEMANGAMES. Bolder has attempted to create an entirely new genre of game in what he classifies as a combination of RTS, tower defense and orbital shooter. The player is given access to a combined total of 21 offensive weapons, 21 defensive towers and 7 hardware levels to battle their way through a massive 49 challenges across 7 different levels. There is also a mix of 13 different music tracks. At first glance I was a little staggered. This appears to be a huge number for a first time Steam developer-publisher. I was more than a little worried that the dev had bitten off more than he could chew. Grandiose plans don’t always function as fully intended.
Given my worry I am going to start with the negatives that I discovered. The game has a few bad control-related bugs that agitated me perhaps more than they ought to have. The first came when I tried to play the game with keyboard and mouse yet had my controller connected to the computer. The game doesn’t like that at all. It wont allow you to play properly with K&M when you have a controller connected. Weapons do not fire as they should and there is no aim. You can even have the weapons land on the enemies and it do nothing. I exited the game, disconnected the controller and reloaded it and the game finally played the way that it was intended.
The other mistake and for a reviewer who loves to alt-tab out to take notes on the fly it was pretty damning. Once I alt-tabbed away from the game going back to it my cursor was gone. It disappeared and I tried everything that I could think of to bring it back but that baby was done. Again, I had to exit the game in order to progress which sadly meant that I had lost my progress.
But that’s exactly where the negatives end. Two bugs that can, I believe, be easily patched out of the game and knowing how hard Thiemo Bolder has worked on his gem will be just as soon as he finds that messy line of coding that needs to be repaired. While on the subject of hard work I sincerely believe that this game is the result of blood, sweat and more than a few tears. It’s an absolute masterclass and showmanship of how a one man developer can create a game as technically sound and enjoyable as what Artificial Defense is.
Not only does the game and the combination of genres marry very well together but the game is both exciting and enjoyable. It’s one game that I will attempt to one hundred percent with achievements. The game incorporates all of the technical aspects and mechanics that make tower defense games so thoroughly challenging. However, the shooter component of the game shines through and makes the game more exciting and fresh than your standard tower defense game. It’s a wicked combination that incorporates more than its fair share of strategy.
Once I overcame my initial bug with (the controller issue causing keyboard and mouse to be unplayable which I’m used to as a tower defense fan) I found that the game was fundamentally very simple to learn. This is in part thanks to the somewhat humorous but very easy to play through tutorials that teach you the basics. This makes the learning curve somewhat marginalized.
The beautiful thing about the game is that it encourages different styles of play. If you’re much more used to playing shooters you can emphasize that more in your playthrough than you would the tower defense aspect. Of course, the most skilled players will probably use a strong combination of both but the choice is ultimately yours and there really isn’t a right or a wrong way to play the game. You can be successful with a number of different strategies. One thing that this enables players to do is to increase their competencies in the weaker of their two chosen genres. Shooter fans may find themselves enjoying tower defense games much more than they may have previously and vice versa.
An intriguing aspect of the strategy that traditional tower defense players need to be wary of is that the avenues to the different parts of the machinery are much more varied and open than they will be traditionally used to. Learning to block paths is important but even more important is understanding and learning which paths will be unable to be blocked so that you are in your best position to thwart the AI attack. Thankfully much of the level design has been thought out to perfection.
Due to its enormous amount of possible gamestyles and fantastic reward and upgrade systems the game offers a lot of replayability. In fact, I don’t believe that a single playthrough will be anywhere close to enough for those of you who become fans of the title. I can easily see players reaching tens of hours with the title.
Artifical Defense is such a fantastic game that I have trouble believing that it was developed by just a single person. An absolute must buy.

This was the first XCOM game that I played.  The learning curve was challenging but rewarding enough to get me hooked.
Management comes in the form of your ship:  you decide what rooms to build, which technologies to research, etc.  You will learn priorities and strategies on your first play through that will have you laughing at yourself the second and third time around.
Each mission you get to assemble your crew.  You can customize your warriors with weapons, armor, etc.  Your soldiers stick with you and level up as you progress through the missions.  You need to determine if you want to share the love and level up all your soldiers, or stick with a core group of hardened veterans.
When ready you launch into a battlefield covered with shroud.. You need to explore quickly to discover your enemies and other challenges awaiting you.  Some missions have timers, others do not.  Enemies react to you once you've been spotted! so keeping your crew in formation while also scouring the map becomes a challenge in itself.  All missions are turned based.  This was difficult getting use to for me, but XCOM2 handles it very well and you never feel slowed down or stuck due to it.
The environment becomes as much of a challenge as the enemies are as you navigate over cliffs, through buildings, and around cover.  Tactics that are available to your troops become increasingly important as you progress through the game so get started using them right away.  This is a game where you want to utilize the 'Save' button often.  Good luck.

Artificial Defense is a real-time-strategy, orbital-shooter game in an artificial, virtual reality setting. You are a mighty computer-system, defending its servers against swarms of intruding creeps.
Fire off miniguns, launch hellfire missiles, drop incinerating hades-bombs and asteroids, deploy mighty railgun and acid towers and spawn your own Intrusion Counter Measures (ICMs) to re-conquer corrupted databases and firewalls. Earn RAM and upgrade your arsenal and hardware-level. Start as an analog punch-tape system and evolve to a quantum A.I. computer.
Well, the game has 3 main game mechanics:

There are 21 offense weapons available, reaching from outdated flintlocks, over maverick-missiles to devastating
meteors and neutron-bombs.

There are 21 defense towers available, reaching from pistol-sentry-towers, over incinerating flame-throwers to
powerful long-range railgun-towers. Additionally there are production towers which produce your main-resource: RAM
(Random Access Memory). Yes, building up a small RAM economy is very important.


Spawn Intrusion Counter Measures (ICMs) in order to conquer corrupted system-structures like databases, honeypots
and firewalls. Databases e.g. spawn datablips which carry valuable data out of the system (backup). In this case you
will have to secure a safe path to the backup-devices, by using your offense and defense equipment.

This game is a fantastic turn-based tactics game, with a solid real-time strategy layer to give it context. I would recommend it to anyone who likes difficult strategy games which require a lot of thought.
The tactics layer revolves around stealth and combat with a squad of 4-6 soldiers. There are 5 classes and many gadgets and upgrades to allow you to customize your team to suit your tastes. The most important and best-designed system of the layer is the cover system. If you choose cover wisely, your soldiers will be have a very low chance of being hit, while at the same time having the opportunity to flank enemies for an advantage. It is simple to understand, but difficult to master.
The strategy layer involves customizing your research, equipment, and buildings, and then basically going to the world-map and waiting. The base-building is quite fun, but I'm personally not a huge fan of the waiting mechanic. Basically you fly your ship around and try to gain resources while waiting for new resources and battles to pop up. The key phrase being "pop up". For most missions there is not much warning for when their prompts will appear, so it's kind of jarring and annoying. You will often find yourself very close to harvesting an important resource, but then suddenly having a mission prompt in your face which you basically can't ignore if you want to win. Not my favourite UX decision in the game.
With respect to difficulty, I would say the game's 4 difficulties are nicely balanced. The most common complaint about this game is that it is too RNG-based for the difficulty to be fair, but that's not really true. The game is really one about risk-management, and there are many ways to mitigate risk in the tactical layer. If you are leaving the success of the game up to the hit-chance of a single soldier, you are probably not playing the situation correctly. As for the difficulty curve, the game is actually most difficult at the beginnings and endings of campaigns. In the mid-game certain tech is perhaps too powerful in that combat can start to become trivial. This unevenness is a little jarring, but it doesn't detract too much from the game for me.
Overall, a clear thumbs up from me. If you enjoy it I would also recommend looking into the War of the Chosen DLC after completing a campaign or two. It adds a lot of new systems to the game(especially in the strategy layer) and is generally fantastic as well.

Now I must stress one thing, if you do not meet the recommended PC requirements, DO NOT attempt to run this game. I purchased this game as a gift to one of my friends who I frequently play with. My assumption was that since he and I could play together in other titles, that he would be able to run this. I was of course horribly mistaken. I neglected to take into account my own PC's capabilities and not his. Does this mean I will request a refund, just because he cannot run it? ABSOLUTELY NOT. I made my gift purchase for the sole purpose of supporting this game, as it is the only way that I can further it's development.
Now the game itself. Why do I recommend it? For it's potential. I cant recommend it as a good game (yet). As of right now the first thing I noted was the clearly unoptimized rendering of the game. I knew this going in that an unoptimized game running on Unity was likely to cause severe drops in frames, and it would be nearly impossible for a low end PC to run. For those people I do not recommend it. I also cannot recommend it to the players of other dinosaur games. If you come here with certain expectations about what the life of a dinosaur should be, expect to be disappointed, because it's likely that you wont have your expectations met. Life can be dull, many already know this. The life of any animal can be dull, but that doesn't mean that, if nothing exciting happens, it must be doing something wrong. That isn't what Saurian is about. Saurian is about survival. For me it is the release into nature that keeps me coming back. There isn't a single thing that keeps me coming back other than just being able to be lost in the life of a simulated animal.
What needs improvement? I think that with future updates, the level of interaction with the AI needs to be improved. Right now the AI feels random and misguided. Upon spotting other AI or the player, the NPC's should engage in meaningful actions. As an adult Dakotaraptor, you will find that Pachys will often stroll randomly, ignoring your presence instead of attempting to stand their ground or fleeing as necessary. Then, once a certain age is reached, you become unable to use the fantastic RPR mechanic on Pachys, as the damage you put out can simply take them down in a single bite, all while being completely immune to their attacks. This has been what is killing the game for me, the lack of a struggle at the end game. A Pachy should be entirely capable of fighting off a dakotaraptor. A well placed headbutt needs to be able to break bone. Put those two things together and you already have more interesting combat.
Again, I only recommend this game because I see its potential and I do not want to spoil its chances as an Early Access game so early in its development. However, if improvements are not made I will change my review as necessary.

(Base game Review, I have not purchased any of the DLC yet, though I will update the game once I've logged sufficient playtime on the game with the DLC installed, assuming I purchase it. [Spoiler: I'm probably going to purchase it.]
*My Opinion In A Nutshell*:
Good game, buy it if you like turn-based strategy games. It's worth buying on sale, and if you're like me, you'll easily get 2-3 challenging playthroughs before even touching the DLC. Each Playthrough takes quite a chunk of time, so you'll get your moneys worth in gametime.
The Good:
-XCom 2 plays very similiarly to Xcom 1 with some new mechanics thrown in, and with harder enemies. I did my first playthrough on Veteran and felt quite challenged, always doing my best to properly position my troops and make use of their abilities in the most effecient way possible. I'm currently looking forward to my next playthrough, and I'm eager to see how well I do against XCom 2's most difficult, well, difficulty.
-XCom 2 offers a more diverse set of choices to you than X1 did. You now have a world map, where instead of simply setting up satellites and all this hoobla hoobla, you now must make use of your time, choosing what resources are most valueble to you on the map at any given period. Scanning Sites can offer different rewards in exchange for your time, and you as the player must continue expanding your contacts on the map in a semi-timely manner, taking out Alien facilities so Doomsday doesn't come quite so quickly. Manage your time wisely, ensure you are prepared, and stay on top of your resources: The Macro game is just as important as the Micro.
-Soldiers are super customizable in terms of appearence, you can even write them a backstory now. Weapons also have a full modding system behind them, and each different type of armor gives a soldier different strengths, as well as different weaknesses.
-There is fall damage, so don't get the floor blown out from under you up on that big fancy tower. Also blow the floor out from under the non-floating aliens. They'll be super p/o'd, and missing an additional chunk of health. You'll also be pretty p/o'd and missing a few chunks of health if you let that Muton get too close and grenade the building out from under your squad. Don't let that happen.
-Utility items are friggin gud man, Xcom 2 has alllll kinds of em, and they're tons of fun.
-Dark Events can be really engaging, as the Aliens will work, month by month, to complete 'Research', which will give them an edge against your most frequently used tactics. You research that Armor buff first thing? Well crap, the Aliens are researching armor too. Better stop that. Been sneaking around a lot, getting WAY too many kills with those perfect Concealment ambushes? Well... Crap, they're researching something to widen their detection radius. Better stop that. It can lead to a lot of interesting gameplay decisions on the Macro level, as well as changing how you would approach situations in combat on a per-month basis. (Each research completion only lasts one month. Don't worry, they won't spam Armor research and give all their units 10 armor by the end of the game. Won't happen. The bonuses cycle in and out per each month of in-game time.)
The Bad:
-Critical hits can feel a bit BS-ey, especially in the early game. Your favorite soldier hiding behind full cover, probably not gonna get hit by that Advent Commander on the second/third mission in your playthrough? Might... Maybe. Just maybe, get hit, critted, and instakilled, because you don't have Tier 2 armor yet. It's not a very likely thing to happen, and most critical hits happen when your soldiers get flanked, but me personally: I'd rather this 'Lucky or not lucky' mechanic didn't exist. It doesn't feel like it belongs in an in-depth strategy game like XCom. I'd much rather have a hit or miss chance as the only element of luck at play, rather than the chance to do, or receive double damage at random as well.
-The Dodge mechanic is almost as equally bad as the Critical mechanic, allowing soldiers (Equipped with certain armor, or hunkering down), and some aliens (Mostly aliens) to only take a small portion of the damage they would have otherwise taken from a hit. You cannot shred it, it's based on RNG, and overall its quite a random wrench thrown into things, having few counters in the early to mid game (Aside from explosives spam). I would, personally, prefer something more consistant and counterable. It feels very 'Thrown in there', and not very well thought out.
-You cannot reinforce cover in this game, and no one form of cover is usually any better than another. All of it can get destroyed by an explosion, and your soldier (Or the enemy alien) can be sitting out there without jack protecting them. It's a semi-fair mechanic most of the time, and hasn't led to many soldier deaths in my playthroughs, but it does feel like being able to reinforce your cover (Or deploy very hard cover), would be a great addition to the game. Not having different explosive resistances to different types of cover in XCom 2 makes no 'One' type of half-cover or full-cover much better than any other, as most cover in the game can be destroyed just with a single grenade.
-Hacking is, in my opinion, somewhat bad. There's no sort of deduction, guesswork, or challenge to it at all. The game will simply roll your soldiers 'Technology Score' against the Items (Whatever it is your trying to hack, that is. A Robot, a Control Tower, a Cache...), rather than giving you any sort of little mini-game or puzzle. Feels like a missed opportunity to do something interesting.
-Mimic Beacons are just plain stupid. Overextend your favorite soldier into a complete and utter dogbowl of a mess? A Sectopod looking to light him THE FLUFF UP next turn? Pfsh. PFSH I SAY! Just throw a Mimic Beacon. ALL OF THE ALIENS WILL ABSOLUTELY ATTACK IT, RATHER THAN ATTACK YOUR SOLDIER. Essentially, it acts as a 100% Taunt mechanic to any Alien which is in it's Line of Sight. I expressly forbade myself from equipping these items on my upcoming playthrough. They're really cheesy, and really should've been adjusted by now. TLDR: Wanna easily beat the game on max difficulty without losing any soldiers? Abuse Mimic Beacons.
The Nuetral: (Or the Ugly, if you prefer. But it's not actually that bad. Heh, get my stupid reference?)
-Proper Dossiers for all of the Alien enemies aren't really a thing. There will be some random 'Quirks' about the Aliens you'll just find out by random, without any warning about. Say you've got a Ranger, for example, and you go to melee attack a Muton with it... LOL. NOPE BRO. That Muton just slapped your soldiers sword out of the way and stabbed him dead. Even if you've completed the Muton Autopsy, no mention of this hidden mechanic is... Anywhere in the game, really. Personally, I would like detailed dossiers regarding these 'Hidden' mechanics to be added to future games, allowing players to find these sorts of things out by other means than random experience and soldier deaths. Really, this is a small thing however, and it could be argued that these hidden mechanics add some form of 'Knowledge Check' to the playerbase. Still, it left a bad taste in my mouth.
-The AI seems to 'Forgive' you of your mistakes sometimes. That one soldier way out of position, flanked by three units, gets cut down to 2 HP? The last enemy Alien with a turn might just... Ignore them for some reason, to shoot at one of your other Soldiers. I'm not sure if this changes with the difficulty or not, but it felt like this happened semi-frequently in my gameplay.
Overall:
-Good game, but could be better. I understand the Developers are trying some new things in this version, tossing in mechanics like crit and dodge, but it just disrupts the consistency of my strats. Still, time well spent, and I'm planning to spend even more time. Get the base game for at least 40$, its worth it.

The problem so far seems to be Nvidia's drivers that have caused the slow down in SFV. Currently running a Radeon 7870 and an i7 5820k @3.8Ghz. Though after putting some time into the game I see that the connection is terrible to everyone. I have 6Mb/s upload and 60Mb/s download. My ping is usually 20ms near me and across the country it is 50-60ms. (1 frame is roughly 16 ms in a 60fps game). The netcode for SFV (GGPO) uses rollbacks to give a smooth or seemingly lagless environment online. The problem with that is capcom totally has it messed up. So you're Ryu and you throw an EX fireball from full screen and the other player is hit by your hadouken. Then in a fraction of a second the player teleports from in the hit stun of the fireball to in your face. Their health literally goes back up, you lose the EX bar and they do a full punish. I am not kidding... this is how online is. Now USFIV has been out for a long time and the netcode, as bad as it was, was polished to a degree so this comparrison is a little unfair. I could, in USFIV, play someone from Japan with a 3 frame lag online connection (which is really good) and it would be impeccably stable. I can't play my friend in the same room online without lag in SFV.
Here is some more info.
My friend has dual 860ms in sli and an I7 4720MQ. Both of our laptops supprt wireless AC and so does my router. The connection over wifi from my router to either of our laptops is sub 1ms. So stop complaining that wireless creates lag. It might on wireless B but wireless N and AC are pretty safe bets on not being the cause of a bad connection. And my desktop is wired directly to my modem. I've tested it and the connection problems are not on my end and usually not on another persons end either. The game is simply laggy and nearly unplayable online. Even the best connections will have teleporting. Buy it in March if you really want the game when the problems have a good chance of being slightly better than they are now.

Mad Games Tycoon is a good, fun game with questionable staying power.
It combines the elements of Game Dev Tycoon and Theme Hospital (to a lesser extent). Much like other games in this genre you hire employees, program games (or piece work), research and repeat. Mad Games Tycoon adds to this forumla by including (a few) random events and allowing you to build your offices. This is where the Theme Hospital part comes in - setting up your various rooms for development, QC, breaks, etc. There's not a lot of strategy involved besides getting the room size right and making sure people don't have to walk a mile to the bathroom but the building part is limited.
Still, it's great fun for a while. You start off just on your own, programming games without an engine and can blossom into a massive gaming empire with dozens of employees at your beck and call. The larger things get, the more risk you're taking because the weight of salaries can drain you of money before you can get your next game out. Then you do well and can expand into a larger space to build an even larger empire. Mad Games Tycoon keeps the graphics light and attractive, the music is decent if nondescript and throws an ever-increasing number of market options for the user.
It's all fun and it's worth your money.
However, don't expect to get too many hours out of this title. It's fun but the game gets redundant. Outfitting a new office for the 3rd or 4th time gets quite old. As you get bigger it's easier to get higher rated games by simply polishing them more. The feedback on prior games isn't very good and so if you're looking for the best "mix" you probably have to consult the forums (which I don't do because I like to think that there's more than one way to make a very good game in a given genre). After a while you've seen it all. The systems don't get complex enough to cause a player any real difficulty and eventually you get to the point where you're just a factory churning out 80+ rated games, self publishing them and making gobs of money. At that point the game is essentially over and it may only take 10 game years or so for a skilled player to hit that point.
