My Grand Replay of all things Fallout has come to its conclusion. Maybe my daughter will one day wonder how dad managed to play hundreds of hours of video games around the time she was born. Or maybe Steam will be long dead by 2030. This kind of peek into one's parents' past is unprecedented if you think about it. Pretty soon 2000s kids will start scrolling through the detailed life log that is the Facebook feed of their parents, asking all sorts of questions : )
Fallout 4 has it's flaws. It is clearly a sibling of Fallout 3, yet again featuring a far too lifelike (as in boring) depiction of an East Coast city. Thankfully we were spared the generic metro tunnels, which makes post apocalyptic Boston a tad bit better than post apocalyptic D.C., but it still doesn't hold a candle to New Vegas or even New Reno. The Institute has been in the works for longer at Bethesda and is therefore more fleshed out than the Enclave of F3, but again pales compared to Caesar's Legion or The Master.
This time around we've sadly been deprived of the 'consequences slides' at the end of the game and the dumbed down family friendliness of Bethesda's newer RPGs is digging it's roots ever deeper. Of the DLCs, Far Harbor was cliche but good, the rest I wouldn't recommend buying at their individual price points. There's going to be a GotY edition pretty soon so that won't really be a problem. Nuka World surprises positively with its amount of content, but forces you to either end everything prematurely or suddenly become the bad guy. As a completionist you have to become evil. The other DLCs might as well not have been.
Objectively though, there are few games that are better than Fallout 4. Lots to explore, good story, interesting companions, satisfying combat. You can spend a hundred hours on the settlement building part of the game alone. They've made the Brotherhood a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s for a change, so there's a creative twist for you. Maxed out, the graphics are exquisite. Upgrading weapons is interesting enough, if heavy on the adhesive stockpiling : )
Fortunately I'm the kind of guy who likes canon playthroughs so the Creation Club BS, while disappointing, really doesn't ruffle my feathers all that much.

artifical defense is a tricky game to talk about because, unfortunately, it doesn't have a lot going on mechanically. I found it to be a very stock-standard tower defense game where you are tasked with placing down towers which will protect your stationary base against oncoming attackers. Layered over this is a direct-shooting mechanic which feels very similar to using an AC-130. You aim at targets from an overhead view, fire a shot, and then it makes impact a moment later, hopefully killing some targets. Firing shots in this manner costs the same resource as deploying turrets, but I didn't find that this all that interesting. I just prioritized towers, given that direct-shooting is somewhat inefficient and only ocasionally necesarry. That aside, Artificial Defense is an exceedingly well-polished game. The visuals are clean, crisp, and vibrant, the music is strong, and the menus are all quite sleek. If you're a fan of tower defense games, you could do a lot worse than Artificial Defense. If you aren't a fan of the genre, then don't expect this game to win you over.

Early access is usually the downfall of most indie games. It happened to ARK, DayZ, and all those popular games that everyone loved to play, then the devs forgot their original plan and the game was either unfinished or changed for the worse. With what I've seen so far in this game, Blackwake's devs do NOT plan on doing that.
These devs are dedicated. They actively communicate with the community, they've set up dedicated servers (more than Ubisoft did for a full-price, AAA title that 's slowly sinking like a navy frigate full of holes), they've made their plan explicitly clear; not with words, with actions. You can tell that when you're having loads of fun with a title that's barely even in beta yet that there's room for something even better to come along.
As far as the game goes, it's fairly minimalistic. The real fun doesn't come from flashy bonus gear and overcomplicated crafting systems; it comes from player involvement. Half of the times I've played the game everybody's been speaking like pirates. Working together to fire cannons at the right time, guide the ship, repair holes in the hull and sails, pumping the water out of the ship, and boarding an enemy vessel to slaughter her crew and send her to the sea floor doesn't feel overwhelming at all. Everything you do helps and feels like it makes an impact. This is a game that is impossible not to have fun with, and we need more of those games.
I think that if the devs of this game are truly dedicated and want to see the game through to a full release, this could be one of the greatest co-op games of all time and a testament to developer integrity and to the power of early access when it's done right.

Once every few years, a JRPG arrives that blends together good world-building, a story that is both fascinating and thought-provoking, challenging your own worldview, philosophy and beliefs and a combat system that, while simple at first, makes you feel like a glorious badass having fun killing hordes after hordes of enemies.
This is Tales of Berseria. Review is spoiler-free, minus the intro stuff.
The game puts you in the boots of Velvet - an average village girl that one day gets to see her little brother being murdered right in front of her by her own brother-in-law, she turns into a daemon and then she gets thrown in prison to feast on other daemons for 3 years. As she manages to escape with someone's help, she learns that her brother-in-law now is mankind's greatest hope against daemons, and the whole world praises him as a saviour. Filled with rage for the injustice she and her brother tasted, she embarks on a journey to kill him.
Let me start off with the world-building. I was having a discussion with a few friends over how games stopped bothering with giving attention to details due to how gamers nowadays tend not to care much about information that gives you a clue on how X village works, how they survive in Y conditions etc. For that I'm glad that Berseria doesn't do that. Here, in the form of completely optional NPC's, you'll find stuff like a father looking for his lost son, a group of teenagers who become interested in music and decide to start their own band and dogs that are criticizing humanity. For that I praise the creators of the game who decided to not restrict themselves to "what information is useful" but also to "what information makes you immerse". I found myself returning to a city wondering whether a couple of NPC's got married.
I can't criticize the English voice acting because I play the game in Japanese voice acting, and there's some great quality to be found there. One of the characters in the group, for example, is the same voice actor behind Jojo's bizarre adventure part 4 antagonist, Yoshikage Kira, and he's doing a glorious job here, too.
Combat system time! People will bash the game for having "button-mashing combat". And they are right, combat is button mashy, BUT... It would be wrong to stop here. See, this is first and foremost a JRPG that has an "exploit weakness system". Your typical dungeon/area visit will be  to first identify the enemy population's weaknesses, compile combos that hit every weakness they have then mash that button against them. For example (oversimplified), if an area has worms, knights and bats I end up identifying and crafting 3 different combos so I'll mash Y for bats, X for knights and B for worms (Xbox controller). This is the equivalent of scrolling through menus in a turn-based JRPG to find the ice spell versus enemies that are weak to ice, the armor penetration move for armored enemies etc. Later in the game the enemy variety becomes large enough that not only you craft combos for each but you make sure you can weave them. So you'll start with X for the first move of the X-combo then Y because the second move of the Y-combo works not only for bats but for armored, etc. Then you get moves called mystic artes that make your characters go full blown crazy killing machines. All in silky smooth 60 frames per second, even for my poverty rig (there's a demo on Steam that you can check out if you're not sure about your PC's performance). Add to that the amazing A.I. behind your teammates, which is also one of the best, if not the best in a Tales game ever and can easily play better than 70% of the players! I can even put everyone on "auto" and go to the bathroom knowing that we will almost certainly win a fight.
Now for the downsides: So far, I find the game quite linear - on rails, so to speak, and the optional areas that I have unlocked so far (I haven't finished the game yet, have mercy) are simple arenas that lack in the difficulty and satisfaction department, compared to the rest of the content. I found myself visiting them once, go "is that it?" then leave in disappointment. Maybe this will change as the game goes on. I heard very good things about the post-game content. There are also the occasional sidequests and mini games that (thankfully) are so many and diverse that you can "play favorites" without losing the rewards (you win coins that let you buy stuff, but its shared across mini-games, thanks Namco).
The difficulty settings are Simple - Normal - Moderate - Hard, with Intense and Chaos being unlocked after you do something in the game. On the other hand, there's a way to make fights so hard you'll almost always get a couple of party members or everyone dead. To give you a clue, my winrate in normal fights is around 90% but for dangerous fights it's at 10%, but that's just me not accepting winning a fight with people being knocked out left and right (the game rewards you with in-game score, called Grade, if you win fights without deaths and without using items, who would say no to that?!?). Maybe it's also me being used to JRPG's throughout the years. Someone can also play the game with the combat system in full automatic mode - AI doing everything - in case you just want to experience the story without bothering with learning how the combat works (I wouldn't do that but some people could). NINJA EDIT: Something else that I noticed and I gotta say: Contrary to most JRPG's, on higher difficulties the enemies not only get the usual stat increases but also different attack frequency and in bosses it can be a change of movesets and spells!
Overall, this isn't simply one of the top Tales games ever (and easily the best modern Tales game - RIP Zestiria) but a great JRPG. I said it on my Zestiria review and I'll say it again: "Tales of" games are the only JRPG series on Steam that combines fast-paced flashy combat system with immersive storytelling. Does it worth paying full price? For me that's a resounding yes. But I hope that my review was informative enough to draw your own decision. Meanwhile, I'll be finishing my playthrough and prepare for my next one. And if you choose to get into it, I would advise you to take it slow and savor every minute, instead of speed through it. JRPG's like this one deserve to be enjoyed like good wine or chocolate.

I'm about 70% in the YES Recommend category and about 30% to NOT Recommend, but I'm not as torn on this game as I am on others.
The reason for this split recommendation is that the game is in serious need of balancing and some bug fixing, polishing and optimization. Even at version 1.5.? (Chinese/French), there is a lot to be desired.
That being said, this is probably one of the more solid Zombie RPGs. In a genre drowning in mediocrity, this game happens to capture the old PS2 days of playing garbage JRPGs (which we all loved and 10/10 star rated... cough cough nostalgia). And it pulls off the survival element rather well (albeit with more than a few frustrating moments and annoying bugs). So in a simple sense this game is a pretty good first attempt. If the dev were to make a second one, I would likely wait in line to purchase it. But as a gamer, I would like to see a lot more go into the game in terms of balancing and QA.
Dead Age has some pretty big gameplay issues, most of which I can look over as "life's not fair, Zombie life is even less fair." But here are the ones that I feel are the major issues that need to be addressed:
1, Tools - the game requires tools to do just about everything and are only available via quests and random loot drops. In about 5 play throughs I've had 4 games where I found maybe a handful (not even close to enough) and one game where I had just enough to keep going. This mechanic needs to be reworked. Speaking frankly, half the things you need tools for in game, you wouldn't need tools to do the activity in real life. Whether or not the game is going for realism is a different issue, but for the sake of immersion, it detracts from the suspension of disbelief and can be a pretty large center of frustration. Especially when you need tools for the radio tower mission and you can't even find one tool.. Then the one tool you were saving up gets stolen. And it's game over. Sucks, but more importantly unbalanced. Btw, why do we need a Radio Tower to repel the punks anyways? Hmm....
2. The Healing Mechanic - in game you need a medical item and a medical skill to heal others. No problem there. But it is a problem that the medical character cannot heal themselves. It may come down to personal choice and the dev decided not to add it. And we can argue all day about it. But when the medical item is shown graphically in the game as a syringe shot and the animation is to inject someone with it, the medic should be able to give themselves the shot. Period. But from a gameplay standpoint, it's a huge problem because healing items are really rare. And that crucial in-fight heal can be a life saver. If they changed it to allow the medic to heal themselves, I imagine the game would be easier. But the game should not be difficult because common sense features are left out, sure it makes the game less survivable, but it also makes it less fun. In fact, speaking of survivability, I think the survivability rate of the "maps" would only be about 25% higher if medics could heal themselves; people still need to craft or loot them after all.
3. Performance - If you've read any of my reviews before, you know that I run a lot of these games on my "craptop.” It's a bargain bin, years-old, integrated graphics POS connected to a TV via HDMI. I mostly do this because I'm a cheapskate, but also because it's rather fun to see what can run on it. This game DID run on it, so cheers to the devs for having good minimum specs. Huzzah! However, the game does experience a huge slow down in framerate in the 3D rendered battle sequences. I switched from high to low graphics in the launcher (though didn't notice much of a difference visually) and was able to get a playable framerate. So that's manageable. But the game glitches out and shows animations at different times, delayed, or sometimes not at all. This could be a series of bugs, but I have a feeling it has to do with how the game renders and manages memory, processing power, etc. In fact, it is likely both. However, IF this is only an issue on my craptop, then I'm 100% willing to concede this point.
In addition to those large issues there's a lot of little things. Strange bugs where you can't see your inventory, or the party screen will scroll but it immediately jumps to the top, grammar errors, etc. The game could use another pass through in the QA phase and I'm sure an open beta (for the next version) would fix a lot of those issues. Most of these things are completely trivial and can be worked around so I'm not sweating any of this, just making a point to let you know that they're in the game and you will experience them.
With all the negatives, this is still a good game. And as I have stated above, I would really like to see a sequel, but it would need some careful attention to detail and I expect it to be more polished than this installment. This game, however, is fun for more than a couple play throughs, and maybe 20 hours of gameplay before you want to give up. At 25 hours in, currently, I didn't scratch the surface of the main game, but like I said.. 20 is the cut off point for not wanting to spend more time in game on some of the bad luck random events and that tool problem.
I definitely feel like I got a lot of enjoyment out of this and buying it 60% off at $5.09 was a steal. I think the perfect price point is $9.99, but had I known the game was this fun I'd have bought it at full price and had no qualms about it. But then I'm a cheapskate playing on a craptop computer, what do I know? 7/10.

GOTY 2012
edit: Game of the Year All Years

Bastion gets storytelling right.  The one prominent voice actor hits it out of the park.  Dialog is punchy, spaced well, and adapts to little details in your game (whether or not you cleared a screen of enemies, that sort of thing).
The gameplay rocks.  Most of the weapons are fun, a few are impractical (the mortar comes to mind), one or two rock my world (pair a shotgun musket and a calamity cannon, enjoy your day).  Level design is smart and rarely frustrating.  The difficulty curve is smooth (though expect to change up your tactics and weapon choices as you progress).  The dream sequences (survival gauntlets) are fun to come back to again and again.  Most of the weapon training levels are fun (a couple are quite flawed, particularly the cannon's).
The one major downside is that it's not modder-friendly, so no user-made content to keep you coming back.
It's gorgeous, it sounds good, it has replay value due to the customizable difficulty and new game plus.  Gamepad controls are awkward, but mouse and keyboard works just fine.  And you don't need a fancy computer to run the game.  Buy it, tell your friends to buy it, disown anyone who does not comply.

Along the way you meet a couple of other survivors and gather them at the bastion, a flying fortress that has the power to make everything right again. You love clicking your mouse.
You love stalker narrators with raspy voices.
You like falling off cliff edges and dying.
You are a masochist with all 10 shrine idols invoked for impossible-to-beat who-knows-wheres.
Even if you don't like any of these things, play this game. It's brilliant.

Don't understand why this game is so highly rated on steam.  Bought this because of the Steam Awards nomination but I'm actually regretting my decision a bit now because the gameplay is just awful.  It distracts from the story.  Just some examples of what I mean:
1) Moving around feels unnatural.  Only 4-axis in 360 degree space.  Terrible when trying to get away from zombies.
2) Sometimes you don't even have control over which direction you can move.  Just forward/back.
3) Camera/view control is limited sometimes.  Can't see 360 degrees around room.
4) Attacking/protecting yourself from zombies is confusing:
a)  Sometimes you have to push them away by pressing Q's and E's.  Doesn't make sense at all.
b)  Other times, you have to go for the head.  Cursor control is slow and clunky, and if you miss the head, you're dead.
c)  Last and my least favorite, sometimes the only thing you can do is decide who to help.  No control of Lee whatsover.  All scripted actions thereafter.  No option to help both people.
5) For a game that prides itself on adjusting the story based on your decisions, in some cases, there isn't enough time to read responses and properly make a decision what to say or do.  The text flashes on screen too fast.
6) Decisions are very limited anyway.  Story feels too linear/scripted.  What if I just want to ditch/ignore people.  Nope, can't do that.  At least with games like Resident Evil, I can run around in any direction around town and not die immediately when I run into zombies, which is more realistic because they walk around so damn slow anyway.
7) Worse thing ever... no real save points/slots.  Apparently, the game autosaves, but you don't really know where or when until you die.  If you quit mid-game and restart later, you may have lost some game progress.  For instance, you may think you've already talked to certain people before you quit the game, but it comes back to a point before you actually did that.  Story is now a little bit different from where you left off.
8) Looking around and interacting with objects is pretty hard because of camera angles/view sometimes.
9) After picking up items, there's no way to inspect objects in your inventory.  You can only use them on people/zombies.
10) Interacting with people is strange.  You walk up to them, hover mouse over them, and then press 1/2/3/etc... to choose how to interact with them based on your inventory of items and whether you can use items on them or not.  Again, too scripted... in a bad way.
There were lots of other things that bugged me about the game, but this list is already way too long.  I found it really hard to be immersed in the story, which is the main reason I bought this game.  Really surprised this won over To the Moon in the Steam Awards. Golden Rush has a fair number of 'new' mechanics for a moba game. such as full rpg equipment drops in-game ranging from normal-set items. Obviously the 4 player mode is also a different change of pace from mainstream mobas, but lacks the same smooth charm as Deep Silver's Dead Island Epidemic.
The game is still quite unpolished. The skills of the current playable champions are subpar and unbalanced. Certain AoE ultimates that cast at the drop of a hat- .5, while other level 1 skills take upwards of ,75-1 to cast. Random creep camps spawn with elite mobs that aoe 2/3 of your life on death, makes farming a bit rediculous at times. Then there is the golden frog- a nice little addition- if only the pathing of it was fair. Some games the frog simlpy dances around one side of the map giving teams on that side a grossly  unfair gold advantage.
Taking towers are also a pain, as every time an enemy sets foot into the cap circle, the capture is reset until the enemy leaves. It also either appears that the number of players do not affect capture speed or give such a negligible buff that teamates are better off defending the circle while 1 teamate captures. This makes capturing towers immensely difficult and annoying. Then there are the checkpoint portals, which would have been a neat addition, had it not been placed directly on top of creep camps, making them inaccesible most of the time. They are also randomly spawned, but certain locations also need rebalancing and give certain sides heavy advantage.
The UI needs work, a lot of work. There is guide or list of commands. You're left to figure everything out yourself, search the forums, or ask other players. Too bad 60% of the players don't speak english and the lobby chat doesn't appear to be working, but at least they do have an option to open the forums through the game.
Overall it's a game that is attempting new things, but there are many kinks that still need to be worked out. If you're looking for something new or were a fan of DI: Epidemic, it might be worth your time to check out this game.
I would recommend friends to try it themselves as it is a small download, but I wouldn't play it again until they start rebalancing the heroes and the checkpoint portals.

I've been waiting for this game for awhile. My first experience with it however, was less than I would have hoped. My very first experience I couldn't even move. A lot of it was my error, but that first impression was less than optimal. I've tried other wild animal sims and quickly left them behind because they were boring. I hated Ark because I couldn't even make it off the beach I died so much. to me, dying without progression is no fun at all. That being said, until recently, my PC's had a 100% mortality rate. This game is unforgiving and brutal.

I found it engaging even though right now, in early access, it is sparcely populated and not everything is behaving as desired. The animal models are well designed and georgous. Since I have an older machine, I'm running it on low settings, but the vegetation and water still look acceptable to me. Running around as a little raptor against all the odds staked against me evokes a sense of accomplishment and elation when I've overcome what's killed me over and over again. I squeaked happily as I grew for a second time, only to die from starvation once again. (my last few attempts at hunting those damned lizards did not go in my favor.)
The game environment and world is unforgiving. You will die a lot. You will starve a lot. You will be killed by other dinos. Your parents will ignore you entirely - at least untill you get big enough. Once you manage to survive past babyhood, you will still die alot, likely to starvation. Your biggest obsticles will be eating and not being eaten, and you will die a lot. The world is currently not terribly populated and it's easy to go a long time without seeing or smelling anything. There is also nothing else to do currently than eat, drink and survive.
Even with all of that, I'm going to keep playing because as challenging as it is for me to keep my poor Dakotaraptor alive, I want to see what else is coming. I want to play as other species. Currently, only the Dakotaraptor is available, but five other species will be available at some later date, as well as multiplayer and a more lively world. The developers have stated that it will get better, eventually. The evolution will take a couple years but it's been promised to evolve. I'm willing to patient and impatiently see whats around that next shrub.

Fallout 4 has it's flaws. It is clearly a sibling of Fallout 3, yet again featuring a far too lifelike (as in boring) depiction of an East Coast city. Thankfully we were spared the generic metro tunnels, which makes post apocalyptic Boston a tad bit better than post apocalyptic D.C., but it still doesn't hold a candle to New Vegas or even New Reno. The Institute has been in the works for longer at Bethesda and is therefore more fleshed out than the Enclave of F3, but again pales compared to Caesar's Legion or The Master.
This time around we've sadly been deprived of the 'consequences slides' at the end of the game and the dumbed down family friendliness of Bethesda's newer RPGs is digging it's roots ever deeper. Of the DLCs, Far Harbor was cliche but good, the rest I wouldn't recommend buying at their individual price points. There's going to be a GotY edition pretty soon so that won't really be a problem. Nuka World surprises positively with its amount of content, but forces you to either end everything prematurely or suddenly become the bad guy. As a completionist you have to become evil. The other DLCs might as well not have been.
Objectively though, there are few games that are better than Fallout 4. Lots to explore, good story, interesting companions, satisfying combat. You can spend a hundred hours on the settlement building part of the game alone. They've made the Brotherhood a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s for a change, so there's a creative twist for you. Maxed out, the graphics are exquisite. Upgrading weapons is interesting enough, if heavy on the adhesive stockpiling : )
Fortunately I'm the kind of guy who likes canon playthroughs so the Creation Club BS, while disappointing, really doesn't ruffle my feathers all that much.

I agree with a lot of other reviews, so some of what I'll say might echo them. This game is gorgeous, and the time the devs have spent researching the Hell Creek formation and bringing it to life really show. The game is sort of bare, there aren't many creatures moving around, but those that do are very fluid.
The controls are relatively simple. Movement doesn't feel as fluid as it does in some other games but it is easy to adjust to. The UI could use a little work, it's really simple right now, but it gets the job done.
The AI is a little strange and unpredictable (but what animal isn't?) I have seen critters walking into trees which kind of breaks the experience a little.
Again there is a clear lack of content. Only 1 of 6 planned dinos are currently playable, and there is only a handful of other creatures in the world around you. I spent a lot of time wandering the forest with nothing else in sight, even small critters for me to eat were pretty scarce. The game is currently in development, and there has already been a bug fix patch within a week of release, so the content should flow relatively quickly. The devs are super open and really interact with the community which is great to see.
TL;DR: This game is sort of bare, but the premise looks great. If you love dinosaurs I would highly recommend picking it up. Otherwise, put it on your follow list and watch the development and pick it up when it has more stuff for everyone to do.

As interesting as the concept sounds, I can't see this game being playable much beyond a few hours at best. It looks ok (until it gets dark, then it just looks weird, not sure if the dev is trying to simulate some kind of night vision, but it looks kind of like the gamma is jacked up at night), and I know it sounds weird, but during the day everything is just too green, I feel like there needs to be a little more colour variety. The game runs smoothly enough for an early access title (occasional screen freezes here and there). But, you pretty much just run around a jungle eating and drinking. I lost my parents on the first day, because I "rested" without reading the hint properly, my fault entirely, but it seemed like a strange time to let you know you can rest to recover stamina, I assumed it meant sit down and you recovered it faster, had I read on I would have noted that 8 hours pass when you rest, so my parents peaced out. I then spent the next 18 minutes running about trying to find water in the dark, this wasn't made easy by the confusing music that made me think I was being persued the whole time. I guess the music was supposed to be creating tension, but it just served to confuse me. Then a pachycephalosaurus stepped on me and I died.
I found, as with most Unity games, the controls were sluggish. Jumping appeared to be something that worked randomly. I couldn't get a feel for when it should and shouldn't work, like there was some kind of condition that needed to be met before I could jump (ie. running at a certain speed, having a certain amount of stamina, an invisible cooldown) And for some reason, for such a small, light and agile critter my dakotaraptor appeared to have incredible difficulty getting up to running speed. I mean, I would expect a predator like this one to be able to accelerate to full speed in a very short time, but it was like trying to roll start a locomotive.
Perhaps the developers are going for an edutainment angle with this title. They do repeatedly mention  the maticulous care spent on getting the game as "scientifically correct" as possible, even down to accurately reporoducing the landscape and ecosystem. As mentioed before, as a game, I mean something to do that's fun, this seems to have very little replayability, or playability for that matter.

Preparing for NG+, so might as well do a review now. It is my first game of the Tales series, and it is a fantastic game. I'll start with what i disliked, but I was really blown away by the game.
(-) maps/dungeons : very linear maps (corridors). Exploration often feels like a chore, there's just too much loot and chests, and rewards aren't anything special (but still often important, that's why it feels like a chore). With the exceptions of the cities, all the maps are empty of anything besides loot and monsters.
(-) design : i'm really not one to criticize the graphics, but i felt a bit let down by the artistic design. While i didn't expect any 'breathtaking views', nothing in particular strikes the eye. It's all kinda meh. Dungeon design is also severely lacking, close to zero 'classic' mechanisms , and those who are present are laughable.
(neutral) costumes : i don't mind the cute costumes, funny hats etc, but i would have liked more options in terms true costumes / armor. Too few options that don't feel out of place during cinematcis.
(neutral) music : it's kinda hit&miss, the OP is really good, there are a few good tracks but some are also annoying after having spent several hours in an area, not a lot of variation.
(+++) combat : one of the strength of the game, that makes not a single combat boring. Although it doesn't require a lot of dexterity skills, you still have to planify your combos before starting the fight, and you have to deal properly with all your ressources (life, souls, break souls point), so you can't mash mindlessly the buttons. Once you have enough spells (artes), it really feels satisfying to chain the combos, get bonus damage because you got all the weaknesses etc. All the playable characters have a different feel, and are really enjoyable. Minor complain : main character (velvet) feels a bit OP, and some characters are a bit frustrating to play against bosses.
(+++) story : incredible story. Some surprisingly heavy and touching scenes. Overall, it is quite dark and dramatic, and I now that I finished the game, i have the same feeling of emptiness i have after finishing an amazing book. All characters have a lot of developement, and it's really smoothly done, little by little. They really feel human.
Also, animated cinematics are gorgeous (but way too rare!)
(+) tutorial : since i said i'm a first time Tales player, i really want to add this one : the game really does a great job teaching you the mechanisms of the game, little by little (instead of 1 huge info dump tutorial). There are still many things that are left for you to understand alone, and a few confusing things, but overall I never felt completely lost despite the depth of some mechanisms.
There are many other things I really enjoyed (gearing system, sidequests, postgame & ng+,...) but the review is already quite long, and i think i exposed the main strength/weaknesses of the game for me. Really a solid 8-9/10 !

I was doubtful at first, especially because of the price, but when I looked up at Velvet a bit more, I instantly grabbed it.  Velvet is very similar to a character I've imagined a while back, a black haired girl with a demon arm with desires of vengeance.
For 65$ cdn, this game gave me 60 hours of gameplay on my first playthrough. The game has a really good story and the characters have great designs. The soundtracks were also somewhat decent.
The combat mechanicss are really fun. Instead of "Mana Points" that older "Tales of" games may have, you have a stamina-like ressources called Soul. Each artes cost a different amount of SG(Soul Gauge) and each Soul Orb contains 30 SGs. You are limited by Soul Orbs when it comes to combo-ing, but those are not lost unless specific conditions are met. There's no basic attacks in this game, so you will be using a variety of artes until you find your favorite combo, smootest combo or combo for the weakness of enemies, etc.
The price is indeed steep, but it's a high quality game.

is a short adventure game that packs a truck load of emotion, inviting you to investigate a painful mystery. When I was browsing through adventure games in Steam, the title took my attention, yet I never got the will to actually try the game while other games that I purchased before were in the waiting line. Now that I did, I'm positive that the story will haunt me for a while. I have to declare here and now: it is immensely difficult for one to write a review about this game without giving any kind of spoilers; but I will try my best.
We play the game as a middle aged man that shares a small cabin out in nowhere with his wife, Serena. He sits on the table and looks at a photo of him and his wife. He is unable to recognize his wife's face. What did her face look like? Her eye color? Was she smiling when they took the photo? Come to think of it, where actually is Serena? She is not there... and doesn't seem to be returning soon either. We take a stroll within the cabin, and try to find some clues about our wife's whereabouts. Every furniture, every memento, every stain makes a life. Every tiny detail scattered around presents us a fragment of our memory with her. What happened to her?
The game is your basic adventure. The only place you got is the small cabin itself, in which the developers managed to fit in a grand deal of story. The atmosphere is a marvelous success, accompanied by beautiful background music that reflects the mood in echoes. Everything around is dim, dark and dusty, as if the reality is old and static as our protagonist's perception. What is certainly remarkable for the gameplay is that; as our memory comes back and our perception change, associations that we have through objects do change also. That is key for the progress within this game. You click on an object for the millionth time - ok, I exaggerate, but at least 15 or so in given progress - , and you still discover something new about the story. The mood starts with faint, content reminiscence, growing to become heavy suspense and conflict; finally calling the trumpet to make room for pure wrath and agony.
You won't be using anything else besides your mouse to go through our protagonist's memory lane. And take note, the game IS really short. I've run through the game 2 times already, and it took me a bit more than an hour to complete it for the first time. Considering the length, the game doesn't have a save game option. You launch, you play, you complete and you exit. That's all there is. I believe the length of the game is one of the reasons that the game was startling. The last moment comes as a punch to your conscience.
is a wonderful short story that you'll keep with yourself even long time after you finish the game. I've made some research and discovered that the developers' intention for the production bears a story of its own. The game is made to correct a wrong and outweigh the pleasant as an intention in gaming community. That's why the game is free to play. So, if you are an adventure player and enjoy high quality, yet disturbing narration, what are you waiting for?

The Walking Dead Season 1 is a triumph in interactive-storytelling. Harrowing and heartbreaking, Telltale has narrated a tale from the dead that's both accurate to the mood of its souce-material (the comic it's based from) and so confident in its take on the canon, that, at times, reaches higher highs than its source-material.
Brilliantly voice acted and wonderfully animated, you can find immidiate affection or resentment from the stories characters; and as you wage through the zombie-infested world, you'll experience tremdenous moments of satisfaction, followed by times of grief. The Walking Dead hits almost every wave-length of human emotion. Few games have done this.
For as well as the story is told, this is still a game, and so, as a game, its puzzles are its gameplay - fairly straightforward and for the most part intuitive. I'm one of the people who enjoyed the comic and the early series' of The Walking Dead more because they were more about the decisions and choices the characters make in different situations and scenarios and helped to show that human nature is an ugly beast, but very complex and interwoven, and never black and white. The video game facilitates this same process- showing the results of our different choices and decisions through the characters, and because you're playing one of those characters and vested in their outcome, everything that affects the world affects you on an emotional level.
When it came out it was a somewhat unique gameplay mechanic for Point & Click Adventure games, and it's still limited- most choices don't actually affect the world or the linear story, yet it absolutely reaches you and makes the story and the things happening on screen more vivid and real.

This is one game that I just cannot drop!
The social element of it is what really sucks me in: depending on your role, you are either working with the "townies" to find and kill all the evildoers, trying to kill everyone, or simply looking out for yourself, no matter what happens to the townies or the evildoers.
The roles are varied (currently there are 30 different roles) and, in my opinion, all fun to play, assuming you are really engaged with the roles in question.  One of my favorites is the Executioner, where you're assigned a random person in the town to have killed by lynching by any means necessary.  That usually means convincing the town that your target is something that they are not in order to get them on trial and ultimately executed.  It is SO satisfying when you get your target lynched, therefore accomplishing your objective and ultimately win, no matter what happens!
The graphics are simplistic (Town of Salem originated as a Flash game), but they work.  The kill animations are always a joy (or painful, depending on who's on the stand) to watch and hear.  There is an in-game store that allows you to purchase new characters, houses, and pets, the money for which can be either earned by playing matches (regardless of the outcome, you'll get at least 5 coins) or dropping real money to get coins in bulk.  The coin purchases are purely cosmetic and have no impact on the gameplay.
If you're an achievement hound, you won't be disappointed here, as over 200 achievements await you, all of which earn you bonus coins for spending in-game.
The core problem for me, as of this review, is people quitting games, which can be REALLY disadvantagous for a town.  Most people that quit do so because they simply didn't like the role they were randomly assigned, which can be understandable... but not really.  When Investigators, Sheriffs, and Lookouts quit on Day 1, it can make winning the game for the town (the good guys) really challenging.  The most people I've seen quit on Day 1 was four.  Combined with the killing overnight, by Day 2 six people were dead (when you quit, you are labeled as committing suicide for that game), all townies, making my life as a Mafioso VERY easy.
Overall, for five bucks, I cannot recommend this game enough.  It's really fun to play, whether it's in short 15-minute spurts or multi-hour sessions.

Golden Rush is a newly developed MOBA made by Gravvit, the same people that made My Lands: Black Gem Hunting. Although there is a lot of potential for this MOBA, I think there are a lot of things that Golden Rush does wrong, including a very substantial cash grab and microtransaction store. You will need money to play this game and you get steep advantages if you shell out the money.
Since Golden Rush has beautiful graphics, menus, and characters, I decided that I would make an entire review based on my experience with the game. Hopefully the developers will realize that microtransactions are horrible for games like this, especially when it requires the purchasing of your own characters abilities. Maybe they'll fix their game, which I think has wonderful potential without the cash grab and sluggish gameplay.
- Artwork is gorgeous, very well done.
- Game offers a unique experience, just needs more fine tuning.
- Character abilities seem fun.
- Menus are very well put-together.
- Microtransactions - seriously, a lot of them.
- Premium membership and cash grab.
- Sluggish gameplay, games are too long.
- No standard MOBA gametype.
- Lots of Russians.
For the pros, a lot of it is subjective.
I think the artwork on the menus are simply astounding and it actually made my jaw drop from looking at it. If you don't believe me, go ahead and look at the art they posted on their store page and you tell me. I think the attention to detail and high resolution of the pictures make them look very well put-together and incredibly professional. Again, subjectivity.
As for the unique experience, this is really a personal preference. Some people enjoy the MOBA games that are more about killing your enemies, taking towers, and crushing the Nexus/Ancient/Titan. For this game, it seems more about farming minions, setting the enemy team back by stealing their gold and killing them before they can farm, and taking down major objectives.
Unfortunately, with this type of game mode, comes the inherently sluggish process of roaming around the map, killing creeps, and shoving the gold into teams wallet. Since there are four teams of three on a large-scale map, sometimes you don't even meet enemy players and are instead met with the same routine: farm, farm, farm. While this is poor design, with a bit of tinkering with the pace of the game, it could actually be really fun.
The character abilities aren't all that dull, in my opinion. They're pretty standard for a game of this genre, but it's not as if they have very many characters, so there is much room for improvement. Giving developers the potential to make their game great is what we should doing, which is why I don't mind the characters being a bit more default than other games in the genre that have spent a good decade in existence.
Now, for the cons, which is undoubtedly one of the biggest reasons why you'll want to quit this game. Microtransactions are an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥. The elixirs in the game alone cost 6 black gems each. To put that in perspective, 5 dollars worth of gems gives you around 500 and if you're playing consistently, that isn't much at all. Players should never have to buy parts of a game, especially if it's a pivotal part of the game and gives players a huge advantage.
Just looking at the store front on the main menu, they're charging up to $400 to purchase some of their gems, which is a completely outrageous price. Developers, if you read this, Golden Rush will die so quickly because of what you've done to the microtransactions - right your wrong, fix this immediately. No players should spend their own money to get a leg up on the competition, ever, period.
Another con, which is pretty substantial, is that there isn't any standard MOBA gametype. You know, the one where you lane for awhile, take down enemies, and push their towers to win? I'm all for new and unique gamemodes, but I think players would benefit from a standard gamemode. There is such a huge difference between the gold farming gamemode and the standard MOBA gamemode because both of them appeal to different crowds. To get more people behind this game, Golden Rush would need to have a more standard mode.
Lastly, lots of Russians. This game was made by a developer that is Russian and, therefore, you're going to see a lot of that coming through the chat. If you feel like dealing with that and you don't mind playing a couple games before the cash grab waves its beckoning finger, go ahead and give this game a whirl. However, I refuse to give it a thumbs up because of the microtransactions and, until they take that out, I will not be recommending this game.

I loved Game Dev Tycoon. If you're thinking about buying this game, there's a chance you do as well. But after having put some real time into Mad Games tycoon, I can say quite frankly that I'm probably never playing it again. It's not meant to be a diss toward them -- it's a great game, through and through -- but MGT is better in almost every sense of the phrase.
MGT is a tycoon game wherein you build a game studio, release games (no, you don't actually make them/ can't play them), and eventually work your way up to producing consoles, MMOs, and more. If you've played GDT, MGT probably sounds pretty familiar. But in this game, you're actually doing floor layouts for your buildings. Your options when hiring workers are better. The gameplay feels smoother and more polished. You can self-produce your games and go into publishing the works of others. There's even an admittedly-dodgy stock market system where you can buy out your competition. All told, MGT is a lot like GDT... only there's more of everything, and everything feels better-refined.
Well, almost everything.
MGT does come up short in a few aspects, most notably with its failure to include a Steam-like distribution service that would cut out physical media production altogether. When was the last time you bought a game in a brick-and-mortar store, with a disc and everything? 2005? Yeah... this game needs to offer players the ability to publish on/ create a service similar to Steam. GDT has something sort of like this, so why doesn't MGT?
Another problem, one that befalls most tycoon games in general, is an utter lack of creative throughput. When designing a game, you can basically that game a name, a broad genre, and a couple of basic topics... and that's it. Where are the sliders for making stories more intricate? Where's the mad-libs-style topic input where I'm defining protagonists, antogonists, and setting? Where do I design the game to feature open-world? Offering these sorts of customization options can make a game considerably more fun and addictive, even if your choices don't have real consequences. Rock God Tycoon lets you write music. The Movies allowed you to make films and watch your creations (why the crap isn't that game being remade?!?!). I want more options when making games, even if I can't play them!
All told, Mad Games Tycoon is a very fun, addictive game. It has its drawbacks, but every game does. If you're into tycoon games, this is one I very strongly recommend picking up.

You’re about to enjoy a tasty burrito when you see the girl of your dreams drop her phone. She disappears, but you need to find her phone to track this woman down, presumably so you can have fart children together. In order to find the phone, you need to clear out the burrito restaurant. Now, asking people to politely move is just unheard of in this day and age, so what do you do? You fart, of course! Lots of farting. Some wet, I assume.
is a 99 cent game, so you can obviously assume that there isn’t much to it. And there isn’t. You use WASD to move, and spacebar to fart. Or d-pad to move and pretty much every other button but start to do your business. You move around the various locations, farting at people to get them to leave. The goal of each level is to clear it of all people. Starts off easy with 20-odd people at the burrito place, then you need to clear a couple hundred from the airport.
You have two bars you need to take care of; gas and time. Your gas depletes the more you fart, so you’ll want to chain together the disgust of people to build up combos. A combo of ten will instantly refill your meter. If you can’t chain ten, maybe because people are spread around, you can run over the randomly spawning burritos that will fill it for you.
Your other piece of management is time. Each level has a time limit that continues from the previous one. If you complete the burrito restaurant with 15 seconds left, you’ll begin the parking lot with only having 15 seconds of time. Running over the clock powerups will increase your time. If you do run out of time, you don’t restart the game, you simply restart the level itself. This is all based on the default difficulty, which is Toot. I have not tried it on Fart or Shart difficulties. Man, it’s actually kind of hard to write this with a straight face.
And that’s the game. Work your way from restaurant to airport to wedding and marry the girl of your dreams.
The cons are, to be honest, not really cons. They are the “bad” parts about this game, but it’s also one whole dollar, they’re to be expected. Unless you download this and never play it, you will, no question, get your money’s worth. Besides, if trading cards are added at some point, you’re bound to make back a quarter of the cost at least.

I personally purchased this game. I reviewed it for my 99 Cent Gaming series.
When I logged into Steam today looking for another game to review for my series, I never thought I'd be hit in the face with a game like CropDuster Supreme. Unphased, I let the gust of insipration take me through the entire game in one video to see if it was worth the dollar or if it was just full of hot musky air...
CropDuster Supreme is a game that is very very simple in it's execution. Every level has the player tasked with clearing out rooms by using your powers of flatulence on demand, aiming to hit as many people as possible with your clouds of stench. On top of the number of people you need to clear is a timer that counts down to 0 making you restart the level if the room isn't cleared in time. You also have a limited number of on demand toots you can use before running out of those as well.
There are two power ups to help which are the clock (which adds time) and the burrito (which adds more ammo). These seem to pop up at random but definitely help out when you really need them the most. I've found myself at the tail end of a level with a couple of people to go screaming "where is a clock?!" and having it pop up just in time. Pun intented.
There were a few couple of things that caused me to get a little frustrated which I want to point out before getting to the verdict. First was the combo system. Now it may have been because I went into the game blind and bought it right as I saw the release, but I had no idea how the combos worked. Every so often I would see the word COMBO and sometimes with a x2 or x3 but I couldn't figure out how I was getting them. At one point in the game it tells you getting a x10 combo refills your bar. I managed to complete the entire game without once reaching that amount, so it's not necessary to beating it...but I do wish that there was some way of knowing how it could have happened.
The other thing that caused frustration was losing myself in the crowds. There were a few levels that had a ton of people you had to clear out, and once the chaos began it was too easy to get lost in the shuffle. I evenutally found myself after stopping to really look, but I think having some sort of identifier or indication of where your character is at all time would bring down the frustration level.
Outside of those two things, I have to say the game brought me pretty decent entertainment for what I purchased. Now granted the game was very short (it took me about 30 minutes to complete) but it was fully featured, bug free (from what I played), grammar was on point and I want to support developers who manage to do that. I've also not played the higher difficulties yet and can only imagine the insanity that it will bring.
I have more to say and reactions to give in my video below, but overall...is the game worth .99? Absolutely! It's a fun distraction, and with the game being in Early Access I hope the developers take notice with the two points of frustration I encountered and work in things like a combo explination tutorial and a player identifier. I'd love to revisit this as updates are made.

This was the first XCOM game that I played.  The learning curve was challenging but rewarding enough to get me hooked.
Management comes in the form of your ship:  you decide what rooms to build, which technologies to research, etc.  You will learn priorities and strategies on your first play through that will have you laughing at yourself the second and third time around.
Each mission you get to assemble your crew.  You can customize your warriors with weapons, armor, etc.  Your soldiers stick with you and level up as you progress through the missions.  You need to determine if you want to share the love and level up all your soldiers, or stick with a core group of hardened veterans.
When ready you launch into a battlefield covered with shroud.. You need to explore quickly to discover your enemies and other challenges awaiting you.  Some missions have timers, others do not.  Enemies react to you once you've been spotted! so keeping your crew in formation while also scouring the map becomes a challenge in itself.  All missions are turned based.  This was difficult getting use to for me, but XCOM2 handles it very well and you never feel slowed down or stuck due to it.
The environment becomes as much of a challenge as the enemies are as you navigate over cliffs, through buildings, and around cover.  Tactics that are available to your troops become increasingly important as you progress through the game so get started using them right away.  This is a game where you want to utilize the 'Save' button often.  Good luck.

This game is a fantastic turn-based tactics game, with a solid real-time strategy layer to give it context. I would recommend it to anyone who likes difficult strategy games which require a lot of thought.
The tactics layer revolves around stealth and combat with a squad of 4-6 soldiers. There are 5 classes and many gadgets and upgrades to allow you to customize your team to suit your tastes. The most important and best-designed system of the layer is the cover system. If you choose cover wisely, your soldiers will be have a very low chance of being hit, while at the same time having the opportunity to flank enemies for an advantage. It is simple to understand, but difficult to master.
The strategy layer involves customizing your research, equipment, and buildings, and then basically going to the world-map and waiting. The base-building is quite fun, but I'm personally not a huge fan of the waiting mechanic. Basically you fly your ship around and try to gain resources while waiting for new resources and battles to pop up. The key phrase being "pop up". For most missions there is not much warning for when their prompts will appear, so it's kind of jarring and annoying. You will often find yourself very close to harvesting an important resource, but then suddenly having a mission prompt in your face which you basically can't ignore if you want to win. Not my favourite UX decision in the game.
With respect to difficulty, I would say the game's 4 difficulties are nicely balanced. The most common complaint about this game is that it is too RNG-based for the difficulty to be fair, but that's not really true. The game is really one about risk-management, and there are many ways to mitigate risk in the tactical layer. If you are leaving the success of the game up to the hit-chance of a single soldier, you are probably not playing the situation correctly. As for the difficulty curve, the game is actually most difficult at the beginnings and endings of campaigns. In the mid-game certain tech is perhaps too powerful in that combat can start to become trivial. This unevenness is a little jarring, but it doesn't detract too much from the game for me.
Overall, a clear thumbs up from me. If you enjoy it I would also recommend looking into the War of the Chosen DLC after completing a campaign or two. It adds a lot of new systems to the game(especially in the strategy layer) and is generally fantastic as well.

(Base game Review, I have not purchased any of the DLC yet, though I will update the game once I've logged sufficient playtime on the game with the DLC installed, assuming I purchase it. [Spoiler: I'm probably going to purchase it.]
*My Opinion In A Nutshell*:
Good game, buy it if you like turn-based strategy games. It's worth buying on sale, and if you're like me, you'll easily get 2-3 challenging playthroughs before even touching the DLC. Each Playthrough takes quite a chunk of time, so you'll get your moneys worth in gametime.
The Good:
-XCom 2 plays very similiarly to Xcom 1 with some new mechanics thrown in, and with harder enemies. I did my first playthrough on Veteran and felt quite challenged, always doing my best to properly position my troops and make use of their abilities in the most effecient way possible. I'm currently looking forward to my next playthrough, and I'm eager to see how well I do against XCom 2's most difficult, well, difficulty.
-XCom 2 offers a more diverse set of choices to you than X1 did. You now have a world map, where instead of simply setting up satellites and all this hoobla hoobla, you now must make use of your time, choosing what resources are most valueble to you on the map at any given period. Scanning Sites can offer different rewards in exchange for your time, and you as the player must continue expanding your contacts on the map in a semi-timely manner, taking out Alien facilities so Doomsday doesn't come quite so quickly. Manage your time wisely, ensure you are prepared, and stay on top of your resources: The Macro game is just as important as the Micro.
-Soldiers are super customizable in terms of appearence, you can even write them a backstory now. Weapons also have a full modding system behind them, and each different type of armor gives a soldier different strengths, as well as different weaknesses.
-There is fall damage, so don't get the floor blown out from under you up on that big fancy tower. Also blow the floor out from under the non-floating aliens. They'll be super p/o'd, and missing an additional chunk of health. You'll also be pretty p/o'd and missing a few chunks of health if you let that Muton get too close and grenade the building out from under your squad. Don't let that happen.
-Utility items are friggin gud man, Xcom 2 has alllll kinds of em, and they're tons of fun.
-Dark Events can be really engaging, as the Aliens will work, month by month, to complete 'Research', which will give them an edge against your most frequently used tactics. You research that Armor buff first thing? Well crap, the Aliens are researching armor too. Better stop that. Been sneaking around a lot, getting WAY too many kills with those perfect Concealment ambushes? Well... Crap, they're researching something to widen their detection radius. Better stop that. It can lead to a lot of interesting gameplay decisions on the Macro level, as well as changing how you would approach situations in combat on a per-month basis. (Each research completion only lasts one month. Don't worry, they won't spam Armor research and give all their units 10 armor by the end of the game. Won't happen. The bonuses cycle in and out per each month of in-game time.)
The Bad:
-Critical hits can feel a bit BS-ey, especially in the early game. Your favorite soldier hiding behind full cover, probably not gonna get hit by that Advent Commander on the second/third mission in your playthrough? Might... Maybe. Just maybe, get hit, critted, and instakilled, because you don't have Tier 2 armor yet. It's not a very likely thing to happen, and most critical hits happen when your soldiers get flanked, but me personally: I'd rather this 'Lucky or not lucky' mechanic didn't exist. It doesn't feel like it belongs in an in-depth strategy game like XCom. I'd much rather have a hit or miss chance as the only element of luck at play, rather than the chance to do, or receive double damage at random as well.
-The Dodge mechanic is almost as equally bad as the Critical mechanic, allowing soldiers (Equipped with certain armor, or hunkering down), and some aliens (Mostly aliens) to only take a small portion of the damage they would have otherwise taken from a hit. You cannot shred it, it's based on RNG, and overall its quite a random wrench thrown into things, having few counters in the early to mid game (Aside from explosives spam). I would, personally, prefer something more consistant and counterable. It feels very 'Thrown in there', and not very well thought out.
-You cannot reinforce cover in this game, and no one form of cover is usually any better than another. All of it can get destroyed by an explosion, and your soldier (Or the enemy alien) can be sitting out there without jack protecting them. It's a semi-fair mechanic most of the time, and hasn't led to many soldier deaths in my playthroughs, but it does feel like being able to reinforce your cover (Or deploy very hard cover), would be a great addition to the game. Not having different explosive resistances to different types of cover in XCom 2 makes no 'One' type of half-cover or full-cover much better than any other, as most cover in the game can be destroyed just with a single grenade.
-Hacking is, in my opinion, somewhat bad. There's no sort of deduction, guesswork, or challenge to it at all. The game will simply roll your soldiers 'Technology Score' against the Items (Whatever it is your trying to hack, that is. A Robot, a Control Tower, a Cache...), rather than giving you any sort of little mini-game or puzzle. Feels like a missed opportunity to do something interesting.
-Mimic Beacons are just plain stupid. Overextend your favorite soldier into a complete and utter dogbowl of a mess? A Sectopod looking to light him THE FLUFF UP next turn? Pfsh. PFSH I SAY! Just throw a Mimic Beacon. ALL OF THE ALIENS WILL ABSOLUTELY ATTACK IT, RATHER THAN ATTACK YOUR SOLDIER. Essentially, it acts as a 100% Taunt mechanic to any Alien which is in it's Line of Sight. I expressly forbade myself from equipping these items on my upcoming playthrough. They're really cheesy, and really should've been adjusted by now. TLDR: Wanna easily beat the game on max difficulty without losing any soldiers? Abuse Mimic Beacons.
The Nuetral: (Or the Ugly, if you prefer. But it's not actually that bad. Heh, get my stupid reference?)
-Proper Dossiers for all of the Alien enemies aren't really a thing. There will be some random 'Quirks' about the Aliens you'll just find out by random, without any warning about. Say you've got a Ranger, for example, and you go to melee attack a Muton with it... LOL. NOPE BRO. That Muton just slapped your soldiers sword out of the way and stabbed him dead. Even if you've completed the Muton Autopsy, no mention of this hidden mechanic is... Anywhere in the game, really. Personally, I would like detailed dossiers regarding these 'Hidden' mechanics to be added to future games, allowing players to find these sorts of things out by other means than random experience and soldier deaths. Really, this is a small thing however, and it could be argued that these hidden mechanics add some form of 'Knowledge Check' to the playerbase. Still, it left a bad taste in my mouth.
-The AI seems to 'Forgive' you of your mistakes sometimes. That one soldier way out of position, flanked by three units, gets cut down to 2 HP? The last enemy Alien with a turn might just... Ignore them for some reason, to shoot at one of your other Soldiers. I'm not sure if this changes with the difficulty or not, but it felt like this happened semi-frequently in my gameplay.
Overall:
-Good game, but could be better. I understand the Developers are trying some new things in this version, tossing in mechanics like crit and dodge, but it just disrupts the consistency of my strats. Still, time well spent, and I'm planning to spend even more time. Get the base game for at least 40$, its worth it.

Excellent combat, beautiful scenery and a gripping story - ★★★★☆
Let's be honest, you know why you're here; you're here because you love the sinister and divisive nature of the tales series. You love having your heart toyed with in inhumane ways, evoking emotion within you that you never thought could even exist in that dark void that you call a soul. If you're looking to do that while exploring a beautiful world through the eyes of a completely badass demon, then this my good sir, is your game.
The strongest feature of this game is its ability to make you feel like an absolute beast. Be warned, a byproduct of this game is sleep deprivation, but also intense adrenaline production when you feel like you have just raised all two-hundred layers of hell, slapped Satan in the face, snorted cocaine off his wife's butt cheeks and then injected heroin through one of his horns.
That being said, there are a lot of things that could be improved. Recycling monsters is something that annoys me to no end, it is incredibly lazy of the developer to just reskin monsters ten times in a row and change their loot tables. The character customization is very lackluster, the combat could be so much more interesting if they actually gave you the ability to switch things up a little. The world could also do with being a little bigger, this size is okay for a game made in the 2000s, but you should know better by now.
I'm also very disappointed that there isn't a city hub in this game - players love to have a place they can ground themselves, do arena, explore and try out different things, a very lazy choice by the developers to not have one in my opinion. Speaking of which, are they serious with the adventure packs? TL;DR Tales of Berseria is a good jRPG and if you're a fan of the genre you should do yourself a favour and buy it right now.
Now, onto more detailed opinion.
Tales of Berseria follows Velvet Crowe, a young woman with traumatic past, that embarks on a journey to murder a man who destroyed her life. One problem is that this man is now a respected world leader and pretty much considered its saviour. Along the way other people join her - each with different agendas, but pretty much sharing a common goal - which creates pretty much one of the most morally grey parties in jRPGs to date. Very refreshing after standard 'good vs evil' trope found in other games.
Plot itself is... Let's just say that Hidetaka Miyazaki (Dark Souls) is not the only person in Namco that is "inspired by" Berserk. From characters, to names (Holy Midgand Empire!), to themes of conflict between emotion and reason. Parallels are undeniable. That aside I found overall story to be okay and it was characters that really kept me playing. From cursed pirates, through samurai demons to self-proclaimed witches, each person in Velvet's band of misfits is very well written and their often clashing personalities create entertaining conversations. Berseria achieves this through skits, optional animated cutscenes, providing additional dialogue that really add depth to the characters.
Aside from few minigames (optional, cosmetic stuff), bulk of gameplay lays in real-time combat. Berseria gradually introduces player to its intricacies and it is not uncommon to get a pop-up tutorial even after few hours. Basically, it all comes down to managing your stamina (souls) bar which allow you to put out more attacks. Starting from few simple kicks and slices to unleashing devastating multi-hit combos, combat system actually gets more fun as you go. Despite all that chaos that is happening on the screen it never becomes overwhelming as you can always pause to adjust party members, AI, equipment, items or even camera height. I controlled Velvet 95% of the time in combat but every other character plays a little different. It is also worth noting that putting yourself at disadvantage by allowing multiple enemies to attack your party will result in more XP, money and items.
Not everything is shiny though in Berserk(ia). First of all it really takes its time to get rolling. First few hours with our brooding edgelord lady could put people off. Thankfully once more people join your merry band and Velvet starts to come out of her shell it becomes much more interesting. Second culprit is sadly backtracking, before you have handy consumables to warp between areas. Couple that with many tedious, bland-looking "dungeons" with linear and constrained corridors and an occasional puzzle where you have to hit a switch to open a door. This is remedied somewhat by obtaining a funky "hover board" that allows faster travel. Lastly, I found music rather bland and forgettable. After 55+ hours, I can't remember any single theme that stands out.
Despite it's flaws however, Berseria is well worth picking up, with enough quality content to satisfy even a veteran player. Recommended.

Artificial Defense takes simple abstract graphics and makes them feel clustered and complete for a full, if very casual, tower defense / orbital bomber defense.
Full video:
Summary:
The sound and graphics make this game gel, giving it much needed activity and ambiance where it would otherwise be a more bland and abstract tower defense hybrid.
The variety of challenges and levels do provide a nice bit of progression, but while they look, feel and behave just great, I do have concerns in the pacing with some of the games. Especially the "survive X time" and "get X Ram" challenges can end up being a game of see and wait. Higher difficulty does alleviate a bit of this, but there are some issues with that...
..as the higher difficulties are flat out "upgrade" locked, and impossible if you don't unlock the higher end upgrades, so there is no reason to revisit an older challenge once you complete it at gold, because it'll only become easier due to higher upgrades.
The upgrade system is the games weakest part, being a flat and linear upgrade system. No reason to mix and match and no thinking needed. Just get the next one asap to make challenges easier / possible to complete. I feel this is also the part where the game lets me down the most. I have no reason to "switch it up" based on a challenge, i know that if i fail, i just wait to upgrade and that does remove some of the tension of otherwise pretty compelling game play.
And while the game is limited in it's scope, the game play and map design does make up for it a fair bit. With towers being restricted, resources limited and a need to switch between Shooting manually using towers, getting resources and balancing these aspects, the game throws in a few curve balls with map design and unit variety (in mechanic, if not look and feel). Forcing you to be active across the map and keep track of several things at the same time makes this game shine at it's best.
It feels great to switch between dropping a tower, jumping to a missile to blow up a clump of enemies, using a CPU module to start my resource chain, switching to my machine gun to take out a roaming ram unit switching to different part of the map to make sure i'm not getting overwhelmed on that side... it's pretty good fun and most challenges take 5-10 minutes to complete - win or lose.
Overall a nice and fun casual experience for short bursts, not something i would play hours on end, but not a bad game to enjoy in short bursts.

- Lastly, no flying vehicles (less verticality).

Sleeping Dogs in many ways is just your average GTA clone. It does nothing much groundbreaking or new but manages to provide a decent open world experience that will entertain for as long as it should.
You start of as Wei, an undercover police detective that's working his way into the power structure of a local triad. Of course he has a number of personal connections and vendettas that he is secretly trying to solve however the lack of choice often means you won't really get to care about his developing identity crisis.
Unlike most games in this genre guns are fairly rare and you will only really use them in the missions that require it, the rest of the time you will be depending on your martial arts skills.
Although the developers did quite a lot of talking up the fighting system in this game, even going as far as comparing it to the Arkham games, it doesn't quite meet that standard, you got your heavy attack and your light attack as well as a grapple and can use those in a variety of combos. Unfortunately Sleeping Dogs also takes a page from the first Assassins Creed game and gives you an end all counter button. You can win almost any fight by just standing still and countering the enemy attacks without much effort.
The driving feels pretty good, not quite the cartoon style of Saints Row but not the annoying wannabe realistic style of later GTAIV either it manages to strike a nice balance where cars are still fun but it doesn't get too silly. For some bizarre reason though motorcycles have much greater road grip than even the best of cars.
Instead of multi-player Sleeping Dogs have a social hub feature wherein you can compete with your friends for high scores on missions and races as well as a number of challenges but it is a feature easily forgotten or ignored.
What separates Sleeping Dogs from the pack is the location. Instead of being situation in yet another differently named version of New York City the game takes place in Hong Kong and everything about the game, from the mini games to the radio stations and the street vendors create a different feel than we're used to in this sort of game. When was the last time you bet on cockfighting in a video game?
Although the Hong Kong vibe manages to make Sleeping Dogs rise somewhat above the pack it is still a fairly unimpressive game underneath, not much new and not much improved over the many other games in the same genre out there now. Also it is much lighter on content than is normal for a game in this genre and 100% the game, achievements and DLC shouldn't take much more than 25-30 hours of game time.
Still, it's a game I had quite a bit of fun with and the Hong Kong vibe was interesting to play around with, it's a pretty game despite originating on the consoles and although I would probably feel a little cheated if I had gotten it at it's original 50$ price tag with the current sales and discounts it's an enjoyable experience.

I was quite worried when Namco announced that the next Tales game would be a distant prequel to Tales of Zestiria. I enjoyed Zesteria, but the game had many issues, one of which was the setup of the world. A sequel, I thought, could clean up some of the plot problems that Zesteria had, but what could a prequel do? My interest in the game dwindled as I waited for more information and the release.
Well, I was wrong.
Berseria is a good game. It's a very good game. It took nearly every good thing that Zesteria did with it's combat system, threw out the bad things, mixed in a whole bunch of new mechanics, all of which are good, and threw it in a blender with a story that's actually good. It's not the best Tales story, but it's definitely not the worst, either, and, unlike Zesteria, is one that will likely be looked back on fondly.
Having played the game, I can now say that making it a prequel to Zesteria was a really good idea. This game feels in a lot of ways like an apology to everyone who was so disappointed with Zesteria. Not only does it fix a lot of Zesteria's systems without throwing out all the good ideas, it also provides much needed world-building. There are so many references, both little and not so little, that players who played Zesteria will catch that I can't list all of them.
While you by no means need to have played Zesteria in order to like this game, those who have done so will find that not only is this the game that they hoped Zesteria was, but the game provides so much backstory and support for Zesteria that if you found yourself disappointed by Zesteria then this is a game that you should not miss.
Honestly, now I'm hoping for a Zesteria sequel to tie the games together even more.
