The original Half-Life is an FPS masterpiece which kickstarted a narrative and mechanical revolution that's still ongoing in the genre to this day.
Because of its understated, minimalist plot using environmental and gameplay-based storytelling, it's aged incredibly well and still makes for a very engaging experience. The gameplay is every bit as excellent and solid as it was all those years ago, the sound design is still phenomenal and the stylized-yet-realistic art direction makes for a look that still holds up today. Buying it also gives you access to a huge, huge quantity of great quality mods developed for the game over the course of almost 20 years, and that's definitely worth the price of admission.
But looking beyond its legacy in modding, and the standard also set by later entries in the series, Half-Life is still a remarkable game and an absolute must-have.
I would say pick it up for 5 bucks while you can if you like an oldschool turn-based rpg.

You move very sluggishly. This makes any sort of dodging hard as you usually won't be able to jump in time to get out of the way. At least you're bullets move fast right? Nope. The speed of the bullets is about a centimeter per second. Most bullets anyway. Because of the lack of velocity with the bullets, you're going to be missing a lot, because by the time they've arrived at their target, he's already 50 feet away in the air. Intrusion 2, as I stated previously, is a game whose developers have shown utter disrespect to the laws of game design. They could have made a really fun game, the core mechanics of Intrusion 2 are actually quite good. But they had to completely ruin it because they wanted to look cool. The game tries WAY too hard to be "cool". Oh look you can ride on a wolf oh look you're fighting a huge mech serpent after snowboarding down a mountain avoiding a grenadier's bombs LOOK HOW COOL THIS GAME IS!!!!11! When in reality no one cares. If your game is not fun because of it's mechanics people aren't going to care how good you make it look or how hard you try to be cool. Now if you want a game that's like Intrusion 2 but actually tries to... well.. be a GAME look at Capsized. Capsized is Intrusion 2 with infinitely better execution. Heck, it even looks cooler and doesn't need to throw it in your face constantly like Intrusion 2.

This is an old but amazing game. I played it quite a few years ago.
You click to reveal a little of an item until you're pretty sure you know what it is and then you type it in. The game is good about giving you credit. For instance, I typed in mannequin once and it was "dress form" but the game gave it to me. Or if you type in watch instead of wrist watch, you'll still get it right. There are different types of guessing games as well. Some are blurry and get clearer with each click. Some are twisted and go more towards their natural shape with each click. Etc. Each stage has a theme so if you can guess that, it's much easier to figure out the object. Between stages, you'll get a "hidden object" type of room but instead of finding items, you complete them. A chair will be missing a leg so you draw that in (just click on it and your pen does the rest). A column will be missing or a bow on a present or half of a pair of scissors. You get the picture. As you progress through the game, you get power ups that will help your guessing when activated. And you'll also open up bonus stages where you can guess even MORE items if you don't get your fill in the main game.
If you like puzzle games, I wholeheartedly recommend this. It is just so much fun.

At this ponit there really isn't anything more to say about Bastion that isn't already said. I think Bastion will be viewed as one of those essential indie games you just have to have played. It's an example of a game that does everything right: fun mechanics, great visual style and soundtrack, but most of all a beautiful and emotional story  presented in a brilliant way through the wonderfull narrator of the game.

As the game goes on things become a lot more interesting and once you get to the very end things become extremely intense. This game takes patience to complete and you must be able to pay attention to detail. I'll rate this game 8.5/10, in what it sometimes lacks in excitement it makes up for in story. The game always seems to keep you guessing and keep you on your toes. As the game progresses the main character is looking for Serena in a getaway cabin. He seems to get harsher, and more assertive and angry as you click on more items and bring up more memories. Setting up the finish for an intense final scene. Takes about 45 minutes to complete, but its worth it.

This game flourished off the back of the success of the TV series, but it's every bit as enjoyable and well made in its own right. I'm one of the people who enjoyed the comic and the early series' of The Walking Dead more because they were more about the decisions and choices the characters make in different situations and scenarios and helped to show that human nature is an ugly beast, but very complex and interwoven, and never black and white. The video game facilitates this same process- showing the results of our different choices and decisions through the characters, and because you're playing one of those characters and vested in their outcome, everything that affects the world affects you on an emotional level.
When it came out it was a somewhat unique gameplay mechanic for Point & Click Adventure games, and it's still limited- most choices don't actually affect the world or the linear story, yet it absolutely reaches you and makes the story and the things happening on screen more vivid and real.

Excellent. Very creative.
Your objective is to guess the object in the hidden picture. You can reveal a small portion of the picture by clicking, and of course, the fewer clicks you need, the better. There are hundreds of pictures for you to guess. And various potions to help you.
Aside from these normal problems, there are some bizarre challenges, such as guessing a twisted picture, a mosaic-ed picture, a scrambled picture, and more.
Each chapter contains 16 puzzles, and between chapters there are search-for-hidden-object levels. What's creative about this is that, you don't just search for listed objects in the scene. Instead, you search for listed objects that SHOULD be in the scene but actually are NOT.

Sleeping Dogs in many ways is just your average GTA clone. It does nothing much groundbreaking or new but manages to provide a decent open world experience that will entertain for as long as it should.
You start of as Wei, an undercover police detective that's working his way into the power structure of a local triad. Of course he has a number of personal connections and vendettas that he is secretly trying to solve however the lack of choice often means you won't really get to care about his developing identity crisis.
Unlike most games in this genre guns are fairly rare and you will only really use them in the missions that require it, the rest of the time you will be depending on your martial arts skills.
Although the developers did quite a lot of talking up the fighting system in this game, even going as far as comparing it to the Arkham games, it doesn't quite meet that standard, you got your heavy attack and your light attack as well as a grapple and can use those in a variety of combos. Unfortunately Sleeping Dogs also takes a page from the first Assassins Creed game and gives you an end all counter button. You can win almost any fight by just standing still and countering the enemy attacks without much effort.
The driving feels pretty good, not quite the cartoon style of Saints Row but not the annoying wannabe realistic style of later GTAIV either it manages to strike a nice balance where cars are still fun but it doesn't get too silly. For some bizarre reason though motorcycles have much greater road grip than even the best of cars.
Instead of multi-player Sleeping Dogs have a social hub feature wherein you can compete with your friends for high scores on missions and races as well as a number of challenges but it is a feature easily forgotten or ignored.
What separates Sleeping Dogs from the pack is the location. Instead of being situation in yet another differently named version of New York City the game takes place in Hong Kong and everything about the game, from the mini games to the radio stations and the street vendors create a different feel than we're used to in this sort of game. When was the last time you bet on cockfighting in a video game?
Although the Hong Kong vibe manages to make Sleeping Dogs rise somewhat above the pack it is still a fairly unimpressive game underneath, not much new and not much improved over the many other games in the same genre out there now. Also it is much lighter on content than is normal for a game in this genre and 100% the game, achievements and DLC shouldn't take much more than 25-30 hours of game time.
Still, it's a game I had quite a bit of fun with and the Hong Kong vibe was interesting to play around with, it's a pretty game despite originating on the consoles and although I would probably feel a little cheated if I had gotten it at it's original 50$ price tag with the current sales and discounts it's an enjoyable experience.

Get used to seeing it crash.
"Pure virtual function being called while application was running (gisrunning == 1)".
Idiots will tell you it's because of mods. Or there's a memory leak, and messing with your Virtual Memory settings will fix it (anyone telling you to mess with Virtual Memory settings is a dangerous idiot). Or that more RAM will help. I have been monitoring my system, it's not even coming close to using my 64Gb of RAM.
Firaxis tells us it's because of bad programming. They're right there, it's just not the mod authors. Because I'm running it with no mods at all. I even turned off the DLC. And asked Steam to verify the cache. I have adequate system cooling (AiO water units, one for GPU, one for CPU). I have adequate power, I've measured it.
Funny thing is though, I've been a programmer for 20 years, and I do know what a Pure Virtual function is. It's used in C++, specifically in Inheritance, when you create a parent class that is designed to be implemented from child classes that inherit from it, you can decalre a method to be pure virtual, which means any child class absolutely must implement that method themselves, they can not default to using the parent implementation. Which makes me wonder how this error could happen at all, as this is supposed to be compile time. What must have happened is someone created a dummy child class that implemented that Pure Virtual method as just calling a MessageBox() and crashing the game, rather than quietly logging that someone doesn't know their tools properly.
If it sounds like I'm a bit grumpy, it's because this error is common. I've started a new game, and it's occured in the intro mission within 5 minutes of starting the game. The "Shen's Last Gift" DLC is unplayable, as in I can't get past the first room without this crash. The longest the game has lasted for me is about one hour.

Reviewed at 6th of August 2017, Immediately after Early access release. (Will update as necessary.) I was a kickstarter backer for this game.
Positive recommendation based on understanding these pointers:
1. Only buy the game if you are into experiencing the long term route of seeing how it develops! As of right now, there isn't that much content to experience, the game is very bare bones as well as has a lot of glitches and roughness. I am on a very high end PC and am experiencing occasional performance issues. Lower end machines will likely struggle.
2. The game is dependent on simulation of life gathered from currently known scientific fact and as such relies heavily on a "make your own adventure" style gameplay experience. A lot of it's charm comes from as accurately as possible depicted dinosaurs.
If you're not into the abovementioned thematics, or want a more finished product, this might not be a game for you right now. Wait until it's further into development. That being said, if you're a hardcore dinosaur fan, you'll probably have a good time.
Now that's out of the way, here are some of my opinions:
The game is very atmospheric, you feel constantly on your guard which gives you a sense of belonging into the game world. Night time can even be a bit spooky, since it gets hard to spot any predator that's hunting you... And at first you also don't know all the things that are out there, so you're especially wary. Immersion is already rather good! I think going forward the game needs to push this angle to keep a grip on the player.
That being said, one thing that breaks the immersion are the way the controls respond as of right now. They're not terrible by any means, but very rough in some spots. You don't always feel in tune with your character, and especially at times some input may lag or not register at all and you're not sure why it happens. Did I do something wrong as a player, or did the game just buckle. These are minor complaints all in all, but do erode the immersion aspect of the game ever so slightly, when at times you feel like you're struggling to get your character to do what you need it to do. Some more fluidity and responsiveness would go a long way.
My other bigger issue with the game right now is the map. Meanwhile it's not terrible, it doesn't particularly stand out in any spots either. There doesn't feel to be much to see, which in turn doesn't make you feel like exploring. I understand the importance of keeping it close to real life simulation to hold true to the game's intent, but looking around, life has a lot of variety. I hope going forward the developers will add a bit more character to the environment. Some more distinct landmarks, small streams, boulder formations strewn around and that kind of thing...  I'm not sure if I'm expressing my thoughts on this matter very well, but let me summarize by saying that the world needs to feel a bit more full and alive.
The feature for using scent to hunt is currently a bit underwhelming and I find myself playing mostly without it, relying more on watching my character's head movements and listening for skittering sounds. Both of which, are actually very neat ways of incorporating your senses into gameplay.
Saurian is definitely worth your try if you're open minded towards experimental games and don't mind it if things aren't running smoothly straight away. The models for the animals are very beautiful as are their animations, so I got myself a bunch of good time from just admiring those. Saurian is trying to make an educational piece in a way that has quality as well as entertainment incorporated, and for these reasons alone it already deserves praise.

I got this yesterday and stayed up all night playing it. It's been years since I've done that with a new video game. Nearly every moment has been fantastic.
Pros:
1. Runs extremely well. After playing a lot of games that are horribly optimized for the PC or are just flat out terribly coded, this game runs beautifully. I have an AMD card so there's always an underlying sense of dread when I purchase a new game. No issues whatsoever here, and I haven't had to update any drivers. Running it on ultra with 60 fps even with a lot going on in battles and my GPU is roughly 4-5 years old now.
2. Absolutely beautiful. The cutscenes are superbly animated and the in-game graphics are great as well.
3. Velvet is an amazing character. It would be have been very easy to make her into a stereotype, but you can tell she's very complicated. Most of the characters are awesome, although a couple are annoying.
4. The combat . . . where do I begin? This is easily the best combat I've played in an RPG, and I've played the other Tales games as well. I have only used Velvet so far but she's extremely fun. The combat has a ton of depth in between combos, having different "breaks" based on what enemies you're fighting, and choosing when to use the breaks (because using it too early is bad as it shortens how long your combos can be).
**SPOILERS**
5. The storyline and the morality behind it is very mature. It's not your typical "angels are good demons are bad" type of affair that many games trend towards. In this game we see that neither side is really right or wrong. The antagonist had reasons for his actions and might have saved humanity, but the means that he used to do it were terrible. I think the general theme is, when have you fallen so far that life is no longer worth living?
**END SPOILERS**
Cons:
1. The beginning is so idyllic that it's unbelievable. Also, it doesn't really have a lot impact because you know what's going to happen her (even from the cover art it's clear that something changes her).
2. The witch is very annoying. Not really a big issue though, there's usually one really annoying character per game.
3. Hard is too easy . . . outside of the "elite" encounters, which range from being difficult to being very challenging. Unfortunately, these encounters are somewhat rare. I would have liked to see more difficulty in normal fights. If there are four difficulty settings, the highest one should be very hard. Hard feels more like what "challenging" should have been.
It seems like you need to grind a lot in hard mode to keep up with the average levels of the monsters you're facing. I don't get why they reduce the exp in challenging / hard. You can say "you don't have to grind and the game will be easier!" but you kinda do need to grind a bit in order to fight the elite monsters. The problem is, when you're at a level where you can take them on then the normal fights become trivial because the "elite" monsters tend to be 6-7 levels higher than the rest of the zone (you can usually fight them when you're 6 levels below them though).
4. Score penalties for your NPCs getting KOd is lame. They should have moved the penalty to the resurrection item instead, because sometimes the NPCs are just dumb and they're basically guaranteed to die.
Overall, the cons are somewhat irrelevant in the grand scheme of things. I would give this game a solid 9.6/10 overall.

This game is absolutely marvellous. I did like the Tales of Xillia and was excited about Zestiria... but Zestiria turned out to be rather meh in everything. The characters were dull, story was so-so, combat was ruined by the stupid camera... actually, i was about to skip Berseria, but the "overwhelmingly positive" mark made me try the game.
Turns out, Tales of Berseria is a really wonderful game, probably among the best ones in Tales of... series and one of the best RPGs in recent years. The game does a much better job than Zestiria in every aspect. First of all, the combat is just better. Equipment system is better. Characters are really awesome, i love them. Their personalities are so well-written. These guys just feel alive... natural.. logical. They are not your average game characters that can be described in 8-10 sentences. In this game, there`s a lot of background, story involvement, reasoning and character development throughout all the 60+ hours it took me to finish the game.
Story is awesome as well. It is a lot darker that in the previous games. And i really love how the story flows from the beginning till the very end of the game, with several twists and turns you can`t call obvious or stupid. It`s great how the details that seemed insignificant and decorative in the beginning play their part in the story later. It`s really a rare thing to be seen in videogames nowadays.
As for me, i really adore this game and i think that, as a story- and character-driven RPG, Tales of Berseria is probably among the best games released in the few recent years, probably rivaling the Witcher in terms of story and characters (i love the Witcher too, so i`m serious)

This game flourished off the back of the success of the TV series, but it's every bit as enjoyable and well made in its own right. The video game facilitates this same process- showing the results of our different choices and decisions through the characters, and because you're playing one of those characters and vested in their outcome, everything that affects the world affects you on an emotional level.
When it came out it was a somewhat unique gameplay mechanic for Point & Click Adventure games, and it's still limited- most choices don't actually affect the world or the linear story, yet it absolutely reaches you and makes the story and the things happening on screen more vivid and real.
Honestly, If I could go back in time, I probably would not spend 60 dollars out the gate for what essentially feels like a demo.

Starbound is almost a good game. I actually enjoy it, mostly. Surprisingly, it's gotten worse in many ways as time has gone on.
I won't speak about bugs in detail, because it's early access, and there really aren't any gameplay bugs that cause any trouble, mostly. The game runs better now than it did a long time ago, but as far as playability goes there, little has changed. Main problem is that it not infrequently hangs/crashes when trying to start the game.
The graphics are nothing spectacular. They get the job done, which is good enough for me. Nothing looks bad, doesn't impact your ability to play, so no problems there.
The audio is also nothing special. The music is fine, though the sound effects are a bit limited. Nothing problematic here.
The controls are fine, but it doesn't behave like you may expect it to at first.  But, the controls work, haven't had any problems actually playing the game. Fully responsive, fairly simple, can just start it up and play, more or less.
The interface is pretty awful, I'm afraid. Menus can be moved around on screen, but more often than not, closing and re-opening a menu results in the menu appearing in the default location, which is highly irritating, and makes accomplishing basic inventory management(crafting/placement of objects) frustrating. Tooltips do not exist for interface aspects, and the tooltips for items are not very useful(although that's due in part to the fact that many items are almost identical to eachother). There's a query tool which is equally useless; next to nothing has a unique description, and nearly all descriptions contain zero information.  I will say that the interface DOES WORK, however. There are almost never problems with actually accomplishing a menu-related task. Buttons work, no bugs to speak of. Just frustrating and lacking descriptions. Partly an early-access issue.
Broadly speaking, the mechanics of the game are good. Basically identical to Terraria, but lacking polish. Sadly, below the surface of things, the mechanics are unfortunate. Combat is depressing, as the enemies lack any real diversity, and the damge dealt by enemies is VERY badly balanced. Sometimes you'll be dying in one hit, sometimes you'll be immortal, with nothing actually creating that distinction except on a per-planet basis. Item progression is very badly implemented, and has only gotten worse as the game has developed. Simply, don't expect to get much out of your time spent. You are unlikely to improve your equipment in a timely manner. That's including the craftable items, and finding weapons in chests, etc. Progression is simply far too slow. There's now a questing system, which is unspectacular. NPCs will ask you to do menial tasks, like most games. The game contains farming, which is massively over-simplified:  hit ground with hoe, plant seed, harvest crop within minutes(or less...), literally no other steps. One major change to things is mining tools; originally, picks/drills were EXTREMELY annoying to craft(vast quantities of materials), and required a progression of upgrades. They also had durability, but could be repaired at any time using various ores(to varying levels of effect, depending on the ore), including once the durability reached zero(could use the item still, but to basically no effect).  Now, however, picks are simple to craft, but BREAK when their now-massively-reduced durability runs out, and they can no longer be repaired(as far as I have seen). And believe me, they break VERY quickly.
Once upon a time, it was possible to see every tier of item(but not every item, mind you) inside 6-10 hours of dedicated grinding, which included fighting bosses and going to new planets to find better materials to craft with. In the most recent incarnation, a couple of hours may not even get you to a new star system(or even another planet...), and almost certainly won't let you see beyond the first tier of items. There's also the issue of the total lack of incentive to build anything on-world, even with the now-halted progression. SFV is very different than IV. Here are some notable differences:
- 1f links are gone, combos are shorter and easier to do
- Light attacks are weakened, no longer can you combo into high damage just by using light attacks.
- Not many if any option selects
Which brings up the next big change:
- The element of risk vs reward is back. You must commit to your attacks, there are no longer second chances (fadc). And since high damage can't be done by hit confirming with light attacks, you have to use the slower and more risky normals (mediums and heavies) to do so. Making the risk much higher than before.
These will be big changes for players who began their SF career with IV. But for long term SF players none of these changes should be a big deal. SF has always been a game that focused on solid fundamentals: Footsies, spacing and mind games. Its a welcome change.
With that being said, RIP SFIV. I will not miss you...except maybe playing Hakan!

What a brilliant concept to offer gamers a simulation of the gaming industry, making sure that every player has a positive emotional connection to the virtual goods he deals with - games are fun! I know this one is not the first to use the idea, but it is an advantage nevertheless in comparison with other simulations that take you into a cookshop or a truck cabin. At least for me, it worked very well.
Visuals and music do not show that this is an indie production at all - it is all well done, in the bright and cheerful spirit of Sims 3. You can even play dollhouse by choosing and positioning furniture until everything is perfect, but this is optional. Just like for many other things like repeated tasks, you can choose automation and grouping functions for that and avoid tedious micromanagement if you don't care for that. Like all tycoon games, this one gets repetitive anyway after a while because you just amass more and more money by doing similar things. However, this one is superior to others because of the historically accurate technological progress from 1980-2018 that gradually unlocks more and more features and increases complexity, until you can really feel the effort of years of development and cooperation of four or five different departments until a big AAA title can be released to the market - and receive its ratings.
Getting a perfect review, making a 100 % perfect game that gives my customers a good time, that was the lifetime dream I started with when I built my first little office next door to my garage. I studied new inventions, I struggled with my bank loans, I hired more and more staff (gamers and nerds like me whom I could very well have befriended in a real-life situation like that) - and together we grew bigger and more respected in the industry, until one day, I finally achieved my first 100 % score. It felt amazing! After that, game development lost a lot of its appeal, but I could choose a completely different path: I made money, as much as I could, by doing contract work for other companies and creating MMOs - my biggest title was online 20 years and earned me 12 billion dollars! And with those riches, I bought out all my competitors and made them produce games for my very own gaming console, making it market leader eventually - while I sat back, drank my coffee and watched the cash flow in.
This was my journey in this game, and even though it lasted only 20 hours, I found this virtual life experience to be very memorable.
The game is still in development (updated regularly), and it still has some little flaws. But in the end, they did not bother me that much. I am very satisfied and give Mad Games Tycoon a 7.5/10.

In Liveza: Death of the Earth you play as a gnome with a hood and an assault rifle, he travels around various levels with clunky animations and depressing colour palette. Your primary goal is to repair your weapon and shoot weird squares that are quite difficult to hit because of the inability to look up, these great sequences are occasionally interrupted by boring “storyline”
In Liveza the world has been destroyed, apart from the generic story it’s a quite straight forward platformer with some occasional shooting In each level. Your primary goal is to shoot all the enemies and reach the end. To a developer this probably doesn’t sound too hard to accomplish yet somehow they managed to make it annoying on all the important bits. I can see how much effort went into it and how it was all wasted on things that didn’t improve anything; in some scenarios made it worse.
Movement overall is fairly responsive, though that is not my main problem with it; my problem with it is the ridiculous control while in the air, so right after you’ve jumped. Some platformers make you jump precisely once with no air control so that you take enough time to make the jump. Others have lots of air control to make it a bit more arcady. Liveza can’t decide which style it wants to choose, so instead it has a bad form of both combined with a blender. The jumping is imprecise with slow and annoying air control that more than often makes me miss the target.
Apart from the jumping the character itself also moved like a turtle on wheels, Much preferring the ground and walking in straight lines; slowly, then actually having some fast paced platforming. This might’ve been intentional as the game is set in a post apocalyptic  world; though the soundtrack doesn’t match it’s speed I’ll give it the benefit of the doubt.

In Liveza you fight cubes, yes various sized cubes I’m not joking. Now if this incredibly original design wasn’t already a nail in the coffin for the combat they only appear above you, this is a problem since you cannot shoot up and you just so have to find a platform to shoot them; after which you have to find a new one since they move like Russian cruise missiles.
Shooting your weapon overall is fine, it feels like you’re not firing a haystack at your enemies which is a lot better than I had expected. Besides from it doing no damage at all at least it felt like I was doing damage.
Your character has quite a lot of health, almost like the developer knew that you were going to get hit a lot by enemies you cannot hit for 70% of their visibility to you, this would be fine if this was just a mistake; but knowing that the developer intentionally designed it this way annoyed me more then anything else.
The game has a retro look with the screen being warped on the outskirts to replicate those rounded television screens from the eighties. Overall this looks quite nice as I did enjoy the colour pallet that although grim, still gave me the idea of a post-apocalyptic world.
The largest problem is not with its looks directly but more about depth, when walking over the various platforms to reach whatever goal the game has put for you there are objects that look like you can walk over them since they look the same, by brightness and contrast, as normal objects; of course you will be unpleasantly surprised as you fall straight through to your death because the developer hasn’t made a graphical difference in depth.
The soundtrack in general is enjoyable and doesn’t wear out over time, the one that does is the one that triggers after you “repair” your weapon and get ready for the cube shooting phase; this soundtrack at first is enjoyable but later it gets very repetitive as the same loop screams into your ear many minutes later after you have shot up all the cubes.
A for the remaining sound design, when picking up items it sounds like a needle popping open your eardrum, these sounds are so annoying that I genuinely felt discouraged picking them up only doing so when necessary.
It’s this which I think has made this game such a pain to play, it combines all the bad elements into one large cesspool.
Liveza is although a great idea a platformer with lacking time and effort that could’ve been used for other things. Though I wish it could’ve been better it just isn’t. Perhaps the developer should write a book and revise his story to truly create it into a story driven adventure like he aims that it is. Although it’s not very expensive I wouldn’t recommend it at this time since it’s just not worth your time. Perhaps if the developer kept working on the project it could become a lot better but now it’s not.

XCOM 2 is a great sequel to the original.  The tactics, story, and RPG style elements improve in almost every aspect.  I purchased this game with the Chosen DLC, and you can see how they inserted the characters and additional storyline into the base game.  While not perfect, it adds a level of variety to the characters and missions.  Many aspects of the world map are improved upon, although it may take some time to understand what is a worthwhile task and which are not.  I would recommend purchasing the DLC due to the additional content.
Tactics gameplay on normal difficulty is improved.  The AI is punishing at the start and missions are quite difficult, but this levels off once you have higher level soldiers.  In comparison to XCOM 1, the overwatch ability has been nerfed, and the ranger class has become OP.  The devs clearly want you to think tactically and reward your characters with experience points when you utilize them.
Go ahead and buy it, you will not be disappointed.

This is a tragically underplayed game. A simple story filled with characters that have lost their minds guides you through what is essentially a vehicle-building sandbox. Firstly, you are the "commander" of XCOM, a once globally funded military organisation tasked with one job: to keep aliens from invading Earth. But after almost 20 years having passed XCOM have failed, and alien overlords, referred to as "Advent", occupy planet Earth.
As a result of this, XCOM was forced to go off the radar to avoid certain doom, and now operates as a resistance force, attempting to maliciously sabotage alien activity, blacksites and research labs whilst striving to spread "dissident propaganda" to help humanity open their eyes to the atrocities of Advent, all from their new mobile base, "The Avenger".
XCOM is highly luck based. Things will go wrong. Sometimes you will fail miserably; sometimes you won't. The first step to playing XCOM is accepting that things will not always go your way, you will miss 99% chances to hit, you will be outmatched, and you will lose many soldiers along the way, especially on higher difficulties and in the early game.
As you progress, however, you will research better weaponry, armour, abilities for soldiers to use, weapon attachments, etc. This combined with making use of the new concealment mode will give opportunities for powerful ambushes.
The customisation options are decent with a good amount of items to wear and customise but lacks real depth, being able to choose from very few faces and haircuts.
The modding scene more than makes up for this though, with a rather extensive wardrobe and customisation options available to download, along with some more appealing gameplay overhauls to compliment it.
Not much to add here other than that I've personally never had any issues with how the game runs or experienced a single crash in all my hours of gameplay.
The art and aesthetics of XCOM 2 are absolutely beautiful. It perfectly captures and envisions how Earth might look after 20 years of alien colonisation. Everything from the modern, vibrant and clean look of the Advent city centres to the abandoned towns, which feel like they were once bustling cities that people actually lived in, now lie in complete ruins. This combined with the superb map generation, beautiful animations and character aesthetics make it an absolutely gorgeous game.
XCOM 2 is not only a fantastic game but a fantastic sequel. It improves on almost every aspect from its predecessor and is an absolute must buy. Although it becomes particularly easy towards the end game, it is still incredibly satisfying to play and ultimately about out-thinking your enemy. If you do not own XCOM 2, I strongly recommend purchasing it, even at full price.

Let me start off by saying that I love this game. I love what the developers are trying to accomplish. I was a KickStarter supporter. And I say with certainty that this game will improve--and when it does, I will be excited to change my review to positive. So why is it negative right now?
"Early Access" is something that far too many developers abuse, and far too many players use as an excuse for poor content. "You can't judge it now because it's in early access," is invalid. When a game launches to Early Access, the whole point of it is to criticize it. You can't really judge a game that is in pre-alpha stages, because there is a lot to do, and it is in a closed group of testers / developers. But Early Access is meant for games that have left that stage and are ready for the public. Saurian is not ready for the public to take part. It is clearly in a pre-alpha state, but launched in Early Access regardless. This is what makes it tough to judge. You can't really say much because it is so underdeveloped, but on the other hand, it has fully launched for the public to play. So I'm left with judging the actual decision of bringing Saurian live.
Saurian has many issues. From♥♥♥♥♥♥poor optimization (30-50 fps + big stutters on a GTX 1070--which is well above recommended specs) to a massive amount of gamebreaking or simply obnoxious bugs. There is also a great lack of content and pretty mediocre AI. Obviously, most Early Access games will have similar types of issues, just not to this extent. There are certain expectations that Early Access games should live up to--it's not really meant to be a dumping ground for demos. Saurian is not ready for Steam, and certainly not the $20 price tag.
I suggest waiting until massive improvements are made. I believe that I will get the opportunity to change my review, and I look forward to that day. But it is not today.

Intrusion 2 is a modern take on Contra/Metal Slug. And when I say modern, it is not an empty word!
However, let's start with what is familiar: Intrusion 2 is a 2D side-scroller with action and platforming, shooting soldiers and robots (some of which can be piloted) while occasionally negotiating some jumps. A lot of games have tried to ape the aforementioned classical games, but very few have come close to touch their greatness. Usually, they are dull with scarce enemies, repetitive levels and clunky controls.
The controls of Intrusion 2 are not beyond any criticism. There is some floatiness to the main character, but it does not make it clunky. It just feels weird, but it is still reactive and shooting is instant. One of the reasons for this feeling is that the characters are not sprites with all their animation frames pre-rendered. Every limb, every object in the game is actually controlled like a puppet by the physics engine. A modern spin that sets this game apart from its ancestors, in addition to the ability to shoot at 360°. The physics make the game feel both awkward and awesome at the same time, as robot legs fly around and kill soldiers in their fall. And there are mechas with grappling hooks battling by throwing rocks at each other when they are not flying around pulled by their ropes before a sword finish.
Sounds cool? Wait until you see the boss fights. I have rarely seen such amazing boss fights. They have tons of different stages and are hard while still being easy to learn, making them an entertaining challenge. They also look good, which helps making those fights memorable.
However, if the game keeps things fresh and cool during the first hour, once the novelty factor wears off the levels feel too lengthy and look-alike. There is very little variation in the settings and formula despite the promising snowboard chase at the start. The music is not especially interesting and too repetitive/annoying rather quickly. The robots have terrific art and animation, but the backgrounds look oddly photo-realistic and not very awe-inspiring. Since I am tackling the negative points, the difficulty associated with whimsical physics might frustrate quite a number of players. If you are not a good player, set the game on easy and enjoy the awesome beginning. If you like a good challenge with still more leeway than a very demanding game like Contra, you will no doubt pull through the short campaign and have a good time despite the less entertaining later levels.
A concession to make to the physics engine is that the game runs slowly. The framerate does not go higher than 30 frames per second, and some slow-downs can be experienced even on a good machine. This is most likely due to the fact that the game was coded in Flash, just like the original Binding of Isaac. Surprisingly, despite the intensive use of physics, there are very few bugs and issues. The controls are well tuned so that the player can instinctively achieve any action without pestering, such as grabbing cords or moving over physics-bound objects.
As a conclusion, this game is not perfect but an impressive example of what a modern Metal Slug/Contra would be. There are a lot of very cool stuff in here, so I definitively recommend trying out this game. Especially for the battles against larger enemies and the boss fights. The game feels like it is great and could almost be placed up there with Metal Slug/Contra, but it is dragged down by a few negative aspects and lack of variety once the beginning is behind.
Good news, most if not all of my gripes appear to have been corrected in the next game from the same developer: Jetpack Squad. This is something very promising that I am definitively looking forward to, and hopefully Intrusion 2 was the stepping stone to a masterpiece!

So I'm 17ish hours in and am assuming I just beat the first act of the game...
Story: 4/5
ToB deviates from its main setup for their games. This game is dark for a tales of game, its about revenge... not saving a world, nor chasing a dream. It's about a girl who wants revenge and will do anything to get it. There are still quirky skits, puns (for those of us who enjoy dad jokes), cameos/easter eggs to other tales of games, and characters that fit the typical JRPG mold (comedic releif, serious person, random little kid that shsould never be in these dangerous situations). Overall the story is intriguing after you push through the "prologue" and will make you want to keep playing whether you are a long time Tales of... fan like me, or a newcomer to the series.
Combat 3.75/5
Combat is a real-time action combat stop and battle game. Overall typical for some rpgs but with their own little twist. Instead of MP you start out with 3 souls which can go up or down throughout the battle depending on your actions and kills. Combat is definitely an improvement to the last game in the series (Tales of Zesteria), but I'm still partial to symphonia and vesperia's combat systems. I like the inclusion of souls/break souls and the "build your own combos" skills list. Combat also seems to go at a faster pace, which I personally enjoy.  Again, vast improvement over Zesteria.
Graphics 2.5/5
Tales of games are never known for their top of the line graphics. They purposefully make an anime-like game which is a JRPG. so they get an average score from me. nothing special to look for in this department.
Extra Features/intangibles 3/5
The best improvement this game has compared to its predecessor, is the equipment system. Equipment has skills which you can learn by fighting with it equipped (kind of like vesperia, but not really). You can improve stuff  using a watered-down crafting system of enhancing/dismantling, super simple stuff.
I enjoy that this game is expanding on the world of Zesteria, meaning you do see some old characters.
Also Typical level up system
Overall: 7.5/10
Overall ToB is an above average game. If you are a JRPG fan definitely get this because the story deviates from the norm and takes a darker driven story, while the gameplay can keep you wanting to fight. I do recommend playing on a difficulty of moderate or higher becasue normal/easy is just too boring and not nearly challenging enough (unless you just want to run through the story)

At heart, this is a turn-based combat game based on surviving zombies. But it does work within a storyline and has some interesting (but not THAT interesting) characters who join your main character's squad. Each day these guys and gals can accompaning the main character on a roam around the highways or the woods, in daylight or dark, to pick up materials and parts to improve the lot of the camp. But, if you want to eat and fight, someone has to stay behind to guard the camp, to hunt for food and to craft new weapons, ammo and health items. You only have 5 or so people and all these bases are hard to cover in one turn. That's what makes the game interesting.
Pro: It has a storyline which is not always the same. The combat is simple but requires thought. The atmosphere and background music are great. It's a clever little indie game that should be enjoyed.
Con: It's very unclear exactly how things like jobs and crafting actually work. You spend a lot of time searching for ways to do what you want (make traps, shotgun shells etc) and some items you make are actually required for characters to perform their chosen roles (medic etc). This is never made clear but everntually you find out.
7/10

is a sandbox in which you can construct different vehicles to either traverse the air, ground or underwater.
There are some vague objectives in the main mode of the game. It is technically sandbox-esk in that mode but its more constrained. The proper sandbox mode has basically no rules and no form of currency to hold back on your design process.
The aforementioned currency is that of FUN. Derived from providing pleasure to the weird little naked  infant/adult hybrid humanoid creatures. Don't be lewd. The pleasure is from well.. kicking them and sort of dragging them around on the vehicles you craft by attaching life savers.
The crafting actually has two options, you can either in-act the use of blueprints that are collected by exploring the world or you can build your own from scratch. Admittedly, the latter is much more difficult. However you can scrap parts, find parts and sell them or spend a lot of time kicking those weird babies. The building from scratch isn't as robust as you might like; but as the game is only $10 and is ostensibly a budget title its really more effective than you might expect.

This game is absolutely fantastic. Not run into many in game bugs.
If you're going to buy this, I highly recommend playing it with friends.

Firstly, you are the "commander" of XCOM, a once globally funded military organisation tasked with one job: to keep aliens from invading Earth. But after almost 20 years having passed XCOM have failed, and alien overlords, referred to as "Advent", occupy planet Earth.
As a result of this, XCOM was forced to go off the radar to avoid certain doom, and now operates as a resistance force, attempting to maliciously sabotage alien activity, blacksites and research labs whilst striving to spread "dissident propaganda" to help humanity open their eyes to the atrocities of Advent, all from their new mobile base, "The Avenger".
XCOM is highly luck based. Things will go wrong. Sometimes you will fail miserably; sometimes you won't. The first step to playing XCOM is accepting that things will not always go your way, you will miss 99% chances to hit, you will be outmatched, and you will lose many soldiers along the way, especially on higher difficulties and in the early game.
As you progress, however, you will research better weaponry, armour, abilities for soldiers to use, weapon attachments, etc. This combined with making use of the new concealment mode will give opportunities for powerful ambushes.
The customisation options are decent with a good amount of items to wear and customise but lacks real depth, being able to choose from very few faces and haircuts.
The modding scene more than makes up for this though, with a rather extensive wardrobe and customisation options available to download, along with some more appealing gameplay overhauls to compliment it.
Not much to add here other than that I've personally never had any issues with how the game runs or experienced a single crash in all my hours of gameplay.
The art and aesthetics of XCOM 2 are absolutely beautiful. It perfectly captures and envisions how Earth might look after 20 years of alien colonisation. Everything from the modern, vibrant and clean look of the Advent city centres to the abandoned towns, which feel like they were once bustling cities that people actually lived in, now lie in complete ruins. This combined with the superb map generation, beautiful animations and character aesthetics make it an absolutely gorgeous game.
XCOM 2 is not only a fantastic game but a fantastic sequel. It improves on almost every aspect from its predecessor and is an absolute must buy. Although it becomes particularly easy towards the end game, it is still incredibly satisfying to play and ultimately about out-thinking your enemy. If you do not own XCOM 2, I strongly recommend purchasing it, even at full price.

Spider: Rite of the Shrouded Moon is a unique experience and I highly recommend it if you're looking for a change of pace.
As a spider, you will puzzle your way through each level by catching insects, either in your webs or with your swift predatory leap. Once you've caught enough, a portal will open somewhere enabling you to finish the level. Scuttle everywhere: under the floorboards, up the walls, and inside the many cracks and crevices of the old estate, seeking prey.
As a player, you will be driven by curiosity about the story behind the scenes your spider explores, and the secret, hidden spaces that your spider finds its way into. A winning example of "show, don't tell", Spider succeeds in striking an unusual balance. Finding secrets and "Clues" to solve the mysteries of this place feels rewarding and it's often unexpected. You will learn to eagerly search everywhere you can to uncover the things that may be hidden in unexpected corners, or in a place which will open to you when you find the right mechanism and figure out how to trigger it.
The artwork and aesthetic are remniscient of old books and maps, with quite beautiful hand-drawn furniture, objects and scenes to explore. The story left behind in the humans' footprints and their belongings after they are gone creates a world of eerie promise. It invites you to notice the suggestions of something sinister afoot early just by including suspicious details in the background of some of the beautiful scenes.

This is the third of Ice-Pick Lodge’s games – the first being a depressing story of an epidemic outbreak in Pathologic, and the second a dark yet wonderful world of The Void. Their third game is called “Cargo! The quest for gravity” – the only game by IPL that cannot be described as gloomy, dark and hostile. Quite the opposite, actually, as Cargo! is a very colorful game.
The game begins with an intro where a crew of two flies over an island in a hot air balloon. The island is their destination, however, they do not land, but crash instead. One of the crew members – a woman – is the player’s character throughout the game. After the intro, the little naked midgets talk to the player using rhymes. The player is supposed to go around and kick the midgets for “FUN”, after which they often explode in colors. Soon afterwards, three machine God-heads speak explaining that the world is destroyed and must be rebuilt by reconnecting various flying around parts of it, which the player can do with paying with the collected FUN. Collecting FUN does is not limited to running around and kicking midgets, fortunately. Among other things, you can attack them to your vehicle and give them a ride or leave on the ground a tune for them to dance around. The main activity of the player is completing various quests he is given – from saving drowning midgets through racing against them to maneuvering a tornado. To complete them one must build different vehicles. Some quests are not obvious and I had to scratch my head coming up with ideas what developers could possibly want me to do at this particular stage of the game. One quest I even completed randomly without knowing what to do until I accidentally did it. Note, however, that it’s not because quests in Cargo! are too difficult – they are banal – but they are often too random! Sometimes the player is not provided with a clear description what he must do and what is expected of him is to perform an action that was neither encountered before nor one that uses common sense.
Building vehicles is the focus of the game, however, it is very undeveloped. To build a vehicle, first it is needed to find a base of it, then gather parts – either by finding them around the map or buying them with FUN. You can build your own vehicles, and you are free to customize existing ones, which  you get from finding blueprints. Interestingly, during the game the player will make land and flying vehicles as well as submarines. The game always provides you with a working blueprint of what you need though, so it is not Kerbal Space Program by any means – assembling a vehicle you need is just a few clicks at best, customizing them or coming up with your own ideas is redundant. I have to add that this game is arcade and nor vehicles nor anything else behaves like it would in real life, so don’t expect any kind of simulation from it. Once you build a necessary vehicle you may complete a quest. There’s only a handful of quests and the game is only few hours long. After each quest there’s a lot of colorful sparks flying around and a sound of clapping so the player can feel awesome.
The gameworld is exceptionally tiny. It’s just one location which can be flied through in a matter of one minute. At least there’s also an underwater part, but it doesn’t add much. Cargo!’s world is the smallest I have ever seen in a video game and I don’t think it even has any competition in this regard. When you fly too far away you are presented with a message telling you to turn back and if you don’t the game will teleport you back. At least not to make the location too boring the game is divided into four different seasons: Autumn, Winter, Spring, and Summer, which make the world look quite different.
While the graphics are very nice and the game is quite pretty, the sounds are very basic and voice overs are terrible. I did not want to listen to them anymore after a short time and just read the text and skipped listening to them. What’s worse the quality of writing is equal to voice overs – it’s so bad that the sole reason why I read it was only for the purpose of letting you know in this quickie how bad it is – it’s atrocious! Not only it barely makes sense, but also it’s just simply dumb and tries hard to be funny but fails at it terribly. Music is not much better either and it didn’t annoy me only because the game is so short that I barely begun to play it when I have already finished it through the end… actually not quite. I did not manage to complete the last quest available in the game because of a game-breaking bug, even though I did not encounter any bugs before. I only watched a walkthrough of this quest and outro on the Internet. This means, however, that the bug does not affect everyone and I had happen to have been just unlucky. In addition to the story mode there is also a sandbox mode, but because of a tiny gameworld and arcade physics it does not really provide any pleasure nor will it allow you to come up with crazy ideas for vehicles as there aren’t that many parts to build with anyway. The game has two endings, which depend on the player’s performance in saving naked midgets.
There isn’t much more to the game. Cargo! The quest for gravity is a game that doesn’t really have anything amusing to offer and can be completed in just six hours. Although the game tells the player to do a lot of things for FUN, there isn’t much fun in it. I can’t really recommend it to anyone as the only interesting point of this game, perhaps besides its weirdness, is building vehicles, but since it’s so simplified and undemanding it’s hardly a reason to play Cargo!. There’s at least one game that does it much better and can be played much longer than what Ice-Pick Lodge presented to us.

That outta the way, lets get to why I can't recommend this game in the current state.
I mean, it works. You can age and survive just well in the current game (my game time of 3.3 hours shows how long I needed to get from baby to adult. This is plus/minus a few, since I died a lot and tried things out) but that's about it. It gets fairly boring after a while, due to bugs and currently boring environments/gameplay.
Just to name a few current issues:
-The Juvenile Dakota has model issues with false weightpaint, the hatchling looks very messy and has almost no details
-Hunting is hard due to jumping delay and the pounce being hard to control.
My biggest issue though, is with the accuracy thing that this game's aiming for. I am sure that these guys put in all their effort to study scientific accuracy of dinos, plants and environment of Hell Creek and have implemented the basics of that in this game.
However, I am told that Dakotaraptors are bad parents right at the start, having the two supposed parents walking off from me and my sibling to handle their own duties.  (Most birds of prey actually share tighter bonds, but I do not know if this applies to Dakota raptor parents also, so I will give them that.)
I get that we start in an age stage where hunting becomes a thing for us so that it doesn't start boring and I do not expect to literally be fed lizards to survive either... however, since birds and our fluffy Dakotaraptors are related, I think that they might share some traits with current day birds as well, given that evolution picks and chooses traits that ensure survival and reproduction... and that most birds of prey will take care of their young, until they are almost teens or even adults themselves, meaning that this is probably a favorable trait to keep. I may be wrong, but I also do not think that parents will turn on their own fledglings if they don't run away fast enough as hatchlings. To me, that's just not.. well... accurate.
Of course it's hard to determine how an extinct animal actually behaved, but it feels more like an attempt to get out of actually programming in AI that cares for you or acts as if it wants to teach you how to hunt. Future updates will tell if this is true or not, since there are still five more dinosaurs to be presented that might have caring parents.
The stamina issue has been also discussed in the forums, but from what I read, Dakotaraptors were big, but lightweight predators made for sprints or general fast traversing. If the argument is that "sprinting" means "A small stamina bar" I can understand that. But let us take an animal made for sprinting: The Cheetah. This may sound extreme at first, but this is an animal with top speed and little stamina, meaning it is the highest extreme in the "top speed" = "low stamina" issue. Even an animal that powers itself out with an up to 110km/h sprint, can run between 300-500 meters whilst sprinting.
This should give the Dakotaraptor, who is made for far smaller speeds, have a bit more than the current ~100 meters maximum to run.
And it is also said the Dakotaraptor was most likely an ambush predator. If so and this is the reason the stamina is so low, then give it a way to actually ambush. There is no way to sneak up on prey, no way to make sure it does not see you, be it watching the direction of the wind to hide your scent, rolling in things to hide your scent or even just to crouch and wait for prey to stroll your way.
I adore that scientific accuracy is being taken into this game, but it doesn't feel like it at the moment, because too many things appear to just not be thought of in the long run. If and how this ends up later on the development, I can not say and I will gladly wait it out, because I do have my hopes that this game WILL turn out good.
As mentioned before, once these changes do occur, I will change my review to reflect this accourdingly.

This is without a doubt my favorite side-scrolling shooter ever, and it should come highly recommended to anybody who likes games that can deliver both incredible spectacle and intense difficulty. And when I say spectacle, I do mean it: if anybody ever tells you indie games just cannot deliver the same kind of epic setpieces as AAA-titles, just point them towards this game.
The more difficult the level, the more awesomely ridiculous the setpieces: from fist-pumping gunships, to wielding grenade-launchers off the backs of giant wolves, to a gun that is also a Tron-bike. And that's not even getting into the final boss, who I won't spoil here. So yeah, the presentation: awesome. The graphics are pixelly but more than detailed enough to convey the awesome action-scenes, and the soundtrack does an excellent job backing it all up. It's exactly the kind of fist-pumping hard rock you want out of a title like this, and it gets absolutely zero complaints from me.
But I also mentioned difficulty, didn't I? Oh boy, the difficulty in this game... Okay, for the record: *yes* there is an Easy option, and it should at least let you get as far as the first boss fight. But this is not the kind of game where people who're just interested in the story can just coast along on Easy without having to worry about dying. This is a game where you pay attention, or you die. Literally, since the boss fights are all about memorizing their attack patterns and figuring out how to dodge them. And you won't do that on your first go. Or your second. Or third.
But for as challenging as they are, it is not as though these fights are hard because it's unclear what to do. All the attacks make it pretty clear how to go about dodging them; it's just that the bosses have so much health that it's hard to perfectly remember and dodge those attacks so many times over the course of a fight. You *will* take damage: the trick is just doing more damage to them first.
If you're the kind of person who saw this game or saw a Let's Play and thought, "Man I wanna try that" then you'll probably make it to the final boss on Easy. But if you're thinking of recommending this to someone as a casual indie title, forget it. This is not something you play on the bus home from work: this is something you play til 1 in the morning, when you finally beat that boss after 2 hours of trying & failing and you unironically shout, "IN YOUR FACE!" at your monitor.
That's the Easy setting. As for Medium, it is exclusively the domain of hardcore fans or shooter veterans. Nobody else need apply. The Hard setting is for masochists who think Metal Gear Solid 2 at European Extreme just isn't challenging enough (yes I'm serious). However it is worth noting that despite those insane challenges, the game *does* actually have an initial difficulty curve. You won't get blown away in the first 10 minutes, if that's what worries you.
If there are any downsides to the game, it's that (A) all that great challenging gameplay doesn't really have a narrative to go with it, and (B) the developer seems sadly reluctant to fix the downloading issue mentioned above (or tell people how to circumvent it: I spent a good hour finding out that tip I put at the start). The narrative is... barely there, to be honest. There's so little of it that you can't really call it bad or distracting: it certainly doesn't detract from the experience. It's just kind of a missed opportunity for the game to show that all your hard work actually has in-universe consequences.
The downloading issue is annoying yes, but to be fair: when the game was originally released it wasn't there. It appeared after a patch and was never fixed. So I'm counting that as a mark against the dev, not the game itself. And again, the tip up top should work.
So who would probably like this?
- People who like side-scrolling shooters.
- People who like a lot spectacle in their action games.
- People who like seriously challenging/punishing difficulty.
- People who like cheap indie games that are nonetheless stuffed with content.
If you fall into any of those categories, the game is definitely worth its retail price and *ABSOLUTELY* worth picking up if it's on sale.
But who probably wouldn't like this?
- People who play games mainly for the story or characters.
- People who don't like high challenge that's based on pattern-recognition.
- People who don't like side-scrolling shooters.
- People who don't like fist-pumping gunships.
Those people should stay far away from this title. It will not float their boat, or any other flotation device for that matter.
This game is the perfectly distilled essence of Side-Scrolling Shooter. What that means for you is your call. But for me, it means a 9/10.
(Oh, and the final boss is Top 3 material. I'm not even kidding.)

Over the last few years, there has been somewhat of a resurgance of the tycoon genre, and this is a further product of that. The 'game development tycoon' genre popularity started a while back with games such as Kairosoft's Gave Dev Story, and since then different studios and developers have improved and refined the formula.
Out of all the various options out there, I feel like this game has the potential to stand out in the crowd. It allows the player much more freedom that we have come to expect from this style of game. You start off in your humble office and rather than the predictable start of just grinding out the games from the get go, there is a bit of extra work to do, and that is where this game plays its ace.
The design element of this product is very good, you place down the walls, door and features of a room and then start to utilise the area to it's full potential. This game reminded me after a few minutes of the Bullfrog classic, Theme Hospital, and that is high praise.
There is still a little 'polish' that could be done, mainly with some of the mechanics and the game interface, however, for an Early Access game, you'd be mad not to give it a go...

Good indie games find their own original concept, but great indie games also explore that concept to its fullest. Spider: Rite of the Shrouded Moon is one such game.
So it's a spider simulator. You shoot web lines by jumping off surfaces and any enclosed space between multiple lines becomes a web that traps insects. Then you eat them. Yum!
But the devil is in the details, as the insect types behave differently: some will only get caught in a very large web, some you can scare away into getting caught and others will avoid your web unless you build it right on top of them. Some insects have to be physically tackled, so there's a nice variety. So it's mostly a puzzle game with a bit of action when timing your jumps. Finishing levels is easy, but hitting each level's target score is a lot more tricky, but it's a fun challenge. A cool addition is that you can look at your bug collection from the menu and some insects are rare finds.
Some things can only be done/found in certain weather, as levels have variations. There are 30 levels, each with 4 weather variations, for 120 levels. That's a decent package. The only annoyance is that the weather is tied to the real world weather in your location and even with that gimmick turned off, there doesn't seem to be a reliable way to choose what variation you want to play. Kind of annoying if you can't be there at the "correct" time and weather.
The game's slighty absurd subtitle comes from the fact that the game is set in larger setting where the mansion you hunt in is apparently the abode of a secret occult organization or "something". There are secret levels to find through puzzles, with clues that have to be gathered from multiple levels and the rooms contain details of the story of the Blackbird family. The music is relaxing and airy, but also a bit odd and creepy, so it sets the overall mood of the game very well. The interior of the mansion is not as well realized as say, Bad Mojo (another "insect simulator"), but the added layer of atmosphere and depth is very welcome.
Give Spider a shot if you want an original puzzle game. Recommended!

Loaded with awkward 'features' that make gameplay unbearable such as the stale, randomly generated enemies that all manage to feel and act about the same way have ruined this experience. Speaking from playing this game and watching its development from its early days up until now, I can tell you that the more finished this game gets, the more vile it becomes. Possibly because the charm has all worn off, or maybe because the development team keeps making the -dumbest- decisions. Now, I don't really know the dev team so I don't know what their vision is, but trying to patch up this game by having forced mission sequences when the core of the game is about exploration, building, and player-driven advancement is more than a little wrong. Instead of finding new, awesome, and cool things on planets, you find that every single place you go to is exactly the same with a different coat of paint. It's the same -everywhere-. The hazards feel like background noise, the enemies all look and feel the same, the combat is dull, and no matter what you do or what you run into, it's always -disappointing- in the end. That's what this game is summed up in one word: Disappointment.
How a game that started out with such crass graphics and such a small development team as Terraria could far surpass this particular endeavour in every way, that started with a -modest- goal, and as more or less a 2D minecraft clone is beyond baffling. Terraria doesn't boast multiple worlds, and the only thing that's randomly generated is the terrain, but I'd still rather waste my time in the world of Terraria than this game. Why? Because when you explore you find things that -matter-. It feels like you're in control. Everything -- even building -- has a point to it. So basically, Starbound managed to completely ruin itself by being the exact opposite of Terraria. You're not in control of anything, everything is pointed out to you, exploration renders nothing satisfying, and there's so much randomly generated content that it all blends together into one static mess.
Understandably, this game is early access which means that the developers are constantly working on fixing it, and at some point in the future, say, maybe 2020, they might have all of the bugs and quirks in this game fixed, but until then, it's not going to be fun for anyone.
If you like disappointment, this is the game for you. Otherwise, just leave it alone, buy and/or play Terraria, and save yourself the grief.
Post August '15 Update Edit: This review might've been written with more venom than what was intended, but I stick to my guns on this: You're better off playing Terraria or Minecraft. The update I've noticed has added a lot of features that seemed interesting, but ended up, again, not adding much to the actual meat of the game. You can dress a mess up however you want and even throw some neon lights on there to attract the rave kids, but at the end of the day, it's still a mess.

An interesting ambience-style game similar in gameplay mechanics to games like Dear Esther. While the game only takes place in one main area, there is plenty to look at over time. One interesting point in the gameplay is that descriptions of items around the area change as you examine more things and uncover the story. The graphics are nice, as well.
One main con of the game revolves around the length. It is not, by any means, a long game. It took me less than an hour to play through it, and that included time taken commentating. It is a very intersting story, and it may have benefitted from being at least a little bit longer. It is also quite possible that being longer would only hurt the story. It's hard to tell.
The voice acting in this game is nice. It's not fantastic, but the main character's audio quality is pretty good. All in all, the voices certainly aren't unenjoyable.
In simple terms, Serena was a good game. It might seem boring or uneventful to some people, but to anyone that loves a good ambience-style game, this is certainly a game to pick up. Besides, it's free!

A great game with a great story. This game, back in the day, skyrocketed telltale;s fame and led to the establishment and growth of a genre of games solely based on one developer, a telltale style game. Of course, games in this niche genre that are not developed by telltale do exist, but the vast majority of this specific type of games are telltale.
Now, if you've read a couple of reviews here, you should know that the walking dead is a cinematic story-focused game with some similarities to point and click, and the main gameplay of the walking dead is the choices. Now, as someone who played some of biowares titles, the accusation that this game is basically mass effect without the gameplay in between,  is so wrong. Mass effect 2 was my favorite game of all time for a while, so believe me when I say that the choices in mass effect series don't come close to the impact of the choices (or at least the impact the game makes you feel) in the walking dead. Each and every choice feels like it has a consequence. When someone dies due to your choice, the emotional impact that you experience is unparalleled to any choice you ever make in the mass effect series. Even if your choices really didn't matter, even if that character was going die anyway, the game succeeds to make you feel as though it does really matter. It makes you feel that you did kill that character by making that choice. Due to the nature of the game, searching for what choice x does before making that choice is not reccomended, as it breaks the illusion of choice.
Besides the choice system, the story in of itself is great, while the gameplay portions are sufficient, although they could've made the shooting better. All in all, a great game and a must play for fans of this genre.

Mad Games Tycoon is like the Name already says a Tycoon Game.
Your task is to build a Game Studio from scratch.
I am a huge fan of “Game Dev Tycoon” so I wanted to play this one for quite a while, and I’m glad that I finally found the time to do so.
It all starts small…in a garage...
Mad Games Tycoon plays like a typical Tycoon game. You start off with some Employees and a few basic skills. As the game progresses you can hire new Employees and build different rooms for the different aspects of Game Design.
For Examples: Development/Research/Marketing and many more!
When you earned enough Money you can buy a new Building for your Studio.
What I really like is that you have to build the Studio by yourself, there are no set rooms. It is all in your hands, and you have to decide how much, of the limited, space each Department gets.
Also it is to you furnish every room and check if your Employers like to work for you. Each NPC has their own set of skills in different categories like Game Design, Programming and Sound etc.
Besides that, the game offers you a huge variety of different genres and topics for your games to experiment with.
The Game mechanics are working well together and supplement each other.
Also Mad Games Tycoon never gives you the feeling to be lost. Beside the good tutorial, the new Gameplay features are added with good time intervals in-between them so you will never feel overwhelmed. I was always exited for what comes next.
The game has 4 different difficulties from Easy to Legendary and different “speeds” so it offers a challenge for casuals as well as for pros.
Nothing I can complain here. The graphic is good and helps to keep an overview, which gets important later when you are moving into the bigger Buildings. I never had a single stutter or anything else in my whole playtime. Only the music got annoying for me after some time.
If you want a Story this game is not for you.
If you are a fan of games like Game Dev Tycoon or other tycoon games I can definitely recommend the game to you. You will get a great and fun Tycoon Game which offers you many hours of Gameplay.
If you’re new to such games but interested in the topic I would say “go for it”
The game has a good tutorial that will help you to get into it and it never overruns you with its features.
