Liveza: Death of the Earth is a platformer/gunner game that tries to releate back to the older more retro platformers like Super Mario Bros and tries to bring back that sort of nostalgia feeling that you get when playing retro games now a days.
Liveza: Death of the Earth takes upon a platforming, gunner game whereby you play as a survivor and your objective is to investigate the anomalies that have settled upon Earth. With the game having barely any story at all, you are set to play through the game as you normally would any of game. As you might of already guessed from just watching the trailer, there is a fair amount of platforming and shooting up enemies. That's bascially the whole game. A few issues with the game that I would like to point out first though.
The first point being you can only shoot horizontally and the enemies move diagonally. This wouldn't be a problem if your character could shoot upwards but for some reason you are unable to do so. This means that you will most probably lose a lot of health and have a lot of cheap deaths with the enemies just moving into you diagaonally. As you can imagine this will most probably cause a few people to rage when you are trying to shoot the enmeies before they get to you. Along with the odd controls (seem more about the controls below), it's kinda diffcult to jump and shoot at the same time as shooting again leading to more cheap deaths throughout the game.
Next, the games controls are a bit odd from the way that the game could be played out. They are very responsive though, but for a game of this type of genre I am suprised that the developer hasn't actually added controller support for this game. I feel like the game would be much easier to play on a controller rather than on a keyboard with these odd keybinds for controls. Above all the game, doesn't even allow you to rebind the keys so you are going to have to stick with these odd controls throughout the entire game. On the topic of optitions, there isn't a optition menu. I mean I get that this game (might?) be trying to replicate a retro platformer but for a steam game you need a options menu. This means that there is no way to mute the music or any of the sound effects that are played in the game, and funnily enough the sound effects are very annoying bleeps so have fun listening to those.
+ Nice music
+ Cheap price
+ Good game for hardcore gamers who like a challenge
- Bare storyline
- Overall difficult game
- Can only shoot horizontally while enemies move diagonally leading to cheap deaths
- Control sheme is odd, and unable to rebind the keys
- No options menu, meaning no control over sound effects, music or switch to window mode
So the final verdict of this game for me. The game tries to be a retro platformerbut is so much more difficult than the game needs to be. No options menu to control sound or to change to window mode. I would only really recommened this game to hardcore gamers who really like a challenge.

Intrusion 2 is a sci-fi sidescrolling 2D shooter/platform with progressive difficulty and a surprisingly good mechanical (mecha) design for bosses and vehicles.
It shares a lot of elements from Gunstar Heroes or other games from Treasure soft.(with the exception of combining weapons) for the intense action and creativity with the environment and boss encounters which are few, but hellish.
Could be enjoyed with a gamepad, in that case it uses the 2nd lever to command the shooting direction.
Otherwise it's done with the mouse.
On the net there're a lot of quoting Metal Slug as similar to this game.
Mostly wrong, the game plays very differently from the almost carefree action of the Neo Geo serie, don't get this game right away thinking it's M.S., accept that's different or you'll get a wrong opinion and get disappointed.
This is a GREAT and original game not a clone of anything.
In I2 the use of vehicles like mechs is possible, but only for few occasions, the rest of the action relies on this man/cyborg and the arsenal of weapons found during the mission.
There're no power ups, only ammo available from crates or weapons dropped by enemies and health capsules of various refill capacity.
No lives, only a health bar and free re-trials from checkpoints.
It's not divided in stages, anyway it's possible to try several times portions of the game using checkpoints or/and loading from the pause menu.
It's possible on a few situations to ride/use the following:
A giant wolf
Gunner Mech
Sword Mech
Grapple Mech
Gameplay:
The controls are not so easy to master, especially it requires a lot of practice dodging while shooting. It's available the remapping option and regardless its limit, helps many different playstyles.
It's not a senseless action what this game gives: it's a challenge. In some parts of the game there's a slight difficult peak if no ammo has been saved previously.  And the unique in-game physics it's a constant part of both trouble and an additional weapon for the player: while a bit strange or awkward used correctly you could use boulders, crates, even dropped weapons to kill enemies. And not only using the Grapple Mech, since each different weapon has has a different knockback power.
Graphics:
Great mecha design, bosses are unforgettable (and unforgiving), wonderful backgrounds. Soldiers and wolfs are affected by the physics so animation seems strange and not quite natural.
Storyline:
If played without interruptions is quite clear that the "intrusion" in enemy territory is a wonder spawned from an action movie. Looking on some sequences is far from being without sense.
It's a shame that even if it's structured as a single mission no hints are given on who's and why the main protagonist have to battle his way to the final boss. There's an android in the game, maybe the main chara is a cyborg? Only pure personal speculation.
Music:
Maybe the worst part. A bit repetitive even for the techno-addicted, anyway works well with the hardboiled action of some parts of the game.
Overall:
For the low price this game offers a lot of challenge, and some replayability for that reason. It's worth for the ending boss encounter alone.
One of the worst for difficult and best for what it does/looks like/challenge.
Surely would love a Intrusion 3 for more mechs and crazy bosses.

As I'm typing this, this game has 34 reviews, but 33 of which are positive, and 2 of which are actually viewable, weird.  I guess the rest are in a different language.
Normally i don't review a game until I beat it, or until I've spent enough time with it, but this state of "reviews" made me decide to review it early.  I may change my mind as I play more.
What it is:
An artsy platformer-gunner.
The Good:
+It is cheap.
+The graphics are sorta attractive, in a retro kind of way.
+The controls, as they are, are responsive enough.
+The music is actually pretty good - at least until you pick up ammo (you start every level with none) and the combat song or whatever kicks in (some may like it though, you can hear it in the trailer and decide for yourself.)
+Infinite lives (respawn at the beginning of the level)
+When you reenter the game, you can continue from last level you reached
The bad:
-Framerate seems lower at times, even though shows as steady 60fps.  NOT as low as you see in the trailer though, don't worry - unless you're using a "slow time" powerup.
-Unlike the music, the "sound effects" are beeps that belong on an Atari 2600.
-These are the controls:
(+E to activate inventory powerups):  They are not rebindable.  There is no gamepad support, it's keyboard-only gameplay.  The menus are MOUSE-only.  During the gameplay the mouse cursor uselessly dangles on the screen (perhaps it's used in later levels, but I doubt it as the platforming and shooting takes both hands on the keyboard.)
-There are no options of any kind, not even windowed mode.  The game seems to be some sort of Chrome app actually, so maybe that's how they work? I dunno.
-Enemies fly at you quickly diagonally from above.  You can only shoot horizontally.  It is almost impossible to not get hurt while you try to shake them off and fire a few shots at them, but you have a lot of health so the game obviously expects you to get hurt a lot. Strange design choice.
-Obstacles that hurt you on contact look like part of the background.
-Pick-up-looking objects floating in the air are actually part of the scenery.
-The extended barrler of your gun is part of your hit-box.
-If you decide to try the "SUPERHOT Mode" whatever that is, you lose all your progress in the game.
-In some levels you pick up a journal entry, which covers the screen for maybe 30 seconds to let you read a couple sentences, and can't be dismissed manually.
-The New Game intro is several minutes long and unskippable

A great, complete, and unique little puzzle platformer with only a few hiccups which I'll get out of the way first.
The player's field of view is restricted to being 'zoomed in' unless using a 'free look' button requiring them to be stationary. This type of camera is likely descended from mobile development with smaller screens. There is no guide or indicator informing the maximum length of a web to the player until after the attempt is made. This changes the gameplay challenge from using the environment to testing how precise the players ability to eyeball distances is. However lines failed by being overextended do not consume resources. There is no way to reconsume or (for purposes of game balancing ignoring real spiders can reconsume webs) at least destroy your own lines requiring level restarts to capture some bugs that require 'Strong Webs' which are webs with large areas that are not bisected. The in game guide to how specific insects are captured is not in the pause menu but the main menu requiring you to quit the level to consult.
The decision to withhold sublevels, for lack of a better term, to arbitrary real world weather conditions is questionable at best.
However besides that the trailer is completely indicative of the final gameplay. It is consistent and a joy to grasp moving around many varied environments designed greatly in both art and gameplay directions.

Quite frankly they are terrible with customer service, after asking a simple question one of their admins gave a short response (did not answer the question) then proceeded to lock the thread. Not the best way to handle a customer.
The game itself has its high and low points. Despite what the designers state, it does feel a little repetitive no matter how you play the game. The limited customization of characters, the fact that characters don't have traits upon creation or their experiences working make the player character feel bland. The personal interactions are also very bland and don't do much to bring the player into the world of the officer they are playing.
Enforcer does provide a large playing area where you can explore, yet the world feels a bit empty. In a day and age with so much attention paid to how Police Officers perform their job, you do not get any of this in the game. You do not even have other officers, events that change how the community sees the police, or a Chief that imposes training on the force.
Unfortunately, it causes the game to feel a bit hollow. While you have the option to choose from a number of police vehicles, and freedom to patrol where you want, there's just a great deal missing that causes the game to not feel satisfying.  I am recommending the game only based on the fact it's the only one of its kind and it's not terrible if you have low expectations.
The developers also should take a hard look at how they respond to customers as well.
Of note, I definitely logged more than the six hours of game time it is showing.
True Score: 5.5/10

So, when I saw this game, I thought it was going to be like Police Quest and be a police sim with some kind of accuracy about it.
However, it's a good deal more like GTA from the police perspective.
Honestly, I think the thing that throws me off the most is the dialog.  A lot of what's said from dispatch, or the written text, is odd and strikes me as non-English speakers who've never watched Cops trying to write dialog.  I would expect less "There's a murderer on the loose" and more "Shots fired; civilian casualties" or "Armed suspect reported" or the like.  Google searches reveal that the dialog used to be even worse, so this is *after improvement*.
There isn't much polish; the little things will constantly eat at you.  Like, trying to back up your squad car feels clunky, or having it slide backwards down a hill when it's parked (which I guess is fixed in the latest patch).  You basically harass and pull over random people to try and make your quotas, with only a few traffic violations being "externally visible".  I will say I was really impressed when, at night, I could actually see people with their headlights broken and ticket them for it.  That was cool, I'll give them that!
You can't pull people over for running lights, you can't issue tickets for accidents.  The game doesn't seem to care if you, yourself, drive recklessly and there doesn't seem to be a penalty for damaging innocent cars.  Scarface: The World Is Yours had better traffic law mechanics.  I couldn't even pull over a truck that ran a light, then rammed into a street light and blocked an intersection.
And finally, the weather; when it started raining, the sound of the storm was really overwhelming and irritating.  And it was raining inside the police station, which was great.  In my house, at least it wasn't raining in there but it was still equally loud as outside.  Really obnoxious.
One of the things that made Police Quest cool was they actually hired law enforcement folks to help design the game.  I'd love these guys to take another shot at this game, with Enforcer 2, and actually hire a cop to help them make it.  Despite all my problems with this game, I really want to love it, and I really tried to, so please try again.

As you can already tell by my playtime, I love XCOM 2. I highly suggest playing it for any fan of the first game or fans of the genre in general. What I would like to do in this review instead is to focus on the many steps that players could take to improve their experiences with this game significantly. I will be focusing on two things: mods and War of the Chosen.
Let's talk about mods:
I'm just going to flat out say it; if you don't play XCOM 2 with mods, then you're playing it wrong. Mods add options and improvements to your experiences in more ways than you can even imagine. For the average players, we are content with playing the base game and seek mods only to add more information and conveniences. However, there are also mods like Long War 2 that completely change the game. It all depends on you. One thing for sure, if you don't play this game with mods, you are doing yourself an enormous disservice, and you only have yourself to blame if you do.
War of the Chosen:
Playing XCOM 2 without the WotC expansion is like playing Civilization 5 without Brave New World. It's a vast expansion, so much so, that it could practically be considered its own game. To thoroughly go over everything will require its own video, so trust me when I say if you are going to buy XCOM 2, you NEED to purchase War of the Chosen. It's a fantastic addition to the base game, and you will be thankful that you did.
In conclusion, XCOM 2 is a must-played for any fan of the turn-based strategy genre. It's addicting, annoying, and entertaining as hell. I can't wait to see what is in store for the sequel!

Saurian was the first Kickstarter I ever backed, andI don't at all regret backing this game or supporting the crew who worked on it - however, in its current state, I don't reccomend this game very highly.
The game isn't very well optimized, which, at this early stage, is understandable yet still gets a negative mark from me. More than once a game has loaded in the background quite a while before it's able to be played, and once the loading screen was gone I was greeted with a 'game over' screen because I was killed before I could even play. The game is surprisingly lacking visually, with shadows that are harsh, bizzarely pure black and jpeg-esque (my graphical settings are currently on the second highest setting, and it looked the same on the highest). Trying to hunt the tiny lizards, the only thing that won't try to kill you back, is sort of a gamble when you get frame drops and lose your prey in the flat black underbrush.
Speaking of prey...It feels weird to say, but the game feels oddly balanced? The Dakotaraptor dies if it gets caught up in a stiff breeze. Not just as a young stage, either. On my most successful run so far, my parents teamed up on and were both
one-shot by some jerk crocodile that walked away unscathed. I mean, I got a free meal out of it, so it wasn't all bad, but it was kind of eye-opening as to how weak the 'raptor is even as an adult.
Just all around, it's not too terribly fun to play at the moment. Watching the dinosaurs go about their business is very cool, though. I found myself spending a while creeping after a t. Rex hoping to steal some of its leftovers when I saw it stalking prey, only to be disappointed when it swallowed its meal whole. I saw another sort of raptor bully a Pachy without actually trying to attack it. I nipped at a Triceratops' ankles and booked it, watching over my shoulder as it chased me down. There is so much potential for when more playable dinos are added that I can't help but be exited about it.
I will be watching this game closely for updates just as I had before it was released onto Steam, but at the moment find myself more frustrated than entertained when playing it. I will most definitely change this review to reflect my opinion as the game changes and continues to update along the way. I very dearly hope that it's not too long before I can change my reccomendation to a yes!

Bastion is overall a solid action RPG (with touches of beat 'em up gameplay) wrapped in a wonderfully crafted world. This game has a complete and unique story and a beautiful enivronment with its art style and music standing out and being different from other games.
As an action RPG, Bastion consists of running around levels destroying enemies and gaining money and experience from them. Weapons consist of various melee weapons like in most fantasy games, while expanding to firearms and explosives for a more technologically advanced loadout. In addition to the variety of weapons, special abilities, upgrades, and passive abilities are addedd to allow progression as the game goes on. The game isn't terribly difficult, but there are some surprise parts that may cause some deaths first time around. Other sources of difficult parts can be remedied by using a better strategy or weapon and skill loadout, and then it doesn't become very hard anymore. With a good amount of options along with a not too difficult except in some parts difficulty, the gameplay is mostly relaxing and fun while not going too deep in gameplay mechanics.
The art and music in this game are simply gorgeous. Each screen is adorned with painted objects in each level, ranging from the destroyed ruins to forests and mines. Sometimes the level pieces literally fall into place, which is a nice touch. The characters and other NPCs themselves are also designed nicely and look great in the game's environment. As the high quality of the art is good, so is the well composed music. The music, like the game, is a bit different than most games, in that it carries a sort of apocalyptic fantasy with traditional instruments backed with some modern electronic styling. The vocal music in the game also carries well into the story, which is a strong part of the game.
When you first start Bastion, you will be a bit disoriented and confused at the start of its story. Gradually however, the game opens itself up by telling backstory of what happened from the ever popular Narrator, who also goes by The Stranger and Rucks. Just hearing his voice and commentary for almost every action you do is pleasing and is the person who does the most story explanation. Once the backstory is mostly told, a series of events start to happen at the middle of the game, which shifts the game from a mostly cheery place to a more serious set of matters. The characters are more complex than at first, giving a good story. The short lines from Rucks can be funny and also be more dramatic as serious events unfold. The story in Bastion is very interesting and can be sad at parts once the game decides to pick up.
Bastion is a well designed action RPG that offers a good amount of fighting and strategy to players. The luscious world with the rich art and music along with a unique story are more powerful points that make for a great game experience. The gameplay is fairly straightforward, but the art, music, and story are very pleasing and one of a kind in Bastion.

I bought this game on sale after reading a lot of its reviews. So far I made it from a single person studio in 1980 to a AAA giant in 2016 (with one failed and three super successful MMO titles that grossed hundreds of millions), but I hear you can play this well into the future. As a gamer in real life, the choices I make as a developer in the game echo reality: should I release the 6th installment of my uber successful series, where profit is certain but creativity is nonexistent, should I maybe probe the market with a cheaper title that explores a radical new genre/combination, or do I dare invest all of my effort into making a brand new concept for an MMO, knowing there are dozens of millions of development and production dollars at stake? There's a lot more of this type of openness - you can decide to be an SDK focused busienss and sell engines to other companies. You can venture into console development and production. You can develop titles for other publishers, you can publish other developers games, you can create annoying candy crush clones with a F2P model. The game's biggest strength is how it puts you in this historically accurate simulation of gaming history and lets you be part of it in whatever way you choose.
Since the game offers no real guidance about how to succeed, I was left with my background of playing a lot of video games since the late 80s. So far they seem to have served me well in picking genre and topic combinations, making target age group and game balance decisions (when you make a game you need to set a series of sliders to balance things like graphics vs gameplay, functions vs atmosphere and so on). I did not read anything about how to play, because I didn't want to ruin the experience, and this led to me learning some game mechanics (like the effects of reputation and the fine balancing act of pricing and packaging) fairly late in the game, so I am curious how I would fare in a second run. I'm also curious to try to play in hard mode - would it be arbitrarily punishing or a well thought difficulty curve?
UPDATE: On my second run I became a multimilionaire by 1986 and by 1990 retired from the business because it's really hard to manage such a big company. I bought out most of the other development companies and made them make games exclusively for my consoles.

Do not buy this game unless you cannot live your life without having some form of a police simulator game in it. When the game was first released in Early Access, it looked fairly promising. Sometimes you get emergency calls, there are about 3 different ones and they are all exactly the same each time over. It is just a barren, empty shell of a game that has been abandoned by the developer.
The reason I say it has been abandoned is that the game literally did not change whatsoever from the first day it was released in Early Access, up until now, when it is in its "complete" form. Don't take this as a "waaaah developer ripped me off because I bought a game in Early Access" This is just my observations of the direction development took in this game, and in my opinion it was a miserable failure all things considered.
The developer, Odin Studios, has also released another Early Access zombie survival game, Better Late Than Dead (lol) on the same broken engine, so I would avoid that too! :^)

I love this game.  I mean, love, like I want to take it home and snuggle it.  The first release of Spider (The Secret of Bryce Manor) is one of my favorites to date, and the changes they've made in the newest release are amazing.
This is a much beefier game than the first.  Bryce Manor was more exploratory, and hints of story were revealed as your spider progressed through each section of the house.  However, this game has puzzles, levels that can be replayed for different results (and bugs) depending on the time of day and weather.  That it uses your local time and weather in the game is, well, nifty.  :-)  Some of the levels are a real challenge, too. I'm not a hardcore gamer and am making my way through.  So, don't be scared.
About the weather, there's also a weather/time machine that you can use periodically.  I'm glad they included this because it's not likely to rain in Central Texas anytime soon, and that would mean I'd have to wait weeks to play some of the levels.
As of now, I've already played nearly 8 hours, and I would have played more if it weren't for that pesky job.  :-D  This game will keep me busy for awhile, and I'm enjoying every minute.  Thank you, Tiger Style.

"Oh look, Bastion, another indie game with a unique art style and shallow gameplay" - Yep, that pretty much summed up my thoughts when I first saw the game. However, I decided to give it a chance before judging it so harshly, and I'm glad I did.
Okay, credit given where credit is due. The art style of bastion really did blow me away. The way that every level builds itself as you go through it as well as the general design and even the characters themselves really won me over. Not to mention the narrator truly making the game feel unique.
Where I expected it to fail, the gameplay, actually turned out not only to be fun and diverse, but extremely polished. Each of the 12 weapons behaves completely differently and you can mix up any two of your choice, combined with one of 30 secret skills, providing LOADS of ways to play.
You slowly upgrade the Bastion however you want after completing each level, unlocking more options. There are some challenges to do here and there but besides that, the game is fairly linear. An average playthrough to one of the 4 endings will last about 5 hours but more content is offered in the much appreciated New Game+ Mode w, allowing for a lot more replay value.
I'm trying to think of something bad to say but I find it difficult. Technically there is only 5 hours of content, so for £11.50, that is a lot. Also, the game may not appeal to everyone, it took a lot of self-encouragement to actually force myself to play the game. It doesn't do a good job at drawing people in initially.
Bastion gets an 8 out of 10 from me on 60 Second Reviews.

So, what are you doing here reading ? Go buy the game!

I think this may be one of the best Indie games I have ever played. The controls and combat is smooth and flowing, and handles beautifully. The art style is flat out amazing, and works extremely well with the environment and atmosphere. Even while the overall feel of the game was fantastic, neither (to me, anyway) even held a candle to the Storytelling and narration.
As for the weapons, each weapon felt insanely well designed. They each were varied from every other weapon in how they were useful and upgraded enough so that each weapon had a unique handle and style of playing with it, and there weren't so many as to feel like they were just haphazardly thrown in the game. The big thing I love about how the weapons are used is one is bound to the LMB and one is bound to RMB, so you can only carry 2 at a time, and you can balance out, using pistols for fast attacks and movement in addition with your much slower, but harder hitting Hammer or Rifle.
I truly recommend this game to just about everyone, it is so close to perfection, I can't really find good complaints about it. About the only thing I had slight issues with was the diagonal moving (up does not move you up, it moves you to the top right) and even then, you get used to that and adjust yourself before you even realize it. About the only other thing I felt disappointed about was how the shield worked. There was no choice of different shields (maybe one that allows you to take partial damage, but move while using it or something), the shield would block all damage, no matter what, and you can't really upgrade it. However, there is also a Parry mechanic which you cause damage if you raise your shield just as you get attacked, and that did take timing and skill.

I will not give this game any discounts just because the game is cheap. I cannot recommend this game even for short relaxing experience by several reasons.
1. It does not work well with multimonitor setup. It only runs on main screen and cannot be ran on secondary one. RIP my intentions to casually play it on my bed from secondary screen. To be fair, you CAN get it to render on secondary screen via Alt + Enter, but if screen have different rendering resolution, like in my case, you gonna have fun with disproportional rendering of the game.
2. It's slow. Painfully slow. So slow in fact, that I had to use CE speedhack to make it at least a little bit playable. But because this game uses physics for completely unknown reason - with speedhack it have collision issues. I was unable to run it stable at more than 1.5 speed increase. At higher (and even sometimes on 1.5) speeds physics freak out and you often find yourself locked out of controls or rotators rotate you as if you entered it from another direction. I came here to think on the puzzles, not to watch slow animations of how I solve said puzzles.
3. Four. Damn. Achievements. Per. Level. Seriously!? Giving an achievement for every level is already bad idea, but GODDAMN FOUR OF THEM!? It's very distracting and completely redundant.
4. Overall puzzles are extremely easy and rarely levels had me to actually even start to think on what I'm doing, as most of them just solve themselves with very little thinking on my side, as I just move block in only possible next direction. Neither challenging or engaging. Boring.
5. Visuals. A bunch of levels are very crowded and I personally had hard time understanding when the block will end up at because of visual overload. Often it ended up in death and level reset.
Conclusion:
Puzzles: 1/10. Boring, not engaging and insultingly easy;
Visuals: 5/10. Problems with level readability;
Audio: Not rated.
Technical implementation: 3/10. Physics for simple animations? Really? Also make it even slower next time.
Total: 3/10. Poor implementation, boring gameplay.
Total according to prices: 5/10. Still won't recommend.

As you can already tell by my playtime, I love XCOM 2. I highly suggest playing it for any fan of the first game or fans of the genre in general. What I would like to do in this review instead is to focus on the many steps that players could take to improve their experiences with this game significantly. I will be focusing on two things: mods and War of the Chosen.
Let's talk about mods:
I'm just going to flat out say it; if you don't play XCOM 2 with mods, then you're playing it wrong. Mods add options and improvements to your experiences in more ways than you can even imagine. War of the Chosen:
Playing XCOM 2 without the WotC expansion is like playing Civilization 5 without Brave New World. It's a vast expansion, so much so, that it could practically be considered its own game. In conclusion, XCOM 2 is a must-played for any fan of the turn-based strategy genre. It's addicting, annoying, and entertaining as hell. I can't wait to see what is in store for the sequel!

A really cool little game I learned about on r/spiders of reddit. Basically, you play a cute little jumping spider with leaping abilities to put Jordan to shame and the ability to make webs once a geometric pattern of criss crossing silk has been made. You use these webs to catch wandering bugs (many with different AI patterns), such as flies and crickets, while other techniques, such as tackling, are needed to take down hornets. Similarly, these insects give you more silk to work with as your supply is finite. You make use of the web's design and the insects you eat to get points as you clear your way to the next area. Meanwhile, there's secrets to be found throughout the stages as you try to uncover the background story of the manor you're hunting in.
The game is one of those 'easy to learn, hard to master' sorts. You have to plan out the best way to keep your point modifiers high (leaping web from web, instead of touching the ground) and you need to strategize how to make your approach, which is made harder with obstacles, finite resources, and bugs that don't necessarily stay where you want them to. All of this adds up to a surprisingly cerebral game.
Sure, people who don't like spiders or bugs to point of burning their house down and screaming like a little girl miiiight not like the imagery used, but nothing is terribly graphic. The imagery is realistic, but don't expect to see more macabre stuff for the most part. There's really a damn good title to be had here that I don't think will squeam out the nervous crowd too much.
There's a lot to do in this game, from the planning, to figuring out the web physics, finding secrets, unlocking new spider skins(!), and even getting a bestiary of sorts of the insects you've defeated on a small board, where you can see a little information about them. Btw, this game utilizes an option to mirror the local weather and time of day of your ISP's location (assuming you allow it), so you might play in Spider's world during a night time rain storm or on a clear sunny day, given your location. How cool!
I have nothing but good things to say about this title, honestly. I wish the developers the best and hope they make more content for Spider. I think the only thing I can give as constructive criticism is I would have preferred a slightly more involved tutorial for the various mechanics of the game. It can be fine to figure out things on your own but some bugs don't get special descriptions concerning what needs to be done versus others, for example.

Spider is a very fun, satisfying experience.
Stacking up multiple bugs in one web, after you've carefully strategised the best way to do it, feels badass.
A video showcasing all the features I'm about to talk about
The controls make sense and feel good in your hand, which is important for a game like this.
Different bugs react differently, which means you need to alter your strategy. Be it simply tackling them to eat them, or needing to scare them into your web.
You have a finite amount of web to spin, but you regain the amount of silk you hold by eating bugs.
You can either eat bugs immediately to refill it, or save multiple bugs in one web to achieve a combo for the highest score possible.
This game has very good replay value because of that reason, and if you are a fan of getting high-scores, then this is a very good choice.
The game has a very interesting IP detection system, which looks at your time of day and weather in your city. (You have the option to turn it off). This will change the type of bugs in levels according to your environment outside.
To sum up, the game is a very fun, unique experience that you should give a go!

A fun, easy-going, strategic spider game that I am incapable of griping too much about, and I'm a real complainer. Excellently polished.
I've been playing this great little game since the beta.
It's a fun game that's a bit difficult to categorize. You play as a spider, you make webs, and, for the most part, these webs catch bugs that you in turn eat. Move from level to level, rinse, wash, repeat. Yet it's a lot better than that, and a lot more interesting. The lovely backgrounds --- which likely look better on the small screen than on the large screen --- are for the attentive suggestive of a story, and the story is told this way without dialogue or, indeed, a plot. Intrigue is in the background, and entirely in the mind of the player. Your little spider avatar is just busy eating bugs.
I want to say that this is a puzzler, and it is in a way, but its points-and-combos scoring system is about all it has in common with one. Is it a platformer when it isn't run-and-jump from left to right? Playing the part of a spider means that you're only nominally susceptible to gravity, and so the feeling of being a platformer is lost entirely. I spend most of the game upside-down or sideways on walls or, what's more interesting, on a web I've carefully planned at the nexus of the flight paths of several bugs.
Not only this, but each level has four different versions --- while the landscape is the same, the number of and kinds of bugs are different, and this radically changes the best approach for the level. It's like four games in one this way. In-game weather is based on your actual IRL local precipitation, though you can change the weather in the game options.
My favorite parts of the game are the calm bits, where I can strategize where to wait and what to do and do it at my own pace. I can easily place webs because the landscape doesn't move and the threads which make up my webs are stable. That is, until the middle to the end of the game when several levels begin to have moving landscape. When some stable bit of the level itself moves, a thread connecting that moving piece of scenery to anywhere else will break. Suddenly, a game I enjoyed for being relaxed became very tense instead. In these levels, I now have to rely on quick movement to chain the combo from bug to bug.
Secondly, during the beta --- I don't know about the finished game, so I hope this changes --- the weather machine has a limited number of uses and it refreshes based pn the phases of the moon, (see title.) IRL interaction is a fun little feature for mobile gaming --- think Pokemon Gold/Silver, when nighttime was based on real-world time --- but in PC gaming that kind of real-world interaction is more a hassle and less interesting. I hope they change it so that the PC user has complete control over the in-game weather.
Though I disagree with these two minor design decisions, they are still not bad design decisions! I can't emphasize this enough. With all the crap on Steam these days, it's wonderful to see an indie dev hit every note they mean to play just right.

Edit:
After messing around with the game a little more the game finally decided to run a little more smoothly. I can now play, albeit in a very jerky mannner and I can't enter an area with too many trees. But I can play.
So, with that said.
The game is still slow to run, understandably on my PC. something confusing was that any stage below adult tended to have steps that slipped into one another, whereas the adult didn't and moved at a more bearable walkspeed.
In terms of food, it's hit and miss. Sometimes you can be in an area with plenty of food about and be just fine and other times you're going to starve. You're best bet is to find some water source and wait for something to come to you. As a baby dakotaraptor you're absolute best bet is to stick with your siblings and cannibalise them. So be thankful you have some siblings because you're parents are probably going to get themselves killed very quickly. The AI absolutely sucks and is by far the thing that needs the most work in this game.
Other than your siblings, you'll struggle to find food because lizards are almost impossible to catch Everything else will kill you immediately and your parents are long gone. You can always eat their corpses. Except, you can't because they've probably already disappeared. Corpses don't hang around very long and you don't know when they're going to disappear because they don't have decomosition/eaten stages.
But other than that, the models are fine, the map is fine, eating and drinking is easy to do, the game forces you to be very weary for better of for worse, which I don't personally mind and it's doing okay. There's definitely worse pre-alphas out there. Don't get me wrong, don't buy it unless your intention is to support the devs more. It's not something that should be sold at the price it is yet, especially after the amazing kickstarter it had.
Onto the other bad points as it stands.
- Glitches. It's in pre-alpha release so expect these around every corner.
- You're dead if anything hits you at dakotaraptor juv/sub-adult stage. It's basically impossible to hunt herbivores with my kind of performance until adult stage. You have to rely on killing other dakotaraptors or whatever the other little raptor is or scavenging if you happen to find  some tasty corpses.
- The stats drain so fast. I think they might've slowed the food down at least since there was an update released. I'm actually pretty happy with hunger now, it's more thirst now. I can't really explore much because I have to keep running up hills then down to a water source then up and down and up and that is very tedious.
- Progression is rather fast. I wouldn't be opposed to slowing progression down just a bit more. I'm thankful that it isn't painfully slow (because the game only plays when you're on it and you don't progress when sleeping. You must play it.) but it could do with coming down a notch.
- The AI is entirely braindead. I can't say anything positive for the AI simply because it's just so basic and slow to do even basic things. I'm expecting them to add and work on the AI because it really is what is going to make the game work in the long run given how many bots there are. But as it stands, everything moves downhill to a water source and swims about in it in circles until some croc comes and eats it. If you bite something, it attacks you, might chase you for a second, then forgets you ever existed. Nothing runs away despite there being a threat in the area. Most things just tend to walk up to a trex and die if one hapens to be there. Trexes will immediately fight  upon seeing eachother as well - I assume thing might change later down the line to have a bit more of a roaring contest go on before a fight breaks out to see if things can be settled peacefully. In terms of drinking, things manage but then they tend to step into the water and go into their circle of death for some reason. In terms of eating they half-manage. On the rare occasion you see something take a bite it'll probably be fien, but occasionally they'll jsut sit and stare. In general, the AI just isn't any fun and is just about functioning. It isn't a nice experience to play with an AI that's just so unaware of everything around it though. Each bot goes about its own little life with no interaction with anything else except food, water and maybe you.
So, all in all, no. I can't recommend it as a game. It is good for something that isn't even an alpha and it functions, eventually. But it's not worth the pricetag and if you buy it, really only consider it something to support the devs with.

I've spent over 500 hours in this game. 260+ hours were on one play-through in the hardcore mode. In that run, I finished the game plus DLCs, got every settlement to maximum population with at least 100 defense, and have generally done about everything.
I've waffled between giving this a good or bad review. It is certainly good at what it is: an open world FPS with RPG elements. It is a good game. But it isn't a good Fallout game. Let me explain.
There's very limited dialog choice, with your options usually being Yes (Good), Yes (Sarcastic) or No (Yes). You can choose between a few faction endings, but not much within those endings. There aren't many scripted quests compared to New Vegas. Plenty of procedurally-generated generic "Go to the place and kill one thing" quests, though. Until they get bugged and you can't do them anymore. This won't stop Preston from mentioning them. Send him to the settlement you visit the least.
Speaking of the settlements, the much-advertised settlement building feature is lackluster, especially on the non-hardcore modes. There is little point to them besides the creative outlet they provide. In hardcore mode they at least provide a save point and food/water as you traverse the wasteland.
The weapon crafting system is interesting but generic.
The whole game is interesting but generic. There is a little bit of lore building, but not enough for my tastes. A few terminal entries here and there is all you really get. Less terminal entries than F:NV or FO3, for sure.
This game is recommended for what it is.

Rustangelo has the possibilty to be great but there's just so many problems with it (Not all of them are the developers faults)
Rustangelo takes a LONG time on anything above black and white, simple paintings. You could be waiting up to an hour just to paint a simple 3 color symbol. Rustangelo also seems to want to add more colors than are necessary. For example I had a picture that had a black outline with a blue and red interior. After dithering the program tried adding blue and red dots to the outline, even though they weren't there originally. This is probably due to a problem with dithering but it's annoying none the less. It's problematic because it can mess up minimalist designs and it causes drawing times to skyrocket.
Some other problems with the program are that there's a lack of developer support from rust. Minimal color choice means high detail paintings get wrecked by the dithering process and make beautiful paintings look like aids.
On top of this there seems to be no way to speed up paint times because it's all based on mouse clicks. Sure, straight lines helps but only to an extent. Sign painting in rust is in a really sorry state and not even this program can fix that.

"Oh look, Bastion, another indie game with a unique art style and shallow gameplay" - Yep, that pretty much summed up my thoughts when I first saw the game. However, I decided to give it a chance before judging it so harshly, and I'm glad I did.
Okay, credit given where credit is due. The art style of bastion really did blow me away. The way that every level builds itself as you go through it as well as the general design and even the characters themselves really won me over. Not to mention the narrator truly making the game feel unique.
Where I expected it to fail, the gameplay, actually turned out not only to be fun and diverse, but extremely polished. Each of the 12 weapons behaves completely differently and you can mix up any two of your choice, combined with one of 30 secret skills, providing LOADS of ways to play.
You slowly upgrade the Bastion however you want after completing each level, unlocking more options. There are some challenges to do here and there but besides that, the game is fairly linear. An average playthrough to one of the 4 endings will last about 5 hours but more content is offered in the much appreciated New Game+ Mode w, allowing for a lot more replay value.
I'm trying to think of something bad to say but I find it difficult. Technically there is only 5 hours of content, so for £11.50, that is a lot. Also, the game may not appeal to everyone, it took a lot of self-encouragement to actually force myself to play the game. It doesn't do a good job at drawing people in initially.
Bastion gets an 8 out of 10 from me on 60 Second Reviews.

So, what are you doing here reading ? Go buy the game!

I think this may be one of the best Indie games I have ever played. The controls and combat is smooth and flowing, and handles beautifully. The art style is flat out amazing, and works extremely well with the environment and atmosphere. Even while the overall feel of the game was fantastic, neither (to me, anyway) even held a candle to the Storytelling and narration.
As for the weapons, each weapon felt insanely well designed. They each were varied from every other weapon in how they were useful and upgraded enough so that each weapon had a unique handle and style of playing with it, and there weren't so many as to feel like they were just haphazardly thrown in the game. The big thing I love about how the weapons are used is one is bound to the LMB and one is bound to RMB, so you can only carry 2 at a time, and you can balance out, using pistols for fast attacks and movement in addition with your much slower, but harder hitting Hammer or Rifle.
I truly recommend this game to just about everyone, it is so close to perfection, I can't really find good complaints about it. About the only thing I had slight issues with was the diagonal moving (up does not move you up, it moves you to the top right) and even then, you get used to that and adjust yourself before you even realize it. About the only other thing I felt disappointed about was how the shield worked. There was no choice of different shields (maybe one that allows you to take partial damage, but move while using it or something), the shield would block all damage, no matter what, and you can't really upgrade it. However, there is also a Parry mechanic which you cause damage if you raise your shield just as you get attacked, and that did take timing and skill.

So before I go into each category, I want to give a brief TLDR. This game is most definitely worth getting and you will enjoy your time with it even though it does not have the standardish battle style of "Tales of" games, and it ranks up among the top made in my opinion.
Now that that is out of the way, there is one other thing to address. One of the things that draws you into a "Tales of" game is the battle system, and this one is much different in that you do not have TP and do not bind Artes (techs) like normal. Instead, every "attack" is an arte that is set in a 4x4 grid that you decide which button will have that arte and which "attack" number that arte will be in the combo. Basically, what this comes down to is you will either have to do a lot of micromanaging to get it perfect or just get a general setup for each button for different purposes and never worry about it again. This isn't necessarily bad, but it takes away the feel of using an arte for just attacking.
-------------------------
Character Design - 10/10
Velvet could not be any more perfect. Not much to say other than extremely well done characters. Whichever you choose to go with, the English or Japanese voice actors, they both did a good job (though it is generally decided that the majority of JP voice actors do a much better job).
Map/Level Design - 6/10
I almost give it a pass, but I generally do not like this newer style of going through areas. Instead of going to a "World Map" where you travel, it is similar to Tales of Xillia where you travel through different areas by going through small groups of maps to simulate an open world, which looks nice, but you have very little area to go and little to explore. It is worth noting that Xillia does this better and does not feel as similar as some of the places in this game do, and you will find yourself going back to the same areas to farm up more spirits. This is the weakest part of the game but does not prevent enjoyment.
Story - 10/10
A very dark story, this is a refreshing change of pace from most other games. This game is about vengeance, and if the world had to be burned or saved for that to happen, Velvet would make it happen.
Combat - 9/10
I know in the begining I gave this a bit of a hard time, but it is simply different, and it not only feels good, but makes sense in terms of the story. The system of absorbing souls becomes very intuitive and just feels right. The only problems I have with this are 1) The artes do not feel like artes, they feel like regular attacks. 2) The Mystic Artes do not feel like mystic artes, they feel more like burst artes from Tales of Vesperia. Again, this does not detract much if at all, and the mystic artes do make a big impact, but they just don't feel like they are as strong as Mystic Artes from previous games.
Itemization - 10/10
This is worth mentioning here that the way that herbs grow back where you found them, the way skill you learn from gear becomes permanent on each character after learning them, the upgrades to equipment, loot drops, the special items dropped from bosses all make a huge impact on the game in a very positive way. Worth putting here and noting it for sure. Also worth noting, definitely starting difficulty should be at least moderate and you may want to go up from there.
Minigames - 9/10
You have to know that there are a TON of minigames within the game, as well as a bunch of spirits to collect to open katz chests. You will not get bored at having to grind the same minigame to unlock a bunch of new items and tokens.
Replayability - 9/10
High replayability. This is where "Tales of" games usually shine the most, where you have the ability to play them for an absolutely obscene amount of hours and not be bored of it. With a new game + feature, you are able to start a new game with whatever you were able to purchase in the grade shop. The grade shop is something you visit when you load up data from after beating the game and you use all the grade that you have been earing throughout the game to purchase things like keep skills, more XP, more health, a grade multiplier, and much more.
--------------------
Ending Comments
I give it an overall score of 9/10
Velvet Crowe might be my favorite "Tales of" character, and Berseria does rank among the top "Tales of" games, Vesperia, Symphonia, Abyss, and Xillia (except we only got one of those previous ones in what can now be called working condition). However, the ultimate of "Tales of" games is still Tales of Vesperia. It is the culmination of everything they had been doing up to that point and everything came together perfectly for it, and it is the only one that I can give a perfect score. This is a good quality port, so we know they can make a good port when they put the effort into it, so you might want to keep an eye out in case one of those comes out. In the mean time, you will have a great time playing Tales of Berseria.

Incredible story experience. Forces a lot of harsh split second decisions. My only complaint is sometimes the game mis-interprets your decision. In the first episode
. But you need to keep going when such things happen. I consider it a way to simulate making bad calls in rough situations, and actually enhances immersion because the player will still make the occassional mistake purely out of a missunderstanding of your options this way even though you're sitting comfortably playing a game.
For the most part the game looks like a comicbook and even somewhat reads like one. There are puzzles to be solved and decisions to make on the fly and the story really does change based on seemingly unimportant decisions made either a few scenes ago or even a few episodes ago. I especially like that the game is *not* a survival game, but still feels tense, like you are really trying to keep people alive until you can't. And then it makes you suck it up and keep going.

The game is essentially just the sliding block on ice puzzles you see in tons of RPGs and action adventure games, Pokemon and Zelda being the most prominent examples (it has a few mechanics that differentiate it later on with different types of blocks you can collide with, but at it's core it's still just a sliding block on ice puzzle).  That on it's own is enough to make it pretty uninteresting but combine that with the fact that the pure white background makes it difficult to actually judge if shots are lining up and you get a game that's pretty irritating to play.  Some sort of grid or even just light grey lines emanating from your piece could have easily fixed that but I suppose the demands of their minimalist aesthetic made that impossible.
On top of the uninspired puzzles and the minimal aesthetic getting in the way of the actual gameplay, the game constantly showers you with achievements making it feel like one of those pieces of shovelware that just throws in achievements to draw in the people who just want to get a huge number of achievements as fast as they can to watch the numbers on their steam profile steadily rise.  An achievement for visiting the main menu, an achievement for starting the game up, two achievements every time you beat a level, one for beating the level and one for accessing the next level, it's obnoxious and whatever merit their minimalist aesthetic has is ruined by the constant achievement notifications popping up in the corner.
It's not the worst game ever made or anything but I found it completely mindnumbing.

The tales series has become something that I don't want it to be, and I want to go into this saying I realize that when changes happen someone isn't going to like it. I happen to be on the bad end of the stick in this case.
I've played every single tales game in the series since symphonia except for symphonia DotNW, and all of those games (save Zesteria and Graces F) have had the same relative "Tales of" feel. In those games, you have normal attacks, then you have 3 steps of artes that can be performed in a sequence to create comboes in exchange for TP (the equivalent to MP in any other RPG). As you progressed through those games, you would eventually unlock new tiers of artes, sometimes through cutscenes, sometimes through leveling, and sometimes you would unlock artes that were better versions of previous ones that you used frequently. As you unlocked new teirs of artes,
. When your old comboes used to be 3 normal attacks and a single arte, you now have that same combo followed by a new arte. This system made artes feel powerful, it made them feel valuable. You could mix and match new artes for different situations, and develop your own style of play. Additionally, as you progress through the game sometimes you unlock more attacks in your basic attack combo, making you have significantly higher damage output.
The Berseria battle system completely ruins all of that. The way it works now is that every attack is an arte. The TP system has been scrapped and replaced with a "soul" resource system. At the start of a battle, you have 3 "souls" in your gauge. Each souls has 30 points (there is a name for the point, but it escapes me at the moment), and your artes use a certain number of points after you use them. If you stun or inflict an enemy with another status effect, you will steal a soul from said enemy, and other enemies will do the same to you. When enemies are stunned, they are vulnerable for a time, allowing you to do massive damage, and again, enemies can do the same to you. Now for balancing purposes this seems fine, but when you are stunned, all of your controls are ripped from you and you just have to sit there, it feels awful for a system that boasts fluidity.
The ally AI (at least while I was playing) is bugged into doing nothing but attacking once and retreating. This is only a problem with the PC full version (the demo on PC and all the PS4 versions work fine). This means that in a fight against, say, seven wolves that stun, you are essentially trying to accomplish the impossible task of doing a 1V7 where you do not get hit at all, because if you do get hit you'll sit there FOREVER and get ripped to shreds as your useless party members laugh at your woes.
***EDIT*** The AI has since been patched, so this is no longer a problem.
The other problem is that this system makes
. Now instead of sequences of attacks with progressing strength, you are simply able to just spam attacks in any order and have them link together. Instead of everything feeling like artes, I feel like I'm just doing a sequence of different normal combo attacks. The only real progression throughout the game is that you unlock new artes from time to time while leveling. These artes are usually a bit more effective then the previous ones, making them useless after you get objectively better ones. In the old tales games, no arte was useless; sometimes they used less TP than the other artes in their tier, sometimes they hit enemies in the air, etc. Every arte in a tier had a purpose, and the way the comboing system worked in the old games made even the first arte you started out with useful to the end of the game. Aditionally, the way the souls system works, you never unlock new combo potential later in the game (as far as I've seen), so you don't end up feeling like a more experienced and skilled player, you feel likea player who has accumulated better moves.
The one thing I like about the battle system is enemy weakness chains. Essentially, if you exploit multiple enemy weaknesses in a combo you will do more and more damage throughout the combo depending on the number of said exploited weaknesses. This makes an otherwise "set the combo with the most damage to the X button and spam X" system a bit more strategic. I think the hope would be that this makes every attack have a use, but as you progress some attacks are so weak that it's better to just use a strong attack because the one from the start of the game is so weak that it negates the weakness chaining system.
Also, the gear mastering system is kind of awful. Every piece of equipable gear will give you small (seemingly pointless) skills, and you can unlock the skills by equipping the item and earning grade to learn them. This leads to a bunch of grinding for something that you're not even sure you want. It honestly just feels like it's there to pad out the game.
My main gripe was with the gameplay, but I must say the story is awful. I give it a Linkin Park out of 10.
TL;DR: If you like old tales games because of the battle system and good storytelling you'd better look somewhere else. If you like samey combat, and you crawl in your skin and/or your wounds will not heal, play to your heart's content.

This game has missed several launch dates, as far back as 2012 and grows more stagnant by the month when it usually gets an update. Updates have been pointless add-ons like NPC idle animations, monster name generator, a few chairs, experiments by devs that won't be in the game, ingame minigames that no one plays. The quests are incredibly long and boring, you have to go through the same dungeon over and over to brute force your way through it since it's essentially a time sink barrier. Game lacks basic features like setting spawn points, tree growing animations (or sprites), tons of items are not named correctly and/or the icons don't match the item.
**RANT WARNING**
Yes, it is a beta and that's exactly my point, the developers spend more time playing around with experiments and creating silly NPC animations when they should be working on the core game aspect, questing, making unique enemies, unique dungeons, expand crafting, etc. The current iteration of the game is what you are going to get at launch with some NPC housing elements and that's it. The stretch goals might get into the game at launch but I expect them to simply fall back on the disclaimer that was attached to most of those goals which is to add them in post launch. Save your money and just pirate the game, the first thing the devs did after selling over a million copies was take a 6 month vacation and blew all the cash so the development slowed down dramatically. Obviosuly poor leadership and management since I've watched a couple of the devs stream and they seemed to know thier stuff, but without proper direction people will do whatever they feel like doing, the fun stuff.
tl;dr: pirate it.

the addition of the chosen makes each mission harder. i keep thinking "am i going to get a chosen this mission, should i bring their counter unit even though they are tired?" and it keeps you on your toes and is far more difficult than vanilla was. they also got rid of the insane load times. everything is FAST now. use to take 30 second to a minute per load screen on vanilla now it's 10 seconds or less. these are on a SSD btw. on a regular HD vanilla load times were... lets just say i could make coffee and get back before the damn game loaded. also what firaxis did with the UI is great. they added alot of the mods and just shoved them in the game. so you don't have to load even more mods you shouldn't have to into the game. this being in fights it now shows everything on your hp bar like a mod in vanilla did before.

the gameplay is also improved ALOT in this game. with new additions to the game like soldiers bonds. where if you get them up to rank 3 compatibility they can dual strike. so both will shoot the same target. they can also inspire the other unit to give them a second move. it's a nice addition to the gameplay in the game. they also created a training room that allows you to use AP to get traits from the other line along with personal traits that unit might have. like one of my rangers had a personal trait you can get through the trainer that gave him shredding. it's not available in either line of the ranger. you can use personal AP or group AP which is for the entire team. i turned my sniper into a sniper and gunslinger. when i beat the sniper chosen i gave him both of his gear and he hit like a truck...
overall xcom vanilla. good game. timers suck with war of the chosen they improve on every aspect of this game and make it a better experience overall. i give the game with war of the chosen about a 9.5/10. i just don't see many games as addicting and as hard as xcom can be now adays.

After a few hours of playing i think im ready to review. I have to admit i have a hard bias towards this game in some regards as i was a backer and contiously followed in it's development, i will always recommend that people support the game as it develops simply because the potential here is something users like me have been begging for in a game since we were kids.
The wait for this game has been long and daunting but the result was a decent demo of things to come but, let me get some of the negatives out of the way. *Note* half of the stuff im about to complain about aren't fair since most is subject to change.
*****Negatives That I Hope Are Fixed In Time*****
Optimization
- Super early access, the demo (thats what it feels like) surely wasnt ready for release, when i heard Saurian was being made public finally after years of waiting i thought we were getting a gorgeous looking game thats somewhat smoothly optimized. But suffice it to say i was dissapointed, the transition between afternoon to night is a laggy nightmare and i ended up dying constantly during those time periods.
Graphics
- foliage textures,  this is mostly subjective but it is increasingly frustrating to see how plain everything looks, some of the larger trees look like rip offs of modern day trees under a "scientifically accurate" blanket. The trees have really poor textures even under ultra settings (There is no noticeable difference between two of the top graphical settings). You would not be able to distinguish a regular piece of foliage from the games own assets. Makes you feel like they wasted time working on their own when could have imported better looking assets from somewhere else.
- Night time especially suffers, instead of being pitch black with a nightvision mode, everything is slightly visible but makes the neutral colours look extreamly flat, it suffers even more during sunsets where everything takes on a orange tone that destroys the look of the enviornment and makes everything look flat and 2D-ish. I found myself always sleeping through the night, even when i wanted to be a nocturnal hunter.
Gameplay
- Ai in general,  first time i played the game, i spawned near a river where my parents rushed to their deaths by attacking a pachy on the other side. The parents Ai puts no emphaces on survival as every time i respawn, the parents will charge to their deaths and the baby dakota Ai will often just stay frozen in place, waiting for whatever wants to kill it. Prey Ai seems especially stupid, when i attack it, it will flinch then go on with its business like nothing happened, the only good Ai seems to be the timid lizards that always dissapear into the greenery.
- Controls, this aspect of the game ceartinly feels rushed, some default key bindings are awkwardly mapped and non existent on console controls. Theres also an issue where the altered key bindings are reset to their default everytime i close the game.
- Camera, seems like the most apparent issue is the fact that the camera seems to operate in fixed angles that are hard to get use to, ill often try to get a look at my dakotaraptor or try to change direction, only to have the camera bug out and swing wildly to some other angle, it's more forgiveable when playing with a controller.
- Action delays, i see more and more indie games dealing with this issue and can't tell if it's deliberate or not but often times when i make my dakotaraptor jump, it'll ignore the first two actions and jump once really slowly, i have an anti ghosting keyboard which makes this even more frustrating.
- Lack of explanation in the use of the different smells, green means lizards? ya dont say.
- Missing assets or features such as spectator mode, dino fight club, plant collision, climbing, turtles, marine life, turtles, other dinosaurs, and turtles.
*****Positives, Things I Hope Will Continue To Improve****
Graphics & Gameplay
- Amazingly detailed dinosaur models.
- Beautifally animated dinosaur motions, clean, and clear sign of attention to detail.
- Incredibly engaging goal of survival while balancing curiousity, you truly feel like a baby dinosaur really experiencing the world for the first time, not knowing whether something will chase after you or is just curious.
- Seeing what is supposed to be a "scientifically accurate" depiction of the climate millions of years ago does wonders for the experience in the educational front and has a potential to bring interest to many new kids in a brand new way of learning.
- Breath taking graphics during the early morning when shadows and hard light help bring more dimension to the animals and plants.
- Cool looking growth mechanic that is stage based but is applied in a way that almost seems seamless, you could just barely see the dakotaraptors hair colours change from brown to black, to white, it was like it was growing in real time. Movements and animations continued to compliment that aspect of the game.
Overall Saurian is a remarkably fresh game that brings a great deal of satisfaction in its execution with downfalls that should be fixed as the game continues to progress. While the long wait seems unwarranted and somewhat weird seeing the current state of the game, it is somewhat forgiveable seeing the size of the team. I can only hope they continue to do the game the justice it deserves. Hopefully more competition sparks from the release of this game too.

Fallout, need I say more? Yes probably.
Fallout 4 is very dfferent from the other titles in this series. Huge weight has been put on crafting and building and managing settlements. Now if you played Fallout 3 and New Vegas and was happy with just the crafting part, the story and building your charecter, then this new layer might scare you off. My advice is to avoid having too many settlements, because suddenly all you are doing is fasttravel from one settlement to the next to manage their needs. My first playthrough I made the mistake of setting up shop at every possible location, with the result that I was suddenly not playing Fallout I was playing a sim and it was driving me nuts.  I have recently started my second playthrough and I have decided to keep only two settlements because I want to focus the many other aspects the game has to offer.
Many things have been added to this game, the whole game area is just huge, amazingly so. The story is new, you wake up and have to locate and find your son and in true Fallout fashion you come across different fractions and quests and side quests. So in an effort not to make this novel length I will make a pro/con list as I see it.
Pros
- Graffic is acceptable (get a whole of those Nexus mods to make it much better)
- The amount and variety of choice of companions
- Weapons crafting
- Amount of quests
- Two of DLCs are superb in their own right
- The length of the game
- The re-playablity is high
- Refreshing main storyline (though it has its faults)
Cons
- Settlements, that can easially ruin the game experince
- many quest are just fetch this and that quest, way to cheap and you're left feeling violated because they take up so much time in the game. For once I actually feel that Bethseda decided the easy rute to make a lengthy game. At some point you start to get irretated at the fact, that all the factions sends you out on fects missions that really does not have any substance to them, in reality a waste of time, but something you need to do you move forward with the main story.
- Radiostations are a bore. Suddenly you find yourself missing 3Dog. Again go to Nexus Mods and get help.
- Having to built a whole lot of stuff, if you had not put in the settlements it might have worked, but the two together simply is just TOO MUCH.
- Graffic is acceptable, having taking so long to make the game you would have thought that the graphics would have been more up to date.
I could add more I am sure. Even though I have some major issues with the game I still recommend it to players of RPGs and Fallout fans. But it sadly does not, in my eyes, come near the previous installments. I know that Bethseda wanted to do something new and different, but I am of the opinion that this whole settlement thing was the wrong way to go about it. And I sadly thing that the whole focus on settlements is the reason for the amount of fetch quest that would drive most people insane with boredom after the first 20 missions of its kind.
So if you can get it a good price, go buy the G.O.T.Y edition so that you get all the DLCs because they are by far some of the best in the whole game. I will not tell you to buy the game no matter what, but if you get a good deal like around the 20€ line then get it.

Bastion is a really wonderful game. The mechanics are enjoyable and well-balanced if perhaps a little repetitive. Although you'll likely find your favorite weapons and largely stick with them, Bastion has better weapon design than many games, and you'll appreciate the different properties of the weapons you use less often. Bastion also offers a wide number of options to tweak the difficulty through a systom of "idols" that can be activated or deactivated to gvie your enemies various bonuses. It's the storytelling and sound design that really made Bastion shine for me. The strange old-west style narration sold me in the very first level and provides a great impetus to keep making progress through the game. The story itself lags a bit in the middle, with minor characters having very little efffect beyond providing plot points, but the way it is told is great.
All in all I would definitely recommend Bastion for a short, self-contained action game with good design and storytelling.

qop is a simple little block sliding puzzle game. You can move your block up, down, left, or right as you try to reach the goal. There are two types of special blocks that add a little flavor to your movement. There is a block that moves you around a right angle and there are teleports.
There are 60 levels in the game. The early levels are rather easy, but they increase in difficulty a bit as you go along. While the levels never get too hard or complex I did still find myself having to plan out my moves in advance and having to restart a few times because I screwed up. It will get you thinking, but it won't strain your brain too much. It's great if you like casual puzzlers.
The background music is peaceful yet upbeat. I never found it to be obtrusive or annoying. (Though there is the option to turn it off if you do.) The movement felt pretty responsive and I encountered zero bugs during my playtime. The achievements were easy to get if that's your sort of thing. There aren't nearly as many as in the Zup games, but anyone who enjoyed actually playing those games will probably enjoy this one as well.
I consider myself a pretty competent puzzle solver and it took me a little over an hour to complete the game. While this is short and I found myself wanting more, I think this game is absolutely worth it at this price point.

Review: 4.5/5
Plot:
A tale of emotion versus reason.
Tales of Berseria's main theme is masterfully carried out throughout the main story. The side events function both as a hint to the main theme and to flesh out ToB's wonderfully written characters.
Characters:
Strong female protagonist done right. It's hard to say much without spoiling too much of the story, but I can say that the Tales' games charm lends itself well to the Berseria party. I hope, very much, for story DLC.
Gameplay:
Way better than zestiria. Controls are fluid, fast, and the battle system is responsive and fair. The dungeons do sometimes feel like a chore to slog through with the uninspired design and re-using of Zestiria's assets. Somehow despite the less-than-ideal dungeons, I kept coming back for more.
Content:
I felt that for the price, Berseria delivered value for my money and then some. I wish for more post game content.
