Compared to the XCOM game before it (excluding the Enemy Within expansion pack of course) its definitel more. More challenge, both in combat with enemies that have seemingly countless tricks and stick to cover like glue, but also a more complex world map. To add to all of that, the combat missions have the added bonus of being timed, so you're always on aa timer... and the mission map is also timed, counting down to something called the Avatar Project which is essentially a Game Over screen.
With all they've added... you know what they left out? Fun.  This game is not fun.  Challenging? Yes. Stressful? Yes. Tedious? Hell yes. Because of the constant timers and reliance on "stealth" for the first part of the missions, you find yourself doing the same thing, rushed by the same timers, again and again...
The stealth segments sound like a great idea, and their fun the first few times you play them. You have to set up an ambush and set most of the squad on overwatch and cause a shooting gallery massacre to 2 or 3 guys right away, to make up for the 2 to 1 odds in a small map where you can be surrounded and bum rushed with ease. To set these death traps up, you have to wander around the map carefully (But also quickly cuz... timers) avoiding the watch towers and turrets, and waiting for the patrols of troops to rander around, hopefully in a position you can surround with enough space to set most of your troops in overwatch, while one member takes the shot.
Sound fun? Do it a dozen times, then ask yourself if its fun again. After awhile it was tedious. The whole game was tedious. All the new enemy types, and added difficulty seems fun at first, more more more after all... but it was just more annoyances.
Take the Sectoids for example... a simple enemy in the first game, and they have returned in XCOM 2. Now they have more health, that need 2 or 3 hits to go down, can cause panick, disorientation from incredibly long range that ignores cover, and can also now raise fallen units as zombies... all this combined with they stick to cover like glue, only engaging themselves when no one else is left to carry on the fight... which means you have to priortize these jerks, or deal with their BS while they remain in near safety.... every time I fight these things, I'm annoyed... and their a very common enemy.
That really sums up the game well for me. Comparing the Sectoids from XCOM 1 to 2. Now with more health, sticks to cover, more psionic spells, more irritation. In the end, I didnt want to play anymore because everything about the game was frustrating or tedious. From the main map to the base building... I had very little fun.

This is, without a doubt, Telltale's masterpiece.  And this is coming from someone who doesn't like any other Telltale game except Sam & Max.  Compared to their other titles they absolutely nailed two critical elements needed for this title to succeed.  1) Choices have consequences.  Your decisions make tangible differences in the game.  It's not like, if you choose this, a character will be mad but the ultimate outcome is still the same.  While there is some of that, here you can actually cause characters to die where they may have lived.  Even the choices that may be "irrelevent" in strict sense, at least have emotional weight which leads to: 2) Characters.  The characters are very fleshed out and the dialogue options are superb.  Your emotional connection and understanding of the characters makes every dialogue option and hard choice an intimate experience as you challenge your ethics in this destroyed, dangerous world.
I think this is one of the quintessential titles of the genre and is a must-play. 9/10.

N.B. This is a review for both XCOM 2 and War of the Chosen.  The base game is great for lovers of turn-based tactics and this review is not meant to imply that the base game is without its merits.  However, I find the War of the Chosen expansion to be brilliant.
The modern incarnation of XCOM has been brilliant.  It's filled with difficult combat, awesomely over-the top weaponry, and difficult strategic choices in all aspects of the game.  The game constantly puts you in dilemnas where you have to choose between haste and caution.  The game also handles scaling difficulty brilliantly, steadily introducing new mechanics, enemies, weapons, and abilities.
The other thing the game does is regularly crush you in new, interesting, and painful ways.  You can miss an easy shot.  Your cover can be destroyed and an enemy can find a new flanking position.  An enemy that you've fought before might use an ability you'd never seen, catching you unawares.  And sometimes, soldiers have to die so that others may live.
War of the Chosen takes all of that and adds a lot of heart.  Where the base game is a steady drumbeat of harder and harder situations, War of the Chosen adds in a larger story, new allies who each have a different worldview, new persistent enemies who take pride in your suffering and have unique talents, and new mechanics that develop your soldiers' stories.  Where the base game was a great strategy game, the expansion is a great strategy game where you care about the characters.  Even Enemy Within never felt this full or emotional.
Take, for instance, the new bondmate mechanic.  Now, your soldiers can become friends and bond on the battlefield, giving you advantages to sending them on missions together.  For me that was my specialist, Hack and my ranger, Slash.  All of a sudden, I really care about these characters.  They're a deadly duo.  With minimal ingredients, I've created a small fiction that now comes up in the game.
Or the photobooth.  I've spent too much time using it, but now, my soldiers have propaganda that makes them persistent characters in the world.  Hack and Slash were my first pair, a symbol of resistance to the alien overlords.  And my small fiction becomes bigger.
The Chosen are new and interesting enemies with various strengths and weaknesses.  They taunt you in battle, pointing out the type of soldier who moved against them.  They taunt you on the home screen.  I can't tell you how satisfying it is to wipe the smile off their face.  Not only that, but they can also abduct these soldiers you've grown to care about.  You'd better believe I'm going after my troops.
The factions add troops with special abilities and backstories.  You can do various missions for them and they will help you in turn.  The one criticism I have for the game is I never really felt like the factions were at odds, despite significant backstory that talks about how much the factions hate each other.  It seems like a missed opportunity.  Then again, balancing how many different mechanics the game has is already very tough.  The faction mechanic further introduces covert missions, which feels right for a game where you're playing the resistance.
The game also introduces a zombie-like enemy called "The Lost."  These guys hunger for brains, yours or the enemy's.  It's particularly fun to draw The Lost towards the aliens and let them do the hard work while you maneuver into a better position.
The last little thing that I love about War of the Chosen is the addition of breakthroughs to research.  Before this tiny addition, I had gotten stuck in a rut of progression, unlocking things in a particular order.  Now, each playthrough gets different breakthroughs, changing how I go through the game.  It keeps the game fresh and personal.
Overall, this is my favorite strategy game to date.  It's robust, challenging, and heartfelt.  It also can kick your♥♥♥♥♥ but it makes those moments of improbable triumph feel even more amazing.

Copies its gameplay substantially from other "game development sim" games. Lacks a lot of "why can't I just do that options", e.g. you can delay a release but while it's delayed developers can't work on known bugs - you can only develop a patch to fix the bugs after you ship the game off to the publisher. Also, how the heck can I publish a patch so cheaply in 1980?? This is just one example - the interactions are not very carefully thought out.
Edit: Some commenters have pointed out that known bugs can be fixed in the QA room. But that's not what QA does - QA discovers bugs, it doesn't fix them, nor is there any reason it should be impossible to fix bugs on an unreleased game without a dedicated QA staff. I consider it a vindication, not a refutation, of the above point about things not being thought out.

I've waffled between giving this a good or bad review. It is certainly good at what it is: an open world FPS with RPG elements. It is a good game. But it isn't a good Fallout game. Let me explain.
There's very limited dialog choice, with your options usually being Yes (Good), Yes (Sarcastic) or No (Yes). You can choose between a few faction endings, but not much within those endings. There aren't many scripted quests compared to New Vegas. Plenty of procedurally-generated generic "Go to the place and kill one thing" quests, though. Until they get bugged and you can't do them anymore. This won't stop Preston from mentioning them. Send him to the settlement you visit the least.
Speaking of the settlements, the much-advertised settlement building feature is lackluster, especially on the non-hardcore modes. There is little point to them besides the creative outlet they provide. In hardcore mode they at least provide a save point and food/water as you traverse the wasteland.
The weapon crafting system is interesting but generic.
The whole game is interesting but generic. There is a little bit of lore building, but not enough for my tastes. A few terminal entries here and there is all you really get. Less terminal entries than F:NV or FO3, for sure.
This game is recommended for what it is.

That said, it's an Early Access game for a reason and I can see the potential everywhere I look. The graphics are gorgeous even if the saturation is a bit off at times (particularly at night), the soundtrack is great, the animals look stunningly realistic even if their AI needs work, and the attention to detail and scientific accuracy are nothing short of amazing, and the game in general is still quite enjoyable if you keep your expectations relatively low. If it continues to get the attention and support it truly deserves, then I have no doubt that it will eventually grow into something incredible. So by all means, purchase this game and support its development, just keep the words "Early Access" in mind.

Bastion is a really wonderful game. The mechanics are enjoyable and well-balanced if perhaps a little repetitive. Although you'll likely find your favorite weapons and largely stick with them, Bastion has better weapon design than many games, and you'll appreciate the different properties of the weapons you use less often. Bastion also offers a wide number of options to tweak the difficulty through a systom of "idols" that can be activated or deactivated to gvie your enemies various bonuses. It's the storytelling and sound design that really made Bastion shine for me. The strange old-west style narration sold me in the very first level and provides a great impetus to keep making progress through the game. The story itself lags a bit in the middle, with minor characters having very little efffect beyond providing plot points, but the way it is told is great.
All in all I would definitely recommend Bastion for a short, self-contained action game with good design and storytelling.

It's been a bit of time since I've played Serena, but I find this game always tends to haunt me. Ooh, we're punning already...
There is one thing that Serena did well that I want to start off with. Serena tells an amazing story in a short period of time. You're in a cabin trying to recall what happened to your beloved and once your memories are becoming a little more clear, you're not so sure if it's madness or clarity. Things are not what they seem. This is a basic writing scenario. The point is to take these things, elaborate on them, and make them very strong. Serena excells at this and gives you a twist ending that leaves you staring at the screen and (at least for me) scrambling for more answers because I just couldn't believe what I saw.
It's a story that starts off simply enough and leaves you to click around for your answers. Things start off sweet and loving and shortly they become a more twisted vision of those "love goggles" your character had on.
Serena is a simple point-and-click style game that is more of an interactive story than a heavy game. There are no heavy puzzles you need to solve other than progressing your mystery you're wrapped up in. You don't ever leave your cottage so there's no heavy exploration. This is not a walking sim. It's just you and your obsessive searching of your cottage and your grisly discoveries.
It really is a lovely game and for what it does, it does well. It is perfect in that respect. I love the attention to detail. There are slight changes made to your surroundings the further along you get. What was once beautiful suddenly becomes ugly and...well...disgusting.
Of course, there is the caveat that it's just really a short story that's interactive. It doesn't do much else. Some people have mentioned their irritation with the narrator. Considering the short length of the game, I'd suggest if you can't stomach him, you'd just have to turn off your volume. Personally I found him fine. Maybe a little dull and uninspired at some moments, but nothing awful enough that I'd have to turn him off. Sure, he talks a lot because you have to click on everything (no exaggeration) to progress the story, but I really didn't get that irritated. In fact I kept clicking on the bookshelf because I wanted more Lovecraft references read to me.
This isn't a game for everyone. There's no action. None. Zero. This is your best example of "a free game to kill an hour or less". It's also something I'd probably suggest to people who are trying their hand at horror writing just to see an example of how to do slow reveals. This is a great learning piece of material as opposed to something that's perfect gaming-wise.
I loved this more as a reader than I did as a gamer. It's simple and it's just plain nice. Though admittedly, if someone is getting into horror games, this is probably the best thing you could offer them to get their feet wet before introducing them to more combat oriented games.
Serena is like an ex I compare other games to. Shamelessly I admit this.

Mad Games Tycoon suffers from a major lack of feedback.  Unfortunately in the beginning there isn't much of an indication of what you're doing wrong.  Worst yet, when your game does somehow succeed, there's no real indication of why it did well either.
Let's start off with what this game did right.
The progression of building your business is really there.  For example: Upon your third year you can make a marketing department or when you have enough fans you'll need Customer support to continue to make them happy.  Once you have enough money you can expand to a larger building site and create break rooms and larger toilet facilities for your staff.
Developing your own game engine.  This really helps out on the profits.  This also gives you a good feeling of what technology is out there and what other engines you are competing against.
Researching is extremely important.  It isn't just about developing games and engines, it is also about researching what topics and genre's and components are out there as well.  If you don't keep your research up, you will certainly fail!
Different staff are available at all times.  There are even such "legendary" workers that you can hire such as Sid Maier (misspelled on purpose)
Now for the reasons for not recommending this game:
There really isn't much feedback at all to why your game did well or badly.  I've made so many consecutive worst game of the year's that I simply feel extremely frustrated rather than having fun.   You would think that the higher the numbers the better right?? Nope.  What about the stars next to the numbers??  Nope.  I still don't understand why one game fails and another succeeds!!
The game does an extremely poor job of explaining all of the features once you do become a bit more successful.  I suppose it's a bit self explanatory, but if you're not ready to trial and error you'll never know it was there.
I will state here that it's not like I didn't try to understand this game, I tried looking up what other people has done.  I've asked my buddy who purchased this game during beta.  Yes, once in a while I hit a beauty and I do well but most everything I've tried blows up in my face. I've even tried to avoid creating games until the trends lineup and then trying with the proper engine and legendary workers.. and my game STILL falls flat on it's face.... AND I DON'T KNOW WHY!!!!
Mad Games Tycoon? More like driving you mad while making games tycoon.

As a fan of sim & tycoon games, I'm very glad I supported this Early Access game.  It provides a great mix of simulating some small details as well as the big picture of the game development industry. It ranges from picking physical game package contents to buying out other game developers and publishing their games. I find that type of end-game stuff to be more satisfying than comparable games. They've also added specific development departments/studios like for testing (gameplay) and audio, which for a price help boost certain aspects of the games being developed.
The game difficulties are true to their names, and I appreciate that genre-specific tips earned with dev time don't just give away precise levels for what it takes to make the best games. The trial-and-error nature exists, but the Game Reports help indicate when certain things like casual vs core gamer balance are just right, and trending topic & genre can help. Even if you get all the sliders right, its still really tough to get 100% on a game - As I've only done it once - On Easy.  More elaborate MMO and F2P mechanics have to be handled different than retail games.  The devs addressed all the bug reports I've provided during Early Access, and I like the choice community-fed ideas that have been put into the game.

I highly recommend waiting before you purchase this game. I also want to point out that a lot of the hypey reviews were posted merely minutes after this game was put on store. Don't trust the hype.
The core content during this stage is eating, drinking, "hunting" and growing up as a small carnivorous raptor on single player. The 'secondary level' content is interacting with the animals in the world around you, and obversing them.
Eating is simple, even in the worst of times where there was nothing to scavenge a little lizard would scurry out of the bush and provide enough to keep me going for while. This was by far the most enjoyable part of the game especially when you're just a little youngling look for scraps. Overall though, once you eat, there is little to nothing left to do.
Drinking is a breeze. Despite the small amount of hazards in the marsh areas including aligators and extra foot traffic from all kinds of dinos... once you've drank you don't have too for a long period of time. So once it's done, just like with hunger, there is nothing to do except sit around and wait. Maybe roam.
Hunting is by far the worst aspect of this game at the moment, which is unforunate considering how much of a core element in plays in the games overall enjoyment. Apart from the small lizard, you can hunt almost anything you find. APPARENTLY. In my experience, the aligators were impossible to kill (and could kill you in one bite while out of water). Other creatures weren't only impossible to kill from time to time, but almost immediately killed ME with one bite. In other words, if the animals weren't outright immune to my damage, only some of the hits worked, and the ones that did dealt almost no damage... but for them, I was merely a one or two hit kill even while I was an adult. As an attempt at faining content, this game is constantly trying to kill you so you're forced to restart.
Growing up is enjoyable and right now genuinely the only thing 'to do' in this games current state. Although once you become an adult, there is little drive to play any more. All attempts at hunting will result in instant death or extremely buggy AI ruins the experience. I'd say only 1/6th of the dinosaurs in this world are opperating properly, and even then its only a short amount of time till they too end up bugging out. I also bring up AI because it affects the 'parenting system'. Which in of itself isn't actually a system at the moment. Rather, the adult AI just doesn't hunt you. In reality, you're just following a buggy AI trying to scrap up its kills for food or eat its body once it's died. There is no interaction, let alone actual 'system' in place for parenting at the moment. It's a thinly veiled way of making it seem like you have parents, when its in fact just AI you spawned next too, perhaps for early food.
All of that being said, the animal interaction is nul. It's just simply not in the game at the moment. Generally all AI have the same behaviour, just different 'kill / ignore' parameters. Which are buggy as well. Even the camera you're playing with is buggy and extremely difficult to work with. If your graphic settings aren't on high then nighttime is a nightmare. Everything turns into a mess of green and it becomes completely impossible to move around in the world let alone distinguish plant from empty air. After saving a 4 hour long save file every time I try to spawn in Pachy swarm and kill me, even though they weren't there when I saved. It's also worth mentioning that just having this game loaded makes my computer constantly nonresponsive, even when parked in the main menu. And yeah... as the loading screen warns about... the game WILL crash within 2 hours or so... So once you begin playing, it completely becomes obvious as to why there were delays. This game was not ready to be shipped, and is absolutely walking the borderline on it being an 'actual' game.
Lets hope we see some fast improvements, and good content in the future.

Unlike some people I see complaining about the game being in a "lack of content state" as of right now, I knew that not all 3 years were spent working on assets specifically for EA launch and putting them into the belt line of production....But rather to create assets as they saw fit in the growing ecosystem. Those 3 years were divided up into a few things. 1.Research. 2.Artwork/Concept designs. 3.Figuring out what will and what will not be in the game, deciding if it felt in the range of a "game". 4.Modeling. 5.Programing. 6.Animation.7.Music/Sounds. Yes, I'm well aware that not all of those things are done by the sae person, they have a decently sized staff team for an Indie game, and not all of those were going on at once. To furter that point, adding creatures/features takes longer than you might origionally think, by doing moding, animations, skin ideas, using those skin ideas, texturing, vocalizations, A.I, stats, and whatever "unique" feature said animal would have. Side note, about the people complaining about the lag/unoptimization, I seriouslly hope you knew this was a brand new EA game, and not a 100% full release. Ark is leaving EA soon, and it's still extremely unoptimized. Overall, this game is amazing/fun as it is right now, and yeah, sure, there's bugs here and there, and teh occasional crash too, but yah know what...that's what EA games are known for, and I'm ok with that <3 .I hope you guys enjoy this game as much as I do, and soak in all of the potentional it has for the future! After finding this on Arvalis's art account, I was rather excited. I had adored dinosaurs when I was a kid, but sadly no game lived up to my expectations. This is the best dinosaur simulator I have played despite its many flaws as of now, although most are either extremely hard to control mobile games on janked up sci-fi crossovers.
I would not buy it if you are looking for extremely gripping and fulfilling gameplay or a bug free experience right from the get-go. There are some bugs (surprisingly few for pre-Alpha), and quite a lot of the game is empty (spaces for additional dino species I wonder? 6_6). As well as this, the AI isn't extremely intelligent. It's better than what you would get from ARK, but still. Some dinosaurs will get locked into the face-to-face bite contest (particularly rexes), and I saw a rex throwing a triceratops up into the air at one point through glitches and some dinosaurs just flat out walk into trees.
The crocodile (I.... forgot what it was called) seems to have the best AI so far. It lurks in the water and quickly goes toward any dinosaur that is unfortunate enough to come to the edge. It also does some hefty damage if it gets you from the front, so be prepared to run. Note: Do NOT use RPR on these guys, they can hit you even if you're on its back. This will kill you instantly.
Pachys seem to like coming after me, and they tend to stick in groups if others are in the area. Triceratops seem to be solitary despite the females supposedly being in groups. I expect this will be fixed in the future. Rexes and Dakotas only attack me when they are hungry, a refreshing change from the perpetually rampaging ones from ARK and a realistic one at that.
This is more of a note to the devs because I'm not sure where the bug report is.
-Killing something with RPR causes you to clip below the ground into the water underneath.
-Killing something with RPR whilst in the water causes you to endlessly sail away, and nothing stops you. You clip through trees, the ground, everything.
Pros
-A realistic looking simulator with a nicely sized world.
-Huge potential
-Some AI works as intended
-Oh thank Jeebus the dinosaurs have feathers
-A couple of hours of fun before it becomes more of a bug test
-Most bugs are rather humourous
-I actually came across Dakotaraptors of differing age groups, which was a pleasant surprise
Cons
-After a while it does get rather monotonous
-Little content, however, as the game is updated I expect this to become less of an issue
-Game looks rather terrible at night
-RPR is finicky, and has quite a few bugs
-Scent mechanic is borked
If you are willing to follow the game and help the devs weed out bugs then I would recommend it. If not, I would wait.
Oh, and I am neutral on this game for the most part, I just want to see it be supported and become much better than it is, which I believe will happen with time and the help of the community. In other words, I am hopeful. Good on you Urvogel.

This game is a piece of history. Upon release, Valve's debut title was regarded as one of the greatest FPS games of all time, and that claim definitely still stands today. The game tells its story in a way only a video game can, by using the actual game and its scenery to progress the plot. Almost never taking away control from the player, and never using cutscenes. The plot itself is pretty basic, science experiment goes wrong, you have to escape, the government tries to cover it up. But it's the presentation that really makes the game's plot shine. Speaking of presentation, Half-Life's visuals haven't aged well, even with the HD models included with Blue Shift. Oftentimes the game's models blend in with background scenery making it hard to tell what you can interact with, but this is hardly an issue. Gunplay is another thing that hasn't aged well, as a lot of the guns don't really have much impact with the absence of ragdoll physics, and it's pretty clunky in general. My last complaint with this game is the platforming segments. I don't know who came up with the whole crouch jump thing, (not the jetpack, just crouching mid-jump to get to higher places) but it seems kind of unnecessary. Also, Xen's platforming segments were kind of a drag, and kind of took away from the flow of the game. This game shines in atmosphere, storytelling, and pacing, but fails in combat, and some of the late-game segments. 8.8/10

This game is breathtaking. It's simply amazing, and without this game, there would be NO Steam. The enemies are really varied and unique. Houndeyes are the pack hunting weak enemies that can emit soundwaves that vary in difference depending on the pack size, Vortigaunts are the Intelligent but weak goons with electricity powers that are powerful in squads, Alien Grunts are the powerful and tanky brutes that can pummel a soldier through a wall and are usually the backbone of the Xenians, the Headcrabs are the annoying weak pests that can manipulate you into danger, Headcrab Zombies are dumb and slow yet powerful Melee experts, HECU Marines are the extremely Intelligent and common bullet sponges that can absolutely DESTROY you in squads, especially with a Tank, Ichthyosaurs are the strong water enemies that can take a chunk out of your health, Leeches are pests that can put you in danger if on low health similar to headcrabs, Alien controllers are the Miscellaneous but terrifying enemy that can severely wound you, and there are many more but I can't explain them all in one review. The Weapons all serve important purposes, the 9MM Is your accurate and deadly pistol, the Crowbar is your trusty Melee weapon that is useful for clearing out objects and winning a close combat encounter, the MP5 is an automatic weapon that is great for clearing out waves, the Shotgun is a powerful weapon that is extremely powerful at close ranges, the Revolver is your backup weapon that can save you if used right and is a weakness of many enemies, and there are alot more guns, same with the enemies. The designs on the levels are so unique and have great ideas, like the shark cage level with the Ichthyosaurs or the amazing Xen levels with beautiful atmospheres. I also noticed some negative comments on this awesome game. Sure, the graphics aren't good and it looks unrealistic, but I strongly disagree with those people who say Black Mesa is better. The reason we still play this is because of those awesome little details Valve added in, they put all their blood and sweat into making even the TINIEST details in here. But in all seriousness, this game is GREAT, put it on your wishlist because this is a MUST BUY.

I've spent over 500 hours in this game. 260+ hours were on one play-through in the hardcore mode. In that run, I finished the game plus DLCs, got every settlement to maximum population with at least 100 defense, and have generally done about everything.
I've waffled between giving this a good or bad review. It is certainly good at what it is: an open world FPS with RPG elements. It is a good game. But it isn't a good Fallout game. Let me explain.
There's very limited dialog choice, with your options usually being Yes (Good), Yes (Sarcastic) or No (Yes). You can choose between a few faction endings, but not much within those endings. There aren't many scripted quests compared to New Vegas. Plenty of procedurally-generated generic "Go to the place and kill one thing" quests, though. Until they get bugged and you can't do them anymore. This won't stop Preston from mentioning them. Send him to the settlement you visit the least.
Speaking of the settlements, the much-advertised settlement building feature is lackluster, especially on the non-hardcore modes. There is little point to them besides the creative outlet they provide. In hardcore mode they at least provide a save point and food/water as you traverse the wasteland.
The weapon crafting system is interesting but generic.
The whole game is interesting but generic. There is a little bit of lore building, but not enough for my tastes. A few terminal entries here and there is all you really get. Less terminal entries than F:NV or FO3, for sure.
This game is recommended for what it is.

Bastion is one of the best games I have ever had the pleasure of playing.
The above statement will probably adorn the majority of the reviews of this game, and for good reason; it really is that good!
For starters; the gameplay and weapons, Bastion is essentially a story driven action RPG.  It offers a large variety of different weapons whith which to disptach the mariad of foes who will opposes you.  Each type of weapon offers a very different esperience when it comes to combat; for example you have the Cael Hammer, a hefty hard hitting meele weapon, and on the opposite side of the meele spectrum you have the Hunter's Machete, a quick and agile blade that when the attack butto is held for a short amont of time can be thrown at your oppnents. Now afterthat dont go thinking that Bastion is a close quarters only affair, as the game quickly introduces weapons whith long range capabilities like the Breaker's Bow, a strong bow with a fairly slow draw time, also, my personal favorite ranged weapon is the Scrap Musket, a shotgun like weapon that is incredibly effective at short range, and features a wide spread shot.
Next up is possibly the best thing Bastion has going for it; the presentation.  Bastions artwork is done in a pseudo-watercolour style that looks absolultly beautiful.  Each and every one of the environments are painstakeinly detailed down to the most minute details.  The levels range from psychotropic jungles to old abandoned scrapyards, and as I mentioned they are all exquisite! The next bit of presentation that should not be forgotten is the phenomenal soundtrack composed by the wonderful Darren Korb.  Every single trak inthe game is wonderful and memorable, I even caught myself bobbing my head and humming along to the catchy as heck battle theme.  Bastion's soundtrack is the first OST that I simply HAD to buy,an dit was a purchase that I know I will not regret.
Finally I want to touch upon the story, which is (big surprise) top notch!  The entire game it narrated by a gravelly voiced old man named Rusk, voiced by Logan Cunningham. One of the coollest things about it is that the narratiion is dynamic, as in the fine people at Supergiant Games had Mr. Cunningham record thousands of lines of dialogue to fit into nearly every context.  I'd rather not discuss the story in too much depth as I would hat to ruin it for anybody, but here's a basic rundown: you play as a nameless young man referred to only as "The Kid" who wakes up in the ruins of a destroyed wall and makes his way towards the Bastion, "Where everybody agreed to go incase of Calamity". After collecting a Core he makes he arrives at the Bastion and Rusk informs him that he must collect more Cores in order to restore Caelondia to it's former glory.
Overall I recommend this game to anybody who has working fingers and/or eyeballs. Of course I'm ancxiously awaiting the 2014 release of Supergiant's opcoming Transistor (featuring the talents of Logan Cunningham and Darren Korb!!)

I had a tremendous amount of fun playing sleeping dogs. It's a really creative chapter in the third person sandbox genre. Think grand theft auto with a healthy dose of chinese culture and kung-fu.
Gameplay

The cars and motorcycles handle well and are generally very fun to drive around the richly designed at populated game world.
Story
The story is where Sleeping Dogs really shines, I dont' want to spoil anything but I was fully enthralled in the story as I was playing it and found myself attached to several of the main characters. There are enough twists and turns in the plot to keep the game fresh well into double-digit hours of play.
Final Word:
This game is worth your money if you're a fan of the genre or chinese culture. It represents a refreshing departure into an infrequently explored culture and the story and action-oriented game play will keep your playing for hours.

Here are my spoiler-free pros and cons as well as my opinion on the censored scene and the Denuvo controversy after playing a good portion of the game:
Pros:
1. The combat is fun, especially after the AI bug has been fixed. The arte tree in previous titles is no longer there and is instead replaced with a much more customisable arte tree allowing you to place your artes where ever you want.
2. The game is optimised really well, so well that even potatoes have been able to play it well (even without the highly recommended TBFix mod by Kaldaien).
3. The equipment system is much more engaging  and much less complicated than Zestiria's allowing you to keep skills from a piece of equipment after mastering it by earning grade from battles.
4. The characters are great and the dark-themed story is a refreshing change from previous titles, the skits are also entertaining as always.
5. The graphics look nice.
Cons:
1. I personally use controllers for PC Tales of games but from what I've seen the keyboard and mouse controls in Tales of Berseria look rather confusing, especially the battle controls. The menu has also been known to be rather broken when using keyboard and mouse so I highly recommend that you use an Xbox 360/One controller or if you want to use a PS3/4 controller you can do so with Kaldaien's button replacement mod.
About the censored scene and Denuvo:
The censored scene in Berseria has no effect on the rest of the game what so ever, they changed it a bit so that ESRB wouldn't give it the M rating, while Valve doesn't mind this too much they also had Sony and PSN to worry about but don't worry, the scene still has the same outcome so it doesn't change the story.
If you look on the Berseria dscussions page people have been whining about Denuvo and how it causes problems. This is not the case, if you are online all the time you won't even notice it there. The stories about it damaging people's hard drives are complete lies and should just be ignored. I should also mention that Denuvo prevents piracy, not it's modding capability so if you want to use texture mods go ahead, Kaldaien''s TBFix mod has recently improved the support of texture mods so get this before you decide to mod the game.
My final verdict is 4.5/5... It's not perfect but it's still a great game nonetheless and I say it's worth it's full price.

You can't save, change the music, change the voices, get rid of subtitles, nothing. So you'll need to set aside half an hour or an hour to play this game, but that's not too bad at all (and the little quirks like the stances of the hand will be easy to figure out if you just experiment a little).
I would recommend trying on your own to figure out the game for 30 minutes, and then (or if you get horribly stuck before that), look up a spoiler free guide. Don't use them to breeze through the game, please. It's a quick game, it's well done, and it deserves your time.

Xcom 2 is a fantastic game and one of my favorite games of all time. between the genre-making unique gameplay and the awesome ayy designs, it just srikes me as an amazing game.
***GAMEPLAY***
Xcom 2 is divided into two states, A base building section and a tactics section. the main gameplay is the tactics section.
*TACTICS*
the main part of this game feels very much like a chess game, and relies heavily on your ability to think ahead of the enemy. as well as common sense.  if your guys are in the wrong place at the wrong time it'll end up being more violent than a saw movie. on the other hand if your guys are placed in just the right way, and the ayys aren't moving a whole lot, you can set up an awesome overwatch ambush and it's seriously one of the most satisfying moments in gaming for me.
you have a certain amount of soldiers on the battlefield at a single time. they have two actions that can be taken up by various things, such as: moving, shooting (which always ends a soldier's turn), throwing a grenade (which does less damage but has a 100% chance of hitting and always ends a soldier's turn), running, (which always ends a soldier's turn),
a few class specific abilities and a few moves used by the sci operatives.
moving is grid-based and utilizes a cover system, which depending on the object in front of the soldier, can give you low or high cover. Which thows off an ayy's aim either a little or a lot, respectivley. But be careful, as most ayys can also use cover to the same effectiveness as your soldiers. using cover also grants the ability to have enemies get flanking shots on you from a side not protected by cover, which often do more damage. you can also get flanking shots on ayys in cover to the same effect.
taking the stealthier approach is also available, where your soldiers can get the jump on the ayys by staying out of their sight. If you put multiple soldiers in overwatch, you can set up massive overwatch ambushes. These can and will often wipe out whole squads in the early game. My only gripe about the stealth, or "concealment" system is that alien squads get bigger over time and they start becoming less effective.
I feel like this has been said before but, this game is very RNG heavy. missing 60% shots will happen often. And if you have below a 90% hit chance with your melee guy, don't even bother with it.
this has also been said before, but this game is timed. 60% of missions have a certain amount of turns before you flat out lose. even for missions that don't make sense at all. as in, "your soldiers must gather a box and return it to the ship before it detonates itself." umm, why is the box detonating at all? the ayys don't know i'm here yet. so they just have it rigged to explode for no reason? the timers still tick down duing stealth.
speaking of timers, the whole game is timed. the "avatar project" is a doom meter that's constantly ticking up at all times. let the bar fill completely, and you lose the game. this never really becomes that much of a problem, seeing as you can always delay it longer, but it's very annoying. "oh let me drop everything and do this mission or i'll lose the game in 30 minutes" is never a thought you want your players to be thinking, devs.
also, every month you'll unlock a new cool ayy to fight. exept chryssalyds. I don't think they're cool. Just annoying.
*BASE BUILDING*
The other part of the game is about managing your power, crew, soldiers, and research. you can clear out rooms caved-in rooms with engineers, and make research go faster with scientists. both available at the HQ and missions. In cleared-out rooms of your ship, you can build rooms with special effects. a lab will make research quicker, a proving grounds is essential for making cool armors and grenades, a psi lab trains psi operatives, a GTS will allow you to re-train soldiers to get different classes, an advanced warfare center will heal your soldiers faster, a shadow chamber is essential for story things and detects enemies in missions,  and there's a couple of other rooms I didn't bother with.
research unlocks new items, and engineering builds them.
Over time you'll get very attached to your soldiers. you can change thier names, armor colors, hair styles and much more. you'll actually be very suprised at how fun it is to play virtual barbie with your most well-trained and badass soldier. also this game has permadeath. your soldiers WILL die. and it'll make you sad.
you can speed up time, travel to different places, scan for missions and buy things from the geoscape.
***STORY***
"Story in a video game is like story in a porn movie. It's expected to be there, but it's not that important."
-John Remero, co-creator of DOOM
while I don't always agree with this quote, it's definitley true here. The story to XCOM 2 is: "Aliens have taken over and you gotta stop them, cause you're the chosen one." oh yeah, I haven't played 38 other games with THAT plot. this game could have a story that consits of a couple of guys flying around and shooting very ugly police, and it wouldn't affect the game much.
***GRAPHICS***
they're pretty good.
***FINAL THOUGHTS***
it's pretty good.
***PROS AND CONS***
*PROS*
-great gameplay
-great graphics
-great voice acting
-great aliens
-great music
-great grates
-great snektits
*CONS*

-RNGsus doesn't like you

TL;DR: At it's core, this is a more fleshed out Game Dev Tycoon.  Unfortunately, there are a lot of small annoyances born from sloppy design that before long start to add up.  Unless you have a lot of patience, it isn't worthwhile in its present state.  Only recommended if it's on sale, or if a patch cleans things up.
I'm writing this review because, honestly, I like this game.  At the same time, though, I can't really recommend it, because of a lot of small issues that add up to a few big ones.
This game is, at its heart, a combination of Game Dev Tycoon and Theme Hospital.  It's different enough from the former that things will go very badly for you if you try to use any prior experience.  The latter was what initially drew me to the game, but unfortunately the implimentation leaves a lot to be desired.  In fact, that's where the first big problems start to show up.
Much like in Theme Hospital, the player has to create several specific rooms, each with their own unique function.  These must be furnished with a number of items, including generic work stations, cabinets, trash cans, and so on and so forth.  Rooms can only be rectangular, and must have a non-blocked door, but not next to a corner.  This seems like a really, really minor thing, except that it inevitably leads to having to Tetris rooms, sliding them around with the 'move' function until you finally manage to squeeze everything together.
The second nuisance is the variety of things rooms require for furnishing.  Having a lot of things you can add based on your tastes is a good thing.  Having a lot of things you HAVE to add, lest you incur a penalty until you find a way to squeeze them into the already-cramped space, is just annoying.
The biggest offender is the First Aid stations: you need one of these in every room people are going to frequent, lest they randomly become 'injured' and unable to work for an obnoxiously long span of time.  And even if you've added them to every room, sometimes they just don't work; having to delay a release for a month while you wait for the one specialist you need to recover from a random injury gets old quickly.
But the thing that REALLY bugs me is that, if characters don't have a clear path from place to place, they'll just teleport there.  This isn't a bug, there's an animation for it.  This severely undercuts the need to try to be ergonomic, and considering the ratio of space to crap is already a problem, it quickly becomes easier to just stop caring.  At which point a good chunk of the game becomes a tedious distraction, rather than something fun and interesting.
The 'Game Dev Tycoon' half of the game fares better, but still has its share of annoying issues.  The biggest of these is that the game is somewhat player-hostile.  The tutorial doesn't explain the stats, failing to intuit what the sliders have to be set to will result in games that fail to make back their development cost, and relevant information is frequently stuck in sub-menus far away from where it might be relevant.
Game Reports are an excellent example of this: for starters, you're unlikely to even be able to get them before Year 3, at which point you'd have to already know a good chunk of what they tell you.  Before that, all you'll get is cryptic reviews and the rare email from fans telling you that one of the sliders was too far in one direction or another.
Once you've managed to unlock the QA room - WHY they're tied to the QA room instead of the Reaserch Room I cannot begin to fathom - you have to have one or more developers tie themselves up with writing them.  The menu for selecting which games to get reports from is buggy; there is no button to start the queue, the only way I could get it to start required checking off reports until the menu closed itself and the devs started writing them.  While Game Reports are being written, you can't look at existing Game Reports unless you build a second office, or start development on a new game.
The entire interface feels kludgy: the Bank icon appears in SOME menus when making selections that have an associated cost, but not others; the escape key does different things depending on where in the menu system you happen to be; information alternates between being readily available and hidden behind several layers of menus; the stats don't have tool-tips, but the engine add-ons do; you get a little picture of your in-game avatar at the start of a new game, but you have no means of customizing it at all, not even the option of picking from among the various pre-fabs that will make up your employees; vital explanations for what things actually MEAN are nowhere to be found; the game remembers slider positions from the last game you made of ANY genre, so you have to either write down their previous positions or avoid making more than one type of game; and so on, and so on.  This feels like an Early Access title that got released six months too early.
And the most frustrating thing of all is that past all of the irritation and clutter, a solid game is THIS close to happening.  There is a much greater importance on employee management, and it's a ton of fun to create developer teams for several genres.  But more often than not a parade of things will get in the way, and before long the slog through the sloppy interface and the constant micromanagement of trashcan-radiator-shelf-desk-photocopier arrangments drag the experience down, until it isn't worth it anymore.

I was very dissapointed in this Tonguc Bodur game. I am a fan of many of their games, but this one is just.... dull.
First of all, exploration is very limited. When you emerge from the starting location, you see the mountains and lake reaching out in front of you and you want to go there and explore it, but the "path through" funnels you throught steep cliffs and ravines, and quickly turns you into the direction it wants you to go. Other than the mountains rising up on either side of you so you can't really explore much except the grass in front of you, there are invisible walls that stop you getting to the lakes and things, which feels very lazy and restrictive.
A second negative point is how repetitive the first chapter is. You wak and walk and walk through the path that funnels you between these really steep cliffs so you can't see any landscape, and each turn in the path feels just like the one before. Nothing new to see, nothing engaging in the landscape. They could have done with putting more animals in (like the deer and white horse - there are two encounters and that's it) or opening up the mountains for more viewpoints. It honestly feels like you're just trundling through the heathers past the redwoods. There feels very little purpose other than getting you from A to B when the whole point of a walking simulator is to immerse you in the landscape as the story unfolds.
As for the story, I was underwhelmed and not interested. The story does not drop in enough hints to "something more" that keep you engaged. The story chunks are very short and don't give you enough or hint at enough to spur you on into reaching the next story chunk. I didn't feel engaged enough to walk to the very end of the level. In fact, I had enough and put it down.
Tl;dr: This is a very underwhelming walking simulator. It's restrictive and unengaging, and I think more could have been done to emmerse you into the world of The Hunting God.

As a veritable connoisseur of Tonguc Bodur games, I must say that The Hunting God is among his best works. That is not to say that I would recommend it to anyone, but it is a noticeable improvement upon his previous titles. In The Hunting God, you play as some Irish deity who walks around pretty landscapes talking to himself occasionally in nonsensical voiceovers and very occasionally clicking on a couple of stock assets to proceed. The story is basically about a god whose realm gets besieged by werewolves and then saved by a magic woman. So far, all of this is pretty standard fare for a TB production—however, there are some dynamic new changes to this game that make it stand out from the rest of Mr. Bodur’s library. Firstly, a big difference between the Drizzlepath, Nephise, and Bottle games and THG is that THG has a male narrator. Yes, Bottle’s protagonist was male, but his two lines were both Easter eggs, if we are being frank. The Hunting God’s narrator and protagonist is a male character. You can’t understand anything he says due to the writer’s affinity for flipping to a random thesaurus page and scrawling the first word they see, plus quite a lot of Gaelic (?), and the voice actor is too busy broguing to emote, but still. The second big unique factor in this game is that there’s no cave section. I’m fairly certain that ALL TB games except this one has a cave that you walk through. Thirdly, THG has separate chapters, which none of his other games have. This means there are varied environments, varied music, and most importantly the game autosaves after every chapter. I was particularly relieved to find this out when, after playing the first level, I was literally falling asleep while playing (the game is just that exciting). It was nice not to lose all my progress. TB always includes a save feature asset in his games, since he always credits it, so I’m glad he’s finally figured out how to use it. Fourth but not last, The Hunting God is the first Tonguc game with cutscenes. There’s no, like, animation in them or anything, or dialogue, or events, but they’re still honest-to-god cutscenes, and I was astounded to see them. Though this game has 3.25 chapters, it is more or less congruous with other TB titles in taking “a little while” to beat. My playtime represents one complete playthough with minimal dawdling (I only goofed around enough to find the hidden texts, which are not well hidden at all), and I did not return to the final level to see the alternate ending. For reference, in case I do wind up doing the last level again, that’s 70 minutes. However, the brevity is always excusable in these titles because there’s so little going on that you get bored as it is*. Now, I imagine that you will see some reviews about this game raving about its beautiful graphics. Let me break that down for you. I’m almost certain that every single post-processing and lighting effect ever produced for the Unreal Engine is turned up to turbo in THG. The skybox assets are genuinely pretty. He even downloaded a few stock texture packs to intersperse around the maps. However, what bugs me when people talk about how nice the graphics are in these games is that it’s the current year and yet TB still cannot be bothered to cover up repeating ground textures. He could just use textures broad enough that you wouldn’t notice, or include something, ANYTHING, to draw your eye away from the immersion-destroying diamond pattern of the path, but he doesn’t. The only other notable thing to discuss regarding this game is the poems that appear twice in each level. This is one aspect that is common to all TB walking simulators, which is to say that they are not very good. It is clear that all six poems writhe to contort themselves into rhyming iambic pentameter, like so much fat into a girdle, but it just doesn’t work, and in some lines they flat-out give up. There is nothing sonically pleasing about the words or their placement, no wordplay, and nothing about the verse seems even remotely organic. Nor do the poems build up to anything. One is about a queen who’s a tough queen, one’s about the theft of a salmon of knowledge, and I can’t even remember the others. Although I have enjoyed some walking simulators (and even others by the same developer, notably Nephise Begins..) I have not enjoyed my brief time spent with The Hunting God. A lot of my gripes with the game are personal preference (most notably in how the narrative is delivered..) however its lack of a traditional save function and its artificial feeling world are primarily what have put me off of bothering to experience more of the game.
The Hunting God is a relaxing, average Walking Simulator in which the player slowly plods along while listening to the narrator / player character regale them with a plethora of background "story" which came off more as overblown mysticism to me than anything interesting or engaging. I prefer when a walking simulator is more left to the player's interpretation with sparse dialog (if any) than having a narrator constantly blabbing through walls of text about some obscure subject. This may craft background story to a degree and can add to the immersion of the player here and there, but at times it comes off as trying too hard (to me) to seem mystical or exotic when it's so unyielding and bashed over the player's head than just letting the game be as-is, with moments of silence, and having the player's interest emerge naturally as they explore the unknown environments.
The Hunting God isn't an ugly game per se, but it is probably one of the least visually impressive of the genre that I have played. This is especially puzzling as the Nephise series (and even Drizzlepath: Genie) from the same developer seem to be quite polished. The Hunting God's washed out, foggy initial environment with its oddly-arranged trees and boulders fails to impress and doesn't feel organic or "real" (whereas Nephise excels at doing this within the first few seconds of playing...) This may change as the environments / time of day change in the game, but having not progressed far enough to trigger a checkpoint at the next chapter I find the idea of shuffling along through the same areas hearing the same dialog seeing the same sights just in the hope of activating an autosave unappealing. Why do walking simulators almost exclusively lack a "save anywhere" option??? The exclusion of a player-determined save has put me off of other titles in this genre before and their absence here is no different. Say a player progresses or wanders around for 20 minutes before having to go do something else but hasn't progressed to whatever arbitrary area triggers the checkpoint, well, if you quit then have fun booting the game up to see you're starting from the beginning and doing the same thing again. The rationale of "the game is intended to be completed in a short amount of time" is a poor excuse for the feature being absent.
The Hunting God does present some unique elements to the walking simulator genre, including a section where you need to sneak up on a slumbering dragon and avoid stepping on branches that will snap and wake it up (which sounds more exciting than it is, you're simply shown a picture of a paw stepping on a broken branch and then restart the area) and at times I found myself engaged with what was being presented (as light breaks between the trees and enjoying the music, etc..) however the vague, frequent rambling from the narrator about things I could care less about, as well as its artificial-feeling world failed to immerse me into much of what it was presenting.

The Hunting God is the seventh and most recent walking simulator crafted by Tonguç Bodur, who has shown an ability to craft wonderful and brief experiences that allow you to wander through interesting stories without the need to commit to a several days long stay. As with Tonguç’s past games, The Hunting God is meant to be enjoyed in a single sitting. What I found while playing this game was a beautiful experience with an interesting story and stellar design. So, what about specifics? Well, here you go:
According to the Steam product page, The Hunting God is described as “a short walking simulator in which you play as Nodens the hunting god and listen to what he has been through accompanied by a white wolf named Draiochta.”
While this is quite apt, it really only scratches the surface of the telling such as it is. The story for this game was written by Simon Kolbe Strange and Stephanie Muscari, and features a jaunt through folklore and seems to specifically blend aspects of both the the Gaelic/Celtic Ulster Cycle (or Red Branch Cycle) and the Mythological Cycle. Perhaps it even pulls from the other two great Cycles of Gaelic/Celtic origin (Fenian Cycle and The Cycle of the Kings). Anyway, the fusion of different cycles creates and interesting story for sure. Essentially it represents the end of an era and an introspective look at how misunderstandings and blind decision lead to strife and chaos. By my mind anyway.
My only critique regarding the story is that it can be difficult to follow and you really need to pay attention to piece together some aspects of it. That said, it was still engaging and the writing style was more elegant that what you typically see in games.
8 out of 10
If you are familiar with true walking simulators and especially if you have played any of Tonguc’s previous games, then you know what to expect. You will walk a path, taking in the sights and sounds and interact with a limited amount of objects in the game. There are three puzzles in the game, easily solved by simply paying attention to your environment and the story as it is being told. This is a perfect example of how a walking simulator should function, suffered from no technical issues, and basically was flawless in its execution.
I would also like to note that The Hunting God pulls an idea from Tonguc’s previous best work, Drizzlepath: Glass, and breaks up the experience with a sudden, almost shocking and scary moment that allows you to re-focus and reinvest yourself, at  just the perfect time during the game. I loved that moment and it really speaks to an awareness of what you, the gamer, are feeling and experiencing while playing.
10 out of 10
The Hunting God easily represents Tonguc’s finest work as it pertains to graphics. I don’t know what aspects of the Unreal Engine he was able to include in the development of this game, but this is a huge step up from his previous games, which were already pretty amazing in their own right. This is flat out a stunning game to take in. During the hour and twenty minutes my playthrough took, I snapped off about a hundred screenshots and could have taken much much more.
10 out of 10
The audio in The Hunting God was also immaculate. The voice work was pretty cool and fit the story perfectly. However, it was the orchestrations that really set this game on a whole different level that most other games. Each section and change in mood was represented perfectly by the music, and was perfect in every moment. The music was also eminently listenable outside of the game. You could easily play these tunes on your own time and enjoy every bit of what you are hearing.
10 out of 10
A lot of people play walking simulators because they are looking for quick, relaxing, and atmospheric experiences. The Hunting God is all of that. Me personally though, I play to witness the developers vision and the world’s being crafted, and The Hunting God did an amazing job of drawing me in and keeping my interest throughout. I would consider this a must own must play title.
9.5 out of 10

This is one of the few games I'd recommend for absolutely everyone. It's absolutely superb in every way possible. Story, art, music, gameplay... Everything.
The art in this game is absolutely stunning. The art style, the multitude of colors and the way the scenery is composed makes the player feel like he/she is playing inside one of the world's greatests works of art.
Gameplay is simple and easy to play, yet mastering the game requires practice. There are no irrelevant weapon upgrades, each and every one of them are great improvements to their respective weapon. Likewise, spirits are also huge improvements. The combination of different weapons, different weapon upgrades, spirits and secret skills makes for an extremely varied gameplay, going from full heads-on approaches towards enemies to more tactical approaches.
The game lasts long enough to have the player invest at least a few hours in the game in his/her first playthrough, while also not being too long so that it feels unnecessarely stretched. Extra modes like New Game Plus add a lot to the game's replay value.
It's hard to even come up with any flaws to mention here. The only one I could think of are some of the Shrine Idols, that can cause the game to become way too hard and not make up for the bonuses they give. But since Idols are completely optional, I wouldn't consider it a flaw.

If there's anything I can say about Bastion, it's that it looks absolutely beautiful. The art style just blew me away, and it was admittedly the reason I got this game in the first place. But of course, good looks aren't the only thing Bastion has going for it. The combat style is very enjoyable due to the variety of customisations available, especially as you progress further into the game and unlock more weapons and potions, which affect your character's base stats. For those looking for a challenge, the interesting gameplay mechanic of invoking idol statues of gods further increases the difficulty of combat, with extra XP and money rewards.
But the most interesting thing about this game for me was the fact that you're accompanied by a deep-voiced narrator, telling you the story as you play through Bastion. Whenever you progress through the story, whether it's finding a new ability, walking into a new area, or even falling off the edge, the narrator will have something to comment about it right as it happens, more often witty than not. The live narration very effectively immerses the you in the game, making you feel as if you are part of the story itself. I have never seen a game do this kind of narration before, so it was a new and often amusing experience for me.
Despite how great this game is, there is one thing I'd like to point out, and that is the game's lack of definitive area borders, making it very easy to fall off ledges sometimes. For example, there would be something like a chunk of land that you think you can walk on, but when you walk over to it, it was actually in the background and so you end up falling off the ledge. This was a bit annoying particularly when I was low on health, but it's not a huge problem I would deduct any theoretical points for.
With a compelling story, great soundtrack and amazing art, I thoroughly enjoyed playing Bastion and wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a good adventure RPG.

Xcom 2 is a fantastic game and one of my favorite games of all time. between the genre-making unique gameplay and the awesome ayy designs, it just srikes me as an amazing game.
***GAMEPLAY***
Xcom 2 is divided into two states, A base building section and a tactics section. the main gameplay is the tactics section.
*TACTICS*
the main part of this game feels very much like a chess game, and relies heavily on your ability to think ahead of the enemy. as well as common sense.  if your guys are in the wrong place at the wrong time it'll end up being more violent than a saw movie. on the other hand if your guys are placed in just the right way, and the ayys aren't moving a whole lot, you can set up an awesome overwatch ambush and it's seriously one of the most satisfying moments in gaming for me.
you have a certain amount of soldiers on the battlefield at a single time. they have two actions that can be taken up by various things, such as: moving, shooting (which always ends a soldier's turn), throwing a grenade (which does less damage but has a 100% chance of hitting and always ends a soldier's turn), running, (which always ends a soldier's turn),
a few class specific abilities and a few moves used by the sci operatives.
moving is grid-based and utilizes a cover system, which depending on the object in front of the soldier, can give you low or high cover. Which thows off an ayy's aim either a little or a lot, respectivley. But be careful, as most ayys can also use cover to the same effectiveness as your soldiers. using cover also grants the ability to have enemies get flanking shots on you from a side not protected by cover, which often do more damage. you can also get flanking shots on ayys in cover to the same effect.
taking the stealthier approach is also available, where your soldiers can get the jump on the ayys by staying out of their sight. If you put multiple soldiers in overwatch, you can set up massive overwatch ambushes. These can and will often wipe out whole squads in the early game. My only gripe about the stealth, or "concealment" system is that alien squads get bigger over time and they start becoming less effective.
I feel like this has been said before but, this game is very RNG heavy. missing 60% shots will happen often. And if you have below a 90% hit chance with your melee guy, don't even bother with it.
this has also been said before, but this game is timed. 60% of missions have a certain amount of turns before you flat out lose. even for missions that don't make sense at all. as in, "your soldiers must gather a box and return it to the ship before it detonates itself." umm, why is the box detonating at all? the ayys don't know i'm here yet. so they just have it rigged to explode for no reason? the timers still tick down duing stealth.
speaking of timers, the whole game is timed. the "avatar project" is a doom meter that's constantly ticking up at all times. let the bar fill completely, and you lose the game. this never really becomes that much of a problem, seeing as you can always delay it longer, but it's very annoying. "oh let me drop everything and do this mission or i'll lose the game in 30 minutes" is never a thought you want your players to be thinking, devs.
also, every month you'll unlock a new cool ayy to fight. exept chryssalyds. I don't think they're cool. Just annoying.
*BASE BUILDING*
The other part of the game is about managing your power, crew, soldiers, and research. you can clear out rooms caved-in rooms with engineers, and make research go faster with scientists. both available at the HQ and missions. In cleared-out rooms of your ship, you can build rooms with special effects. a lab will make research quicker, a proving grounds is essential for making cool armors and grenades, a psi lab trains psi operatives, a GTS will allow you to re-train soldiers to get different classes, an advanced warfare center will heal your soldiers faster, a shadow chamber is essential for story things and detects enemies in missions,  and there's a couple of other rooms I didn't bother with.
research unlocks new items, and engineering builds them.
Over time you'll get very attached to your soldiers. you can change thier names, armor colors, hair styles and much more. you'll actually be very suprised at how fun it is to play virtual barbie with your most well-trained and badass soldier. also this game has permadeath. your soldiers WILL die. and it'll make you sad.
you can speed up time, travel to different places, scan for missions and buy things from the geoscape.
***STORY***
"Story in a video game is like story in a porn movie. It's expected to be there, but it's not that important."
-John Remero, co-creator of DOOM
while I don't always agree with this quote, it's definitley true here. The story to XCOM 2 is: "Aliens have taken over and you gotta stop them, cause you're the chosen one." oh yeah, I haven't played 38 other games with THAT plot. this game could have a story that consits of a couple of guys flying around and shooting very ugly police, and it wouldn't affect the game much.
***GRAPHICS***
they're pretty good.
***FINAL THOUGHTS***
it's pretty good.
***PROS AND CONS***
*PROS*
-great gameplay
-great graphics
-great voice acting
-great aliens
-great music
-great grates
-great snektits
*CONS*

-RNGsus doesn't like you
***AWARDS***

My only complaint with the multiplayer is that there's no way to fight the other players, at least not that I know of.
In recent updates, they've added more quest stuff and missions and things like that if you like a more structured RPG. I like the open endedness of it, so I like that the missions aren't necessary to enjoy the game. You do have to complete a few missions to get your ship fully up and running to jump between systems, but that adds to the experience of the game.

Edit and Important Note: As of the 23rd of June, Kabam Announced that they would transfer ownership of the game to an Indie Company named Deca Games.  Deca games is a brand new company with the idea to acquire old games with dedicated playerbases and "breathe life into them."  However, this will be Deca Games's first attempt at reviving an old game, and have made many promises to fix the massive issues with balance and exploits.  My review will remain unchanged until they officially take over on the 15th of july, and announce official plans.  So if you're reading my review, take it with a grain of salt.  Give the game some time and see where Deca decides to take it.
Edit 2: Deca has taken over, and has done more in a few days than Kabam did in 6 months.  Please, please give this game a chance, you will not regret it.
Now, let's get one thing straight, I know it says I have something like 6 hours on record... That's not even CLOSE to how much I've played since it came out on kongregate.  I've played probably 100+ something hours on that account, and easily over 1500 hours on the website.  I have made multiple maxed out characters, and lost just as many.  I think I'm qualified to give a review, so here goes.
Pros:
Days upon days of enjoyment.
Hardcore gameplay (permadeath)
Amazing pixel art
Random dungeon generation
Super high skill cap
Fast leveling
You don't need to buy anything
literally the most addictive game I've played in a while
Cons:
Takes a while to get into
Deca has inherited Kabam's fairly P2W system, and there's not a lot they can do about it (pets)
Very grindy
So like I said, i've spent thousands of hours on this game by now, I have a great legendary pet, I've had multiple (and lost multiple) maxed characters, but there's something about this game that just keeps me coming back.  The pixel art is incredible, reminiscent of OG Legend of Zelda or even Terraria.  The community, for the most part, is actually super nice.  I've died on maxed characters and been messaged by multiple people, "Yo man, sorry about your death, can I give you some stuff to rebuild?" The randomly generated dungeons allow for easy group, and solo content if you prefer.  There's an incredible trading market that players have created, allowing for someone to buy and trade whatever potion or item they may need.
The grind to get the really rare drops like Doom Bows and Ancient Stone Swords is incredibly satisfying, and no matter how many times I just say "♥♥♥♥ this I'm never coming back to this game" after dying, I always return after a few hours.  Even though its annoying, permadeath provides an interesting "risk/reward" aspect.  Do I want to run this Shatters to see if I could maybe get a high tier piece of armor or a life pot? Or is the risk too great that I'll die and lose everything I've gotten?
Also, Deca has already proven themselves to be more than capable of handling the massive amount of bots/dupers/multis that plagued the game for so long when Kabam had the game Sil3x took it upon himself to server hop and banhammer every bot he could find, which isn't a permanent fix, but it did more than Kabam did in 6 months.  As soon as they took over they gave players Month of the Mad God, one of the most awesome events ever.  So finally, after over a year, I can now recommend this game.  Deca has shown themselves to be capable devs and that they know how to run a game.  So please, give this game a chance, spend a few hours on it.  I hope you'll enjoy it as much as I have.

Blackwake is awesome.
I haven't owned the game for very long, but I can't stop playing it, and I haven't even played every gamemode for very long. I personally prefer 1v1 Hoy (I prefer a duel-esque 1v1 setting and I find Galleons to require too large of a crew to be able to function efficiently in a casual setting) and I enjoy playing as the Captain. And no, it's not for the reason a lot of players pick Captain, ("ZOMG IM THW CAPTEN IM IN CHARGE NOU" they say as they don't even try to steer the ship, don't say a word to their crew and forget they're the captain halfway through the game.) but because I feel I can efficiently command a good crew. While a mic is, of course, recommended, a Captain can still lead a team to victory with just the ingame voice commands. And the pleasure you get from leading a good crew to victory as they follow your orders is unparraleled.
Even so, the joy of the game doesn't just come from playing Captain. Even as a simple crewman, the game is still amazing. As long as your Captain is competent and knows how to give orders, coordinating with them is extremely satisfying. You know you have a good crew when you tell them your plans and you can see them react accordingly. "I'm pulling away for repairs!" You say as all their crew immediately leave their spots on the cannons and get to work fixing the ship. "Turning around to Port!" And just like that, the crew dismounts their starboard cannons and, like a magestic line wave of bearded sailor men, they swing over to the Port cannons and ready themselves.
You might have guessed by now that this game is very reliant on a good team. And yes, that's very true. While it's an amazing experience, it does demand that your crew be competent, and a bad crewman who doesn't listen to orders can easily ruin the fun. But fear not, for the majority of the Blackwake community is competent and eager to help you and every else on your little Canoe paddle their way to victory. I'm not a perfect Captain, I've lost a good amount of times from my own faults, and sometimes when I do, my Crew are quick to suggest strategies and ways of doing things easier, and I'm happy to listen. And when you do sail into victory after a long-fought battle of coordination, the humble feeling of your crew all voting for you as Captain the next round is probably one of the most satisfying things in the game.
Also, the soundtrack. Lord, the soundtrack. After my first game, I immediately went to search it up so I could listen to it again. I would have bought it on steam if I had any spare money.
So yeah. Buy Blackwake. Just don't be toxic and ruin the game for everyone else, please.
