An entertaining, if confusing, game
Story Summary: Three bumbling Gods responsible for recreating Earth as an experiment hire a zeppelin captain and his pilot/mechanic Flawkes to deliver parts so they can repair their planet-building machine. The devil, who sabotaged the planet-building machine, talks Flawkes into editing the Earth into his own image. Flawkes must entertain the proto-humans (called Buddies) to produce FUN, a currency that can be used to build machines and pull heavy objects out of the stratosphere.
This game is a mix of puzzle-solving and building and driving around in your own crazy vehicles. The faster/higher they go, the more entertained the Buddies will become and the more FUN you earn.
Playtime: about 6 hours to complete the story mode
Pros:
* The story and visuals are hilarious at times: the first time I had a “Buddy dance party”, I was laughing so hard I couldn’t breathe.
* Vehicle building is easy and fun, designs can be saved and reloaded at will. Or, if you don't enjoy it, you can use pre-made blueprints and skip vehicle building altogether.
* Game lets you import and use your own music for Buddy dances.
Cons:
* Crashes, bugs, and insufficient auto-saves. Twice I managed to strand a submarine underneath the seafloor, once while going past a loading screen and another while editing the submarine when it was resting on the sea floor. The game only autosaves at the beginning of a new season, and seasons are very long. I’ve also read reports of the game failing to load saves made at particular times.
*** Important: if you decide to play this, save your game often and save in a new slot each time. ***
* Sometimes it’s hard to know what the game expects you to do. I had to consult a walkthrough for the volcano restarting section in winter, and for the tornado sequence in summer. I also had to look up online what the key for placing clefs was. (Enter.) This might be due to poorly-done translation of the guiding text (Cargo was originally developed in Russian.)
* Airplanes don’t control well.
If you’re a fan of games with weird characters and settings, like Zeno Clash, a fan of games where you build vehicles, like Spore or Kerbal Space Program, or a fan of silly nonsense humor, I think you'll enjoy this game.

This game is a odd, wacky, and just plain weird. I can imagine this game being thought of one late night at the office with nothing better to do. Theories asside, lets talk about the game.
The story of the game is somewhat hard to follow, but without trying to give out spoilers here, you must help these mechanical "gods" re-create the world with your engineering and creative powers. There are four seasons in the game, each one with different themes, like winter freezes all the water so you can drive on it. The game took me about six hours to finish, and thats with me messing around a bit. After you finish the story mode there are little to no reasons to do it again. The only thing for replay is sandbox mode, where you play around on the island with many (but limited) tools, making any vehicle your heart desires.
One small thing this game did horribly is sound, the begining sequence the voice acting was bad enough to make me want to quit the game. It got better from there, but the sound just isnt there in this game.
Throughout the game there is a little bar at the bottom of the screen that tells you what to do next, but I would of rather seen a check list menu or really anything other than this. It doesnt grab your attention easily, and I offen times would find my self forgeting about it and wondering what to do next. Other times when I did see it, what it said didnt make sence, one example that tool me awile to figure out was, near the end of the game it told me to "Find a large object" and it tool me almost fifteen minutes to figure out what I was suppost to do.
Now the big grabber in the game, making your own vehicle, is somthing this game does fairly well, you startout with a base for your vehicle and build from there. So, say you want to build a car, start with a car base, add a few connectors, add wheels to the connectors. and you are all set! However, on occasion you will run into problems. The game gives you blueprints that you can find, these are pre-made vehicles that
A. get the job done,
B. Are faster to make and,
C. Look cooler than anything I could make.
By the end of the second season I found myself going to these rather than building anything myself. Also the gravity and physics in this game dont feel right. Planes and helicopters feel like they're made from paper, the cars are too drifty, and the boats feel like your anchor is alwase down.
All in all this game is a quirky, fun, just plain weird building game that lets you be creative in a world full of weird things. But the story isnt there, the gameplay is diffferent and it really feels like its incomplete. But if you have six plus hours to burn, this isnt the worst of all choices. (Just dont get it for full price) :)

This is the 7th walking sim released by Tonguc Bodur. If you are not familiar with the genre here's a short description: walking simulators (or FPE, first person exploration games) put a lot of emphasis on walking instead of shooting (hence the missing word "shooter" from the name of the genre). The emphasis is on immersion and these games often showcase the capabilities of a particular engine and are relatively short (which explains why the price is significantly lower than that of an AAA game). They are slow-paced, have relaxing, atmospheric music and can usually be completed in an hour or two.
As the title suggests, the protagonist in his latest FPE is a deity himself. Similarly to the Nephise series a narration is done at regular intervals as we make progress throughout the 3 chapters the game offers. These chapters offer different landscapes, music and they take place at a different time of the day. My favourite was the 2nd chapter titled Moon which takes place at night and as we look up to the sky we can see a green moon and the constantly shining aurora borealis.
The game showcases the features of the 4th iteration of the Unreal engine. It is a bit too heavy on effects (e.g. shining grass) and it could have used a bit more water; the landscapes I now found more diverse and interesting than in previous titles of the creator. Also, there's more story here (do note the advanced level of English grammar here along with the excellent poems encountered regularly at statues) and, interestingly, 2 endgames depending on the choice we make.
This is a must-grab for those loving this genre as well as for those who are about to grab their first walking sim. You'll get a relaxing 2 hours and a game with 6 easy achievements.

Video games, at least the vast majority of them on Steam, seem geared towards one simplistic goal or another. Kill this, gather that resource, reach a new high score. Why can’t there be more titles which just focus on peaceful exploration and poetry? Tonguç Bodur realized that there’s a palpable need for precisely the aforementioned features and he delivers compelling stories with varying degrees of interaction. The Hunting God is the developer’s seventh Steam project and he’s come a long way, both technically and stylistically since the initial Drizzlepath from 2015.
As the game’s title suggests, players shall explore through the eyes (and narration) of Nodens, the Celtic deity associated with hunting, healing and seafaring. Pinpointing the exact time & location in which the game takes place, is easier than in Tonguç’s previous titles. The Hunting God features locations and stories relating to the Emerald Isle. Ireland and its mythology play a central role in the game, but Nodens does mention the ancient Kingdom of Gwynedd (Northern part of Wales) as well, so it confirms that as a deity, he was worshipped far beyond the borders of Hibernia (Latin for Ireland). Regardless of the exact location which may or may not be Banagher Forest, players shall travel across a diversified scenery which spans over mountainous terrain by The Hunting God’s conclusion.
Powered by Unreal Engine 4, in what I shall name as one of the most satisfying portrayal of optimization, for this graphics engine in an indie title. I could run The Hunting God maxed out@4K without exhibiting massive frame rate drops. It never strayed far from 40fps and I know I could’ve went down the 2K route and play at solid 60fps at all times, yet if you read a sufficient number of my articles already, you know that long after I have played and reviewed a game, all that remains are my memories of it and the many screenshots which serve as an even better memento. In other words, I care about those screenshots and I want them to be with as few flaws as possible. The Hunting God didn’t disappoint me in the slightest. I had plenty of points of interest to snapshoot and the game looks gorgeous without being as heavy on foliage use as with similar games from this developer. A balance between level of detail and stability has been achieved without compromise. What could I complain about?
Certainly not about the sounds, since everything was top notch. From the relaxing soundtrack (with occasional classic instrumentals) to the convincing voice acting. Nodens was obviously voice by an actor fluent in English with an Irish accent. The English subtitles didn’t feature any typos, yet some accent marks were omitted, such as the one in “draíochta”, the Irish word for “magic”. In any case, that’s scraping the barrel at this point.
At least one puzzle section which was rather brief and simple, yet the game doesn’t consider itself as belonging to the conventional Adventure genre in gaming. The Hunting God, much like its series’ predecessors is more about the journey itself than the obstacles standing between players and the game’s ending. The abstract structure transcends the narrative and represents a crucial part of the gameplay as well. Yes, it’s a relatively short trip, clocking at around an hour if you’re really in a hurry. I obviously wasn’t and spent a bit more, just looking for perfect screenshot material.
The Steam Achievements are easy to unlock and they relate to six poems toggled by an equal number of statues. Two for each game section (Earth, Moon and Sun). You really can’t overlook them and while they don’t advance the storyline in any manner, they serve their purpose regardless. It’s up to you to decide. It isn’t the type of game that will endear itself to the unpatient or those players that have come to expect and rely on action and clearly stated objectives. It may be an acquired taste, but by no means should it deter anyone from playing The Hunting God or walking sims in general. They may grow on you, as they did in my case, several years back. Keep an open mind, will you?
Steam Trading Cards are on the way (now it’s up to Valve to decide on that matter) yet The Hunting God stays true to the formula and high standards set by Tonguç Bodur’s past projects, while offering more stability and a homogenized Celtic theme which never felt forced at all. Being abstract just for the sake of it, is out of the picture. What remains, is a game which relaxes players and expects very little in return. It also has two endings which ensure at least some limited form of replay value.
+ Abstract experience.
+ Steam Achievements.
+ Gorgeous graphics and sounds.
+ Smoother gameplay than previous titles in the series.
- Brief and with almost no replay value.
- No Steam Trading Cards yet.
- Abstract experience.

I must admit that my initial thought when I first saw the title of the game was something in the lines of: "OMG this is going to be bloody and full of dead animals". I immediately corrected myself because I realized that Tonguç Bodur wouldn't create gore-y games (or will he ever?). I was right,
is, as all the other games developed by him, a peaceful (and harmless), relaxing and beautiful walking simulator.
If you are familiar with any of the developer's previous creations, you'll probably know what to expect: for around 1h - 1h30' you will be transported to a wonderful place in the middle of the mountains, that you can explore at your own pace, accompanied by the narrator's voice that chimes in from time to time. The exploration is one directional, the path is straightforward and you can wander a bit to the left or to the right of it, to catch a better perspective of the stunning views surrounding you. Doing this will allow you to discover several of the many Easter eggs of the game, consisting of funny messages hidden in the least accessible places.
The game is divided into 3 main parts, each of them having a unique atmosphere and particular design. You'll start on journey on Earth, in the middle of a mountain setting, full of vegetation and life, progressing further towards a fictional arid Moon environment, and ending up on top of the mountains, directly under the Sun.
has indeed some alluring visuals. However, its strongest aspect is, in my opinion, the narration. The narrator's voice is so calming, it's a pleasure to listen to him! He also has a  strong exotic accent that makes his recitation even more colorful and attuned to the Celtic / Irish names that his story references. The story itself centers around a Hunting God called Nodens who recounts a few events from his existence - how he met his otherworldly wolf companion Draiochta with whom he develops a strong bond, how one day they went hunting together and uncovered a terrible evil, and how they turned to the druidess Mug for help in defeating it. The story has two possible endings and in order to see them both you'll need to play the entire last chapter twice (one playthrough of it takes around 15 minutes).
Overall, it's a well made game which provides a calming and  soothing experience. If it's worth or not the asking price for 1.5h of gameplay - this is up to you to decide, based on how much you appreciate Tonguç's games and his art direction. One thing to be noted though, before buying the game: please look at the required specs, since having to play it with low settings would most likely ruin your experience.

Would i recommend it? Sure, if it makes the servers Fuller.

Ittle Dew presented a series of interesting challenges one should expect from a rogue-like adventure game. Less emphasis was placed on combat and a lot more was placed on environmental puzzles. A great many challenges were actually difficult, but optional. What little story was written was an amusing, self-aware commentary on the game itself.
Usually, full completion of a game is a chore for me. I end up taking a long break and coming back when I feel like grinding. Fortunately, Ittle Dew isn't about grinding. It's about learning. The more you know, the better off you are. Your protagonist is a powerless little person with a worthless animal companion, but the knowledge you gain makes you hilariously dangerous.
I wholeheartedly approve of the adorable art style, playful sound design, and even the personality of my protagonist. It isn't often that I enjoy a game like this so much, and I'm eager to get the sequel eventually to see if it measures up to the original.
Finally, good luck with the Master Cave. I really mean it. It is ridiculous, but I love it.

It's strange that this genre seems so full when there really aren't many games in it. Grand Theft Auto, Saints Row, Just Cause, Mafia, and now Sleeping Dogs. This game does a really good job of making itself stand out from the crowd, though.
Technically the game is fantastic. It looks great even on medium settings and runs quite well, with the option of full DX11 support and a high resolution texture pack for those with beastly machines. It has the best looking rain I've ever seen and an amazing amount of detail in the cities, rivaling GTA4 while looking far better and running with similar performance to Saints Row 3.
First of all it has a top notch story with great voice acting, only falling short of GTA4 in the motion capture department. The characters are all believable and well written. There's quite a few optional side missions as well, though they unfortunately aren't anywhere near as fleshed out.
The car handling is the best of any of the games, hands down. Think Saints Row 3 but more realistic. Driving is fun and unlike the other games, you are actually rewarded for driving safe. Sometimes you do need to crash though, and the game has a nice ramming mechanic to destroy other cars and push them off the road. In addition you can shoot out car tires when you have a gun which disables them quite quickly.
The combat system is where the game really shines though. It has a freeflow combat system similar to Batman AA/AC, but rather than being a superhero you're a martial arts master. You fight groups of enemies mostly in hand-to-hand combat, unlocking new moves as you gain more experience. The melee weapons you obtain sometimes are not very durable and will usually only take out one enemy. Guns are rare but extremely powerful and attract the police extremely quickly.
Tying in with the combat system is freerunning. You will do a lot of climbing up tall barriers and vaulting over tables, even doing special disarm and takedown moves when you vault into enemies. It's an enjoyable addition to the game and fits in very well with the setting in Hong Kong.
Now one of the biggest strengths and weaknesses is the camera control.  This game has the best driving camera I've ever see.  It uses a novel idea of actually pointing the direction you're moving when you turn a corner!  It does tend to get a bit confused when you reverse though.
The walking camera is another matter altogether.  I lost track of how many different camera angles there are, since there's a different one for every movement speed, and for each weapon type, and a different one while fighting, and combinations of them all.  The walking camera doesn't point the same direction you're moving, the walking and sprinting cameras make the mouse laggy, and some of the weapon cameras give you weird camera angles.  The rest of it's pretty good though.  I don't know why they couldn't just stick to a single good camera angle instead of changing it all the time.
Sleeping Dogs really is a must-have for fans of the genre.

This game had everything going for it before I even added it to my wishlist. Part of a franchise I'm already addicted to. Established world to operate in. Turn-based tile gameplay I've loved since my Heroes of Might and Magic days. Decent graphics, animations and music. It even has support for ultra-wide monitors out of the box.
So did it live up to it's potential? Yes, mostly. It's a very good update on the tried-and tested XCOM formula with some great new elements and some distressing old bugs.
I love the addition of custom soldiers you can design and take on missions. It makes you that much more attached to them and it's super fun to yell out friend and family names in anger when they miss 95% accuracy shots. The class changes are fun too - I've got a couple of pretty OP Rangers now that I would legitimely fell distressed at losing on a mission.
I hate that the ultra-wide monitor support was a little tacked on and almost game breaking in some aspects. Hacking anything becomes difficult because the button to continue falls off the screen. Sometimes clicking on another soldier action will cause them to do the action already seleceted instead because the areas on screen aren't mapped correctly. IT's bearable if you mostly play keyboard-first, but it needs work.
I like the idea of the Spark units and the Boss aliens from the DLC. The story lines seemed very basic for what they could have been, but an enjoyable addition to the vanila game nonetheless. I don't have the Chosen DLC yet but it looks promising and I'm keen to try it (maybe once it goes on sale).
Minor and mission breaking bugs still plague this game (it's XCOM so that's to be expected). Sometimes it gets stuck on Alien Activity or in between turns forcing you to exit the game to continue. Sometimes the action descriptions are innacurate as to whether or not they end a unit's turn. Sometimes units that shouldn't be affected by blasts get knocked through floors or walls even. I could go on.
It's a great game, I love it and I have already sunk 50+ hours into it, with the promise of many more. BUT I'd enjoy much more of that time if so much of it weren't spent backtracking to avoid mission-critical bugs and corrupt save games.

The Walking Dead is a game I would never forget, it is a game I incredibly love for many reasons. Out of all the Telltale Games I have played The Walking Dead would still always be my favourite, it’s not just my favourite Telltale Game maybe even my most beloved single player game that I had ever played in my life.
The Walking Dead has one of the best storylines in video game history, starting from episode 1 to 5 the story is constantly progressing, always getting better. Telltale has really nailed the storyline perfectly. With the incredibly well voice actings played out by Dave Fennoy (Lee Everett) and Melissa Hutchison (Clementine), it has really brought the the characters to life making players actually feel like they are part of the character. The atmosphere of the game changes really maturely, it's never repetitive or filled with cliches and with The Walking Dead’s sound track it greatly supports the tone and atmosphere a lot.
On to the characters, this is another part which I think Telltale has also nailed perfectly. Just from the first episode already Telltale has made the protagonist Lee Everett a legend, A character that players would always remember and respect, he is also my favourite character in videogames.The second character Clementine is also one of the most beloved character in the Walking Dead series,this even makes her the main protagonist in the following up seasons, season 2 & 3 and players truly adore her. As the story progresses the characters relationship develops stronger, players feelings for the characters also builds up. I won’t be sharing any spoilers of the game but I will mention the my feeling at end of the game. There are many reasons why countless players would adore Lee Everett and Clementine and this is because of their bond together. When the game reaches the end I was so attached to the characters and the story. I cried
When I first saw this game I never expected it to be any good, because personally I am more into FPS games, and The Walking Dead was nothing close to FPS. (except for a few minor scenes you have to shoot zombies with your pistol in first person) Even though I read a lot of reviews and watched different game interviews about Telltale’s The Walking Dead, I still wasn’t convinced, but when I finally tried it myself, I completely underestimated The Walking Dead. This is a game I would 100% recommend to everyone, I don’t expect my review to be much of a help because this is a game you would have to experience it yourself to understand. My main point is to just give it a shot, you might like the game or you might not, everyone has different opinions. Its gameplay time is over 20+ hours which is incredibly well for a game priced at US$24.99, but trust me it’s worth it.

Weird. Fun. Weird.
Probably the strangest game I have ever played, where kicking weird little naked baby-like things and driving/flying around at high speed with them hanging onto your vehicle earns "fun" which you can spend on causing houses, Big Ben, icebergs and lots of other random objects to fall from space onto the planet.
The game is played in third person, which is not normally a plus for me, but as you spend most of the time in vehicles it works well enough, and there is a reasonable variety of quests/activities and vehicle types - sailboat, screw propelled boat, wheels, ballons, prop planes, submarines or a mixture of propulsion methods if you like, as well as expanding them meccano style with more parts you can buy over time.
There are various objectives including racing or searching for the buddies, some light puzzling to do, etc., and a kind of storyline/weirdness knitting it all together. Overall you get a fairly simple but reasonably flexible vehicle constructor to play with, and a very weird world to explore. While probably not hugely replayable, it is definitely a lot of fun to experience this strange and innovative world.

Having played though twice, my view of the game is that it needs additional content where the player can drive the story line. For instance, it really is not possible to be an evil player. If you♥♥♥♥♥♥off the members of your base they'll stop interacting (which I only saw happen once), which means they won't craft things or guard while you're off on a mission.
The combat system is simplistic, so you have to be alright with that element in order to enjoy the game. Your team is lined up on the left, and the enemies are on the right. Each team has a max of 4 on screen, though the player can only operate 3 members (you sometimes have a 4th that is computer controlled). The type of squad-based mechanics here is pretty elementary, and does feel repetitive. (I don't mind it though, because it can still be challenging).
The whole concept is to accumulate sufficient stuff (meds. food, cloth, weapons) to survive to the end, and the end-date is pre-set. You have to manage your team, keep people healed if they are going on missions with you, assign others to jobs to craft better armor, and so on. The management aspect is interesting, and there are definitely choices to be made, but ultimately the whole game is linear. That's fine as far it goes, but after two play-throughs I'm not feeling any urge to do it again, because it is essentially an identical experience.
As a rating, I’d give it a 7/10 for the initial experience, but low re-play value due to lack of variability in outcomes. If the designers added new content, such as meaningful decisions that actually alter the direction of the game, I’d gladly play it more.

Well, after years and hundereds of hours on Fallout 3 and then New Vegas on Playstation 3, Fallout became my favourite game franchise. I purchased a gaming PC soley for Fallout 4 and the added benefit of modding, and I have not been dissapointed..
Fallout 4 is an immersive, detailed and polished up next step into the post apocolyptic franchise of fallout, with more weapons, enemies, locations to discover and additions such as in depth weapons, mods, base building and crafting that makes the whole game feel more unique and personal and immersive, making the wasteland 'yours'. I have been easily immersed for hours on end wandering the wastes and completing quests, while appreciating the revamp of all the textures and items from the previous games.
However, as an avid fan, if you want a critical review, continue reading:
I feel the story is very delegated, with little varitation in the quests and little difference in the main story line on multiple playthroughs. New vegas had multiple factions, that could be brought together or fought against similar to fallout 4, however siding with varying factions in F4 has no real benefit or change to the story, meaning missions go the same way and often with the same result.
There is little/no punishment in Fallout 4, theres no need to specialise in character builds as you can become incredibly overpowered with the unlimited level progression, perks become accumulated and there is no hard decisions or concequences when confronting situatations and everything just seems to always.. work out. This makes it easier for novice players and those new to the franchise but somewhat punishes experiences players with a lack of secrets, easter eggs, rare loot and unique items.
The base game is enjoyable, but is only a mere shadow of itself in comparison to a modded game.. Modding F4 WAS THE BEST DECISION IVE EVER MADE. A 5 minute nexus mod installer tutorial and I then had acsess to thousands of gun skins all with custom sounds and effects, custom characters, armor, ammo and settlement builds, improving the game no end and its replayability, while simultaneously highlighting the rough edges of the base game.
Although Fallout 4 is a brilliant game (7/10) with modding it can quickly become an (8.5/10). F4 has however lost aspects of its former self but makes up for the 'softness' of the game with brilliant graphics, cinematic moments, immersion and unique customisations with the added benefit of some top quality mods..
Fallout 4 could never be considered a 'bad purchase' and im glad that ive always have acsess to the wasteland from my steam library.

Dead Age is a Zombie Apocalypse survival simulation game with turn based Rock/Paper/Scissor-like combat and RPG management of survivors. You have been tasked in the management of your camp and you need to survive by finding or crafting enough of the necessary resources (Food/Tools/Materials).
The game is divided between Exploration and Camp activities.
Exploration is done on fixed/named map locations each providing different challenges and rewards. Combat happens mainly during this time and each survivor will have several Combat skills and Armor/Weapons to use. During exploration you can also fulfill mission objectives tasked on you by fellow survivors.
Camp acivities are executed through Jobs and consist in Hunting, Crafting or Guarding the camp. Each survivor has a Job proficiency which can be leveled up with time. The camp can also be attacked by Scavangers/Bandits or Zombies, in which case you'll need to fight to keep your stuff (and lives).
The graphics is very nice and fits the general mood of the game. The AI is smart enough to keep you on your toes so that you need to develop different tactics against different enemies and prioritize targets in a group.
All in all this is a "little" nice and addicting game... just don't expect much freedom on the plot, it's not a sandbox game! :-]

You only play as Dakotaraptor. You start off as a hatchling then overtime, you grow and grow, until you reach a mature age. To stay alive you must hunt and drink water, also avoiding threats.
That's all this game has to offer currently. There is no alternative species to choose from which makes the game feel empty.

They do plan to add more playable dinosaurs but we do not know if they will reach to that point. Indie game developers can become unpredictable since they make games in their spare time, they can bail out the project if they wanted to or just not up for it.
A game developer that works on triple AAA games are hired and paid to get the job done, and are more trusted when they reach a goal that players expect. Indie devs aren't like that hence I said this game is barebones.

You can explore around the map if you wanted to but every terrain is the same to me. It's mostly based on the low lands of Hell Creek. It would be nice for more forests and interesting places to visit time to time. Highland forests and mountains are welocme.
I personally want a redwood excuslsive biome with very tall and big redwood trees with ferns covering the forest floors, along with a interesting hotspot inside the biome. I haven't done much research on Hell Creek,
I do not know much about plant materials that existed back then since I am more of a dinosaur lover, I only stick to what I can understand more.
The AI is bland. The dinosaurs still walk into trees. They do not know their surroundings and often ignore a lot of things that are nearby. You can say mindless walking dinner plates. I cannot tell if it will get better than this so I make it a bad point for now until I see progress.
I said the controls made the Dakotaraptor move like a bus, they seem to have listened. They recently made the movements much more lighter. This does not make the game any better, its a small change that doesn't effect the gameplay but its nice to play control quicker.
The models for the animals are well made. The detailing is well putted. They do research into these species to create what the actual animal would look like.
The animations are well detailed. A animator uses a Emu to simulate dinosaur motions which is attention of research put into animations. The dinosaurs move like birds (mostly the bipedal creatures).
The textures and skins are based off real resources and likely conludsions. The team and artists come up with a plausable result.
The colours of the dinosaurs are guesses, when theres talent and skill put into dinosaur colours, its very eye appearing and grounded.
Overhaul Saurian is still not worth it just yet. Its not a bad game its just empty.
I am confident in the developers judgeing by the patch notes that have been dropped.

As much as I watched this game receive a lot of negative publicity when it first launched, all the glitches, the game breaking glitches, and so on. Just about yesterday did I really give this title a chance. Now I am addicted to it. For some odd reason. Allow me to give some Positives and Negatives on the game. So you can decide to make your purchase.
Positives: -Plenty of Dispatch Missions to take advantage of, which are Challengings and Fun.
-Your Police Vehicle has many customization options.
-Wide vast area with much to explore.
-Plenty of criminals to arrest.
-Responsive Controls.
-Driving feels very fluent, but takes time to get used to.
-Music is actually very good.
-Voice acting is on point.
-There is always something to do, even when there are no missions available.
-Ranking up feels rewarding as you get an increase in pay.
-Weather & Night to Day transitions are wonderfully done.
-You are able to decorate and buy new things for your home.
Negatives: -Aiming can be a chore to pull off, when you are about to get shot.
-Sometimes when doing routine checks on cars, the person driving the car will run sometimes, also very far.
-When you arrest someone, you are forced to walk. When you want to put them in your car, especially if they run a far distance, walking takes forever to get back to your car which will inspire you to call police dispatch to lighten the burden.
-When finished with routine missions, entering the police station for a warrant based on a mission is a problem. When you step back outside the station, the game forces another routine mission on you, removing the perp from the map. Making it difficult to find where they are again. Unless Dispatch decides to update you on their location, which can take a terribly long time.
-illegally parked cars don't spawn often, unless you quit, and restart the game. So when asked to ticket illegally parked cars, there are usually none in the street. There is a way around this by ticketing cars on the street by checking their license plates, and ticketing them that way. Its the only way around it.
-You take no damage by getting hit by cars. They usually flip over you. Also you cannot kill a pedestrian by hitting them.
-You can only arrest one person at a time. When you're after two perps, you have to dispatch the one first, while the other has the chance to escape as you cannot go after them when you have someone handcuffed.
-Sometimes Dispatch missions never show up. Because of a game glitch. You have to sleep 8 hours & restart the game. The glitch is caused by the Stress meter being too low. The game gets confused and doesn't turn back Dispatch calls on.
-AI pedestrians have a habit of endlessly walking into vehicles, perps in houses run endlessly into the wall, or the door with their body peeking out of the door when you try to arrest them.
-The game has a bad habit of throwing you missions even after your shift is over. They should stop. Because when you end your shift with a mission active, even if its routine, you are penalized points. Which you need to rank up.
Even with the negatives I think the game is still very enjoyable. Regardless, its up to the buyer. Happy New Year everyone.

The Hunting God is the seventh game from Tonguc Bodur, a man seemingly dedicated to the art of making "walking simulators". For those familiar with his output, this can perhaps be seen as something of a consolidation of his prior work: it has the voice-over narration of most of his games, the fantastic setting and mythological resonance of Drizzlepath: Genie, and the infrequent and none-too-taxing "puzzles" of the Nephise games.
Which isn't to say that I consider this his most successful work to date - I'd personally give that honour to Drizzlepath: Glass - but it's evidently nice to see a developer not only willing to mix up his own past formulas, but arguably "learn" from past mistakes. This certainly succeeds in feeling more like a fully-fledged "journey" than the two Nephises and Bottle, which were altogether too short for their own good and perhaps resembled accomplished demos more than actual "games" (whereas this one's a decent hour-and-a-half long, give or take).
The nitty-gritty? Well, the graphics as always are lovely - if not quite as consistently detailed and lush as some of his earlier games - the sound suitably immersive, the music by-and-largely excellent, the voice acting mostly solid if occasionally stilted, and the story - while fairly bare-bones and nothing terribly new - gives sufficient context to the scenery you're travelling through and can't be faulted terribly on a literary level (though the language is still a tad "flowery" at times for my tastes, but not as much as some previous Tonguc games).
So what would one buy this for? The story? The writing? The gameplay? The atmosphere? Well, mostly the latter, but a bit of all the above really. Like all half-decent walking sims, it's more about the EXPERIENCE than anything else. The Genre: Keyboard/mouse or twin-stick shooting physics platformer.
The Awesome: Crazy over the top enemy wave and boss design. The first boss is an elaborate, punishing, multi-stage battle where you keep thinking it's dead and it just...keeps...coming! Then it finally dies and you think perhaps the next level will get off to a more relaxing start, and instead you find yourself careening downhill on a fragment of the boss you just killed, while ninjas lob increasingly dangerous explosives at you...and then there are some airstrikes...and then the airstrikes start to include missiles that turn into giant robot snakes. I still haven't gotten past the snakes, so I don't know what else that sequence might hold, but it inspired me to write a review.
The Good: All the things you can do with the game's physics. Lots of movable/destroyable objects, vehicles, enemies with individually destroyable, independently moving sections.
The Bad: The physics and controls feel very loose and floaty. Movement could be tighter and objects could feel like they have more weight and heft. Sometime you try to jump and it doesn't quite happen. It doesn't generally prevent you from being able to move around and do skillful things, but it is annoying.
The Ugly: The game autosaves at checkpoints, and they are very far apart. There are more frequent checkpoints that you return to when you die, but if you actually quit the game, you may find yourself much further back. Some people may appreciate this feature, since it makes the game more challenging and perhaps increases playtime, while others may be annoyed by it.
Verdict: The ideas in here are so cool...with a little bit of tolerance for the imperfect controls/physics you can have a lot of fun with it...especially if you can let your imagination fill in some of the gaps between the execution and the level of awesomeness that the game is aiming at (and mostly achieves).

I am glad this is done. It was the most challenging translation job for me, so far (English - German). And it was worth it. I learned a lot about ancient myths of Ireland and the Celts while researching the background of the narration and the poems.
So, what can you expect?
Well, as usual from a game by Tonguç Bodur, it is at least a "Walking Simulator", so you will travel for quite a while, admiring pretty landscapes. True – they may look a little surreal, partially. But they are mere memories of a God at the end of his existence, in fact; some degree of simplification and exaggeration is just in conformance with the topic.
But even more, it is a "Narrative Game". You don't simply walk and look. You are also told a story, based on celtic myths (and some of Lovecraft's interpretations). And so you get the honor to participate, rudimentarily. Yes, this game has interactive elements. Achievements. Jump scares. Even a few puzzles. A final decision to make. And eastereggs... can you catch them all? Why not become a Screen Archer?
If you enjoyed the previous game series (Drizzlepath..., Bottle, Nephise...), you will probably enjoy this game as well, with more narrative content than before.
And if not ... then you probably don't like this whole genre anyway. This is entertainment without a lot of action. It is relaxing pastime, with visible and audible harmony.
Regarding hardware demands: An Nvidia GT 450 (below recommendation) could handle it (using all "Epic" effect options and reduced motion blur) with semi-fluid speed (probably 15-20 fps) in a 1600x900 window. The optimization is surely better than in previous games.

I love "The Legend of Zelda" series. They're great adventure, action games that any fan of the genre can appreciate. Ittle Dew takes inspiration from the top-down, 2D Zelda games to the point where if you reskinned Ittle Dew with the same textures as "A Link to the Past" you wouldn't be able to tell the difference. On the surface Ittle Dew appears to take more than inspiration, and I'm sure most would even call Ittle Dew a Zelda clone. You explore dungeons, get items from the dungeons, solve the dungeons' puzzles, defeat a boss, use the item from the dungeons to progess further into the game, and eventually it all ends with a final epic boss battle. There's hearts to replenish your life, a fairy-esque follower who guides you on your travels, old men giving you cryptic messages, statues resembling those from the original Zelda 1, hell, you even begin the game waking up from a deep sleep as Zelda games traditonally do. However, to label Ittle Dew simply as just a Zelda clone would be a diservice to this game, because Ittle Dew's puzzles are more intricate, creative, and difficult than any Zelda puzzle to date. Now I know that's a bold statement, but think for a moment, what was the last zelda puzzle that really made you think and put your puzzle solving skills to the test? I can think of only one, and anybody who played "Twilight Princess" will know exactly which puzzle I'm talking about. That's one puzzle. In a game series spanning more than 25 years there's only one puzzle that tests you. Ittle Dew regularly makes you scratch your head and 20 minutes later you're still left scratching.
If you like puzzle games and zelda, check this one out, you won't regret it.

I doubt this will reach many people, but I felt like to give my own input on what this game is and if one should play it. I am a fan of this series. I played most if not all of the "Tales of" series, so I'll do my best to put away my bias.
This game, Tales of Beseria is not the best game there is, and not the best in its series. It uses old hardware and techniques, and its graphics are not the best. However, I beleive that does not make it a bad game. I will go over now what makes this fun, but also what could be off putting. I currently played near 50hrs, and I have beaten it. I got to see pretty much the extent of what it has to offer, while also not spoiling anything.
Story is the most important part of a "Tales of" game. Not just that, bout the amount of work put into every piece of dialogue as well is quite impressive. From the moment, you start, to the end, there’s always something to learn or something to hear and read. The main character will grow, and each team member will win your heart, (or hatred) someway or another. There are lots of filler text and gives the illusion that the world is cohesive enough to stand on its own. I have yet to read every piece of dialogue, however, I did get to see a lot of good moments of foreshadowing and piecing together of the world through text and lore. Fans of the “Tales of” series gets to witness some of the past games origin stories, while new ones still get to learn about the world they are in already.  If anything, the lore, story, the dialogue is what keeps this game up and running.
So, the most important factor I find in this game is that you are playing the “villain” so to speak, and you have a team of mischievous daemons. However, you are not necessarily the bad guy, and they way they try to make you feel like you are, feels a bit underhanded. I feel could have been done better. To avoid spoilers, I’ll only talk as depth as I can without giving to much away. Velvet is a “daemon” more or less, and she does questionable things. However, the bad things only come as consequences. She is not out to kill for fun, she only does it if its required to do so. If the person blocking her path moves out her way, she does not kill. The game makes the mistake of still putting our “villain” as the hero, even giving her motivations that is villainous, but even behind all the “uncaring” and “ruthless” outlook. She never once deliberately did anything villainy like other than stealing a ship and escaping prison. Once you start considering the context and values, you realize that the “Group” of demons, pirates, don’t seem all that villainous. Perhaps that was the point, but it must of fell short on me. The story and growth of characters is still very much pleasant, as you learn that each one of them aren’t as bad as they say they are.
The story, lore, and text is the driving point of this game. Quite frankly, I might say it’s the only thing really keeping it together… because
There is a bit to be desired gameplay wise. The game uses the same ol Linear Motion system that has been spiced up in this iteration. Its very fun to play, and can be rewarding to learn to use it right, but a lot of people, including myself, realized you can really just string together your strongest attack and use that through the game. One would actually have too go out of their way to combo, which there is reward for. If you learn the combat, you will get through fights faster and intact too.
However, the simplicity occasionally makes it boring. Velvets own special is near OP that when I activate it once, when times are best, I can keep it going because I stagger and gain back Souls to continue doing her special. You can control your entire cast if you wish to (one by one I mean) so you don’t have to stick with Velvet. Your you can control your others, and it can be refreshing to do so.
The maps are beautiful, I find. The beginning area had a lot of colours and was quite nice to look at. The same style kept going all the way through, so don’t expect even better sights. In fact, some areas are
. You spend a lot of time walking from one place to the next. Since Combat can get very repetitive, very fast (and quite frankly you don’t need to fight every demon you come across) it can take a while to get from one end, to the other. The speed boost you get halfway doesn’t do much, but rather makes backtracking easier, as you can blow throw daemons instead of fighting them. It helps not, as it still feels
There is a lot of walking around, and the collectables are so frequent that they don’t have the same “effect” as they are intended. They do guide and lead you to secrets, which aren’t very much rewarding (if you play well) but finding a life bottle when you have none. The solution to this is “Denore” and “Inoph” bottles. They teleport you to recently visited locations and can be a time saver. HOWEVER
You are unable to use those teleporting bottles if there are story elements and cutscenes involved on your travel to and from (even if its backtracking). You will have to slowly run through and watch the cutscenes. As I said though with story, the cutscenes are never a bore, and can be quite humorous. In a way, they are the only thing to break the monotony of walking to places, as fighting isn’t always fun to do.  I was never a grinding person though, so I played through it is minor difficulties as I was never TOO high level for any encounter.
There are many factors I am not cutting into, such as the “cut” scene controversy and such as. I find it to be a very minor thing, and the new scene is almost just as dramatic, if no longer blunt and to the point. If you are to purchase this game and not be like Eizen (yar har maties) then the DRM is not all that bad. I managed to play this at school for 3 days WITHOUT internet. After coming on for a connection for only 5 minutes, things updated and continued to work properly. I don’t support it, as it would be much better to not hafta worry about going online what so ever… but to paying customers, one should not have much problems. Other problems consist of the “AI” issue, which may or may not be fixed by now. It made AI occasionally stand still, which can get frustrating.
However, I am here to judge this game on its own merits. So the final verdict is as follows:
This game is not worth its 60 dollar price point, as the DLC, for frivolous costumes are way to pricey. They should have been put in the game to begin with, as costumes to work towards, as theres not to much to look forward to unlocking. The AI bug is also unforgivable, as if they did not playtest the game. DRM is another matter at hand, but for the purchasing customer, this game requires YOU to think a bit on your own.
Do you love story, and an adventure. Do you like any of the previous “Tales of” games. Its up to you as an individual to make a decision.
I told you what “I” felt like was the “Good” and the “Bad” of the game.
I enjoyed the game quite a bit, at a discounted price of 35 dollars
I personally would want to see more of the “Tales of” game come to PC, and was very happy to see another, what used to be a Japanese only series, come to PC. I want them to know they can continue doing it. I enjoyed the story, and to some extent, even the gameplay, despite some shortcomings.
So what do YOU think. I personally give this a “Enjoyable game to play” rating, if you have the money and its on sale, totally buy it and enjoy it as well. If you don’t mind the price, buy it now. You will not get your mind blown, but you will be chucking, and enjoying the moments that the game offers for sure.

Ludosity, you have become one of favourite indie developers, as of late. I’ve played several of your games now and they’ll all good. Guess this means I’m giving this a recommendation already but I still must explain the pros and cons of this game so let’s begin.
Story:
Ittle Dew and her buddy Tippsie were just relaxing on their raft when they get stranded on an island. After some exploring, the duo meet an item carver named Itan Carver who can make them a raft off the island but they must find an artefact in the nearby castle as payment so our adventurers must go find it.
Not much to talk story wise as it’s just an adventure so lets talk characters which isn’t much but it’s something. Ittle is an enjoyable little adventurer who’s very blunt about things like eating what she find on the ground or admitting not understanding what someone said. And there’s Tippsie, her flying fox buddy who gives tips with a tone of “Really, do I have to help.”. Together they make a fun duo, poking fun at the weird things on the island and each other.
And some of the enemies have some personality even if some of them don’t have an intro, like the stone heads who are afraid of heights. But my favourites are the Jennys  who each have a little personalty quark like the frog being laid back.
Gameplay:
I’ve never played a Legend of Zelda game before. Not even the new ones for handheld. Now that we got that out of the way lets talk about the game.
The first few minutes do a decent job of showing how the game works up to your first chest, like pushing blocks, lighting your stick to light bonfires, the different doors that open by defeat all enemies or turning on all switches, etc.  But in order to get to the dungeons, you need money from the castle and after the first chest, you free to do the first dungeon or explore to get more money. And that’s one of the interesting things about this game which is the castle is non-linear as you only need to buy two items to get to the end.
The dungeons are really just tutorials on how the items you get work, and you temporary lose your other items you bought so it’s like being thrown in the middle depth of the pool and have to use your head to get out. I like this as it teaches you how each items works and with all the other mechanics in each dungeon, can teach you how it works with the other items like freezing blocks to break them with you fire sword. And of course each dungeon ends with a boss fight and to be honest, only the forest boss and the final boss are good since they both are test of what you can do. The fire boss was very underwhelming with how you barely him and the ice boss was good but it uses one of the most important ice mechanics you weren’t thought in the dungeon so I had to use a tip to figure it out.
And besides the main dungeons, there are little dungeon rooms just outside them that can teach you more about your new items with it’s cleaver puzzles and reward you with a health upgrade or a card that’s just for flavour. And there’s even a super optional dungeon that have some nasty puzzles, making you think outside the box and making you use ideas you didn’t know you can do.
This is clearly a speed running game too as not only do you just have to do two dungeons but there are also shortcuts that are hard to unlock but can really cut a good chuck of time from the dungeon. But I did found one flaw where if you want to a particular run, it’s very easy to screw yourself over. For me, I wanted to do the one where you don’t kill any Jenny’s and decided to get the fire sword first, but as I explore the castle I couldn’t the chests I needed to get the ice wand so I had to start over.
Presentation:
The music is a mix bag for me. While I like the music for the outside and the castle theme are good, I found the dungeon music to be pretty forgettable.
I love the art in this game. Everything just looks so cute, from Ittle and Tippsie, to the Jenny’s to the fishbuns to even the crystals and blocks. I think it looks really good.
Verdict:
I admit some puzzle were pretty hard but this is a good game. Wonder if Ittle Dew 2 be better?

It's strange that this genre seems so full when there really aren't many games in it. Grand Theft Auto, Saints Row, Just Cause, Mafia, and now Sleeping Dogs. This game does a really good job of making itself stand out from the crowd, though.
Technically the game is fantastic. It looks great even on medium settings and runs quite well, with the option of full DX11 support and a high resolution texture pack for those with beastly machines. It has the best looking rain I've ever seen and an amazing amount of detail in the cities, rivaling GTA4 while looking far better and running with similar performance to Saints Row 3.
First of all it has a top notch story with great voice acting, only falling short of GTA4 in the motion capture department. The characters are all believable and well written. There's quite a few optional side missions as well, though they unfortunately aren't anywhere near as fleshed out.
The car handling is the best of any of the games, hands down. Think Saints Row 3 but more realistic. Driving is fun and unlike the other games, you are actually rewarded for driving safe. Sometimes you do need to crash though, and the game has a nice ramming mechanic to destroy other cars and push them off the road. In addition you can shoot out car tires when you have a gun which disables them quite quickly.
The combat system is where the game really shines though. It has a freeflow combat system similar to Batman AA/AC, but rather than being a superhero you're a martial arts master. You fight groups of enemies mostly in hand-to-hand combat, unlocking new moves as you gain more experience. The melee weapons you obtain sometimes are not very durable and will usually only take out one enemy. Guns are rare but extremely powerful and attract the police extremely quickly.
Tying in with the combat system is freerunning. You will do a lot of climbing up tall barriers and vaulting over tables, even doing special disarm and takedown moves when you vault into enemies. It's an enjoyable addition to the game and fits in very well with the setting in Hong Kong.
Now one of the biggest strengths and weaknesses is the camera control.  This game has the best driving camera I've ever see.  It uses a novel idea of actually pointing the direction you're moving when you turn a corner!  It does tend to get a bit confused when you reverse though.
The walking camera is another matter altogether.  I lost track of how many different camera angles there are, since there's a different one for every movement speed, and for each weapon type, and a different one while fighting, and combinations of them all.  The walking camera doesn't point the same direction you're moving, the walking and sprinting cameras make the mouse laggy, and some of the weapon cameras give you weird camera angles.  The rest of it's pretty good though.  I don't know why they couldn't just stick to a single good camera angle instead of changing it all the time.
Sleeping Dogs really is a must-have for fans of the genre.

This game had everything going for it before I even added it to my wishlist. Part of a franchise I'm already addicted to. Established world to operate in. Turn-based tile gameplay I've loved since my Heroes of Might and Magic days. Decent graphics, animations and music. It even has support for ultra-wide monitors out of the box.
So did it live up to it's potential? Yes, mostly. It's a very good update on the tried-and tested XCOM formula with some great new elements and some distressing old bugs.
I love the addition of custom soldiers you can design and take on missions. It makes you that much more attached to them and it's super fun to yell out friend and family names in anger when they miss 95% accuracy shots. The class changes are fun too - I've got a couple of pretty OP Rangers now that I would legitimely fell distressed at losing on a mission.
I hate that the ultra-wide monitor support was a little tacked on and almost game breaking in some aspects. Hacking anything becomes difficult because the button to continue falls off the screen. Sometimes clicking on another soldier action will cause them to do the action already seleceted instead because the areas on screen aren't mapped correctly. IT's bearable if you mostly play keyboard-first, but it needs work.
I like the idea of the Spark units and the Boss aliens from the DLC. The story lines seemed very basic for what they could have been, but an enjoyable addition to the vanila game nonetheless. I don't have the Chosen DLC yet but it looks promising and I'm keen to try it (maybe once it goes on sale).
Minor and mission breaking bugs still plague this game (it's XCOM so that's to be expected). Sometimes it gets stuck on Alien Activity or in between turns forcing you to exit the game to continue. Sometimes the action descriptions are innacurate as to whether or not they end a unit's turn. Sometimes units that shouldn't be affected by blasts get knocked through floors or walls even. I could go on.
It's a great game, I love it and I have already sunk 50+ hours into it, with the promise of many more. BUT I'd enjoy much more of that time if so much of it weren't spent backtracking to avoid mission-critical bugs and corrupt save games.

Nice game, with some serious flaws. I will give i 6 out of 10, for reasons specified below. Pros gives 2 points, cons take away one point.
Pros:
1. Better than Game Dev Tycoon, and really not that similar, since it is more like Theme Hospital without the patients.
2. There are a lot of things to do and different ways to get money and be successful (design games, design engines, do contract work, and later build games platforms, and manufacture games, and buy-out the competition, and...)
3. You can recruit as many employees as you wish, and get do build your office yourself.
4. The games are evaluated in a pretty logical manner, meaning it is not really a dice-roll whether yo get good ratings or not. You want the game stats to be at the same level, while also be as high as possible, and it also matters which audience you aimed for, and what genres you chose and so on.
5. It is possible to claw yourself out of a bad start. Just take out more of a loan, and make the next game better. Once you make that killer game, you can relax for a while. But not until the end of the game.
Cons:
1. The graphics/UI is so bad that it actively hinders game play. When a room is in use, a menue showing what is happening in the room is shown ABOVE THE ROOM, meaning that you cannot see who is working in the room. All you see is the menues. Yes you can turn those menues off, but then again, if you do that you don't know what is happening in the rooms, so you have to turn them on and off all the time. There must be a better solution. Also, hovering over an employee shows where he works, but hovering over a room does NOT show which employees work there. So if they wander off to the break room, good luck finding them.
2. More on the UI: for example, the only way to close a window is to click the x button in the top right corner of the window. Why does not escape work, or simply clicking the right mouse button anywhere? Also, I would have liked being able to promote employees into a specific line of work: like making some one a grapics designer, meaning he will only work on graphics-related jobs. The game contains too much micro management as it is.
3.  No mod support. I know that this game was made by one single person, and that to make it moddable is hard. It is still a bad thing that the game cannot be modded.
4. Too much is unlocked at the start of the game. For instance, I don't think you could make patches/game updates in the 1980s without giving the player a new floppy disk, or having them mod the game themselves, both of which things you need a marketing/support division to handle.

I like zombie games, try to check them out whenever i can. But i cannot say “i liked Dead Age”. Is it a bad game? No. But unfortunately it’s not a good game either. I think it would have been a good game 10-15 years ago, when we were not yet very spoiled by a quality and number of available experiences. The only 2 things that kept me playing was the progression system unlocked through medals, and the story, the “what’ll happen in the end” kind of question that probably is a basic motivation for why we spend money on games in the first place. Other plus is that quests pop-ups provide a fairly good guidance of the story and sometimes fairly intense situations. Interesting take on the enemies and their abilities, each giving you a distinct feeling they are different. Somewhat. And that’s where good things probably stop.
Combat Gameplay is not really enjoyable and becomes quite stale and boring after a few game days and, after a while it becomes the same grindy experience – melee where can, shoot where it’ss more effective. No strategy or interesting tactics. Some systems like damage multipliers and abilities don’t seem to work. Balance of skills, combat and events feels off. UI/UX experience is far from good, and makes camp, team and any sort of management a struggle. Some of the art style feels almost stolen from previous versions of Rebuild and the last stand. 3D models don’t look good either. I bought the game on 33% discount i feel like overpaying. Would probably not recommend this game for more than 5$.

Saurian has been in production for a few years now and it has a good-sized group of loyal followers. This shows in the reviews  but try not to be fooled by the currently 'Very Positive' overall review score, this game is an investment rather than a product I would consider worth my money at this point in development. I pre-ordered it myself and have eagerly awaited it's release.
First off, this is about as early access as I would ever consider buying into. It is pre-alpha stage and has almost no content. You get to play one dinosaur, a Dakotaraptor, which you start off as a hatchling and slowly progress up to an adult. You would do well to get there at all, since there is little in the way of edibles and everything in the world one-shots you from a few feet away but the progression is fair in timeframe if you can find the food required. This isn't where the problems stop though, Saurian is currently a bit of a mess of mechanics. The AI is still very early (I hope), with other dinosaurs staring into space and ignoring you completely. The graphics are suffering from an excess of contrast in this build making daytime shadows/plants ugly and night time a mess of green and brown. The controls are flaky, delayed and suffer from poor hitboxes, so combat is just clumsy right now and the overall performance of the game is satisfactory at best with mild stutter and freezing when loading new models and landscape. (i5 3570k, 16gb, nvidia 1070)
It's not all bad though, as early as it is, it shows a lot of promise. The lanscape is lovingly created and a good size with some variation to see. The dinosaur models are very detailed and well animated, although still need a little work on tranistions. The health, hunger, hydration and stamina bars all react well, aren't too high or low and look good. It's just that if you aren't an absolute dinosaur junky, this won't be enough to keep you entertained for very long.
Summary: I want to give this game a thumbs up because I think developers are good and the long term plan is awesome but I am struggling to find positives at this early stage that outweigh the negatives to any degree. IF you are a dino junky and have to buy every game with dinosaurs in, then you'll likely have a few hours of fun here but otherwise I would wait a few months for the game to flesh out a bit and for some of the obvious failing to get some dev attention.

Dinosaur video games often suffer from the same problem - A lack of focus on the science, and a complete reliance on pop culture, for instance, the Turok reboot saw dinosaurs as near-zombie minded animals that would attack everything on sight. People seem to have forgotten that dinosaurs were animals no different to the animals surrounding us in our daily lives.
Saurian attempts to (re)create the cretaceous world grounded in fact and accuracy, and educate its players. From the feathers covering the small dromaeosaurids to the drastic growth stages of Tyrannosaurus and even down to the vegetation that would have covered the Hells Creek formation.
The game has a ways to go to truly capture the feeling of a living ecosystem - The foliage needs more movement, combat needs more impact and weight and of course, more life needs to be added. Following Saurian from the beginning has been a pleasure, and the team have made a solid and extremely fun game.

Bastion is a good game, make no mistake, but it's considerable style outweighs its substance. It's certainly a beautiful game, the hand-drawn art style graphics are very pretty and distinctive, fitting well with the general tone, although they can sometimes get a little busy. There were also times where the isometric viewpoint combined with some strange shapes made the safe pathway a little less than obvious. Visually, it's a treat from beginning to end.
The soundtrack, in my opinion, is the Bastion's strongest asset. The score is wonderful, taking old-western guitar twang and mixing it beautifully with other velvety tones that make the soundtrack bundle worth the extra dough. The narration is also great, adding a new and interesting way of framing the story and directing the player with a voice that sounds like molten caramel. The story it frames is also fairly good, if a little bewildering to start with.
On the downside, the actual gameplay is fairly homogenous. Most of the game consists of "go to a place, hack and slash until everything is dead, grab a magical something-or-other and flee before the ground disappears from under you" on a repeating cycle.  The variety of weapons and special attacks and the challenges offered by the Shrines (difficulty-boosting optional extras) and other challenges offer a little bit of variety, but I can't see myself making use of the New Game Plus feature. Despite there being two possible endings, I just didn't enjoy the 5 hours I spent with it enough to want to go back any time soon.
Overall though, considering I paid quite a lot less than the list price for Bastion, I still got my money's worth and would recommend it to anyone who doesn't mind beauty being mostly skin deep.

Coming from a person who's completed every Tales game that is regarded as one of the best of the series, I have to say that Berseria fits right in with that group. I would even go as far to say that it is now the newest member of the "golden trinity" which used to be made up of Tales of Symphonia, Abyss, and Vesperia.
First off, this game is very long. Even after the credits roll there is still a lot of story to be told will fully animated cutscenes and a lot of character development. I beat the game at around 66 hours while doing as many side activities as possible, and I am currently 91 hours in as of writing this review and I still have a lot more to do before I feel like I'm comfortable enough to start a NG+.
The gameplay is very engaging. You can choose at any time which character you want to play as, and though I always like to play as the main characters, I liked the side characters' styles enough that I may occasionally switch in this game.
I do not like the combat as much as Xillia's but that does not mean it is worse in any way, I just loved Xillia's combat to pieces. With that said, I recommend playing this game on at least moderate difficulty. Some claim this game is easy, but I still die a lot on moderate difficulty when I try risky double battles.
Aside from the combat, this game is extremely beautiful. At first glance you may not think the graphics are all that great but once you truly get to explore this world and look around, the artistic design of the world will probably make you forget everything you thought about the graphics.
The story is amazing. My favorite story of the series has always been Tales of Vesperia, and it still has a special place in my heart, but I have to say that Berseria now holds the spot as my favorite Tales game, as well as my favorite video game in general.
The cast is very interesting. The plot is exciting enough to make you not want to put the game down. There are a few easter eggs thrown in at Zestiria, so if you know anything about Zestiria's story, you can see that this game is indeed in the same world, but a knowledge of Zestiria's story is not at all necessary to enjoy this games story. However, this game may cause you to like Zestiria better if you didn't like it that much.
As for the music, the songs definitely serve their purposes well and I found that there were a quite a few memorable tracks as well as forgettable ones, but I found none of them to be annoying or unfitting.
After having finished the game, I do recommend having a little bit of knowledge of Zestiria's plot. It isn't necessary, but it does make this game that much better if you know the connections they share.
Without spoiling anything, the features will keep adding up as you progress through the game. The combat from the beginning of the game will get more complex. At around 11 hours I was still learning some new ways to play this game, both in and out of combat.
So far, I have no complaints. My review may be slightly biased due to the fact that Tales is my favorite rpg series but that does not prevent me from leaving a negative review if I thought negatively of the game. I am a huge fan, but not a fanboy.
If you like action combat, I recommend this game. If you like strong stories, I recommend this game. If you disliked Zestiria, I recommend this game. If you liked Zestiria, oh boy is this the game for you!
Also as a side note, Tales has one of the greatest gaming communities you will ever find. Avoid the steam forums at all costs as it is a terrible representation of the community. Join the facebook groups, discord channel, or reddit, and you will find everyone is friendly, helpful, welcoming, and overall a great community to make friends in.
You probably won't see a single person complaining about denuvo (it does nothing to harm your computer) or censorship as they know that the (very very VERY little) censorship that exists in this game is not due to Bandai Namco wanting to change the (single) scene, but in order to keep this game available to people under 18, they had to change 5 minutes worth of content due to PEGI and/or ESRB's sheltering of the country's media.

After Zestiria, I thought I might be done with this series. I enjoyed it, but it lacked that magic that the others had. When I heard about Berseria, I was unsure. I decided to give them another shot and I'm glad I did.
I've played quite a few of the Tales games. Vesperia, Symphonia, Graces, Xillia 1-2, Abyss, Zestiria, and Hearts. This is my favorite entry in the series. After eighty plus hours I still want more. If you're a Tales fan, or a JRPG fan in general you owe it to yourself to take the plunge.
Pros:
Darker story that doesn't rely on the clichès of the genre. There is no amnesia here!
Most characters are likeable and have a great english VO. Only a few grating ones stand out, but they don't get a ton of screeen time.
The battle system is similar to previous Tales, but the soul gauge and break soul mechanics help to set it apart. Enemies also drop tons of equipment. This makes battling feel more purposeful outside of just grinding level and money.
This game performs great on PC. I played with max settings at 4K with no issues.
Characters can recieve skills and upgrades from equipment. Similar to FFIX. Once you master a skill, it's yours forever. Much improved over Zestiria's RNG based system.
Optional events are listed on the map, so it makes it easier to find all the events. In past Tales, it was easy to miss events.
Souls and materials are sprinkled throughout the world. It makes it feel like everything has a purpose and no time is wasted. Even if that corner didn't have a treasure chest, it had ten souls which will come in handy later.
Mid way through you get an item that helps traverse the landscape quicker. It also allows you to avoid combat with weaker enemies. Wonderful time saver.
Cons:
Berseria suffers from the same bland environments that plagued Xillia 1/2 and Zestiria. There are some spots with beautiful scenery, but there also blue caves, green caves, red caves, and so on.
There isn't a whole lot of post game content. After the main quest is over, there isn't much left to do.
Not as many post battle skits as I would have liked. In past Tales, it seemed like more were added as you progressed, but Berseria seems to lack that.
Final Thought:
If you are a fan of JRPG's or are looking to try one this is a great example of how great they can be. I've been playing RPG's since the 16 bit era and I rarely enjoy them as much as I used to. I truly enjoyed this game and it's characters. By the end, I actually cared about them. After Berseria, I cannot wait to see what they put out next!
Short, but a solid Zelda-like nonetheless.

Intrusion 2 is basically Metal Slug with physics. Objects get thrown around, trees bend and wobble, and enemies wave their mechanical tentacles around.
I didn’t really care much for the physics, but I guess that’s what made the gameplay a bit different from similar games. The mech designs were cool and the boss battles were epic. The final battle in particular was one of the most insane boss battles I’ve ever played in a game.
My main criticism about Intrusion 2 is that the levels just dragged on for a bit too long. Enemies and scenery just repeated a few times too many. It took me over two hours to play through the game, while Metal Slug fits the same amount of content into a much shorter game with more replay-value.

Much better then past few games. Combat system is improved; graphics improved; much more likeable characeters. If you like Tales this is one of the best; up there with Vesperia; Abyss; maybe not as good a xilia 2 as far as characters and combat goes. Now i actually wanna play Zesteria.
Update: I am 15 hours in and this game is such a upgrade and true successor to the old games; as in Tales of Graces. I think Zesteria tried to update the Graces F system but failed because of lack of character control due to the Armatize system. Now you can swap in and out all your characters to form chain combos with the entire party; and with more specialized arte customization this is amazing!
Gone are the normal attacks of the olden tales days tho; which isn't bad. The combat and arte customization is akin to the Ps2 game Godhand! Which is vasty underplayed and rated as well. Which this means to gammers who haven't played Godhand is that you basically chose which moves goes over what button in a sequence of 4. Amazing; I'm juggling enemies in the air with custom combos! To players who haven't played a Tales Game; its a customizable RPG BEAT EM UP with a anime story basically.
UPDATE COMPLETED GAME 80 hours: Yep. I completed the game in 80 hours which is a good length for Tales Games; some games like vesperia and abyss literally DRAG ON. This one was pretty good about just getting to the point and I still have good generic Tales endgame content to deal with; Like a few EX dungeons and side quests. Also a big cheer to the end dungeon; games like Tales of Graces F; and Xillia 2 had some terrible end dungeons. Xillia 2 is hands down the worst dungeon.
Story: Simple; predictable; funny and a bit sad too. This is a good one for the basic for any anime lovers and I particularly like the generic story of Rokurou the Swordsman from the East. The Ending also is very good.
Overal Ratings from a Tales Fan:
